A.label: Section A — Vocabulary MCQ
A.instructions: Choose the word that best fits the meaning of the sentence.

questions.stem: The school hall was as ________ as a beehive on Sports Day — children rushing everywhere and music playing loudly.
questions.trap_type: 'Quiet','empty','dark' = opposite of a busy, noisy place. BUSY = full of people and activity.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! The hall was AS BUSY AS a beehive = comparing the activity to buzzing worker bees. BUSY = full of movement and activity. AS + ADJECTIVE + AS is always the correct simile form.
questions.retry_hint: The sentence compares the hall to a BEEHIVE, and tells you children were rushing everywhere with music playing. Ask: is a beehive famous for stillness, or for non-stop activity? Match the adjective to that picture.

questions.stem: The puppy ran ________ around the garden, chasing a butterfly.
questions.trap_type: Context mood — chasing a butterfly is a playful, energetic action. 'Slowly' and 'quietly' contradict the running and chasing.
questions.learning_tip: Chasing = active and fun → choose an adverb that shows energy and happiness. 'Happily' fits running and playing.
questions.retry_hint: Look at what the puppy is doing: running around and CHASING a butterfly. Ask: does that action sound tired and gloomy, or full of energy and fun? The adverb must match the mood of the action.

questions.stem: After the group project, Mia stayed behind to ________ the art room before the next class arrived.
questions.trap_type: 'Run away','give up on','break into' = negative actions. TIDY UP = organise and clean a space.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: TIDY UP = clean and organise a space. Mia stayed to TIDY UP the room = she put everything away neatly. TIDY + UP work together as one meaning.
questions.retry_hint: Mia STAYED behind on purpose, so the room would be ready before the next class arrived. Ask: would a helpful student damage the room, or leave it in good order? Pick the phrasal verb that helps rather than harms.

questions.stem: When Amy found out she had passed all her exams, she was ________ — she jumped for joy.
questions.trap_type: 'Under the weather' = ill; 'in hot water' = trouble; 'at a loss' = confused. OVER THE MOON = extremely happy.
questions.learning_tip: IDIOM: OVER THE MOON = feeling extremely happy and delighted. Amy was OVER THE MOON = overjoyed at her results. Idioms cannot be understood word by word!
questions.retry_hint: The dash gives you the meaning: she JUMPED for joy. Ask: which idiom means extremely happy? The others describe being ill, in trouble, or confused - none of those make you jump.

questions.stem: Priya raised her hand to give the ________ answer when the teacher asked a difficult question.
questions.trap_type: Subtle logic — a 'difficult question' makes students think the answer might be 'short' or 'simple'. But raising your hand confidently = giving the RIGHT answer.
questions.learning_tip: Raising your hand to answer = you know the answer → it must be the CORRECT answer. The question being 'difficult' just shows Priya is clever.
questions.retry_hint: Priya RAISED her hand on purpose, even though the question was hard. Ask: would you volunteer in front of the class to give an answer you believed was wrong? Do not let the word DIFFICULT trick you into a length-based choice.

questions.stem: Nobody in our class ________ the answers to the surprise quiz — the teacher had not given any hints.
questions.trap_type: NOBODY = singular → verb+S.
questions.learning_tip: NOBODY / EVERYONE / SOMEONE = Singular! Nobody KNOWS = add -S. 'Nobody know' is WRONG. Singular indefinite pronouns always take singular present-tense verbs.
questions.retry_hint: Look at the subject: NOBODY. Words like nobody, everyone and somebody act like ONE person, even though they feel like many. Ask: does a singular subject take the plain verb, or the verb ending in -s?

questions.stem: Our school has ________ a new after-school reading programme for Primary Three students this term.
questions.trap_type: HAS + past participle = present perfect. START → STARTED.
questions.learning_tip: HAS + past participle = present perfect. The school HAS STARTED a new programme = done recently. START → STARTED (regular verb, add -ed).
questions.retry_hint: The helper verb HAS is already in the sentence. Ask: which verb form must follow have/has to build the present perfect? Not the base form, not the -ing form - you need the third form (the past participle).

questions.stem: The children ________ loudly in the playground when the bell rang and called them back to class.
questions.trap_type: 'The bell rang' = sudden event. Past continuous = was/were + -ing.
questions.learning_tip: The bell RANG = sudden past event. Children were already playing = WERE PLAYING (past continuous). Was/were + verb-ing = action in progress when interrupted.
questions.retry_hint: Two things happen here: one long action and one sudden one. The bell RANG is the sudden event that cuts in. Ask: which tense shows an action already in progress when something interrupts it?

questions.stem: The new school library is much ________ than the old one — it has three times as many books.
questions.trap_type: 'Biggest' = superlative; 'more bigger' is WRONG. BIGGER = comparative.
questions.learning_tip: Short adjective + -ER = comparative. Big → BIGGER (double G). BIGGER THAN the old library = comparing two libraries. 'More bigger' is ALWAYS WRONG — never add BOTH.
questions.retry_hint: The word THAN is your signal - you are comparing exactly TWO libraries, not three or more. Ask: does comparing two things need the comparative or the superlative? And never stack 'more' in front of an -er ending.

questions.stem: Tom ________ the bag off the chair so that Mia could sit down.
questions.trap_type: Past tense context. TAKE → TOOK (irregular).
questions.learning_tip: TAKE → TOOK (irregular past). In a completed past action, use TOOK. 'Tom take the bag' = WRONG. TAKE → TOOK. Irregular verbs must be memorised.
questions.retry_hint: The sentence describes something that already happened, so that Mia COULD sit down. Ask: what is the past form of this verb? Careful - it is irregular, so adding -ed will not work.

questions.stem: Learning to read and write is one of the most important things you do in primary school, ________ it?
questions.trap_type: Positive present 'to be' ('is') → negative question tag.
questions.learning_tip: Positive present 'to be' → negative tag. Learning to read IS important, ISN'T it? POSITIVE → NEGATIVE. IS → ISN'T.
questions.retry_hint: This is a question tag. The main clause is positive and its verb IS the 'to be' verb. Ask: does a positive statement take a positive tag or a negative one? The tag must also reuse the same verb from the statement.

questions.stem: She did not ________ her homework before the teacher collected it.
questions.trap_type: After 'did not', use BASE FORM of the verb.
questions.learning_tip: DID NOT + BASE FORM. 'Did not finish' = base form FINISH. After auxiliaries (did, does, will, can), always use the BASE FORM.
questions.retry_hint: The helper DID not already carries the past tense for you. Ask: once a helper verb has shown the tense, what form does the main verb take? Do not mark the tense twice.

questions.stem: "Please put ________ books back on the shelf after reading," said the librarian.
questions.trap_type: The librarian is talking TO the students → 'your'.
questions.learning_tip: YOUR = belonging to you (second person possessive). The librarian is talking to the students: put YOUR books back. 'You books' = WRONG.
questions.retry_hint: The LIBRARIAN is speaking directly TO the students, not about herself or about other people. Ask: from the speaker's point of view, whose books are these? Match the possessive to the person being addressed.

C.label: Section C — Grammar Cloze
C.instructions: Read the passage below. Choose the most suitable word from the box and write its letter in each blank. Use each word ONCE only.
C.passage: Last Monday, my class went on a field trip to the Singapore Botanic Gardens. Our form teacher, Ms Tan, led (1)___ there by bus. When we arrived, (2)___ told everyone to stay together and not wander off. My friend Raju was very excited. (3)___ kept pointing at the different flowers. Ms Tan smiled at (4)___ and explained that the gardens had more than two thousand types of plants. Raju wrote the names of the flowers in (5)___ notebook. Later, we met two gardeners. (6)___ showed us how to plant a small cutting. (7)___ all tried it and got our hands dirty! At the end of the day, we thanked Ms Tan and gave (8)___ a card to say how much we had enjoyed the trip.

questions.trap_type: Object pronoun — Ms Tan led 'us' (we = subject, us = object after verb).
questions.learning_tip: After an action verb like 'led', use OBJECT pronoun: led US (not we). US is the object of 'led'.
questions.retry_hint: Ms Tan LED the whole class onto the bus - the writer is one of the people being led. Ask: which pronoun means 'me and the people with me' in the OBJECT position, after the verb? Not the doing form 'we'.

questions.trap_type: Corrected: 'told them' — referring to the students as 'them' (3rd person view from narrator who is also part of group). Actually in first-person narration, 'told us' is correct. Passage redesigned so blank 2 uses E (them) in a different sentence.
questions.learning_tip: After 'told', use object pronoun. Here, Ms Tan told the students (them) = E.
questions.retry_hint: The person doing the telling is MS TAN - one woman, and the pronoun starts the sentence, so it is the one acting. Ask: which pronoun is the SUBJECT form for a single female? The object form only comes after a verb or a preposition.

questions.trap_type: My friend Rita (female) → she = D. Students may confuse with 'they' (thinking of all friends).
questions.learning_tip: A single female friend = SHE (subject pronoun). D = she.
questions.retry_hint: The excited one is RAJU - one boy, and this pronoun starts the sentence, so it is doing the pointing. Ask: which pronoun is the SUBJECT form for one male? Not 'him', which comes after a verb.

questions.trap_type: 'Asking her teacher' — her = A, referring to Ms Tan (female teacher). Students may pick D (she) but that is subject, not possessive.
questions.learning_tip: Before a noun (teacher), use possessive: HER teacher = A. 'She teacher' is wrong.
questions.retry_hint: Ms Tan SMILED AT Raju - he is receiving the smile, and the pronoun comes after 'at'. Ask: which pronoun for one male goes AFTER a verb or preposition? The subject form cannot sit there.

questions.trap_type: Redesigned: friend is Raju (male) → smiled at HIM = B. Students pick D (she) confusing subject/object.
questions.learning_tip: After 'smiled at' (preposition), use OBJECT pronoun: smiled at HIM (not he). B = him.
questions.retry_hint: The NOTEBOOK belongs to RAJU. Ask: which word shows that something belongs to one male? Careful: two of the choices sound similar, but only one can sit in front of a noun to show ownership.

questions.trap_type: Two gardeners = they = F. Students may pick D (she) thinking of one person.
questions.learning_tip: Two or more people = THEY = F. Use 'they' as subject pronoun for plural people.
questions.retry_hint: The ones showing the class how to plant are the TWO GARDENERS - more than one person, and the pronoun begins the sentence. Ask: which pronoun is the SUBJECT form for several other people? Not the form that comes after a verb.

questions.trap_type: 'We all tried it' — G = we (subject). Students may pick H (us) confusing subject/object.
questions.learning_tip: WE is the SUBJECT (we did the action). US is the OBJECT (someone did something to us). 'We all tried' = WE = G.
questions.retry_hint: '___ all tried it and got OUR hands dirty' - the word OUR tells you exactly who this is. Ask: which pronoun is the SUBJECT form for me and my classmates together? Not the object form used after a verb.

questions.trap_type: 'She was very proud' — Ms Tan (female singular) = she = D. Students may pick F (they) thinking of multiple teachers.
questions.learning_tip: Ms Tan is ONE female person → SHE = D. 'They' is for more than one person.
questions.retry_hint: They GAVE a card to MS TAN - one woman, receiving the card. Ask: which pronoun for one female goes after a verb, in the object position? The subject form 'she' cannot receive anything.

C.passage_final: Last Monday, my class went on a field trip to the Singapore Botanic Gardens. Our form teacher, Ms Tan, led (1)___ there by bus. When we arrived, Ms Tan told (2)___ to stay together and not wander off. My friend Raju was very excited. (3)___ kept pointing at the different flowers and asking (4)___ teacher about them. Ms Tan smiled at (5)___ and explained that the gardens had more than two thousand types of plants. Later, we met two gardeners. (6)___ showed us how to plant a small cutting. (7)___ all tried it and got our hands dirty! At the end of the day, Ms Tan said (8)___ was very proud of how well we had behaved.

answers_final.3: F(they→he, redesign Raju=C his? No — use D she for female)

D.label: Section D — Vocabulary Cloze
D.instructions: Read the passage carefully. Choose the most suitable word from the box and write its letter in each blank. Use each word ONCE only.
D.passage: One afternoon, Mei found a pink water bottle near the school gate. She looked at it (1)___ and saw the name 'Amy' written on the side. Mei was worried that Amy had (2)___ her bottle. She picked it up and walked (3)___ to the school office to hand it in. The teacher smiled and said, 'Well done for being honest!' The next morning, Amy ran up to Mei and said, 'Thank you! I was looking everywhere for it!' Mei felt (4)___ that she had helped a classmate. That same afternoon, the office teacher (5)___ the bottle to Amy.

questions.trap_type: Manner adverb for looking at an object — 'carefully' fits examining something. Students may pick 'quickly' but you look at things carefully, not quickly, when checking.
questions.learning_tip: 'Carefully' = with great attention. When you check a name on a bottle, you look at it CAREFULLY to read it clearly.
questions.retry_hint: She was able to READ THE NAME 'Amy' on the side, so she must have taken her time looking. Ask: does the blank describe HOW she looked? Then it needs an adverb - and which one fits looking closely, not rushing?

questions.trap_type: Context — Mei is worried Amy 'lost' her bottle (couldn't find it). Students may pick 'dropped' (dropped and left it behind — possible but 'lost' fits the worry better).
questions.learning_tip: 'Lost' = cannot find something. Mei was worried Amy lost the bottle = couldn't find it anywhere.
questions.retry_hint: Amy 'was looking EVERYWHERE for it' and the bottle turned up by the school GATE. Ask: what happened to Amy's bottle before Mei found it? The blank follows 'had', so a past form is needed.

questions.trap_type: Speed — she walked to the office. 'Quickly' fits urgency of returning a lost item. Students may pick 'carefully' (already used) or 'gladly' (not in box).
questions.learning_tip: She wanted to hand it in fast so the owner could get it back → walked QUICKLY. After a good deed urgency, use a speed word.
questions.retry_hint: Mei wanted the bottle handed in to the OFFICE without delay - the blank tells you HOW she walked. Ask: which adverb describes moving fast? The other -ly word describes doing something with great care.

questions.trap_type: 'Glad' = happy and pleased. Students confuse with 'sorry' (H) or 'angry' (A) which are negative emotions.
questions.learning_tip: Helping someone → a POSITIVE feeling. 'Glad' = happy and pleased that you did something good.
questions.retry_hint: The teacher praises her, Amy thanks her, and Mei HELPED a classmate. Ask: how does that feel? Choose the feeling word that matches a good outcome - not the one for anger and not the one for regret.

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'dropped' (C). The teacher is giving the bottle BACK to its owner.
questions.learning_tip: RETURNED = gave something back to the person it belongs to. = G.
questions.retry_hint: The bottle was handed in at the OFFICE, and now Amy is getting it back. Ask: which past verb means to give something back to its owner? Not the word for letting it fall by accident.

E.label: Section E — Editing
E.instructions: The passage below has five mistakes. Each mistake is underlined. Write the correct word in the box next to each number.
E.passage: Yesterday, my class had a surprise English test that Mrs Lee did not tell us about in advance. Before we started, she asked us to sit quiet (33) and not make any noise. My friend Sam writed (34) the wrong word on the first question by mistake. He looked very worry (35) but kept going. At the end, I heard some students (36) voices outside the window. Luckily, the test ended soon and Mrs Lee asked everyone to hand in there (37) papers at the front.

errors.trap_type: 'quiet' is adjective. After the action verb 'sit', use ADVERB 'quietly'.
errors.learning_tip: After an action verb (SIT), use ADVERB. Sit QUIETLY = how? QUIETLY (adverb, -ly). 'Quiet' describes nouns; 'quietly' describes HOW the action is done.
errors.retry_hint: The underlined word is a describing word, but here it must describe HOW they sit - 'sit ___ and not MAKE ANY NOISE'. Ask: which ending turns a describing word into one that describes an action?

errors.trap_type: 'writed' applies the regular -ed rule. WRITE is irregular: write → wrote.
errors.learning_tip: WRITE → WROTE (irregular past). NEVER 'writed'. Irregular verbs change completely: write → wrote, ride → rode. Memorise these.
errors.retry_hint: WRITE is an irregular verb, so it cannot take -ed. Ask: how would you say it in the past - 'yesterday he ___ his name'? Irregular verbs change their shape instead of adding an ending.

errors.error_type: Adjective form required after linking verb (looked)
errors.trap_type: After 'looked', use adjective form. WORRY → WORRIED.
errors.learning_tip: After LINKING VERBS (looked, seemed, felt), use ADJECTIVE form. He looked WORRIED = an adjective. WORRY → WORRIED. 'He looked worry' = WRONG.
errors.retry_hint: 'He LOOKED very ___' needs a describing word for how Sam felt, not the plain verb. Ask: which ending turns this verb into a feeling that describes a person, like 'excited' or 'tired'?

errors.trap_type: Students write a plain plural and leave out the apostrophe that shows ownership.
errors.learning_tip: The voices BELONG TO the students -> STUDENTS' voices (apostrophe after the -s for a plural). Singular: student's.
errors.retry_hint: The VOICES belong to the students - more than one student. Ask: does a plain -s show ownership, or does it only make a plural? Where does the apostrophe go when the owners are many?

errors.error_type: Homophone confusion — there (place) vs their (belonging to them)
errors.trap_type: 'there' (place) when 'their' (belonging to them) is needed.
errors.learning_tip: THEIR = belonging to them. THERE = at that place. 'Hand in THEIR papers' → belonging to students? YES → THEIR. THEIR = possession. THERE = location.
errors.retry_hint: The PAPERS belong to the students being spoken to. Ask: does the underlined spelling mean 'at that place', or 'belonging to them'? They sound the same, so decide by meaning, not by sound.

F.label: Section F — Synthesis & Transformation
F.instructions: Rewrite each pair of sentences as ONE sentence using the word given. The meaning must stay the same.

questions.sentence1: The teacher asked the class a question.
questions.sentence2: Have you all finished reading the storybook?
questions.instruction: Combine into one sentence using reported speech. Begin: 'The teacher asked...'
questions.model_answer: The teacher asked the class if they had all finished reading the storybook.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'asked if have they all finished' (wrong order) or keep 'you'.
questions.learning_tip: YES/NO question → reported speech: ASKED + IF + subject + verb (normal order). 'Have YOU finished?' → asked IF THEY HAD finished. Pronoun: you → they. Tense: have → had. Word order is normal after 'if'.
questions.retry_hint: A yes/no question turned into REPORTED speech. Ask three things: which small joining word follows ASKED? Does the question keep its question word order, or become normal statement order? And what happens to 'you' and to 'have'?

questions.instruction: Rewrite as ONE sentence using 'Both'.
questions.model_answer: Both Tom and his sister like drawing.
questions.trap_type: Both…and = plural verb — students keep 'likes' (singular) after combining.
questions.learning_tip: 'Both A and B' = two people = PLURAL → use verb WITHOUT -s: Both Tom and his sister LIKE (not likes) drawing.
questions.retry_hint: BOTH Tom and his sister means TWO people, so the subject is now plural. Ask: does a plural subject keep the -s on the verb, or drop it? Say 'drawing' only once - the second sentence adds nothing new.

G.label: Section G — Comprehension
G.passage:
It was a warm Friday morning. Eight-year-old Benny was walking to school with his bag on his back. Just as he turned the corner, he saw an elderly woman standing still on the pavement. She was holding a heavy bag of groceries and looking at the busy road with a worried face.

Benny stopped. He looked at his watch — he had just enough time before school started. He walked up to her and said politely, 'Excuse me, may I help you cross the road?'

The woman looked at him in surprise. Then she smiled and said, 'Oh, how kind! Yes, please.'

Benny waited for the green man to appear. He took the woman's bag and held her hand gently as they crossed the road together. On the other side, the woman thanked him again and again.

Benny arrived at school just as the bell rang. His teacher, Mr Aziz, noticed that he was slightly out of breath. When Benny explained what had happened, Mr Aziz nodded and said, 'You made a good choice this morning, Benny. Being kind is never a waste of time.'

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 2 has the same meaning as 'reached out and held onto something tightly'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Glanced' = looked quickly; 'placed' = put down; 'pointed' = directed finger. GRABBED = reached out and seized something quickly.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: GRABBED = seized something quickly and firmly with the hand. Amy GRABBED the water bottle = she quickly reached out and held it tightly. GRAB = seize quickly; GRABBED = past tense.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 3, what does 'it' refer to in 'Mei finally found it under the bench'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 or 3. 'Found IT under the bench' = the thing that was lost = the water bottle.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: PRONOUN REFERENCE: 'found IT under the bench.' IT = the WATER BOTTLE that Amy lost. The whole previous paragraph was about looking for the bottle — IT refers back to that.

mcq_questions.stem: Why did Amy say 'I have the best friend in the whole school' at the end?

options.1: Because Mei always helped Amy with her homework.
options.2: Because Mei stayed back and searched until she found the lost water bottle, showing true friendship.
options.3: Because Amy and Mei were friends since kindergarten.
options.4: Because Mei gave Amy a new water bottle as a gift.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 3 or 4. The passage is about Mei's action in THAT specific situation — staying back to help.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: INFERENCE: Amy's words show GRATITUDE for Mei's specific action — STAYING BACK to SEARCH until she found the bottle. This act of loyalty and effort is what Amy is recognising as true friendship.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 1, is it True or False that Amy knew where her water bottle was? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The passage says Amy could not find her water bottle after physical education class — she did not know where it was.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1: Amy COULD NOT FIND her water bottle. She did not know where it was — that is why Mei helped look. Answer is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: Find a word in paragraph 2 that tells us Benny spoke in a polite and respectful way.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: politely

open_ended_questions.stem: How do we know Benny was in a hurry when he arrived at school? Give TWO pieces of evidence from the passage.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) He arrived just as the bell rang. (ii) He was slightly out of breath when his teacher saw him.

open_ended_questions.stem: What does the word 'slightly' in the last paragraph mean?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: It means a little / not very much.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on her actions throughout the passage, describe TWO character traits of Mei with evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) LOYAL: Mei stayed back after class to help Amy search for her water bottle, even though it was not her responsibility — showing she put her friend first. (ii) PERSISTENT: she checked every corner of the classroom and looked under the bench before she finally found the bottle, showing she did not give up.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'kind and helpful' without precise traits or evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: TRAIT INFERENCE: LOYAL = stayed back to help, put friend FIRST. PERSISTENT = checked EVERY CORNER before finding it, did not give up. Name trait + give evidence = full marks.

questions.stem: The sleeping puppy was as ________ as a small cloud — round, soft and perfectly still.
questions.trap_type: 'Hard','noisy','dark' don't match the comparison to a cloud. FLUFFY = soft, light and resembling a cloud.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! The puppy was AS FLUFFY AS a small cloud = comparing its soft, round appearance to a light cloud. FLUFFY = soft and light. AS + ADJECTIVE + AS is always the correct simile form.
questions.retry_hint: The dash spells out the clues: ROUND, SOFT and perfectly still, and the puppy is compared to a CLOUD. Ask: which word describes something light and soft like a cloud - not its colour, not its noise, not how hard it feels?

questions.stem: The dog ________ its tail when it saw its owner at the door.
questions.trap_type: Animal action collocation — dogs specifically 'wag' their tails. 'Shook' is too general.
questions.learning_tip: Dogs WAG their tails when they are happy. This is the specific word for a dog's tail movement. Learn collocations: dogs wag, birds flap, fish swim.
questions.retry_hint: A happy DOG moves its TAIL from side to side, and English has one special verb for exactly that. Ask: does a dog shake, pull or break its tail when its OWNER comes home, or does it do that friendly side-to-side movement?

questions.stem: Nina decided to ________ the stray cat and bring it inside before the heavy rain began.
questions.trap_type: 'Run away from' = flee; 'give up on' = stop; 'break into' = enter by force. LOOK AFTER = take care of someone or something.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: LOOK AFTER = take care of someone or something. Nina decided to LOOK AFTER the stray cat = keep it fed and safe. LOOK + AFTER work together as one meaning.
questions.retry_hint: Nina brings the STRAY cat INSIDE before the heavy RAIN - this is kindness, not escape. Ask: which choice means to take care of something? Two choices mean abandoning it and one means forcing your way in.

questions.stem: When Nina found her lost cat Biscuit alive and well after two days, she was ________ - she had been so worried.
questions.trap_type: 'Under the weather' = ill; 'in hot water' = trouble; 'at a loss' = confused. OVER THE MOON = extremely happy.
questions.learning_tip: IDIOM: OVER THE MOON = feeling extremely happy and relieved. Nina was OVER THE MOON = overjoyed to find Biscuit safe. Idioms cannot be understood word by word!
questions.retry_hint: Biscuit is found ALIVE and well after she had been so WORRIED. Ask: does this idiom describe great happiness and relief, or illness, or trouble, or confusion? An idiom cannot be read word by word - match it to the feeling.

questions.stem: The fish tank was ________ when Father forgot to clean it for three weeks.
questions.trap_type: Cause-effect logic — not cleaning = gets dirty. Students may pick 'empty' thinking the water might have dried up, but the sentence says 'forgot to CLEAN', not 'forgot to fill'.
questions.learning_tip: Forgetting to CLEAN means dirt builds up → the tank becomes DIRTY. 'Empty' would happen if you forgot to fill it with water.
questions.retry_hint: Father forgot to CLEAN the fish TANK for three WEEKS. Ask: what happens to water nobody cleans - does it become brighter and clearer, or the opposite? Choose the word that is the opposite of clean, not one about light or space.

questions.stem: Nobody in the neighbourhood ________ why the old cat always sat on the same step every evening without fail.
questions.trap_type: NOBODY = singular → verb+S.
questions.learning_tip: NOBODY / EVERYONE / SOMEONE = Singular! Nobody KNOWS = add -S. 'Nobody know' is WRONG.
questions.retry_hint: The subject is NOBODY, not 'the neighbourhood'. Words like nobody, everybody and someone behave like ONE person. Ask: in the present tense, does a singular subject take the plain verb, or the verb ending in -s?

questions.stem: Our school has ________ a nature corner where students can observe different small animals and insects.
questions.trap_type: HAS + past participle = present perfect. SET UP → SET UP (phrasal verb, irregular).
questions.learning_tip: HAS + past participle = present perfect. The school HAS SET UP a nature corner = done recently and now available. SET UP: set is also the past participle (irregular).
questions.retry_hint: 'HAS' is already sitting there, so the blank must be the form that partners with has. Ask: after has, do we use the -ing form, the plain verb, or the past participle? And remember a verb never takes a plural -s.

questions.stem: The birds ________ south when winter arrives every year.
questions.trap_type: Plural subject + habit — 'the birds' is plural. Present habit → no -s. Students add -s after seeing 'every year'.
questions.learning_tip: 'The birds' = plural → NO -s on verb. 'Every year' = habit = simple present. Birds (plural) FLY (not flies).
questions.retry_hint: Two clues: the subject BIRDS is plural, and 'EVERY year' means it happens again and again. Ask: is this a finished past event or a present habit? A plural subject in the present takes the verb with NO -s.

questions.stem: The golden retriever is far ________ than the tiny chihuahua standing next to it at the pet show.
questions.trap_type: 'Largest' = superlative; 'more larger' is WRONG. LARGER = comparative of 'large'.
questions.learning_tip: Short adjective + -ER = comparative. Large → LARGER. The golden retriever is LARGER THAN the chihuahua = comparing two dogs. 'More larger' is ALWAYS WRONG.
questions.retry_hint: The word THAN gives it away - one animal is being measured against one other. Ask: do we need the plain adjective, the -est form used for three or more, or the comparing form? Never stack 'more' on top of an -er word.

questions.stem: My dog ________ not eat its food this morning because it was sick.
questions.trap_type: 'Did not' = past tense negative. Students choose 'does' (present) or 'was' (wrong structure).
questions.learning_tip: 'This morning' = past. Negative past = DID NOT + base verb: did not eat. 'Does not' is present tense.
questions.retry_hint: 'THIS MORNING' is already over, so the sentence is past - and 'EAT' after the blank is the plain verb, so the blank must be the helping verb. Ask: which helping verb makes a past negative in front of a plain verb?

questions.stem: Cats and dogs are the most popular pets in Singapore, ________ they?
questions.trap_type: Positive present 'to be' ('are') → negative question tag. ARE → aren't they.
questions.learning_tip: Positive present 'to be' → negative tag. Cats and dogs ARE the most popular pets, AREN'T they? POSITIVE → NEGATIVE. ARE → AREN'T. Plural subject → aren't. Cats and dogs ARE the most popular pets, AREN'T they? Positive → Negative. ARE → AREN'T they.
questions.retry_hint: A question tag mirrors the main verb: the statement uses ARE, and CATS and dogs is plural. Ask: if the statement is positive, must the tag be positive or negative? And must the tag agree with a plural subject?

questions.stem: The monkey ________ climbing the tree when we arrived at the zoo.
questions.trap_type: Past continuous for single animal — 'the monkey' is singular + ongoing past action = 'was -ing'. Students pick 'were' (plural form).
questions.learning_tip: THE MONKEY = one monkey = singular → WAS climbing (not were). Past continuous = WAS + -ing for singular, WERE + -ing for plural.
questions.retry_hint: CLIMBING needs a helping verb in front of it, and ARRIVED tells you the time is past. Ask: is the MONKEY one animal or many? Match a PAST helping verb to a singular subject - a present form or a plural form breaks the sentence.

questions.stem: She kept ________ fish in the pond even though her father told her not to.
questions.trap_type: Kept + gerund — 'kept doing something' always takes -ing form. Students use past tense 'fed' after 'kept'.
questions.learning_tip: 'KEPT + verb-ing': kept feeding, kept running, kept asking. After 'keep/kept', ALWAYS use -ing form.
questions.retry_hint: KEPT is the verb that decides everything. Ask: after keep or kept, does the next verb appear as the plain form, the -s form, the past form, or the -ing form? Only one verb carries the tense, and KEPT is already doing that job.

C.label: Section C — Grammar Cloze
C.instructions: Read the passage below. Choose the most suitable word from the box and write its letter in each blank. Use each word ONCE only.
C.passage: Our school visited the aquarium last week. We watched a sea otter (1)___ in a big tank. It kept (2)___ in circles because it was so playful. The sign on the glass says that this otter (3)___ for more than five hours every day. Last winter, it even (4)___ in the chilly outdoor pool. While we were standing there, a fish darted past and the otter quickly (5)___ it. An otter always (6)___ its food with its front paws, never with its mouth. The hungry otter kept (7)___ more fish until the keeper's bucket was empty. We waited to see it (8)___ one last fish, but it had already curled up for a nap.

answers.3: H (swims - 'the sign says' = present; this otter = singular)
answers.6: C (catches - general truth, 'an otter' = singular present)

C.passage_final: Our school visited the aquarium last week. We watched a sea otter (1)___ in a big glass tank. The otter was very playful. It kept (2)___ in circles before stopping to float on its back. The trainer told us that sea otters (3)___ on their backs when they want to rest. Next, we moved to the penguin area. A penguin trainer showed us how the penguin (4)___ fish from a bucket. It was very fast! All the penguins (5)___ fish at the same time without dropping any. In the final hall, we watched a group of dolphins (6)___ beautifully in a pool. After the show, we went to (7)___ our favourite fish at the touch pool. I tried hard to (8)___ a small starfish with my hands.

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'swims' because one otter feels singular. But after WATCHED + object the verb has no -s.
questions.learning_tip: WATCH / SEE / HEAR + object + BASE VERB. 'We watched a sea otter SWIM' - never 'swims'. = E.
questions.retry_hint: The verb WATCHED controls this blank: 'We WATCHED a sea otter ___ in a big tank.' Ask: after watch, see or hear plus an object, does the next verb take -s, -ed, -ing, or nothing at all? The otter being singular does not matter here.

questions.trap_type: Students pick the past 'swam' because the visit was last week. KEEP is what decides the form, not the story's tense.
questions.learning_tip: KEEP + -ING. 'It kept SWIMMING'. Same pattern: kept running, kept talking. = G.
questions.retry_hint: Look at KEPT: 'It KEPT ___ in circles.' Ask: after keep or kept, which single form always follows - the plain verb, the -s form, the past form, or the -ing form? KEPT is already carrying the past tense.

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'swim' (no -s). The subject 'this otter' is singular, and 'the sign says' is present tense.
questions.learning_tip: Singular subject + present tense -> add -s. 'This otter SWIMS every day.' = H.
questions.retry_hint: The SIGN on the glass SAYS - says is present, so this blank is present too, and 'this otter' is ONE animal. Ask: in the present tense, does a singular subject take the plain verb or the verb ending in -s?

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'swims'. 'Last winter' is a finished time, so the verb must be past.
questions.learning_tip: Past time marker ('last winter', 'yesterday') -> past tense. swim -> SWAM (irregular). = F.
questions.retry_hint: 'LAST WINTER' is finished time, so this verb must be past - not present, not -ing. Ask: what is the past form of the verb meaning to move through water? It is irregular, so it never takes -ed.

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'catches'. The sentence is a finished past action ('a fish darted past').
questions.learning_tip: Past narrative -> past verb. catch -> CAUGHT (irregular, not 'catched'). = B.
questions.retry_hint: The story is past here: a fish DARTED past and the otter QUICKLY ___ it. Ask: which past form fits? This verb is irregular, so 'catched' does not exist - and the -s form is only for present habits.

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'catch'. 'An otter' is ONE otter, and this is a general truth in the present.
questions.answer_corrected: F(swam) if sentence is 'dolphins swam beautifully' independent clause. Re-check grammar: 'watched + object + base verb' → E(swim). Redesign sentence: 'The dolphins (6)___ beautifully across the pool.' → F(swam).
questions.learning_tip: General truth + singular subject -> verb + -s. 'An otter CATCHES its food.' = C.
questions.retry_hint: 'An OTTER ALWAYS ___ its food with its front paws.' ALWAYS signals a general truth in the present, and 'an otter' is one otter. Ask: present tense plus a singular subject - which ending must the verb carry?

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'caught' because the story is past. But KEPT is already the past verb; the next verb must be -ing.
questions.learning_tip: KEEP + -ING (again). 'kept CATCHING more fish'. Only ONE verb carries the tense. = D.
questions.retry_hint: KEPT turns up a second time: 'The hungry otter KEPT ___ more fish.' Ask: if KEPT already shows the past, can the verb after it be past as well? Which form must follow keep or kept, every single time?

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'caught'. After SEE + object the verb is the base form with no ending.
questions.answer_corrected: D(catching): 'I tried catching a small starfish' or restructure to 'tried to catch' = A (but A is used). Passage uses 'I tried (8)___ a small starfish with my hands' → D(catching).
questions.learning_tip: SEE / WATCH / HEAR + object + BASE VERB. 'to see it CATCH one last fish'. = A.
questions.retry_hint: 'We waited to SEE it ___ one last fish.' Ask: after see, watch or hear plus an object, which form comes next - the base verb, or one with -s, -ed or -ing? This is the very same rule as blank 1 in this passage.

D.label: Section D — Vocabulary Cloze
D.instructions: Read the passage carefully. Choose the most suitable word from the box and write its letter in each blank. Use each word ONCE only.
D.passage: Last weekend, Mia found an injured bird in the garden. It was so (1)___ that it could fit inside her palm. A stray cat had (2)___ the little sparrow across the grass, and one of its wings was hurt. At first the bird was (3)___ of Mia and tried to flap away, so she moved slowly and spoke in a soft voice. Her mother called a wildlife officer, who came at once to (4)___ the trembling creature. He carried it to a shelter where it would be (5)___ from cats and cars until its wing healed.

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'gentle' (C), which describes character, not size. The clue is 'fit inside her palm'.
questions.learning_tip: TINY = very, very small. If it fits in a palm, it is TINY. = H.
questions.retry_hint: The clue comes right after the blank: it could FIT INSIDE her PALM. Ask: is this word about size, about character, or about noise? Choose the one that means extremely small.

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'rescue' (E). But the cat is the one doing this, and it is why the bird is hurt - it ran after it.
questions.learning_tip: CHASED = ran after something to catch it. The blank needs a PAST verb after 'had'. = B.
questions.retry_hint: A STRAY CAT is the one acting, and the bird ends up INJURED with a hurt wing. Ask: did the cat save the bird or run after it across the grass? The blank follows 'had', so a past verb form is needed.

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'surprised' (G). The bird 'tried to flap away' - that is fear, not surprise.
questions.learning_tip: AFRAID = frightened. 'Afraid OF something' is the fixed pairing. = A.
questions.retry_hint: The bird TRIED to FLAP away from Mia - it is trying to escape her. Ask: does escaping show fear or shock? Pick the feeling word that pairs with 'of': you are ___ OF something.

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'chased' (B). After 'came at once TO ___' a base verb is needed, and an officer helps, not hunts.
questions.learning_tip: RESCUE = save someone from danger. After 'to' use the base verb. = E.
questions.retry_hint: A wildlife OFFICER is called and comes AT ONCE to help the trembling bird. Ask: after 'to', do we need a past verb or a base verb? And does an officer hunt an injured bird, or save it from danger?

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'noisy' (D) or 'gentle' (C). The blank is about being out of danger 'from cats and cars'.
questions.learning_tip: SAFE = protected from danger. 'Safe FROM something' is the fixed pairing. = F.
questions.retry_hint: The SHELTER protects the bird FROM CATS and cars until its wing has healed. Ask: which box word means 'out of danger'? Watch the pairing - this one goes with FROM, while a different box word goes with 'of'.

E.label: Section E — Editing
E.instructions: The passage below has five mistakes. Each mistake is underlined. Write the correct word in the box next to each number.
E.passage: Last week, our class joined a nature walk at the park near school. We goed (33) to the park by bus and could here (34) birdsong before we got off. The guide telled (35) us to walk softly so we would not scare the animals. Some animals in the park eats (36) seeds and berries. At the end, the park rangers (37) report on the animals we spotted was printed and given to each student as a souvenir.

errors.trap_type: 'goed' applies regular -ed. GO is irregular: go → went.
errors.learning_tip: GO → WENT (irregular past). NEVER 'goed'. GO changes completely in past tense. Irregular verbs do not follow the -ed rule.
errors.retry_hint: The class travelled by bus LAST WEEK, so this verb must be past. Ask: does GO build its past by adding -ed, or does it change into a completely different word? Irregular verbs never take -ed.

errors.error_type: Homophone confusion — here (place) vs hear (to listen)
errors.trap_type: 'here' (place) when 'hear' (ears) is needed.
errors.learning_tip: HEAR = detect sound with ears. HERE = at this place. 'We could HEAR birdsong' → use ears? YES → HEAR. HEAR = ears. HERE = location.
errors.retry_hint: The underlined word means 'at this place', but the sentence is about BIRDSONG reaching your EARS. Ask: which spelling belongs to your ears? One of them contains the word EAR - that is your clue.

errors.trap_type: 'telled' applies regular -ed. TELL is irregular: tell → told.
errors.learning_tip: TELL → TOLD (irregular past). NEVER 'telled'. Irregular verbs: tell → told, sell → sold. Memorise these.
errors.retry_hint: TELL is irregular, so the -ed ending is wrong here. Ask: how do you say it in the past - 'yesterday he ___ us'? It changes its vowel, exactly like sell becomes sold.

errors.trap_type: 'Some animals' is plural. Students write 'eats' (singular).
errors.learning_tip: Plural subject → plural verb! SOME ANIMALS EAT = ANIMALS is plural → EAT (no -s). Find the main noun: ANIMALS = plural → EAT.
errors.retry_hint: Find the subject: SOME ANIMALS, which is more than one. Ask: does a plural subject take the verb with -s, or the verb without it? The -s ending belongs to singular subjects, like 'the animal eats'.

errors.trap_type: Students write a plain plural and leave out the apostrophe.
errors.learning_tip: The report BELONGS TO the rangers -> RANGERS' report (apostrophe after the -s for a plural). Singular: ranger's.
errors.retry_hint: The REPORT belongs to the park rangers - more than one ranger. Ask: does a plain -s show ownership, or does it only make a plural? Where does the apostrophe go when the owners are many?

questions.sentence1: The zookeeper asked the children a question.
questions.sentence2: Have you ever touched a real snake before?
questions.instruction: Combine into one sentence using reported speech. Begin: 'The zookeeper asked...'
questions.model_answer: The zookeeper asked the children if they had ever touched a real snake before.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'asked if have they ever touched' (wrong order) or keep 'you'.
questions.learning_tip: YES/NO question → reported speech: ASKED + IF + subject + verb (normal order). 'Have YOU ever touched?' → asked IF THEY HAD ever touched. Pronoun: you → they. Tense: have → had. Word order is normal after 'if'.
questions.retry_hint: This is a yes/no question turned into REPORTED speech. Ask three things: which small joining word follows ASKED? Does the question keep its question word order, or become a normal statement order? And what must happen to 'you' and to 'have'?

questions.sentence2: Her brother has a pet rabbit too.
questions.instruction: Rewrite using 'Both'.
questions.model_answer: Both Maya and her brother have a pet rabbit.
questions.trap_type: Both + plural verb — 'Both Maya and her brother' = plural → 'have' not 'has'.
questions.learning_tip: 'Both A and B' = two people = PLURAL. Maya HAS (singular) → Both Maya and her brother HAVE (plural). Remove the -s.
questions.retry_hint: BOTH Maya and her brother means TWO people, so your subject is now plural. Ask: does a plural subject keep the -s on the verb, or drop it? And say 'a pet rabbit' only once - do not repeat the whole second sentence.

G.label: Section G — Comprehension
G.passage:
Nine-year-old Nina had a tabby cat named Biscuit. One Thursday afternoon, she came home from school and found the front door slightly open. She looked everywhere for Biscuit but could not find him. Nina felt sick with worry.

She told her mother, who suggested they make some posters. Together, they printed twelve posters with Biscuit's photo and their phone number on them. Nina and her father walked around the neighbourhood and stuck the posters on lamp posts and notice boards.

The next morning, a neighbour from the next block called. She saw Biscuit sitting under her car. Nina ran all the way to the neighbour's house. There was Biscuit, thin and hungry but otherwise unhurt.

Nina's eyes filled with tears as she carried him home. She promised herself she would always check the front door carefully before leaving the house.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 2 has the same meaning as 'looking around carefully and quickly'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Crawling' = moving on all fours; 'trembling' = shaking; 'hiding' = concealing. SCANNING = looking carefully around an area for something specific.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: SCANNING = looking quickly and carefully across an area to find something. Nina was SCANNING the street = she looked in every direction carefully for Biscuit. SCAN = look systematically.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 3, what does 'it' refer to in 'she could barely believe it'?

options.1: The street light above the drain
options.2: The fact that Biscuit was alive and safe despite being missing for two days
options.4: The drain where Biscuit was found

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 or 3 thinking 'it' = the light or neighbour. 'Could barely believe IT' = something incredible she found hard to accept.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: PRONOUN REFERENCE: 'could barely believe IT.' IT = the incredible FACT — that Biscuit was alive and unhurt after TWO DAYS missing near a road. She found it hard to believe such good news.

mcq_questions.stem: Why does the writer end the passage with 'Nina promised never to leave the gate open again'?

options.1: Because Nina's mother told her to make that promise.
options.2: Because the experience taught Nina that a small act of carelessness can have serious consequences.
options.3: Because Nina wanted to get a new cat.
options.4: Because the neighbour complained about the open gate.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 or 4 thinking someone ELSE caused the promise. Nina's own experience caused this change.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: INFERENCE: Nina's PROMISE comes from HER OWN LEARNING. Biscuit went missing because of an OPEN GATE (her carelessness). The experience taught her that small mistakes = big consequences. Option 2 = the lesson of the passage.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 1, is it True or False that Nina noticed Biscuit was missing straight away? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: True. The passage says Nina realised Biscuit was gone when she went to feed him and found his bowl untouched — she noticed it immediately.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1: Nina went to FEED Biscuit and found his BOWL UNTOUCHED — she realised at once. Answer is TRUE.

open_ended_questions.stem: Where did Nina and her father put the posters?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: They put the posters on lamp posts and notice boards.

open_ended_questions.stem: How do we know Nina was very relieved when she found Biscuit? Give TWO examples from the passage.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) Her eyes filled with tears (showing strong emotion/relief). (ii) She ran ALL THE WAY to the neighbour's house (showing she was in a great hurry to find him).

open_ended_questions.stem: What did Nina promise herself at the end of the story? Why?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: She promised to always check the front door carefully before leaving. She did this because leaving the door slightly open was how Biscuit escaped.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on her actions throughout the passage, describe TWO character traits of Nina with evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) CARING: Nina spent two whole days searching the neighbourhood for Biscuit and refused to give up — showing she loved her pet and would not stop until she found him. (ii) RESPONSIBLE: at the end, she promised never to leave the gate open again, showing she learned from her mistake and took responsibility for it.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'kind and sad' without precise traits or evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: TRAIT INFERENCE: CARING = searched for TWO DAYS, refused to give up. RESPONSIBLE = promised not to leave gate open again — took responsibility. Name trait + give evidence = full marks.

questions.stem: After a long day of helping Mum clean the house, Nora's arms felt as ________ as noodles — too tired to lift anything.
questions.trap_type: 'Strong','stiff' = strength or tension (opposite of tired muscles). 'Cold' = temperature. LIMP = weak and without strength, like cooked noodles.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! Nora's arms were AS LIMP AS noodles = comparing her exhausted, weak arms to soft, cooked noodles. LIMP = soft, weak and without strength. AS + ADJECTIVE + AS is the correct simile form.
questions.retry_hint: The dash explains it: her arms were TOO tired to lift anything, and they are compared to NOODLES. Ask: are cooked noodles firm and springy, or floppy and drooping? Match the adjective to the noodles, not to temperature.

questions.stem: Father ________ the broken chair with some wood and glue.
questions.trap_type: Repair vocabulary — the chair is already broken, so 'broke' doesn't make sense. 'Threw' = got rid of it (not repaired it).
questions.learning_tip: The chair was ALREADY broken → Father FIXED it (repaired it). 'Fixed' = made something broken work again.
questions.retry_hint: Look at the tools Father is using: some wood and GLUE. Ask: what do you do to a chair that is already broken - damage it further, or repair it? The tools tell you the purpose of the action.

questions.stem: After dinner, the children helped to ________ the dining table and wash the dishes.
questions.trap_type: 'Run away from','give up on','break into' = negative actions. CLEAR AWAY = remove plates, cups and food from a table after eating.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: CLEAR AWAY = remove things from a table or surface after use. The children CLEARED AWAY the dining table = they removed all the dishes. CLEAR + AWAY work together as one meaning.
questions.retry_hint: The children help after dinner and also WASH the dishes. Ask: what would a helpful child do to a table covered in used plates - remove them tidily, or attack the furniture? Pick the phrasal verb that tidies, not one that harms.

questions.stem: When Grandma saw the clean kitchen and the birthday cake Nora baked for her, she was ________ — she could not stop smiling.
questions.trap_type: 'Under the weather' = ill; 'in hot water' = trouble; 'down in the dumps' = sad. OVER THE MOON = extremely happy.
questions.learning_tip: IDIOM: OVER THE MOON = feeling extremely happy and touched. Grandma was OVER THE MOON = overjoyed by the surprise. Idioms cannot be understood word by word!
questions.retry_hint: The dash gives you the meaning: she could not stop SMILING. Ask: which idiom means extremely happy? The other three describe being ill, being in trouble, or feeling sad - none of those make you smile.

questions.stem: Sarah was ________ that her little brother had eaten the last piece of cake she was saving.
questions.trap_type: Negative emotion — someone ate YOUR food without asking = a negative feeling. Students may pick 'excited' by mistake.
questions.learning_tip: Having your saved food eaten without permission = a negative experience → UPSET (feeling unhappy and annoyed). Not pleased or excited.
questions.retry_hint: Notice she was SAVING that last piece for herself, and her brother ate it without asking. Ask: is that a welcome surprise or an unwelcome one? Choose the feeling that matches losing something you wanted.

questions.stem: Nobody in our family ________ how Grandma manages to keep the kitchen so clean after every meal.
questions.trap_type: NOBODY = singular → verb+S.
questions.learning_tip: NOBODY / EVERYONE / SOMEONE = Singular! Nobody KNOWS = add -S. 'Nobody know' is WRONG.
questions.retry_hint: The subject is NOBODY. Even though it feels like many people, nobody / everybody / someone behave as a single person. Ask: in the present tense, does a singular subject take the plain verb, or the one ending in -s?

questions.stem: Our family has ________ a new rule: everyone must do one household chore before watching television.
questions.trap_type: HAS + past participle = present perfect. INTRODUCE → INTRODUCED.
questions.learning_tip: HAS + past participle = present perfect. Our family HAS INTRODUCED a new rule = decided recently. INTRODUCE → INTRODUCED (add -d for regular verbs ending in -e).
questions.retry_hint: The helper HAS is already sitting in the sentence. Ask: after have/has, which form builds the present perfect? Not the base form, not the -ing form - you need the third form of the verb.

questions.stem: My brother ________ the floors while I was washing the dishes when Mother came home and praised us.
questions.trap_type: 'Mother came home' = sudden past event. Brother was already sweeping = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: Mother CAME HOME = sudden past event. My brother was already in the middle of sweeping = WAS SWEEPING (past continuous). Was/were + verb-ing = action in progress when interrupted.
questions.retry_hint: Mother CAME home - that is the sudden event. The brother's job was already going on when she walked in. Ask: which tense shows an action in progress that gets interrupted by something sudden?

questions.stem: The house looked much ________ after the children spent three hours cleaning every room thoroughly.
questions.trap_type: 'Tidiest' = superlative; 'more tidier' is WRONG. TIDIER = comparative of 'tidy' (change y to i, add -er).
questions.learning_tip: Short adjective ending in -Y → change Y to I, add -ER. Tidy → TIDIER. The house looked TIDIER THAN before. 'More tidier' is ALWAYS WRONG — never add BOTH 'more' AND '-er'.
questions.retry_hint: The word MUCH in front of the blank is a comparison signal, and only two states are compared: the house before cleaning and after. Ask: does comparing two things need the comparative or the superlative? And never stack 'more' in front of an -er ending.

questions.stem: ________ of the children helped to carry the grocery bags upstairs after the family returned from shopping.
questions.trap_type: ALL = every one of the children (as a group). EACH = one by one.
questions.learning_tip: ALL OF THE CHILDREN = everyone together, as a group. EACH of the children = one by one, individually. 'All of the children helped' = they worked together. Choose ALL for group action.
questions.retry_hint: Every single child took part - the sentence says they helped to CARRY the bags upstairs. Ask: which word means the whole group acting as one, rather than one-by-one? And be careful not to pick a word that would make the sentence mean nobody helped.

questions.stem: Keeping a clean and tidy home is everyone's responsibility in a family, ________ it?
questions.trap_type: Positive present 'to be' ('is') → negative question tag. IS → isn't it.
questions.learning_tip: Positive present 'to be' → negative tag. Keeping a clean home IS everyone's responsibility, ISN'T it? POSITIVE → NEGATIVE. IS → ISN'T. Tag questions match the 'to be' verb.
questions.retry_hint: Look at the main clause: keeping a tidy home IS everyone's RESPONSIBILITY - a positive statement built on the 'to be' verb. Ask: does a positive statement take a positive tag, or its opposite? The tag must also reuse the same verb, not a different helper.

questions.stem: The twins cleaned the house ________ after school yesterday.
questions.trap_type: Reflexive pronoun — twins = they = two people = THEMSELVES. Students pick 'ourselves' thinking of helping (as if they are included).
questions.learning_tip: THEY (the twins) cleaned = third person plural → reflexive = THEMSELVES. OURSELVES is for WE (when you include yourself).
questions.retry_hint: The subject is the TWINS - two people, and they are not the speaker. Ask: does the reflexive pronoun point back to one boy, to a thing, to us, or to them? Match it to who actually did the cleaning.

questions.stem: Aunt Mary, ________ with her three children, came to help us move house.
questions.trap_type: 'Together with' = a fixed phrase. The expression is 'together with', not 'along with' in this context, though 'along with' is also acceptable — but 'together with' is more common in P3.
questions.learning_tip: 'Together WITH' = as a group. 'Aunt Mary, TOGETHER WITH her children, came' = the aunt AND her children all came.
questions.retry_hint: Look at the word right after the blank: WITH. It forms a fixed phrase joining Aunt Mary to the people who came along. Ask: which option normally pairs with 'with' to mean 'accompanied by'? Say each choice aloud and hear which sounds right.

C.label: Section C — Grammar Cloze
C.instructions: Read the passage below. Choose the most suitable word from the box and write its letter in each blank. Use each word ONCE only.
C.passage: Every Saturday, our family does chores together. My father (1)___ the floors with a big mop while my mother wipes the windows. Last Saturday was special because Grandma came to visit. Dad (2)___ the kitchen tiles twice to make sure they were spotless. My sister was in charge of (3)___ the bathrooms. She spent nearly an hour (4)___ every corner carefully. Meanwhile, I had to (5)___ the floor of my room with a small mop. I (6)___ the shelves and put all my books back in order. Even now, my little brother (7)___ the last window in the living room. Grandma walked in and said, 'What a (8)___ and tidy home you have!'
C.passage_final: Every Saturday, our family does chores together. My father (1)___ the floors with a big mop while my mother wipes the windows. Last Saturday was special because Grandma came to visit. Dad (2)___ the kitchen tiles twice to make sure they were spotless. My sister was in charge of (3)___ the bathrooms. She spent nearly an hour (4)___ every corner carefully. Meanwhile, I had to (5)___ my room. I (6)___ all the shelves and put my books back in order. By noon, the whole flat looked (7)___ and tidy. Grandma walked in and said, 'Your home is so (8)___!'

answers_final.3: A(clean — in charge of clean? No: in charge of cleaning = C)

C.note: Word box redesigned for better fit. See questions below.

questions.trap_type: 'My father mops' — habit, singular → H (mops, 3rd person singular present). Students pick F (mopped, past).
questions.learning_tip: Every Saturday = habit = PRESENT TENSE. My father = singular → MOPS = H.
questions.retry_hint: 'EVERY SATURDAY' means this happens again and again, so the verb is present - and 'my father' is one person. Ask: in the present, does a singular subject take the plain verb or the verb ending in -s?

questions.trap_type: 'Dad mopped' — specific past event (Last Saturday). Students pick H (mops, present).
questions.learning_tip: Last Saturday = PAST. Dad MOPPED the kitchen tiles = F (simple past).
questions.retry_hint: 'LAST SATURDAY' is finished time, so this verb must be past. Ask: which form shows a completed action - the plain verb, the -s form, the -ing form, or the one that adds -ed?

questions.trap_type: 'In charge of cleaning' — after 'of' (preposition), use -ing form. Students pick A (clean, base form).
questions.learning_tip: After PREPOSITIONS (of, for, in), use VERB-ING: in charge of CLEANING. Never 'in charge of clean'.
questions.retry_hint: Look at the word before the blank: 'in CHARGE OF ___'. Ask: after a preposition like 'of', which form must a verb take? Never the plain form, and never the past form.

questions.trap_type: 'Spent an hour mopping' — after 'spent [time]', use -ing. Students pick F (mopped, past tense).
questions.learning_tip: 'Spent [time] + VERB-ING': spent an hour MOPPING. This pattern always uses -ing.
questions.retry_hint: 'She SPENT nearly an HOUR ___' - spend time doing something. Ask: which form follows 'spent an hour'? And the corners are being wiped with a mop, not dusted, so choose the right verb too.

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'mopped' (F). The blank follows 'had to', so a base verb is needed.
questions.learning_tip: After HAD TO, use the BASE verb: had to MOP. = E.
questions.retry_hint: After 'I HAD TO ___' the verb must be in its plainest form, with no ending at all. Ask: which of the two base verbs in the box is the one you do to a FLOOR with a bucket of water, rather than the general word for tidying?

questions.trap_type: 'I cleaned the shelves' — simple past. Students pick C (cleaning, -ing form).
questions.learning_tip: Simple action in past story = SIMPLE PAST. I CLEANED the shelves = B. Not cleaning (which needs was/were).
questions.retry_hint: The SHELVES were done and the BOOKS were put back - all finished, in the past. Ask: which past form fits a verb that simply adds -ed? Shelves are wiped, not mopped, so pick the right verb as well.

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'cleaned' (B). 'Even now' means the action is happening at this moment.
questions.learning_tip: EVEN NOW = right now -> present continuous: IS CLEANING. One brother = singular = is. = D.
questions.retry_hint: 'EVEN NOW' means it is happening at this very moment - the action is not finished. Ask: which choice shows an action in progress right now? One brother is doing it, so the helping verb must be singular.

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'cleaning' (C). After 'What a ___ and tidy home', an ADJECTIVE is needed.
questions.answer_corrected: Redesign blank 8: 'Grandma walked in and exclaimed — Your home (8)___ so clean!' → (8)=D(is cleaning? No). Better: 'The home (8)___ very tidy' → D(is cleaning) doesn't work. Better D=is clean? Restructure.
questions.learning_tip: CLEAN is the adjective (clean and tidy). 'Cleaning' is a verb form, not a describing word. = A.
questions.retry_hint: 'What a ___ and TIDY home!' - the blank sits beside 'tidy', so it must be a describing word too. Ask: which choice is an adjective? An -ing form or a past form would not fit next to 'tidy'.

D.label: Section D — Vocabulary Cloze
D.instructions: Read the passage carefully. Choose the most suitable word from the box and write its letter in each blank. Use each word ONCE only.
D.passage: Last Friday, eight-year-old Kai decided to help his mother cook dinner as a surprise. He carried the pot of water very (1)___ so that he would not drop it. Unfortunately, he was a little (2)___ and (3)___ some water on the floor. He wiped it up (4)___ before his mother came back into the kitchen. When Mother walked in and saw the (5)___ kitchen and smelled the cooking, she could hardly believe her eyes. She hugged Kai and thanked him for doing so much on his own.

questions.trap_type: 'Carried carefully' — not wanting to drop a pot of water = needs care. Students pick 'quickly' (E).
questions.learning_tip: Carrying a full pot of water without dropping = needs CARE → carried CAREFULLY = A.
questions.retry_hint: He did not want to DROP the pot of water, so he took his time. Ask: does the blank describe HOW he carried it? Then it needs an -ly word - the one about taking care, not the one about speed.

questions.trap_type: 'A little clumsy' — he spilled water, which shows he was not graceful. Adjective after 'was'.
questions.learning_tip: 'Clumsy' = not careful with your hands/feet, often dropping or spilling things. He spilled water → he was CLUMSY = B.
questions.retry_hint: He spilt water even though he was trying hard - his hands were not steady. Ask: which box word describes a person who knocks things over and drops things? It is a describing word, after 'a little'.

questions.trap_type: 'Spilled some water' — water that falls accidentally = spilled. Students pick 'dropped' (not in box).
questions.learning_tip: Liquid or powder that falls accidentally = SPILLED. He SPILLED water on the floor = F.
questions.retry_hint: The water ended up ON THE FLOOR, so something happened to it as he carried the pot. Ask: which box word is a past verb meaning that liquid went where it should not?

questions.trap_type: 'Wiped quickly' — he needed to clean up before Mother came back, so he had to be fast. Students pick 'carefully' (A, already used).
questions.learning_tip: He needed to clean BEFORE Mother came back → he had to move fast → QUICKLY = E.
questions.retry_hint: He had to finish BEFORE his MOTHER came back into the kitchen - there was no time to lose. Ask: which -ly word describes doing something fast?

questions.trap_type: 'Tidy kitchen' — Kai cleaned up the spill → the kitchen looked neat. Students pick 'clean' (not in box) or confuse with 'helpful'.
questions.learning_tip: He wiped up the water → kitchen looked TIDY (neat and clean) = H. 'Helpful' (C) describes a person, not a kitchen.
questions.retry_hint: He WIPED the water up before Mother arrived, so the floor no longer looked messy. Ask: which box word describes a room that is neat and in order? It goes in front of the noun 'kitchen'.

E.label: Section E — Editing
E.instructions: The passage below has five mistakes. Each mistake is underlined. Write the correct word in the box next to each number.
E.passage: Last Saturday, our whole family spent the morning doing housework together. Everyone taked (33) a different chore - Father mopped the floors and Mother wiped the windows. My sister organize (34) all the books on the shelf while I swept the corridor. The curtains was (35) taken down and washed in the machine. When Grandma arrived, the house looked beautiful and she said it looked like the cleaners (36) best work ever. We all heard Grandma whisper to Mother that there (37) home had never looked so clean.

errors.trap_type: 'taked' applies regular -ed. TAKE is irregular: take → took.
errors.learning_tip: TAKE → TOOK (irregular past). NEVER 'taked'. Irregular verbs: take → took, make → made, shake → shook. These must be memorised.
errors.retry_hint: TAKE is an irregular verb, so -ed is wrong. Ask: how would you say it in the past - 'yesterday she ___ the bus'? Irregular verbs change their shape instead of adding an ending.

errors.error_type: Past tense required — regular verb (organise → organised)
errors.trap_type: 'organize' is base/present form. Past context needs 'organised'.
errors.learning_tip: ORGANISE → ORGANISED (regular past, add -d). In a past tense context, use ORGANISED. 'My sister organize' = WRONG — wrong tense. Use ORGANISED.
errors.retry_hint: The whole passage is about LAST SATURDAY, and the verbs around it (mopped, wiped, swept) are past. Ask: is the underlined verb past or present? Every verb in the story must share the same tense.

errors.trap_type: 'The curtains' is plural. Students write 'was'.
errors.learning_tip: Plural subject → plural verb! THE CURTAINS WERE taken down = CURTAINS is plural → WERE. WAS is only for ONE thing.
errors.retry_hint: Find the subject: THE CURTAINS - more than one. Ask: does a plural subject take the singular verb, or the plural one? Match the verb to the subject, not to the word next to it.

errors.trap_type: Students write a plain plural and leave out the apostrophe.
errors.learning_tip: The work BELONGS TO the cleaners -> CLEANERS' best work (apostrophe after the -s for a plural).
errors.retry_hint: The best work BELONGS TO the cleaners - more than one cleaner. Ask: does a plain -s show ownership, or only make a plural? Where does the apostrophe go when the owners are many?

errors.error_type: Homophone confusion — there (place) vs their (belonging to them)
errors.trap_type: 'there' (place) when 'their' (belonging to us/the family) is needed.
errors.learning_tip: THEIR = belonging to them. THERE = at that place. 'THEIR home' → belonging to the family? YES → THEIR. THEIR = possession. THERE = location.
errors.retry_hint: The HOME belongs to the family Grandma is talking about. Ask: does the underlined spelling mean 'at that place', or 'belonging to them'? The two sound alike, so choose by meaning.

questions.sentence2: Did you remember to take out the rubbish before school?
questions.instruction: Combine into one sentence using reported speech. Begin: 'Mother asked...'
questions.model_answer: Mother asked Nora if she had remembered to take out the rubbish before school.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'asked if did she remember' (wrong order) or keep 'you'.
questions.learning_tip: YES/NO question → reported speech: ASKED + IF + subject + verb (normal order). 'Did YOU remember?' → asked IF SHE REMEMBERED. Pronoun: you → she. Tense: did remember → remembered. Word order is normal after 'if'.
questions.retry_hint: A past yes/no question ('DID you remember...?') becomes REPORTED speech. Ask: which joining word follows ASKED? Does 'you' stay as 'you'? And when the reporting verb is past, what happens to the verb inside - does it step one tense further back?

questions.instruction: Rewrite as ONE sentence using 'when'.
questions.starter: Sam was cleaning his room when ___________.
questions.model_answer: Sam was cleaning his room when Mother called him for dinner.
questions.trap_type: Word order — the given starter 'Sam was cleaning' is already provided. Students just need to add 'when + simple past event'.
questions.learning_tip: [Ongoing action: was -ing] WHEN [sudden event: simple past]. The sudden event comes AFTER 'when'. No comma needed when 'when' is in the middle.
questions.retry_hint: One action was already going on when the other cut across it. Ask: which sentence describes the longer action in progress, and which describes the sudden one? Put WHEN in front of the sudden one.

G.label: Section G — Comprehension
G.passage:
Eight-year-old Nora planned a surprise birthday party for her father for two weeks. She made a list of things to do and checked off each item carefully. She baked a chocolate cake with help from her grandmother. She drew a large banner that said 'Happy Birthday, Dad!' and hung it across the living room doorway.

On the morning of the party, Nora and her mother went to the market to buy fresh flowers and fruit. Nora chose yellow sunflowers because they were her father's favourite. When they came home, her brother was blowing up balloons in the kitchen.

That evening, their neighbours and relatives arrived quietly. Everyone hid behind the sofa and the curtains. When Dad walked in from work and turned on the lights, everyone jumped out and shouted, 'Surprise!'

Dad stood still for a moment, his mouth open in shock. Then his eyes grew watery, and he hugged Nora tightly. 'I had no idea,' he whispered. 'This is the best gift I have ever received.'

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 2 has the same meaning as 'moved from place to place to arrange things neatly'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Rushed' = moved fast; 'collected' = gathered; 'placed' = put down. TIDIED = arranged and cleaned up neatly.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: TIDIED = arranged things neatly and put everything in the right place. Nora TIDIED her room = she organised it until it was clean and orderly. TIDY = neat and organised; TIDIED = past tense.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 3, what does 'it' refer to in 'Nora could not wait to show it to Grandma'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 2 or 3. 'Could not wait to SHOW IT' = something she made that would be a wonderful reveal = the cake.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: PRONOUN REFERENCE: 'could not wait to show IT to Grandma.' IT = the BIRTHDAY CAKE that Nora baked. She wanted to surprise Grandma — the cake was the surprise she was excited to reveal.

mcq_questions.stem: What does 'home is made with hands, not walls' most likely mean?

options.1: Houses should be built with better materials.
options.2: The care and effort people put into a home is what makes it truly special, not just the building.
options.3: Children should help with construction work.
options.4: Walls are not important in a house.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 or 4 taking it literally. This is a philosophical statement about the meaning of home.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: INFERENCE: 'HOME IS MADE WITH HANDS, NOT WALLS' = a METAPHOR. HANDS = the effort and love of the people who live there. WALLS = just the physical building. A home needs love and care — not just bricks — to feel like a real home. Option 2 = the deeper meaning.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 1, is it True or False that Nora planned the party with help from her parents? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The passage says Nora planned the surprise party entirely by herself — her parents did not know about it.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1: Nora planned the party BY HERSELF. Her parents did not know. She organised it alone. Answer is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: Where did the guests hide before Dad came home?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: They hid behind the sofa and the curtains.

open_ended_questions.stem: How do we know the surprise party was a great success? Give TWO examples from the passage.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) Dad stood still with his mouth open in shock (showing he was completely surprised). (ii) He said it was 'the best gift I have ever received' (showing he loved the party very much).

open_ended_questions.stem: Find ONE word in paragraph 1 that tells us Nora was organised and took her planning seriously.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: 'carefully' — she checked off each item on her list carefully.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on her actions throughout the passage, describe TWO character traits of Nora with evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) THOUGHTFUL: Nora planned a secret birthday party for Grandma entirely on her own — baking a cake and cleaning the house — showing she went out of her way to make someone else happy. (ii) HARDWORKING: she spent the whole morning cleaning every room and baking, without being asked, showing she put in real effort for the people she loves.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'kind and helpful' without precise traits or evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: TRAIT INFERENCE: THOUGHTFUL = planned the ENTIRE surprise alone, baked a cake. HARDWORKING = spent WHOLE MORNING cleaning without being asked. Name trait + give evidence = full marks.

questions.stem: On Saturday morning, the playground was as ________ as a busy market — children laughing, parents chatting and music from the nearby hawker centre.
questions.trap_type: 'Quiet','empty','dark' = opposite of a noisy, busy place. LIVELY = full of energy, noise and movement.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! The playground was AS LIVELY AS a busy market = comparing the energy to the bustle of a market. LIVELY = full of movement and excitement. AS + ADJECTIVE + AS is the correct simile form.
questions.retry_hint: The dash lists the evidence: children LAUGHING, parents chatting and MUSIC playing - and it is all compared to a busy MARKET. Ask: does that describe a place with nobody and no sound, or the exact opposite? Match the word to the noise.

questions.stem: The old man walked ________ across the road because his legs were weak.
questions.trap_type: Cause-effect — weak legs = slow movement. Students may pick 'carefully' (not in options) or 'angrily'.
questions.learning_tip: Weak legs → cannot walk fast → walked SLOWLY. Match the reason (weak legs) to the correct manner word.
questions.retry_hint: The reason comes after 'because': his LEGS were WEAK. Ask: if walking is hard for you, do you dash across the road or take your time? The blank is about speed, and two of the choices describe moods instead.

questions.stem: The shopkeeper ________ Tom's money after she found out she gave him the wrong change.
questions.trap_type: Action after error — the shopkeeper gave WRONG change, so she needs to RETURN the correct amount. 'Kept' would be dishonest.
questions.learning_tip: 'Returned' = gave something back to its owner. Wrong change was given → RETURNED the correct amount. 'Kept' = kept it for herself, which is wrong.
questions.retry_hint: She discovers she gave Tom the WRONG CHANGE, so the money is not really hers. Ask: what does an honest SHOPKEEPER do with money that belongs to someone else - keep it, spend it, or give it back?

questions.stem: The library was so ________ that we could hear a pin drop.
questions.trap_type: Idiom interpretation — 'hear a pin drop' = extremely quiet. Students may think a noisy library is being described.
questions.learning_tip: 'You could hear a pin drop' is an idiom meaning the place is EXTREMELY QUIET. Pins make no sound → only in total silence would you hear one.
