questions.retry_hint: 'We could HEAR a PIN DROP' is the clue - a pin makes almost no sound, so the room must be perfectly still. Ask: which word is the opposite of noisy? The others describe light, or how many people are inside.

questions.stem: The elderly lady was struggling with her heavy groceries, so Ali decided to ________ and help her carry them home.
questions.trap_type: 'Run away' = flee; 'give up' = stop; 'break in' = enter by force. STEP IN = become involved in a situation to help.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: STEP IN = get involved in a situation to help or take action. Ali decided to STEP IN and help = he got involved when he saw someone struggling. STEP + IN work together as one meaning.
questions.retry_hint: The lady is STRUGGLING with HEAVY groceries and Ali chooses to HELP her carry them. Ask: which phrase means to move forward and take action for someone? The others mean escaping, quitting, or entering by force.

questions.stem: Nobody in our neighbourhood ________ why the old well behind the community centre has been sealed up for so many years.
questions.trap_type: NOBODY = singular → verb+S.
questions.learning_tip: NOBODY / EVERYONE / SOMEONE = Singular! Nobody KNOWS = add -S. 'Nobody know' is WRONG.
questions.retry_hint: Do not be fooled by 'in our NEIGHBOURHOOD' - the true subject is NOBODY, and that counts as ONE person. Ask: in the present tense, does a singular subject take the plain verb or the verb with -s? This is a fact, not an action happening right now.

questions.stem: The town council has ________ a new community garden in the open space between the two housing blocks.
questions.trap_type: HAS + past participle = present perfect. BUILD → BUILT (irregular).
questions.learning_tip: HAS + past participle = present perfect. The council HAS BUILT a new garden = completed recently and now open. BUILD → BUILT (irregular past participle).
questions.retry_hint: 'HAS' is already there, so the blank must be the form that partners with has. Ask: after has, do we use the plain verb, the -s form, the -ing form, or the past participle? Only one of them can finish a present perfect.

questions.stem: While the cleaner ________ the corridor, a boy ran past and knocked over the mop bucket.
questions.trap_type: While + past continuous — the cleaning was ongoing when the boy ran past (interrupting event).
questions.learning_tip: WHILE = two things at same time. The cleaner WAS MOPPING (ongoing) when the boy ran past (interrupted). Past continuous = WAS -ing.
questions.retry_hint: WHILE tells you the cleaner's action was already in progress when the boy RAN past and interrupted it. Ask: which choice shows an action in the middle of happening in the PAST? A plain past verb, or a present form, cannot show that.

questions.stem: The new community centre is far ________ than the old one — it has a pool, a gym and a rooftop garden.
questions.trap_type: 'Most modern' = superlative; 'moderner' is WRONG. MORE MODERN = comparative.
questions.learning_tip: Long adjective → MORE + adjective = comparative. MORE MODERN THAN the old one = comparing two buildings. 'Moderner' is ALWAYS WRONG. For longer adjectives, use MORE.
questions.retry_hint: THAN is the signal: the new centre is measured against the OLD one, and 'modern' is a long adjective. Ask: do long adjectives take -er, or a comparing word in front? And is 'most' correct when only two things are compared?

questions.stem: The supermarket is ________ the MRT station.
questions.trap_type: Preposition of location — 'beside' = next to. 'Behind of' is wrong (no 'of' after behind). 'Inside' = within a building.
questions.learning_tip: BESIDE = next to (same level). BEHIND = at the back of. Note: 'behind' has NO 'of' after it. 'Behind of' is ALWAYS wrong.
questions.retry_hint: The supermarket and the MRT STATION are two separate buildings standing next to each other. Ask: which preposition means 'at the side of'? Of the rest, one puts you inside a building, one is about time, and one is not proper English.

questions.stem: Being a good neighbour is one of the most important responsibilities of living in a community, ________ it?
questions.trap_type: Positive present 'to be' ('is') → negative question tag.
questions.learning_tip: Positive present 'to be' → negative tag. Being a good neighbour IS important, ISN'T it? POSITIVE → NEGATIVE. IS → ISN'T.
questions.retry_hint: A tag question mirrors the main verb: this sentence uses IS ('Being a good neighbour IS one of...'). Ask: if the statement is positive, must the tag be positive or negative? And should the tag repeat the same verb, or switch to a form of 'do'?

questions.stem: Father drove ________ to the hospital because Tom had hurt his knee.
questions.trap_type: Adverb after action verb — 'drove slowly'. 'Slow' is an adjective. 'Most slow / more slowly' = comparative/superlative, not needed here.
questions.learning_tip: After action verb DROVE, use ADVERB: drove SLOWLY. 'Slow' is an adjective (a slow car). Adverbs describe HOW something is done.
questions.retry_hint: The blank describes HOW Father DROVE - it tells you about the verb, not about a noun. Ask: which form of the word is used to describe an action? And is anything being compared here, which would call for a comparing form?

questions.stem: ________ of the rubbish bags was left at the wrong bin.
questions.trap_type: 'One of the bags WAS left' — singular verb 'was' follows. Only 'one' is singular. 'All/some/any' are plural or require specific contexts.
questions.learning_tip: 'One of [plural noun] + singular verb': ONE of the bags WAS left. 'One' = a single item → singular verb (was).
questions.retry_hint: Look at the verb: 'WAS LEFT' is singular, even though BAGS is plural. Ask: which choice makes the subject a single item rather than several? Three of the choices would force you to change 'was' to 'were'.

C.label: Section C — Grammar Cloze
C.instructions: Read the passage below. Choose the most suitable word from the box and write its letter in each blank. Use each word ONCE only.
C.passage: My neighbourhood has many useful places. There is a small market (1)___ our block, just two minutes away on foot. It opens every morning (2)___ six o'clock. (3)___ the market and the post office, there is a small park where children play after school. My grandmother likes to sit (4)___ a bench (5)___ the park and watch the children. On Sundays, there is a food fair (6)___ the community centre, in the car park at the back. People come (7)___ all over the neighbourhood to buy food and crafts. My father once walked right (8)___ a lamp post because he was looking at his phone!

questions.trap_type: Students reach for 'at' (A), but AT is needed for the exact clock time in blank 2 and each word is used only once.
questions.answer_corrected: A(at) — 'at the end of our street'
questions.learning_tip: NEAR = a short distance away. 'Just two minutes away on foot' = NEAR our block. = G.
questions.retry_hint: The clue follows the blank: just TWO MINUTES away on FOOT. The market is close by - not inside your block, not at its back. Ask: which preposition simply means 'a short distance away from'?

questions.trap_type: Students write 'on six o'clock' or 'in six o'clock'.
questions.answer_corrected: Redesigned: blank 1 = E(in) 'in our street / in the area', blank 2 = A(at) 'at six o'clock'. Both can coexist.
questions.learning_tip: AT + an exact time: AT six o'clock, AT noon, AT midnight. = A.
questions.retry_hint: 'SIX O'CLOCK' is an exact point in time, not a stretch of time. Ask: which preposition goes in front of clock times? Try each word aloud in the blank - only one sounds right before a time like six.

questions.trap_type: 'Between the market and the post office' — C = between. Students pick E (in) or G (near).
questions.learning_tip: 'BETWEEN A and B' = in the space separating two things. The park is BETWEEN two buildings = C.
questions.retry_hint: The park has the MARKET on one side and the POST OFFICE on the other - exactly two places, with the park in the middle. Ask: which preposition describes being in the space that separates TWO things?

questions.trap_type: 'Sit ON a bench' — H = on. Students may pick E (in) thinking of sitting inside something.
questions.learning_tip: 'ON a bench/chair/seat' = sitting on the surface. ON is used for surfaces you sit or place things on.
questions.retry_hint: Grandmother rests her body upon the surface of the BENCH. Ask: which preposition shows resting upon a surface, rather than being inside a space or beside it? Think how you would finish: she sat ___ the chair.

questions.trap_type: 'In the park' — E = in. Students pick G (near). In = inside the park area.
questions.learning_tip: 'IN the park' = inside the park. NEAR = close to but possibly outside. She is sitting IN (inside) the park.
questions.retry_hint: The BENCH stands within the PARK - the park is an area that surrounds it. Ask: which preposition shows being inside an area? Not a surface, not a direction of movement, not merely close by.

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'near' (G, already used) or 'at'. The clue is the car park AT THE BACK of the building.
questions.answer_corrected: Redesign for uniqueness. Passage reworked so each blank uses a different letter.
questions.learning_tip: BEHIND = at the back of something. The fair is in the back car park = BEHIND the centre. = B.
questions.retry_hint: The extra detail is the giveaway: the fair is in the car park AT THE BACK of the building. Ask: which preposition means 'at the back of' something? Not in front, not inside, not simply close to.

questions.trap_type: 'Come FROM all over' — D = from. Students pick E (in) or G (near).
questions.learning_tip: 'FROM' shows origin/starting point: came FROM all over the neighbourhood. People travelled from different places.
questions.retry_hint: 'People come ___ ALL OVER the neighbourhood' - they start somewhere else and travel here. Ask: which preposition shows the origin, the starting point of a journey, rather than where someone ends up?

questions.trap_type: 'Walked INTO a lamp post' — F = into (collision direction). Students pick E (in) or B (behind).
questions.learning_tip: 'Walk INTO something' = collide with it accidentally. He walked INTO a lamp post = crashed into it. INTO shows direction of impact.
questions.retry_hint: Father was staring at his PHONE and walked right ___ a LAMP POST - he collided with it. Ask: which preposition shows movement that ends in a crash against something? This is not a resting position; he was moving.

C.passage_revised: My neighbourhood has many useful places. There is a small market (1)___ our street. It opens every morning (2)___ six o'clock. (3)___ the market and the post office, there is a small park where children play after school. My grandmother likes to sit (4)___ a bench and enjoy the fresh air (5)___ the park. On Sundays, there is a food fair (6)___ the open field nearby. People come (7)___ all parts of the neighbourhood to buy food and crafts. My father once walked right (8)___ a lamp post because he was looking at his phone!

answers_revised.6: B(behind? No) — H is used. Use D? 'a food fair FROM the field?' No. Use 'on' a different way. Simplify: blank 6 = H(on) BUT H used in blank 4. Swap blank 4 to use different option.
answers_revised.resolution: Reassign: blank 4 = 'sit on a bench' → need 'on'. blank 6 = 'food fair in the open field' → E(in). But E used in blank 5. Final resolution: redesign word box to avoid conflicts by using enough distinct prepositions for 8 unique slots.

D.label: Section D — Vocabulary Cloze
D.instructions: Read the passage carefully. Choose the most suitable word from the box and write its letter in each blank. Use each word ONCE only.
D.passage: The bus stop near our block is always (1)___ in the morning, with people going to work and school. Last Tuesday, a long queue of neighbours stood there, (2)___ for the bus. An old man reached for his wallet and accidentally (3)___ his bag, and oranges rolled all over the pavement. A girl on a bicycle (4)___ got off to help before anyone else moved. She picked up every orange and (5)___ him put the fruit back into his bag.

questions.trap_type: Context — many people at a bus stop = crowded = busy. Students pick 'loud' (E) thinking of noise.
questions.learning_tip: BUSY = full of activity or people. A bus stop with many people waiting = BUSY = A.
questions.retry_hint: The clue is 'people going to WORK and SCHOOL' in the morning rush. Ask: does that describe an empty stop or a full one? Careful: a crowd can be noisy, but the blank is about how much is happening, not about sound.

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'busy' (A). The blank follows a comma after 'stood there' and needs an -ing verb.
questions.learning_tip: WAITING = the -ing form after 'stood there, ___ for the bus'. People WAIT for a bus. = H.
questions.retry_hint: The neighbours STOOD there in a long QUEUE, doing nothing yet. Ask: which form can follow after that comma - a past verb, or an -ing verb? And what do people at a bus stop actually do until the bus arrives?

questions.trap_type: 'Dropped his bag' — B = dropped (let it fall by accident). Students pick 'lost' (not in box).
questions.learning_tip: DROPPED = let something fall accidentally. The old man accidentally DROPPED his bag = B.
questions.retry_hint: The ORANGES ROLLED all over the PAVEMENT, so the bag must have fallen as he reached for his wallet. Ask: did he do it on purpose? The word 'accidentally' before the blank tells you, and the blank needs a past verb.

questions.trap_type: 'Quickly got off her bicycle' — acting fast to help. Students pick 'kindly' (not in box) or 'slowly'.
questions.learning_tip: She saw someone in trouble → moved fast to help → got off QUICKLY = F.
questions.retry_hint: The blank tells you HOW the girl GOT OFF her bicycle - so it must be an adverb. Ask: which box word ends in -ly? She acted 'before anyone else moved', so she did not take her time.

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'smiled' (G). Smiling is an expression, not the action of putting fruit back.
questions.learning_tip: HELPED = did something to make another person's task easier. She HELPED him put the fruit back. = C.
questions.retry_hint: She PICKED UP every orange and then did something more for the old man: she made his task easier. Ask: which past verb in the box names that action? Smiling is only a face; it does not put fruit back into a BAG.

E.label: Section E — Editing
E.instructions: The passage below has five mistakes. Each mistake is underlined. Write the correct word in the box next to each number.
E.passage: Last Sunday, our family spent the morning at the neighbourhood community day. Many residents came out to clean the park and plant flowers. We saw Ali, who lives close to the MRT station, picking up litter besides (33) the drain. The organisers said there (34) favourite activity was the colouring contest for children. Some stalls order (35) extra food because the crowd turned out to be much bigger than expected. Every helper receive (36) a free drink and a packet of biscuits. One helper said the event shows that our neighbourhoods (37) spirit is stronger than ever.

errors.error_type: Confused words - besides (= in addition) vs beside (= next to)
errors.trap_type: Students use 'besides' when they mean 'next to'.
errors.learning_tip: BESIDE = next to / at the side of. BESIDES = in addition, as well. Litter BESIDE the drain = next to it.
errors.retry_hint: The LITTER lies next to the DRAIN. Ask: does the underlined word mean 'next to', or does it mean 'in addition, as well'? One of the two spellings has an extra -s, and that -s changes the meaning completely.

errors.error_type: Homophone confusion - there (place) vs their (belonging to them)
errors.trap_type: 'there' (place) written where 'their' (ownership) is needed.
errors.learning_tip: THEIR = belonging to them. THERE = at that place. THEY'RE = they are. 'THEIR favourite activity' = the activity that belongs to them.
errors.retry_hint: The favourite activity belongs to the ORGANISERS. Ask: does the underlined spelling mean 'at that place', or 'belonging to them'? They sound the same, so decide by meaning: whose activity is it?

errors.error_type: Tense - past narrative needs the past form
errors.trap_type: Students leave the verb in the present because the sentence looks like a fact.
errors.learning_tip: The whole passage is about LAST SUNDAY = past. order -> ORDERED (add -ed). Keep every verb in the same tense as the story.
errors.retry_hint: Everything in this passage happened LAST SUNDAY - the stalls acted before you arrived. Ask: is the underlined verb in the past or the present? Match it to the tense of the rest of the story.

errors.trap_type: 'Every' feels like many people, so students drop the -s.
errors.learning_tip: EVERY + noun = SINGULAR. Every helper RECEIVES, every child GOES. Singular subject in the present -> verb + -s.
errors.retry_hint: The subject is EVERY HELPER. 'Every' feels like many people, but it points at them one at a time. Ask: does a singular subject in the present take the plain verb, or the verb with -s?

errors.trap_type: Students add a plain -s instead of an apostrophe + s.
errors.learning_tip: The spirit BELONGS TO the neighbourhood -> NEIGHBOURHOOD'S spirit. A plain -s only makes a plural (two neighbourhoods).
errors.retry_hint: The spirit BELONGS TO the neighbourhood - one neighbourhood, not several. Ask: does a plain -s show ownership, or does it just make a plural? What small mark shows that something belongs to someone?

questions.sentence1: The community officer asked the residents a question.
questions.sentence2: Are you happy with the new recycling bins?
questions.instruction: Combine into one sentence using reported speech. Begin: 'The community officer asked...'
questions.model_answer: The community officer asked the residents if they were happy with the new recycling bins.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'asked if are they happy' (wrong order) or keep 'you'.
questions.learning_tip: YES/NO question → reported speech: ASKED + IF + subject + verb (normal order). 'Are YOU happy?' → asked IF THEY WERE happy. Pronoun: you → they. Tense: are → were. Word order is normal after 'if'.
questions.retry_hint: A yes/no question becomes REPORTED speech. Ask three things: which small joining word follows ASKED? Does the question keep its question word order, or turn into normal statement order? And what happens to 'you' and to 'are'?

questions.sentence1: Ali waited for the bus for thirty minutes.
questions.sentence2: Then he decided to walk home.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as ONE sentence using 'when'.
questions.model_answer: When Ali had waited for thirty minutes, he decided to walk home.
questions.model_answer_simple: When the bus did not come after thirty minutes, Ali decided to walk home.
questions.trap_type: Students may write 'When Ali waited for thirty minutes, he decided...' (present tense intrusion) or restructure incorrectly.
questions.learning_tip: WHEN + [past event], [result in past]. Keep all verbs in PAST TENSE. 'When [situation], [what happened next]'.
questions.retry_hint: Put WHEN in front of the action that came FIRST - the thirty minutes of standing at the bus stop - and let the second sentence become the main part. Ask: which tense shows an action already finished before another past action?

G.label: Section G — Comprehension
G.passage:
On a stormy Wednesday, heavy rain flooded the market near Greenwood Estate. Water rose quickly to ankle level, and some stalls had to close. Mrs Chen, who ran a fruit stall, was packing up her unsold mangoes in a hurry.

Suddenly, she heard a splash behind her. She turned around and saw an elderly man called Mr Siva sitting on the wet ground. He had slipped on the flooded floor. His groceries were scattered everywhere.

Mrs Chen called for help loudly. Three young men who were nearby rushed over. Two of them helped Mr Siva to his feet while the third picked up his groceries. They found a dry spot under a stall roof and sat Mr Siva down there.

Mr Siva rubbed his knee and said he was all right. One of the young men offered to take him home in a taxi. At first, Mr Siva said it was not necessary. But they insisted, and he finally agreed.

The next day, Mr Siva returned to the market. He went to the fruit stall and left a bag of oranges for Mrs Chen with a note that said: 'Thank you for shouting for help. You saved me from sitting in the rain alone.'

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 2 has the same meaning as 'moving steadily and slowly'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Rushing' = moving fast; 'drifting' = floating; 'jumping' = leaping. WADING = walking slowly through water or a difficult surface.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: WADING = walking slowly through water, mud or a difficult surface. The elderly man was WADING through the flooded market = he was slowly stepping through the floodwater. WADE = move slowly through.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 3, what does 'it' refer to in 'Ali could not pretend he did not see it'?

options.1: The market stall that was flooded
options.2: The elderly man struggling alone through the floodwater with heavy bags
options.3: The puddle in front of the gate

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking 'it' = the stall. But 'could not pretend he did not see IT' = something Ali felt compelled to respond to.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: PRONOUN REFERENCE: 'could not pretend he did not see IT.' IT = the ELDERLY MAN'S STRUGGLE — he was alone in the water with heavy bags. The passage says Ali stopped when he noticed this sight. IT = the man struggling.

mcq_questions.stem: Why does the writer end the passage with 'sometimes a neighbourhood is just one person'?

options.1: Because not many people live in the neighbourhood.
options.2: Because a single act of kindness by one person can define the spirit and warmth of a whole community.
options.3: Because Ali was the only person at the market that day.
options.4: Because Ali was the most important person in the neighbourhood.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 3 or 4 taking it literally. This is a reflective statement about community spirit.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: INFERENCE: 'sometimes a neighbourhood is just ONE PERSON' = a METAPHOR. ONE PERSON doing something kind can represent the whole community's spirit. Ali's act showed the neighbourhood's warmth — he embodied it single-handedly. Option 2 = the deeper meaning.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 1, is it True or False that the market was flooded on purpose? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The passage says a sudden heavy storm caused the flooding — it was not planned.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1: a SUDDEN HEAVY STORM caused the flooding. 'Sudden' = not planned. Answer is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: What did the three young men do to help Mr Siva? Give TWO actions.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: Two of them helped Mr Siva to his feet (stood him up) and the third picked up his groceries / they took him to a dry spot.

open_ended_questions.stem: At first, Mr Siva did not want the young men to take him home. Why did he change his mind?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: He changed his mind because the young men insisted / kept pressing him to accept their offer.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on his note, what does Mr Siva think would have happened without Mrs Chen's help?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: He thinks he would have sat in the rain alone (nobody would have come to help him).

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on his actions in the passage, describe TWO character traits of Ali with evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) OBSERVANT: Ali noticed the elderly man struggling in the floodwater even though many others walked past — showing he was paying attention to those around him. (ii) SELFLESS: he stopped and helped carry the man's heavy bags all the way home without being asked, showing he put the man's needs before his own plans.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'kind and helpful' without precise traits or evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: TRAIT INFERENCE: OBSERVANT = noticed the man when OTHERS WALKED PAST. SELFLESS = helped carry bags ALL THE WAY HOME without being asked. Name trait + give evidence = full marks.

questions.stem: The hawker centre on a Saturday morning was as ________ as an ant colony — every stall busy, every seat filled and the air thick with delicious smells.
questions.trap_type: 'Quiet','empty','cold' = opposite of a busy, lively place. BUZZING = full of excited activity and energy.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! The hawker centre was AS BUZZING AS an ant colony = comparing the non-stop activity to worker ants. BUZZING = full of energy and movement. AS + ADJECTIVE + AS is the correct simile form.
questions.retry_hint: The dash explains it: every STALL busy, every SEAT filled, and the place is compared to an ANT COLONY. Ask: does an ant colony sit still and silent, or hum with movement and sound? Match the word to that hum.

questions.stem: The hawker uncle ________ the rice onto the plate in one smooth movement.
questions.trap_type: Action precision — rice is scooped, not poured (that is for liquids) or thrown.
questions.learning_tip: 'Scooped' = took a portion using a spoon or ladle with a curving motion. Rice is SCOOPED onto a plate. Liquids are POURED.
questions.retry_hint: The clue is 'in ONE SMOOTH MOVEMENT' onto the PLATE. Ask: how do you move rice with a spoon or ladle - by pouring liquid, by throwing, by cutting, or by lifting it up in one curved motion?

questions.stem: The hawker uncle always made sure to ________ the extra chilli and sauce before he served the noodles to regular customers.
questions.trap_type: 'Run away from','give up on','break into' = negative actions. ADD ON = include something extra as an addition.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: ADD ON = include something extra on top of what is already there. The uncle ADDED ON extra chilli = he put additional chilli on the dish. ADD + ON work together as one meaning.
questions.retry_hint: He gives regular CUSTOMERS EXTRA CHILLI and SAUCE, so he is putting more in, not taking anything away. Ask: which phrase means to include something extra? The others mean escaping, quitting, or forcing your way in.

questions.stem: When Sam tasted Mr Lim's famous fishball noodles for the first time, he was ________ — it was the most delicious thing he had ever eaten.
questions.trap_type: 'Under the weather' = ill; 'in hot water' = trouble; 'at a loss' = confused. OVER THE MOON = extremely happy.
questions.learning_tip: IDIOM: OVER THE MOON = feeling extremely happy and delighted. Sam was OVER THE MOON = overjoyed by the taste. Idioms cannot be understood word by word!
questions.retry_hint: It was the MOST DELICIOUS thing Sam had ever EATEN - so how must he feel? Ask: does this idiom describe great delight, or illness, or trouble, or confusion? An idiom cannot be read word by word.

questions.stem: The cook ________ the vegetables into the wok and a big burst of steam rose up.
questions.trap_type: 'Tossed into the wok' = threw quickly with a flipping motion. 'Placed' = set down gently (no steam burst).
questions.learning_tip: 'Toss' = throw something quickly into a pan or wok with a flipping motion. Cooking uses TOSS for putting ingredients into a hot pan. The steam burst shows speed and heat.
questions.retry_hint: A burst of STEAM rose the instant the vegetables hit the hot WOK - they went in fast, not gently. Ask: which verb means to throw something quickly into a pan? 'Placed' is slow and careful, and 'carried' puts nothing in.

questions.stem: Nobody in the class ________ how Mr Lim manages to keep the same recipe so perfect every single day without ever measuring anything.
questions.trap_type: NOBODY = singular → verb+S.
questions.learning_tip: NOBODY / EVERYONE / SOMEONE = Singular! Nobody UNDERSTANDS = add -S. 'Nobody understand' is WRONG.
questions.retry_hint: The subject is NOBODY, not 'the CLASS'. Words like nobody and everybody behave like ONE person. Ask: in the present tense, does a singular subject take the plain verb or the verb with -s? This is a fact, not an action in progress.

questions.stem: There ________ only a little bit of curry left in the pot.
questions.trap_type: 'A little bit of curry' = uncountable, singular amount → 'is'. Students pick 'are' confusing curry with plural.
questions.learning_tip: 'A little bit' = a small amount of uncountable thing. Uncountable + singular → IS. 'There IS a little bit of curry'.
questions.retry_hint: 'Only a LITTLE BIT of CURRY' - how many things are you counting? Ask: does the amount left in the POT count as one single thing, or as many things? Match the verb to that amount, and remember the curry has not been eaten yet, so do not reach for a past form.

questions.stem: We ________ our food when the waiter suddenly dropped a tray of dishes.
questions.trap_type: Past continuous for ongoing background action — we were already eating when the waiter dropped the tray (interruption).
questions.learning_tip: We WERE EATING (ongoing past) when the waiter dropped the tray (sudden interruption). The eating was already happening → past continuous.
questions.retry_hint: The waiter SUDDENLY DROPPED the tray right in the middle of your meal. Ask: which choice shows an action already going on in the past when something else cut across it? A plain past verb only shows a finished action.

questions.stem: Mr Lim's fishball noodles are far ________ than anything Sam had ever tasted from a restaurant.
questions.trap_type: 'Most delicious' = superlative; 'deliciouser' is WRONG. MORE DELICIOUS = comparative.
questions.learning_tip: Long adjective → MORE + adjective = comparative. MORE DELICIOUS THAN restaurant noodles = comparing two things. 'Deliciouser' is ALWAYS WRONG. For long adjectives, use MORE.
questions.retry_hint: THAN tells you two things are being compared, and 'delicious' is a long adjective. Ask: do long adjectives take -er, or do they need a helper word in front? The -est form is for three or several, and 'deliciouser' is not English.

questions.stem: "________ you tried the new roti prata stall yet?" asked Min.
questions.trap_type: 'Have you tried' = present perfect (experience up to now). Students use 'Did you try' (simple past, also possible but less natural with 'yet').
questions.learning_tip: 'Have you [done something] YET?' = asking about experience up to now → present perfect: HAVE you tried. 'Yet' is a signal for present perfect question.
questions.retry_hint: The word YET at the end, together with TRIED (a past participle), tells you the question is about any time up to now. Ask: which helping verb goes with a past participle to make the present perfect? 'Did' would need the plain verb 'try'.

questions.stem: The hawker centre is one of the most important parts of Singapore's food culture, ________ it?
questions.trap_type: Positive present 'to be' ('is') → negative question tag.
questions.learning_tip: Positive present 'to be' → negative tag. The hawker centre IS important, ISN'T it? POSITIVE → NEGATIVE. IS → ISN'T.
questions.retry_hint: A tag mirrors the statement's verb: the sentence uses IS ('The hawker centre IS one of...'). Ask: after a positive statement, must the tag turn negative or stay positive? And should the tag keep the same verb rather than borrow 'do'?

questions.stem: The auntie at the drinks stall gave Sam ________ glass of barley water free.
questions.trap_type: 'A glass' — 'glass' starts with a consonant sound → 'a'. Students may pick 'an' over-applying vowel rules.
questions.learning_tip: 'A' + consonant sound: a glass, a bowl, a plate. 'AN' + vowel sound: an orange, an egg. 'Glass' starts with G (consonant) → A glass.
questions.retry_hint: GLASS begins with the consonant sound /g/, and the auntie is not pointing to one particular glass the reader already knows. Ask: which article goes before consonant sounds, and which goes before vowel sounds?

questions.stem: ________ the food was spicy, the children ate it happily.
questions.trap_type: 'Although' = concession — the food was spicy BUT they still ate it happily. This is a contrast.
questions.learning_tip: ALTHOUGH = even though (surprising contrast). Spicy food + children happily eating = a contrast (usually spicy food makes children not want to eat). ALTHOUGH introduces the surprise.
questions.retry_hint: The two halves of the sentence pull against each other: the food was SPICY, yet the children ate it HAPPILY. Ask: which joining word signals a contrast or surprise? 'Because' gives a reason, and 'so' gives a result.

C.label: Section C — Grammar Cloze
C.instructions: Read the passage below. Choose the most suitable word from the box and write its letter in each blank. Use each word ONCE only.
C.passage: My family loves going to the hawker centre near (1)___ house. Last Saturday, my father took the whole family there for lunch. We sat at a round table and looked at all the stalls. My sister pointed at the chicken rice stall and said, '(2)___ food always smells so good!' Father went to order and came back with five plates of chicken rice. He placed (3)___ carefully on the table. The chicken rice uncle saw (4)___ sitting together as a family and smiled. He walked over with a small bowl of soup. '(5)___ is a gift from me,' he said kindly. My mother thanked (6)___ warmly and said the soup had a rich flavour all of (7)___ own. Before we left, my sister gave (8)___ mother a big hug for bringing us.

questions.trap_type: 'Near our house' — E = our (possessive, first person plural). Students may pick F (their).
questions.learning_tip: MY FAMILY = we/our. 'Near OUR house' = belonging to us. OUR = E (first person plural possessive).
questions.retry_hint: The writer says MY FAMILY loves going there - the house belongs to the writer together with the family. Ask: which possessive word means 'belonging to me and the people I live with'? Not one person alone, and not somebody else's.

questions.trap_type: 'Brought us there' — H = us (object pronoun). Students pick G (them).
questions.learning_tip: Father brought US (the family, including the speaker) there. US = object pronoun for WE. H = us.
questions.retry_hint: These words are inside the SISTER's speech, and she is pointing at the CHICKEN RICE STALL - the food belongs to the people who run that stall. Ask: which possessive word points to other people, not to you?

questions.trap_type: 'Their food' — F = their (possessive for the stall/the people running it). Students pick D (its).
questions.learning_tip: The chicken rice stall's food = THEIR food (belonging to the stall people). THEIR = F (third person plural possessive).
questions.retry_hint: Father comes back with FIVE PLATES and puts those plates down on the table. Ask: which pronoun stands for more than one thing that is being acted upon? The plates are objects, and there are several.

questions.trap_type: 'Placed them on the table' — G = them (object pronoun for 'five plates'). Students pick C (it).
questions.learning_tip: Five plates = plural → object pronoun = THEM = G. 'IT' (C) is for singular objects.
questions.retry_hint: The uncle SAW the whole family sitting TOGETHER - and the writer is part of that family, seen from outside. Ask: which pronoun means 'me and the people with me' when we are the ones being looked at, not the ones doing the looking?

questions.trap_type: H is already used in blank 2. Must redesign. 'He saw us sitting' → H(us). But H used. Redesign blank 2 or 5.
questions.answer_corrected: Blank 5: 'He saw (5)___ sitting together as a family' → needs US (H). But H is used in blank 2 too. Re-examine: If blank 2 uses a different word... OR redesign passage so only one blank needs 'us'. Resolution: blank 2 = 'brought (2)___ there' → could use G(them) if narrator speaks of family as 3rd person. But passage uses first person 'we'. Final fix: use 'the family' in blank 2 to free up H for blank 5.
questions.learning_tip: HE SAW US = he saw the family (object pronoun: us = H).
questions.retry_hint: He is speaking about the small BOWL of SOUP he has just brought over. Ask: which pronoun stands for a single thing that is neither male nor female? The blank starts the sentence, so you need the subject form.

questions.trap_type: 'This/It is a gift from me' — C = it (referring to the soup bowl). Students pick D (its).
questions.learning_tip: 'IT is a gift from me' = referring to the soup bowl. IT = C (pronoun for a thing). ITS = possessive (its colour, its taste).
questions.retry_hint: Mother THANKED the chicken rice UNCLE - one man, and he is the person receiving her thanks. Ask: which pronoun replaces a single male in the object position? Not the possessive, and not the subject form 'he'.

questions.trap_type: 'Thanked him' — the uncle is male. B = his? No: 'thanked him' = object pronoun = B(his)? No — 'him' is not in the box. Redesign: replace B(his) with B(him).
questions.answer_corrected: Word box redesigned: B = 'him'. 'My mother thanked HIM = B (the uncle, male, object).'
questions.learning_tip: After THANKED (verb), use object pronoun: thanked HIM (the male uncle). HIM = B.
questions.retry_hint: 'A rich FLAVOUR all of ___ OWN' - the flavour belongs to the SOUP, and soup is a thing, not a person. Ask: which possessive word belongs to a thing? Careful: the look-alike with an apostrophe is short for 'it is'.

questions.trap_type: 'It was her best' — A = her (possessive for 'my mother'). Students pick E (our) thinking of the whole family.
questions.learning_tip: MY MOTHER said the chicken rice was HER best = belonging to her (the mother's own experience). HER = A.
questions.retry_hint: The SISTER hugs the MOTHER, and that mother belongs to the sister - one girl. Ask: which possessive word shows something belonging to a single female? Match the pronoun to who the mother belongs to.

D.label: Section D — Vocabulary Cloze
D.instructions: Read the passage carefully. Choose the most suitable word from the box and write its letter in each blank. Use each word ONCE only.
D.passage: Last Saturday, my mother took me to the market to choose some fish for dinner. The (1)___ of fried garlic and grilled fish floated through the whole market. There were many people standing in a long (2)___ at the popular fish stall. We (3)___ patiently for our turn. When it was our time, Mother (4)___ two big sea bass because they looked very (5)___. The fishmonger weighed them, wrapped them neatly and handed them to us. On the way home, Mother told me that sea bass is the fish Father likes best, and that he would be very happy when he saw what we were having for dinner.

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'fresh' (D). The blank is a noun after 'The', and it is what your nose notices.
questions.learning_tip: SMELL = what you take in through your nose. The blank needs a NOUN, not an adjective. = G.
questions.retry_hint: Your NOSE notices it first: FRIED GARLIC and GRILLED FISH, floating through the whole market. Ask: which box word names something you take in through your nose? The blank follows 'The', so it must be a noun.

questions.trap_type: 'Standing in a long queue' — F = queue (line of people waiting). Students pick 'crowd' (not in box).
questions.learning_tip: A QUEUE = a line of people waiting their turn. At a popular stall, people stand in a QUEUE = F.
questions.retry_hint: Many people are STANDING in a LONG line at the POPULAR fish stall. Ask: which box word names a line of people waiting for their turn? The blank comes after 'a long', so it has to be a noun.

questions.trap_type: 'Waited patiently for our turn' — H = waited. Students pick 'stood' (not in box).
questions.learning_tip: You WAIT for your turn in a queue. WAITED = H (past tense). 'Patiently' tells us HOW they waited.
questions.retry_hint: The blank sits between 'We' and PATIENTLY, so it is a verb - and the story happened LAST SATURDAY, so it must be past. Ask: what do you do while you stand in that long line?

questions.trap_type: 'Mother chose two sea bass' — A = chose (selected). Students pick 'bought' (E = paid) confusing choosing and paying.
questions.learning_tip: CHOSE = selected/picked. She CHOSE two sea bass = picked them. Paying comes AFTER choosing. 'Chose' (past of choose) = A.
questions.retry_hint: Mother had to pick TWO BIG SEA BASS out of everything on the stall. Ask: which box word is the past form of 'choose'? Careful - 'choose' is irregular, so it does not simply take -ed.

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'favourite' (C). The fish is not chosen because it is anyone's favourite, but because of how it LOOKED.
questions.learning_tip: FRESH = newly caught, not old. 'They looked very FRESH' explains why Mother chose them. = D.
questions.retry_hint: The reason follows the blank: 'because they LOOKED very ___'. Ask: what does a good fish look like at the market - newly caught, clear-eyed and shiny? Which box word means 'not old, just caught'?

E.label: Section E — Editing
E.instructions: The passage below has five mistakes. Each mistake is underlined. Write the correct word in the box next to each number.
E.passage: Last weekend, my family visited the famous Maxwell Food Centre in Chinatown. We arrived early so that we could eat before the crowd came. Many families were already waiting outside there (33) favourite breakfast stall. The uncle and his wife works (34) at their stall seven days a week, and they recognised us at once. He knowed (35) our order by heart and started preparing the food before we even spoke. He show (36) us how he makes the stock by simmering bones for over six hours. At the end, we read the stall owners (37) story on the sign and felt even prouder to be regular customers.

errors.error_type: Homophone - there (place) vs their (belonging to them)
errors.trap_type: 'there' sounds the same as 'their', so students write the place word.
errors.learning_tip: THEIR = belonging to them. THERE = at that place. The stall belongs to those families = THEIR stall.
errors.retry_hint: The breakfast stall belongs to those FAMILIES. Ask: does the underlined spelling mean 'at that place', or 'belonging to them'? The two sound alike, so choose by meaning, not by sound.

errors.error_type: Subject-verb agreement - compound subject is plural
errors.trap_type: Students match the verb to 'his wife' (the nearest noun) instead of the whole subject.
errors.learning_tip: 'The uncle AND his wife' = two people = PLURAL -> WORK (no -s). Find the FULL subject before choosing the verb.
errors.retry_hint: Read the whole subject: the UNCLE AND HIS WIFE - that is two people. Ask: does a plural subject take the verb with -s, or without it? Do not match the verb to the nearest noun alone.

errors.trap_type: Students add -ed to an irregular verb.
errors.learning_tip: KNOW -> KNEW. Irregular verbs change their whole form; they never take -ed. 'Knowed' does not exist.
errors.retry_hint: KNOW is an irregular verb, so it cannot take -ed. Ask: how would you say it in the past - 'yesterday he ___ the answer'? Irregular verbs change their shape instead of adding an ending.

errors.error_type: Tense - past narrative needs the past form
errors.trap_type: The verb is left in the present although the whole passage is about last weekend.
errors.learning_tip: The story happened LAST WEEKEND = past. show -> SHOWED. Keep every verb in the story's tense.
errors.retry_hint: The visit happened LAST WEEKEND, and the verbs around it (started, simmered) are past. Ask: is the underlined verb past or present? Every verb in a story must share the same tense.

errors.trap_type: Students write a plain plural and forget the apostrophe that shows ownership.
errors.learning_tip: The story BELONGS TO the owners -> OWNERS' story (apostrophe AFTER the -s for a plural). Singular: owner's. Plural: owners'.
errors.retry_hint: The STORY belongs to the stall OWNERS. Ask: does a plain -s show ownership, or only make a plural? Where does the apostrophe go when the owners are more than one person?

questions.sentence1: Sam's mother asked the hawker a question.
questions.sentence2: Do you make the fishballs by hand every morning?
questions.instruction: Combine into one sentence using reported speech. Begin: 'Sam's mother asked...'
questions.model_answer: Sam's mother asked the hawker if he made the fishballs by hand every morning.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'asked if does he make' (wrong order) or keep 'you'.
questions.learning_tip: YES/NO question → reported speech: ASKED + IF + subject + verb (normal order). 'Do YOU make?' → asked IF HE MADE. Pronoun: you → he. Tense: do make → made. Word order is normal after 'if'.
questions.retry_hint: A yes/no question turned into REPORTED speech. Ask three things: which small joining word follows ASKED? Does the question keep its question order, or switch to normal statement order? And what happens to 'you' and to 'do you make'?

questions.instruction: Rewrite using 'Both'.
questions.model_answer: Both Rani and her father like chicken rice.
questions.trap_type: Students keep 'likes' (singular) after 'Both A and B'.
questions.learning_tip: 'Both A and B' = plural → plural verb: Both Rani and her father LIKE (not likes) chicken rice.
questions.retry_hint: BOTH Rani and her father means TWO people, so the subject is now plural. Ask: does a plural subject keep the -s on the verb, or drop it? And write 'chicken rice' only once - do not repeat the second sentence.

G.label: Section G — Comprehension
G.passage:
Every morning, Mr Lim arrived at his stall at five o'clock, long before the rest of the hawker centre opened. He boiled the fishball soup for at least two hours to get the right taste. Mr Lim sold fishball noodles at Tampines Food Centre for over twenty years.

One rainy Tuesday, a young boy came to the stall alone. He looked at the menu and counted his coins carefully. 'Uncle,' he said quietly, 'I only have one dollar and fifty cents. Is that enough for a small bowl?'

Mr Lim looked at the boy. He knew the price was two dollars. But the boy's wet uniform and tired eyes told him the boy had come a long way in the rain. 'Of course,' said Mr Lim with a smile. 'One dollar fifty is enough today.'

He served the boy a full bowl — not a small one. He even added extra fishballs. The boy ate every bit of it and looked up at Mr Lim with bright eyes. 'Thank you, Uncle. This is the best I have ever eaten.'

Mr Lim waved his hand. 'Come back any time,' he said. And he meant it.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 2 has the same meaning as 'cooked something slowly and gently in hot liquid'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Boiled' = high heat with large bubbles; 'fried' = cooked in oil; 'grilled' = cooked over flame. SIMMERED = cooked gently in liquid just below boiling.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: SIMMERED = cooked slowly and gently in hot liquid just below boiling point. Mr Lim SIMMERED the bones for six hours = kept them at a low, steady heat. SIMMER = gentle, slow cooking.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 3, what does 'it' refer to in 'Sam could not explain it'?

options.1: The way the stall was decorated
options.2: Why the fishball noodle soup tasted so different from anything he had eaten before
options.3: How Mr Lim made the broth
options.4: The amount of time he waited in the queue

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 3 thinking 'it' = the broth recipe. But 'could not explain IT' = a feeling about the taste, not a recipe.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: PRONOUN REFERENCE: 'Sam could not explain IT.' IT = the mysterious quality of the taste — WHY the soup tasted so different and so much better. He could taste the difference but could not put it into words.

mcq_questions.stem: Why does the writer say Mr Lim's secret ingredient was 'time'?

options.1: Because Mr Lim was very old and experienced.
options.2: Because the long hours of slow cooking and years of practice were what made the soup taste so special.
options.3: Because Mr Lim's stall was open for a very long time.
options.4: Because Mr Lim took a very long time to serve each customer.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 3 thinking TIME = how long the stall has been open. But 'secret ingredient = time' refers to the COOKING PROCESS.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: INFERENCE: The 'SECRET INGREDIENT = TIME' = a METAPHOR. Mr Lim SIMMERED the bones for SIX HOURS and spent YEARS perfecting his recipe. TIME = the patience and sustained effort that cannot be shortcut. Option 2 = the full meaning of 'time' here.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 1, is it True or False that Sam had eaten Mr Lim's fishball noodles before? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The passage says it was Sam's first visit to the stall — his mother told him about it but he had never tasted it before.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1: it was Sam's FIRST VISIT. He had heard about it from his mother but never tasted it. Answer is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: How did Mr Lim know the boy had come a long way in the rain?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: He could see that the boy's uniform was wet and the boy looked tired.

open_ended_questions.stem: Apart from accepting the lower price, what else did Mr Lim do to help the boy? Give TWO things.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) He served the boy a FULL bowl instead of a small one. (ii) He added EXTRA fishballs to the bowl.

open_ended_questions.stem: At the end of the passage, the writer says 'And he meant it.' What did Mr Lim mean?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: Mr Lim meant that the boy was truly welcome to come back any time — it was a sincere invitation, not just something polite to say.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on the passage, describe TWO character traits of Mr Lim with evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) DEDICATED: Mr Lim arrived every morning at four o'clock to prepare his stock and did so for thirty years — showing total commitment to his craft without shortcuts. (ii) HUMBLE: when Sam's mother complimented the soup, Mr Lim simply smiled and said 'same recipe, every day' — showing he did not seek praise and just focused on his work.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'hardworking and kind' without precise traits or evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: TRAIT INFERENCE: DEDICATED = arrived at FOUR O'CLOCK every morning for THIRTY YEARS. HUMBLE = just smiled and said 'same recipe, every day' — no boasting. Name trait + give evidence = full marks.

questions.stem: On the hottest day of the year, the playground was as ________ as a frying pan — even the metal slide was too hot to touch.
questions.trap_type: 'Cold','dark','wet' are opposite to the description. SCORCHING = extremely hot, like being near a flame.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! The playground was AS SCORCHING AS a frying pan = comparing the intense heat to a hot pan on a stove. SCORCHING = extremely hot. AS + ADJECTIVE + AS is always the correct simile form.
questions.retry_hint: The dash proves it: even the metal SLIDE was TOO HOT TO TOUCH, and the playground is compared to a FRYING PAN. Ask: which word describes extreme heat? The others are about cold, darkness or water.

questions.stem: After the rain stopped, a beautiful ________ with seven colours appeared across the sky.
questions.trap_type: Thunder is a sound and lightning is a flash — neither has seven colours. Only a rainbow shows seven colours after rain.
questions.learning_tip: A RAINBOW appears when sunlight passes through water droplets after rain and splits into seven colours.
questions.retry_hint: It appears AFTER THE RAIN, stretches ACROSS THE SKY and has SEVEN COLOURS. Ask: which of these do you see rather than hear? Thunder is a sound, and lightning is a flash - neither has colours.

questions.stem: When the rain finally stopped, the children rushed outside to ________ the puddles and enjoy the cool air.
questions.trap_type: 'Run away from','give up on','break down' all describe negative actions. SPLASH AROUND IN = play happily in shallow water.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: SPLASH AROUND IN = play in water by hitting it and creating spray. Children SPLASHED AROUND IN the puddles = they jumped and played in the rain water. SPLASH + AROUND + IN work together as one meaning.
questions.retry_hint: The rain has STOPPED, the air is COOL, and children are running to the PUDDLES to enjoy themselves. Ask: which phrase means to play happily in water? The other choices mean avoiding, quitting or breaking.

questions.stem: After the family survived the terrible flood with everyone safe and their home intact, they were ________ — it felt like a miracle.
questions.trap_type: 'Under the weather' = ill; 'in hot water' = trouble; 'down in the dumps' = sad. OVER THE MOON = extremely happy and relieved.
questions.learning_tip: IDIOM: OVER THE MOON = feeling extremely happy and relieved. The family was OVER THE MOON = overjoyed that everyone was safe. Idioms cannot be understood word by word!
questions.retry_hint: Everyone is SAFE, the home is INTACT, and it feels like a MIRACLE. Ask: does the idiom describe great joy and relief, or sickness, or trouble, or sadness? An idiom cannot be read word by word.

questions.stem: Mother ________ us to bring our umbrellas before we left for school that rainy morning.
questions.trap_type: 'Suggested' implies a new idea; 'reminded' means telling someone about something they should already know but might forget.
questions.learning_tip: REMINDED = told someone again about something they might have forgotten. Mother REMINDED us = made sure we did not forget our umbrellas.
questions.retry_hint: They already knew it was a RAINY MORNING - Mother was telling them not to forget the UMBRELLAS. Ask: which verb means to make someone remember something? 'Suggested' offers a new idea; 'discovered' finds something out.

questions.stem: Nobody in the village ________ a storm as powerful as the one that struck last Thursday night.
questions.trap_type: NOBODY = singular → verb+S.
questions.learning_tip: NOBODY / EVERYONE / SOMEONE = Singular! Nobody REMEMBERS = add -S. 'Nobody remember' is WRONG. Singular indefinite pronouns always take singular present-tense verbs.
questions.retry_hint: The subject is NOBODY, not 'the VILLAGE'. Words like nobody and everybody behave like ONE person. Ask: in the present tense, does a singular subject take the plain verb, or the verb with -s?

questions.stem: The Meteorological Service has ________ a weather warning for heavy rain and strong winds this weekend.
questions.trap_type: HAS + past participle = present perfect. ISSUE → ISSUED (regular).
questions.learning_tip: HAS + past participle = present perfect. The service HAS ISSUED a warning = done recently and now in effect. ISSUE → ISSUED (regular verb, add -d).
questions.retry_hint: 'HAS' is already in the sentence, so the blank must partner with has. Ask: after has, do we use the plain verb, the -s form, the -ing form, or the past participle? Only one of them completes a present perfect.

questions.stem: The children ________ in the park when the sky suddenly darkened and the first drops of rain began to fall.
questions.trap_type: 'The sky darkened' = sudden interrupting event. Children were already playing = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: The sky DARKENED = sudden past event. Children were already in the middle of playing = WERE PLAYING (past continuous). Was/were + verb-ing = action in progress when interrupted.
questions.retry_hint: The children's action was already going on when the SKY SUDDENLY DARKENED and cut across it. Ask: which choice shows an action in progress in the PAST? A plain past verb only shows a finished action.

questions.stem: After the storm, the river was far ________ than before — it had swallowed the lower path completely.
questions.trap_type: 'Widest' = superlative; 'more wider' is WRONG. WIDER = comparative of 'wide'.
questions.learning_tip: Short adjective + -ER = comparative. Wide → WIDER. The river was WIDER THAN before = comparing two states. 'More wider' is ALWAYS WRONG — never add BOTH 'more' AND '-er'.
questions.retry_hint: THAN tells you the river now is being measured against the river BEFORE - just two states compared. Ask: does a short adjective take -er, or 'most'? And can you ever put 'more' in front of a word that already ends in -er?

questions.stem: We could not go to the beach ________ the weather was too stormy that afternoon.
questions.trap_type: 'So' would reverse the order, placing the result before the reason. 'Because' correctly links the result to its reason.
questions.learning_tip: Could not go BECAUSE the weather was stormy. BECAUSE introduces the reason. The reason comes AFTER 'because'.
questions.retry_hint: The second half gives the REASON why the beach was impossible: the weather was too STORMY. Ask: which joining word introduces a reason? 'So' gives a result, and 'although' would signal a contrast instead.

questions.stem: The rainy season in Singapore usually arrives in November and December, ________ it?
questions.trap_type: Positive present simple ('arrives') → negative question tag. ARRIVES → doesn't it.
questions.learning_tip: Positive present simple → negative tag. The rainy season ARRIVES in November, DOESN'T it? POSITIVE → NEGATIVE. Present simple → DOES/DOESN'T. 'Doesn't it' (not 'isn't it' — that is for 'to be').
questions.retry_hint: A tag mirrors the main verb. The statement has no 'is' or 'are' - it uses the plain verb ARRIVES. Ask: which helping verb stands in for a plain present verb? And after a positive statement, is the tag positive or negative?

questions.stem: The typhoon ________ the island early yesterday morning, causing great damage.
questions.trap_type: 'Yesterday morning' = past. 'Hit' is invariant: hit → hit. Students often write 'hitted'.
questions.learning_tip: 'Hit' never changes its form: hit → hit → hit. 'Yesterday morning' = past → HIT. Never write 'hitted'.
questions.retry_hint: 'EARLY YESTERDAY MORNING' is finished time, so the verb must be past. Ask: what is the past of this verb? Careful - it is irregular, so its past form looks exactly like the plain form.

questions.stem: "Look at ________ puddles outside! We must wear our boots today," said Mother.
questions.trap_type: 'Puddles' is plural so we need 'these' or 'those'. 'Look at' means the puddles are visible right outside = nearby = these.
questions.learning_tip: 'Puddles' = plural → these or those. 'Look at' = they are visible nearby. Near + plural = THESE.
questions.retry_hint: PUDDLES is plural, and they are right OUTSIDE where Mother can point at them. Ask: which word points at more than one thing that is CLOSE BY? 'That' and 'this' point at one thing only.

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Prepositions of time and place)

questions.trap_type: Students write 'in' or 'on' for a clock time. AT is the correct preposition for specific times.
questions.learning_tip: Use AT for specific clock times: AT six o'clock, AT noon, AT midnight.
questions.retry_hint: 'SIX O'CLOCK' is an exact point on the clock. Ask: which preposition goes in front of clock times? Say each choice aloud before 'six o'clock' - only one sounds right.

questions.trap_type: Students write 'in' or 'at'. DURING means throughout a whole period of time such as a journey.
questions.learning_tip: DURING = throughout a period: DURING the journey, DURING the holiday, DURING the match.
questions.retry_hint: The tunnel was driven through while the JOURNEY was still going on - the blank covers a whole stretch of time. Ask: which preposition means 'all through a period of time'?

questions.trap_type: Students write 'in' which means inside without motion from one end to the other. THROUGH means entering one side and exiting the other.
questions.learning_tip: THROUGH = enter one side and come out the other: drive THROUGH a tunnel, walk THROUGH a forest.
questions.retry_hint: A TUNNEL has an entrance at one end and an exit at the other, and the car goes in one side and out the other. Ask: which preposition shows movement from one end of something to the other?

questions.trap_type: 'Arrived by noon' — 'by' shows the deadline or latest time. Students write 'at' (already used in blank 1) or 'in'.
questions.learning_tip: BY = no later than a specific time: arrived BY noon = got there no later than noon. It shows a deadline, not a precise moment.
questions.retry_hint: They reached the hotel some time before NOON, or just as noon struck - noon is the deadline. Ask: which preposition means 'not later than' a given time? The one for an exact clock time is already used in blank 1.

questions.trap_type: Students write 'at' or 'on'. The rule is IN the morning / afternoon / evening for parts of the day.
questions.learning_tip: IN the morning, IN the afternoon, IN the evening — use IN for parts of the day. Exception: AT night.
questions.retry_hint: 'The AFTERNOON' is a part of the day, not an exact clock time. Ask: which preposition do we use with parts of the day, like the morning or the evening?

questions.trap_type: 'During' is already used in blank 2. The jackets were worn ahead of entering the cold farm, so BEFORE is correct.
questions.learning_tip: BEFORE = earlier than an event. They wore jackets BEFORE the visit = put them on before going inside the cold farm.
questions.retry_hint: The jackets went on FIRST, and the VISIT came afterwards. Ask: which preposition puts one event EARLIER than another? It is the opposite of the word you need in blank 7.

questions.trap_type: The fireplace scene happened when dinner was finished. AFTER is correct. 'Before' is already used in blank 6.
questions.learning_tip: AFTER = when something is finished. AFTER dinner = when dinner ended. Events happen in order: first dinner, then fireplace.
questions.retry_hint: DINNER came first, and sitting by the FIRE came later. Ask: which preposition puts one event LATER than another? It is the opposite of the word needed in blank 6.

questions.trap_type: Students write 'at' or 'in' for a named day. ON is always used before specific days of the week.
questions.learning_tip: ON + specific day: ON Saturday, ON Monday morning, ON Christmas Day. Always ON for named days.
questions.retry_hint: 'SATURDAY MORNING' names a particular day. Ask: which preposition goes with days and dates - the one for exact times, the one for parts of the day, or the one for days of the week?

C.passage: Last December, my family went on a trip to Cameron Highlands. We left home (1)________ six o'clock in the morning. (2)________ the journey, we drove (3)________ a long tunnel in the mountains. We arrived (4)________ noon and checked into our hotel. (5)________ the afternoon, we visited a strawberry farm. We had to put on our jackets (6)________ the visit because it was very cold there. (7)________ dinner, we sat by the fire and drank hot chocolate. We had to leave (8)________ Saturday morning because Father had to return to work.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: Last Sunday, the weather (1)________ on television warned of heavy rain in the afternoon. My brother and I ignored it and cycled to the park anyway. When the first drops fell, we ran to take (2)________ under the roof of the bus stop. Our shirts were already (3)________ and water dripped from our hair. Ten minutes later the rain stopped, a cool (4)________ blew across the field, and the sun came out again. On the way home, we cycled around the (5)________ that had formed along the path.

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'thunder'. The blank is the report that WARNED of rain before it fell.
questions.learning_tip: FORECAST = what the weather is expected to do. 'The weather FORECAST warned of rain.'
questions.retry_hint: It appeared on TELEVISION and WARNED of rain before a single drop had fallen. Ask: which box word names the report that tells you what the weather will do? Thunder and lightning are things you see or hear, not reports.

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'raincoat'. You do not 'take a raincoat under a roof' - you TAKE something else there.
questions.learning_tip: TAKE SHELTER = go somewhere to be protected from the rain. A fixed phrase.
questions.retry_hint: They RAN UNDER THE ROOF of the bus stop to get out of the rain. Ask: which box word completes the fixed phrase 'to take ___'? You take it in order to be protected from the weather.

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'raincoat'. The blank describes the shirts after the rain.
questions.learning_tip: SOAKED = completely wet through. 'Our shirts were SOAKED.'
questions.retry_hint: WATER DRIPPED FROM THEIR HAIR - so how wet were the shirts? Ask: which box word describes something completely wet through? It is a describing word here, after 'were already'.

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'thunder' or 'lightning'. The blank BLEW across the field, so it is moving air.
questions.learning_tip: BREEZE = a light, gentle wind.
questions.retry_hint: It BLEW ACROSS THE FIELD and it was COOL - so it is moving air, and a gentle kind. Ask: which box word names a light wind? Thunder and lightning belong to the storm, not to the calm after it.

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'shelter'. The blank names the small pools of water left on the path.
questions.learning_tip: PUDDLES = small pools of rainwater on the ground. Plural, because there are many.
questions.retry_hint: The rain has stopped, but water is still lying ALONG THE PATH, so the cyclists must steer around them. Ask: which box word names small pools of water on the ground? It must be plural, because there are many.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.error_type: Homophone confusion — here (place) vs hear (to listen)
questions.trap_type: 'here' (place) when 'hear' (ears) is needed.
questions.learning_tip: HEAR = detect sound with ears. HERE = at this place. 'We could HEAR the thunder' → use ears? YES → HEAR. HEAR = ears. HERE = location.
questions.retry_hint: The underlined word means 'at this place', but the sentence is about THUNDER reaching your ears. Ask: which spelling belongs to your ears? One of them has the word EAR hidden inside it.

questions.trap_type: 'falled' applies the regular -ed rule. FALL is irregular: fall → fell.
questions.learning_tip: FALL → FELL (irregular past). NEVER 'falled'. Irregular verbs change completely: fall → fell, tell → told, sell → sold. These must be memorised.
questions.retry_hint: FALL is an irregular verb, so -ed cannot be right. Ask: how would you say it in the past - 'yesterday the rain ___ heavily'? Irregular verbs change their shape instead of taking an ending.

questions.trap_type: 'telled' applies the regular -ed rule. TELL is irregular: tell → told.
questions.learning_tip: TELL → TOLD (irregular past). NEVER 'telled'. Irregular verbs do not follow the -ed rule: tell → told, sell → sold, feel → felt.
questions.retry_hint: TELL is irregular too, so -ed is wrong. Ask: what is its past form - 'yesterday she ___ me a story'? It changes its vowel, exactly as sell becomes sold.

questions.error_type: Subject-verb agreement — compound subject (Father and I = plural)
questions.trap_type: 'Father and I' = two people = plural subject → WERE.
questions.learning_tip: FATHER AND I = two people = plural subject → WERE. 'Father and I WAS soaking wet' is WRONG. Compound subjects joined by AND are always plural → WERE. Think: two people = they → WERE.
questions.retry_hint: Read the whole subject: FATHER AND I - that is two people. Ask: does a plural subject take the singular verb or the plural one? Do not match the verb to the word nearest to it.

questions.trap_type: Students write a plain plural and leave out the apostrophe.
questions.learning_tip: The group chat BELONGS TO the neighbours -> NEIGHBOURS' group chat (apostrophe after the -s).
questions.retry_hint: The GROUP CHAT belongs to the neighbours - more than one neighbour. Ask: does a plain -s show ownership, or only make a plural? Where does the apostrophe go when the owners are many?

E.passage: Last Thursday, a sudden thunderstorm hit our neighbourhood. We could here (1) the thunder long before the lightning appeared in the sky. The rain falled (2) so heavily that the drain outside our house overflowed within minutes. Our neighbour telled (3) us to move our bicycles to higher ground immediately. Father and I was (4) soaking wet by the time we managed to get back indoors. Later that evening, we read the neighbours (5) group chat and saw that several trees had fallen across the road.

questions.sentence_a: The weather officer asked the reporter a question.
questions.sentence_b: Will the storm reach the city by midnight?
questions.instruction: Combine into one sentence using reported speech. Begin: 'The weather officer asked...'
questions.model_answer: The weather officer asked the reporter if the storm would reach the city by midnight.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'asked if will the storm reach' (wrong order).
questions.learning_tip: YES/NO question → reported speech: ASKED + IF + subject + verb (normal order). 'WILL the storm reach?' → asked IF the storm WOULD reach. Tense shifts: will → would. Word order is normal after 'if'.
questions.sentence1: The weather officer asked the reporter a question.
questions.sentence2: Will the storm reach the city by midnight?
questions.retry_hint: A yes/no question turned into REPORTED speech. Ask three things: which small joining word follows ASKED? Does the question keep its question word order, or become normal statement order? And what happens to 'will'?

questions.sentence_a: Father was driving home.
questions.sentence_b: It started to hail.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'when'.
questions.model_answer: Father was driving home when it started to hail.
questions.trap_type: Students drop 'was', writing 'Father driving home when it started to hail'.
questions.learning_tip: Father WAS DRIVING (ongoing background) when it STARTED to hail (sudden event). Keep WAS for the background action.
questions.retry_hint: One action was already going on when the other one suddenly began. Ask: which sentence is the longer action in progress, and which is the sudden one? Put WHEN in front of the sudden one.

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
It rained for three days without stopping. The river near Kai's village began to rise higher and higher. On the third morning, Kai woke up to find that water had seeped under the front door of their house.

'We have to leave now,' said Grandfather. He was a farmer who lived in the village all his life and saw floods before. 'Take only what you need,' he told the family.

Kai quickly grabbed his schoolbag and packed it with his books, a change of clothes and his grandmother's old photo album. His little sister Maya carried her favourite toy rabbit. Mother packed some food and medicine.

The family waded through ankle-deep water to reach higher ground. Neighbours helped each other along the way. At the community hall, volunteers were handing out blankets and hot drinks.

Three days later, the rain stopped and the water went down. When the family returned home, they found mud on the floors and some furniture damaged. But Grandfather looked around and smiled. 'We are safe. We can clean and fix the rest,' he said.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 2 has the same meaning as 'swirling or spinning with force'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Rushing' = moving fast; 'gathering' = coming together; 'rising' = going up. CHURNING = moving in a circular, agitated way with great force.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: CHURNING = moving in a powerful, swirling, circular way. The brown water was CHURNING = it swirled and turned with great force. Washing machines CHURN clothes; storms CHURN the sea.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 3, what does 'it' refer to in 'Grandfather said it would pass'?

options.2: The storm and flooding that was frightening the family

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 or 3. 'It would pass' = something unpleasant that will eventually end = the storm.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: PRONOUN REFERENCE: 'IT would pass.' IT = the STORM AND FLOODING — the frightening situation that the family was experiencing. Grandfather was reassuring the family that the danger would not last. IT = the dangerous situation.

mcq_questions.stem: Why did Grandfather say 'The river gives and the river takes — that is its nature' at the end?

options.1: He was angry that the river had flooded their home.
options.2: He wanted to teach the family that nature has both gifts and dangers, and one must accept both with wisdom.
options.3: He was explaining that rivers produce fish for the village to eat.
options.4: He was telling the family to move away from the river permanently.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking he was angry. His tone is philosophical and wise, not angry.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: INFERENCE: 'The river GIVES and the river TAKES — that is its NATURE.' Grandfather is teaching a philosophical lesson: nature provides (gives rice fields, water) and nature destroys (floods). One must live wisely alongside both. Option 2 = wisdom, not anger or simple description.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 1, is it True or False that the family was surprised by the flood? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. Grandfather had a boat ready and lived by the river all his life — he saw floods before and had already prepared for one.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1: Grandfather SAW FLOODS BEFORE and HAD A BOAT READY. He was already prepared — so the family was NOT surprised. Answer is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: What were the volunteers doing at the community hall?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: The volunteers were handing out blankets and hot drinks.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'helping people' which is too vague. The passage gives specific details.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 4: 'volunteers were handing out BLANKETS and HOT DRINKS'. Use the specific details from the text.

open_ended_questions.stem: What damage did the family find when they returned home? Give TWO things.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) There was mud on the floors. (ii) Some furniture was damaged.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students describe the flooding instead of the damage found after the water went down.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 5 names TWO things: MUD on the floors AND damaged FURNITURE. Both details are in the last paragraph.

open_ended_questions.stem: Find a phrase in paragraph 4 that shows the community worked together to help each other.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: 'Neighbours helped each other along the way.'
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students quote the volunteer sentence instead of the neighbour sentence about mutual community help.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 4: 'NEIGHBOURS HELPED EACH OTHER along the way.' This shows community members helping one another, not just the volunteers.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on his actions throughout the passage, describe TWO character traits of Grandfather with evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) PREPARED: Grandfather had a boat ready before the flood arrived, showing he planned ahead and thought calmly about how to protect his family. (ii) WISE: instead of panicking, he guided the family to safety and then calmly explained that floods are part of living by the river — showing deep experience and calm acceptance.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'strong and brave' without precise traits or evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: TRAIT INFERENCE: PREPARED = had a BOAT READY before the flood. WISE = guided family to safety, then explained nature calmly ('the river gives and the river takes'). Name trait + give evidence = full marks.

questions.stem: At the finish line, the runner's face was as ________ as a tomato - flushed with colour from the effort and the heat.
questions.trap_type: 'Pale','calm','cold' describe the opposite. RED = flushed with colour from effort or heat.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! The runner's face was AS RED AS a tomato = comparing the flushed colour to a ripe tomato. RED = flushed with colour. AS + ADJECTIVE + AS is always the correct simile form.
questions.retry_hint: The comparison is with a ripe TOMATO, and the face is FLUSHED WITH COLOUR from the EFFORT and the HEAT. Ask: what colour does skin turn after running hard - paler, calmer, cooler, or the colour of that tomato?

questions.stem: The coach ________ the team to keep trying even though they were losing by three goals.
questions.trap_type: 'Scolded' and 'punished' are negative responses. A good coach gives positive support when a team is losing.
questions.learning_tip: ENCOURAGED = gave support and confidence to keep going. A good coach ENCOURAGES the team even when they are losing.
questions.retry_hint: The team was LOSING BY THREE GOALS, yet the coach still wanted them TO KEEP TRYING. Ask: would a good coach scold, punish or ignore his players at that moment, or pour courage into them? Match the verb to his purpose.

questions.stem: After winning the gold medal, Priya had to ________ her tears of joy as she stood on the podium in front of the whole school.
questions.trap_type: 'Put off' = delay; 'run away' = flee; 'break down' = stop working. HOLD BACK = stop a strong feeling from bursting out.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: HOLD BACK = keep a strong feeling from showing. You HOLD BACK tears, anger or laughter. HOLD + BACK work together as one meaning.
questions.retry_hint: She has just won the GOLD MEDAL, so the TEARS OF JOY are already rising and must be kept in. Ask: does 'put off' (delay), 'run away' or 'break down' fit tears? A phrasal verb must be learnt as one whole unit.

questions.stem: When the underdog team scored the winning goal in the last minute, every supporter in the stadium was ________ — no one could believe it.
questions.trap_type: 'Under the weather' = ill; 'in hot water' = trouble; 'at a loss' = confused. OVER THE MOON = extremely happy.
questions.learning_tip: IDIOM: OVER THE MOON = feeling extremely happy and excited. The supporters were OVER THE MOON = overjoyed at the unexpected victory. Idioms cannot be understood word by word!
questions.retry_hint: The UNDERDOG team scored in the LAST MINUTE and NO ONE COULD BELIEVE IT. Ask: does the idiom describe wild happiness, or illness, trouble, or confusion? An idiom cannot be worked out word by word.

questions.stem: The athletes trained every single day to reach their ________ performance during the championship.
questions.trap_type: 'Peak performance' is a fixed sports phrase meaning the highest level an athlete can achieve.
questions.learning_tip: PEAK means the very highest point. PEAK performance = the best you have ever performed. Athletes train hard to reach their PEAK.
questions.retry_hint: They trained EVERY SINGLE DAY for the CHAMPIONSHIP, so the blank names their very best level. Ask: would anyone train that hard to reach their laziest, weakest or usual performance? Choose the word meaning 'highest point'.

questions.stem: Nobody in the swimming club ________ how to do a perfect butterfly stroke without practising for months.
questions.trap_type: NOBODY = singular → verb+S.
questions.learning_tip: NOBODY / EVERYONE / SOMEONE = Singular! Nobody KNOWS how to do the butterfly stroke = add -S. 'Nobody know' is WRONG. Singular indefinite pronouns always take singular present-tense verbs.
