questions.retry_hint: The subject is NOBODY, not the SWIMMING CLUB. Words like nobody and everyone act like ONE person. Ask: in the present tense, does a singular subject take the plain verb, or the verb ending in -s?

questions.stem: Our school has ________ three gold medals at the National Primary School Swimming Championships this year.
questions.trap_type: HAS + past participle = present perfect. WIN → WON (irregular).
questions.learning_tip: HAS + past participle = present perfect. Our school HAS WON three gold medals = started winning this year. WIN → WON (irregular past participle). HAS + WON = present perfect.
questions.retry_hint: HAS is already in the sentence, so the blank must be its partner. Ask: after has, do we use the plain verb, the -s form, the -ing form, or the past participle? WIN is irregular, so its participle is not made with -ed.

questions.stem: The goalkeeper ________ for the ball when the striker kicked it into the top corner of the net.
questions.trap_type: 'The striker kicked it' = sudden interrupting event. The goalkeeper was already reaching = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: The striker KICKED it = sudden past event. The goalkeeper was already in the middle of reaching = WAS REACHING (past continuous). Was/were + verb-ing = action in progress when interrupted.
questions.retry_hint: The STRIKER KICKED it - a sudden action that cut across what the goalkeeper had already begun. Ask: which form shows an action IN PROGRESS in the past? A plain past verb would only show a finished action.

questions.stem: The new indoor stadium is far ________ than the old outdoor track — it can be used in any weather.
questions.trap_type: 'Most useful' = superlative; 'usefuler' is WRONG. MORE USEFUL = comparative for long adjectives.
questions.learning_tip: Long adjective (3+ syllables) → MORE + adjective = comparative. MORE USEFUL THAN the outdoor track = comparing two venues. 'Usefuler' is ALWAYS WRONG. For long adjectives, always use MORE.
questions.retry_hint: THAN tells you two venues are being compared, and the adjective is long. Ask: do long adjectives take -er, or a helper word in front? 'Usefuler' is not English, and 'most' is for a group of three or above.

questions.stem: The referee blew the whistle and all the players ________ running immediately.
questions.trap_type: 'The referee blew' = past. The players' immediate reaction is also a completed past action.
questions.learning_tip: The referee BLEW = past. All players STOPPED = simple past completed reaction to the whistle.
questions.retry_hint: The referee BLEW the whistle - a finished past action - and the players reacted IMMEDIATELY. Ask: should the second verb sit in that same finished past, or drift into the present? Both verbs share one time frame.

questions.stem: Regular exercise is one of the best ways to stay healthy and reduce stress, ________ it?
questions.trap_type: Positive present 'to be' ('is') → negative question tag. IS → isn't it.
questions.learning_tip: Positive present 'to be' → negative tag. Regular exercise IS one of the best ways, ISN'T it? POSITIVE → NEGATIVE. IS → ISN'T. Tag questions: match the 'to be' verb of the main clause.
questions.retry_hint: A tag mirrors the main verb, and the statement uses IS ('Regular exercise IS one of the best ways'). Ask: after a positive statement, does the tag stay positive or turn negative? Keep the same verb - do not borrow 'do'.

questions.stem: The team trained very hard ________ they did not win the trophy in the end.
questions.trap_type: Trained hard (positive effort) + did not win (negative result) = a contrast, not a cause-effect. Use 'but'.
questions.learning_tip: BUT joins two contrasting ideas. Trained hard = positive. Did not win = negative. Contrast → BUT.
questions.retry_hint: TRAINED VERY HARD is a positive effort, yet DID NOT WIN THE TROPHY is a disappointing result. Ask: does this need a reason word like 'because', a result word like 'so', or a word that signals a surprise? Two clashing ideas need a contrast link.

questions.stem: There ________ not enough players available, so the practice match was cancelled.
questions.trap_type: PLAYERS is plural, so 'was' can never agree with it. Students match the verb to 'enough' instead of to the noun that follows.
questions.learning_tip: THERE + plural noun -> WERE. 'There WERE not enough players available.' The verb agrees with the noun after it: one player WAS, many players WERE.
questions.retry_hint: Look at the noun straight after the blank: PLAYERS - many, not one. And the match WAS CANCELLED, so the time is past. Ask: does a plural noun take the singular past verb, or its plural partner? Never match the verb to 'enough'.

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Verb forms of 'run')

questions.trap_type: After 'enjoys', only the gerund (-ing form) is possible. Students write 'to run'.
questions.learning_tip: ENJOY + verb-ing: enjoys RUNNING every morning. 'Enjoys to run' is never correct.
questions.retry_hint: The verb in front of the blank is ENJOYS. Ask: after enjoy, can the next verb ever carry 'to', or must it wear the -ing ending? Try each box word in the gap and listen - only one shape may follow enjoy.

questions.trap_type: 'Each day' = regular habit = simple present. 'He' is singular so the verb needs -s.
questions.learning_tip: 'Each day' = habit = simple present. He (singular) → RUNS five kilometres.
questions.retry_hint: EACH DAY WITHOUT FAIL signals a habit, so the tense is simple present - not past, and not this very moment. Ask: HE is one person, so does the present verb stay plain, or does it need -s on the end?

questions.trap_type: 'Last Tuesday' = past. 'Run' is irregular: run → ran. Students write 'runned'.
questions.learning_tip: 'Last Tuesday' = past. 'Run' is irregular: run → RAN. Never write 'runned'.
questions.retry_hint: LAST TUESDAY is finished time, so the action is over and done. Ask: is this verb regular? Its past form does not take -ed at all, and 'runned' is not a word. Irregular verbs change their vowel instead.

questions.trap_type: 'While he ___' past the fountain = ongoing background action. Singular he = was running.
questions.learning_tip: 'While he ___' = ongoing background past action = past continuous. He WAS RUNNING when he spotted Mr Lim.
questions.retry_hint: WHILE tells you the action was already going on when he SPOTTED Mr Lim. Ask: which past form shows an action in progress? And is HE one person or many? That decides whether the helping verb is singular or plural.

questions.trap_type: 'Several other students' = plural subject + ongoing past action. Plural = were running.
questions.learning_tip: Several students = plural. They were in motion at the same moment = WERE RUNNING (past continuous).
questions.retry_hint: The subject is SEVERAL OTHER STUDENTS - more than one, and they are in the middle of moving at that same moment. Ask: which helping verb belongs to a plural subject in the past, and which to one person? Then add the -ing form.

questions.trap_type: After 'tried', use the infinitive 'to run'. Using 'running' would change the meaning.
questions.learning_tip: 'Try TO + base verb': tried TO RUN faster to catch up with them.
questions.retry_hint: TRIED is followed by an infinitive: he attempted the action on purpose. Ask: which box word carries the little marker that shows an infinitive? The -ing form has already been claimed by ENJOYS at the start of the passage.

questions.trap_type: After the modal verb 'should', always use the base form with no -s or -ing.
questions.learning_tip: Modal + base verb: should RUN, must swim, can jump. Never 'should runs' or 'should running'.
questions.retry_hint: SHOULD is a modal verb, like must, can and will. Ask: after a modal, does the verb ever carry -s, -ing or 'to'? Pick the plainest shape in the box - the one a dictionary would list.

questions.trap_type: 'Right now' = present continuous. 'My cousin' = singular → is running.
questions.learning_tip: 'Right now' = present continuous. My cousin (singular) → IS RUNNING her first race right now.
questions.retry_hint: RIGHT NOW means at this very moment, as we speak. Ask: does a habit tense fit that, or a tense that shows the action still unfolding? HIS COUSIN is one person, so choose the singular helping verb.

C.passage: Wei Ming enjoys (1)________ every morning before school. He (2)________ five kilometres around the park each day without fail. Last Tuesday, he (3)________ his fastest time ever — just twenty minutes! While he (4)________ past the fountain, he spotted his teacher Mr Lim also out for a jog. Several other students (5)________ ahead of him on the track. Wei Ming tried (6)________ faster to catch up with them. Mr Lim called out, 'You should (7)________ with your arms held higher!' Wei Ming smiled and pushed on. Right now, his cousin (8)________ in her very first school race.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: The school basketball final was the most exciting game of the year. Thousands of (1)________ filled the stands, cheering loudly for their favourite teams. In the same final last year, our team had been (2)________ by eight points, so few people expected us to win. At half-time, our captain Reza looked calm but (3)________. He told everyone to believe in themselves and keep fighting. In the second half, one of our players got (4)________ when he twisted his ankle. Even so, the remaining players pushed on and won the match. Reza held up the trophy as our school's (5)________ for the very first time.

questions.trap_type: Spectators watch; supporters cheer. 'Spectators' is the precise word for people watching a live sport event.
questions.learning_tip: SPECTATORS = people who watch a sport or event. They fill the stands and cheer for their teams.
questions.retry_hint: They FILLED THE STANDS and cheer loudly for their FAVOURITE TEAMS. Ask: which box word names the people who WATCH a game rather than play in it? A coach and a referee are never counted in thousands.

questions.trap_type: Students think our team lost this match. Read again: the eight-point loss happened in LAST YEAR's final, not in this one.
questions.learning_tip: DEFEATED = beaten by an opponent. 'Our team had been DEFEATED by eight points' = the other team beat them.
questions.retry_hint: Mind the time: this happened IN THE SAME FINAL LAST YEAR, not today - our team actually WON THE MATCH this time. Ask: which box word means 'beaten by the other team'? After HAD BEEN, only a past participle fits.

questions.trap_type: The captain gives a motivating speech showing firm resolve, not tiredness. 'Determined' = firmly decided to succeed.
questions.learning_tip: DETERMINED = firmly decided to succeed no matter what. A captain who rallies the team despite being behind is DETERMINED.
questions.retry_hint: CALM BUT warns you the next word must contrast with calm, and Reza tells the team to KEEP FIGHTING. Ask: which box word describes someone who has firmly decided to succeed? It must describe a person, so 'coach' cannot fit.

questions.trap_type: A twisted ankle is a physical injury. 'Got injured' = was hurt during play.
questions.learning_tip: INJURED = hurt during physical activity. A twisted ankle is a sports INJURY.
questions.retry_hint: The clue comes right after the blank: he TWISTED HIS ANKLE. Ask: which box word describes a player who has been hurt during play? 'Got' plus this word tells you what happened to his body.

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'coach'. Reza is the captain who lifts the trophy, so the blank names the WINNER of the competition.
questions.learning_tip: A CHAMPION is the player or team that wins a competition. Holding up the trophy = being the CHAMPION.
questions.retry_hint: He HELD UP THE TROPHY after the team WON THE MATCH, so the blank names the title they earned. Ask: is Reza the school's coach or referee, or the winner of the whole competition? Choose the word for the top prize-winner.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.error_type: Homophone confusion — here (place) vs hear (to listen)
questions.trap_type: 'here' (place) when 'hear' (ears) is needed.
questions.learning_tip: HEAR = detect sound with ears. HERE = at this place. 'We could HEAR the excitement' → use ears? YES → HEAR. HEAR = ears. HERE = location.
questions.retry_hint: The underlined word means 'at this place', but the sentence is about the EXCITEMENT reaching your ears. Ask: which of the two look-alikes has the word EAR hidden inside it? They sound the same, so choose by meaning.

questions.trap_type: 'holded' applies the regular -ed rule. HOLD is irregular: hold → held.
questions.learning_tip: HOLD → HELD (irregular past). NEVER 'holded'. Irregular verbs change completely: hold → held, sell → sold, tell → told. These must be memorised.
questions.retry_hint: HOLDED forces the regular -ed rule onto a verb that refuses it. Ask: how would you say it about yesterday? Think of sell becoming sold and tell becoming told - the vowel changes instead of an ending being added.

questions.trap_type: 'runned' applies the regular -ed rule. RUN is irregular: run → ran.
questions.learning_tip: RUN → RAN (irregular past). NEVER 'runned'. Irregular verbs do not follow the -ed rule: run → ran, begin → began, swim → swam.
questions.retry_hint: RUNNED is not a word: the -ed rule has been pushed onto an irregular verb. Ask: how do you say it about yesterday? Think of swim becoming swam, and begin becoming began - the vowel does the work.

questions.error_type: Simple past — regular verb (drop → dropped, double p)
questions.trap_type: 'drop' is base form. Past tense context requires 'dropped' (double p + ed).
questions.learning_tip: DROP → DROPPED (regular past, double the -p). Rule: short vowel + single consonant → double before -ed. DROP: D-R-O-P, ends vowel+consonant → DROPPED. 'One runner drop the baton' = WRONG. Use DROPPED.
questions.retry_hint: Everything around it is past: this was LAST SATURDAY, and WE HAD TO RESTART. Ask: is DROP a past form, or the plain base verb? And in a short word ending in one vowel + one consonant, what happens to that last letter before -ed?

questions.trap_type: Students write a plain plural and leave out the apostrophe that shows ownership.
questions.learning_tip: The results sheet BELONGS TO the coordinators -> COORDINATORS' results sheet (apostrophe after the -s for a plural). Singular: coordinator's.
questions.retry_hint: The RESULTS SHEET belongs to the COORDINATORS - more than one person. Ask: does a plain -s show ownership, or does it only make a plural? When the owners are many, where must the apostrophe go?

E.passage: Last Saturday, our school held its annual sports day on the field. We could here (1) the excitement from the classrooms before we were even allowed outside. One athlete holded (2) his breath before the race and began to look nervous. Our class team runned (3) the four-by-one-hundred relay, but one runner drop (4) the baton and we had to restart. At the end, the sports coordinators (5) results sheet was read aloud and the top three teams were cheered by the whole school.

questions.sentence_a: The coach asked Priya a question.
questions.sentence_b: Did you feel nervous before the final race?
questions.instruction: Combine into one sentence using reported speech. Begin: 'The coach asked...'
questions.model_answer: The coach asked Priya if she felt nervous before the final race.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'asked if did she feel' (wrong order) or keep 'you'.
questions.learning_tip: YES/NO question → reported speech: ASKED + IF + subject + verb (normal order). 'Did YOU feel nervous?' → asked IF SHE FELT nervous. Pronoun: you → she. Tense: did feel → felt. Word order is normal after 'if'.
questions.retry_hint: The COACH ASKED a yes/no QUESTION and you must now report it. Ask: which small joining word follows asked? Does the reported part keep question order, or normal statement order? And what must 'you' and 'did' become?

questions.sentence_a: Sara was practising her free kicks.
questions.sentence_b: Her coach arrived at the field.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'when'.
questions.model_answer: Sara was practising her free kicks when her coach arrived at the field.
questions.trap_type: Students drop 'was', writing 'Sara practising her free kicks when her coach arrived'.
questions.learning_tip: Sara WAS PRACTISING (ongoing background) when her coach ARRIVED (sudden event). Keep WAS for the ongoing background action.
questions.retry_hint: One action was already going on; the other one cut across it. Ask: which sentence is the long background action, and which is the sudden event? WHEN goes in front of the sudden one - and never drop the helping verb of the ongoing action.

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
It was the final race of the year — the 1500-metre run. Twelve-year-old Priya stood at the starting line, her heart beating fast. She had trained for months for this moment.

The race began. For the first two laps, Priya stayed in third place, pacing herself carefully. Her coach, Mr Rajan, had always told her: 'Save your energy for the last lap.'

On the third lap, the girl in first place stumbled and fell. She got up quickly, but she lost precious time. Priya pushed forward and moved into second place.

With one lap to go, Priya's legs felt heavy. She thought about giving up. But then she heard the crowd cheering and she remembered why she started running — not to win, but to prove to herself that she could finish.

She crossed the finish line in second place. As she caught her breath, she felt a deep sense of pride. Mr Rajan ran over and shook her hand. 'That,' he said, 'was your best race ever.'

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 2 has the same meaning as 'breathing in short, quick bursts from effort'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Sprinting' = running fast; 'stretching' = extending; 'stumbling' = tripping. GASPING = breathing in short quick bursts, especially from exhaustion.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: GASPING = breathing in short, urgent bursts because of great effort or shock. Priya was GASPING at the finish line = she was out of breath from running so hard. GASP = one sharp intake of breath.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 3, what does 'it' refer to in 'she almost did not believe it'?

options.2: That she was still in second place despite losing time when she fell
options.4: The timing board above the track

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 3 thinking 'it' = the cheering. But 'almost did not believe IT' = an incredible situation she found herself in.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: PRONOUN REFERENCE: 'almost did not believe IT.' IT = the SITUATION — that she was STILL IN SECOND PLACE even after falling and losing time. She could hardly believe she was still competitive after the setback.

mcq_questions.stem: Why does the writer say Priya 'was not last' at the end of the passage?

options.1: To show that Priya won a medal at the end.
options.2: To show that finishing without giving up — even in difficult circumstances — is itself a form of victory.
options.3: To explain that Priya ran faster than expected.
options.4: To show that the other runners were slower than Priya.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 3 thinking speed is the point. But the emphasis is on persistence, not speed.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: INFERENCE: 'She was NOT LAST' = the ending focuses on the fact that she FINISHED and did not give up — not on medals or speed. The passage celebrates PERSISTENCE. Option 2 = the message is about the value of continuing despite difficulty.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 1, is it True or False that Priya was the fastest runner in her school? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The passage says Priya had never won a race before — it was her dream, not something she was already known for.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1: Priya NEVER WON A RACE before. She was not the fastest — winning was her DREAM, not her current status. Answer is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: What did Mr Rajan do when Priya crossed the finish line?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: Mr Rajan ran over and shook her hand.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'he congratulated her' which is too vague. The passage gives specific physical actions.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Last paragraph: Mr Rajan 'RAN OVER and SHOOK HER HAND'. Give the specific actions described in the text.

open_ended_questions.stem: How do we know Priya almost gave up during the last lap? Give TWO pieces of evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) Her legs felt heavy. (ii) She thought about giving up.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students give one piece of evidence twice in different words.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 4 gives TWO separate facts: (1) 'her legs felt HEAVY' and (2) 'she THOUGHT ABOUT GIVING UP'. These are two distinct pieces of evidence.

open_ended_questions.stem: What made Priya keep going when she felt like giving up?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: She heard the crowd cheering and remembered why she started running — to prove to herself that she could finish.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students give only one reason and miss the deeper personal motivation.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Two things helped her: the CROWD CHEERING and remembering she wanted to PROVE to herself she could finish. Include both.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on her actions throughout the passage, describe TWO character traits of Priya with evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) DETERMINED: after falling and losing precious time, Priya got up immediately and kept running instead of stopping — showing she refused to give in to difficulty. (ii) BRAVE: despite the pain of her fall and the knowledge that she was behind, she continued to the finish line without complaint.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'fast and hardworking' without precise traits or evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: TRAIT INFERENCE: DETERMINED = fell, but GOT UP and KEPT RUNNING. BRAVE = continued despite pain and setback, no complaint. Name trait + give evidence = full marks.

questions.stem: The shopping mall during the Great Singapore Sale was as ________ as a beehive — shoppers moving in every direction.
questions.trap_type: 'Quiet','empty','dark' describe the opposite of a crowded mall. BUSY = full of people and activity.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! The mall was AS BUSY AS a beehive = comparing the frantic movement of shoppers to worker bees in a hive. BUSY = full of activity and people. AS + ADJECTIVE + AS is the correct simile form.
questions.retry_hint: The mall is compared to a BEEHIVE, with SHOPPERS MOVING IN EVERY DIRECTION. Ask: is a beehive quiet, empty and dark, or humming with constant activity? Match the adjective to the movement, not to the building.

questions.stem: The shopkeeper ________ the price by half during the year-end sale.
questions.trap_type: 'Raised' and 'doubled' mean the price went up. A sale means the price goes down.
questions.learning_tip: REDUCED = made lower. During a sale, prices are REDUCED — cut to a lower amount.
questions.retry_hint: The clue is BY HALF, during the YEAR-END SALE. Ask: in a sale, does a price climb or come down? 'Raised' and 'doubled' both push it up, and 'ignored' does nothing to it at all.

questions.stem: After comparing prices at three different stores, Ben decided to ________ forty dollars on a new pair of running shoes.
questions.trap_type: 'Throw away','give away' = get rid of; 'run out of' = use up. SPLASH OUT = spend a larger amount of money than usual as a treat.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: SPLASH OUT = spend more money than usual on something you want as a treat. Ben SPLASHED OUT on new shoes = he spent a good amount as a special purchase. SPLASH + OUT work together as one meaning.
questions.retry_hint: Ben COMPARED PRICES at three stores first, so he spent the forty dollars on purpose, as a treat. Ask: do 'throw away' or 'give away' fit money he meant to spend? 'Run out of' means having none left.

questions.stem: When Marcus found the lost wallet and returned it to its owner, he was ________ — the owner's relief and gratitude made his day.
questions.trap_type: 'Under the weather' = ill; 'in hot water' = trouble; 'at a loss' = confused. OVER THE MOON = extremely happy.
questions.learning_tip: IDIOM: OVER THE MOON = feeling extremely happy. Marcus was OVER THE MOON = overjoyed that his honesty brought someone else relief. Idioms cannot be understood word by word!
questions.retry_hint: The owner's RELIEF AND GRATITUDE MADE HIS DAY. Ask: does the idiom describe someone bursting with happiness, or someone ill, in trouble, or confused? An idiom cannot be worked out word by word.

questions.stem: The wet market was ________ with shoppers looking for fresh ingredients for their new year feast.
questions.trap_type: 'Silent', 'deserted' and 'empty' all suggest few or no people. A busy new year market is the opposite.
questions.learning_tip: BUSTLING = very busy and full of movement and noise. A market BUSTLING with shoppers = many people rushing about, lively and active.
questions.retry_hint: The WET MARKET is packed with SHOPPERS hunting for FRESH INGREDIENTS before a FEAST. Ask: could 'silent', 'deserted' or 'empty' ever fit a market full of people? The blank needs the opposite of empty.

questions.stem: Nobody in the family ________ where Mother hid the emergency savings — it was her best-kept secret.
questions.trap_type: NOBODY = singular → verb+S.
questions.learning_tip: NOBODY / EVERYONE / SOMEONE = Singular! Nobody KNOWS where the savings are = add -S. 'Nobody know' is WRONG. Singular indefinite pronouns always take singular present-tense verbs.
questions.retry_hint: The subject is NOBODY, not THE FAMILY. Words like nobody and everyone behave like ONE person. Ask: does a singular subject take the plain present verb, or the one ending in -s? The -ing form is not used with this thinking verb.

questions.stem: The supermarket has ________ a new self-checkout system that allows customers to pay without a cashier.
questions.trap_type: HAS + past participle = present perfect. INSTALL → INSTALLED (regular).
questions.learning_tip: HAS + past participle = present perfect. The supermarket HAS INSTALLED a new system = done recently and now available. INSTALL → INSTALLED (regular verb, add -ed).
questions.retry_hint: HAS is already in the sentence, so the blank must be its partner. Ask: after has, do we need the plain verb, the -s form, the -ing form, or the past participle? This verb is regular, so the ending follows the usual rule.

questions.stem: The cashier ________ the items when the customer's phone suddenly rang and distracted everyone.
questions.trap_type: 'The phone rang' = sudden interrupting event. Cashier was already scanning = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: The phone RANG = sudden past event. The cashier was already in the middle of scanning = WAS SCANNING (past continuous). Was/were + verb-ing = action in progress when interrupted.
questions.retry_hint: The customer's phone SUDDENLY RANG - that cut across something already happening. Ask: which form shows an action in progress in the past? A plain past verb would show only a finished, closed action.

questions.stem: The online prices are far ________ than the in-store prices at most electronics shops.
questions.trap_type: 'Cheapest' = superlative; 'more cheaper' is WRONG. CHEAPER = comparative of 'cheap'.
questions.learning_tip: Short adjective + -ER = comparative. Cheap → CHEAPER. Online prices are CHEAPER THAN in-store prices = comparing two types of prices. 'More cheaper' is ALWAYS WRONG — never add BOTH 'more' AND '-er'.
questions.retry_hint: THAN sets ONLINE PRICES against IN-STORE PRICES, and the adjective is short. Ask: does a short adjective add -er, or take 'most' in front? And can you ever put 'more' before a word that already ends in -er?

questions.stem: She chose the red bag ________ it was her favourite colour.
questions.trap_type: 'So' would reverse the order, putting the result before the reason. 'Because' correctly links the choice to its reason.
questions.learning_tip: She chose the bag BECAUSE it was her favourite colour. BECAUSE = the reason. The reason comes AFTER 'because'.
questions.retry_hint: The second half gives the REASON for her choice: it was her FAVOURITE COLOUR. Ask: which joining word introduces a reason? 'So' would put a result there instead, and 'although' would signal a contrast.

questions.stem: Spending more than you earn is a sure way to end up in debt, ________ it?
questions.trap_type: Positive present 'to be' ('is') → negative question tag. IS → isn't it.
questions.learning_tip: Positive present 'to be' → negative tag. Spending more than you earn IS a way to end up in debt, ISN'T it? POSITIVE → NEGATIVE. IS → ISN'T. Tag questions match the 'to be' verb of the main clause.
questions.retry_hint: A tag mirrors the main verb, and this statement uses IS ('Spending more than you earn IS a sure way'). Ask: after a positive statement, does the tag stay positive or flip to negative? Keep the same verb - do not borrow 'do'.

questions.stem: The shop assistant ________ the customer where the toys section was.
questions.trap_type: The story is set in the past. 'Tell' is irregular: tell → told. Students write 'telled'.
questions.learning_tip: 'Tell' is irregular: tell → TOLD. The event is in the past → TOLD the customer.
questions.retry_hint: Look at the last word of the sentence: WAS. The whole scene sits in the past. Ask: is this verb regular? 'Telled' does not exist - think of sell becoming sold. Every verb in the sentence must share one time.

questions.stem: The children ________ themselves in the toy aisle while Mother paid for the shopping.
questions.trap_type: The blank is a past tense verb in the same time frame as 'paid'. 'Amusement' is a noun; 'amusing' is an adjective.
questions.learning_tip: 'Amused themselves' = entertained themselves = simple past verb. The children AMUSED themselves while waiting.
questions.retry_hint: Mother PAID for the shopping - a past verb - so the blank must sit in the same past time. Ask: is 'amusement' a naming word and 'amusing' a describing word? The blank needs an action that matches PAID.

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Personal pronouns — subject, object, possessive)

questions.trap_type: Before a noun like 'mother', use a possessive adjective. Students write 'I' (subject pronoun).
questions.learning_tip: Before a noun ('mother'), use a possessive adjective: MY mother. 'I mother' is wrong.
questions.retry_hint: The blank stands in front of the noun MOTHER, so it must show whom she belongs to. Ask: can a subject pronoun like 'I' ever sit before a naming word? A possessive form is needed there.

questions.trap_type: After the verb 'took', use the object pronoun. Students write 'I' (subject form).
questions.learning_tip: After a verb like 'took', use the OBJECT pronoun: took ME. 'Took I' is wrong.
questions.retry_hint: The blank comes straight after the verb TOOK, so the writer is being taken, not doing the taking. Ask: does a subject form like 'I' ever follow a verb? Test the gap on its own: 'Mother took ___'.

questions.trap_type: The blank is the subject of 'wanted'. Speaker + sister together = we. Students write 'us' (object form).
questions.learning_tip: The blank is the SUBJECT of 'wanted'. Speaker and sister = WE. 'Us wanted' is wrong.
questions.retry_hint: This blank opens the sentence and is the subject of WANTED - the writer plus the SISTER, two people. Ask: can an object form like 'us' ever act as a subject? Say it aloud: 'Us wanted shoes' is wrong.

questions.trap_type: 'My sister and I' — I is the subject. Students write 'me' by false analogy with 'my sister and me'.
questions.learning_tip: Test: remove 'my sister and' → 'I tried on shoes' is correct. 'Me tried' is wrong. Use I as the subject.
questions.retry_hint: Use the removal test: take away MY SISTER AND, and read what is left - '___ TRIED ON MANY PAIRS'. Ask: does a subject form or an object form fit there? The subject of TRIED can never be 'me'.

questions.trap_type: After the verb 'helped', use the object pronoun. The assistant helped the speaker and sister = us.
questions.learning_tip: After 'helped', use the OBJECT pronoun. The shop assistant helped US (the speaker + sister).
questions.retry_hint: The blank follows the verb HELPED, so the two shoppers are receiving the help, not giving it. Ask: which form comes after a verb - the subject one, or the object one? 'The assistant helped we' sounds wrong for a reason.

questions.trap_type: Before a noun ('belongings'), use a possessive adjective. Students write 'we' or 'us'.
questions.learning_tip: Before a noun ('belongings'), use a possessive adjective: OUR belongings. 'We belongings' is wrong.
questions.retry_hint: The blank stands in front of the noun BELONGINGS, so it must show who owns them. Ask: can 'we' sit before a naming word? Before a noun you need a possessive form, never a subject or an object form.

questions.trap_type: After 'take good care of', use the object pronoun. Students write 'they' (subject form).
questions.learning_tip: After a verb + preposition like 'take care OF', use the OBJECT pronoun: take good care of THEM.
questions.retry_hint: The blank follows TAKE GOOD CARE OF, so the belongings are receiving the action. Ask: after a verb and the little word 'of', do we use the subject form 'they', or its object partner? Pronouns change shape with their job.

questions.trap_type: The blank is the subject of 'will last'. Students write 'them' (object form).
questions.learning_tip: THEY = subject pronoun for things. 'THEY will last a long time' = the belongings last. THEY is the subject of 'will last'.
questions.retry_hint: This blank is the subject of WILL LAST - the belongings are doing the lasting. Ask: can the object form 'them' ever act as a subject? Say it aloud: 'Them will last a long time' is wrong.

C.passage: Last Saturday, (1)________ mother took (2)________ and my sister to the shopping centre. (3)________ wanted to buy new school shoes. My sister and (4)________ tried on many pairs before finding the right ones. The shop assistant helped (5)________ find the correct size. Our parents always remind us to look after (6)________ belongings carefully. If we take good care of (7)________, (8)________ will last a long time.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: Last Monday, my aunt went to a department store with a strict (1)________ of fifty dollars. She found a handbag she liked, but the original price was eighty dollars. Luckily, it was on sale — she got a great (2)________ at only forty-five dollars. However, when she got home, she found the zip was broken. She went back to the store and had to join a long (3)________ at the customer service counter. She asked to (4)________ it for a new one in good condition. The sales assistant agreed and also gave her a small (5)________ for the inconvenience.

questions.trap_type: A budget is a fixed amount of money you decide to spend. Students may write 'plan' which is not in the box.
questions.learning_tip: A BUDGET = a fixed amount of money you decide to spend. Staying within your BUDGET means not spending more than that amount.
questions.retry_hint: The word STRICT and the exact sum of FIFTY DOLLARS point to a limit fixed before shopping began. Ask: which box word names the amount you decide to spend and must not go over? A receipt is only proof of what you paid.

questions.trap_type: 'A great bargain' = something bought at a much lower price than normal. Students may write 'deal' which is not in the box.
questions.learning_tip: A BARGAIN = something bought at a much lower price than normal. Getting an 80-dollar bag for 45 dollars = a great BARGAIN.
questions.retry_hint: Compare the two figures: the ORIGINAL PRICE WAS EIGHTY DOLLARS, but she paid only FORTY-FIVE. Ask: which box word names something bought far below its normal price? The blank follows 'a great', so it is a naming word.

questions.trap_type: 'Join a long queue' = stand in a line and wait. Students may write 'line' which is not in the box.
questions.learning_tip: QUEUE = a line of people waiting for something. She had to join a long QUEUE at the customer service counter.
questions.retry_hint: You JOIN it, it is LONG, and it forms at the CUSTOMER SERVICE COUNTER. Ask: which box word names a line of people waiting for their turn? A cashier is a person, and a trolley is a thing you push.

questions.trap_type: 'Exchange it for a new one' = return the broken one and get a different one. Students may write 'return' which is not in the box.
questions.learning_tip: EXCHANGE = return a faulty item and get a different working one in its place. She wanted to EXCHANGE the broken bag.
questions.retry_hint: The blank follows ASKED TO, so it must be a doing word, and the pattern is '___ IT FOR A NEW ONE'. Ask: which box word means handing back a faulty item and taking a working one in its place?

questions.trap_type: A refund = money given back. Last word by context and elimination.
questions.learning_tip: A REFUND = money given back when you return a product or when there is a problem. A partial REFUND = some money back.
questions.retry_hint: She has already been promised the new bag, so this last thing is given FOR THE INCONVENIENCE. Ask: which box word names money handed back to a customer? A receipt is only a slip of paper - it is not money.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.error_type: Homophone confusion — here (place) vs hear (to listen)
questions.trap_type: 'here' (place) when 'hear' (ears) is needed.
questions.learning_tip: HEAR = detect sound with ears. HERE = at this place. 'We could HEAR the music' → use ears? YES → HEAR. HEAR = ears. HERE = location.
questions.retry_hint: The underlined word means 'at this place', but the sentence is about the CHEERFUL MUSIC reaching your ears. Ask: which of the two look-alikes has EAR hidden inside it? Choose by meaning, since both sound the same.

questions.error_type: Irregular past — go → went (not go, base form)
questions.trap_type: 'go' is base form. Past tense context requires 'went'.
questions.learning_tip: GO → WENT (irregular past). NEVER 'goed'. In a past tense context, use WENT. 'A salesperson go up to us' = WRONG — wrong tense. Use WENT.
questions.retry_hint: Everything around it happened LAST SATURDAY, so the story is finished and past. Ask: is GO a past form, or the plain base verb? This verb is irregular - its past looks nothing like it, and 'goed' is not a word.

questions.trap_type: 'tries' is present tense third person. Past tense context requires 'tried'.
questions.learning_tip: TRY → TRIED (regular past, change -y to -i and add -ed). In a past tense context, use TRIED. 'Mother tries on shoes' = WRONG — wrong tense. TRY → TRIED.
questions.retry_hint: TRIES carries the -s of the present tense, yet the whole passage is set in the past. Ask: what is this verb's past form? When a verb ends in -y after a consonant, the y must change before the ending is added.

questions.trap_type: 'Some items' is plural. Students write 'was'.
questions.learning_tip: Plural subject → plural verb! SOME ITEMS WERE placed in a box = ITEMS is plural → WERE. WAS is only for ONE thing. Find the main noun: ITEMS = plural → WERE.
questions.retry_hint: Find the subject of the underlined verb: SOME ITEMS - many things, not one. Ask: can a plural subject ever take 'was'? Match the verb to the main noun, never to the BOX that comes after it.

questions.trap_type: Students write a plain plural and leave out the apostrophe that shows ownership.
questions.learning_tip: The purchases BELONG TO the shoppers -> SHOPPERS' purchases (apostrophe after the -s for a plural). Singular: shopper's.
questions.retry_hint: The PURCHASES belong to the SHOPPERS - many owners, not one. Ask: does a plain -s show ownership, or does it only make a plural? When the owners are many, where must the apostrophe sit?

E.passage: Last Saturday, Mother took us to the new mall near the expressway for the school sale. We could here (1) the cheerful music playing even before we reached the entrance. Inside, a salesperson go (2) up to us immediately and offered us a loyalty card. Mother tries (3) on several pairs of shoes before choosing the blue ones with the special grip. There were not enough bags at the counter — some items was (4) placed in a box instead. At the end, the shoppers (5) purchases were checked against their receipts before they passed through the exit gates.

questions.sentence_a: The shopkeeper asked the customer a question.
questions.sentence_b: Are you looking for something specific today?
questions.instruction: Combine into one sentence using reported speech. Begin: 'The shopkeeper asked...'
questions.model_answer: The shopkeeper asked the customer if he was looking for something specific.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'asked if is he looking' (wrong order) or keep 'you'.
questions.learning_tip: YES/NO question → reported speech: ASKED + IF + subject + verb (normal order). 'Are YOU looking?' → asked IF HE WAS looking. Pronoun: you → he. Tense: are looking → was looking. Word order is normal after 'if'.
questions.retry_hint: The SHOPKEEPER ASKED a yes/no QUESTION and you must now report it. Ask: which small joining word follows asked? Does the reported part keep question order, or normal statement order? And what must 'you' and 'are' become?

questions.sentence_a: Mother was checking the prices.
questions.sentence_b: The children ran to the toy section.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'while'.
questions.model_answer: While Mother was checking the prices, the children ran to the toy section.
questions.trap_type: Students drop 'was', writing 'While Mother checking the prices, the children ran'.
questions.learning_tip: Mother WAS CHECKING (ongoing background) while the children RAN (different simultaneous action). Keep WAS.
questions.retry_hint: WHILE goes in front of the longer action that was already under way. Ask: which of the two sentences is the background action, and which one happens inside it? Keep the helping verb of the ongoing action - never drop it.

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
Nine-year-old Marcus was helping his mother carry the groceries when he saw a brown wallet on the floor near the checkout counter. He looked inside and found some cash and a name card that read: 'Mr David Tan, Block 44, Maple Avenue.'

'Mum, someone dropped this,' Marcus said, holding up the wallet. His mother smiled. 'What do you think you should do?' she asked.

Marcus thought carefully. He could keep the money — there was quite a lot inside. But he knew that was wrong. He handed the wallet to the customer service counter and told the officer what he found.

The officer took down Marcus's name and phone number. That evening, Mr Tan called their home. He sounded very relieved. He told Marcus's mother that the wallet contained money for his daughter's school trip, which was the very next day.

'Your son is a very honest boy,' Mr Tan said. He visited the next day and brought a box of biscuits as a thank-you gift. Marcus felt happier about returning the wallet than he would have felt keeping the money.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 1 has the same meaning as 'extremely busy with lots of noise and movement'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Quiet' = opposite; 'crowded' = full of people (but less vivid); 'colourful' = visually bright. BUSTLING = extremely busy, full of noisy activity and movement.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: BUSTLING = very busy, noisy and full of movement. A BUSTLING market = one where many people are moving, talking and trading energetically. BUSTLE = busy activity; BUSTLING = currently very busy and lively.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 3, what does 'it' refer to in 'Marcus knew he had to return it'?

options.2: The wallet he found on the ground
options.3: The shopping bag he was carrying
options.4: The amount of money in the wallet

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 or 4 thinking 'it' = money or receipt. But 'return IT' = the whole object he found.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: PRONOUN REFERENCE: 'had to return IT.' IT = the WALLET — the complete item Marcus found on the ground. He had to return the entire wallet (including everything inside) to its owner. IT = the wallet.

mcq_questions.stem: Why did the writer describe Marcus as feeling 'lighter' as he walked away from the police station?

options.1: Because Marcus had put down the heavy wallet.
options.2: Because returning the wallet relieved him of a moral burden — doing the right thing made him feel free and good about himself.
options.3: Because Marcus was tired from walking and finally felt relaxed.
options.4: Because the officer told Marcus to walk faster.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking 'lighter' = less physical weight. This is a metaphor for emotional relief.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: INFERENCE: 'felt LIGHTER' = a metaphor for EMOTIONAL RELIEF. Returning the wallet removed the moral weight of carrying something that was not his. Doing the right thing made him feel FREE and at ease. Option 2 = the emotional/moral reading, not the physical one.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 1, is it True or False that Marcus immediately knew what to do when he found the wallet? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The passage says Marcus picked it up and stood still for a moment — showing he paused to think about what to do rather than acting immediately.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1: Marcus STOOD STILL FOR A MOMENT — he paused, suggesting he was not sure what to do right away. He then made the decision to report it. Answer is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: What did Mr Tan bring when he visited Marcus the next day?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: Mr Tan brought a box of biscuits as a thank-you gift.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'he brought a present' which is too vague. The passage gives a specific detail.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Last paragraph: 'a box of BISCUITS as a THANK-YOU GIFT'. Give the specific detail from the text.

open_ended_questions.stem: In paragraph 3, Marcus thought about keeping the money. Give TWO things that helped him decide not to.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) He knew that keeping the money was wrong. (ii) He decided to hand the wallet to the customer service counter instead.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students give one reason twice in different words, or describe what he did rather than why he decided.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 3: He KNEW IT WAS WRONG = the moral reason. He then ACTED by going to CUSTOMER SERVICE = the decision. State both.

open_ended_questions.stem: Find the exact word in paragraph 4 that shows Mr Tan was very glad the wallet was found.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: relieved
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students write 'happy' or 'glad' — these are synonyms but NOT the exact word used in the passage.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 4: 'He sounded very RELIEVED.' The question asks for the exact word from the passage, not a synonym.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on his actions throughout the passage, describe TWO character traits of Marcus with evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) HONEST: even though the wallet was full of cash, Marcus chose to hand it in at the police station instead of keeping it — showing strong personal integrity. (ii) RESPONSIBLE: he acted on his own conscience without being told to, and followed through by going to the police station immediately.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'kind and good' without precise traits or evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: TRAIT INFERENCE: HONEST = handed in the wallet with FULL CASH inside. RESPONSIBLE = acted on his OWN CONSCIENCE, went to police station immediately. Name trait + give evidence = full marks.

questions.stem: After the rain, the forest floor was as ________ as a newly washed carpet - green, clean and sparkling with droplets.
questions.trap_type: 'Dry','grey','noisy' describe the opposite or unrelated qualities. FRESH = clean, new and full of life.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! The forest floor was AS FRESH AS a freshly washed carpet = comparing its clean, renewed quality after rain to a clean carpet. FRESH = new, clean and full of life. AS + ADJECTIVE + AS is the correct simile form.
questions.retry_hint: AFTER THE RAIN the forest floor is compared to a NEWLY WASHED CARPET - green, clean and SPARKLING WITH DROPLETS. Ask: does that sound dry, grey or noisy? Match the adjective to the just-washed look, not to the weather.

questions.stem: The forest fire ________ thousands of trees and left many wild animals without a home.
questions.trap_type: 'Grew', 'watered' and 'planted' are positive actions. A fire causes destruction, not growth.
questions.learning_tip: DESTROYED = completely ruined or wiped out. The fire DESTROYED the trees = burned them all down.
questions.retry_hint: A FOREST FIRE swept through, and the animals were LEFT WITHOUT A HOME. Ask: can a fire grow, water or plant trees? The verb must match the damage the fire left behind.

questions.stem: Every weekend, the students came to ________ the abandoned plot of land and turn it into a community garden.
questions.trap_type: 'Run away from','give up on','break into' all describe negative actions. CLEAN UP = tidy and remove rubbish or dirt from a space.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: CLEAN UP = remove dirt, rubbish and mess from an area. The students came to CLEAN UP the abandoned plot = they removed all the rubbish and tidied it. CLEAN + UP work together as one meaning.
questions.retry_hint: The plot is ABANDONED, and the students turn it into a COMMUNITY GARDEN, so the rubbish must go first. Ask: do 'run away from', 'give up on' or 'break into' fit students who came to help? A phrasal verb works as one unit.

questions.stem: When the old tree that the students had worked so hard to save finally survived and bloomed again in spring, everyone was ________ — all their effort was worth it.
questions.trap_type: 'Under the weather' = ill; 'in hot water' = trouble; 'down in the dumps' = sad. OVER THE MOON = extremely happy.
questions.learning_tip: IDIOM: OVER THE MOON = feeling extremely happy and relieved. Everyone was OVER THE MOON = overjoyed that the tree survived. Idioms cannot be understood word by word!
questions.retry_hint: The old tree SURVIVED and BLOOMED AGAIN, and ALL THEIR EFFORT WAS WORTH IT. Ask: does the idiom describe great joy, or illness, trouble, or sadness? Idioms cannot be read word by word.

questions.stem: The wildlife officer released the injured turtle back into the sea after it ________ fully.
questions.trap_type: 'Disappeared', 'shrank' and 'drowned' are all negative outcomes. An officer releases an animal only after it gets better.
questions.learning_tip: HEALED = became healthy again after being injured. The turtle HEALED → the officer released it safely back into the sea.
questions.retry_hint: The turtle was INJURED, and only afterwards was it RELEASED back into the sea. Ask: would an officer let it go if it had shrunk, drowned or disappeared? The blank names the good change in its body.

questions.stem: Nobody in the class ________ how much plastic ends up in the ocean every year — the numbers are shocking.
questions.trap_type: NOBODY = singular → verb+S.
questions.learning_tip: NOBODY / EVERYONE / SOMEONE = Singular! Nobody REALISES how much plastic = add -S. 'Nobody realise' is WRONG. Singular indefinite pronouns always take singular present-tense verbs.
questions.retry_hint: The subject is NOBODY, not THE CLASS. Words like nobody and everyone act like ONE person. Ask: does a singular subject take the plain present verb, or the verb ending in -s? The -ing form is not used with this thinking verb.

questions.stem: Our school has ________ a zero-waste campaign this term to reduce the amount of plastic used in the canteen.
questions.trap_type: HAS + past participle = present perfect. LAUNCH → LAUNCHED (regular).
questions.learning_tip: HAS + past participle = present perfect. Our school HAS LAUNCHED a zero-waste campaign = started recently and now running. LAUNCH → LAUNCHED (regular verb, add -ed).
questions.retry_hint: THIS TERM shows the campaign began recently and still counts now, and HAS already sits before the blank. Ask: after has, do we need the plain verb, the -s form, the -ing form, or the past participle?

questions.stem: The birds ________ loudly in the trees when the bulldozer suddenly started clearing the forest.
questions.trap_type: 'The bulldozer started clearing' = sudden interrupting event. Birds were already chirping = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: The bulldozer STARTED = sudden past event. The birds were already in the middle of chirping = WERE CHIRPING (past continuous). Was/were + verb-ing = action in progress when interrupted.
questions.retry_hint: The BULLDOZER SUDDENLY STARTED clearing - that cut across something already happening. Ask: which form shows an action in progress in the past? And THE BIRDS are many, so the helping verb must be the plural one.

questions.stem: The coral reefs in our oceans are far ________ now than they were fifty years ago — pollution and warming have taken a heavy toll.
questions.trap_type: 'Most damaged' = superlative; 'damageder' is WRONG. MORE DAMAGED = comparative for long adjectives.
questions.learning_tip: Long adjective → MORE + adjective = comparative. MORE DAMAGED THAN fifty years ago = comparing two points in time. 'Damageder' is ALWAYS WRONG. For longer adjectives, use MORE.
questions.retry_hint: THAN sets the reefs NOW against the reefs FIFTY YEARS AGO, and the adjective is long. Ask: do long adjectives take -er, or a helper word in front? 'Damageder' is not English, and 'most' is for three or above.

questions.stem: There ________ a family of otters living in the river near our school.
questions.trap_type: 'A family of otters' — the head noun is 'a family' = singular. Present fact. Students write 'are' looking at 'otters'.
questions.learning_tip: 'A family' = ONE family = singular → THERE IS a family. Even though otters are plural, the head noun 'a family' is singular.
questions.retry_hint: Find the head noun straight after the blank: A FAMILY - one family, even though many OTTERS live inside it. Ask: does the verb follow 'a family', or the otters? And the sentence describes now, not the past.

questions.stem: Protecting the environment is everyone's responsibility, not just the government's, ________ it?
questions.trap_type: Positive present 'to be' ('is') → negative question tag. IS → isn't it.
questions.learning_tip: Positive present 'to be' → negative tag. Protecting the environment IS everyone's responsibility, ISN'T it? POSITIVE → NEGATIVE. IS → ISN'T. Tag questions: match the 'to be' verb of the main clause.
questions.retry_hint: A tag mirrors the main verb, and the statement uses IS ('Protecting the environment IS everyone's responsibility'). Ask: after a positive statement, does the tag stay positive or flip to negative? Keep the same verb - do not borrow 'do'.

questions.stem: Each of the young trees ________ watered by the students every morning.
questions.trap_type: 'Each of the trees' = each tree individually = singular. Students write 'are' seeing 'trees' (plural).
questions.learning_tip: 'Each of the trees' = each tree one at a time = singular → IS watered. Look at 'each', not 'trees', to decide.
questions.retry_hint: Do not be fooled by TREES. The subject begins with EACH, and each tree gets watered on its own. Ask: does 'each of...' mean one at a time, or many at once? Match the verb to EACH, not to the noun beside it.

questions.stem: "We must stop cutting ________ so many trees in the forest," the environmentalist said firmly.
questions.trap_type: 'This', 'that' and 'these' are demonstratives and cannot stand between 'cutting' and 'so many'. CUT DOWN is a fixed phrasal verb.
questions.learning_tip: 'Cut DOWN trees' = chop trees so that they fall. STOP CUTTING DOWN = stop chopping them. The two words work as one verb.
questions.retry_hint: CUTTING is only half of the verb here - it needs its partner to mean chopping trees so that they fall. Ask: can 'this', 'that' or 'these' ever squeeze between CUTTING and SO MANY? A phrasal verb is two words acting as one.

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Verb forms of 'plant')

questions.context_check: Subject: 'Our school' (singular). Signal: 'Every year' = habit = simple present. Singular subject + simple present = plants.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'plant' (plural form) forgetting 'our school' is a singular subject.
questions.learning_tip: 'Every year' = habit = simple present. Our school (singular) → PLANTS trees along the road each year.
questions.retry_hint: EVERY YEAR signals a habit, so the tense is simple present - not past, and not this very moment. Ask: OUR SCHOOL is one thing, so does the present verb stay plain, or must it take -s?

questions.context_check: Signal: 'Last Earth Day' = past. 'Plant' is regular: plant → planted.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'plant' (base form) ignoring the past time signal 'Last Earth Day'.
questions.learning_tip: 'Last Earth Day' = past. 'Plant' is regular: plant → PLANTED.
questions.retry_hint: LAST EARTH DAY is finished time, and the action is over. Ask: does the sentence need a form still in progress, or a plain completed past? This verb is regular, so its past is made in the ordinary way.

questions.context_check: Signal: 'While half the class ___' = ongoing background action in the past. Subject 'half the class' = plural group = were planting.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'planted' (simple past) and miss the ongoing background signal 'while'.
questions.learning_tip: 'While the older BOYS ___' = an action in progress in the past = past continuous. Plural subject -> WERE PLANTING.
questions.retry_hint: WHILE tells you this action was still going on while THE GIRLS WATERED the saplings. Ask: which past form shows an action in progress? THE OLDER BOYS are many, so pick the plural helping verb.

questions.context_check: Signal: 'reminded us ___' = infinitive structure. 'Remind someone TO do something' → to plant.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'planting' instead of the infinitive that follows 'reminded us'.
questions.learning_tip: 'Reminded us TO + base verb': reminded us TO PLANT each seedling carefully. Always use the infinitive after 'reminded someone'.
questions.retry_hint: REMINDED US is always followed by an infinitive. Ask: which box word carries the little marker of an infinitive? 'Reminded us planting' is not English - the pattern is fixed: remind someone, then the infinitive.

questions.context_check: Signal: 'while she ___' = ongoing background action. Subject 'Lin' = singular she = was planting. Interrupted by dropping the bottle.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'planted' (simple past) missing the ongoing signal 'while she'.
questions.learning_tip: Lin WAS PLANTING (ongoing) when she dropped her water bottle (sudden event). Singular subject → WAS PLANTING.
questions.retry_hint: She DROPPED her water bottle - a sudden event that cut across what Lin was already busy doing. Ask: which past form shows the longer background action? LIN is one person, so choose the singular helping verb.

questions.context_check: Signal: 'Right now' = present continuous. Subject: 'my brother's class' = singular group = is planting.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'plants' (simple present habit) missing the 'right now' signal for present continuous.
questions.learning_tip: 'Right now' = present continuous. My brother's class (one class, singular) → IS PLANTING trees behind the canteen.
questions.retry_hint: RIGHT NOW means at this very moment, as we speak. Ask: does a habit tense fit that, or a tense that shows the action still unfolding? MY BROTHER'S CLASS is one class, so the helping verb is singular.

questions.context_check: Signal: 'loves ___' = gerund after 'loves'. Pattern: love + verb-ing.
questions.trap_type: After 'enjoys', only the gerund is possible. Students write 'to plant'.
questions.learning_tip: ENJOY + verb-ing: enjoys PLANTING trees. 'Enjoys to plant' is never correct.
questions.retry_hint: The verb in front of the blank is ENJOYS. Ask: after enjoy, can the next verb ever carry 'to'? Only one shape may follow it - and the infinitive has already been claimed by REMINDED US earlier in the passage.

questions.context_check: Signal: 'should ___' = modal verb + base form. Never add -s or -ing after a modal.
questions.trap_type: Students add -s or use 'planting' after the modal verb 'should'.
questions.learning_tip: After modal verbs (should, must, can, will), always use the BASE form: should PLANT. Never 'should plants' or 'should planting'.
questions.retry_hint: SHOULD is a modal verb, and modals are always followed by the same shape. Ask: after should, must or can, does the verb take -s, -ing or 'to'? Pick the plainest form in the box, the one with no ending at all.

C.passage: Every year, our school (1)________ trees along the roadside as part of its green programme. Last Earth Day, students from all classes (2)________ over two hundred seedlings in the school compound. Class 3A was especially enthusiastic - while the older boys (3)________ trees near the science block, the girls watered the young saplings. Our teacher reminded us (4)________ each seedling carefully so the roots would take hold. My friend Lin (5)________ a small mango tree when she accidentally dropped her water bottle. Right now, my brother's class (6)________ trees behind the canteen. Our principal enjoys (7)________ trees and has said we should (8)________ at least one new tree every month.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: Our neighbourhood park used to be a beautiful place. Sadly, (1)________ has become a serious problem there - drink cans and food wrappers are dropped on the grass every day. Along our coast, (2)________ has left the sea with far fewer fish than before, because too many are caught at one time. Last month, our class started a green project. We collected leftover food and vegetable peels and turned them into (3)________ for the school garden. Our teacher explained that this is a (4)________ way to enrich the soil, as no chemicals are used at all. If every one of us does a little, we can (5)________ our environment for the animals and for ourselves.

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'recycle'. The clue is the drink CANS and food WRAPPERS left on the grass.
questions.learning_tip: LITTERING = dropping or throwing rubbish in public places. It spoils the surroundings and harms animals.
questions.retry_hint: The clue follows the dash: DRINK CANS and FOOD WRAPPERS ARE DROPPED ON THE GRASS every day. Ask: which box word names the act of throwing rubbish in a public place? The blank is the subject, so it must be a naming word.

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'extinct'. The blank must be a THING that has left the sea with fewer fish, not a describing word.
questions.learning_tip: OVERFISHING = catching too many fish from the sea, leaving too few to breed. 'Over-' = too much.
questions.retry_hint: The reason is spelt out: TOO MANY ARE CAUGHT AT ONE TIME, leaving FAR FEWER FISH. Ask: which box word names the act of taking too much from the sea? 'Extinct' is a describing word, so it cannot be the subject.

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'habitat'. Leftover food and vegetable peels are turned into food for the SOIL.
questions.learning_tip: COMPOST = decayed food and plant material mixed into soil to make it richer.
questions.retry_hint: LEFTOVER FOOD and VEGETABLE PEELS were TURNED INTO something useful for the SCHOOL GARDEN. Ask: which box word names rotted plant matter that feeds the soil? A habitat is a place, not a material.

questions.trap_type: The blank sits before 'way', so it must be a describing word. The clue is that NO CHEMICALS are used.
questions.learning_tip: NATURAL = happening in nature, without man-made chemicals.
questions.retry_hint: The blank sits between 'a' and WAY, so it must be a describing word - and the clue is that NO CHEMICALS ARE USED AT ALL. Ask: which box word means 'made by nature, not by people'?

questions.trap_type: The blank follows 'we can', so it must be a base verb. Students pick a noun.
questions.learning_tip: PROTECT = keep something safe from harm. We must PROTECT the environment for every living thing.
questions.retry_hint: The blank follows WE CAN, so it must be a plain doing word, not a naming word like compost. Ask: which box word means to keep something safe from harm, so that the ANIMALS and the ENVIRONMENT survive?

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.error_type: Homophone confusion — here (place) vs hear (to listen)
questions.trap_type: 'here' (place) when 'hear' (ears) is needed.
questions.learning_tip: HEAR = detect sound with ears. HERE = at this place. 'We could HEAR the birdsong' → use ears? YES → HEAR. HEAR = ears. HERE = location.
questions.retry_hint: The underlined word means 'at this place', yet the sentence is about BIRDSONG reaching your ears. Ask: which of the two look-alikes contains the word EAR? They sound the same, so choose by meaning.

questions.trap_type: 'jointed' adds -ed to 'joint' not 'join'. The correct base is JOIN → JOINED.
questions.learning_tip: JOIN → JOINED (just add -ed). 'Jointed' = a different word (connected by a joint). NEVER 'jointed' for JOIN. Spell clearly: J-O-I-N + ED = JOINED.
questions.retry_hint: Look at the base verb hiding inside JOINTED. A joint is a part of a body or a pipe - that is a different word altogether. Ask: what do you get when you simply add -ed to JOIN, with no extra letter squeezed in?

questions.trap_type: 'telled' applies the regular -ed rule. TELL is irregular: tell → told.
questions.learning_tip: TELL → TOLD (irregular past). NEVER 'telled'. Irregular verbs: tell → told, sell → sold, fall → fell. These must be memorised.
questions.retry_hint: TELLED forces the regular -ed rule onto a verb that refuses it. Ask: how would you say it about yesterday? Think of sell becoming sold - the vowel changes instead of an ending being tacked on.

questions.trap_type: 'The students' is plural. Students write 'was'.
questions.learning_tip: Plural subject → plural verb! THE STUDENTS WERE amazed = STUDENTS is plural → WERE. WAS is only for ONE thing. STUDENTS = plural → WERE.
questions.retry_hint: Find the subject of the underlined verb: THE STUDENTS - many people, not one. Ask: can a plural subject ever take 'was'? Match the verb to the subject, not to the VARIETY of birds that follows.

questions.trap_type: Students write a plain plural and leave out the apostrophe that shows ownership.
questions.learning_tip: The observation sheets BELONG TO the participants -> PARTICIPANTS' sheets (apostrophe after the -s for a plural). Singular: participant's.
questions.retry_hint: The OBSERVATION SHEETS belong to the PARTICIPANTS - many owners. Ask: does a plain -s by itself show ownership, or does it only make a plural? When the owners are more than one, where must the apostrophe go?

E.passage: Last Sunday, our class joined a nature walk at the reservoir nature trail. We could here (1) birdsong from the moment we stepped off the bus. Our guide jointed (2) us at the entrance and explained the rules: no litter, no loud noise. She telled (3) us that even a small piece of rubbish can harm the wildlife living near the water. As we walked, the students was (4) amazed by the variety of birds and insects they spotted along the way. At the end, the participants (5) observation sheets were collected for a class display back at school.

questions.sentence_a: The nature guide asked the children a question.
questions.sentence_b: Have you ever seen a wild otter before?
questions.instruction: Combine into one sentence using reported speech. Begin: 'The nature guide asked...'
questions.model_answer: The nature guide asked the children if they had ever seen a wild otter before.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'asked if have they ever seen' (wrong order) or keep 'you'.
questions.learning_tip: YES/NO question → reported speech: ASKED + IF + subject + verb (normal order). 'Have YOU ever seen?' → asked IF THEY HAD EVER seen. Pronoun: you → they. Tense: have → had. Word order is normal after 'if'.
questions.retry_hint: The NATURE GUIDE ASKED a yes/no QUESTION and you must now report it. Ask: which small joining word follows asked? Does the reported part keep question order, or normal statement order? And what must 'you' and 'have' become?

questions.sentence_a: The students were collecting fallen leaves.
questions.sentence_b: A butterfly landed on one of the bags.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'when'.
questions.model_answer: The students were collecting fallen leaves when a butterfly landed on one of the bags.
questions.trap_type: Students drop 'were', writing 'The students collecting fallen leaves when a butterfly landed'.
questions.learning_tip: The students WERE COLLECTING (ongoing background) when a butterfly LANDED (sudden event). Keep WERE for the ongoing action.
questions.retry_hint: One action was already going on; the other one suddenly broke in. Ask: which sentence is the long background action, and which is the sudden event? WHEN goes in front of the sudden one, and the ongoing action keeps its helping verb.

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
At the centre of Birchwood Primary School stood a magnificent old raintree. Its wide branches spread across the entire field, giving shade to students during recess. According to the school's history book, the tree was planted by the school's founder over eighty years ago.

One morning, the principal announced that the raintree had to be cut down because its roots were cracking the floor of the school hall. Many students were upset. A group of Primary 5 students decided to do something about it.

They started a petition and collected over three hundred signatures from students, teachers and parents. They also researched ways to save old trees without cutting them down. One student found that roots could be guided away from buildings using special underground barriers.

The principal read the petition carefully. Impressed by the students' effort and research, she agreed to bring in a tree expert before making the final decision.

The expert visited and suggested installing root barriers underground to guide the roots away from the hall. It would cost more, but the tree could be saved.

A month later, the work was done. The old raintree still stood, and students still gathered under its shade during recess, just as they always did.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 2 has the same meaning as 'not moving at all, completely still'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Whispering','leaning','reaching' all involve some movement. MOTIONLESS = completely still, not moving at all.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: MOTIONLESS = completely without movement. The children stood MOTIONLESS = they did not move a single muscle while watching the birds. MOTION = movement; MOTIONLESS = no movement at all (-LESS = without).

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 3, what does 'it' refer to in 'Kai realised he had never noticed it before'?

options.1: The bird that landed on the branch
options.2: How much beauty and life existed in nature close to his home, which he had walked past without seeing
options.3: The notebook he used to record his observations

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking 'it' = the bird. But 'never noticed IT before' = something that was always there but unseen.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: PRONOUN REFERENCE: 'never noticed IT before.' IT = THE NATURAL WORLD around his home — the birds, the trees, the sounds. Kai realised he had walked past all this BEAUTY without ever paying attention to it. IT = the richness of nature near his home.

mcq_questions.stem: Why does the writer end the passage with 'the old tree was still there — and so were they'?

options.1: To show that the students were tired and did not want to leave.
options.2: To show that protecting the tree and caring for nature helped both the tree and the students grow and endure.
options.3: To explain that the tree was so old it would outlast the students.
options.4: To suggest the students should come back to visit more often.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 or 3. The ending is poetic and symbolic — 'they' = the students and the relationship between humans and nature.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: INFERENCE: 'the old tree was still THERE — and so WERE THEY.' Both the tree AND the students endured and grew. The writer is drawing a parallel: just as the tree survived through care, the students' CONNECTION TO NATURE also survived and deepened. Option 2 = the symbolic parallel meaning.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 1, is it True or False that the old tree was in danger of being cut down? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: True. The passage says the town council planned to remove the old tree to make way for a road — showing it was under threat.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1: the TOWN COUNCIL PLANNED TO REMOVE the old tree to make way for a road. This means the tree was in danger of being cut down. Answer is TRUE.

open_ended_questions.stem: How many signatures did the students collect for their petition?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: They collected over three hundred signatures.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'many signatures' which is too vague.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 3: 'over THREE HUNDRED signatures'. Use the exact number from the text.

open_ended_questions.stem: What TWO things did the group of Primary 5 students do to try to save the tree?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) They started a petition and collected signatures. (ii) They researched ways to save old trees without cutting them down.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students give one action twice or mention the expert, who was brought in by the principal — not by the students.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 3: (1) they started a PETITION and (2) they RESEARCHED ways to save trees. The expert was the principal's decision later.

open_ended_questions.stem: What was the raintree used for by students at recess?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: Students gathered under its shade during recess.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'to play' or 'to rest' which are too general.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1: 'giving SHADE to students during RECESS'. The tree gave shade and students gathered beneath it at recess.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on their actions throughout the passage, describe TWO character traits of the students with evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) DETERMINED: the students wrote letters, made signs and appealed to the council to save the tree — showing they did not give up even when facing official opposition. (ii) CARING: they gave up their weekends to water and tend to the tree, showing genuine concern for nature beyond their own personal gain.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'hardworking and kind' without precise traits or evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: TRAIT INFERENCE: DETERMINED = wrote letters, made signs, appealed to council — did not give up. CARING = gave up weekends to water and tend the tree. Name trait + give evidence = full marks.

questions.stem: Grandma's kitchen smelled as ________ as a bakery — warm bread, cinnamon and butter filled every corner.
questions.trap_type: 'Cold','noisy','empty' don't match the warm comforting smell description. SWEET = pleasant, warm, sugary smell.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! The kitchen smelled AS SWEET AS a bakery = comparing the home's smell to a freshly baked bakery. SWEET = pleasantly fragrant. AS + ADJECTIVE + AS is always the correct simile form.
questions.retry_hint: The clue is the list after the dash: WARM BREAD, CINNAMON and BUTTER. Ask: does a BAKERY smell cold, noisy or empty? The blank must describe a smell, so match it to that sugary, comforting scent.

questions.stem: The chef added a ________ of salt to the dish to improve its flavour.
questions.trap_type: A bowl, bucket and bottle are all large amounts. Salt is added in tiny amounts — a pinch.
questions.learning_tip: A PINCH = a very small amount you can pick up between two fingers. Recipes say 'a pinch of salt' for a tiny amount.
questions.retry_hint: Think how much SALT a dish needs TO IMPROVE ITS FLAVOUR - a bowl, a bucket, a bottle? Ask: how much salt can a CHEF hold between his thumb and one finger? Any more would ruin the whole dish.

questions.stem: After the big meal, Mother asked the children to ________ the dishes and put them away in the cupboard.
questions.trap_type: 'Put off' = delay; 'run away' = flee; 'give in' = surrender. WASH UP = clean the dishes after a meal.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: WASH UP = clean the dishes and utensils after eating. Mother asked them to WASH UP the dishes = clean them with soap and water. WASH + UP work together as one meaning.
questions.retry_hint: AFTER THE BIG MEAL the DISHES are dirty, and they must go back into the CUPBOARD clean. Ask: do 'put off', 'run away' or 'give in' get a single plate clean? A phrasal verb must be learnt as one unit.

questions.stem: When the judges tasted Grandma's secret recipe soup and gave her first prize, she was ________ — it was her dream come true.
questions.trap_type: 'Under the weather' = ill; 'in hot water' = trouble; 'at a loss' = confused. OVER THE MOON = extremely happy.
questions.learning_tip: IDIOM: OVER THE MOON = feeling extremely happy and delighted. Grandma was OVER THE MOON = her happiness was at its very highest. Idioms cannot be understood word by word!
questions.retry_hint: The JUDGES gave her FIRST PRIZE, and it was her DREAM COME TRUE. Ask: does the idiom describe someone bursting with joy, or someone ill, in trouble, or confused? An idiom cannot be read word by word.

questions.stem: The recipe said to ________ the mixture until it became smooth and there were no more lumps.
questions.trap_type: 'Fry' uses oil; 'fold' = gently combine; 'peel' removes skin. Only 'whisk' = beat rapidly to make smooth.
questions.learning_tip: WHISK = beat a mixture quickly to make it smooth and airy. You whisk eggs or cake batter. The clue 'no more lumps' tells you the action makes things smooth.
questions.retry_hint: The clue sits at the end: SMOOTH, with NO MORE LUMPS. Ask: does frying, folding or peeling ever break up lumps? The blank names a quick beating action that smooths a MIXTURE.

questions.stem: Nobody in the cooking class ________ how to make roti prata from scratch — it is one of the hardest dishes to master.
questions.trap_type: NOBODY = singular → verb+S.
questions.learning_tip: NOBODY / EVERYONE / SOMEONE = Singular! Nobody KNOWS = add -S. 'Nobody know' is WRONG. Singular indefinite pronouns always take singular present-tense verbs.
questions.retry_hint: The subject is NOBODY, not the COOKING CLASS. Words like nobody and everyone act like ONE person. Ask: does a singular subject take the plain present verb, or the verb ending in -s?
