It was the last week of term and Class 3C had to complete their science project on insects. Each group had to observe an insect for two weeks, record what they saw and present their findings to the class.

Ten-year-old Maya was in a group with her friends Deen and Siti. Their insect was the ant. Every day after school, the three of them crouched by the ant colony near the school drain and watched carefully.

One afternoon, Siti noticed that the ants were carrying tiny white eggs. 'The queen is moving her eggs to a safer place,' Maya said. She read about this in a library book. Deen quickly took notes while Maya pointed out each ant's role.

On presentation day, their group went last. Maya spoke clearly about the ant colony's structure. Deen explained the roles of the queen, the worker ants and the soldier ants. Siti showed the photographs she took during their observations.

When they finished, Mrs Chen, their science teacher, nodded slowly. 'You three clearly spent a lot of time observing,' she said. 'This is what real science looks like.'

Maya smiled. She started the project thinking insects were boring. She ended it thinking they were one of the most fascinating creatures on Earth.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 2 has the same meaning as 'carefully watched to check progress'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Ignored' = paid no attention; 'organised' = arranged; 'distributed' = gave out. MONITORED = regularly checked on progress or activity.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: MONITORED = regularly watched or checked to see how something is developing. The teacher MONITORED the groups = she kept an eye on each team's progress throughout the session.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 3, what does 'it' refer to in 'Siva suggested they try it once more'?

options.2: The failed experiment that the group wanted to abandon

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 or 3. 'Try IT once more' = try the experiment again.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: PRONOUN REFERENCE: 'try IT once more.' What had they been doing that failed? The EXPERIMENT. IT = the failed experiment. Siva is encouraging the group not to give up and to attempt the experiment again.

mcq_questions.stem: Why does the writer say Siva 'surprised even himself' when the experiment worked?

options.1: Because Siva usually got everything right without any effort.
options.2: Because Siva had doubted whether he could lead the group to success.
options.3: Because Siva had expected to win first place easily.
options.4: Because no one in the class expected anyone to succeed.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking he always succeeded. 'Surprised himself' means he doubted his own ability.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: INFERENCE: 'Surprised HIMSELF' = even he did not believe they could succeed. He doubted his own ability. Option 2 = he was uncertain but pushed through. This shows internal doubt overcome by determination.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 1, is it True or False that Siva's group chose their project topic easily? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The passage says the group spent two whole lessons arguing about what to investigate — showing it was not easy at all.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1: the group SPENT TWO LESSONS ARGUING. ARGUING = disagreeing strongly. This shows it was NOT easy. Answer is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: What did each group member do during the presentation? Name all three roles.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: Maya spoke about the ant colony's structure. Deen explained the roles of the different ants. Siti showed the photographs she took.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students describe only one person's role instead of all three.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 4: MAYA spoke about structure, DEEN explained roles, SITI showed photographs. All three had different roles.

open_ended_questions.stem: What did Siti notice one afternoon? What did Maya say about it?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: Siti noticed that the ants were carrying tiny white eggs. Maya said the queen was moving her eggs to a safer place.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students describe only one part — what Siti saw OR what Maya said — instead of both.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 3 has TWO parts: (1) Siti NOTICED the ants carrying EGGS; (2) Maya explained the queen was moving them to a SAFER PLACE. Include both.

open_ended_questions.stem: How did Maya's opinion of insects change from the beginning to the end of the project?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: At the start, Maya thought insects were boring. By the end, she thought they were one of the most fascinating creatures on Earth.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students describe only the end opinion without mentioning how she felt at the start.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Last paragraph: she STARTED thinking insects were BORING and ENDED thinking they were FASCINATING. Always describe both the before and the after.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on his actions throughout the passage, describe TWO character traits of Siva with evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) PERSISTENT: when the experiment failed the first time, Siva suggested they try again rather than giving up — showing he did not quit when faced with difficulty. (ii) ENCOURAGING: he kept the group calm and motivated throughout, praising their efforts even when things went wrong.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'clever and hardworking' without precise traits or evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: TRAIT INFERENCE: PERSISTENT = suggested trying AGAIN after failure. ENCOURAGING = kept group CALM and MOTIVATED. Name trait + give evidence from passage = full marks.

questions.stem: A doctor's work is as ________ as a tightrope walk — one small mistake can have very serious consequences.
questions.trap_type: 'Easy' and 'safe' are opposites. 'Quick' doesn't capture the precision needed. DELICATE = requiring great care and precision.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! A doctor's work is AS DELICATE AS a tightrope walk = comparing the precision required to balancing on a tightrope. DELICATE = requiring extreme care. AS + ADJECTIVE + AS is the correct simile form.
questions.retry_hint: The comparison is a TIGHTROPE WALK, where ONE SMALL MISTAKE brings very serious consequences. Ask: does that call for something easy and safe, or for extreme care and precision? Match the adjective to the tightrope.

questions.stem: The surgeon had to ________ carefully so that the patient would recover well afterwards.
questions.trap_type: Only 'operate' relates to a surgeon's work. The other words belong to completely different contexts.
questions.learning_tip: To OPERATE = to perform a medical procedure on a patient. A surgeon OPERATES in a hospital theatre.
questions.retry_hint: The person doing it is a SURGEON, and afterwards the PATIENT must RECOVER well. Ask: which verb names the medical procedure a surgeon performs? 'Decorate', 'celebrate' and 'navigate' belong to completely different jobs.

questions.stem: The plumber decided to ________ the old leaking pipes and replace them with new ones.
questions.trap_type: 'Give in' = surrender; 'run away' = flee; 'put off' = delay. TAKE OUT = remove something from its place.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: TAKE OUT = remove something from where it is fixed or stored. The plumber TOOK OUT the old pipes = he removed them completely. TAKE + OUT work together as one meaning.
questions.retry_hint: The old LEAKING PIPES are going to be REPLACED with new ones, so they must first be removed. Ask: which phrasal verb means to pull something from where it is fixed? 'Give in' means surrender, and 'put off' means delay.

questions.stem: When the young chef's dish won first prize at the competition, she was ________ — all her late nights of practice had paid off.
questions.trap_type: 'Under the weather' = ill; 'at a loss' = confused; 'in hot water' = in trouble. ON CLOUD NINE = extremely happy.
questions.learning_tip: IDIOM: ON CLOUD NINE = feeling extremely happy and delighted. She was ON CLOUD NINE = her happiness was at its highest. Idioms cannot be understood word by word!
questions.retry_hint: Her dish WON FIRST PRIZE and all her LATE NIGHTS of practice paid off. Ask: does the idiom describe pure delight, or illness, or confusion, or trouble? An idiom cannot be read word by word.

questions.stem: The lawyer studied all the evidence carefully before ________ her client in court.
questions.trap_type: 'Arresting' is done by police, not lawyers. 'Defending' = arguing in support of someone in a legal case.
questions.learning_tip: DEFENDING = arguing on behalf of someone in a court of law to prove they are not guilty. A defence lawyer DEFENDS her client.
questions.retry_hint: The lawyer STUDIED ALL THE EVIDENCE and now speaks for her CLIENT IN COURT. Ask: which verb means to argue in support of someone? 'Arresting' is police work, and 'ignoring' would abandon the client.

questions.stem: Everyone in the operating theatre ________ completely silent while the surgeon carries out a procedure.
questions.trap_type: EVERYONE = singular → verb+S.
questions.learning_tip: EVERYONE / NOBODY / SOMEONE = Singular! Everyone STAYS = add -S. 'Everyone stay' is WRONG. Singular indefinite pronouns always take singular present-tense verbs.
questions.retry_hint: The subject is EVERYONE, not 'the operating theatre'. Words like everyone and nobody behave like ONE person. Ask: in the present tense, does a singular subject take the plain verb, or the verb with -s?

questions.stem: The head chef has ________ a brand-new menu for the restaurant's grand reopening this month.
questions.trap_type: HAS + past participle = present perfect. CREATE → CREATED (regular).
questions.learning_tip: HAS + past participle = present perfect. The chef HAS CREATED a new menu = done recently and ready now. CREATE → CREATED (regular verb, add -d).
questions.retry_hint: HAS already stands in the sentence, so the blank must partner with it. Ask: after 'has', do we need the plain verb, the -s form, the -ing form, or the past participle? Only one of them builds a present perfect.

questions.stem: The nurse ________ the patient's temperature when the doctor suddenly called for her assistance.
questions.trap_type: 'The doctor called' = sudden interrupting event. The nurse was already checking = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: The doctor CALLED = sudden past event. The nurse was already in the middle of checking = WAS CHECKING (past continuous). Was/were + verb-ing = action in progress when interrupted.
questions.retry_hint: The doctor SUDDENLY CALLED for help, cutting across something the nurse had already started. Ask: which choice shows an action still in progress in the past? A plain past verb only reports a finished action.

questions.stem: The surgeon's hands are far ________ than most people's — years of practice have made them extremely precise.
questions.trap_type: 'Most steady' = superlative; 'more steadier' is WRONG. STEADIER = comparative of 'steady' (short adj ending -y: change y to i, add -er).
questions.learning_tip: Short adjective ending in -Y → change Y to I, add -ER. Steady → STEADIER. 'More steadier' is ALWAYS WRONG. STEADIER THAN = comparing the surgeon's hands to others'.
questions.retry_hint: THAN compares the surgeon's hands with MOST PEOPLE'S, and this adjective ends in -y. Ask: does a short adjective take an ending, or does it need 'most' in front? And never place 'more' before a word that already carries that ending.

questions.stem: The pilot landed the plane safely ________ the storm was getting stronger by the minute.
questions.trap_type: 'Because' introduces a reason; 'so' introduces a result. The pilot landing safely despite a storm = a contrast = although.
questions.learning_tip: ALTHOUGH = despite the fact that. The pilot landed safely ALTHOUGH the storm was strong = he succeeded despite the difficulty.
questions.retry_hint: The two halves fight each other: the plane landed SAFELY even while the STORM was getting stronger. Ask: which joining word signals a contrast? 'Because' gives a reason, and 'so' gives a result.

questions.stem: Becoming a doctor takes at least ten years of study and training, ________ it?
questions.trap_type: Positive present simple ('takes') → negative question tag. TAKES → doesn't it.
questions.learning_tip: Positive present simple → negative tag. Becoming a doctor TAKES ten years, DOESN'T it? POSITIVE → NEGATIVE. Present simple → DOES/DOESN'T. 'Doesn't it' (not 'isn't it' — that is for 'to be').
questions.retry_hint: The statement has no 'is' or 'are' - it runs on the plain present verb TAKES. Ask: which helping verb stands in for a plain present verb inside a tag? And after a positive statement, is the tag positive or negative?

questions.stem: "Please show ________ identification card to the officer at the gate," the guard said.
questions.trap_type: Before a noun ('identification card'), use a possessive adjective. 'You' is a subject pronoun and cannot describe a noun.
questions.learning_tip: Before 'identification card' (a noun), use a POSSESSIVE ADJECTIVE: YOUR identification card. 'You card' is wrong.
questions.retry_hint: The blank sits in front of the noun IDENTIFICATION CARD, so it must show who the card belongs to. Ask: can a subject pronoun like 'you' describe a noun? 'Yours' must stand alone, and 'yourself' points back at the doer.

questions.stem: The construction workers built the entire bridge ________ without any outside help.
questions.trap_type: 'The construction workers' = they = plural third person → reflexive = themselves. 'Ourselves' = first person plural.
questions.learning_tip: 'The construction workers' = THEY (plural, third person). Reflexive = THEMSELVES. They built it THEMSELVES = without outside help.
questions.retry_hint: The subject is THE CONSTRUCTION WORKERS - several people, and they are not the speaker. Ask: does the reflexive pronoun point back at one man, one woman, at us, or at them? Match it to who actually did the building.

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Verb forms of 'work')

questions.context_check: Passage: 'My father enjoys (1)________ as a paramedic.' Signal: 'enjoys + ___' = gerund (verb-ing). Pattern: enjoy + verb-ing → working.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'to work' instead of the gerund after 'enjoys'.
questions.learning_tip: ENJOY + verb-ing: enjoys WORKING as a paramedic. After 'enjoys', always add -ING.
questions.retry_hint: Look at the verb right in front: ENJOYS. Ask: after enjoy, do we use an infinitive, a bare verb, or the -ing form? Enjoy is one of those verbs that only ever accepts a gerund.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'He (2)________ at the hospital every day, including weekends.' Signal: 'every day' = regular habit = simple present. Subject 'He' = singular → works.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'work' (plural form) forgetting that 'He' is a singular subject.
questions.learning_tip: 'Every day' = habit = simple present. He (singular) → WORKS at the hospital including weekends.
questions.retry_hint: EVERY DAY, INCLUDING WEEKENDS signals a repeated habit, and HE counts as one person. Ask: does a singular subject in the present tense take the plain verb, or the one ending in -s?

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Last year, he (3)________ a night shift for three months in a row.' Signal: 'Last year' = past. 'Work' is regular: work → worked.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'work' (base form) ignoring the past signal 'Last year'.
questions.learning_tip: 'Last year' = past. 'Work' is regular: work → WORKED.
questions.retry_hint: LAST YEAR closes the time off - those night shifts are over. Ask: is this verb regular? If it is, which ending does the plain form take for a completed past action?

questions.context_check: Passage: 'While he (4)________ on a difficult case, a second emergency call came in.' Signal: 'While he ___' = ongoing background action in the past. Subject 'he' = singular → was working. Interrupted by 'a second emergency call came in'.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'worked' (simple past) missing the ongoing background signal 'while he'.
questions.learning_tip: 'While he ___' = ongoing background past action = past continuous. He WAS WORKING on a case when the call came in.
questions.retry_hint: WHILE HE marks a long background action, and then a SECOND EMERGENCY call cut across it. Ask: which form shows an action still running in the past? A plain past verb would report it as finished.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Two other paramedics (5)________ alongside him at the same time.' Signal: same past time frame, plural subject 'two other paramedics' + ongoing parallel action → were working.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'worked' (simple past) instead of the past continuous for an ongoing parallel action.
questions.learning_tip: Two other paramedics = plural. They were doing it at the same past moment = WERE WORKING (past continuous).
questions.retry_hint: TWO OTHER PARAMEDICS are plural, and they act AT THE SAME TIME as he does. Ask: which past form shows several people in the middle of an action? Match the helping verb to a plural subject.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Father always wanted (6)________ in a job that helps people.' Signal: 'wanted + ___' = infinitive. Pattern: want + to + base verb → to work.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'working' instead of the infinitive after 'wanted'.
questions.learning_tip: 'Want TO + base verb': wanted TO WORK in a job that helps people. Always use the infinitive after 'wanted'.
questions.retry_hint: Father WANTED something, and that verb calls for an infinitive after it. Ask: after 'wanted', do you use the -ing form, the bare verb, or the infinitive with its particle in front? Say each one aloud.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'He says all paramedics should (7)________ calmly even in the most difficult situations.' Signal: 'should + ___' = modal verb + base form. Never add -s or -ing after a modal.
questions.trap_type: Students add -s or -ing after the modal verb 'should'.
questions.learning_tip: After modal verbs (should, must, can, will), always use the BASE form: should WORK. Never 'should works' or 'should working'.
questions.retry_hint: SHOULD belongs with the modal family, and a modal never allows an ending on the verb after it. Ask: do you add -s, add -ing, or leave the verb bare after should, must and can?

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Right now, Father (8)________ the early morning shift at the ambulance station.' Signal: 'Right now' = present continuous. Subject 'Father' = singular → is working.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'works' (simple present habit) missing the 'right now' signal for present continuous.
questions.learning_tip: 'Right now' = present continuous. Father (singular) → IS WORKING the early morning shift right now.
questions.retry_hint: RIGHT NOW points at this very moment, and FATHER counts as one person. Ask: which form shows an action happening as we speak? A plain present verb would only describe a habit.

C.passage: My father enjoys (1)________ as a paramedic. He (2)________ at the hospital every day, including weekends. Last year, he (3)________ a night shift for three months in a row. While he (4)________ on a difficult case one evening, a second emergency call came in. Two other paramedics (5)________ alongside him at the same time to manage both situations. Father always wanted (6)________ in a job that helps people in their darkest moments. He says all paramedics should (7)________ calmly even in the most difficult situations. Right now, Father (8)________ the early morning shift at the ambulance station.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: My aunt is a nurse at a government hospital. She chose this (1)________ because she wanted to care for sick people and make a difference in their lives. Every day, she puts on her white (2)________ before heading to the ward. She looks after many (3)________ who are recovering from illnesses and operations. The work is demanding and she often comes home (4)________ after a long shift. But she never complains. She is one of the most (5)________ workers I know — she gives her best every single day without fail.

questions.trap_type: Students may write 'job' which is not in the box. PROFESSION = a type of work that requires special training or education.
questions.learning_tip: A PROFESSION = a type of work requiring special training. Nursing is a PROFESSION because nurses need years of study and training.
questions.retry_hint: She CHOSE THIS one because she WANTED TO CARE FOR SICK PEOPLE, and nursing needs years of study. Ask: which box word names a kind of work that requires special training? 'Medicine' is a substance, not a job.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'white... before heading to the ward' = nurses wear a uniform at work.
questions.learning_tip: A UNIFORM = a special set of clothes worn by people in the same job or group. Nurses wear a white UNIFORM.
questions.retry_hint: The clue is WHITE, and she puts it on BEFORE HEADING TO THE WARD. Ask: which box word names the special clothing worn by everyone in the same job? An 'appointment' is a fixed meeting, not clothing.

questions.trap_type: Students may write 'people' which is not in the box. PATIENTS = people receiving medical treatment.
questions.learning_tip: PATIENTS = people who are receiving medical care in a hospital or clinic. A nurse looks after PATIENTS in the ward.
questions.retry_hint: She LOOKS AFTER many people who are RECOVERING FROM ILLNESSES AND OPERATIONS. Ask: which box word names the people who receive medical care? Careful - one distractor describes somebody who cannot wait.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'after a long shift' and 'demanding work' = very tired = exhausted.
questions.learning_tip: EXHAUSTED = extremely tired after a lot of physical or mental effort. Nurses are often EXHAUSTED after a long shift.
questions.retry_hint: The work is DEMANDING and she COMES HOME after A LONG SHIFT. Ask: which box word means tired right to the bone? The blank describes her, not the job she does.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'gives her best every single day without fail' = committed and hardworking = dedicated.
questions.learning_tip: DEDICATED = fully committed to a job or cause and working hard for it. A DEDICATED nurse gives her best every single day.
questions.retry_hint: The clue follows: she GIVES HER BEST EVERY SINGLE DAY WITHOUT FAIL and NEVER COMPLAINS. Ask: which box word means fully committed to the job? 'Impatient' would say the exact opposite.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.error_type: Homophone confusion — here (place) vs hear (to listen)
questions.trap_type: 'here' (place) when the sentence needs 'hear' (ears).
questions.learning_tip: HEAR = detect sound with ears. HERE = at this place. Test: 'We could HEAR the excitement' → use ears? YES → HEAR. HEAR = ears. HERE = location.
questions.retry_hint: The sentence is about the EXCITEMENT reaching you along the CORRIDOR - a sound, not a place. Ask: does the underlined word belong to your ears, or does it mean 'at this spot'? One spelling hides EAR inside it.

questions.trap_type: 'buyed' applies the regular -ed rule. BUY is irregular: buy → bought.
questions.learning_tip: BUY → BOUGHT (irregular past). NEVER 'buyed'. Irregular verbs change completely: buy → bought, teach → taught, catch → caught. Memorise these — they do not follow the -ed rule.
questions.retry_hint: BUYED has been built with the regular -ed rule, but this verb refuses it. Ask: what did the paramedic do about the FIRST AID KIT back then? The verb changes shape completely, exactly as 'catch' becomes 'caught'.

questions.trap_type: 'taked' applies the regular -ed rule. TAKE is irregular: take → took.
questions.learning_tip: TAKE → TOOK (irregular past). NEVER 'taked'. Irregular verbs do not follow the -ed rule: take → took, make → made, give → gave. These must be memorised.
questions.retry_hint: TAKED copies the regular -ed pattern onto a verb that will not accept it. Ask: how do you say it about last Friday - 'she ___ her seat'? Think of how 'shake' changes, and follow the same path.

questions.error_type: Subject-verb agreement — plural subject (some of the chairs)
questions.trap_type: 'Some of the chairs' is plural. Students write 'was' (singular).
questions.learning_tip: Plural subject → plural verb! SOME OF THE CHAIRS WERE broken = CHAIRS is plural → WERE. Find the main noun: CHAIRS = plural → WERE, not WAS.
questions.retry_hint: Find the real subject: SOME OF THE CHAIRS - more than one. Ask: does a plural subject take the singular form of 'to be', or the plural one? Do not match the verb to the little word 'some' alone.

questions.trap_type: Students write a plain plural and leave out the apostrophe that shows ownership.
questions.learning_tip: The cards BELONG TO the speakers -> SPEAKERS' cards (apostrophe after the -s for a plural). Singular: speaker's.
questions.retry_hint: The THANK-YOU CARDS belong to the SPEAKERS, and there were several of them. Ask: does a plain -s show ownership, or does it only make a plural? Where must the apostrophe sit when the owners are many?

E.passage: Last Friday, we had a 'Careers Day' at school and many professionals came to speak to us. We could here (1) the excitement in the corridor before the first visitor arrived. A paramedic explained that he buyed (2) his first aid kit during his very first year of training. Then a lawyer entered and taked (3) her seat at the front of the hall. Some of the chairs was (4) broken and had to be replaced quickly before the session began. At the end, we signed the speakers (5) thank-you cards and placed them in individual envelopes.

questions.sentence_a: The interviewer asked the young doctor a question.
questions.sentence_b: Do you enjoy your work at the hospital?
questions.instruction: Combine into one sentence using reported speech. Begin: 'The interviewer asked...'
questions.model_answer: The interviewer asked the young doctor if he enjoyed his work at the hospital.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'asked if does he enjoy' (wrong word order) or keep 'you/your'.
questions.learning_tip: YES/NO question → reported speech: ASKED + IF + subject + verb (normal order). 'Do YOU enjoy YOUR work?' → asked IF HE ENJOYED HIS work. Pronoun: you → he, your → his. Tense: do → did (enjoy). Word order is normal after 'if'.
questions.retry_hint: A yes/no question becoming REPORTED SPEECH. Ask three things: which joining word follows 'asked'? Does the question order survive, or does it turn into statement order? And what must happen to 'you', 'your' and the helper 'do'?

questions.sentence_a: The road was blocked by an accident.
questions.sentence_b: The ambulance could not reach the hospital on time.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'so'.
questions.model_answer: The road was blocked by an accident, so the ambulance could not reach the hospital on time.
questions.trap_type: Students reverse the clauses, writing 'The ambulance could not reach the hospital on time so the road was blocked by an accident'.
questions.learning_tip: Blocked road = CAUSE. Ambulance could not reach = RESULT. Cause + SO + result. The cause always comes BEFORE 'so'.
questions.retry_hint: The road BLOCKED by an accident is the cause; the ambulance's delay is the result. Ask: which half must stand first when you join them with 'so'? The cause always comes before the result.

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage_title: The Best Job in the World
G.passage:
Nine-year-old Preethi could never make up her mind about what she wanted to be when she grew up. One week she wanted to be a scientist, the next a pilot, and the week after that, a baker.

One afternoon, her school organised a Career Day. Parents came in to talk about their jobs. The first speaker was Mr Hassan, a police officer. He told the students about the importance of keeping the community safe and working as a team.

The second speaker was Dr Lim, a children's doctor. She said the best part of her job was seeing a sick child recover and go home healthy. 'Nothing makes me happier,' she said with a warm smile.

The last speaker was Mrs Gomez, a school librarian. She spoke softly about how books could take a person anywhere in the world. 'Every book I shelve is a door to a new adventure,' she said.

After Career Day, Preethi sat quietly in the garden at home. She thought about all three speakers. Each of them loved what they did. Each of them helped people in a different way.

Preethi picked up the book she was reading and smiled. She still did not know what she wanted to be. But she knew one thing for certain — the best job was the one that made you feel proud every single day.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 1 has the same meaning as 'moved very quickly because of urgency'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Strolled' = walked slowly; 'waited' = stayed put; 'gathered' = collected. RUSHED = moved very fast because of urgency.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: RUSHED = moved very quickly, driven by urgency or a deadline. The paramedic RUSHED to the scene = she moved fast because every second counted.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 3, what does 'it' refer to in 'she said it was the most rewarding job she had ever done'?

options.2: Being a doctor and caring for patients

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking 'it' = the hospital. But 'it was the most rewarding job' = IT = the work/job itself.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: PRONOUN REFERENCE: 'IT was the most rewarding job.' IT = the JOB of being a doctor. The sentence is about what SHE DOES — her career of caring for patients — not where she works.

mcq_questions.stem: Why does the writer end the passage with the question 'What will you be?'

options.1: Because the writer does not know what job they want.
options.2: To suggest that every reader is capable of becoming whatever they choose to work hard for.
options.3: Because the passage is only about one type of job.
options.4: To prove that being a doctor is the best career.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 or 4. The question is directed at the reader and opens a possibility.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: INFERENCE: 'What WILL YOU be?' = the question is directed at the READER. It implies that every reader has the potential to choose their own path — the passage is about the value of all occupations. It invites reflection, not prescription.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 1, is it True or False that all the jobs described in the passage are dangerous? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The passage describes many types of jobs — including chefs and teachers — that are not dangerous. Only some, like firefighters and paramedics, involve danger.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1 lists many jobs: chefs, teachers, firefighters, doctors. Only SOME involve danger. Not ALL are dangerous. Answer is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: What did Mrs Gomez say about books?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: She said that every book she shelved was a door to a new adventure.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'she liked books' which is too vague. The passage gives a specific quote.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 4: 'Every book I shelve is a DOOR TO A NEW ADVENTURE.' Use the specific words from the passage.

open_ended_questions.stem: What did Preethi notice about all three speakers after Career Day? Give TWO things they had in common.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) Each of them loved what they did. (ii) Each of them helped people in a different way.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students describe individual speakers instead of identifying what the three had in common.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 5: (1) 'Each of them LOVED what they did' and (2) 'Each of them HELPED people in a different way.' These are the two things in common.

open_ended_questions.stem: Find a phrase in paragraph 2 that tells us what Mr Hassan said was important about his job.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: 'Keeping the community safe and working as a team.'
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students describe his job title (police officer) instead of quoting the specific phrase about what he valued.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 2: Mr Hassan spoke about 'KEEPING THE COMMUNITY SAFE and WORKING AS A TEAM.' Find and quote the specific phrase.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on the passage, describe TWO character traits of the young doctor with evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) DEDICATED: the doctor said she worked night shifts for three years before becoming a fully qualified surgeon — showing she put in sustained effort over a long time. (ii) COMPASSIONATE: she said the most rewarding part of her job was seeing patients recover and return to their families — showing she genuinely cared about others.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'hardworking and kind' without precise traits or evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: TRAIT INFERENCE: DEDICATED = worked night shifts for THREE YEARS. COMPASSIONATE = moved by seeing patients RECOVER and return to families. Name trait + give evidence = full marks.

questions.stem: The lion's roar was as ________ as thunder — every visitor in the zoo stopped what they were doing and turned to look.
questions.trap_type: 'Soft' and 'quiet' are opposites of thunder. 'Distant' = far away. LOUD = producing strong powerful sound.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! The roar was AS LOUD AS thunder = comparing the lion's roar to the power of thunder. LOUD = producing great sound. AS + ADJECTIVE + AS is the correct simile form — never use an adverb.
questions.retry_hint: The roar is compared to THUNDER, and every VISITOR stopped and turned to look. Ask: is thunder soft, quiet or distant - or does it fill the whole sky with sound? Match the adjective to the thunder.

questions.stem: The zookeeper ________ fresh fruit and vegetables to the elephants at feeding time every morning.
questions.trap_type: 'Threw away' means discarded. 'Hid' means concealed. Only 'distributed' = handed out to multiple animals.
questions.learning_tip: DISTRIBUTED = gave things out to several people or animals one by one. The zookeeper DISTRIBUTED food to the elephants.
questions.retry_hint: The zookeeper hands FRESH FRUIT AND VEGETABLES to the ELEPHANTS at feeding time. Ask: which verb means to give things out to many animals, one by one? 'Threw away' discards the food, and 'collected' brings it back instead.

questions.stem: After a long day at the zoo, the children were too tired to ________ and had to be carried to the car.
questions.trap_type: 'Stay on' = remain; 'sit down' = take a seat; 'give up' = stop trying. WALK ON = continue walking forward.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: WALK ON = continue moving forward without stopping. The children were too tired to WALK ON = they could not continue walking. WALK + ON work together as one meaning.
questions.retry_hint: The children were TOO TIRED and had TO BE CARRIED TO THE CAR - their legs could not keep going. Ask: which phrasal verb means to continue moving forward? 'Sit down' stops, and 'give up' means quitting.

questions.stem: When the baby elephant walked up and touched the little girl's hand with its trunk, she was ________ — it was the best moment of her life.
questions.trap_type: 'Under the weather' = ill; 'in hot water' = in trouble; 'at a loss' = confused. OVER THE MOON = extremely happy.
questions.learning_tip: IDIOM: OVER THE MOON = feeling extremely happy and excited. She was OVER THE MOON = the best feeling of happiness. The moon is so far — being 'over' it means the very highest happiness!
questions.retry_hint: The baby elephant TOUCHED THE LITTLE GIRL'S HAND, and it was THE BEST MOMENT OF HER LIFE. Ask: does the idiom describe the highest joy, or illness, or trouble, or confusion? Idioms cannot be read word by word.

questions.stem: The zoo's ________ programme helped bring the number of endangered rhinos back from very low numbers.
questions.trap_type: 'Destruction' and 'hunting' harm animals. 'Decorating' is irrelevant. Only 'breeding' = a programme to reproduce and increase animal numbers.
questions.learning_tip: BREEDING = producing offspring, especially as part of a conservation programme. A BREEDING programme helps endangered animals reproduce safely.
questions.retry_hint: The programme helped the number of ENDANGERED RHINOS climb back up from very low numbers. Ask: which word names work that helps animals produce young? 'Hunting' and 'destruction' would push the numbers down instead.

questions.stem: Nobody in our group ________ the polar bear clearly when it hides behind the rocks at the back of its den.
questions.trap_type: NOBODY is singular, so the plain verb and 'are seeing' are both wrong, and 'have seen' cannot agree with a singular subject either.
questions.learning_tip: NOBODY / EVERYONE / SOMEONE = singular. Nobody SEES = add -s in the present tense. 'Nobody see' and 'nobody have seen' are both wrong.
questions.retry_hint: The subject is NOBODY, however many people the group holds. Words like nobody act like ONE person. Ask: in the present tense, does a singular subject take the plain verb, or the verb ending in -s?

questions.stem: The zoo has ________ a new underwater viewing tunnel for visitors to watch the sea lions swim.
questions.trap_type: HAS + past participle = present perfect. OPEN → OPENED (regular).
questions.learning_tip: HAS + past participle = present perfect. The zoo HAS OPENED a new tunnel = it was completed recently and is now available to visitors. OPEN → OPENED (regular verb).
questions.retry_hint: HAS is already there, so the blank has to partner with it. Ask: after 'has', which form completes a present perfect - the plain verb, the -s form, the -ing form, or the past participle?

questions.stem: The monkey ________ from branch to branch when the keeper called it back for feeding time.
questions.trap_type: 'The keeper called it back' = sudden interrupting event. The monkey was already swinging = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: The keeper CALLED IT BACK = sudden past event. The monkey was already in the middle of swinging = WAS SWINGING (past continuous). Was/were + verb-ing = action in progress when interrupted.
questions.retry_hint: The keeper CALLED IT BACK for feeding time: a sudden event that cut across something the monkey had already started. Ask: which choice shows an action still in progress in the past?

questions.stem: The giraffe enclosure is far ________ than the lion area — you can walk all the way around it in ten minutes.
questions.trap_type: 'Largest' = superlative; 'more larger' is WRONG. LARGER = comparative of 'large'.
questions.learning_tip: Short adjective + -ER = comparative. Large → LARGER. The giraffe enclosure is LARGER THAN the lion area = comparing two areas. 'More larger' is ALWAYS WRONG — never add BOTH 'more' AND '-er'.
questions.retry_hint: THAN compares two enclosures, and this adjective is short. Ask: does a short adjective take an ending, or does it need 'most' in front? And you can never use 'more' together with that ending.

questions.stem: We queued for twenty minutes ________ we could watch the sea lion feeding show.
questions.trap_type: 'Because' introduces a past reason. 'So that' introduces a forward-looking purpose — they queued FOR THE PURPOSE of watching the show.
questions.learning_tip: SO THAT = in order to achieve a goal. We queued SO THAT we could watch the show. This shows the purpose of the action.
questions.retry_hint: They QUEUED FOR TWENTY MINUTES with a goal in mind: watching the sea lion show. Ask: which joining phrase gives the PURPOSE of an action, rather than a past reason or a contrast? 'But' and 'although' both signal opposition.

questions.stem: The penguin feeding show is one of the most popular attractions at the zoo, ________ it?
questions.trap_type: Positive present 'to be' ('is') → negative question tag. IS → isn't it.
questions.learning_tip: Positive present 'to be' → negative tag. The show IS popular, ISN'T it? POSITIVE → NEGATIVE. IS → ISN'T. Tag questions: match the 'to be' verb of the main clause.
questions.retry_hint: A tag mirrors the main verb, and the statement uses IS. Ask: after a positive statement, does the tag turn negative or stay positive? And should it keep the same verb rather than borrow 'does'?

questions.stem: "Look at ________ baby orangutan over there — it is holding on to its mother!" said Jas.
questions.trap_type: 'Baby orangutan' is singular (→ this or that). 'Over there' = far away from the speaker = that.
questions.learning_tip: 'Baby orangutan' = singular → this or that. 'Over there' = the animal is far away = THAT baby orangutan.
questions.retry_hint: OVER THERE tells you the baby ORANGUTAN sits far from the speaker, and there is only ONE animal. Ask: which pointing word suits a single thing at a distance? 'These' and 'those' are for several things.

questions.stem: The children enjoyed ________ so much that they asked to visit the zoo again the very next weekend.
questions.trap_type: 'The children enjoyed themselves' = reflexive pronoun for third person plural. Students pick 'them' (object) or 'they' (subject).
questions.learning_tip: 'The children enjoyed THEMSELVES' = they had a great time. THEMSELVES is the reflexive pronoun for 'they' (third person plural).
questions.retry_hint: The children ENJOYED the day so much that they asked to VISIT THE ZOO AGAIN. Ask: which pronoun points back at the same plural people who did the enjoying? 'Them' and 'they' cannot do that job.

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Prepositions of place and movement)

questions.context_check: Passage: 'We arrived (1)________ the zoo entrance at half past nine.' Signal: specific location point = AT. 'Arrived AT the entrance' = AT is used for arrival at a specific place.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'in' (inside the zoo) or 'on' (surface). AT is correct for a named arrival point.
questions.learning_tip: Use AT for a specific location point: arrived AT the zoo entrance, waited AT the gate. AT shows you are at that exact spot.
questions.retry_hint: The class ARRIVED, and the blank names one exact point: THE ZOO ENTRANCE, a single spot. Ask: which preposition marks an exact arrival point, rather than being enclosed or resting upon a surface?

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The flamingos were standing (2)________ a shallow pool near the entrance.' Signal: inside the pool (enclosed water area) = IN. Animals stand IN water, not ON it.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'on' (surface) instead of 'in' (inside an enclosed space or liquid).
questions.learning_tip: IN = inside an enclosed space or immersed in something. The flamingos stood IN a shallow pool = their legs were inside the water.
questions.retry_hint: The flamingos STOOD with their LONG LEGS HIDDEN UNDER THE WATER - they are surrounded by the pool, not perched above it. Ask: which preposition means enclosed or immersed, rather than resting upon a surface?

questions.context_check: Passage: 'We walked (3)________ the winding path that led to the big cat section.' Signal: following the length of a path = ALONG. 'Walked ALONG the path' = followed its direction.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'on' (surface of the path) instead of 'along' (following the path's direction and length).
questions.learning_tip: ALONG = following the line or length of something: walk ALONG a path, walk ALONG the river. It shows movement in the direction of something extended.
questions.retry_hint: The blank comes before a WINDING PATH that FOLLOWED THE EDGE OF THE LAKE. Ask: which preposition means moving from one end of something long towards the other, following its whole length? 'On' would only touch the surface.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'We walked (4)________ a glass tunnel where sharks swam above our heads.' Signal: entering one side and exiting the other side of an enclosed space = THROUGH. 'Walked THROUGH a tunnel' = passed inside from one end to the other.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'in' (inside but not passing through) instead of 'through' (entering and exiting).
questions.learning_tip: THROUGH = enter one side and come out the other: walk THROUGH a tunnel, drive THROUGH a forest. It shows complete passage inside something.
questions.retry_hint: They had to PASS a DARK TUNNEL and COME OUT AT THE OTHER END. Ask: which preposition shows entering one side of something and leaving by the other side? 'In' would leave them stuck inside.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'We then walked (5)________ the reptile house without going inside.' Signal: moved beside and beyond a place without entering = PAST. 'Walked PAST the reptile house' = went by it without stopping.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'through' (they did not go inside) or 'along'. PAST = go by something without entering it.
questions.learning_tip: PAST = moved alongside and beyond a place without stopping or entering. We walked PAST the reptile house = we went by it without going in.
questions.retry_hint: They walked by the REPTILE HOUSE WITHOUT GOING IN, because some were afraid of snakes. Ask: which preposition means going alongside a place and beyond it, without ever entering?

questions.context_check: Passage: 'My little brother sat (6)________ me on the bench while we rested.' Signal: next to, at the side of a person = BESIDE. 'Sat BESIDE me' = sat right next to me.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'on' (the bench) instead of the word that shows position next to a person.
questions.learning_tip: BESIDE = right next to someone or something. My brother sat BESIDE me on the same bench.
questions.retry_hint: The brother SAT ON THE SAME WOODEN BENCH and SHARED HIS SANDWICHES - the two of them are side by side. Ask: which preposition means right next to a person? 'On' is already doing the work of the bench.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The zookeeper placed a large watermelon (7)________ the ground for the elephant.' Signal: resting on the surface of the ground = ON. 'Placed ON the ground' = put it on the surface.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'in' (inside the ground) or 'at' (a specific location point). ON = resting on a surface.
questions.learning_tip: ON = resting on a surface: placed ON the ground, put ON the table. Use ON for things touching the top of a surface.
questions.retry_hint: The banana was left lying against the flat surface of THE GROUND, where a cheeky MONKEY could snatch it. Ask: which preposition shows something resting upon a surface, rather than enclosed or moving?

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The elephant picked it up with its trunk and dropped it (8)________ its mouth.' Signal: movement entering an enclosed space = INTO. 'Dropped INTO its mouth' = the watermelon moved and entered the mouth.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'in' (location inside) instead of 'into' (movement entering). INTO shows the direction of entry.
questions.learning_tip: INTO = movement entering a space: dropped INTO its mouth, jumped INTO the water. INTO shows something moving and entering an enclosed space.
questions.retry_hint: The monkey PEELED THE BANANA and POPPED IT somewhere IN ONE QUICK MOVEMENT: the fruit travels and ends up inside its mouth. Ask: which preposition shows movement entering a space, not just sitting there?

C.passage: Our class arrived (1)________ the zoo entrance at eight o'clock sharp. The first animals we saw were the flamingos, which stood (2)________ a shallow pool with their long legs hidden under the water. We then walked (3)________ a winding path that followed the edge of the lake all the way to the monkey house. To reach the butterfly garden, we had to pass (4)________ a dark tunnel and come out at the other end. On the way back, we walked (5)________ the reptile house without going in, because a few of us were afraid of snakes. At lunchtime, my brother sat (6)________ me on the same wooden bench and shared his sandwiches. Someone had left a banana (7)________ the ground, and a cheeky monkey snatched it up. It peeled the banana and popped it (8)________ its mouth in one quick movement.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: At the zoo's safari section, we saw animals that live in the wild in Africa. The zebras and giraffes (1)________ freely across a wide open area that looked like their natural (2)________. The zookeeper explained that some of these animals are (3)________ because their numbers in the wild are very low. One of the tigers was in a large (4)________ surrounded by thick glass so visitors could watch it safely. During the visit, we also (5)________ a rare white lion resting in the shade. It was the first time I had ever seen one.

questions.trap_type: Students may write 'walked' which is not in the box. ROAMED = wandered freely over a large area.
questions.learning_tip: ROAMED = wandered or moved freely over a wide area. The zebras ROAMED across the open space = moved around freely.
questions.retry_hint: The zebras and giraffes moved FREELY ACROSS A WIDE OPEN AREA, with no fences to stop them. Ask: which box word is a past verb meaning to wander over a large space? 'Hibernate' means sleeping through the winter.

questions.trap_type: Students may write 'home' which is not in the box. HABITAT = the natural environment where an animal lives.
questions.learning_tip: HABITAT = the natural environment where a plant or animal normally lives. The savannah is the natural HABITAT of zebras and giraffes.
questions.retry_hint: The wide open area LOOKED LIKE THEIR NATURAL home in the wild. Ask: which box word names the natural surroundings where an animal normally lives? The blank follows 'natural', so it must be a noun.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'their numbers in the wild are very low' = at risk of dying out = endangered.
questions.learning_tip: ENDANGERED = at serious risk of becoming extinct because the population is very low. ENDANGERED animals need protection.
questions.retry_hint: The clue follows the blank: THEIR NUMBERS IN THE WILD ARE VERY LOW. Ask: which box word describes animals at serious risk of dying out? Careful - one distractor names the dying-out itself and is a noun.

questions.trap_type: Students may write 'cage' which is not in the box. ENCLOSURE = a fenced or walled area where animals are kept in a zoo.
questions.learning_tip: An ENCLOSURE = a fenced or walled area in a zoo where animals are kept. The tiger was in a large glass ENCLOSURE.
questions.retry_hint: The tiger was SURROUNDED BY THICK GLASS so that visitors could WATCH IT SAFELY. Ask: which box word names a fenced or walled space in a zoo? The blank follows 'a large', so it has to be a noun.

questions.trap_type: Students may write 'saw' which is not in the box. SPOTTED = noticed or caught sight of something, often something rare.
questions.learning_tip: SPOTTED = noticed something, especially something that is rare or hard to find. We SPOTTED a rare white lion = we caught sight of it.
questions.retry_hint: The white lion was RARE and RESTING IN THE SHADE, and it was the FIRST TIME the writer had ever seen one. Ask: which box word is a past verb meaning to catch sight of something hard to find?

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.error_type: Homophone confusion — here (place) vs hear (to listen)
questions.trap_type: 'here' (place) when 'hear' (ears) is needed.
questions.learning_tip: HEAR = detect sound with ears. HERE = at this place. 'We could HEAR the animals' → use ears? YES → HEAR. HEAR = ears. HERE = location.
questions.retry_hint: The class could not SEE the animals yet, but the sound still reached them. Ask: does the underlined word mean 'at this place', or does it belong to your ears? The two sound alike, so choose by meaning.

questions.trap_type: 'goed' applies the regular -ed rule. GO is irregular: go → went.
questions.learning_tip: GO → WENT (irregular past). NEVER 'goed'. GO changes completely in past tense: go → went. Irregular verbs do not follow the -ed rule.
questions.retry_hint: GOED has been built with the regular -ed rule, but this verb throws that rule away. Ask: how do you say it about last Saturday - 'we ___ straight to the reptile section'? Its past form looks nothing like the plain one.

questions.trap_type: 'finded' applies the regular -ed rule. FIND is irregular: find → found.
questions.learning_tip: FIND → FOUND (irregular past). NEVER 'finded'. Irregular verbs change completely: find → found, bind → bound, wind → wound. Memorise these.
questions.retry_hint: FINDED copies the -ed pattern onto a verb that refuses it. Ask: what did the keeper do with the small GECKO? The vowel changes instead, exactly as 'bind' becomes 'bound'.

questions.trap_type: 'The children' is plural. Students write 'was' (singular).
questions.learning_tip: Plural subject → plural verb! The CHILDREN WERE amazed = CHILDREN is plural → WERE. WAS is only for ONE thing. CHILDREN = plural → WERE.
questions.retry_hint: Find the real subject: THE CHILDREN - more than one person. Ask: does a plural subject take the singular form of 'to be', or the plural one? Match the verb to the subject, not to the nearest noun.

questions.trap_type: Students write a plain plural and leave out the apostrophe that shows ownership.
questions.learning_tip: The guestbook BELONGS TO the zookeepers -> ZOOKEEPERS' guestbook (apostrophe after the -s for a plural). Singular: zookeeper's.
questions.retry_hint: The GUESTBOOK belongs to the ZOOKEEPERS, and there are several of them. Ask: does a plain -s show ownership, or does it only make a plural? Where must the apostrophe sit when the owners are many?

E.passage: Last Saturday, our class visited the city zoo as part of a school excursion. When we arrived, we could here (1) the animals before we could see them. The guide showed us the map and we goed (2) straight to the reptile section first. There, a keeper finded (3) a small gecko hiding behind a rock and showed it to us carefully. The children was (4) amazed by the number of different species in just one enclosure. At the end, we signed the zookeepers (5) guestbook and left our feedback about the visit.

questions.sentence_a: The zookeeper asked the children a question.
questions.sentence_b: Can you guess what the cheetah eats?
questions.instruction: Combine into one sentence using reported speech. Begin: 'The zookeeper asked...'
questions.model_answer: The zookeeper asked the children if they could guess what the cheetah ate.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'asked if can they guess' (wrong word order) or keep 'you'.
questions.learning_tip: YES/NO question → reported speech: ASKED + IF + subject + verb (normal order). 'Can YOU guess?' → asked IF THEY COULD guess. Pronoun: you → they. Tense: can → could. Word order is normal after 'if'.
questions.retry_hint: A yes/no question turning into REPORTED SPEECH. Ask three things: which joining word follows 'asked'? Does the question order stay, or become statement order? And what happens to 'you' and to 'can'?

questions.sentence_a: The queue for the elephant ride was very long.
questions.sentence_b: We decided to skip it and watch the bird show instead.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'so'.
questions.model_answer: The queue for the elephant ride was very long, so we decided to skip it and watch the bird show instead.
questions.trap_type: Students reverse the clauses, writing 'We decided to skip it so the queue for the elephant ride was very long'.
questions.learning_tip: Long queue = CAUSE. Decided to skip = RESULT. Cause + SO + result. The cause always comes BEFORE 'so'.
questions.retry_hint: The QUEUE was VERY LONG - that is the cause, and skipping the ride is what followed. Ask: which half must stand in front when you join them with 'so'? The cause comes first, the result second.

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
Class 3B was on a school trip to the wildlife park. The students were excited, clutching their clipboards and worksheets. Their task was to observe one animal closely and write down three interesting facts about it.

Most students rushed to the lion enclosure or the elephant zone. But ten-year-old Faiz walked quietly to a smaller enclosure at the side. There, lying in the shade of a tall rock, was a cheetah.

The cheetah was asleep. Its spotted coat rose and fell with each slow breath. Faiz sat down on a bench and watched. He did not write anything yet. He just looked.

After ten minutes, the cheetah opened one eye. It looked directly at Faiz. Then it stretched, yawned and curled up again.

Faiz smiled and began to write. He wrote about the cheetah's spotted coat, its long tail that helped it balance when running, and the black lines on its face that looked like tear marks.

'You spent the whole time at one enclosure?' his friend asked after the trip.

'Yes,' said Faiz. 'And I learned more than anyone else today.'

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 2 has the same meaning as 'not moving at all and very still'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Crouched' = bent down; 'stretched' = extended; 'alert' = watchful and ready. MOTIONLESS = completely still, not moving at all.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: MOTIONLESS = completely without movement. The cheetah was MOTIONLESS = it did not move even a single muscle. MOTION = movement; MOTIONLESS = no movement at all (the suffix -LESS = without).

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 3, what does 'it' refer to in 'Kira pressed her nose against it and stared'?

options.2: The glass viewing panel of the cheetah enclosure

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 3 thinking 'it' = the camera. But 'pressed her nose against IT and stared' = she was pressing against the glass to look at the cheetah.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: PRONOUN REFERENCE: 'pressed her nose against IT.' What do you press your nose against to look into an enclosure? The GLASS PANEL. IT = the glass viewing panel. Context clue: she stared at the sleeping cheetah through it.

mcq_questions.stem: Why did Kira say 'I think it's dreaming about running' at the end of the passage?

options.1: Because she could see the cheetah's legs moving in its sleep.
options.2: Because she imagined that even a sleeping cheetah's spirit belonged to the wild, where it would run free.
options.3: Because the zookeeper told her cheetahs dream about running.
options.4: Because Kira wanted to make her classmates laugh.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking she saw movement. The sentence is poetic/imaginative — Kira is projecting her idea of the cheetah's inner nature.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: INFERENCE: Kira said 'I THINK it's dreaming about running.' This is her IMAGINATION — she sees a wild animal constrained in a zoo and imagines its spirit longing to run free. It is a poetic, empathetic statement, not a factual observation.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 1, is it True or False that Kira visited the zoo many times before? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The passage says it was Kira's first visit to the zoo — she had never seen most of the animals in real life before.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1: 'FIRST visit to the zoo.' FIRST = it had never happened before. Answer is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: What did the cheetah do after it opened one eye and looked at Faiz?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: It stretched, yawned and curled up again.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'it went back to sleep' which misses the specific actions described.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 4: the cheetah 'STRETCHED, YAWNED and CURLED UP again.' Give the specific sequence of actions.

open_ended_questions.stem: What THREE facts did Faiz write about the cheetah? Name any TWO.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) Its spotted coat. (ii) Its long tail that helped it balance when running. (Accept also: the black lines on its face that looked like tear marks.)
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students describe what the cheetah did (stretched, yawned) instead of the facts Faiz wrote down.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 5: Faiz wrote about (1) the SPOTTED COAT, (2) the long TAIL that helped it balance, and (3) the black lines like tear marks. Give any two.

open_ended_questions.stem: Find a phrase in paragraph 3 that shows Faiz was observing the cheetah very patiently.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: 'He just looked.'
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students quote 'He sat down on a bench' which describes his position, not his patient observation.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 3: 'He did not write anything yet. He JUST LOOKED.' This phrase shows he was simply watching patiently without rushing to write.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on her actions throughout the passage, describe TWO character traits of Kira with evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) OBSERVANT: Kira noticed the sleeping cheetah before anyone else in the group and was the first to press her nose against the glass to look — showing she paid close attention to her surroundings. (ii) IMAGINATIVE: rather than simply noting the cheetah was asleep, she imagined it was dreaming about running — showing a creative and empathetic way of seeing the world.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'curious and kind' without precise traits or evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: TRAIT INFERENCE: OBSERVANT = noticed the sleeping cheetah FIRST, pressed nose against glass. IMAGINATIVE = said it was 'dreaming about running' — a creative, empathetic statement. Name trait + evidence = full marks.

questions.stem: The puppy's eyes were as ________ as two shining buttons — black, round and full of life.
questions.trap_type: 'Dull' = lacking light; 'large' = big (but doesn't capture the shining quality); 'rough' = not smooth. BRIGHT = giving off a strong, clear light.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! The puppy's eyes were AS BRIGHT AS shining buttons = comparing the sparkle of the eyes to polished buttons. BRIGHT = giving off a clear, strong light. AS + ADJECTIVE + AS is the correct simile form.
questions.retry_hint: The eyes are compared to TWO SHINING BUTTONS - black, round and full of life. Ask: does something shining look dull and rough, or does it throw the light back at you? Match the adjective to the shine, not to the size.

questions.stem: The vet ________ the injured cat carefully to check for any broken bones.
questions.trap_type: 'Dropped' and 'released' would harm or free the cat. Only 'examined' = looked at and checked carefully.
questions.learning_tip: EXAMINED = looked at something or someone very carefully to find out information. A vet EXAMINES an animal to check its health.
questions.retry_hint: The vet needs to CHECK FOR ANY BROKEN BONES in the INJURED CAT. Ask: which verb means to look at something very carefully to find out its condition? 'Dropped' and 'released' would only make matters worse.

questions.stem: Before going on holiday, Priya asked her neighbour to ________ her goldfish while she was away.
questions.trap_type: 'Give up' = stop trying; 'run away' = flee; 'break into' = enter by force. LOOK AFTER = take care of someone or something.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: LOOK AFTER = take care of someone or something, especially while the owner is away. Priya asked her neighbour to LOOK AFTER her goldfish = keep it fed, alive and safe. LOOK + AFTER work together.
questions.retry_hint: Priya will be away on HOLIDAY, so somebody else must feed and care for the GOLDFISH. Ask: which phrasal verb means taking care of something while the owner is absent? 'Give up' means quitting, and 'break into' means forcing entry.

questions.stem: When the vet confirmed that the dog's leg was not broken, the whole family was ________ — they were so worried.
questions.trap_type: 'Under the weather' = ill; 'in hot water' = in trouble; 'at a loss' = confused. OVER THE MOON = extremely happy and relieved.
questions.learning_tip: IDIOM: OVER THE MOON = feeling extremely happy, delighted or relieved. The family was OVER THE MOON = they were overjoyed to hear good news about their pet. Idioms cannot be understood word by word!
questions.retry_hint: The vet CONFIRMED that the leg was NOT BROKEN, and the family had been SO WORRIED. Ask: does the idiom describe relief and delight, or illness, or trouble, or confusion? Idioms cannot be read word by word.

questions.stem: The fish tank needed to be kept ________ to keep the tropical fish healthy and active.
questions.trap_type: 'Frozen' = too cold; 'dim' = dark; 'arid' = very dry. Only 'immaculate' = perfectly clean, which is what a fish tank needs.
questions.learning_tip: IMMACULATE = perfectly clean, without any dirt or mess. A fish tank must be kept IMMACULATE so the fish stay healthy.
questions.retry_hint: The tank must stay this way TO KEEP THE TROPICAL FISH HEALTHY AND ACTIVE. Ask: which word means perfectly clean, with no dirt at all? 'Frozen' is about cold, 'dim' about light, and 'arid' about dryness.

questions.stem: Nobody in our neighbourhood ________ a pet as well-trained as Scout the golden retriever.
questions.trap_type: NOBODY = singular → verb+S.
questions.learning_tip: NOBODY / EVERYONE / SOMEONE = Singular! Nobody OWNS = add -S. 'Nobody own' is WRONG. Singular indefinite pronouns always take singular present-tense verbs.
questions.retry_hint: The subject is NOBODY, not 'our neighbourhood'. Words like nobody and everyone behave like ONE person. Ask: in the present tense, does a singular subject take the plain verb, or the one ending in -s?

questions.stem: The animal shelter has ________ over two hundred dogs to loving families since it opened last year.
questions.trap_type: HAS + past participle = present perfect. REHOME → REHOMED (regular).
questions.learning_tip: HAS + past participle = present perfect. The shelter HAS REHOMED two hundred dogs = started last year and still going. REHOME → REHOMED (regular verb, add -d).
questions.retry_hint: HAS stands in front of the blank, and the time stretches SINCE IT OPENED LAST YEAR right up to today. Ask: after 'has', which form builds a present perfect - the plain verb, the -s form, the -ing form, or the past participle?

questions.stem: The dog ________ on its blanket when the doorbell rang and startled it awake.
questions.trap_type: 'The doorbell rang' = sudden interrupting event. The dog was already sleeping = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: The doorbell RANG = sudden past event. The dog was already in the middle of sleeping = WAS SLEEPING (past continuous). Was/were + verb-ing = action in progress when interrupted.
questions.retry_hint: The DOORBELL RANG and STARTLED IT AWAKE - a sudden event breaking into something already happening. Ask: which choice shows an action still in progress in the past? A plain past verb only reports a finished action.

questions.stem: Priya's cat is much ________ than the vet expected — it ran to the door as soon as they arrived home.
questions.trap_type: 'Most lively' = superlative; 'more livelier' is WRONG. LIVELIER = comparative of 'lively' (ending in -y: change y to i, add -er).
questions.learning_tip: Short adjective ending in -Y → change Y to I, add -ER. Lively → LIVELIER. The cat is LIVELIER THAN expected = comparing current state to expectations. 'More livelier' is ALWAYS WRONG.
questions.retry_hint: THAN compares the cat now with what THE VET EXPECTED, and this adjective ends in -y. Ask: does a short adjective take an ending, or does it need 'most' in front? Never put 'more' before a word that already carries that ending.

questions.stem: The parrot ________ the words it hears so often that it can now say full sentences.
questions.trap_type: 'So often' = a regular habit = simple present. 'The parrot' is singular → repeats.
questions.learning_tip: 'So often' = a regular, habitual action = simple present. The parrot (singular) → REPEATS the words it hears.
questions.retry_hint: SO OFTEN describes something the parrot does again and again, as a habit - and the bird is ONE creature. Ask: does a habit take the present or the past? And does a singular subject take the plain verb, or the -s form?

questions.stem: Looking after a pet is a big responsibility that requires daily care, ________ it?
questions.trap_type: Positive present simple ('requires') → negative question tag. REQUIRES → doesn't it.
questions.learning_tip: Positive present simple → negative tag. Looking after a pet REQUIRES daily care, DOESN'T it? POSITIVE → NEGATIVE. Present simple → DOES/DOESN'T. 'Doesn't it' (not 'isn't it' — that is for 'to be').
questions.retry_hint: The statement has no 'is' or 'are' - it runs on the plain present verb REQUIRES. Ask: which helping verb stands in for a plain present verb inside a tag? And after a positive statement, is the tag positive or negative?

questions.stem: The vet told Priya ________ her cat twice a day and bring it back in a week.
questions.trap_type: 'Told someone to do something' = reported speech structure: told + object + to + base verb → to medicate.
questions.learning_tip: 'Told someone TO + base verb': told Priya TO MEDICATE her cat. After 'told + object', use the infinitive with 'to'.
questions.retry_hint: The vet TOLD PRIYA, and 'told + person' calls for an infinitive next. Ask: after 'told Priya', do you use the -ing form, the bare verb, the plain past, or the infinitive with its particle in front? Say each one aloud.

questions.stem: The injured bird ________ by a kind student who found it on the playing field.
questions.trap_type: The bird was the receiver of the action (it did not rescue itself). Past passive = was rescued.
questions.learning_tip: The bird did not rescue itself — someone rescued it. Use the PASSIVE: was RESCUED. Passive = was/were + past participle.
questions.retry_hint: The BIRD did not do the saving - it received the action, and A KIND STUDENT did it. Ask: when the subject receives the action, which structure do we need? Passive = the verb 'be' plus a past participle.

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Verb forms of 'feed')

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Lily enjoys (1)________ her two goldfish every morning before school.' Signal: 'enjoys + ___' = gerund (verb-ing). Pattern: enjoy + verb-ing → feeding.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'to feed' instead of the gerund after 'enjoys'.
questions.learning_tip: ENJOY + verb-ing: enjoys FEEDING her goldfish. After 'enjoys', always add -ING.
questions.retry_hint: The verb right before the blank is ENJOYS. Ask: after enjoy, does English want an infinitive, a bare verb, or the -ing form? Enjoy is one of the verbs that accepts only a gerund.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'She (2)________ them exactly the right amount each time so they stay healthy.' Signal: 'each time' = regular habit = simple present. Subject 'She' = singular → feeds.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'feed' (plural form) forgetting that 'She' is singular.
questions.learning_tip: 'Each time' = a regular habit = simple present. She (singular) → FEEDS them the right amount.
questions.retry_hint: EACH TIME points at a repeated habit, and SHE counts as one person. Ask: in the present tense, does a singular subject take the plain verb, or the one with -s on the end?

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Last week, she (3)________ them a little too much and the water turned cloudy.' Signal: 'Last week' = past. 'Feed' is irregular: feed → fed.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'feeded', not knowing 'feed' is irregular.
questions.learning_tip: 'Last week' = past. 'Feed' is irregular: feed → FED. Never write 'feeded'.
questions.retry_hint: LAST WEEK closes the action off in the past. Ask: what is the past form of this verb? It is irregular, so the -ed ending is impossible - 'feeded' does not exist in English.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'While she (4)________ them one morning, she noticed one fish was not moving.' Signal: 'While she ___' = ongoing background action in the past. Subject 'she' = singular → was feeding. Interrupted by 'she noticed'.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'fed' (simple past) missing the ongoing signal 'while she'.
questions.learning_tip: 'While she ___' = ongoing background past action = past continuous. She WAS FEEDING the fish when she noticed the problem.
questions.retry_hint: WHILE SHE marks the long background action, and then she NOTICED ONE FISH in trouble. Ask: which form shows an action still running in the past? A plain past verb would only report it as finished.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Her younger brothers (5)________ the family rabbit in the garden at the same time.' Signal: same past time frame, plural subject 'her younger brothers' + ongoing parallel action → were feeding.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'fed' (simple past) instead of past continuous for an ongoing parallel action.
questions.learning_tip: Her younger brothers = plural. They were doing it at the same past moment = WERE FEEDING (past continuous).
questions.retry_hint: HER YOUNGER BROTHERS are plural, and they act AT THE SAME TIME as Lily. Ask: which past form shows several people in the middle of an action? Match the helping verb to a plural subject.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The vet reminded Lily (6)________ her fish only once a day from then on.' Signal: 'reminded + object + ___' = infinitive. Pattern: remind someone + to + base verb → to feed.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'feeding' instead of the infinitive after 'reminded Lily'.
questions.learning_tip: 'Reminded someone TO + base verb': reminded Lily TO FEED her fish only once a day.
questions.retry_hint: The vet REMINDED LILY, and 'remind + person' calls for an infinitive. Ask: after 'reminded Lily', do you use the -ing form, the bare verb, or the infinitive with its particle in front? Say each one aloud.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'She says we should never (7)________ pet fish more than they need.' Signal: 'should + ___' = modal verb + base form. Never add -s or -ing after a modal.
questions.trap_type: Students add -s or -ing after the modal verb 'should'.
questions.learning_tip: After modal verbs (should, must, can, will), always use the BASE form: should FEED. Never 'should feeds' or 'should feeding'.
questions.retry_hint: The word SHOULD belongs with the modals, and a modal never allows an ending on the verb after it. Ask: do you add -s, add -ing, or leave the verb bare after should, must and can?

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Right now, Lily (8)________ her fish carefully, making sure she gives them just the right amount.' Signal: 'Right now' = present continuous. Subject 'Lily' = singular → is feeding.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'feeds' (simple present habit) missing the 'right now' signal for present continuous.
questions.learning_tip: 'Right now' = present continuous. Lily (singular) → IS FEEDING her fish carefully right now.
questions.retry_hint: RIGHT NOW points at this very moment, and LILY counts as one person. Ask: which form shows an action happening as we speak? A plain present verb would only describe a habit.

C.passage: Lily enjoys (1)________ her two goldfish every morning before school. She (2)________ them exactly the right amount each time so they stay healthy. Last week, she (3)________ them a little too much and the water turned cloudy. While she (4)________ them one morning, she noticed one fish was not moving. Her younger brothers (5)________ the family rabbit in the garden at the same time, so she called out to her mother for help. The vet reminded Lily (6)________ her fish only once a day from then on. She says we should never (7)________ pet fish more than they need, as overfeeding can harm them. Right now, Lily (8)________ her fish carefully, making sure she gives them just the right amount.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: When my family adopted Max, a young golden retriever, the vet did several important things for him on his very first visit. First, Max was (1)________ against common dog diseases so that he would not fall ill. He was also (2)________, so that if he ever got lost, any vet could scan him and read our address. At home, we brush his thick coat every Sunday to (3)________ him, and he sits perfectly still while we work. Max is very (4)________ as well - he follows every command without any fuss. Best of all, he is the most (5)________ dog I have ever known, because he loves to cuddle up beside us and lick our hands.

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'microchipped'. The clue is 'against common dog diseases so that he would not fall ill'.
questions.learning_tip: VACCINATED = given an injection that protects against disease. A dog must be VACCINATED before it can mix with other dogs.
questions.retry_hint: The clue is AGAINST COMMON DOG DISEASES, so that he WOULD NOT FALL ILL. Ask: which box word describes a pet given an injection that guards it from illness? A tiny chip cannot fight a disease.

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'vaccinated'. The clue is that a vet could SCAN him and read the owner's address if he got lost.
questions.learning_tip: MICROCHIPPED = had a tiny electronic chip placed under the skin. A vet can SCAN it to find the owner's details.
questions.retry_hint: The clue is that ANY VET COULD SCAN HIM and read our address if he GOT LOST. Ask: which box word describes a pet carrying a tiny electronic tag under its skin? An injection cannot store an address.

questions.trap_type: The blank follows 'to', so it must be a base verb. The clue is BRUSHING his thick coat.
questions.learning_tip: GROOM = clean and tidy an animal's coat, nails and appearance. We brush Max every Sunday to GROOM him.
questions.retry_hint: We BRUSH HIS THICK COAT every Sunday, and the blank follows 'to', so it must be a base verb. Ask: which box word means to clean and tidy an animal's coat, nails and appearance?

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'affectionate'. The clue is that he FOLLOWS EVERY COMMAND without any fuss - that is about training, not love.
questions.learning_tip: OBEDIENT = does what it is told. A well-trained dog is OBEDIENT and follows its owner's commands.
questions.retry_hint: The clue follows the blank: he FOLLOWS EVERY COMMAND WITHOUT ANY FUSS. Ask: which box word describes a dog that does exactly what it is told? That is about training, not about love.

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'obedient'. The clue is that he CUDDLES up and LICKS our hands - that is about love, not training.
questions.learning_tip: AFFECTIONATE = showing love and warmth through cuddling and touching.
questions.retry_hint: The clue is that he LOVES TO CUDDLE UP beside us and LICK OUR HANDS. Ask: which box word describes a pet that is full of warmth and love? The word about obeying commands is already used in an earlier blank.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.error_type: Homophone confusion — here (place) vs hear (to listen)
questions.trap_type: 'here' (place) when 'hear' (ears) is needed.
questions.learning_tip: HEAR = detect sound with ears. HERE = at this place. 'We could HEAR the mewing' → use ears? YES → HEAR. HEAR = ears. HERE = location.
questions.retry_hint: The TINY MEWING SOUNDS reached the family through a closed door - that is a sound, not a place. Ask: does the underlined word belong to your ears, or does it mean 'at this spot'? One spelling hides EAR inside it.
