questions.trap_type: 'bringed' applies the regular -ed rule. BRING is irregular: bring → brought.
questions.learning_tip: BRING → BROUGHT (irregular past). NEVER 'bringed'. Irregular verbs change completely: bring → brought, buy → bought, catch → caught. Memorise these.
questions.retry_hint: BRINGED applies the regular -ed rule to a verb that will not take it. Ask: how do you say it about last week - 'Ben ___ a small blanket'? This verb changes shape completely, just as 'buy' does.

questions.error_type: Subject-verb agreement — singular subject (the mother cat)
questions.trap_type: 'The mother cat' is singular. Students write 'were' thinking of the kittens.
questions.learning_tip: Singular subject → singular verb! The MOTHER CAT WAS gentle = THE MOTHER CAT is one animal → WAS. Find the main noun: THE MOTHER CAT = singular → WAS, not WERE.
questions.retry_hint: Find the real subject: THE MOTHER CAT - one single animal, even though her KITTENS are all around her. Ask: does a singular subject take the plural form of 'to be', or the singular one? Do not be pulled by the nearby nouns.

questions.trap_type: 'careful' (adjective) after action verb 'held'. A verb needs an adverb.
questions.learning_tip: After an action verb (HELD), use an ADVERB. Ben held the kitten CAREFULLY = how did he hold it? CAREFULLY (adverb, -ly). 'Careful' describes nouns; 'carefully' describes HOW the action is done.
questions.retry_hint: The underlined word describes HOW Ben HELD the kitten, and 'held' is an action verb. Ask: does an action verb need an adjective, or an adverb ending in -ly? Adjectives describe nouns; adverbs describe actions.

questions.trap_type: Students write a plain plural and leave out the apostrophe that shows ownership.
questions.learning_tip: The journal BELONGS TO the pets -> PETS' observation journal (apostrophe after the -s for a plural). Singular: pet's.
questions.retry_hint: The OBSERVATION JOURNAL belongs to the PETS - more than one animal. Ask: does a plain -s show ownership, or does it only make a plural? Where must the apostrophe go when the owners are many?

E.passage: Last week, our neighbour's cat had kittens and my family went next door to visit them. We could here (1) the tiny mewing sounds before we even opened the door. Ben bringed (2) a small blanket to keep the kittens warm during the visit. The mother cat were (3) very gentle but kept a watchful eye on each kitten the whole time. Ben held the smallest kitten careful (4) in both hands so as not to disturb it. Later, he wrote down his thoughts in the pets (5) observation journal that the vet kept at the clinic.

questions.sentence_a: The vet said to Priya, 'Your rabbit needs more fresh vegetables in its diet.'
questions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence using reported speech: The vet told Priya that ________.
questions.model_answer: The vet told Priya that her rabbit needed more fresh vegetables in its diet.
questions.trap_type: Students keep 'your' instead of changing to 'her', or keep 'needs' instead of changing to 'needed' in reported speech.
questions.learning_tip: In reported speech: (1) change 'your' → 'her', (2) change 'needs' → 'needed'. The vet told Priya that HER rabbit NEEDED more fresh vegetables.
questions.retry_hint: Direct speech becoming REPORTED SPEECH after 'told Priya that'. Ask two things: what must the word 'your' become when the vet speaks about Priya's rabbit? And once 'told' is in the past, can a present verb stay as it is?

questions.sentence_a: The vet asked Priya a question.
questions.sentence_b: Does your rabbit eat fresh vegetables every day?
questions.instruction: Combine into one sentence using reported speech. Begin: 'The vet asked...'
questions.model_answer: The vet asked Priya if her rabbit ate fresh vegetables every day.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'asked if does her rabbit eat' (wrong word order) or keep 'your'.
questions.learning_tip: YES/NO question → reported speech: ASKED + IF + subject + verb (normal order). 'Does YOUR rabbit eat?' → asked IF HER rabbit ATE. Pronoun: your → her. Tense: does eat → ate. Word order is normal after 'if'.
questions.retry_hint: A yes/no question folded into REPORTED SPEECH after ASKED. Ask three things: which joining word comes next? Does the question order survive? And what must 'your' and the helping verb 'does' become?

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
When Aiden was six years old, his parents brought home a small brown puppy. Aiden named him Scout. From the first day, the two were inseparable. Scout slept at the foot of Aiden's bed and waited by the door every afternoon for him to come home from school.

As Scout grew older, Aiden took on more responsibility. He learned to measure Scout's food carefully, brush his coat every evening and take him for walks even when it was raining. His mother watched quietly and smiled. Her shy, quiet boy was growing more confident every day.

One morning in Aiden's third year of primary school, Scout fell ill. He refused to eat and lay still in his basket with dull, half-closed eyes. Aiden was frightened. He sat beside Scout and stroked his fur gently, whispering, 'You'll be okay.'

At the vet's clinic, the doctor examined Scout and said he had a stomach infection. 'He will need medicine twice a day for five days,' she said.

Aiden gave Scout his medicine every morning and evening without missing a single dose. By the fifth day, Scout was wagging his tail again.

That evening, Aiden hugged Scout tightly. He realised that caring for a pet was not just about the fun parts. It was about being there — even on the hard days.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 2 has the same meaning as 'moved back and forth with great energy'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Cowered' = crouched in fear; 'leaped' = jumped; 'barked' = made dog sound. WAGGED = moved tail back and forth repeatedly with excitement.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: WAGGED = moved a tail back and forth rapidly, usually showing excitement or happiness. Scout's tail WAGGED = it moved from side to side energetically when Scout was happy.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 3, what does 'it' refer to in 'Ben could not believe it'?

options.2: That Scout recognised Ben after three whole years apart
options.3: That the vet said Scout was healthy
options.4: The size of Scout's new kennel

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 3 thinking 'it' = health news. But 'Ben could not believe IT' = the incredible moment of Scout recognising him after years.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: PRONOUN REFERENCE: 'Ben could not believe IT.' What was unbelievable? That SCOUT RECOGNISED BEN after THREE YEARS apart. IT = that remarkable reunion moment of being remembered.

mcq_questions.stem: What does 'he grew up, but Scout had not aged' most likely suggest about how Ben felt?

options.1: Ben was happy that Scout was younger than him.
options.2: Ben felt a mix of tenderness and sadness, realising that his childhood bond with Scout still existed even though time had passed.
options.3: Ben was disappointed that Scout was still a puppy.
options.4: Ben felt that Scout did not recognise him because dogs age differently.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 4 thinking the dog didn't recognise him. The sentence is reflective and emotional — Ben is moved by the bond that time cannot break.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: INFERENCE: 'he grew up but Scout had not aged' = Ben is moved by the contrast — he is older and changed, but the DOG'S LOVE and RECOGNITION remain unchanged. Option 2 = emotional insight into the lasting bond between boy and dog.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 1, is it True or False that Ben still lived with Scout? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The passage says Ben had not seen Scout for three years because his family moved away — so Scout was left with his grandparents.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1: Ben had not seen Scout for THREE YEARS because his family MOVED AWAY. Scout stayed with his grandparents. Ben no longer lived with Scout. Answer is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: What did the vet say was wrong with Scout?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: The vet said Scout had a stomach infection.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'he was sick' which is too vague.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 4: 'he had a STOMACH INFECTION.' Give the specific diagnosis from the passage.

open_ended_questions.stem: How did Aiden's mother know that caring for Scout was changing Aiden? Give TWO pieces of evidence from paragraph 2.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) Aiden learned to measure Scout's food carefully and brush his coat every evening. (ii) He took Scout for walks even when it was raining, which showed growing responsibility. His mother noticed her shy, quiet boy growing more confident.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students describe what Aiden did without linking it to the change his mother observed.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 2: His mother saw Aiden becoming more RESPONSIBLE (measuring food, brushing, walking in rain) and growing more CONFIDENT. Link the actions to the change.

open_ended_questions.stem: How do we know Aiden was a caring and dedicated owner when Scout was ill? Find ONE piece of evidence from paragraphs 4 and 5.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: Aiden gave Scout his medicine every morning and evening without missing a single dose.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'he took Scout to the vet' which was his parents' action. The question asks about Aiden's own dedication.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 5: Aiden gave medicine EVERY MORNING AND EVENING WITHOUT MISSING A SINGLE DOSE. This shows dedication — he did not skip once.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on the passage, describe TWO character traits of Ben with evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) CARING: when Ben saw Scout after three years, he immediately knelt down and embraced the dog — showing he had not forgotten their bond and still deeply loved his pet. (ii) REFLECTIVE: Ben noticed that 'he grew up, but Scout had not aged' — showing he could think about the passage of time and what their relationship meant.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'loving and sad' without precise traits or textual evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: TRAIT INFERENCE: CARING = immediately embraced Scout, showing lasting love. REFLECTIVE = said 'he grew up but Scout had not aged' = thinking about time, change and their bond. Name trait + evidence = full marks.

questions.stem: On a dark rainy evening, the wet road was as ________ as a mirror - two cars slid right across the junction and could not stop in time.
questions.trap_type: 'Rough' is the opposite of a mirror-smooth surface; 'dull' and 'dark' say nothing about grip. Only SLIPPERY explains why the cars slid.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adjective + AS = simile. A wet road is AS SLIPPERY AS a mirror = so smooth that tyres cannot grip it. Read the clue AFTER the dash - it tells you which quality is being compared.
questions.retry_hint: The clue comes after the dash: two cars SLID right across the junction. Ask: which word explains why tyres cannot grip a wet road? 'Rough' would give more grip, and 'dull' or 'dark' say nothing at all about grip.

questions.stem: The safety officer reminded the students to ________ their bicycle helmets before riding on the road.
questions.trap_type: 'Remove' is the opposite — it means take off. 'Fasten' = click and secure in place.
questions.learning_tip: FASTEN = click or secure something in place. Always FASTEN your helmet before riding so it stays on and protects your head.
questions.retry_hint: A helmet only protects you if it stays ON your head, and this must happen BEFORE riding. Ask: which verb means to clip a strap shut and hold it in place? 'Remove' is the opposite, and 'lose' or 'tear' would ruin the helmet.

questions.stem: In a fire emergency, it is important to ________ the building immediately and gather at the designated meeting point.
questions.trap_type: 'Stay in' and 'run into' are the opposite of safe behaviour. 'Break into' = enter by force. GET OUT OF = leave a place or situation.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: GET OUT OF = leave a place, especially in an emergency. In a fire, GET OUT OF the building immediately = leave it at once. GET + OUT + OF work together as one meaning.
questions.retry_hint: In a FIRE EMERGENCY you must leave the building at once and gather at the meeting point. Ask: which phrase means to leave a place quickly? 'Stay in' keeps you inside, and 'run into' or 'break into' send you the wrong way.

questions.stem: After the fire drill ended and everyone was found safe and accounted for, the principal was ________ — no one was hurt.
questions.trap_type: 'Under the weather' = ill; 'in hot water' = in trouble; 'down in the dumps' = sad. OVER THE MOON = extremely happy and relieved.
questions.learning_tip: IDIOM: OVER THE MOON = feeling extremely happy and relieved. The principal was OVER THE MOON = overjoyed that everyone was safe. Idioms cannot be understood word by word — the moon has nothing to do with it!
questions.retry_hint: Everyone was SAFE and NO ONE WAS HURT, so the principal's feeling must match that relief. Ask: does the idiom describe great happiness, illness, trouble or sadness? An idiom cannot be read word by word.

questions.stem: The paramedic acted ________ and reached the scene of the accident within three minutes of the call.
questions.trap_type: 'Leisurely' = slowly and without hurry; 'reluctantly' = unwillingly; 'carelessly' = without attention. Only 'promptly' = quickly and without delay, which is essential in emergencies.
questions.learning_tip: PROMPTLY = quickly and without any delay. In an emergency, paramedics must arrive PROMPTLY so they can help as soon as possible.
questions.retry_hint: The paramedic reached the accident WITHIN THREE MINUTES of the call. Ask: does that describe acting slowly, unwillingly, carelessly, or with no delay at all? Match the adverb to the speed the sentence shows you.

questions.stem: Everyone in the fire safety class ________ how important it is to check smoke detectors every month.
questions.trap_type: EVERYONE = singular → verb+S.
questions.learning_tip: EVERYONE / NOBODY / SOMEONE = Singular! Everyone KNOWS = add -S. 'Everyone know' is WRONG. Singular indefinite pronouns always take singular present-tense verbs.
questions.retry_hint: The subject is EVERYONE, not 'the class'. Words like everyone and nobody act like ONE person. Ask: in the present tense, does a singular subject take the plain verb, or the verb ending in -s? This is a fact, not an action in progress.

questions.stem: The town council has ________ new traffic lights at the busy junction near the school this month.
questions.trap_type: HAS + past participle = present perfect. INSTALL → INSTALLED (regular).
questions.learning_tip: HAS + past participle = present perfect. The council HAS INSTALLED new traffic lights = done recently and now in use. INSTALL → INSTALLED (regular verb, add -ed).
questions.retry_hint: HAS is already sitting in front of the blank, and the work was finished THIS MONTH. Ask: which form partners with 'has' to build the present perfect - the plain verb, the -s form, the -ing form, or the past participle?

questions.stem: The children ________ on the pavement when a car suddenly swerved onto the kerb.
questions.trap_type: 'The car suddenly swerved' = sudden interrupting event. Children were already walking = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: The car SUDDENLY SWERVED = sudden past event. The children were already in the middle of walking = WERE WALKING (past continuous). Was/were + verb-ing = action in progress when interrupted.
questions.retry_hint: A car SUDDENLY SWERVED onto the kerb and cut across an action the children had already begun. Ask: which choice shows an action in progress in the PAST? A plain past verb only reports a finished action.

questions.stem: The new pedestrian crossing is much ________ than the old one — it has flashing lights and a countdown timer.
questions.trap_type: 'Most safe' = superlative; 'more safer' is WRONG. SAFER = comparative of 'safe'.
questions.learning_tip: Short adjective + -ER = comparative. Safe → SAFER. The new crossing is SAFER THAN the old one = comparing two crossings. 'More safer' is ALWAYS WRONG — never add BOTH 'more' AND '-er'.
questions.retry_hint: THAN tells you two crossings are being compared, and 'safe' is a short adjective. Ask: do short adjectives add -er, or take 'most' in front? And can 'more' ever stand before a word that already ends in -er?

questions.stem: Always look both ways before crossing ________ you do not get hit by oncoming traffic.
questions.trap_type: 'Because' introduces a past reason. 'So that' introduces a forward-looking purpose — you look both ways FOR THE PURPOSE of not getting hit.
questions.learning_tip: SO THAT = in order to achieve a goal. Look both ways SO THAT you do not get hit — this is the purpose of the action.
questions.retry_hint: Looking both ways is done for a PURPOSE: to avoid being HIT by oncoming traffic. Ask: which joining word introduces a purpose, a goal you want to reach? 'Because' gives a past reason, and 'but' signals a contrast.

questions.stem: Wearing a helmet when cycling can save your life, ________ it?
questions.trap_type: Positive present 'can' → negative question tag. CAN → can't it.
questions.learning_tip: Positive modal verb → negative tag. Wearing a helmet CAN save your life, CAN'T it? POSITIVE → NEGATIVE. Modal 'can' → 'can't'. Match the auxiliary verb of the main clause.
questions.retry_hint: A tag mirrors the helping verb of the statement, and this statement uses CAN. Ask: after a POSITIVE statement, must the tag turn negative or stay positive? And should the tag borrow 'do', or keep the verb already there?

questions.stem: The safety officer told the pupils ________ their phones while crossing the road.
questions.trap_type: Negative reported speech: 'told someone not to do something' = told + object + not to + base verb → not to use.
questions.learning_tip: Negative reported speech: told them NOT TO + base verb. The officer told pupils NOT TO USE their phones while crossing. Always put 'not' before 'to'.
questions.retry_hint: The officer TOLD the pupils something they must avoid doing. Ask: after 'told + someone', which form follows - the plain verb, the -ing form, or the infinitive? And where does the word 'not' sit, before that little word 'to' or after it?

questions.stem: The broken step on the staircase ________ by the building manager last Monday.
questions.trap_type: The step did not repair itself — it was repaired by the manager. Past passive = was repaired.
questions.learning_tip: The step was the receiver of the action. Use the PASSIVE: was REPAIRED. Passive = was/were + past participle. 'Last Monday' = past → was repaired.
questions.retry_hint: The STEP did not repair itself; the BUILDING MANAGER did the work. Ask: does the step do the action or receive it? A receiver needs the PASSIVE, and LAST MONDAY tells you which tense that passive must be in.

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Verb forms of 'cross')

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Every child must learn that (1)________ a busy road safely is a skill worth practising.' Signal: subject of the clause = gerund as noun.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'to cross'. The blank is the SUBJECT of 'is a skill', so it needs a gerund.
questions.learning_tip: A gerund (verb + -ing) can act as the SUBJECT of a clause: '... that CROSSING a busy road safely is a skill'.
questions.retry_hint: Read the frame: 'must learn THAT ________ a busy road safely is a skill'. The blank is the SUBJECT of 'is'. Ask: which form of a verb can act like a noun and be the subject - the plain verb, the -ed form, or the -ing form?

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Every day, our school warden (2)________ the road with a long line of pupils behind her.' Signal: 'Every day' = habit = simple present; 'our school warden' = singular -> crosses.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'cross' (plural form) forgetting that 'our school warden' is singular.
questions.learning_tip: 'Every day' = habit = simple present. Our school warden (singular) → CROSSES the road with the students.
questions.retry_hint: EVERY DAY signals a habit, and the subject is ONE school WARDEN. Ask: in the simple present, does a singular subject take the plain verb, or the verb with -s on the end? Match the verb to the warden, not to the pupils behind her.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Last Tuesday, a girl (3)________ at the traffic lights near the market.' Signal: 'Last Tuesday' = past. cross -> crossed.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'cross' (base form) ignoring the past time signal 'Last Tuesday'.
questions.learning_tip: 'Last Tuesday' = past. 'Cross' is regular: cross → CROSSED.
questions.retry_hint: LAST TUESDAY is finished time, and this verb is regular. Ask: which ending turns a regular verb into the simple past? The girl's action is over and done, so no continuous form is needed here.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'While she (4)________, a motorcycle ran the red light.' Signal: 'While' + ongoing past action, interrupted -> past continuous, singular subject.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'crossed' (simple past) missing the ongoing background signal 'while she'.
questions.learning_tip: 'While she ___' = ongoing past action = past continuous. She WAS CROSSING the road when the motorcycle ran the red light.
questions.retry_hint: WHILE she ________, a MOTORCYCLE ran the red light and cut into her action. Ask: which form shows a longer action still in progress in the past when a sudden event interrupts it? And which helper matches a single person?

questions.context_check: Passage: 'At that very moment, two elderly neighbours (5)________ the same road further down the street.' Signal: plural subject + ongoing past action.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'crossed' (simple past) instead of the past continuous needed for a parallel ongoing action.
questions.learning_tip: 'Two elderly neighbours' = plural. They were in the middle of it at that same past moment -> WERE CROSSING (past continuous).
questions.retry_hint: Count the subject: TWO ELDERLY NEIGHBOURS, more than one, and their action was still going on AT THAT VERY MOMENT. Ask: which past form shows an action in progress, and which helper belongs with a plural subject?

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The principal later reminded everyone (6)________ only when the green man appears.' Signal: reminded + object + TO + base verb.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'crossing' instead of the infinitive after 'reminded everyone'.
questions.learning_tip: 'Reminded everyone TO + base verb': reminded everyone TO CROSS only at the green man signal.
questions.retry_hint: The principal REMINDED everyone ________ only when the green man appears. Ask: after a verb like reminded, told or asked, which form follows - the -ing form, the bare plain form, or the infinitive with its little partner word in front?

questions.context_check: Passage: 'He warned that no pupil should (7)________ between parked cars.' Signal: modal 'should' + base form.
questions.trap_type: Students add -es or -ing after the modal verb 'should'.
questions.learning_tip: After modal verbs (should, must, can, will) always use the BASE form: should CROSS. Never 'should crosses'.
questions.retry_hint: SHOULD is a modal verb, and modals never let the next verb change shape. Ask: after should, must or can, do we use the -s form, the -ing form, or the bare plain form with nothing added at all?

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Right now, the warden (8)________ the road with a group of Primary One children.' Signal: 'Right now' = present continuous, singular subject.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'crosses' (simple present habit) missing the 'right now' signal for present continuous.
questions.learning_tip: 'Right now' = present continuous. The warden (singular) → IS CROSSING the road with the students right now.
questions.retry_hint: RIGHT NOW points at this very moment, and the subject, the WARDEN, means one person. Ask: which form shows an action happening as you read, and which helper goes with a singular subject? A simple present verb would only describe a habit.

C.passage: Road safety begins with good habits. Every child must learn that (1)________ a busy road safely is a skill worth practising. Every day, our school warden (2)________ the road with a long line of pupils behind her. Last Tuesday, a girl (3)________ at the traffic lights near the market without looking up from her phone. While she (4)________, a motorcycle ran the red light and swerved past her. At that very moment, two elderly neighbours (5)________ the same road further down the street and stopped in shock. The principal later reminded everyone (6)________ only when the green man appears. He warned that no pupil should (7)________ between parked cars. Right now, the warden (8)________ the road with a group of Primary One children.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: At home, safety is just as important as on the road. Every family should know what to do in an (1)________ such as a fire or a gas leak. One important (2)________ is to keep a working fire extinguisher in the kitchen. Cooking oil and some cleaning products are (3)________ — they can catch fire very easily, so they must be stored safely away from heat. The yellow warning signs on these products are there to signal a (4)________ to users. Whenever you handle such products, do so with great (5)________ and always follow the instructions on the label.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'such as a fire or a gas leak' = a sudden serious situation = emergency.
questions.learning_tip: An EMERGENCY = a sudden and serious situation that requires immediate action. A fire or gas leak at home is an EMERGENCY.
questions.retry_hint: The examples come right after the blank: A FIRE or a GAS LEAK - sudden, serious, needing action at once. Ask: which box word names such a situation? The two look-alike words beside it are about being careful beforehand, not about the crisis.

questions.trap_type: Students may confuse 'precaution' with 'caution' (blank 5). A PRECAUTION = an action taken in advance to prevent a problem.
questions.learning_tip: A PRECAUTION = an action taken ahead of time to prevent something bad from happening. Keeping a fire extinguisher is a PRECAUTION against fires.
questions.retry_hint: Keeping a fire EXTINGUISHER in the KITCHEN happens BEFORE any fire starts. Ask: which box word names a step taken in advance to stop trouble happening? Careful: its look-alike means the care you take while doing something.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'they can catch fire very easily' = able to catch fire easily = flammable.
questions.learning_tip: FLAMMABLE = easily set on fire. Cooking oil and some chemicals are FLAMMABLE and must be kept away from heat and open flames.
questions.retry_hint: The dash explains it: they CAN CATCH FIRE VERY EASILY and must be stored away from HEAT. Ask: which box word describes a material that burns easily? The blank follows 'are', so it must be a describing word, not a noun.

questions.trap_type: Students may write 'danger' which is not in the box. HAZARD = a specific risk or source of danger.
questions.learning_tip: A HAZARD = something that can cause danger or harm. Warning signs on products tell users there is a HAZARD — a specific risk to be aware of.
questions.retry_hint: The YELLOW WARNING SIGNS exist to tell users that one particular risk is present. Ask: which box word names a source of danger? An emergency is the disaster once it happens; this word names the danger waiting to happen.

questions.trap_type: Students may confuse 'caution' with 'precaution' (blank 2). CAUTION = care and attention when doing something.
questions.learning_tip: CAUTION = great care and attention, especially when doing something risky. Handle flammable products with CAUTION = be very careful.
questions.retry_hint: 'Do so with great ________ and always FOLLOW THE INSTRUCTIONS' - this is about HOW you handle the products, at the moment you handle them. Ask: which box word names the care and attention you use while doing something risky?

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.error_type: Homophone confusion — here (place) vs hear (to listen)
questions.trap_type: 'here' (place) when 'hear' (ears) is needed.
questions.learning_tip: HEAR = detect sound with ears. HERE = at this place. 'We could HEAR cars passing' → use ears? YES → HEAR. HEAR = ears. HERE = location.
questions.retry_hint: The underlined word means 'at this place', but the sentence is about CARS PASSING outside reaching your ears. Ask: which of the two spellings has the word EAR hidden inside it? Choose by meaning, never by sound.

questions.trap_type: 'runned' applies the regular -ed rule. RUN is irregular: run → ran.
questions.learning_tip: RUN → RAN (irregular past). NEVER 'runned'. Irregular verbs do not follow the -ed rule: run → ran, begin → began, swim → swam.
questions.retry_hint: RUNNED is built by adding -ed, but this verb is IRREGULAR. Ask: how would you say it in the past - 'yesterday the boy ______ into the road'? Irregular verbs change their vowel instead of taking an ending.

questions.error_type: Adverb required after the action verb 'cross'
questions.trap_type: 'careful' (adjective) is placed after the action verb 'cross'. A verb is described by an adverb.
questions.learning_tip: How do we cross? CAREFULLY. After an ACTION verb use an ADVERB (-ly). Adjectives describe nouns; adverbs describe how the action is done.
questions.retry_hint: The underlined word is describing HOW we CROSS the road, and 'cross' is an action verb. Ask: do we describe an action with an adjective, or with an adverb? An adjective can only describe a noun, so what ending must be added?

questions.trap_type: 'taked' applies the regular -ed rule. TAKE is irregular: take → took.
questions.learning_tip: TAKE → TOOK (irregular past). NEVER 'taked'. Irregular verbs change completely: take → took, make → made, shake → shook.
questions.retry_hint: TAKED follows the -ed rule, but this verb refuses it. Ask: what do you say in the past - 'yesterday the boy ______ a wrong turn'? Think of shake becoming shook, and make the same kind of vowel change.

questions.trap_type: Students leave out the apostrophe, so 'pupils' reads as a plain plural instead of showing ownership.
questions.learning_tip: The drawings belong to the pupils. Plural noun already ending in -s -> add the apostrophe AFTER the -s: PUPILS' drawings. Singular would be pupil's.
questions.retry_hint: The DRAWINGS belong to the pupils, so the word must do more than count them. Ask: does a plain -s show ownership, or only make a plural? And where does the apostrophe go when the owners are many, before or after the -s?

E.passage: Last Wednesday, a traffic police officer came to our school to give a talk on road awareness. She asked us to stay quiet - we could here (1) cars passing outside and needed to concentrate. She told us that a child once runned (2) into the road after a ball and was nearly hit by a lorry. She reminded the class that we must cross the road careful (3) and never rush, even when we are late for school. A boy then taked (4) a wrong turn during the practice drill and had to be guided back by a teacher. At the end, the pupils (5) drawings of road signs were displayed outside the school hall.

questions.sentence_a: The teacher said to the class, 'Never play near the swimming pool without an adult present.'
questions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence using reported speech: The teacher told the class ________.
questions.model_answer: The teacher told the class never to play near the swimming pool without an adult present.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'told the class to never play' (incorrect word order) or keep 'never play' without changing to infinitive form.
questions.learning_tip: Negative reported speech with 'never': told the class NEVER TO PLAY. Change the imperative 'Never play' to 'never to play' in reported speech.
questions.retry_hint: The order was 'NEVER PLAY near the swimming pool'. Ask: after 'told the class', which form must the verb take? And where does 'never' sit - in front of that little word 'to', or squeezed between it and the verb?

questions.sentence_a: The safety officer asked the students a question.
questions.sentence_b: Do you always look both ways before crossing?
questions.instruction: Combine into one sentence using reported speech. Begin: 'The safety officer asked...'
questions.model_answer: The safety officer asked the students if they always looked both ways before crossing.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'asked if do they always look' (wrong word order) or keep 'you'.
questions.learning_tip: YES/NO question → reported speech: ASKED + IF + subject + verb (normal order). 'Do YOU always look?' → asked IF THEY ALWAYS LOOKED. Pronoun: you → they. Tense: do look → looked. Word order is normal after 'if'.
questions.retry_hint: 'Do you ALWAYS LOOK BOTH WAYS before crossing?' is a yes/no question. Ask: which small joining word follows ASKED? Does the question keep its inverted order, or turn into a normal statement? And what must happen to 'you' and to the tense?

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
It was a bright Tuesday afternoon when eight-year-old Nora noticed something that made her stop in her tracks. An elderly man was trying to cross a busy road, but he looked confused and kept stepping forward and pulling back each time a car went by.

Nora hesitated. She was already late for her piano lesson, and her mother was waiting for her at the community centre just two blocks away. But the sight of the old man struggling made her feel uneasy.

She walked up to him. 'Excuse me, sir. Would you like me to help you cross?' she asked politely.

The old man looked at her with grateful eyes. 'Thank you, child. My eyesight is not very good these days.'

Nora held his arm gently and looked both ways carefully before guiding him across at the pedestrian crossing. On the other side, the old man thanked her warmly and went on his way.

When Nora arrived at the community centre, she explained to her mother what happened. Her mother did not say a single word about the lateness. Instead, she pulled Nora close and said quietly, 'I am very proud of you.'

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 1 has the same meaning as 'came to a complete stop'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Rushed' = moved fast; 'watched' = looked carefully; 'signalled' = gave a sign. HALTED = stopped completely, especially suddenly.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: HALTED = came to a complete, sudden stop. The car HALTED at the red light = it stopped completely. HALT = stop; HALTED = past tense of 'halt'.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 2, what does 'it' refer to in 'Kai knew it was his fault'?

options.2: The fact that he had not looked both ways before cycling out of the driveway
options.3: The red light that was not working

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking 'it' = the bicycle. But 'IT was his fault' = IT = the accident/situation that happened because he did not check.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: PRONOUN REFERENCE: 'Kai KNEW IT was his fault.' IT = the SITUATION — the near-accident that happened because HE DID NOT LOOK BOTH WAYS before cycling out. It refers to the careless action, not the bicycle.

mcq_questions.stem: Why does the writer describe Kai's heart as 'pounding for a different reason' at the end of the passage?

options.1: Because Kai was still afraid of the driver who nearly hit him.
options.2: Because his heart pounded from relief and the determination never to be careless again.
options.3: Because he was running very fast to get home.
options.4: Because the road safety officer made him nervous.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 3 thinking he was running. 'A different reason' = not fear anymore — but a new emotion: relief and resolve.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: INFERENCE: earlier, his heart pounded from FEAR. Now it pounds for 'A DIFFERENT REASON' = RELIEF at being safe, combined with a new DETERMINATION to be more careful. Option 2 = the contrast the writer is drawing between fear and resolve.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 1, is it True or False that Kai was concentrating fully on the road when the car nearly hit him? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The passage says Kai was looking at his phone and not paying attention to the road when the car swerved past him.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1: Kai was LOOKING AT HIS PHONE and NOT PAYING ATTENTION to the road. This is why the near-accident happened. Answer is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: Why did the elderly man have difficulty crossing the road?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: His eyesight was not very good, so he could not see the traffic clearly.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'he was old' which is too general. The passage gives a specific reason.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 4: 'My EYESIGHT is not very good these days.' The specific reason is his poor eyesight — not just his age.

open_ended_questions.stem: How do we know Nora crossed the road safely with the elderly man? Give TWO things she did.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) She held his arm gently to guide him. (ii) She looked both ways carefully before crossing at the pedestrian crossing.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students describe only one action or say 'she helped him' which is too vague.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 5: (1) she HELD HIS ARM gently and (2) she LOOKED BOTH WAYS carefully before crossing AT THE PEDESTRIAN CROSSING. Two specific safe actions.

open_ended_questions.stem: How did Nora's mother react when Nora arrived late at the community centre?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: Her mother did not say a word about the lateness. Instead, she pulled Nora close and said she was very proud of her.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'her mother was angry' which is the opposite of what happened.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Last paragraph: her mother 'did not say a single word about the LATENESS' and instead told Nora she was 'very PROUD' of her. The mother approved, not complained.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on his actions throughout the passage, describe TWO character traits of Kai with evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) RESPONSIBLE: after the near-accident, Kai did not make excuses — he admitted it was his own fault for not looking both ways and for using his phone while cycling. (ii) REFLECTIVE: standing at the kerb, he made a firm decision to always check before crossing in future — showing he could learn from a frightening experience.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'careful and scared' without precise traits or evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: TRAIT INFERENCE: RESPONSIBLE = admitted IT WAS HIS FAULT without excuses. REFLECTIVE = made a firm DECISION to change his behaviour. Name trait + give evidence from passage = full marks.

questions.stem: The astronaut floated through the space station as ________ as a feather drifting in still air — weightless and completely silent.
questions.trap_type: 'Heavy','noisy' and 'rigid' describe the opposite of weightless movement. LIGHT = without heaviness.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! The astronaut was AS LIGHT AS a feather = comparing weightless movement to a feather floating. LIGHT = without weight. AS + ADJECTIVE + AS is the correct simile form — never use an adverb.
questions.retry_hint: The comparison is a FEATHER DRIFTING in still air, and the dash adds WEIGHTLESS. Ask: which word matches a body that floats with no weight at all? 'Heavy' and 'rigid' are the opposite, and 'noisy' is about sound, not weight.

questions.stem: Scientists use powerful ________ to study distant stars and galaxies from Earth.
questions.trap_type: 'Microscopes' zoom in on tiny things; 'stethoscopes' are for heartbeats; 'periscopes' are used in submarines. Only 'telescopes' are for viewing distant objects in space.
questions.learning_tip: A TELESCOPE = an instrument that uses lenses to make distant objects appear closer. Scientists use TELESCOPES to study stars and planets far away.
questions.retry_hint: The instrument must bring DISTANT STARS AND GALAXIES close enough to study. Ask: which of these looks far away rather than very near? A microscope enlarges tiny things, a stethoscope listens to hearts, a periscope peeps above the sea.

questions.stem: After years of research, scientists finally managed to ________ the mystery of how black holes are formed.
questions.trap_type: 'Ignore' = pay no attention; 'create' = make something new. FIGURE OUT = understand or solve after thinking carefully.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: FIGURE OUT = understand or solve a problem by thinking carefully. Scientists FIGURED OUT the mystery = they worked out the answer after long research. FIGURE + OUT work together.
questions.retry_hint: After YEARS OF RESEARCH the scientists finally understood HOW BLACK HOLES ARE FORMED. Ask: which phrase means to solve a puzzle after long, careful thinking? 'Ignore' means to pay no attention, and 'create' would mean they made the black holes.

questions.stem: When Priya finally saw the Milky Way through the telescope, she was ________ — it was more beautiful than she ever imagined.
questions.trap_type: 'Under the weather' = ill; 'in hot water' = in trouble. OVER THE MOON = extremely happy and thrilled.
questions.learning_tip: IDIOM: OVER THE MOON = feeling extremely happy and excited. Priya was OVER THE MOON = she was thrilled beyond words. Idioms cannot be understood word by word — being 'over the moon' means reaching the highest happiness!
questions.retry_hint: Priya saw the MILKY WAY and it was MORE BEAUTIFUL than she ever imagined. Ask: does the idiom name great delight, illness, trouble or danger? Read an idiom as one whole meaning, never word by word.

questions.stem: Scientists discovered the asteroid was ________ towards Earth at tremendous speed and raised an alert.
questions.trap_type: 'Retreating' means moving away; 'drifting' means moving slowly without direction; 'hovering' means staying in one spot. Only 'hurtling' = moving at great speed in a specific direction.
questions.learning_tip: HURTLING = moving at very great speed in a particular direction, often dangerously. The asteroid was HURTLING towards Earth = racing towards it at tremendous speed.
questions.retry_hint: The asteroid was moving TOWARDS EARTH AT TREMENDOUS SPEED and an ALERT was raised. Ask: which verb carries both great speed and a clear direction? 'Drifting' is slow and aimless, 'hovering' stays put, and 'retreating' moves away.

questions.stem: Nobody in our science class ________ the meteorite in the display cabinet - it is far too precious to be handled.
questions.trap_type: Students match the verb to 'class' or write the plural 'touch'. NOBODY = singular -> verb + S.
questions.learning_tip: NOBODY / EVERYONE / SOMEONE = singular. Nobody TOUCHES = add -S. 'Nobody touch' is WRONG, and 'have touched' would need a plural subject.
questions.retry_hint: The subject is NOBODY, not 'our science class'. Words like nobody and everyone behave like ONE person. Ask: in the present tense, does a singular subject take the plain verb, or the verb with -s? 'Have' would need a plural subject.

questions.stem: Scientists have ________ more than five thousand planets outside our solar system since the 1990s.
questions.trap_type: HAVE + past participle = present perfect. DISCOVER → DISCOVERED (regular).
questions.learning_tip: HAVE + past participle = present perfect. Scientists HAVE DISCOVERED five thousand planets = started in the 1990s and still finding more. DISCOVER → DISCOVERED (regular verb, add -ed).
questions.retry_hint: HAVE is already in the sentence, and the finding has gone on SINCE THE 1990s. Ask: which form partners with 'have' to build the present perfect - the plain verb, the -s form, the -ing form, or the past participle?

questions.stem: The students ________ through the telescope when the shooting star flashed across the sky.
questions.trap_type: 'The shooting star flashed' = sudden interrupting event. Students were already looking = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: The shooting star FLASHED = sudden past event. Students were already looking = WERE LOOKING (past continuous). Was/were + verb-ing = action in progress when something interrupts.
questions.retry_hint: The SHOOTING STAR FLASHED across the sky: one sudden event cutting into something already happening. Ask: which choice shows an action in progress in the PAST? A plain past verb would only report a finished action.

questions.stem: Jupiter is far ________ than any other planet in our solar system — it is twice the size of all the others combined.
questions.trap_type: 'Largest' = superlative; 'more larger' is WRONG. LARGER = comparative of 'large'.
questions.learning_tip: Short adjective + -ER = comparative. Large → LARGER. Jupiter is LARGER THAN = comparing it to other planets. 'More larger' is ALWAYS WRONG — never add BOTH 'more' AND '-er'. FAR + comparative = much more.
questions.retry_hint: THAN is doing the work here: Jupiter is measured against every other planet, and 'large' is a short adjective. Ask: do short adjectives add -er, or take 'most'? And is it ever right to put 'more' before a word already ending in -er?

questions.stem: The rocket launched ________ midnight so that scientists could observe it against the dark sky.
questions.trap_type: 'Midnight' is a specific time point. 'In' is for months/years/parts of day; 'on' is for days; 'at' is for specific times including midnight.
questions.learning_tip: Use AT for specific time points: AT midnight, AT noon, AT six o'clock. 'Midnight' is a precise moment → AT midnight.
questions.retry_hint: MIDNIGHT is one exact point on the clock - not a day, not a part of the day. Ask: which preposition do we use with exact clock times? Say each choice aloud in front of 'midnight'; only one sounds like English.

questions.stem: The moon landing in 1969 was one of the greatest achievements in human history, ________ it?
questions.trap_type: Positive past 'to be' ('was') → negative question tag. WAS → wasn't it.
questions.learning_tip: Positive past 'to be' → negative tag. The moon landing WAS a great achievement, WASN'T it? POSITIVE → NEGATIVE tag. WAS → WASN'T. Past 'to be': was/were → wasn't/weren't.
questions.retry_hint: The statement uses WAS: 'The moon landing WAS one of the greatest achievements'. Ask: after a POSITIVE statement, does the tag turn negative or stay positive? And should the tag keep the verb already used, or borrow 'did'?

questions.stem: The space probe ________ by engineers at the control centre when it sent back its first images.
questions.trap_type: The probe did not guide itself — engineers guided it. Past passive = was guided.
questions.learning_tip: The probe was the receiver of the action. Use the PASSIVE: WAS GUIDED. Passive = was/were + past participle. Engineers guided it → it WAS GUIDED by engineers.
questions.retry_hint: The PROBE did not steer itself; the ENGINEERS at the control centre did. Ask: does the probe do the action or receive it? A receiver needs the PASSIVE, and 'sent back its first images' fixes the tense in the past.

questions.stem: The science teacher told her students ________ the positions of the planets before the test next Friday.
questions.trap_type: 'Told someone to do something' = reported speech structure: told + object + to + base verb → to memorise.
questions.learning_tip: 'Told someone TO + base verb': told her students TO MEMORISE the positions. After 'told + object', use the infinitive with 'to'.
questions.retry_hint: The teacher TOLD her students what she wanted them to do. Ask: after 'told + someone', which form follows - the plain verb on its own, the -ing form, the past form, or the infinitive with its little partner word in front?

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Verb forms of 'explore')

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Priya has loved (1)________ the night sky ever since she was given a small telescope.' Signal: LOVE + verb-ing (gerund).
questions.trap_type: Students write 'to explore' instead of the gerund after 'loved'.
questions.learning_tip: LOVE + verb-ing: loved EXPLORING the mysteries of space. After 'loved', always add -ING.
questions.retry_hint: LOVED is the verb standing before the blank: 'has LOVED ________ the night sky'. Ask: after love, enjoy or finish, which form of the next verb do we use - the infinitive, or the -ing form? The pattern decides, not the meaning.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Every week, her team (2)________ the new data that the space station sends back.' Signal: 'Every week' = habit; 'her team' = singular collective -> explores.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'explore' (plural form) forgetting that 'her team' is treated as a singular collective subject.
questions.learning_tip: 'Every week' = habit = simple present. Her team (singular collective) → EXPLORES new data every week.
questions.retry_hint: EVERY WEEK signals a habit, and the subject HER TEAM counts as ONE group. Ask: in the simple present, does a singular subject take the plain verb, or the verb with -s? Do not be fooled by the many people inside a team.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Last year, our class (3)________ the science of stars in an exciting project.' Signal: 'Last year' = past. explore -> explored.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'explore' (base form) ignoring the past signal 'Last year'.
questions.learning_tip: 'Last year' = past. 'Explore' is regular: explore → EXPLORED.
questions.retry_hint: LAST YEAR is finished time, and this verb is regular. Ask: which ending turns a regular verb into the simple past? The project is over, so no continuous form is needed here.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'While the rover (4)________ a rocky ridge on Mars, it detected a strange purple stone.' Signal: 'While' + ongoing past action, singular subject.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'explored' (simple past) missing the ongoing signal 'while the rover'.
questions.learning_tip: 'While the rover ___' = ongoing background past action = past continuous. The rover WAS EXPLORING when it detected the unusual rock.
questions.retry_hint: WHILE the rover ________ the rocky ridge, it DETECTED a strange stone: a sudden event cutting into a longer one. Ask: which form shows the longer action still in progress, and which helper matches a single rover?

questions.context_check: Passage: 'At the same moment, two separate probes (5)________ the far side of the Moon.' Signal: plural subject + ongoing past action.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'explored' (simple past) instead of past continuous for an ongoing parallel action.
questions.learning_tip: Two separate probes = plural. They were doing it at the same past moment = WERE EXPLORING (past continuous).
questions.retry_hint: Count the subject: TWO SEPARATE PROBES, more than one. Their work had not finished; it carried on AT THE SAME MOMENT. Ask: which past form shows an action still going on, and which helper belongs with a plural subject?

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Priya and her friends hope (6)________ the moons of Jupiter one day.' Signal: HOPE + TO + base verb.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'exploring' instead of the infinitive after 'hope'.
questions.learning_tip: 'Hope TO + base verb': hope TO EXPLORE the moons of Jupiter. Use the infinitive after 'hope'.
questions.retry_hint: HOPE is the verb in front of the blank: 'Priya and her friends HOPE ________ the moons of Jupiter'. Ask: after hope, want or plan, which form follows - the -ing form, the bare plain form, or the infinitive with its partner word in front?

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Our teacher says that scientists should (7)________ every clue carefully.' Signal: modal 'should' + base form.
questions.trap_type: Students add -s or -ing after the modal verb 'should'.
questions.learning_tip: After modal verbs (should, must, can, will) always use the BASE form: should EXPLORE. Never 'should explores'.
questions.retry_hint: SHOULD is a modal verb, and modals never let the next verb change shape. Ask: after should, must or can, do we use the -s form, the -ing form, or the bare plain form with nothing added? 'Should explores' is never English.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Right now, the newest rover (8)________ a region near the Martian south pole.' Signal: 'Right now' = present continuous, singular subject.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'explores' (simple present habit) missing the 'right now' signal for present continuous.
questions.learning_tip: 'Right now' = present continuous. The newest rover (singular) → IS EXPLORING a region near the Martian south pole.
questions.retry_hint: RIGHT NOW points at this very moment, and the subject, THE NEWEST ROVER, means one machine. Ask: which form shows an action happening as you read, and which helper goes with a singular subject? A simple present verb describes a habit.

C.passage: Space has always fascinated our class. Priya has loved (1)________ the night sky ever since she was given a small telescope. Every week, her team (2)________ the new data that the space station sends back to Earth. Last year, our class (3)________ the science of stars in an exciting project with a real astronomer. While the rover (4)________ a rocky ridge on Mars, it detected a strange purple stone. At the same moment, two separate probes (5)________ the far side of the Moon. Priya and her friends hope (6)________ the moons of Jupiter one day. Our teacher says that scientists should (7)________ every clue carefully before they announce a discovery. Right now, the newest rover (8)________ a region near the Martian south pole.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: Space is vast and full of wonders. Beyond our solar system lie billions of stars grouped into a (1)________ - a huge spinning system held together by gravity. Each planet travels in its own (2)________, a fixed path around the Sun that it follows year after year. The Moon is Earth's only natural (3)________, circling our planet every twenty-eight days. Closer to home, Earth's (4)________ is a thin layer of gases that traps heat and makes life possible. When a space rock crashes into the Moon, it leaves behind a circular hollow called a (5)________.

questions.trap_type: Students may write 'universe' which is not in the box. A GALAXY = a huge system of billions of stars.
questions.learning_tip: A GALAXY = a system of billions of stars held together by gravity. The Milky Way is the GALAXY that contains our solar system.
questions.retry_hint: The clue sits on both sides of the blank: BILLIONS OF STARS grouped together and HELD TOGETHER BY GRAVITY. Ask: which box word names that huge spinning system of stars? An orbit is a path and a crater is a hole - neither is made of stars.

questions.trap_type: Students may write 'path' which is not in the box. ORBIT = the curved path a planet or moon takes around a star or planet.
questions.learning_tip: An ORBIT = the curved path that a planet, moon or satellite travels around a larger body in space. Earth's ORBIT around the Sun takes 365 days.
questions.retry_hint: Read the words right after the comma: A FIXED PATH AROUND THE SUN that the planet follows year after year. Ask: which box word names that path? Careful - a comet also travels, but the blank names the path, not the traveller.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'circles our planet' = a natural satellite. Students may write 'moon' but SATELLITE is the precise scientific term used here.
questions.learning_tip: A SATELLITE = an object that orbits a planet. The Moon is a natural SATELLITE of Earth. Man-made satellites are also sent into orbit.
questions.retry_hint: The Moon is NATURAL and it keeps CIRCLING OUR PLANET every twenty-eight days. Ask: which box word names an object that goes round a planet? An eclipse is an event, not an object, and an asteroid does not circle the Earth.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'layer of gases surrounding the planet' = atmosphere. Students may write 'sky' which is not in the box.
questions.learning_tip: ATMOSPHERE = the layer of gases surrounding a planet. Earth's ATMOSPHERE protects us from harmful radiation and provides the air we breathe.
questions.retry_hint: The blank is followed by its own definition: A THIN LAYER OF GASES that TRAPS HEAT and makes life possible. Ask: which box word names that blanket of gases wrapped around a planet?

questions.trap_type: The clue 'large bowl-shaped holes made when rocks crashed' = craters. Students may write 'holes' which is not in the box.
questions.learning_tip: A CRATER = a large, bowl-shaped hollow on the surface of a planet or moon, formed when a rock from space crashes into it.
questions.retry_hint: A SPACE ROCK CRASHES into the Moon and leaves a CIRCULAR HOLLOW behind. Ask: which box word names that bowl-shaped hole? A comet and an asteroid are rocks that fly; this word names the mark they leave.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.error_type: Homophone confusion — here (place) vs hear (to listen)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'here' (at this place) when the sentence needs 'hear' (to detect sound with ears).
questions.learning_tip: HEAR = detect sound with ears. HERE = at this place. Test: 'We could HEAR the excitement' → use ears? YES → HEAR. HEAR = ears. HERE = place.
questions.retry_hint: The underlined word means 'at this place', but the sentence is about the EXCITEMENT IN THE CROWD reaching your ears. Ask: which of the two spellings has the word EAR hidden inside it? Choose by meaning, never by sound.

questions.error_type: Spelling — -ing rule: silent -e is dropped, consonant is NOT doubled
questions.trap_type: Students double the 'n' in 'shining', producing 'shinning'. 'Shine' ends in a vowel-consonant-e pattern: drop the -e and add -ing. Do NOT double the final consonant.
questions.learning_tip: 'Shine' ends in vowel-consonant-e (-i-n-e): drop the -e and add -ing → SHINING. Only double the consonant when a SHORT vowel precedes a single consonant (e.g., run → running).
questions.retry_hint: SHINNING doubles the N. Look at the plain verb 'shine': it ends in a silent -e. Ask: do we double that consonant, or simply drop the -e before adding -ing? Doubling belongs to short-vowel words like run and sit.

questions.trap_type: 'The stars' is plural, but students match the verb to the nearest idea and write the singular 'was'.
questions.learning_tip: 'The stars' = more than one -> WERE. WAS belongs only to a singular subject. Find the real subject before you choose the verb.
questions.retry_hint: Find the real subject of the underlined verb: THE STARS, and there are far too many to count. Ask: does a plural subject take the singular verb or the plural one? Match the verb to the subject, never to the word beside it.

questions.error_type: Irregular plural — consonant + y → drop y, add -ies
questions.trap_type: Students add -s directly to 'discovery', producing 'discoverys'. When a word ends in consonant + y, change y to i and add -es.
questions.learning_tip: 'Discovery' ends in consonant + y → change y to i and add -es: discovery → DISCOVERIES. Same rule: story → stories, city → cities.
questions.retry_hint: DISCOVERYS just adds -s. Look at the ending of 'discovery': a consonant followed by -y. Ask: what happens to that -y before the plural ending? Think of story and city, and make the same change here.

questions.trap_type: Students leave out the apostrophe, so 'scientists' reads as a plain plural instead of showing ownership.
questions.learning_tip: The report belongs to the scientists. Plural noun already ending in -s -> apostrophe AFTER the -s: SCIENTISTS' report. Singular would be scientist's.
questions.retry_hint: The REPORT belongs to the scientists, so the word must do more than count them. Ask: does a plain -s show ownership, or only make a plural? And where does the apostrophe go when the owners are more than one?

E.passage: Last Saturday, my family went to a star-gazing event at the science park. We could here (1) the excitement in the crowd as the first telescope turned towards the moon. High above us, the stars were shinning (2) brightly in every direction. The stars was (3) so numerous that nobody could count them all. A scientist told us about the recent discoverys (4) made by the Mars rovers. At the end, the scientists (5) report on the night sky was read aloud before we drove home.

questions.sentence_a: The astronaut asked mission control a question.
questions.sentence_b: Is the shuttle ready for launch?
questions.instruction: Combine into one sentence using reported speech. Begin: 'The astronaut asked...'
questions.model_answer: The astronaut asked if the shuttle was ready for launch.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'asked if the shuttle is ready' (no tense shift).
questions.learning_tip: YES/NO question → ASKED + IF + subject + verb (normal order). 'IS the shuttle ready?' → asked IF the shuttle WAS ready. Tense shifts: is → was. Word order is normal after 'if'.
questions.retry_hint: 'IS THE SHUTTLE READY for launch?' is a yes/no question. Ask: which small joining word must follow ASKED? Does the question keep its inverted order, or become a normal statement? And what happens to the tense once it is reported?

questions.sentence_a: A team of engineers built the new space telescope.
questions.instruction: Rewrite in the passive voice: The new space telescope ________.
questions.model_answer: The new space telescope was built by a team of engineers.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'The new space telescope built by a team of engineers' — missing the auxiliary verb 'was'.
questions.learning_tip: Passive = subject + WAS/WERE + past participle + by + agent. The new space telescope WAS BUILT BY a team of engineers.
questions.retry_hint: The instruction says PASSIVE, so the receiver of the action must come first. Ask: what did the ENGINEERS do to the telescope, and which helping verb has to sit in front of that past participle? Do not forget the little word that introduces the doer.

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
Eleven-year-old Priya wanted to be an astronaut from the age of four. Her bedroom ceiling was covered with glow-in-the-dark stars, and her bookshelf held more books about space than about anything else.

One evening, her school organised a visit to the Science Centre for a special planetarium show. Priya arrived thirty minutes early, claiming a seat in the very front row. While the other students chatted and played on their phones, Priya sat perfectly still, staring up at the dark dome above her.

When the show began, the dome lit up with thousands of simulated stars. The narrator explained how stars are born inside giant clouds of gas and dust called nebulae. Priya leaned forward in her seat, her notebook open on her lap. She wrote down every fact, every name and every number.

Afterward, a scientist named Dr Ariff stayed to answer questions. One by one, the other students gave short answers and walked away. But Priya stayed. She asked about the temperature at the core of a star, how long it takes light to travel from the nearest star to Earth and whether any current missions were searching for planets like ours.

Dr Ariff looked at her with a wide smile. 'You know,' he said, 'I have been visiting schools for fifteen years. I have never met a student quite like you.'

Priya did not know what to say. She just looked back up at the dome, which was now dark and still. She smiled quietly to herself.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 2 has the same meaning as 'completely unable to look away due to fascination'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: TRANSFIXED = unable to look away due to fascination.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: TRANSFIXED = completely held by something so fascinating you cannot look away. TRANSFIXED by the stars = staring, unable to move.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 3, what does 'it' refer to in 'Priya leaned forward, her notebook open on it'?

options.3: Her lap where the notebook rested

mcq_questions.trap_type: 'It' = the surface the notebook rests on = her lap.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: PRONOUN REFERENCE: 'notebook open on IT.' The notebook is placed on something. IT = her LAP. A detail showing how focused and prepared Priya was.

mcq_questions.stem: Why does the writer say Priya's hand 'shot up immediately' when Dr Ariff asked for questions?

options.2: Priya was so genuinely curious she could not wait to ask.
options.3: Priya was the only student awake.

mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Shot up IMMEDIATELY' = instinctive genuine curiosity, not showing off.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: INFERENCE: 'Shot up IMMEDIATELY' + notebook open + transfixed throughout = GENUINE BURNING CURIOSITY. Evidence in the text = the real reason.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 1, is it True or False that Priya visited a planetarium before? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The passage says this was Priya's first visit to the planetarium — she had never seen a show like this before.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1: 'FIRST visit to the planetarium.' FIRST = never happened before. Answer is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: Name THREE questions that Priya asked Dr Ariff after the show.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: She asked about (i) the temperature at the core of a star, (ii) how long it takes light to travel from the nearest star to Earth, and (iii) whether any current missions were searching for planets like ours.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students name only one or two questions instead of all three.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 4: Priya asked THREE things — (1) TEMPERATURE at a star's core, (2) how long LIGHT takes to travel from the nearest star, (3) whether missions seek PLANETS like Earth.

open_ended_questions.stem: How did Priya's behaviour during the show differ from that of the other students? Give TWO differences.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) While the other students chatted and played on their phones, Priya sat perfectly still and stared at the dome. (ii) Priya wrote down every fact in her notebook, while the other students did not appear to take any notes.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students give the same difference twice in different words.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 2: students chatted and used phones; Priya sat STILL and stared. Paragraph 3: Priya wrote in her NOTEBOOK; no mention of others doing the same. Two clear differences.

open_ended_questions.stem: What did Dr Ariff mean when he said 'I have never met a student quite like you'?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: He meant that Priya was exceptional — her deep curiosity, focused attention and intelligent questions were unlike anything in his fifteen years of visiting schools.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'he thought she was good' which is too vague.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Dr Ariff visited schools for FIFTEEN YEARS and never met anyone like Priya. He means she was truly EXCEPTIONAL in her curiosity and the depth of her questions — not just 'good'.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on her actions throughout the passage, describe TWO character traits of Priya with evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) CURIOUS: Priya kept a notebook open during the show and immediately raised her hand for questions — showing a deep, genuine desire to learn more. (ii) FOCUSED: while others chatted and used phones, Priya sat still and stared at the dome, not distracted by anything around her.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'smart and excited' without precise traits or evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: TRAIT INFERENCE: CURIOUS = notebook open, hand shot up immediately. FOCUSED = sat still, stared at dome, ignored distractions. Name trait + evidence = full marks.

questions.stem: The freshly painted mural was as ________ as a sunset — brilliant reds, golds and blues stretching from one end of the wall to the other.
questions.trap_type: 'Dull' = lacking colour (opposite); 'small' = limited size; 'rough' = not smooth. COLOURFUL = having many bright, vivid colours.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! The mural was AS COLOURFUL AS a sunset = comparing its vivid colours to a spectacular sunset. COLOURFUL = having many bright, vivid colours. AS + ADJECTIVE + AS is the correct simile form.
questions.retry_hint: The dash lists the proof: BRILLIANT REDS, GOLDS AND BLUES stretching across the wall. Ask: which word describes a surface full of many bright shades? 'Dull' is its opposite, 'small' is about size, and 'rough' is about touch.

questions.stem: The sculptor used a small knife to ________ a horse from a block of wood.
questions.trap_type: 'Pour' is for liquids; 'scatter' means to spread things; 'assemble' means to put parts together. Only 'carve' = cut a shape from a solid material.
questions.learning_tip: CARVE = cut into a solid material like wood or stone to create a shape. A sculptor CARVES figures out of wood or marble.
questions.retry_hint: The sculptor is cutting into a BLOCK OF WOOD with a small KNIFE. Ask: which verb means to cut a shape out of something solid? 'Pour' needs a liquid, 'scatter' spreads things about, and 'assemble' joins ready-made parts.

questions.stem: In the middle of painting, Mei realised she had ________ blue paint and had to mix more from scratch.
questions.trap_type: 'Given away' = given for free; 'looked after' = cared for; 'put away' = stored. RUN OUT OF = used up all of something so none remained.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: RUN OUT OF = use up all of something so there is none left. Mei RAN OUT OF blue paint = she used every last drop. RUN + OUT + OF work together as one meaning — never separate them.
questions.retry_hint: Mei had no blue paint left and had to MIX MORE FROM SCRATCH. Ask: which phrase means that every last drop has been used up? 'Given away' means handed over free, and 'put away' means simply stored.

questions.stem: When Omar's painting won first place, he was ________ — it was the proudest moment of his school life.
questions.trap_type: 'Under the weather' = feeling ill; 'in hot water' = in trouble. ON CLOUD NINE = feeling extremely happy and delighted.
questions.learning_tip: IDIOM: ON CLOUD NINE = feeling extremely happy and elated. Omar was ON CLOUD NINE = he felt wonderful when he won. There is no actual cloud — it means the highest possible level of happiness!
questions.retry_hint: Omar WON FIRST PLACE and it was the PROUDEST MOMENT of his school life. Ask: does the idiom describe joy, illness, trouble or danger? An idiom carries one whole meaning; read it as a phrase, never word by word.

questions.stem: The painting was so ________ in colour and detail that it looked almost like a real photograph.
questions.trap_type: 'Dull', 'faded' and 'blurred' all suggest poor colour or lack of clarity. Only 'vivid' = bright, strong and very clear.
questions.learning_tip: VIVID = very bright, strong and clear in colour or detail. A VIVID painting has rich, striking colours that make it look almost real.
questions.retry_hint: The painting looked ALMOST LIKE A REAL PHOTOGRAPH, so its colours must be strong and sharply clear. Ask: which word means bright, rich and full of life? 'Dull', 'faded' and 'blurred' all describe the opposite.

questions.stem: Everyone in the art class ________ a different style of brush stroke for the shading exercise.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'try'. EVERYONE = singular → verb+S.
questions.learning_tip: EVERYONE / NOBODY / SOMEONE = Singular! Always use verb+S. Everyone TRIES = add -S. 'Everyone try' is WRONG. Singular indefinite pronouns always take singular present-tense verbs.
questions.retry_hint: The subject is EVERYONE, not 'the art class'. Words like everyone and nobody act like ONE person. Ask: in the present tense, does a singular subject take the plain verb, or the verb ending in -s?

questions.stem: Our school has ________ a new art studio this term, with proper easels and professional brushes.
questions.trap_type: HAS + past participle = present perfect. OPEN → OPENED (regular).
questions.learning_tip: HAS + past participle = present perfect. The school HAS OPENED a new studio = it was done recently and the studio is now available. OPEN → OPENED (add -ed for regular verbs).
questions.retry_hint: HAS stands right before the blank, and the studio exists now, THIS TERM. Ask: which form partners with 'has' to build the present perfect - the plain verb, the -s form, the -ing form, or the past participle?

questions.stem: The potter ________ the clay on the wheel when the electricity suddenly went out.
questions.trap_type: 'The electricity went out' = sudden interrupting event. The potter was already shaping = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: The electricity WENT OUT = sudden past event. The potter was already in the middle of shaping = WAS SHAPING (past continuous). Was/were + verb-ing = action in progress when interrupted.
questions.retry_hint: The ELECTRICITY SUDDENLY WENT OUT and cut into something already happening at the wheel. Ask: which choice shows an action in progress in the PAST? A plain past verb would only report a finished job.

questions.stem: Mei's watercolour painting was far ________ than any work she had produced before — the colours blended perfectly.
questions.trap_type: 'Most beautiful' = superlative; 'beautifuler' is WRONG. MORE BEAUTIFUL = comparative of long adjective.
questions.learning_tip: Long adjective (3+ syllables) → MORE + adjective = comparative. MORE BEAUTIFUL THAN = comparing this painting to her earlier work. 'Beautifuler' is ALWAYS WRONG. FAR + MORE = much more beautiful.
questions.retry_hint: THAN compares this painting with all her earlier work, and the adjective being tested is a long one of three syllables. Ask: do long adjectives add -er, or take a comparing word in front? 'Most' is for the top of a group, and 'beautifuler' is not English.

questions.stem: The winning artwork was displayed ________ the main entrance so that all visitors could see it.
questions.trap_type: 'In the entrance' suggests inside an enclosed space; 'on' is for surfaces; 'at' is correct for a specific location point.
questions.learning_tip: AT = at a specific location point: displayed AT the main entrance, waited AT the gate. AT shows you are at that named spot.
questions.retry_hint: The artwork sits by one exact spot, THE MAIN ENTRANCE, so that every visitor passes it. Ask: which preposition points to a specific place-point? 'In' would push it inside the doorway, and 'on' would lay it flat against a surface.

questions.stem: The school art competition is held every year in November, ________ it?
questions.trap_type: Positive present 'to be' ('is held') → negative question tag. 'Is' → isn't it.
questions.learning_tip: Positive present 'to be' → negative tag. The competition IS held every year, ISN'T it? POSITIVE → NEGATIVE. IS → ISN'T. Remember: use 'to be' tags for passive sentences too (is held → isn't it).
questions.retry_hint: The statement uses the verb IS: 'The competition IS HELD every year'. Ask: after a POSITIVE statement, must the tag turn negative or stay positive? And should the tag keep the same verb rather than borrow 'do'?

questions.stem: The mural ________ by a group of student volunteers over the course of three weekends.
questions.trap_type: The mural did not paint itself — volunteers painted it. Past passive = was painted.
questions.learning_tip: The mural was the receiver of the action. Use the PASSIVE: WAS PAINTED. Passive = was/were + past participle.
questions.retry_hint: The MURAL cannot paint itself; a GROUP OF STUDENT VOLUNTEERS did the work. Ask: does the mural do the action or receive it? A receiver needs the PASSIVE, and three weekends that are over fix the tense in the past.

questions.stem: The art teacher told the class ________ their brushes in the wrong container.
questions.trap_type: Negative reported speech: 'told someone not to do something' = told + object + not to + base verb.
questions.learning_tip: Negative reported speech: told them NOT TO + base verb. The teacher told the class NOT TO LEAVE their brushes in the wrong container.
questions.retry_hint: The teacher TOLD the class about something they must avoid doing. Ask: after 'told + someone', which form follows - the plain verb, the -ing form, or the infinitive? And where does the word 'not' sit, before that little word 'to' or after it?

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Verb forms of 'paint')

questions.context_check: Passage: 'My grandfather enjoys (1)________ landscapes in his spare time.' Signal: 'enjoys + ___' = gerund (verb-ing). Pattern: enjoy + verb-ing → painting.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'to paint' instead of the gerund after 'enjoys'.
questions.learning_tip: ENJOY + verb-ing: enjoys PAINTING landscapes. After 'enjoys', always add -ING.
questions.retry_hint: ENJOYS is the verb standing right before the blank. Ask: after enjoy, love or finish, which form of the next verb do we use - the infinitive, or the -ing form? The pattern decides this, not the meaning.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'He (2)________ at least one new picture every month without fail.' Signal: 'every month' = regular habit = simple present. Subject 'He' = singular → paints.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'paint' (plural form) forgetting that 'He' is singular.
questions.learning_tip: 'Every month' = habit = simple present. He (singular) → PAINTS at least one new picture.
questions.retry_hint: EVERY MONTH signals a repeated habit, and the subject HE is one person. Ask: in the simple present, does a singular subject take the plain verb, or the verb with -s on the end?

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Last summer, he (3)________ a large mural on the wall of our community centre.' Signal: 'Last summer' = past. 'Paint' is regular: paint → painted.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'paint' (base form) ignoring the past signal 'Last summer'.
questions.learning_tip: 'Last summer' = past. 'Paint' is regular: paint → PAINTED.
questions.retry_hint: LAST SUMMER is finished time, and this verb is regular. Ask: which ending turns a regular verb into the simple past? The mural was completed, so no continuous form is needed here.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'While he (4)________ the upper section of the mural, a sudden rain shower forced him to stop.' Signal: 'While he ___' = ongoing background action in the past. Subject 'he' = singular → was painting. Interrupted by 'a sudden rain shower forced him to stop'.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'painted' (simple past) missing the ongoing signal 'while he'.
questions.learning_tip: 'While he ___' = ongoing background past action = past continuous. He WAS PAINTING the upper section when the rain shower came.
questions.retry_hint: WHILE he ________ the upper section, a RAIN SHOWER forced him to stop: a sudden event cutting into a longer one. Ask: which form shows the longer action still in progress, and which helper matches a single person?
