questions.trap_type: 'Swallowed' and 'absorbed' suggest taking something in. 'Released' = let something out, which is what an octopus does with ink.
questions.learning_tip: RELEASED = let something out or set something free. An octopus RELEASES a cloud of ink to escape from predators.
questions.retry_hint: The ink travels OUT of the octopus in order to CONFUSE THE SHARK. Ask: does the blank send the ink outwards, or pull it inwards? 'Swallowed', 'collected' and 'absorbed' all take something in - the wrong direction entirely.

questions.stem: The giant manta ray drifted through the water as ________ as a cloud floating across a summer sky — effortless and silent.
questions.trap_type: 'Noisy' and 'rapid' describe opposite qualities. 'Clumsy' = awkward, which contrasts with the image. GRACEFUL = moving in a smooth, elegant and effortless way.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! The manta ray was AS GRACEFUL AS a cloud = comparing its smooth, effortless movement to a drifting cloud. GRACEFUL = elegant and smooth (adjective). AS + ADJECTIVE + AS is the correct simile form — never use an adverb.
questions.retry_hint: The dash gives it away: EFFORTLESS AND SILENT, DRIFTED like a CLOUD. Ask: which adjective describes smooth, elegant, flowing movement? 'Noisy' and 'rapid' contradict the cloud, and 'clumsy' is its exact opposite.

questions.stem: Scientists discovered a new species of deep-sea fish that was completely ________ to science.
questions.trap_type: 'Familiar' and 'common' are the opposite of a new discovery. 'Unknown' = not yet known or recorded by science.
questions.learning_tip: UNKNOWN = not yet discovered, named or recorded. A species UNKNOWN to science is one that no scientist has ever studied or documented before.
questions.retry_hint: It is a NEW SPECIES that scientists have only just DISCOVERED, so nobody had ever recorded it. Ask: which word means 'never yet known to anyone'? 'Familiar' and 'common' would mean scientists had seen it many times already.

questions.stem: The children spent all afternoon exploring the rock pools — they were in ________, pointing at every crab and starfish they found.
questions.trap_type: 'Hot water' = in trouble; 'thin ice' = in a risky situation; 'deep trouble' = serious problems. IN SEVENTH HEAVEN = feeling extremely happy and delighted.
questions.learning_tip: IDIOM: IN SEVENTH HEAVEN = feeling extremely happy, as if you are in a perfect, joyful place. The children were IN SEVENTH HEAVEN = they were absolutely thrilled exploring the rock pools. Idioms cannot be understood word by word!
questions.retry_hint: They spent ALL AFTERNOON at the ROCK POOLS, POINTING AT EVERY CRAB and starfish. Ask: does the idiom describe delight, danger, or trouble? 'Hot water', 'thin ice' and 'deep trouble' all mean something has gone badly wrong.

questions.stem: The documentary warned viewers to ________ single-use plastics that end up in the ocean and harm sea creatures.
questions.trap_type: 'Hold on' = wait; 'run into' = encounter; 'give in' = surrender. CUT OUT = stop using or consuming something entirely.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: CUT OUT = stop doing or using something entirely. CUT OUT single-use plastics = stop using them completely. CUT + OUT work together. 'I need to cut out junk food' = stop eating it.
questions.retry_hint: The documentary WARNED viewers because the plastics HARM SEA CREATURES, so it wants them stopped for good. Ask: which phrasal verb means to give something up completely? 'Hold on' means wait; 'give in' means surrender.

questions.stem: Nobody in the diving team ________ the blue-ringed octopus without feeling a shiver - its venom is deadly enough to kill a person.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'see'. NOBODY = singular -> verb + S. 'Seeing' and 'are seeing' have no place after a singular subject in a simple present statement.
questions.learning_tip: NOBODY / EVERYONE / SOMEONE = Singular! Nobody SEES = add -S. 'Nobody see' is WRONG. Singular indefinite pronouns always take singular present-tense verbs.
questions.retry_hint: The subject is NOBODY, not 'the diving team'. Words like nobody and everyone behave like ONE person. Ask: in a simple present statement, does a singular subject take the plain verb, or the verb ending in -s?

questions.stem: Our school has ________ an online marine life project that students can contribute to from home.
questions.trap_type: HAS + past participle = present perfect. LAUNCH → LAUNCHED (regular).
questions.learning_tip: HAS + past participle = present perfect. Our school HAS LAUNCHED the project = it started recently and is now running. LAUNCH → LAUNCHED (regular verb, add -ed).
questions.retry_hint: HAS is already in the sentence, so the blank must be the form that partners with it. Ask: after 'has', do we use the plain verb, the -s form, the -ing form, or the past participle? This verb is regular, so it simply takes -ed.

questions.stem: The dolphins ________ playfully around the boat when the captain spotted a school of tuna in the distance.
questions.trap_type: 'The captain spotted tuna' = sudden interrupting event. Dolphins were already swimming = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: The captain SPOTTED tuna = sudden past event. The dolphins were already in the middle of swimming = WERE SWIMMING (past continuous). Was/were + verb-ing = action in progress when interrupted.
questions.retry_hint: The captain SPOTTED a school of tuna - one sudden event that cut across an activity already under way. Ask: which form shows an action in progress in the past? A plain past verb reports only a finished action.

questions.stem: The blue whale is far ________ than any other animal on Earth — it can grow up to thirty metres long.
questions.trap_type: 'Largest' = superlative (for 3+); 'more larger' = WRONG double comparative. LARGER = comparative (comparing two groups).
questions.learning_tip: Short adjective + -ER = comparative. Large → LARGER. The blue whale is LARGER THAN any other animal = comparing it to all others. 'More larger' is ALWAYS WRONG — never add both 'more' AND '-er'.
questions.retry_hint: THAN signals a comparison, and this adjective is a short one. Ask: do short adjectives simply add -er, or do they need a word in front? Can you ever put 'more' before a word that already ends in -er? 'Largest' would need three or above.

questions.stem: Scientists have explored less than twenty percent of the deep ocean, so we still know very ________ about the creatures that live down there.
questions.trap_type: 'Many' and 'few' are for countable nouns. 'Very much' cannot be used like this in a positive statement. LITTLE = not much (uncountable).
questions.learning_tip: Know very LITTLE = know almost nothing. LITTLE / MUCH go with uncountable ideas; FEW / MANY go with countable things you can number.
questions.retry_hint: The clue is LESS THAN TWENTY PERCENT explored - our knowledge of the deep ocean is tiny. Ask: is knowledge counted one by one, or measured as an amount? 'Few' and 'many' count separate things; the blank needs the other kind.

questions.stem: Each of the clownfish in the tank ________ bright orange and white stripes on its body.
questions.trap_type: 'Each of the clownfish' = each one individually = singular. Present fact. Students write 'have' thinking of many fish.
questions.learning_tip: 'Each of the clownfish' = each one at a time = singular → HAS bright orange and white stripes. EACH always uses a singular verb.
questions.retry_hint: EACH means one clownfish at a time, however many swim in the TANK. Notice ITS BODY - singular again. Ask: does a singular subject take 'have', or the form ending in -s?

questions.stem: The rare blue whale ________ by a team of marine biologists off the coast of Sri Lanka last month.
questions.trap_type: The whale did not spot itself — the marine biologists spotted it. Past passive = was spotted.
questions.learning_tip: The whale was the receiver of the action. Use the PASSIVE: WAS SPOTTED. Passive = was/were + past participle.
questions.retry_hint: BY A TEAM OF MARINE BIOLOGISTS tells you the whale received the action, and LAST MONTH tells you it is over. Ask: which choice is both passive and past? A passive verb needs a helper plus a past participle.

questions.stem: The marine conservationist told visitors ________ into the water to touch or disturb the coral.
questions.trap_type: Negative reported speech: told someone not to do something = told + object + not to + base verb.
questions.learning_tip: 'Told visitors NOT TO + base verb': told visitors NOT TO REACH into the water. After 'told + object', use 'not to' + base verb.
questions.retry_hint: TOLD + somebody + a negative instruction. Ask: after 'told visitors', does English use the plain verb, the -ing form, or the infinitive? And where does the little negative word sit inside that pattern?

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Be verbs and auxiliary verbs)

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The Great Barrier Reef (1)________ the largest coral reef system in the world.' Signal: singular subject 'The Great Barrier Reef' + present fact = IS. Third person singular + simple present be verb.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'are' thinking of many reefs. 'The Great Barrier Reef' is one named reef = singular.
questions.learning_tip: 'The Great Barrier Reef' = one singular named place → IS the largest coral reef. IS is used for singular subjects in the present tense.
questions.retry_hint: 'The GREAT BARRIER REEF' names ONE single place, however many corals it holds. Ask: in the present tense, which be-verb belongs with a singular subject, and which one belongs with many things?

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Thousands of fish species (2)________ found in its warm waters.' Signal: plural subject 'thousands of fish species' + present passive fact = ARE. Plural + present be verb in passive.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'is' (singular) instead of 'are' (plural). 'Thousands of fish species' is plural.
questions.learning_tip: 'Thousands of fish species' = plural → ARE found in its waters. ARE is for plural subjects in the present tense.
questions.retry_hint: Count the subject: THOUSANDS OF FISH SPECIES. Ask: does a plural subject take the singular be-verb, or the plural one? The time stays present here - the fish live in those WARM WATERS today.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The reef (3)________ first explored by European scientists in the eighteenth century.' Signal: singular subject 'the reef' + past passive = WAS. Singular + past be verb in passive construction.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'is' (present) ignoring the time signal 'eighteenth century' which indicates the past.
questions.learning_tip: 'In the eighteenth century' = past. 'The reef' = singular. Past + singular = WAS first explored. Always match the be verb to the time and number.
questions.retry_hint: The EIGHTEENTH CENTURY is finished time, and 'the reef' is one thing. Ask: which past be-verb goes with a singular subject? Match BOTH the time and the number before you choose.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'In the past, many coral species (4)________ believed to be indestructible by early scientists.' Signal: plural subject 'many coral species' + past passive = WERE. Plural + past be verb in passive construction.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'was' (singular) instead of 'were' (plural). 'Many coral species' is plural.
questions.learning_tip: 'Many coral species' = plural + past = WERE believed. WERE is for plural subjects in the past tense.
questions.retry_hint: Two clues at once: IN THE PAST (finished time) and MANY CORAL SPECIES (more than one). Ask: which be-verb is past AND plural? Do not let the singular word 'past' pull you the wrong way.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Sadly, rising ocean temperature (5)________ caused widespread coral bleaching in recent years.' Signal: singular subject 'rising ocean temperature' + present perfect auxiliary = HAS. Singular + HAS + past participle (caused).
questions.trap_type: Students write 'have' (plural) instead of 'has' (singular). 'Rising ocean temperature' is singular.
questions.learning_tip: 'Rising ocean temperature' = singular → HAS caused bleaching. HAS is the present perfect auxiliary for singular subjects.
questions.retry_hint: CAUSED is a past participle, so the blank must be its helping verb. The subject, RISING OCEAN TEMPERATURE, is one thing. Ask: which present perfect helper goes with he/she/it, and which goes with plural subjects?

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Scientists (6)________ been working for decades to find ways to protect the reef.' Signal: plural subject 'scientists' + present perfect continuous auxiliary = HAVE. Plural + HAVE + been + verb-ing.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'has' (singular) instead of 'have' (plural). 'Scientists' is plural.
questions.learning_tip: 'Scientists' = plural → HAVE been working. HAVE is the present perfect auxiliary for plural subjects.
questions.retry_hint: BEEN WORKING needs a helper in front of it, and the subject SCIENTISTS is plural. Ask: which present perfect helper goes with a plural subject? The singular one is already needed in blank 5.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The reef (7)________ not only shelter sea creatures but also protect coastlines from strong waves.' Signal: singular subject 'the reef' + negative present simple auxiliary for emphasis = DOES. 'Does not only... but also' = emphatic positive construction.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'do' (plural) or reach for a be verb. 'The reef' is singular, and a negative in the simple present needs the DO-family auxiliary.
questions.learning_tip: Simple present negative: singular subject -> DOES not + base verb. 'The reef DOES not grow back quickly.' Plural subject -> DO not.
questions.retry_hint: NOT GROW BACK is a plain verb with a negative in front, so the blank is the auxiliary carrying that negative. 'The reef' is singular. Ask: which member of the DO-family goes with he/she/it?

questions.context_check: Passage: 'What (8)________ we owe to these incredible ecosystems? We owe them our commitment to protect them.' Signal: question with plural subject 'we' + simple present auxiliary = DO. 'What DO we owe' = interrogative form.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'does' (singular) instead of 'do' (plural). 'We' is plural → auxiliary is DO in questions.
questions.learning_tip: In questions: 'What DO we owe?' = auxiliary DO for plural subject 'we'. 'Does' would be for he/she/it (singular).
questions.retry_hint: This sentence is a question, so a helper must jump in front of the subject WE. Ask: which helper goes with 'we' - the plural one, or the he/she/it form that blank 7 already uses? Questions cannot use the bare verb alone.

C.passage: The Great Barrier Reef (1)________ the largest coral reef system in the world. Thousands of fish species (2)________ found in its warm waters. The reef (3)________ first explored by European scientists in the eighteenth century. In the past, many coral species (4)________ believed to be indestructible by early scientists. Sadly, rising ocean temperature (5)________ caused widespread coral bleaching in recent years. Scientists (6)________ been working for decades to find ways to protect the reef. The reef (7)________ not grow back quickly after bleaching, so every visitor must treat it with care. What (8)________ we owe to these incredible ecosystems? We owe them our commitment to protect them.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: Fish are fascinating creatures that have many special features to help them survive. They breathe underwater using (1)________, which absorb oxygen from the water as it flows past them. They use their (2)________ to steer and balance themselves as they swim. Some fish have the ability to (3)________ themselves by changing colour or pattern to match their surroundings, making them nearly invisible. This helps them hide from any (4)________ that might want to eat them. When a fish needs more oxygen, it may rise to the (5)________ of the water and gulp air from above.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'absorb oxygen from the water as it flows past' = the breathing organs of a fish = gills.
questions.learning_tip: GILLS = the organs fish use to breathe underwater. GILLS extract oxygen from water as it flows through them.
questions.retry_hint: The clue sits right beside the blank: they ABSORB OXYGEN from the water so the fish can BREATHE UNDERWATER. Ask: which box word names the breathing organs of a fish? 'Scales' merely cover the skin; they take in nothing.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'steer and balance themselves as they swim' = the flat wing-like parts on a fish's body = fins.
questions.learning_tip: FINS = the flat, wing-like parts on a fish that help it steer, balance and move through the water.
questions.retry_hint: The job here is to STEER AND BALANCE while swimming. Ask: which box word names the flat, wing-like parts on a fish's body? 'Scales' are the small plates covering the skin - they steer nothing at all.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'changing colour or pattern to match their surroundings, making them nearly invisible' = camouflage.
questions.learning_tip: CAMOUFLAGE = disguise by blending in with the surroundings. Some fish CAMOUFLAGE themselves to hide from predators.
questions.retry_hint: CHANGING COLOUR OR PATTERN to MATCH THEIR SURROUNDINGS makes the fish nearly INVISIBLE. The blank follows 'the ability to', so it must be a verb. Ask: which box word means to disguise yourself by blending in?

questions.trap_type: The clue 'might want to eat them' = an animal that hunts and eats other animals = predator.
questions.learning_tip: A PREDATOR = an animal that hunts and eats other animals. Fish camouflage themselves to hide from PREDATORS.
questions.retry_hint: The clue follows the blank: it MIGHT WANT TO EAT THEM. Ask: which box word names an animal that hunts and eats other animals? 'Venom' is a poison, not a hunter, and this blank must name a creature.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'rise to the ___ of the water and gulp air from above' = the top of the water = surface.
questions.learning_tip: SURFACE = the top layer or outer face of something. A fish rises to the SURFACE of the water to gulp air when it needs more oxygen.
questions.retry_hint: The fish must RISE and then GULP AIR FROM ABOVE, so the blank is the very top of the water. Ask: which box word names the top layer of something? 'Current' is the water moving along, not its top.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.error_type: Invariable plural — fish stays fish (not fishes)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'fishes' as a regular plural. FISH is invariable: one fish, fifty fish.
questions.learning_tip: FISH = invariable plural. One fish, two fish, fifty FISH. 'Fishes' is WRONG in standard usage. Unlike most nouns, FISH does not add -S for the plural.
questions.retry_hint: Count them: OVER FIFTY of them in the TANK, so a plural is certainly needed. Ask: does this animal word add -es for its plural, or does it stay exactly the same whether there are one or fifty? Some animal names never change.

questions.error_type: Homophone confusion — there (place) vs their (belonging to them)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'there' (place) when the meaning is 'their' (belonging to the staff).
questions.learning_tip: THEIR = belonging to them. THERE = at that place. Test: 'showed us THEIR favourite exhibit' → does it belong to them? YES → THEIR. THEIR = possession; THERE = location. Never confuse them!
questions.retry_hint: The favourite EXHIBIT belongs to the aquarium STAFF - the sentence is not pointing at a place. Ask: does the underlined spelling mean 'at that place', or 'belonging to them'? Choose by meaning, never by sound.

questions.error_type: Spelling — -ing rule: drop silent -e before adding -ing
questions.trap_type: Students keep the -e: 'shineing'. Drop the silent -e before adding -ing.
questions.learning_tip: Spelling rule: word ending in silent -e → DROP -e before adding -ing. SHINE → SHIN + ING = SHINING (not 'shineing'). Same: make→making, write→writing, love→loving.
questions.retry_hint: The base verb is SHINE, and it ends in a silent -e. Ask: what happens to that -e before -ING is added? The same rule runs through make/making, ride/riding and write/writing.

questions.error_type: Subject-verb agreement - plural subject (the deep-sea creatures)
questions.trap_type: Students match the verb to 'gallery', the noun nearest to the blank, instead of to the real subject 'the deep-sea creatures'.
questions.learning_tip: The subject is THE DEEP-SEA CREATURES = plural -> WERE the strangest of all. WAS is only for a singular subject. Find the head noun, not the nearest noun.
questions.retry_hint: Find the real subject: the DEEP-SEA CREATURES, not the GALLERY that happens to sit next to the blank. Ask: is that subject one thing, or many? Match the verb to the head noun, never to the nearest noun.

questions.trap_type: Students write a plain plural and leave out the apostrophe that shows ownership.
questions.learning_tip: The enclosure BELONGS TO the octopuses -> OCTOPUSES' enclosure (apostrophe after the -s for a plural owner). Singular: octopus's.
questions.retry_hint: The ENCLOSURE belongs to the octopuses - many owners, not one. Ask: does a plain -s show ownership, or only make a plural? When the owners are many, does the apostrophe go before the -s, or after it?

E.passage: Last Saturday, our class visited the aquarium near the harbour. The tank held over fifty fishes (1) from different parts of the ocean. The aquarium staff showed us there (2) favourite exhibit — an enormous manta ray that swam above our heads. A sea horse clung to a strand of seaweed, shineing (3) with pale silver light in the dark tank. The deep-sea creatures in the final gallery was (4) the strangest of all, with glowing bodies and enormous eyes. At the end, the octopuses (5) enclosure was the last stop, and we pressed our faces against the glass.

questions.sentence_a: The marine biologist asked a question.
questions.sentence_b: Are the coral reefs recovering?
questions.instruction: Combine into one sentence using reported speech. Begin: 'The marine biologist asked...'
questions.model_answer: The marine biologist asked if the coral reefs were recovering.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'asked if the coral reefs are recovering' (no tense shift) or 'asked if were the coral reefs recovering' (wrong word order).
questions.learning_tip: YES/NO question → reported speech: ASKED + IF/WHETHER + subject + verb (normal word order). 'ARE the reefs recovering?' → asked IF the reefs WERE recovering. Tense shifts: are → were. Word order flips to normal — no inversion.
questions.retry_hint: A yes/no question turned into REPORTED speech. Ask: which small joining word follows ASKED? Does the question keep its inverted order, or become a normal statement? And what must happen to the verb 'are' when the reporting verb is past?

questions.sentence_a: The coral reef was badly damaged by the storm.
questions.sentence_b: Scientists are now working to restore it.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'although'.
questions.model_answer: Although the coral reef was badly damaged by the storm, scientists are now working to restore it.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'The coral reef was badly damaged by the storm although scientists are now working to restore it' — less emphatic and changes the contrast.
questions.learning_tip: ALTHOUGH + [the difficult fact], [the positive response]. ALTHOUGH the reef was damaged, scientists are working to restore it. Starting with 'although' shows the contrast more powerfully.
questions.retry_hint: ALTHOUGH introduces the setback; the main clause gives the response to it. Ask: which of the two sentences is the bad news, and which is the answer to it? Put the joining word in front of the bad news and keep both halves complete.

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
Of all the creatures in the ocean, the seahorse is one of the most unusual. It does not look like a typical fish. It has a horse-like head, a long curved neck and a body covered in bony rings instead of scales. Its eyes move independently of each other, which means it can look in two different directions at the same time.

Seahorses are very slow swimmers. They move upright through the water by fluttering their tiny dorsal fin very fast — up to fifty times per second. They use their curling tails to grip onto seagrass and coral so that strong currents do not sweep them away.

One of the most surprising facts about seahorses is that it is the male — not the female — that carries and gives birth to the young. The female deposits her eggs into a special pouch on the male's body. The male carries the eggs for several weeks until the baby seahorses are ready to swim out on their own.

Seahorses are also skilled hunters. They creep up slowly behind tiny shrimps and then snap them up with their long tube-like mouths so fast that the shrimp barely has time to react.

Sadly, seahorses are under threat. They are caught in fishing nets, collected for use in traditional medicine and lose their homes when seagrass meadows and coral reefs are destroyed. Conservation groups are working hard to protect them and restore the habitats they depend on.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 2 has the same meaning as 'gripping or holding on tightly'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Drifting' = floating freely; 'curling' = bending in circles; 'swaying' = moving side to side. ANCHORING = fixing firmly in place, gripping tight.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: ANCHORING = fixing firmly in place so as not to drift away. The seahorse's tail acts as an ANCHOR = it grips the seagrass tightly so the current cannot sweep it away.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 1, what does 'they' refer to in 'they move independently of each other'?

options.1: The fins on the seahorse's back
options.2: The two eyes of the seahorse
options.3: The tiny shrimps the seahorse hunts

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking 'they' = fins. But the sentence is about eyes: 'Its eyes move independently of each other.'
mcq_questions.learning_tip: PRONOUN REFERENCE: 'THEY move independently of each other.' What has two parts that can move separately? The EYES. 'Its EYES move independently' = the left and right eyes can look in different directions at the same time.

mcq_questions.stem: Why does the writer describe the seahorse as 'one of nature's most unlikely survivors' in paragraph 5?

options.1: Because seahorses live only in very cold water and few places are cold enough.
options.2: Because despite being slow, armourless and tiny, seahorses have existed for millions of years.
options.3: Because seahorses are too delicate to survive outside of aquariums.
options.4: Because scientists have only recently discovered that seahorses exist.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 3 thinking they are too delicate. The word 'unlikely' = surprising that they survived given their disadvantages.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: INFERENCE: 'UNLIKELY SURVIVOR' = an animal you would not expect to survive — because it is slow, small and has no claws or fangs. Yet seahorses have SURVIVED for millions of years. UNLIKELY = surprising, not what you would predict.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 3, is it True or False that the female seahorse carries and gives birth to the babies? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The passage says it is the MALE seahorse that carries the eggs in a pouch on his belly and gives birth — not the female.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'True' because they assume females give birth in all animals. The passage clearly states it is the male.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 3: 'the MALE seahorse carries the eggs in a pouch on his belly and gives birth.' This is unique in the animal world. The MALE, not the female, gives birth. Answer is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: How does the seahorse catch its prey?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: The seahorse creeps up slowly behind tiny shrimps and then snaps them up with its long tube-like mouth very fast.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'it uses its mouth' without describing the hunting method.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 4: 'they CREEP UP slowly behind tiny shrimps and then SNAP them up with their long tube-like mouths.' Describe the full hunting method.

open_ended_questions.stem: Why is it surprising that the male seahorse gives birth? Explain using information from the passage.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: It is surprising because in almost all other animals, it is the female that carries and gives birth to young. In the seahorse, the female deposits her eggs into a special pouch on the male's body and the male carries them until the babies are ready to swim out.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'it is surprising because seahorses are unusual animals' — too vague. Must explain the reversal of the expected role.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 3: It is the MALE, not the female, that carries the young in a POUCH and gives birth. This is the opposite of what happens in most animals.

open_ended_questions.stem: Give TWO reasons from paragraph 5 why seahorse numbers are falling.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) They are caught in fishing nets. (ii) They are collected for use in traditional medicine. (Accept also: their habitats are destroyed when seagrass and coral reefs are damaged.)
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students give only one reason or use a reason from earlier paragraphs.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 5: (1) caught in FISHING NETS, (2) collected for TRADITIONAL MEDICINE, (3) lose homes when habitats are destroyed. Give any two of these three.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on the passage, describe TWO ways in which the seahorse is unusual compared to most other fish. Give evidence for each.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) MOVEMENT: unlike most fish, seahorses swim upright using a tiny fin that beats up to 35 times per second — they do not use their tail for swimming, only for anchoring. (ii) REPRODUCTION: uniquely, it is the MALE seahorse that carries the eggs in a pouch and gives birth, not the female.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students give general facts ('they are small and live in the sea') without comparing to other fish or giving specific evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: The question asks what makes seahorses UNUSUAL — meaning different from most other fish. MOVEMENT = swim upright (most fish swim horizontally). REPRODUCTION = male gives birth (in almost all other animals, the female does). Evidence from passage = full marks.

questions.stem: The engineer spent three years trying to ________ a robot that could carry heavy boxes in a warehouse.
questions.trap_type: 'Destroy' and 'discard' mean to remove or damage. 'Download' is a digital action. Only 'develop' = design and create something new over time.
questions.learning_tip: DEVELOP = design, build and improve something new over time. Engineers DEVELOP new technologies through research, testing and improvement.
questions.retry_hint: It took THREE YEARS, so this is slow designing, building and improving - not a single click. Ask: which word means to create something new over a long time? 'Download' takes seconds; 'destroy' and 'discard' get rid of things.

questions.stem: The new smartphone screen was as ________ as a mirror — every tiny reflection was perfectly clear.
questions.trap_type: 'Heavy', 'sharp' and 'small' don't describe the surface quality of a mirror. SMOOTH = having an even, flat surface.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! The screen was AS SMOOTH AS a mirror = comparing its perfectly flat surface to a mirror. SMOOTH = no bumps or rough patches — like glass. Similes always use 'as ... as' to compare two things.
questions.retry_hint: The dash explains it: every tiny REFLECTION is perfectly clear, and the screen is compared to a MIRROR. Ask: which adjective describes a flat, even surface with no bumps? 'Heavy' and 'small' say nothing about a surface.

questions.stem: The scientist's new ________ for turning seawater into drinking water could help millions of people.
questions.trap_type: 'Excuse' and 'hobby' are unrelated to scientific solutions. 'Decoration' is aesthetic. Only 'process' = a series of actions that achieves a specific result.
questions.learning_tip: A PROCESS = a series of steps or actions carried out to achieve a specific result. A PROCESS for turning seawater into drinking water = a method with clear steps.
questions.retry_hint: TURNING SEAWATER INTO DRINKING WATER takes a series of steps, one after another. Ask: which word names a method built from ordered steps? An 'excuse' or a 'hobby' could never help millions of people.

questions.stem: When the scientist announced that her invention could charge a phone in thirty seconds, the audience was ________ — nobody expected news this exciting.
questions.trap_type: 'Under the weather' = ill; 'in hot water' = in trouble; 'on thin ice' = risky. OVER THE MOON = extremely happy and excited.
questions.learning_tip: IDIOM: OVER THE MOON = extremely happy and thrilled about something. The audience was OVER THE MOON = absolutely delighted by the news. There is no actual moon — it is an idiom for pure joy!
questions.retry_hint: NOBODY EXPECTED news this exciting, and the invention can CHARGE A PHONE IN THIRTY SECONDS. Ask: does the idiom describe delight, illness, or danger? 'Under the weather' means ill; 'in hot water' means in trouble.

questions.stem: The engineer decided to ________ a complicated feature of the app before its launch to make it simpler.
questions.trap_type: 'Bring in' = introduce; 'break down' = stop working; 'hold up' = delay. TAKE OUT = remove something from a design or plan.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: TAKE OUT = remove something from somewhere. The engineer TOOK OUT a feature = she removed it from the app design. TAKE + OUT work together. 'I need to take out this paragraph' = remove it.
questions.retry_hint: To MAKE IT SIMPLER, the COMPLICATED feature has to go. Ask: which phrasal verb means to remove something from a design? 'Bring in' would add it back, and 'hold up' would only delay the LAUNCH.

questions.stem: Everyone in the engineering team ________ a different role in building the prototype device.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'play'. EVERYONE = singular → verb+S.
questions.learning_tip: EVERYONE / NOBODY / SOMEONE = Singular! Always use verb+S. Everyone PLAYS = add -S. 'Everyone play' is WRONG. Singular indefinite pronouns always take singular present-tense verbs.
questions.retry_hint: The subject is EVERYONE, not 'the engineering team'. Words like everyone and nobody act like ONE person. Ask: in the present tense, does a singular subject take the plain verb, or the verb ending in -s?

questions.stem: Scientists have ________ a new material that is stronger than steel but lighter than paper.
questions.trap_type: HAVE + past participle = present perfect. DISCOVER → DISCOVERED (regular).
questions.learning_tip: HAVE + past participle = present perfect. Scientists HAVE DISCOVERED a new material = they discovered it recently and the result matters now. DISCOVER → DISCOVERED (regular verb, add -ed).
questions.retry_hint: HAVE is already there, so the blank must be the form that partners with it. Ask: after 'have', do we use the plain verb, the -ing form, or the past participle? This verb is regular, so it simply takes -ed.

questions.stem: The students ________ their robot when the battery unexpectedly ran out of power in the middle of the test.
questions.trap_type: 'The battery ran out' = sudden interrupting event. Students were already programming = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: The battery RAN OUT = sudden past event. Students were already in the middle of programming = WERE PROGRAMMING (past continuous). Was/were + verb-ing = action in progress when something interrupts.
questions.retry_hint: The battery RAN OUT - a sudden event breaking into an activity already under way. Ask: which form shows an action still in progress in the past? A plain past verb reports only a finished action.

questions.stem: The latest laptop model is much ________ than last year's version — it processes data twice as fast.
questions.trap_type: 'Most powerful' = superlative (for 3+); 'powerfuller' is WRONG. MORE POWERFUL = comparative (long adjective).
questions.learning_tip: Long adjective (3+ syllables) → MORE + adjective = comparative. MORE POWERFUL THAN = comparing two models. 'Powerfuller' is ALWAYS WRONG. For long adjectives, always use MORE.
questions.retry_hint: THAN compares this laptop with LAST YEAR'S VERSION - exactly two models - and the adjective is a long one. Ask: do long adjectives take -er, or do they need a comparing word in front? 'Powerfuller' is not English; 'most' is for three or above.

questions.stem: Scientists can store so ________ data on a single microchip today that a whole library of books fits inside your pocket.
questions.trap_type: 'Data' is uncountable, so 'many', 'few' and 'a few' are impossible. Students count the books instead of measuring the data.
questions.learning_tip: MUCH = a large amount, for uncountable nouns (data, water, information). MANY / A FEW / FEW = for things you can count one by one.
questions.retry_hint: DATA is one uncountable mass: you never say 'one data, two datas'. Ask: which quantity word measures an amount rather than counting separate items? 'Many', 'few' and 'a few' all count things one by one.

questions.stem: The invention of the internet changed communication forever, ________ it?
questions.trap_type: Positive past simple ('changed') → negative question tag. 'Changed' → 'didn't it' (not 'wasn't it' which is for 'to be').
questions.learning_tip: Positive past simple → negative tag. The internet CHANGED communication, DIDN'T it? POSITIVE → NEGATIVE. Past simple regular verb → DID/DIDN'T. 'Did' is the auxiliary for past simple. CHANGED → DIDN'T it (not 'wasn't').
questions.retry_hint: The statement is positive, and its verb CHANGED is a past simple verb - there is no 'to be' verb anywhere in it. Ask: after a positive statement, is the tag positive or negative? And which helper stands in for a past simple verb?

questions.stem: The first working telephone ________ by Alexander Graham Bell in eighteen seventy-six.
questions.trap_type: The telephone did not invent itself — Bell invented it. Past passive = was invented.
questions.learning_tip: The telephone was the receiver of the action. Use the PASSIVE: WAS INVENTED. Passive = was/were + past participle.
questions.retry_hint: BY ALEXANDER GRAHAM BELL shows the telephone received the action - it could hardly build itself. Ask: which choice is passive, and does it match a year long finished? A passive verb needs a helper plus a past participle.

questions.stem: The tech company told its programmers ________ the new software before the deadline next Friday.
questions.trap_type: 'Told someone to do something' = reported speech: told + object + to + base verb → to complete.
questions.learning_tip: 'Told programmers TO + base verb': told its programmers TO COMPLETE the software. After 'told + object', use the infinitive with 'to'.
questions.retry_hint: TOLD + somebody + an instruction. Ask: after 'told its programmers', does English use the plain verb, the -ing form, or the infinitive with 'to'? Reported orders always follow the one same pattern.

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Basic conjunctions)

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The light bulb changed the world (1)________ it was invented by Thomas Edison in 1879.' Signal: at the time / at the moment = WHEN. 'The world changed WHEN the light bulb was invented' = the invention is the point in time that triggered the change.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'because'. Edison being famous was not caused by the light bulb - the blank marks the POINT IN TIME at which he switched it on.
questions.learning_tip: WHEN = at the time that something happened. He was already famous WHEN he switched on the bulb = the two facts share the same moment.
questions.retry_hint: Edison was ALREADY A FAMOUS INVENTOR, so the light bulb did not make him famous - this is not a reason. Ask: which joining word marks the POINT IN TIME at which he SWITCHED it on?

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Before electricity, people used candles (2)________ they had no other source of light at night.' Signal: reason = BECAUSE. People used candles for the reason that they had no other light source.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'so' (result) instead of 'because' (reason). The lack of electric light is the REASON, not the result.
questions.learning_tip: BECAUSE = the reason. People used candles BECAUSE they had no other light = the reason they used candles was the lack of electric light.
questions.retry_hint: Why CANDLES? The second half tells you: they had NO OTHER WAY of seeing after dark. Ask: which joining word introduces the reason for something? 'So' would give a result instead - the wrong direction.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Today, electric lights are used in homes, schools (3)________ offices all around the world.' Signal: adding to a list = AND. Connecting the third item in a series of places.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'or' (a choice) instead of 'and' (addition). The three places all have electric lights — it is an addition, not a choice.
questions.learning_tip: AND = used to add items in a list. Homes, schools AND offices = all three places have electric lights. AND shows addition.
questions.retry_hint: Three places are being listed: HOMES, SCHOOLS, OFFICES. Every one of them has electric lamps; nobody is choosing between them. Ask: which joining word ADDS the last item of a list? 'Or' would offer a choice.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Early computers were as large as a room (4)________ today's computers fit in the palm of your hand.' Signal: contrast between large old computers and tiny modern ones = BUT. The two facts contrast strongly.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'and' (addition) instead of 'but' (contrast). The size change from room-sized to palm-sized is a sharp contrast, not a simple addition.
questions.learning_tip: BUT = contrast. Early computers were huge BUT today's fit in your hand. BUT shows a strong difference between two ideas.
questions.retry_hint: One machine filled A WHOLE ROOM; the other fits in a POCKET. The two halves clash. Ask: which joining word signals a contrast, a surprise, a sharp difference? 'And' would simply add a second fact of the same kind.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The first computers broke down often, (5)________ engineers worked hard to make them more reliable.' Signal: result/response = SO. Engineers working hard is the result/response to the computers breaking down.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'because' (reason) instead of 'so' (result). 'So' links the cause (breakdowns) to the result (engineers working hard).
questions.learning_tip: SO = as a result. Computers broke down often, SO engineers worked hard = the engineers' effort was the RESULT of the problem.
questions.retry_hint: The machines BROKE DOWN first; the ENGINEERS WORKED LONG HOURS as a consequence. Ask: which joining word introduces the RESULT of a problem? 'Because' would flip the order, making the engineers the cause.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Some people use their phones to listen to music (6)________ they exercise.' Signal: two actions happening at the same time = WHILE. Listening to music and exercising happen simultaneously.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'when' (a point in time) instead of 'while' (two ongoing actions at the same time).
questions.learning_tip: WHILE = at the same time as. People listen to music WHILE they exercise = both actions happen simultaneously. WHEN would suggest the music starts at the moment exercise begins.
questions.retry_hint: Two activities run side by side from start to finish: you LISTEN TO MUSIC for the whole time that you JOG. Ask: which joining word means 'at the same time as', across a stretch of time rather than one instant?

questions.context_check: Passage: '(7)________ technology has made our lives easier in many ways, it has also created new problems.' Signal: contrast showing an unexpected or surprising result = ALTHOUGH. Technology made life easier (positive), BUT it also created problems (negative) — a contrast.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'because' or 'so' instead of 'although'. The sentence has a contrast — technology is helpful but also causes problems.
questions.learning_tip: ALTHOUGH = despite the fact that. ALTHOUGH technology made life easier, it also created problems. 'Although' introduces a contrast between two facts.
questions.retry_hint: The sentence admits a good thing (lives MUCH EASIER), then turns against it (NEW PROBLEMS, TOO MUCH SCREEN TIME). Ask: which joining word opens a sentence to say 'despite this fact'? 'Because' would make the problems a reason.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'In the future, people may travel by self-driving cars (8)________ flying taxis to reach their destinations.' Signal: choice between two options = OR. Self-driving cars and flying taxis are two alternative ways to travel.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'and' (addition) instead of 'or' (choice). The sentence lists two ALTERNATIVE future transport options, not two things used together.
questions.learning_tip: OR = one option or another. Self-driving cars OR flying taxis = two alternative choices. OR shows that one of the two options will be chosen.
questions.retry_hint: EITHER is the giveaway: it always needs a partner, offering one of two choices - a SELF-DRIVING CAR, a FLYING TAXI. Ask: which joining word presents alternatives? 'And' would mean both arrive together.

C.passage: Thomas Edison was already a famous inventor (1)________ he switched on his first electric light bulb in 1879. Before that evening, most families lit their homes with candles (2)________ they had no other way of seeing after dark. Today, electric lamps brighten our homes, our schools (3)________ our offices. Machines have changed just as much: the earliest computers were as big as a whole room, (4)________ the one in my father's pocket is far more powerful. Those early machines broke down almost every week, (5)________ engineers worked long hours to make them more reliable. Nowadays, we can listen to music (6)________ we jog around the park, thanks to tiny earphones. (7)________ technology has made our lives much easier, it has also created new problems, such as too much screen time. Perhaps the next great invention will be either a self-driving car (8)________ a flying taxi.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: Technology has changed the way we live in remarkable ways. Every modern device is designed to be more (1)________ — doing more work in less time and with less effort. A (2)________ is any small electronic device designed to make a task easier, from a smartwatch to a pocket calculator. The most (3)________ inventions are those that solve problems in completely new ways. Before selling a new invention, inventors must register a (4)________ to protect their idea by law. Many devices today use (5)________ technology — sending data through the air without any cables or wires.

questions.trap_type: The blank follows 'more' and comes before a dash, so it must be a describing word. Students pick a noun such as 'gadget'.
questions.learning_tip: EFFICIENT = doing a job well without wasting time or energy. A device that does more work in less time is more EFFICIENT.
questions.retry_hint: The dash explains the blank: DOING MORE WORK IN LESS TIME with LESS EFFORT. It follows 'more', so it must describe the DEVICE. Ask: which box word means getting a job done without waste? 'Gadget' names a thing, not a quality.

questions.trap_type: The clue is 'any small electronic device ... from a smartwatch to a pocket calculator'. The blank follows 'A', so it names a thing.
questions.learning_tip: A GADGET = a small, clever electronic device or tool that does one particular job. A smartwatch is a GADGET.
questions.retry_hint: The sentence defines the blank for you: any SMALL ELECTRONIC DEVICE, from a SMARTWATCH to a POCKET CALCULATOR. It follows 'A', so it names a thing. Ask: which box word is that thing? A 'circuit' is only a part inside it.

questions.trap_type: The clue is 'solve problems in completely new ways'. The blank follows 'The most', so it must be an adjective.
questions.learning_tip: INNOVATIVE = new, original and creative. An INNOVATIVE invention solves a problem in a way nobody has tried before.
questions.retry_hint: The clue comes straight after the blank: inventions that SOLVE PROBLEMS IN COMPLETELY NEW WAYS. Ask: which box word describes something new, original and creative? 'Obsolete' means out of date - the exact opposite.

questions.trap_type: The clue is 'to protect their idea by law' before selling an invention. The blank follows 'register a', so it names a document.
questions.learning_tip: A PATENT = an official document giving an inventor the legal right to an invention. Others may not copy it without permission.
questions.retry_hint: Inventors REGISTER it in order to PROTECT THEIR IDEA BY LAW. Ask: which box word names an official document granting legal rights? A 'circuit' or a 'gadget' is hardware, never paperwork.

questions.trap_type: The clue is 'sending data through the air without any cables or wires'. The blank describes 'technology'.
questions.learning_tip: WIRELESS = sending or receiving information without cables. Wi-Fi and Bluetooth are WIRELESS technologies.
questions.retry_hint: The dash spells it out: SENDING DATA THROUGH THE AIR without any CABLES. Ask: which box word describes technology that needs no cable at all? 'Manual' means done by hand and has nothing to do with cables.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.trap_type: Students over-apply the -es rule and write 'computeres'.
questions.learning_tip: Add -ES only after s, x, z, ch or sh (buses, boxes, watches, brushes). 'Computer' ends in -r, so it simply takes -S: COMPUTERS.
questions.retry_hint: The underlined word is a plural, but the -ES ending has been over-applied. Ask: which nouns truly take -ES? Only the hissing endings: bus/buses, box/boxes, watch/watches, brush/brushes. Does this word end in any of those?

questions.error_type: Homophone confusion — there (place) vs their (belonging to them)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'there' (place) when the sentence needs 'their' (belonging to the guides).
questions.learning_tip: THEIR = belonging to them. THERE = at that place. Test: 'showed us THEIR favourite exhibit' → does it belong to them? YES → THEIR. THEIR = possession; THERE = place. Never confuse them!
questions.retry_hint: The favourite exhibit belongs to the two GUIDES; the sentence is not pointing at a place. Ask: does the underlined spelling mean 'over at that spot', or 'belonging to them'? They sound alike but are spelt differently.

questions.trap_type: Students add -s to 'man', producing 'mans'. 'Man' has a completely irregular plural form.
questions.learning_tip: 'Man' has an irregular plural: man → MEN. Never write 'mans'. Similar: woman → women, child → children.
questions.retry_hint: TWO of them, so a plural is needed - and this noun refuses a simple -s. Ask: how does the word MAN change in the plural? It swaps a vowel, exactly as woman and child change shape rather than take an ending.

questions.error_type: Subject-verb agreement — plural subject (the interactive displays)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'was' because 'displays' comes after a long descriptive phrase and seems singular.
questions.learning_tip: Plural subject → plural verb! The interactive DISPLAYS WERE so popular = DISPLAYS is plural → WERE. WAS is only for ONE thing (singular). Long subjects can trick you — always find the main noun. DISPLAYS = plural → WERE.
questions.retry_hint: Find the subject: the INTERACTIVE DISPLAYS - then count them. Ask: is that one thing, or many? A long subject can trick you, so match the verb to the head noun, never to the word closest to the blank.

questions.trap_type: Students write a plain plural and leave out the apostrophe that shows ownership.
questions.learning_tip: The names BELONG TO the inventors -> INVENTORS' names (apostrophe after the -s for a plural owner). Singular: inventor's.
questions.retry_hint: The NAMES belong to the inventors - many owners, not one. Ask: does a plain -s show ownership, or only make a plural? When the owners are many, does the apostrophe go before the -s, or after it?

E.passage: Last week, we visited the Science and Technology Museum in the city. The first room showed old computeres (1) from fifty years ago that were much bigger than what we use today. The two guides in white coats showed us there (2) favourite exhibit — a robot that could sort objects by colour. Two mans (3) in the robotics gallery demonstrated how the machine learned to recognise shapes. The interactive displays was (4) so popular that students queued for twenty minutes just to press the buttons. At the end, we read the inventors (5) names on the Wall of Innovation before boarding the bus home.

questions.sentence_a: Alexander Graham Bell invented the telephone.
questions.sentence_b: The telephone changed the way people communicate.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using the relative pronoun 'which'.
questions.model_answer: Alexander Graham Bell invented the telephone, which changed the way people communicate.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'Alexander Graham Bell invented the telephone which Alexander Graham Bell changed the way people communicate' — repeating the subject.
questions.learning_tip: Use 'which' to add information about a THING: Alexander Graham Bell invented the telephone, WHICH changed the way people communicate. 'Which' replaces 'the telephone' in the second clause.
questions.retry_hint: The second sentence names THE TELEPHONE all over again. Ask: where must the relative pronoun sit - straight after the noun it stands for? And what must you delete from the second sentence so that the subject is not repeated twice?

questions.sentence_a: The teacher asked the students a question.
questions.sentence_b: Can you name the inventor of the light bulb?
questions.instruction: Combine into one sentence using reported speech. Begin: 'The teacher asked...'
questions.model_answer: The teacher asked the students if they could name the inventor of the light bulb.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'asked the students if can they name' (wrong word order) or 'asked if you could name' (wrong pronoun).
questions.learning_tip: YES/NO question → reported speech: ASKED + IF + subject + verb (normal order). 'Can YOU name...?' → asked IF THEY COULD name... Pronoun changes: you → they. Tense shifts: can → could. Word order is normal — no inversion after 'if'.
questions.retry_hint: A yes/no question turned into REPORTED speech. Ask: which small joining word follows ASKED? Does the question keep its inverted order, or turn into a normal statement? And what happens to 'you' and to 'can'?

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
Nobody in the neighbourhood threw anything away without asking Nadia first. Toasters, fans, radios — if it was broken, they brought it to her. Nadia was eleven years old and her workshop was the corner of her bedroom, but she could fix almost anything with a screwdriver and a lot of patience.

One afternoon, her grandmother brought in an old clock that had stopped working. 'My father gave me this when I was young,' Grandma said. 'I thought it was lost forever.'

Nadia opened the back of the clock and peered inside. The spring was broken. She spent two hours bending and adjusting a replacement spring she made from a piece of wire. When she wound the clock up and placed it on the table, it began to tick again — slowly at first, then with a steady rhythm.

Grandma held the clock with two hands and was quiet for a long time. 'How do you know how to do all this?' she asked.

'I take things apart,' Nadia said simply. 'And then I figure out how to put them back together.'

That evening, Nadia sat in her corner and thought about what she wanted to do when she grew up. She did not think about fame or money. She thought about the sound of a clock ticking again. She thought about her grandmother's face.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 1 has the same meaning as 'never giving up despite difficulties'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Curious' = wanting to know; 'skilled' = having ability. PERSISTENT = continuing despite difficulties.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: PERSISTENT = continuing to try despite difficulties. Nadia was PERSISTENT = she did not give up when repairs were hard. PERSIST = keep trying; PERSISTENT = the quality of never stopping.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 3, what does 'it' refer to in 'Grandma held it with two hands and was quiet'?

options.2: The repaired clock that was now ticking again

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1. 'It' = the clock Nadia had just fixed and handed back.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: PRONOUN REFERENCE: 'Grandma held IT with two hands.' IT = the CLOCK. Nadia fixed it and gave it back → Grandma held the CLOCK gently. Context: Nadia fixed the clock → gave it to Grandma → she held IT.

mcq_questions.stem: What does Nadia mean when she says 'I take things apart. And then I figure out how to put them back'?

options.1: Nadia destroys broken things for fun.
options.2: Nadia learns by disassembling things and then understanding how to reassemble them correctly.
options.3: Nadia only fixes things already in pieces.
options.4: Nadia prefers to buy new parts.

mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Take apart' does not mean destroy — it means disassemble to understand.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: INFERENCE: 'TAKE THINGS APART' = disassemble to examine each part. 'FIGURE OUT HOW TO PUT THEM BACK' = understand how they work and reassemble. This is HOW Nadia learns — by taking apart and understanding each component.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 1, is it True or False that people paid Nadia to fix their broken things? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The passage says people brought broken things to Nadia, but there is no mention of payment. She fixed things out of interest, not for money.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'True, she ran a repair business.' The passage never mentions payment.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1 says people BROUGHT broken things to Nadia — but does NOT mention money or payment. If the passage does not say she was paid, we cannot assume it. Answer is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: How did Nadia fix the broken spring?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: She spent two hours bending and adjusting a replacement spring she made from a piece of wire.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'she replaced the spring' without describing how she made the replacement.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 3: 'She spent two hours BENDING and adjusting a replacement spring she made from a PIECE OF WIRE.' Give the specific method, not just the result.

open_ended_questions.stem: Why was the clock so important to Grandma? Use TWO pieces of evidence from the passage.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) Her father gave her the clock when she was young, so it had deep personal and family meaning. (ii) She thought the clock was lost forever before Nadia fixed it, showing how much she valued it.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students give only one reason or describe the clock's physical features instead of its emotional importance.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 2: (1) 'My FATHER GAVE ME THIS when I was young' = sentimental family value; (2) 'I thought it was LOST FOREVER' = she deeply missed it. Both show its importance.

open_ended_questions.stem: What did Nadia think about that evening, and what does this tell us about what she valued?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: Nadia thought about the sound of the clock ticking again and her grandmother's face. This shows she valued the joy and meaning she brought to others, not fame or money.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'she thought about fixing things' without explaining what this reveals about her values.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 6: she thought about the CLOCK TICKING and her GRANDMOTHER'S FACE — not fame or money. This shows she valued the impact on others, not personal reward.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on her actions throughout the passage, describe TWO character traits of Nadia with evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) DETERMINED: she spent two hours bending and adjusting a replacement spring until it was perfect — showing she did not give up even when the repair was slow and difficult. (ii) EMPATHETIC: she understood how much the clock meant to Grandma and took great care repairing it, knowing its emotional value went far beyond its function as a timepiece.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'clever and kind' without precise traits or textual evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: TRAIT INFERENCE: DETERMINED = spent TWO HOURS adjusting spring until perfect. EMPATHETIC = understood the clock's emotional value to Grandma and cared about the outcome. Name trait + give evidence from passage = full marks.

questions.stem: The soap bubbles on Kai's hands were as ________ as tiny pearls, catching the light as he scrubbed.
questions.trap_type: 'Heavy', 'rough' and 'sharp' are the opposite of what a pearl is like. The bubbles and the pearls share their COLOUR - both catch the light with a milky shine.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! The bubbles were AS WHITE AS pearls = comparing soap bubble colour to the pure white of pearls. Similes always use 'as ... as' to compare two different things directly.
questions.retry_hint: The bubbles are CATCHING THE LIGHT, exactly as TINY PEARLS do. Ask: which quality does a soap bubble truly share with a pearl - its weight, its roughness, or its milky colour? Match the adjective to what your eye actually sees.

questions.stem: Father reminded the children to ________ their hands with soap and water before every meal.
questions.trap_type: 'Dry' comes only after the soap and water; 'hide' means to conceal; 'lotion' is not a verb. Only one word means to clean with soap and water.
questions.learning_tip: WASH your hands = clean them with soap and water to remove germs. Always WASH your hands before meals and after using the toilet.
questions.retry_hint: The clue is SOAP AND WATER: you cannot use soap to dry, hide or lotion anything. Ask: which verb means to clean with soap and water? Read every option back into the sentence before you decide.

questions.stem: Getting enough sleep helps the body to ________ and fight off illnesses more effectively.
questions.trap_type: 'Collapse' and 'weaken' suggest the body getting worse. Only 'recover' = regain strength and health.
questions.learning_tip: RECOVER = regain strength, health or ability after being tired or ill. Sleep allows the body to RECOVER and repair itself overnight.
questions.retry_hint: SLEEP helps the body FIGHT OFF ILLNESSES, so the body is growing stronger, not weaker. Ask: which verb means to regain health and strength? 'Collapse' and 'weaken' point the wrong way entirely.

questions.stem: After eating fresh fruit and vegetables every day, Mia finally felt ________ — full of energy and ready for anything.
questions.trap_type: 'Under the weather' = feeling ill; 'a piece of cake' = easy; 'out of the blue' = suddenly. ON TOP OF THE WORLD = feeling extremely happy and healthy.
questions.learning_tip: IDIOM: ON TOP OF THE WORLD = feeling wonderful, extremely happy and full of energy. Mia felt ON TOP OF THE WORLD = she felt amazing after eating well. Idioms cannot be understood word by word!
questions.retry_hint: The dash tells you exactly how she feels: FULL OF ENERGY and READY FOR ANYTHING. Ask: which idiom means feeling wonderful and healthy? 'Under the weather' means ill, and 'a piece of cake' means easy - neither is a feeling of joy.

questions.stem: The doctor told Omar to ________ on screen time after school and spend more time outdoors instead.
questions.trap_type: 'Break down' = stop working; 'run out' = use up completely; 'give away' = give for free. CUT DOWN = reduce the amount of something gradually.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: CUT DOWN ON = reduce the amount you do or use. The doctor told him to CUT DOWN on screen time = spend less time on screens. CUT + DOWN work together. NEVER separate them!
questions.retry_hint: Omar is to SPEND MORE TIME OUTDOORS instead, so his SCREEN TIME must shrink - though not vanish. Ask: which phrasal verb means to reduce the amount of something? 'Run out' means to finish it completely.

questions.stem: Nobody in our class ________ breakfast before coming to school — everyone knows it is the most important meal of the day.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'skip' thinking 'nobody' = many people. NOBODY = singular → verb+S.
questions.learning_tip: NOBODY / EVERYONE / SOMEONE / EACH = Singular! Always use verb+S. Nobody SKIPS = add -S. 'Nobody skip' is WRONG. Singular indefinite pronouns always take singular present-tense verbs.
questions.retry_hint: The subject is NOBODY, not 'our class'. Words like nobody and everyone behave like ONE person. Ask: in the present tense, does a singular subject take the plain verb, or the verb ending in -s?

questions.stem: Our school has ________ a daily fruit break every morning since the beginning of last term.
questions.trap_type: HAS + past participle = present perfect. 'Introduce' → INTRODUCED (regular).
questions.learning_tip: HAS + past participle = present perfect. Our school HAS INTRODUCED fruit breaks = started in the past, still happening now. INTRODUCE → INTRODUCED (add -d for regular verbs ending in -e).
questions.retry_hint: HAS, plus SINCE the beginning of last term: an action that started in the past and still runs today. Ask: after 'has', which form of the verb do we need - the plain verb, the -ing form, or the past participle?

questions.stem: The children ________ their hands at the sink when the lunch bell rang and reminded them to stop.
questions.trap_type: 'The lunch bell rang' = sudden interrupting event. Children were already washing = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: The bell RANG = sudden past event. The children were already in the middle of washing = WERE WASHING (past continuous). Was/were + verb-ing = action in progress when something interrupts.
questions.retry_hint: The LUNCH BELL RANG - one sudden moment cutting into something already happening. Ask: which form shows an action still in progress in the past? A plain past verb only reports a finished action.

questions.stem: Drinking water is much ________ for your teeth than fizzy drinks, which contain large amounts of sugar.
questions.trap_type: 'Best' = superlative (for 3+); 'more good' is WRONG. BETTER = comparative of 'good' (comparing 2 things).
questions.learning_tip: GOOD → BETTER → BEST (irregular). Comparing two drinks = comparative: water is BETTER for teeth. 'More good' is ALWAYS WRONG. Good → BETTER (never 'gooder' or 'more good').
questions.retry_hint: THAN compares exactly two drinks, so a comparative is needed - and this adjective is irregular. Ask: what does 'good' turn into when two things are compared? 'More good' is never English, and 'best' needs three or above.

questions.stem: Students should drink ________ water during the day to stay hydrated, especially after sports.
questions.trap_type: 'Water' is uncountable → use 'plenty of', 'much' or 'a lot of'. 'Many', 'a few' and 'several' are for countable nouns.
questions.learning_tip: PLENTY OF = a large amount (works with both countable and uncountable nouns). 'Water' is uncountable → drink PLENTY OF water. MANY and A FEW are only for countable nouns.
questions.retry_hint: WATER cannot be counted: you never say 'one water, two waters'. Ask: which quantity phrase works with an uncountable noun? 'Many', 'several' and 'a few' all count separate items one by one.

questions.stem: Each of the students in the health talk ________ given a leaflet about dental care to take home.
questions.trap_type: 'Each of the students' = each one individually = singular. Present passive. Students write 'are' thinking of many students.
questions.learning_tip: 'Each of the students' = each one at a time = singular → IS given a leaflet. EACH always uses a singular verb.
questions.retry_hint: EACH means one student at a time, however many sat in the HEALTH TALK. Ask: does a singular subject take a singular verb or a plural one? Check the time too: the LEAFLET reaches them now, not last year.

questions.stem: The healthy lunch boxes ________ by parent volunteers every day for the school's nutritional programme.
questions.trap_type: 'Lunch boxes' = plural. Present regular action. Passive = are prepared. Students write 'is prepared' (singular) or 'prepared' (simple past).
questions.learning_tip: 'Lunch boxes' = plural + present + passive → ARE PREPARED. Passive = am/is/are + past participle. Plural subject in present passive = ARE.
questions.retry_hint: BY PARENT VOLUNTEERS shows the boxes receive the action, and EVERY DAY shows it happens again and again. Ask: LUNCH BOXES is plural, so which passive helper matches a plural subject in the present tense?

questions.stem: The health coach told the students ________ their screen time to less than two hours a day.
questions.trap_type: 'Told someone to do something' = reported speech: told + object + to + base verb → to limit.
questions.learning_tip: 'Told students TO + base verb': told the students TO LIMIT their screen time. After 'told + object', use the infinitive with 'to'.
questions.retry_hint: TOLD + somebody + an instruction. Ask: after 'told the students', does English use the plain verb, the -ing form, or the infinitive with 'to'? Reported orders always follow one fixed pattern.

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Demonstrative and indefinite pronouns)

questions.context_check: Passage: '(1)________ are the five healthy habits our school nurse shared with us last week.' Signal: blank = subject of the sentence referring to 'the five healthy habits' (plural, nearby in context) = THESE. THESE = plural + nearby reference.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'those' (plural but far away) or 'this' (singular). The habits are being introduced right now = nearby plural = THESE.
questions.learning_tip: THESE = plural things that are nearby or being introduced right now. THESE are the five habits = we are talking about them right now, here.
questions.retry_hint: The FIVE SIMPLE HEALTH RULES have only just been mentioned, so they sit right here in front of us - and there is more than one. Ask: which pointing word is plural AND close by? 'Those' would push them far away.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'First, (2)________ of us should wash our hands regularly, especially before meals.' Signal: blank = 'every single one of us' = ALL. ALL of us = every person without exception.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'some' (partial group) instead of 'all' (every member). The sentence states a universal rule that applies to everyone.
questions.learning_tip: ALL of us = every single person, without exception. Health rules that apply to everyone use ALL: ALL of us should wash our hands.
questions.retry_hint: WITHOUT A SINGLE EXCEPTION: the rule covers every person in the class, leaving nobody out. Ask: which word means every single member of a group? 'Some' would cover only a part of it.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Second, eat (3)________ fruits and vegetables every day to get the vitamins your body needs.' Signal: blank = an unspecified amount of fruits/vegetables = SOME. SOME = a partial, unspecified quantity (positive statement).
questions.trap_type: Students write 'any' instead of 'some'. In positive sentences recommending an action, use SOME, not ANY.
questions.learning_tip: SOME = an unspecified amount, used in positive sentences. Eat SOME fruits and vegetables = eat a portion of them. ANY is used in negatives or questions.
questions.retry_hint: This is positive advice: we SHOULD EAT FRUITS AND VEGETABLES, a certain quantity of them, at every meal. Ask: which word gives an unspecified amount in a POSITIVE sentence? Its partner belongs in negatives.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Third, try not to eat (4)________ junk food after school if you want to stay healthy.' Signal: blank = in a negative sentence (try not to eat) = ANY. ANY is used after negatives to mean 'not even one'.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'some' instead of 'any'. In negative sentences, use ANY, not SOME.
questions.learning_tip: ANY = used in negative sentences or questions. Try NOT to eat ANY junk food = not even a small amount. SOME is for positive sentences.
questions.retry_hint: Look at the negative: TRY NOT TO EAT it. Ask: in a negative sentence, which word means 'not even a little'? Its positive partner belongs in blank 3, where the advice says what we SHOULD EAT.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Fourth, (5)________ habit of sleeping eight hours a night is one of the most important for children our age.' Signal: blank = singular noun 'habit' that is right here being discussed = THIS. THIS = singular + nearby/currently being introduced.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'that' (singular but far away) or 'these' (plural). 'Habit' is singular and is being introduced right now = THIS.
questions.learning_tip: THIS = a singular thing nearby or currently being introduced. THIS habit = this specific habit we are talking about right now.
questions.retry_hint: ANOTHER RULE has just been named - one single habit, sitting right here in the sentence. Ask: which pointing word is singular and near? 'These' would need more than one habit; 'that' would push it far away.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Fifth, (6)________ who exercise regularly tend to feel happier and more energetic.' Signal: blank = refers to a group of people (not specifically named, far away in concept) = THOSE. THOSE who = the people who (a group defined by what they do).
questions.trap_type: Students write 'these' (nearby) or 'they' (personal pronoun, not in word box). THOSE who = a category of people.
questions.learning_tip: THOSE WHO = a group of people defined by what they do. THOSE who exercise regularly = all people who regularly exercise. THOSE who = the ones who.
questions.retry_hint: The blank stands for a whole group of people, defined by what they do: they EXERCISE REGULARLY. Ask: which pointing word can mean 'the people who...' in front of WHO? A singular word cannot cover a whole group.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Of all the bad habits, (7)________ is harder to break than staying up too late every night.' Signal: blank = 'not any / not one' of the bad habits → NONE. NONE is harder = not a single one of them is harder.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'some' or 'any' instead of 'none'. NONE = not any / not one. Used with a comparative to say nothing exceeds something.
questions.learning_tip: NONE is harder = not one bad habit is harder to break than staying up late. NONE = not any, not one. 'None is harder' means 'nothing is harder'.
questions.retry_hint: Nothing among our BAD HABITS beats STAYING UP LATE - not one of them is HARDER TO BREAK. Ask: which word means 'not one, not any at all'? 'Some' would say the opposite.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The nurse said (8)________ keeping these habits requires effort, but the results are worth it.' Signal: blank = 'that' introducing a reported statement / noun clause. The nurse said THAT keeping these habits requires effort = reported speech noun clause.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'this' (demonstrative pronoun, not a clause connector) or 'those'. 'That' introduces a noun clause as the object of 'said'.
questions.learning_tip: 'Said THAT + clause' = reported speech. The nurse said THAT keeping these habits requires effort. THAT here is a conjunction introducing the reported statement.
questions.retry_hint: After SAID comes a whole reported statement: keeping the FIVE RULES REQUIRES EFFORT. Ask: which word links a reporting verb to the clause it introduces? Here it works as a conjunction, never as a pointing word.

C.passage: The school nurse taught our class five simple health rules, and (1)________ rules are easy to follow. First, (2)________ of us should wash our hands with soap before we eat, without a single exception. Next, we should eat (3)________ fruits and vegetables at every meal. We should try not to eat (4)________ junk food after dinner. Brushing our teeth twice a day is another rule, and (5)________ habit protects us from cavities. In her experience, (6)________ who exercise regularly fall sick less often than children who never do. Among our bad habits, (7)________ is harder to break than staying up late. Before she left, the nurse said (8)________ keeping the five rules requires effort, which is well worth it.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: Looking after our bodies requires daily care. We must maintain a (1)________ diet - eating a variety of foods from different food groups instead of only one. Dentists remind us that too much sugar causes a painful (2)________ - a hole in a tooth that forms when bacteria break down leftover food. Staying (3)________ means drinking enough water throughout the day, especially after sports. Good (4)________ - sitting and standing up straight - protects the spine and prevents back pain. At least thirty minutes of (5)________ exercise each day, such as running or skipping, keeps the heart strong and the lungs healthy.

questions.trap_type: The clue is 'a variety of foods from different food groups instead of only one'. The blank describes the diet.
questions.learning_tip: A BALANCED diet = one with all the different kinds of food in the right amounts: proteins, carbohydrates, fats, vitamins and minerals.
questions.retry_hint: The dash defines it: a VARIETY OF FOODS FROM DIFFERENT FOOD GROUPS, instead of only one. Ask: which box word describes a diet holding every kind of food in the right amounts? 'Nutrients' is a noun; it cannot describe a diet.

questions.trap_type: The clue is 'a hole in a tooth ... when bacteria break down leftover food'. The blank follows 'a painful', so it names a single thing.
questions.learning_tip: A CAVITY = a hole in a tooth caused by decay. Sugar feeds bacteria, which produce acid that eats through the enamel.
questions.retry_hint: The dash tells you exactly what it is: A HOLE IN A TOOTH, made by BACTERIA feeding on leftover food. The blank follows 'a painful', so it names one single thing. Ask: which box word is that hole?

questions.trap_type: The clue is 'drinking enough water throughout the day'. The blank follows 'Staying', so it must be a describing word, not a noun.
questions.learning_tip: HYDRATED = having enough water in your body to work well. Stay HYDRATED, especially when you sweat during sports.
