questions.retry_hint: The sentence defines the blank: DRINKING ENOUGH WATER all day, especially after SPORTS. It follows 'Staying', so it must describe you, not name a thing. Ask: which box word means holding enough water inside the body?

questions.trap_type: The clue is 'sitting and standing up straight' and 'protects the spine'. The blank follows 'Good', so it names a thing.
questions.learning_tip: POSTURE = the way you hold your body when you sit or stand. Good POSTURE keeps the spine straight and prevents back pain.
questions.retry_hint: The dashes explain it: SITTING AND STANDING UP STRAIGHT, which PROTECTS THE SPINE. The blank follows 'Good', so it names a thing. Ask: which box word means the way you hold your body?

questions.trap_type: The clue is 'running or skipping' and 'keeps the heart strong'. The blank describes the exercise, so it must be an adjective.
questions.learning_tip: VIGOROUS = needing a lot of energy and physical effort. VIGOROUS exercise makes your heart beat faster and your lungs work harder.
questions.retry_hint: RUNNING OR SKIPPING for THIRTY MINUTES makes the HEART beat hard - this is not gentle exercise. Ask: which box word describes activity demanding a lot of energy? 'Sluggish' means slow and dull, the very opposite.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.trap_type: Students add -s to 'child', producing 'childs'. 'Child' has an irregular plural form.
questions.learning_tip: 'Child' has an irregular plural: child → CHILDREN. Never write 'childs'. Other irregular plurals: tooth → teeth, foot → feet, man → men.
questions.retry_hint: The word CHILD does not build its plural with -s. Ask: what do you call more than one child? The same trick appears in tooth/teeth and foot/feet: the word changes shape instead of taking an ending.

questions.error_type: Homophone confusion — there (place) vs their (belonging to them)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'there' (a place) when the sentence needs 'their' (belonging to the students).
questions.learning_tip: THEIR = belonging to them. THERE = at that place. Test: 'good for THEIR wellbeing' → does it belong to them? YES → THEIR. THEIR = belonging to THEM. THERE = location/place.
questions.retry_hint: The WELLBEING belongs to the PUPILS - the sentence is not pointing at a place. Ask: does the underlined spelling mean 'at that spot', or 'belonging to them'? Choose by meaning, never by sound.

questions.error_type: Spelling — doubling rule: short vowel + single consonant before -ing
questions.trap_type: Students write 'runing' with one 'n'. 'Run' has a short vowel (u) + single consonant (n) → double the n before -ing.
questions.learning_tip: 'Run' has a short vowel + single consonant: run → RUNNING (double the n). Same rule: sit → sitting, swim → swimming, jog → jogging.
questions.retry_hint: The base verb RUN has a short vowel followed by ONE consonant. Ask: what must happen to that final consonant before -ING is added? Compare sit/sitting, swim/swimming and jog/jogging.

questions.trap_type: Students match the verb to 'class', the noun nearest to the blank, instead of to the real subject 'the pupils'.
questions.learning_tip: The subject is THE PUPILS = plural -> WERE given a talk. WAS is only for a singular subject. Find the head noun, not the nearest noun.
questions.retry_hint: Find the real subject: the PUPILS, not the word CLASS that happens to sit beside the blank. Ask: is that subject one, or many? Match the verb to the head noun, never to the nearest noun.

questions.trap_type: Students write a plain plural and leave out the apostrophe that shows ownership.
questions.learning_tip: The report BELONGS TO the two nurses -> NURSES' report (apostrophe after the -s for a plural owner). Singular: nurse's.
questions.retry_hint: The REPORT belongs to the TWO SCHOOL nurses - two owners, not one. Ask: does a plain -s show ownership, or only make a plural? When the owners are many, does the apostrophe go before the -s, or after it?

E.passage: Our school health week last term turned out to be a great success. The childs (1) in every class took part in activities about staying fit and healthy. The teacher told the pupils that these habits are good for there (2) wellbeing throughout life. Then we went outside and practised runing (3) and skipping for thirty minutes without stopping. After the activities, the pupils in our class was (4) given a short talk on healthy eating and good hygiene. At the end of the week, the two school nurses (5) report showed that almost everyone had improved their understanding of good health.

questions.sentence_a: You do not get enough sleep.
questions.sentence_b: You will find it hard to concentrate in class.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'If'.
questions.model_answer: If you do not get enough sleep, you will find it hard to concentrate in class.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'If you will not get enough sleep, you will find it hard to concentrate' — adding 'will' incorrectly in the 'if' clause.
questions.learning_tip: In an 'If' conditional: IF + simple present, simple future. If you DO NOT get enough sleep, you WILL find it hard. Never use 'will' in the 'if' clause.
questions.retry_hint: IF opens the condition; the second sentence gives the consequence. Ask: which tense belongs inside the IF clause - present or future? A common slip is to push 'will' into both halves, yet it belongs in only one.

questions.sentence_a: Lena likes fresh fruit.
questions.sentence_b: Lena does not like sugary snacks.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'would rather ... than'. Begin: 'Lena would rather...'
questions.model_answer: Lena would rather eat fresh fruit than sugary snacks.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'Lena would rather fresh fruit than sugary snacks' — missing the verb 'eat' after 'would rather'.
questions.learning_tip: 'Would rather + base verb + than': Lena would rather EAT fresh fruit THAN sugary snacks. Always include the base verb after 'would rather'.
questions.retry_hint: 'WOULD RATHER' is not a complete verb on its own - an action must follow it. Ask: what does LENA actually do with fresh fruit? Put that action in its plain base form, then use 'than' before the food she likes less.

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
It started as a dare. During lunch on Monday, Kai bet his friend Omar that he could go an entire week without eating any sugar. Omar laughed. 'You won't last a day,' he said.

Tuesday was the hardest. Kai walked past the canteen snack corner without buying anything. He counted the gummy bears in his pencil case and put them back without eating a single one. By afternoon, he had a headache.

On Wednesday, Kai found that drinking water helped when he felt the urge for something sweet. He also ate an apple after lunch, which surprised him — he did not usually like apples much, but it tasted better than he remembered.

By Thursday, the headaches were gone. Kai noticed he felt more alert in class and did not fall asleep during afternoon lessons the way he sometimes did.

Friday arrived, and Kai succeeded. When he told Omar, Omar looked genuinely impressed. 'I honestly thought you would give up on day one,' he said.

Kai smiled. He did not say anything about the packet of sweets he had already bought for Saturday. But he also knew something had changed. He did not crave sugar the way he once did.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 2 has the same meaning as 'an intense desire for something'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Challenge' = difficult task; 'energy' = power. CRAVING = a strong, urgent desire.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: CRAVING = a very strong, almost uncontrollable desire (often for food). CRAVE = desire strongly; CRAVING = the strong desire.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 4, what does 'it' refer to in 'he did not expect it'?

options.3: That water would make the apple taste sweeter and better than before

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1. But 'it' = the surprising discovery that water changed how the apple tasted.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: PRONOUN REFERENCE: 'IT' = the surprising OUTCOME — that after drinking water, the apple tasted better than before. He did not expect THAT to happen.

mcq_questions.stem: What does the last paragraph suggest about Kai at the end of the week?

options.1: Kai was disappointed the challenge ended.
options.2: Kai found it easy from the start.
options.3: Kai's desire for sugar reduced because his body adjusted to eating healthily.
options.4: Kai decided never to eat sugar again.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 4. But 'craving reduced' ≠ 'gave up sugar permanently'.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: INFERENCE: 'His craving for sugar HAD REDUCED' = his body adjusted. This means the week changed his habits. Option 4 goes BEYOND what is written.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 1, is it True or False that Kai planned to give up sugar before Omar challenged him? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The passage says the challenge started as a dare — Kai bet Omar himself, meaning it was a spontaneous challenge, not something he planned in advance.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'True, Kai wanted to be healthy.' The challenge was unplanned — it started as a dare.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1: 'It started as A DARE.' A dare = something done on impulse, not planned. Kai BET Omar — showing it was spontaneous. Answer is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: What did Kai notice about himself on Thursday?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: The headaches were gone and he felt more alert in class. He did not fall asleep during afternoon lessons.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students describe Wednesday's events (apple, water) instead of Thursday's.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 4 (Thursday): the HEADACHES were gone and he felt more ALERT in class and did not fall asleep. These are Thursday's specific improvements.

open_ended_questions.stem: Describe TWO difficulties Kai faced during the challenge.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) On Tuesday, he walked past the canteen without buying anything, showing it was hard to resist. (ii) He had a headache by Tuesday afternoon, likely caused by sugar withdrawal.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students describe what helped Kai (water, apple) rather than the difficulties he faced.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 2 (Tuesday): (1) he had to resist buying from the CANTEEN; (2) he had a HEADACHE by afternoon. Both are specific difficulties from the text.

open_ended_questions.stem: Find a phrase in paragraph 5 that shows Omar was surprised Kai succeeded.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: 'I honestly thought you would give up on day one.'
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students quote 'Omar looked genuinely impressed' which describes his reaction, not his words of surprise.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 5: Omar said 'I HONESTLY THOUGHT YOU WOULD GIVE UP ON DAY ONE.' This quote directly shows he did not expect Kai to succeed.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on his actions throughout the passage, describe TWO character traits of Kai with evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) DETERMINED: Kai resisted sugar for an entire week — on Tuesday, the hardest day, he walked past the canteen without buying anything. (ii) SELF-AWARE: he noticed changes in his own body — headaches gone, more alertness in class, apple tasting different — and reflected on how his choices affected him.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'brave and hardworking' without precise traits or textual evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: TRAIT INFERENCE: DETERMINED = walked past canteen, resisted for FULL WEEK. SELF-AWARE = noticed headaches gone, felt alert, apple tasted better. Name trait + give evidence = full marks.

questions.stem: The museum guide ________ the students through the ancient Egyptian hall, explaining each exhibit.
questions.trap_type: 'Pushed' and 'chased' suggest force or pursuit. Only 'escorted' = accompanied and guided officially.
questions.learning_tip: ESCORTED = accompanied someone to guide or protect them. The museum guide ESCORTED the students = walked with them and showed them around.
questions.retry_hint: The guide walked the students through the hall, EXPLAINING EACH EXHIBIT along the way. Ask: which verb means to accompany someone and show them the way? 'Pushed' and 'chased' use force; 'scattered' would spread the class apart.

questions.stem: The museum's main hall was as ________ as a cathedral — towering ceilings, marble floors and complete silence.
questions.trap_type: 'Noisy' and 'cramped' are opposites of a grand cathedral. GRAND = impressively large and magnificent.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! The hall was AS GRAND AS a cathedral = comparing its impressive size and silence to a great cathedral. GRAND = impressively large, beautiful and important.
questions.retry_hint: The hall is compared to a CATHEDRAL - TOWERING CEILINGS, MARBLE FLOORS, complete silence. Ask: does a cathedral feel small and plain, or huge and magnificent? Match the adjective to the cathedral, not to the noise.

questions.stem: After seeing the exhibit on ancient Singapore, the students were ________ — buzzing with facts they could not wait to share.
questions.trap_type: 'Under the weather' = ill; 'a piece of cake' = easy; 'all ears' = listening. ON CLOUD NINE = extremely happy.
questions.learning_tip: IDIOM: ON CLOUD NINE = feeling extremely happy, excited and delighted. The students were ON CLOUD NINE = thrilled after the trip. There is no actual cloud — it is an idiom!
questions.retry_hint: The students are BUZZING WITH FACTS they COULD NOT WAIT TO SHARE. Ask: does this idiom describe great delight, illness, an easy task, or careful listening? 'Under the weather' means ill, and 'all ears' means listening.

questions.stem: The archaeologist carefully ________ the fragile pottery from the soil using a small brush.
questions.trap_type: 'Crushed' would destroy it; 'buried' is the opposite; 'replaced' = put something else there. Only 'extracted' = carefully removed from a surrounding material.
questions.learning_tip: EXTRACTED = removed carefully from a surrounding material. Archaeologists EXTRACT artefacts from the ground without damaging them.
questions.retry_hint: The pottery is FRAGILE and the archaeologist works with A SMALL BRUSH. Ask: which verb means to remove something gently from the material around it? 'Crushed' would destroy it, and 'buried' does the opposite.

questions.stem: After the tour, the teacher asked the students to ________ the worksheets and hand them to the curator.
questions.trap_type: 'Run away' = flee; 'give up' = stop; 'break down' = stop working. FILL IN = complete a form by writing in the blank spaces.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: FILL IN = complete a form or blank spaces by writing in them. FILL IN the worksheet = write the answers in all the blank spaces. FILL + IN work together as one meaning.
questions.retry_hint: The students must complete the WORKSHEETS before handing them to the CURATOR. Ask: which phrasal verb means to write answers into the blank spaces of a form? 'Give up' means stop; 'break down' means stop working.

questions.stem: Everyone in the museum ________ in a hushed voice so as not to disturb other visitors.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'speak'. EVERYONE = singular → verb+S.
questions.learning_tip: EVERYONE / NOBODY / SOMEONE = Singular! Everyone SPEAKS = add -S. 'Everyone speak' is WRONG. Singular indefinite pronouns always take singular present-tense verbs.
questions.retry_hint: The subject is EVERYONE, not the visitors around him. Words like everyone and nobody act like ONE person. Ask: in the present tense, does a singular subject take the plain verb, or the verb ending in -s?

questions.stem: The National Museum has ________ a new exhibit on Singapore's street food history this month.
questions.trap_type: HAS + past participle = present perfect. OPEN → OPENED (regular).
questions.learning_tip: HAS + past participle = present perfect. The museum HAS OPENED a new exhibit = opened recently and now available. OPEN → OPENED (regular verb, add -ed).
questions.retry_hint: HAS is already in the sentence, waiting for a partner. Ask: after 'has', do we use the plain verb, the -s form, the -ing form, or the past participle? Only one of them builds a present perfect, and 'open' is a regular verb.

questions.stem: The students ________ at a display of ancient coins when the tour guide called them to the next gallery.
questions.trap_type: 'The guide called them' = sudden interrupting event. Students were already looking = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: The guide CALLED THEM = sudden past event. Students were already in the middle of looking = WERE LOOKING (past continuous). Was/were + verb-ing = action in progress when something interrupts.
questions.retry_hint: The guide CALLED THEM in the middle of something. Ask: which choice shows an action already in progress in the past when a sudden event cuts across it? A plain past verb reports only a finished action.

questions.stem: The dinosaur skeleton on display is far ________ than any model Ivan had ever seen in a shop.
questions.trap_type: 'Most impressive' = superlative; 'impressiver' is WRONG. MORE IMPRESSIVE = comparative (long adj).
questions.learning_tip: Long adjective (3+ syllables) → MORE + adjective = comparative. MORE IMPRESSIVE THAN = comparing the skeleton to other models. 'Impressiver' is ALWAYS WRONG. Use MORE for long adjectives.
questions.retry_hint: THAN signals a comparison of just two things, and 'impressive' is a long adjective. Ask: do long adjectives take -er, or do they need a comparing word in front? 'Most' belongs to three or several things, and 'impressiver' is not English.

questions.stem: Only ________ visitors were allowed into the conservation lab at one time for safety reasons.
questions.trap_type: 'Visitors' is countable → use 'a few' or 'many'. 'Much', 'a little' and 'little' are for uncountable nouns.
questions.learning_tip: A FEW = a small number (used with countable plural nouns). Visitors = countable → only A FEW visitors allowed. MUCH and A LITTLE are for uncountable nouns.
questions.retry_hint: VISITORS can be counted one by one. Ask: which choice belongs with countable plural nouns? 'Much', 'a little' and 'little' all go with uncountable things such as water, space or time.

questions.stem: Each of the artefacts in the restoration room ________ handled with white cotton gloves.
questions.trap_type: 'Each of the artefacts' = each one individually = singular. Present rule. Students write 'are' seeing 'artefacts'.
questions.learning_tip: 'Each of the artefacts' = each one at a time = singular → IS handled with gloves. EACH always uses a singular verb.
questions.retry_hint: EACH OF THE ARTEFACTS means one artefact at a time, however many sit in the room. Ask: does EACH take a singular verb or a plural one? The rule describes what happens now, so a past form cannot fit.

questions.stem: The ancient scroll ________ by experts from the National University before it was put on display.
questions.trap_type: The scroll did not authenticate itself. Past passive = was authenticated.
questions.learning_tip: The scroll was the receiver of the action. Past passive = WAS AUTHENTICATED. Passive = was/were + past participle.
questions.retry_hint: The SCROLL did not check itself: EXPERTS FROM THE NATIONAL UNIVERSITY did that, and it happened before the scroll went on display. Ask: which choice is passive (the subject receives the action) and set in the past?

questions.stem: The museum director told visitors ________ flash photography near the fragile watercolour paintings.
questions.trap_type: Negative reported speech: told someone not to do something = told + object + not to + base verb.
questions.learning_tip: 'Told visitors NOT TO + base verb': told visitors NOT TO USE flash photography. After 'told + object', always use 'not to' + base verb.
questions.retry_hint: TOLD VISITORS = a reported command. Ask: after 'told + person', which form follows - the plain verb, the -ing form, or 'to' + verb? And where does the negative word sit: before that little word, or after it?

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Quantity adjectives)

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The museum has (1)________ galleries spread across four floors.' Signal: 'galleries' is countable and plural; large number → MANY. MANY = a large number of countable plural nouns.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'much'. OBJECTS can be counted one by one, so an uncountable word cannot go here.
questions.learning_tip: MANY + countable plural noun: so MANY objects. Use MANY when you can count the things separately.
questions.retry_hint: Count them: FASCINATING OBJECTS can be counted one by one, and the sentence says SO ___ that one visit is never enough. Ask: which box word belongs with countable plural nouns? 'Much' goes with things you cannot count.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'There is so (2)________ history in this building that it would take days to see everything.' Signal: 'history' is uncountable; large amount → MUCH. MUCH = a large amount of an uncountable noun. 'So much history' = a very large amount.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'both' (only two) or 'a few' (two or three). More than two galleries are open, but not all of them.
questions.learning_tip: SEVERAL = more than two, but not a large number. SEVERAL of the galleries = perhaps four or five.
questions.retry_hint: The blank stands in front of OF THE GALLERIES, and more than two are open every day. Ask: which box word means more than two, but still not all of them? 'Both' would mean exactly two.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'We had (3)________ minutes to look at the painting before the guide moved us on.' Signal: 'minutes' is countable; small number → A FEW. A FEW = a small number of countable plural nouns.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'a little', which belongs to uncountable nouns. The galleries are countable.
questions.learning_tip: A FEW + countable plural: explore them all or just A FEW. A LITTLE is only for uncountable nouns.
questions.retry_hint: Blank 3 finishes 'explore them ALL or just ___' - only some GALLERIES, not all. Ask: which box phrase means small number and belongs with countable plurals? The 'little' phrase is only for uncountable nouns.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'I understood (4)________ French, so I could read the captions on the Impressionist paintings.' Signal: 'French' (knowledge of a language) is uncountable; small amount → A LITTLE. A LITTLE = a small amount of an uncountable noun.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'much'. In a positive statement 'much space' sounds unnatural in everyday English.
questions.learning_tip: A LOT OF = a large amount. Natural in positive statements with both countable and uncountable nouns: A LOT OF space.
questions.retry_hint: SPACE cannot be counted, and the MAIN HALL must hold LARGE SCHOOL GROUPS - the amount is big, not small. Ask: which box phrase means large amount and sounds natural in this positive sentence? 'Much' suits negatives better.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The children showed (5)________ enthusiasm when they saw the life-sized dinosaur model.' Signal: 'enthusiasm' is uncountable; large amount in a positive statement → A LOT OF. A LOT OF = a large amount, used with both countable and uncountable nouns.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'many'. TIME is uncountable, and the sentence is negative - the natural partner of a negative is 'much'.
questions.learning_tip: MUCH + uncountable noun, especially in negatives: does not have MUCH time. 'Many time' is always wrong.
questions.retry_hint: Read the whole clause: the team DOES NOT HAVE ___ TIME. It is negative, and time cannot be counted. Ask: which box word partners an uncountable noun in a negative sentence? 'Many' needs things you can count.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'We visited (6)________ rooms before finding the ancient Chinese ceramics section.' Signal: 'rooms' is countable; more than two but not a large number, unspecified = SEVERAL. SEVERAL = more than two but not very many (countable plural).
questions.trap_type: Students write 'either' (one of the two) or 'several'. Exactly two galleries are named and joined by 'and'.
questions.learning_tip: BOTH = the two things together. BOTH the Roman gallery AND the Egyptian gallery = the two of them.
questions.retry_hint: Count the galleries named: THE ROMAN GALLERY and THE EGYPTIAN GALLERY - exactly two, joined by 'and'. Ask: which box word takes two things together? 'Either' would pick only one of them.

questions.context_check: Passage: '(7)________ the ancient map and the compass were displayed side by side in the same glass cabinet.' Signal: exactly TWO things (the map and the compass) = BOTH. BOTH = the two things together, used with exactly two items.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'both'. You cannot walk out through two exits at the same time, and the word 'or' demands a choice.
questions.learning_tip: EITHER ... OR = one out of exactly two choices. EITHER the north exit OR the south exit.
questions.retry_hint: The word OR splits two ways out: THE NORTH EXIT or THE SOUTH EXIT. Ask: which box word partners with 'or' to mean one out of exactly two? You cannot walk out through two exits at once.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'You can enter the exhibition through (8)________ the north entrance or the south entrance.' Signal: a choice between exactly two options = EITHER. EITHER = one of two options (used with 'or').
questions.trap_type: Students write 'a few'. TIME cannot be counted, so a countable word cannot go here.
questions.learning_tip: A LITTLE + uncountable noun: A LITTLE time left. A FEW is for countable plurals such as minutes.
questions.retry_hint: TIME LEFT BEFORE CLOSING cannot be counted, and only some remains. Ask: which box phrase means small amount and belongs with uncountable nouns? The 'few' phrase goes with countable plurals such as minutes.

C.passage: The museum has so (1)________ fascinating objects that one visit is never enough. (2)________ of the galleries are open every day, and visitors can choose to explore them all or just (3)________. There is (4)________ space in the main hall for large school groups to gather before their tours. The conservation team does not have (5)________ time to repair every damaged item, so the most fragile pieces are treated first. (6)________ the Roman gallery and the Egyptian gallery contain objects over two thousand years old. When you leave, you may go out through (7)________ the north exit or the south exit. If you have (8)________ time left before closing, do not miss the shadow puppet display.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: Museums keep history alive. Every object on display is an (1)________ - something made or used by people in the past. Many items have been carefully (2)________ so that they do not decay: experts control the temperature and the light in every room. Some objects are only copies - a (3)________ made to look exactly like the original. Others are given by families who no longer wish to keep them, and each (4)________ is a generous gift to the public. Some exhibits date back to the fifth (5)________, over fifteen hundred years ago.

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'replica'. The clue is 'something MADE OR USED BY PEOPLE IN THE PAST' - every museum object, not only the copies.
questions.learning_tip: An ARTEFACT = an object made or used by people in the past, kept for its historical value.
questions.retry_hint: 'AN' in front of the blank tells you the word starts with a vowel sound, and the dash explains it: SOMETHING MADE OR USED BY PEOPLE IN THE PAST. Ask: which box word names any historical museum object, not only a copy?

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'fragile'. The blank follows 'have been carefully', so it must be a past participle, not a describing word.
questions.learning_tip: PRESERVED = kept in its original condition so that it does not decay. Museums PRESERVE objects with careful light and temperature control.
questions.retry_hint: The blank follows HAVE BEEN CAREFULLY, so it must be a past participle - and the reason comes next: SO THAT THEY DO NOT DECAY. Ask: which box word means kept in its original condition? 'Fragile' only describes.

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'artefact'. The clue is 'only COPIES ... made to look exactly like the ORIGINAL'.
questions.learning_tip: A REPLICA = an exact copy of something. Museums display a REPLICA when the original is too precious to show.
questions.retry_hint: The clue sits in the same sentence: ONLY COPIES, made TO LOOK EXACTLY LIKE THE ORIGINAL. Ask: which box word names an exact copy? An 'artefact' is the real thing, not the imitation of it.

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'artefact'. The clue is that families GIVE the object away and it becomes a GENEROUS GIFT to the public.
questions.learning_tip: A DONATION = something given freely to help others. Each DONATION is a gift the museum did not have to buy.
questions.retry_hint: The families GIVE the object away and it becomes A GENEROUS GIFT TO THE PUBLIC. Ask: which box word names something given freely, with nothing asked in return? A 'ticket' is bought, not given.

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'artefact'. The clue is the number FIFTH and the phrase 'over fifteen hundred years ago' - a length of time.
questions.learning_tip: A CENTURY = one hundred years. The fifth CENTURY = the years 400-499, about fifteen hundred years ago.
questions.retry_hint: THE FIFTH ___ , OVER FIFTEEN HUNDRED YEARS AGO: the blank is counted with an ordinal number and it measures time. Ask: which box word names a period of one hundred years?

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.trap_type: Students omit the 'e' in 'careful', writing 'carful'. The word comes from 'care' + 'ful' → careful.
questions.learning_tip: 'Care' + '-ful' = CAREFUL. The 'e' in 'care' is kept: c-a-r-e-f-u-l. Spelling tip: think of 'full of care' → CAREFUL.
questions.retry_hint: The underlined word is meant to say 'full of CARE'. Ask: when you add -FUL to a word ending in silent -e, does that -e stay or go? Spell the whole word in your head and count the letters you really need.

questions.error_type: Homophone confusion - there (place) vs their (belonging to them)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'there' (place) when the bags belong to the pupils.
questions.learning_tip: THEIR = belonging to them. THERE = at that place. Test: the bags belong to the pupils -> THEIR bags.
questions.retry_hint: The BAGS belong to the PUPILS FROM ANOTHER SCHOOL. Ask: does the underlined spelling mean 'at that place', or 'belonging to them'? The two sound alike, so choose by meaning, never by sound.

questions.trap_type: Students simply add -s to 'knife'. Nouns ending in -f or -fe usually change to -ves.
questions.learning_tip: KNIFE -> KNIVES. Same rule: leaf -> leaves, half -> halves, loaf -> loaves, wolf -> wolves.
questions.retry_hint: KNIFES is the trap: nouns ending in -f or -fe rarely take a plain -s. Ask: how do you write more than one leaf, or more than one wolf? Apply that same change here.

questions.trap_type: 'The exhibits' is plural. Students write 'was' (singular).
questions.learning_tip: 'The exhibits' = plural → WERE labelled. WAS is only for singular subjects.
questions.retry_hint: Find the subject: MANY OF THE EXHIBITS - that is more than one thing. Ask: does a plural subject take the singular past verb, or the plural one? Do not match the verb to the nearest noun alone.

questions.error_type: Spelling — -ing rule: silent -e is dropped, not consonant doubled for 'write'
questions.trap_type: Students double the 't' in 'writing', producing 'writting'. 'Write' ends in a vowel-consonant-e pattern: drop the -e and add -ing. Do NOT double the t.
questions.learning_tip: 'Write' ends in vowel-consonant-e (-i-t-e): drop the -e and add -ing → WRITING. The t is NOT doubled because the vowel before it (i) is long, not short.
questions.retry_hint: WRITTING doubles a letter it should not. Ask: 'write' ends in a silent -e, so when you add -ing, do you drop the -e or keep it? Compare: make becomes making, ride becomes riding.

E.passage: Our class visited the National Museum last Thursday. Our teacher reminded us to be carful (1) not to touch any exhibits without permission. Inside the first gallery, some pupils from another school had left there (2) bags on the floor. The curator showed us two ancient knifes (3) that had been found in a riverbed. Many of the exhibits was (4) labelled in English and Mandarin so that all visitors could read them. At the end, we spent time writting (5) our reflections in our museum journals before boarding the bus back to school.

questions.sentence_a: The ancient vase was discovered by archaeologists in Egypt.
questions.sentence_b: The ancient vase is now displayed in the National Museum.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using the relative pronoun 'which'.
questions.model_answer: The ancient vase, which was discovered by archaeologists in Egypt, is now displayed in the National Museum.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'The ancient vase which it was discovered by archaeologists is now displayed' — adding an extra pronoun 'it' after 'which'.
questions.learning_tip: Use 'which' to add information about a THING. The ancient vase, WHICH was discovered in Egypt, is now displayed. Do NOT add 'it' after 'which'.
questions.retry_hint: Both sentences talk about THE ANCIENT VASE, so name it once and let 'which' carry the second mention. Ask: after 'which', do you still need the word 'it'? And which punctuation mark holds the extra information inside?

questions.sentence_a: The class arrived at the museum.
questions.sentence_b: They went straight to the dinosaur exhibition.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'After'.
questions.model_answer: After the class arrived at the museum, they went straight to the dinosaur exhibition.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'After they went straight to the dinosaur exhibition, the class arrived at the museum' — reversing the correct time order.
questions.learning_tip: AFTER + [the first event], [the second event]. AFTER the class ARRIVED, they WENT to the exhibition. The event after 'after' happened FIRST.
questions.retry_hint: Which happened first - THE CLASS ARRIVED AT THE MUSEUM, or the walk to the dinosaurs? Ask: the event that follows the word 'After' must be the EARLIER one. Then a comma joins the two halves.

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
Class 3E arrived at the Heritage Museum on a Tuesday morning. Their teacher, Mr Loh, had one rule: look with your eyes, not your hands.

The first gallery was full of ancient pottery from South-East Asia. While the guide was explaining the history of a particular clay pot, a boy named Ivan leaned too close. He lost his balance, and his elbow caught the edge of a rope barrier. The barrier toppled, and the museum's smallest pot — a replica, thankfully — fell and shattered on the marble floor.

Everyone went very still. Ivan's face turned red. He looked at Mr Loh.

Mr Loh did not shout. He walked over to the museum attendant, spoke quietly and then came back. 'It was a replica,' he said calmly. 'No harm done. Now, what can everyone learn from this?'

A girl named Rina put her hand up. 'To respect the rules,' she said.

'Good,' said Mr Loh. 'And also — it is easier to break something than to make it.' He picked up one of the large shards and held it up. 'Look at this. A craftsman spent weeks shaping this pot. And it took one second to break.'

Ivan nodded slowly. He did not say anything for the rest of the museum visit. But when they reached the ancient weaving gallery at the end, he was the most careful one there.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 1 has the same meaning as 'broke suddenly into many small pieces'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Toppled' = fell over; 'leaned' = bent. SHATTERED = broke suddenly into many pieces.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: SHATTERED = broke suddenly and completely into many pieces. The pot SHATTERED on the marble floor = it smashed. SHATTER = break violently into small pieces.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 3, what does 'it' refer to in 'Mr Loh already knew what it was'?

options.1: The broken pieces on the floor
options.3: The fact that the pot was a replica, not the real ancient one
options.4: The lesson Mr Loh planned to teach

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1. 'It' = the pot's nature — that it was a copy.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: PRONOUN REFERENCE: 'IT' refers to what the pot WAS — a REPLICA. Mr Loh already knew IT = he knew the pot was a copy. Context: 'He walked over slowly, crouched down, and smiled.'

mcq_questions.stem: Why was Ivan described as 'the most careful one' in the weaving gallery?

options.1: Because he was always the most careful student.
options.2: Because the broken pot taught him to understand how fragile and precious things are.
options.3: Because Mr Loh gave him a warning before the weaving gallery.
options.4: Because the weaving exhibits were more delicate.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Ivan was NOT always careful — he broke the pot. This change was caused by the lesson.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: INFERENCE: Ivan was NOT always careful (he broke the pot by leaning too close). In the weaving gallery, 'he was the most careful.' This CHANGE happened BECAUSE the broken pot taught him a lesson about care.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 2, is it True or False that Ivan broke the pot on purpose? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The passage says Ivan leaned too close, lost his balance and his elbow hit the barrier — it was an accident, not deliberate.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'True, he touched the barrier.' He hit it accidentally when he lost his balance.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 2: 'Ivan leaned too close, LOST HIS BALANCE, and his elbow HIT the rope barrier.' These words show an ACCIDENT. Answer is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: How did the pot break?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: Ivan leaned too close, lost his balance, and his elbow hit the rope barrier. The barrier toppled and knocked the pot off its stand.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'Ivan touched the pot' which is inaccurate — he hit the barrier with his elbow, not the pot directly.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 2: Ivan's ELBOW hit the rope BARRIER, which toppled and caused the pot to fall. He did not directly touch the pot.

open_ended_questions.stem: What TWO lessons did Mr Loh teach the class after the pot broke?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) To respect the rules. (ii) It is easier to break something than to make it.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students give only one lesson or repeat the same lesson in different words.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraphs 5–6: (1) 'To RESPECT THE RULES' (Rina's answer that Mr Loh approved). (2) 'It is EASIER to break something than to make it.' Both are explicit lessons in the text.

open_ended_questions.stem: Find ONE phrase from the passage that shows Ivan truly understood the lesson by the end of the visit.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: 'He was the most careful one there.'
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students quote 'He did not say anything' which shows silence, not necessarily understanding.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Last paragraph: 'he was THE MOST CAREFUL ONE there.' This action shows he genuinely understood and changed his behaviour — the clearest evidence of learning.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on his actions in the passage, describe TWO character traits of Mr Loh with evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) CALM: when the pot shattered, instead of scolding Ivan, Mr Loh walked over slowly and smiled — showing he did not panic or react in anger. (ii) THOUGHTFUL: he used the broken pot as a teaching moment, turning the accident into a lesson about care and respect for things made with effort.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'kind and patient' without precise trait names or specific evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: TRAIT INFERENCE: CALM = walked SLOWLY, SMILED (not angry). THOUGHTFUL = turned the broken pot into a TEACHING MOMENT. Name trait → give evidence from passage = full marks.

questions.stem: The explorer ________ through the dense jungle, pushing branches aside as he searched for the hidden ruins.
questions.trap_type: 'Floated' and 'soared' are for water/air movement; 'tiptoed' is too careful and slow. Only 'trekked' = travelled on foot over difficult terrain.
questions.learning_tip: TREKKED = walked a long, difficult journey on foot, especially through wild terrain. Explorers TREK through jungles and mountains.
questions.retry_hint: The explorer PUSHED BRANCHES ASIDE in a DENSE JUNGLE - slow, hard travel on foot. Ask: which verb means to make a long and difficult journey by walking? 'Floated' and 'soared' belong to water and air.

questions.stem: The old map was as ________ as tissue paper — one wrong touch and it might crumble to dust.
questions.trap_type: 'Thick', 'bright' and 'heavy' don't describe something easily damaged. FRAGILE = easily broken.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! The map was AS FRAGILE AS tissue paper = comparing how easily it could be damaged to thin, delicate tissue paper. FRAGILE = easily broken — handle with care!
questions.retry_hint: The map is compared to TISSUE PAPER, and ONE WRONG TOUCH could make it CRUMBLE TO DUST. Ask: does tissue paper feel strong and heavy, or thin and easily broken? Match the adjective to the paper.

questions.stem: The children ________ their way through the abandoned warehouse, unsure of what they might find.
questions.trap_type: 'Raced', 'stormed' and 'leaped' all imply speed or force. Only 'crept' = moved slowly and quietly, trying not to be heard or noticed.
questions.learning_tip: CREPT = moved slowly, quietly and carefully, trying not to make noise. The children CREPT through the warehouse = moved with caution and silence.
questions.retry_hint: The children were UNSURE OF WHAT THEY MIGHT FIND inside the ABANDONED WAREHOUSE, so they moved with caution. Ask: which verb means to move slowly and quietly? 'Raced', 'stormed' and 'leaped' are all fast or forceful.

questions.stem: Finding a single clue in the enormous abandoned warehouse was like looking for a ________ — almost impossible.
questions.trap_type: 'A piece of cake' = easy (opposite!). NEEDLE IN A HAYSTACK = something extremely difficult to find.
questions.learning_tip: IDIOM: A NEEDLE IN A HAYSTACK = something almost impossible to find among many things. The warehouse was so big that finding one small clue was A NEEDLE IN A HAYSTACK. Idioms cannot be understood word by word!
questions.retry_hint: The warehouse is ENORMOUS, the clue is a SINGLE one, and the sentence itself says ALMOST IMPOSSIBLE. Ask: which idiom describes something nearly impossible to find? 'A piece of cake' means exactly the opposite.

questions.stem: The detective carefully ________ the secret passage and found a trail of muddy footprints leading deeper inside.
questions.trap_type: 'Ran away from' = fled; 'gave up on' = stopped. LOOKED INTO = investigated carefully.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: LOOK INTO = investigate something carefully. The detective LOOKED INTO the passage = she examined it to find clues. LOOK + INTO work together as one meaning.
questions.retry_hint: The detective FOUND A TRAIL OF MUDDY FOOTPRINTS after examining the SECRET PASSAGE. Ask: which phrasal verb means to investigate something carefully? 'Gave up on' means stopped; 'ran away from' means fled.

questions.stem: Nobody in the adventure club ________ a clue this difficult before — it has everyone completely baffled.
questions.trap_type: BEFORE + 'it has everyone baffled' = up to now, so a simple present verb cannot be used. Students also write 'have solved', forgetting that NOBODY is singular.
questions.learning_tip: NOBODY = singular -> HAS, never 'have'. BEFORE (= at any time up to now) needs the present perfect: Nobody HAS SOLVED a clue this difficult before.
questions.retry_hint: The word BEFORE means 'at any time up to now', so a plain present verb cannot work here. Ask: which choice is the present perfect? And NOBODY acts like one person - so must its helping verb be the singular one, or the plural one?

questions.stem: The young detectives have ________ three hidden clues since they started their investigation this morning.
questions.trap_type: HAVE + past participle = present perfect. FIND → FOUND (irregular).
questions.learning_tip: HAVE + past participle = present perfect. The detectives HAVE FOUND three clues = started finding this morning and have three so far. FIND → FOUND (irregular past participle).
questions.retry_hint: HAVE is already in the sentence, and SINCE THIS MORNING stretches right up to now. Ask: after 'have', which form of 'find' fits - the plain verb, the -s form, the -ing form, or the past participle? 'Find' is irregular.

questions.stem: The explorers ________ across the rope bridge when it began to sway violently in the wind.
questions.trap_type: 'The bridge began to sway' = sudden interrupting event. Explorers were already crossing = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: The bridge BEGAN TO SWAY = sudden past event. Explorers were already in the middle of crossing = WERE CROSSING (past continuous). Was/were + verb-ing = action in progress when something interrupts.
questions.retry_hint: The bridge BEGAN TO SWAY suddenly, cutting across something already happening. Ask: which choice shows an action in progress in the past? A plain past verb reports only a finished act, and a present form cannot fit.

questions.stem: The tunnel on the left was much ________ than the one on the right — and far more dangerous to enter alone.
questions.trap_type: 'Darkest' = superlative; 'more darker' = WRONG. DARKER = comparative of 'dark'.
questions.learning_tip: Short adjective + -ER = comparative. Dark → DARKER. The left tunnel was DARKER THAN the right = comparing only two. 'More darker' is ALWAYS WRONG — never add BOTH 'more' AND '-er'.
questions.retry_hint: MUCH ___ THAN tells you two tunnels are being compared, and 'dark' is a short adjective. Ask: do short adjectives take -er, or do they need a word in front? And can you ever put 'more' before a word already ending in -er?

questions.stem: The children searched ________ the attic from morning until evening but still could not find the old diary.
questions.trap_type: 'At' marks a point; 'on' marks a surface; 'into' shows entering, not examining. SEARCH THROUGH = look in every part of a place.
questions.learning_tip: SEARCHED THROUGH = examined every part of something. They searched THROUGH the attic = looked in every corner and box. 'Through' shows comprehensive coverage.
questions.retry_hint: The children looked in every corner of THE ATTIC, FROM MORNING UNTIL EVENING. Ask: which preposition means moving over and examining every part of a place? 'At' marks a point, and 'on' marks a surface.

questions.stem: Each of the coded messages in the detective game ________ a different secret phrase to unlock.
questions.trap_type: 'Each of the coded messages' = each one individually = singular. Present fact. Students write 'contain' thinking of many messages.
questions.learning_tip: 'Each of the coded messages' = each one at a time = singular → CONTAINS a different secret phrase. EACH always uses a singular verb.
questions.retry_hint: EACH OF THE CODED MESSAGES means one message at a time, however many there are. Ask: does EACH take a singular verb or a plural one? The sentence states what is true now, so a past form cannot fit.

questions.stem: The ancient scroll ________ in a clay pot buried under the ruins of the old temple.
questions.trap_type: The scroll did not find itself. Past passive = was found.
questions.learning_tip: The scroll was the receiver of the action. Past passive = WAS FOUND. Passive = was/were + past participle.
questions.retry_hint: The SCROLL could not hide itself IN A CLAY POT - somebody else did the finding, and the ruins are long gone. Ask: which choice is passive (the subject receives the action) and set in the past?

questions.stem: The expedition leader told her team ________ the cave alone under any circumstances.
questions.trap_type: Negative reported speech: told someone not to do something = told + object + not to + base verb.
questions.learning_tip: 'Told her team NOT TO + base verb': told her team NOT TO ENTER the cave alone. After 'told + object', always use 'not to' + base verb.
questions.retry_hint: TOLD HER TEAM = a reported command. Ask: after 'told + person', which form follows - the plain verb, the -ing form, or 'to' + verb? And does the negative word come before that little word, or after it?

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Verb forms of 'discover')

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Young adventurers love (1)________ hidden places and solving puzzles.' Signal: 'love + ___' = gerund (verb-ing). Pattern: love + verb-ing → discovering.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'to discover' instead of the gerund after 'love'.
questions.learning_tip: LOVE + verb-ing: love DISCOVERING hidden places. After 'love', always add -ING.
questions.retry_hint: The verb LOVE stands right in front of the blank. Ask: after love, enjoy and hate, which form do we normally use - the -S form, the past, or the -ING form? A plain verb can never follow 'love' directly.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Every year, someone (2)________ a new piece of ancient history in an unexpected place.' Signal: 'Every year' = regular habit = simple present. Subject 'someone' = singular → discovers.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'discover' (plural form) forgetting 'someone' is singular.
questions.learning_tip: 'Every year' = habit = simple present. Someone (singular) → DISCOVERS a new piece of ancient history.
questions.retry_hint: EVERY YEAR signals a repeated habit, and SOMEONE behaves like one person. Ask: in the simple present, does a singular subject take the plain verb, or the verb ending in -s?

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Last summer, a team of divers (3)________ a sunken ship off the coast of Batam.' Signal: 'Last summer' = past. 'Discover' is regular: discover → discovered.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'discover' (base form) ignoring the past signal 'Last summer'.
questions.learning_tip: 'Last summer' = past. 'Discover' is regular: discover → DISCOVERED.
questions.retry_hint: LAST SUMMER is finished time, so the verb must be simple past. Ask: is this verb regular, and if so, which ending do you add? An -ing form cannot stand alone here without a helping verb.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'While the lead diver (4)________ the lower deck, a shark appeared nearby.' Signal: 'While the lead diver ___' = ongoing background action in the past. Subject 'the lead diver' = singular → was discovering. Interrupted by 'a shark appeared'.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'discovered' (simple past) missing the ongoing signal 'while the lead diver'.
questions.learning_tip: 'While the lead diver ___' = ongoing background past action = past continuous. The lead diver WAS DISCOVERING the lower deck when the shark appeared.
questions.retry_hint: WHILE marks the longer action that had already begun when the SHARK APPEARED - and THE LEAD DIVER is one person. Ask: which past continuous form matches a single subject? A simple past would show only a finished act.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The other divers (5)________ ancient coins in the upper hull at the same time.' Signal: same past time frame, plural subject 'the other divers' + ongoing parallel action → were discovering.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'discovered' (simple past) instead of past continuous for an ongoing parallel action.
questions.learning_tip: The other divers = plural. They were doing it at the same past moment = WERE DISCOVERING (past continuous).
questions.retry_hint: AT THE SAME TIME points back to that same underwater moment, and THE OTHER DIVERS are more than one. Ask: which past continuous form matches a plural subject? A simple past form loses the 'still going on' meaning.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Every explorer dreams (6)________ something truly remarkable.' Signal: 'dreams + ___' = infinitive. Pattern: dream + to + base verb → to discover.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'discovering'. HOPE takes the infinitive, never the -ing form.
questions.learning_tip: HOPE + TO + base verb: hopes TO DISCOVER something remarkable. 'Hopes discovering' is never correct.
questions.retry_hint: HOPES comes right before the blank. Ask: after 'hopes', do we use the -ING form, the -S form, or the infinitive (the plain verb with its little partner word in front)? 'Hopes discovering' is never English.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'One day, scientists may (7)________ what lies beneath the Antarctic ice sheet.' Signal: 'may + ___' = modal verb + base form. Never add -s or -ing after a modal.
questions.trap_type: Students add -s or -ing after the modal verb 'may'.
questions.learning_tip: After modal verbs (may, should, must, can), always use the BASE form: may DISCOVER. Never 'may discovers' or 'may discovering'.
questions.retry_hint: MAY is a modal verb, and modals never change the verb behind them. Ask: after may, can, must or should, do you add -s, add -ing, or keep the base form? 'May discovers' is always wrong.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Right now, a research team (8)________ ancient remains in a cave in Borneo.' Signal: 'Right now' = present continuous. Subject 'a research team' = singular → is discovering.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'discovers' (simple present habit) missing the 'right now' signal for present continuous.
questions.learning_tip: 'Right now' = present continuous. A research team (singular) → IS DISCOVERING ancient remains right now.
questions.retry_hint: RIGHT NOW - the work happens at this very moment, and A RESEARCH TEAM counts as one thing. Ask: which present continuous form fits a single subject acting now? 'Discovers' would mean every year, not today.

C.passage: Young adventurers love (1)________ hidden places and solving puzzles about the past. Every year, someone (2)________ a new piece of ancient history in an unexpected place. Last summer, a team of divers (3)________ a sunken ship off the coast of Batam. While the lead diver (4)________ the treasure in the lower deck, a shark appeared and circled the wreck. The other divers (5)________ ancient coins in the upper hull at the same time. Every explorer hopes (6)________ something truly remarkable that changes what we know about history. One day, scientists may (7)________ what lies beneath the Antarctic ice sheet. Right now, a research team (8)________ ancient remains deep inside a cave in Borneo.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: Mystery stories often begin with something strange or hidden. A key setting is the (1)________ house or location — empty and forgotten, full of secrets. Important clues may be (2)________ — hidden from view by clever tricks or physical barriers. A good mystery always leads to an (3)________ — a careful search for the truth. Many mysteries end when the last thread is (4)________ — the final connection between all the clues. These adventures remind us that even the most (5)________ journey can lead to something remarkable if we are brave enough to begin.

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'concealed'. The clue is 'EMPTY AND FORGOTTEN' - nobody lives there any more.
questions.learning_tip: ABANDONED = left empty and no longer used or cared for. An ABANDONED house has been deserted by its owners.
questions.retry_hint: The dash explains it: EMPTY AND FORGOTTEN, FULL OF SECRETS - nobody has lived there for years. Ask: which box word describes a building everyone has left behind? 'Concealed' means hidden, not deserted.

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'abandoned'. The clue is 'HIDDEN FROM VIEW by clever tricks or physical barriers'.
questions.learning_tip: CONCEALED = deliberately hidden so that it cannot be seen. A clue may be CONCEALED behind a panel.
questions.retry_hint: The dash explains it: HIDDEN FROM VIEW BY CLEVER TRICKS or physical barriers. Ask: which box word means deliberately kept out of sight? 'Abandoned' describes an empty place, not a hidden clue.

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'perilous'. The blank follows 'an', so it must be a noun beginning with a vowel sound, and the clue is 'A CAREFUL SEARCH FOR THE TRUTH'.
questions.learning_tip: An INVESTIGATION = a careful, organised search for the facts. Detectives open an INVESTIGATION to solve a mystery.
questions.retry_hint: 'AN' before the blank means the word starts with a vowel sound, and the dash defines it: A CAREFUL SEARCH FOR THE TRUTH. Ask: which box word names what detectives open the moment a mystery begins?

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'concealed'. The clue is the THREAD image - a tangle being pulled straight until everything makes sense.
questions.learning_tip: UNRAVELLED = came apart thread by thread, so the whole truth became clear. A mystery UNRAVELS clue by clue.
questions.retry_hint: Picture the image: THE LAST THREAD, pulled straight until the FINAL CONNECTION between the clues appears. Ask: which box word describes a tangle coming apart so that the truth shows? It follows 'is', so it is a past participle.

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'abandoned'. The blank sits between 'the most' and 'journey', so it must be a describing word, and the clue is 'BRAVE ENOUGH TO BEGIN'.
questions.learning_tip: PERILOUS = full of danger. A PERILOUS journey is one that could easily end badly.
questions.retry_hint: The blank sits between THE MOST and JOURNEY, so it must describe the journey - and you need to be BRAVE ENOUGH TO BEGIN it. Ask: which box word means full of danger? 'Abandoned' describes a place, not a journey.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.trap_type: Students write 'slow' (adjective) after the action verb 'crept'. A verb needs an adverb to describe how.
questions.learning_tip: After an action verb (crept), use an ADVERB: crept SLOWLY. 'Slow' is an adjective — it describes nouns, not actions.
questions.retry_hint: The underlined word is meant to tell you HOW they CREPT down the corridor - and 'crept' is an action verb. Ask: do we describe an action with an adjective, or with an adverb? Which ending turns one into the other?

questions.error_type: Homophone confusion — its (possessive) vs it's (it is)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'its' (possessive) when the meaning is 'it is'.
questions.learning_tip: IT'S = it is (contraction). ITS = belonging to it (possessive). Test: 'ITS strange' → can you say 'IT IS strange'? YES → use IT'S. IT'S = IT IS. ITS has no apostrophe because possessives (his, her, its) never need one.
questions.retry_hint: ITS with no apostrophe means 'belonging to it'. Ask: in this sentence, does something belong to the wall, or is the writer saying that a situation seems STRANGE? Say the two words out in full and see which meaning fits.

questions.error_type: Spelling — -ing rule: silent -e is dropped before -ing
questions.trap_type: Students keep the final -e when adding -ing to 'hide', producing 'hideing'. Drop the silent -e before adding -ing.
questions.learning_tip: 'Hide' ends in silent -e: drop the -e before adding -ing → HIDING. Same rule: make → making, slide → sliding, give → giving.
questions.retry_hint: HIDEING keeps a letter it should drop. Ask: 'hide' ends in a silent -e, so when you add -ing, does that -e stay or go? Compare: make becomes making, slide becomes sliding, give becomes giving.

questions.error_type: Subject-verb agreement - plural subject (the muddy paw prints)
questions.trap_type: 'The muddy paw prints' is plural. Students match the verb to the nearest word instead.
questions.learning_tip: 'The muddy paw prints' = plural -> WERE all over the dusty floor. WAS is only for singular subjects.
questions.retry_hint: Find the subject: THE MUDDY PAW PRINTS - many prints, not one. Ask: does a plural subject take the singular past verb, or the plural one? Do not match the verb to the nearest word alone.

questions.trap_type: Students write a plain plural and leave out the apostrophe that shows ownership.
questions.learning_tip: The notebook BELONGS TO the detectives -> DETECTIVES' notebook (apostrophe after the -s for a plural). Singular: detective's.
questions.retry_hint: The NOTEBOOK belongs to the detectives, and there is more than one of them. Ask: does a plain -s show ownership, or only make a plural? Where does the apostrophe go when the owners are many?

E.passage: Last Thursday after school, three friends decided to investigate the strange scratching sounds coming from the old storeroom. They crept slow (1) down the corridor, hearts pounding. They turned a corner and spotted a gap in the wall — its (2) strange that nobody noticed it before. They found a small cat hideing (3) behind a stack of boxes. The muddy paw prints was (4) all over the dusty floor. Later, when they wrote up their findings, the detectives (5) notebook was filled with detailed sketches and notes about the little cat's hiding spot.

questions.sentence_a: The explorer was mapping the cave.
questions.sentence_b: She suddenly noticed strange symbols on the wall.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'while'.
questions.model_answer: While the explorer was mapping the cave, she suddenly noticed strange symbols on the wall.
questions.trap_type: Students drop 'was', writing 'While the explorer mapping the cave, she suddenly noticed strange symbols'.
questions.learning_tip: WHILE + ongoing action (past continuous), sudden event (simple past). While the explorer WAS MAPPING, she suddenly NOTICED. Keep WAS for the ongoing action.
questions.retry_hint: 'While' must stand in front of the LONGER action, the one already going on. Ask: which of the two sentences shows that action - and when you move it behind 'while', do you keep its helping verb, or drop it?

questions.sentence_a: The detective found the hidden door.
questions.sentence_b: The hidden door led to a secret underground room.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using the relative pronoun 'which'.
questions.model_answer: The detective found the hidden door, which led to a secret underground room.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'The detective found the hidden door which it led to a secret underground room' — adding an extra 'it' after 'which'.
questions.learning_tip: Use 'which' to add information about a THING. The detective found the hidden door, WHICH led to a secret underground room. Never add 'it' after 'which'.
questions.retry_hint: Both sentences name THE HIDDEN DOOR, so say it once and let 'which' stand in for the second mention. Ask: after 'which', do you still need the word 'it'? And where does the comma belong?

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
It was Priya who noticed it first. While she was leaning against the crumbling wall of the old shophouse, her hand felt something beneath the peeling paint — a raised edge, like the border of a frame. She looked closer. There, barely visible under decades of old white paint, was a map.

She called the others: her neighbour Reuben and her cousin Amara. Together, they spent the next forty minutes carefully brushing away loose paint with their fingers. Slowly, a hand-drawn map of the neighbourhood came into view — but the neighbourhood looked very different from how it did today.

There were pathways that no longer existed. Buildings that were now carparks. And at the centre of the map, circled in red ink, was a location that none of them recognised: 'The Keeper's Room'.

'This must be from decades ago,' Reuben said.

'We have to find out where this room is,' said Amara.

Preya photographed the map with her phone. She knew the local history group met every Saturday morning. She also knew her grandmother once lived in this neighbourhood since she was a child.

That Saturday, she brought the photograph as well as her grandmother.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 1 has the same meaning as 'almost impossible to see'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Crumbling' = falling apart; 'peeling' = coming off in strips. BARELY VISIBLE = almost impossible to see.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: BARELY VISIBLE = almost impossible to see. The map was BARELY VISIBLE under the old paint = so faint that Priya almost missed it. BARELY = almost not at all. VISIBLE = able to be seen.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 3, what does 'it' refer to in 'it was labelled The Keeper's Room'?

options.1: The old map hidden under the paint
options.2: The red circle drawn at the centre of the map
options.3: The wall of the abandoned shophouse

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1. 'It' = the specific red CIRCLE that was labelled.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: PRONOUN REFERENCE: 'IT was labelled The Keeper's Room.' IT = the RED CIRCLE at the centre of the map. 'A circle marked in red ink — IT was labelled...' IT refers to the circle, not the whole map.

mcq_questions.stem: Why did Priya decide to bring her grandmother to the history group meeting?

options.1: Because her grandmother was a member of the history group.
options.2: Because her grandmother might recognise places from when she once lived in the area.
options.3: Because she wanted her grandmother to draw a new map.
options.4: Because the history group required an adult.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1. The grandmother's value was her personal knowledge of the area, not membership.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 5: Priya knew her grandmother ONCE LIVED in this neighbourhood. So the grandmother might RECOGNISE places on the old map. Priya brought her because of personal knowledge of the area.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 1, is it True or False that Priya was looking for a map when she found it? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The passage says Priya was leaning against the wall and her hand felt something by accident — she was not searching for anything.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'True, she found the map.' She found it by accident while leaning, not because she was searching.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1: 'While she was LEANING AGAINST the wall, her hand FELT something beneath the peeling paint.' She was not looking — it was an ACCIDENTAL discovery. Answer is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: What was marked at the centre of the map?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: A location circled in red ink called 'The Keeper's Room'.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'a circle' without naming what the circle marked.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 3: 'at the centre of the map, circled in RED INK, was a location: THE KEEPER'S ROOM.' Name both the marking and the location.

open_ended_questions.stem: How did the map show that the neighbourhood had changed? Give TWO specific examples from the passage.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) The map showed pathways that no longer existed. (ii) It showed buildings that were now carparks.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'the neighbourhood looks different now' without naming the specific changes.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 3: (1) 'PATHWAYS that no longer existed' and (2) 'buildings that were now CARPARKS.' Give both specific changes from the text.

open_ended_questions.stem: Why did Priya think of TWO sources of help to find 'The Keeper's Room'?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: She thought of the local history group and her grandmother, because the history group meets regularly and knows local history, and her grandmother has lived in the neighbourhood since she was a child.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students mention only one source of help.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 6: Priya thought of (1) the LOCAL HISTORY GROUP that meets on Saturdays and (2) her GRANDMOTHER who lived in the neighbourhood since childhood. Two different sources.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on her actions throughout the passage, describe TWO character traits of Priya with evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) OBSERVANT: she was the first to notice the raised edge beneath the paint — most people would lean against a wall without noticing anything unusual. (ii) RESOURCEFUL: when she could not solve the mystery alone, she thought of TWO sources of help — the local history group and her grandmother — using all available resources.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'curious and clever' without precise traits or specific evidence from the text.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: TRAIT INFERENCE: OBSERVANT = FIRST to notice the raised edge beneath the paint. RESOURCEFUL = thought of TWO different sources of help. Name the trait → give specific evidence from the passage = full marks.

questions.stem: The gardener used a small rake to ________ the dry leaves into a pile before composting them.
questions.trap_type: 'Scatter' means spread out; 'bury' means put underground; 'flatten' = press down. Only 'gather' = bring together into a group.
questions.learning_tip: GATHER = bring things together into one place. The gardener GATHERS fallen leaves into a pile before composting them.
questions.retry_hint: The gardener uses A SMALL RAKE and wants the DRY LEAVES INTO A PILE. Ask: which verb brings scattered things together into one heap? 'Scatter' spreads them apart, and 'flatten' only presses them down.

questions.stem: The tomato seedlings were as ________ as little green jewels - tiny, glossy and catching the morning light.
questions.trap_type: 'Heavy' and 'dull' are opposites of bright; 'delicate' describes fragility not colour. BRIGHT = giving off a strong, clear light or colour.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! The seedlings were AS BRIGHT AS little green jewels = comparing their vivid green colour to sparkling jewels. Similes always use 'as ... as' to compare two different things.
questions.retry_hint: The seedlings are compared to LITTLE GREEN JEWELS - TINY, GLOSSY and CATCHING THE MORNING LIGHT. Ask: do jewels look dull and heavy, or clear and shining? Match the adjective to the jewels, not to their size.

questions.stem: The seeds needed rich, ________ soil to germinate quickly and grow into strong seedlings.
questions.trap_type: 'Stony', 'arid' and 'frozen' all describe soil that prevents plant growth. Only 'fertile' = rich in nutrients and ideal for growing plants.
questions.learning_tip: FERTILE = rich in nutrients and ideal for growing plants. FERTILE soil produces healthy crops and strong seedlings.
questions.retry_hint: The soil must be RICH, so that the seeds GERMINATE QUICKLY and grow into STRONG SEEDLINGS. Ask: which adjective describes soil full of the food plants need? 'Stony', 'arid' and 'frozen' all stop things from growing.

questions.stem: Mr Tan has ________ for growing vegetables — everything he plants comes up healthy and full.
questions.trap_type: 'A black eye' = an injury; 'cold feet' = fear; 'a big mouth' = talks too much. A GREEN THUMB = a natural talent for growing plants.
questions.learning_tip: IDIOM: A GREEN THUMB = a natural talent for gardening. 'Mr Tan has A GREEN THUMB' = he is naturally good at growing plants. Idioms cannot be understood word by word — green thumb is NOT about finger colour!
questions.retry_hint: EVERYTHING HE PLANTS COMES UP HEALTHY AND FULL. Ask: does this idiom describe a natural talent for gardening, an injury, sudden fear, or talking too much? An idiom cannot be read word by word.

questions.stem: After the harvest festival, the students decided to ________ the old vegetable beds and plant fresh seeds.
questions.trap_type: 'Give in' = surrender; 'break down' = stop working; 'run out' = exhaust supply. DIG UP = remove something by digging it out of the ground.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: DIG UP = remove something from the ground by digging. The students DIG UP the old beds = they use a spade to lift and clear the soil. DIG + UP work together as one meaning.
questions.retry_hint: The students want to clear THE OLD VEGETABLE BEDS and PLANT FRESH SEEDS in them. Ask: which phrasal verb means to lift something out of the ground with a spade? 'Give in' means surrender; 'run out' means finish a supply.

questions.stem: Everyone in the gardening club ________ a different plant to care for each term.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'choose' thinking 'everyone in the club' = many people. EVERYONE = singular → verb+S in present tense.
questions.learning_tip: EVERYONE / NOBODY / SOMEONE / EACH = Singular! Always use verb+S. Everyone CHOOSES = add -S. 'Everyone choose' is WRONG. Singular indefinite pronouns always take singular present-tense verbs.
questions.retry_hint: The subject is EVERYONE, not the members of the club. Words like everyone and nobody act like ONE person. Ask: in the present tense, does a singular subject take the plain verb, or the verb ending in -s?

questions.stem: The sunflower ________ almost two metres tall by the end of the summer holidays.
questions.trap_type: 'By the end of the summer holidays' = completed past event. 'Grow' is irregular: grow → grew.
questions.learning_tip: 'Grow' is irregular: grow → GREW. By the end of summer = completed past event → GREW almost two metres tall.
questions.retry_hint: BY THE END OF THE SUMMER HOLIDAYS is finished time, so the verb must be past. Ask: is 'grow' a regular verb? It is not, so it does not simply take -ed. Which past form does it change into?

questions.stem: Grandmother ________ the tomato seedlings when a sudden downpour flooded the pots.
questions.trap_type: 'A sudden downpour flooded the pots' is the sudden interrupting event. Grandmother was already repotting = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: The downpour FLOODED the pots = sudden past event. Grandmother was already repotting at that moment = WAS REPOTTING.
questions.retry_hint: A SUDDEN DOWNPOUR FLOODED THE POTS - that cut across something already happening. Ask: which choice shows an action in progress in the past? Grandmother is one person, so match the helping verb to her.

questions.stem: There ________ several caterpillars eating the lettuce leaves in the garden right now.
questions.trap_type: 'Several caterpillars' = plural, and RIGHT NOW = present. Students write 'is' (singular) or a past form.
questions.learning_tip: THERE + plural noun + present -> ARE. 'There ARE several caterpillars ... right now.' One caterpillar IS, several caterpillars ARE.
questions.retry_hint: SEVERAL CATERPILLARS is more than one, and RIGHT NOW puts the sentence in the present. Ask: does a plural subject take 'is' or the plural present form? And can a past form ever sit beside 'right now'?

questions.stem: You planted those seeds last Monday, ________ you?
questions.trap_type: The main clause is positive past ('planted') → the question tag must be negative. 'Planted' = past simple → auxiliary 'did'. Negative tag = didn't.
questions.learning_tip: Question tag for positive simple past: [positive statement] + DIDN'T + subject? 'You PLANTED those seeds, DIDN'T you?' Positive → negative tag; past → 'did'.
questions.retry_hint: The statement is positive and finished: YOU PLANTED THOSE SEEDS LAST MONDAY. Ask: after a positive statement, must the tag turn negative? And which helping verb stands in for a plain past verb?

questions.stem: These herbs are very easy to grow indoors, ________ they?
questions.trap_type: The main clause is positive present ('are') → the question tag must be negative. 'These herbs are' = plural present → negative tag = aren't.
questions.learning_tip: Question tag for 'These herbs ARE': positive present plural → negative tag = AREN'T. 'These herbs ARE easy to grow, AREN'T they?'
questions.retry_hint: The statement already carries the verb ARE, and it is positive. Ask: after a positive statement, does the tag go negative or stay positive? And should the tag repeat that same verb, or borrow 'do'?

questions.stem: The herbs ________ by children in the community garden with guidance from volunteer gardeners.
questions.trap_type: 'Herbs' = plural. Present regular process. Passive = are planted. Students write 'is planted' (singular).
questions.learning_tip: 'Herbs' = plural + present passive → ARE PLANTED. Passive = am/is/are + past participle. Plural subject = ARE.
questions.retry_hint: The HERBS did not plant themselves: BY CHILDREN tells you who does the work, and the herbs receive it. Ask: which choice is passive, present, and plural? 'Is planted' would need a single herb.

questions.stem: The horticulture teacher told the students ________ the seedlings too often or the roots would rot.
questions.trap_type: Negative reported speech: told someone not to do something = told + object + not to + base verb.
questions.learning_tip: 'Told students NOT TO + base verb': told the students NOT TO WATER the seedlings too often.
questions.retry_hint: The warning is a reported command: TOLD THE STUDENTS ... OR THE ROOTS WOULD ROT. Ask: after 'told + person', which form follows - the plain verb, the -ing form, or 'to' + verb? And where does the negative word sit?

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Prepositions: by, with, without, from, to, of, for, about)

questions.context_check: Passage: 'My uncle taught me everything I know (1)________ gardening.' Signal: 'taught me everything about' = the topic or subject matter = ABOUT. 'Know ABOUT gardening' = concerning the topic of gardening.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'of' instead of 'about'. 'Know ABOUT' = concerning a topic; 'know OF' = know that something exists, which is different.
questions.learning_tip: ABOUT = concerning a topic. 'Know ABOUT gardening' = have knowledge concerning gardening. 'About' shows the subject of the knowledge.
questions.retry_hint: KNOW ___ GARDENING: the blank links the knowing with its topic. Ask: which preposition introduces a subject matter? 'Of' after 'know' would only mean knowing that something exists.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'He digs the soil (2)________ a long-handled spade each morning.' Signal: using a tool = WITH. 'Digs WITH a spade' = the spade is the tool used.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'by' instead of 'with'. 'By' shows method in passive sentences; 'with' shows the physical tool being used.
questions.learning_tip: WITH = using a physical tool or instrument. He digs WITH a spade = he uses the spade to dig. 'With' shows what tool is being used.
questions.retry_hint: He DIGS THE SOIL using A LONG-HANDLED SPADE - the spade is the tool in his hands. Ask: which preposition marks the instrument you hold? 'By' introduces a method, not a tool.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'He propagates new plants (3)________ taking cuttings from healthy stems.' Signal: method or means in an active sentence = BY. 'BY taking cuttings' = the method he uses.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'with' instead of 'by'. 'With' is for tools; 'by' shows the method or process used to achieve something.
questions.learning_tip: BY = the method or process used. He propagates plants BY taking cuttings = the method he uses is taking cuttings. 'By' + verb-ing shows how something is done.
