questions.retry_hint: The blank stands in front of TAKING CUTTINGS, and that names a method, not a tool. Ask: which preposition plus an -ing verb explains HOW something is done? A tool word would need an object you can hold.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'A cactus can survive (4)________ water for weeks because it stores moisture in its thick stems.' Signal: in the absence of something = WITHOUT. 'Survive WITHOUT water' = in the absence of water.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'from' (source) or 'for' (duration). 'Without' = in the absence of something.
questions.learning_tip: WITHOUT = in the absence of something. A cactus can survive WITHOUT water = it does not need water the way other plants do.
questions.retry_hint: A CACTUS CAN SURVIVE for weeks although no water reaches it, because it STORES MOISTURE. Ask: which preposition means 'in the absence of something'? 'From' shows a source, and 'for' shows a length in time.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The seeds he plants come (5)________ all over the world.' Signal: origin or source = FROM. 'Come FROM all over the world' = their origin is different countries.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'of' instead of 'from'. 'Come FROM' = originating from a place; 'of' shows membership or composition.
questions.learning_tip: FROM = showing origin or source. The seeds come FROM all over the world = they originate from many different countries.
questions.retry_hint: The seeds COME ___ ALL OVER THE WORLD, and JAPAN, INDIA AND SOUTH AMERICA are named next. Ask: which preposition shows origin - the place something started out? 'Of' shows belonging, not a starting place.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The smell (6)________ jasmine fills the garden every evening at dusk.' Signal: belonging or association = OF. 'The smell OF jasmine' = the smell that belongs to / comes from jasmine.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'from' instead of 'of'. 'The smell OF something' is the fixed noun phrase; 'of' shows association/belonging.
questions.learning_tip: OF = showing belonging or association. 'The smell OF jasmine' = the smell belonging to / characteristic of jasmine. 'Smell of' is a fixed phrase.
questions.retry_hint: THE SMELL ___ JASMINE is one fixed noun phrase: the smell belongs to the flower. Ask: which preposition ties two nouns together in that way? 'From' would suggest travel rather than belonging.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'My uncle has been gardening (7)________ over thirty years.' Signal: duration of time in present perfect context = FOR. 'Gardening FOR over thirty years' = the length of time he has been doing it.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'since' (not in the box) or 'of' instead of 'for'. FOR is used with a duration of time in present perfect sentences.
questions.learning_tip: FOR + duration of time: gardening FOR over thirty years = the length of time he has been doing it. FOR shows how long something has lasted.
questions.retry_hint: OVER THIRTY YEARS tells you how long the gardening has lasted; it does not name a starting date. Ask: which preposition introduces a length in time? 'Since' would need a starting point, and it is not in the box.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'He donates fresh vegetables (8)________ the elderly residents in our neighbourhood every week.' Signal: recipient of an action = TO. 'Donates TO someone' = giving direction toward a recipient.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'for' instead of 'to'. 'Donate TO someone' = the person who receives; 'for' would show purpose, not recipient.
questions.learning_tip: TO = showing the recipient of an action. He donates vegetables TO the elderly residents = they are the ones who receive the vegetables.
questions.retry_hint: He DONATES FRESH VEGETABLES, and THE ELDERLY RESIDENTS are the people who receive them. Ask: which preposition points at the receiver? 'For' would show purpose - who the gift helps - rather than who gets it.

C.passage: My uncle taught me everything I know (1)________ gardening. He digs the soil (2)________ a long-handled spade each morning before the sun gets too strong. He propagates new plants (3)________ taking cuttings and placing them in water until roots appear. He told me that a cactus can survive (4)________ water for weeks because it stores moisture in its thick stems. The seeds he plants come (5)________ all over the world; Japan, India and South America are just three examples. The smell (6)________ jasmine fills the garden every evening at dusk and makes the whole compound feel peaceful. My uncle has been gardening (7)________ over thirty years. Every week, he donates fresh vegetables (8)________ the elderly residents in our neighbourhood.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: A garden needs careful attention all year round. Many gardeners make their own (1)________ from vegetable peels and fallen leaves, and mix it into the earth to feed the plant roots. Warmth and moisture help the seeds (2)________ and push their first shoots through the soil. Once a young (3)________ appears above the ground, it needs regular water and light to grow. Many plants depend on insects like bees to (4)________ them, carrying pollen between flowers. After months of care, gardeners enjoy the (5)________, picking ripe fruit and vegetables to eat or share.

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'fertile'. The blank follows 'make their own', so it must be a noun, and the clue is VEGETABLE PEELS and FALLEN LEAVES rotting down.
questions.learning_tip: COMPOST = decayed food scraps and plant material mixed into soil to feed it. Gardeners make COMPOST from kitchen and garden waste.
questions.retry_hint: The clue is what it is made from: VEGETABLE PEELS AND FALLEN LEAVES, mixed into the earth to FEED THE PLANT ROOTS. Ask: which box word names rotted-down waste that enriches soil? It follows 'their own', so it is a noun.

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'seedling' (a noun). The blank follows 'help the seeds', so it must be a base verb, and the clue is the FIRST SHOOTS pushing through.
questions.learning_tip: GERMINATE = begin to grow from a seed. Warmth and moisture make a seed GERMINATE.
questions.retry_hint: The blank follows HELP THE SEEDS, so it must be a plain verb, and the clue is the FIRST SHOOTS pushing through the soil. Ask: which box word means to begin growing from a seed? 'Seedling' names the plant, not the process.

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'germinate' (a verb). The blank follows 'a young', so it must be a noun - the little plant itself, not the process.
questions.learning_tip: A SEEDLING = a very young plant that has just come up from a seed.
questions.retry_hint: The blank follows A YOUNG, so it must be a noun - the little plant itself. Ask: which box word names a plant that has just come up ABOVE THE GROUND? 'Germinate' is the action, not the thing.

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'germinate'. The clue is BEES CARRYING POLLEN BETWEEN FLOWERS.
questions.learning_tip: POLLINATE = carry pollen from one flower to another so that fruit and seeds can form. Bees POLLINATE as they feed.
questions.retry_hint: The clue is BEES CARRYING POLLEN BETWEEN FLOWERS, and the blank follows 'bees to', so it must be a plain verb. Ask: which box word means to carry pollen from one flower to another so that fruit can form?

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'compost'. The blank follows 'enjoy the', so it must be a noun, and the clue is PICKING RIPE FRUIT AND VEGETABLES after months of care.
questions.learning_tip: The HARVEST = the gathering in of ripe crops, and the crops themselves. Farmers wait all season for the HARVEST.
questions.retry_hint: AFTER MONTHS OF CARE, the gardeners are PICKING RIPE FRUIT AND VEGETABLES. Ask: which box word names the gathering in of the ripe crops? The blank follows 'enjoy the', so it must be a noun.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.trap_type: Students write 'careful' (adjective) after the action verb 'pruned'. A verb needs an adverb to describe how the action was done.
questions.learning_tip: After an action verb (pruned), use an ADVERB: pruned CAREFULLY. 'Careful' is an adjective — it describes nouns, not actions.
questions.retry_hint: The underlined word is meant to tell you HOW the volunteer PRUNED the bushes - and 'pruned' is an action verb. Ask: do we describe an action with an adjective, or with an adverb? Which ending turns one into the other?

questions.trap_type: Students add -s to 'leaf', producing 'leafs'. Words ending in -f often change to -ves in the plural.
questions.learning_tip: 'Leaf' follows the -f → -ves rule: leaf → LEAVES. Same pattern: knife → knives, half → halves, loaf → loaves.
questions.retry_hint: LEAFS is the trap. Ask: how do you write more than one knife, or more than one wolf? Nouns ending in -f or -fe change that ending before the -s; they do not simply take one.

questions.trap_type: Students insert an extra 'c' in 'sprinkling', writing 'sprinckling'. The word comes from 'sprinkle' + -ing (drop silent e).
questions.learning_tip: 'Sprinkle' ends in silent -e: drop -e and add -ing → SPRINKLING. No extra 'c'. Spell it: s-p-r-i-n-k-l-i-n-g.
questions.retry_hint: SPRINCKLING has one letter too many. Ask: how do you spell the base verb 'sprinkle' - is there a c anywhere in it? Drop the silent -e, add -ing, and change nothing else.

questions.trap_type: 'The sunflowers' is plural. Students write 'was' (singular).
questions.learning_tip: 'The sunflowers' = plural → WERE all facing east. WAS is only for singular subjects.
questions.retry_hint: Find the subject: THE SUNFLOWERS, and they are ALL FACING EAST - many flowers, not one. Ask: does a plural subject take the singular past verb, or the plural one? Do not match the verb to the nearest word.

questions.trap_type: Students write a plain plural and leave out the apostrophe that shows ownership.
questions.learning_tip: The toolshed BELONGS TO the gardeners -> GARDENERS' toolshed (apostrophe after the -s for a plural). Singular: gardener's.
questions.retry_hint: The TOOLSHED belongs to the gardeners, and there is more than one of them. Ask: does a plain -s show ownership, or only make a plural? Where does the apostrophe go when the owners are many?

E.passage: Last Saturday, we visited a community garden near the market. A volunteer pruned the rose bushes careful (1), removing all the dead branches near the base. We also noticed that some of the leafs (2) were eaten by insects. Another volunteer began sprinckling (3) water gently over the young seedlings in the shade house. By midday, the sunflowers was (4) all facing east, tracking the movement of the sun. We were shown the gardeners (5) toolshed, which was filled with rakes, hoses and bags of fertiliser.

questions.sentence_a: She waters her plants every day.
questions.sentence_b: She will have a beautiful garden in spring.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'If'.
questions.model_answer: If she waters her plants every day, she will have a beautiful garden in spring.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'If she will water her plants every day, she will have a beautiful garden' — incorrectly adding 'will' in the 'if' clause.
questions.learning_tip: Conditional: IF + simple present, simple future. If she WATERS her plants, she WILL HAVE a beautiful garden. Never 'will' in the 'if' clause.
questions.retry_hint: 'If' introduces the condition - SHE WATERS HER PLANTS EVERY DAY - and the result follows in the other half. Ask: may you put 'will' inside the 'if' half, or must that half stay in the simple present?

questions.sentence_a: The gardener planted a row of sunflowers.
questions.sentence_b: The sunflowers brighten up the whole neighbourhood.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using the relative pronoun 'which'.
questions.model_answer: The gardener planted a row of sunflowers, which brighten up the whole neighbourhood.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'The gardener planted a row of sunflowers which they brighten up the neighbourhood' — adding 'they' after 'which'.
questions.learning_tip: Use 'which' to add information about a THING. The gardener planted sunflowers, WHICH brighten up the neighbourhood. Do NOT add 'they' after 'which'.
questions.retry_hint: Both sentences talk about the same SUNFLOWERS, so name them once and let 'which' take over the second mention. Ask: after 'which', do you still need the word 'they'? And which punctuation mark holds the extra information?

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
When the principal of Greenfield Primary announced that an unused rooftop would be turned into a garden, the students were curious but unconvinced. 'What is the point of growing vegetables at school?' one student asked.

By the end of the year, those same students could not imagine school without it.

The project began in January with the students digging compost into large planters and sowing seeds of spinach, chilli and cherry tomatoes. At first, progress was slow and some seeds did not sprout at all. But by March, the rooftop had green shoots pushing upward from every planter.

The garden changed the way many students thought about food. Before the project, several admitted they had never thought about where vegetables came from. After growing them, they paid more attention to what they ate and wasted far less food at lunch.

The garden also brought students together. Children from different classes worked side by side during gardening sessions, learning each other's names. A boy named Darren, who had previously kept to himself, became one of the most active gardeners. By the end of the year, he made three close friends through the garden.

In December, the students organised a small harvest festival. They cooked a simple vegetable soup using everything they grew, and invited parents and teachers to join them.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 1 has the same meaning as 'full of enthusiasm and interest'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Curious' = wanting to know; 'confused' = not understanding; 'satisfied' = content. EAGER = full of enthusiasm and keen to do something.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: EAGER = showing keenness and enthusiasm. The students were EAGER = they were enthusiastic and ready to begin. Look for word clues: 'full of enthusiasm' = EAGER.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 3, what does 'this' refer to in 'None of them expected this'?

options.1: The arrival of the gardening tools
options.2: That their plants would grow so quickly and produce real vegetables to eat
options.3: The instruction to water the plants every day
options.4: That Darren would become interested in the garden

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking 'this' = the tools. But the paragraph shows surprise at the actual results — real food growing from their work.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: PRONOUN REFERENCE: 'THIS' refers to the nearest previous idea. In paragraph 3, 'this' = the fact that their plants actually GREW and produced real vegetables — an unexpected outcome.

mcq_questions.stem: What does Darren's story in paragraph 5 suggest about the garden's effect on students?

options.1: The garden was only useful for students who were already interested in nature.
options.2: The garden helped students who struggled academically improve their grades.
options.3: The garden could bring out new strengths in students who seemed quiet or withdrawn.
options.4: The garden was most useful for teaching students how to cook.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 2 thinking the garden helped grades. The passage focuses on Darren's social transformation, not academics.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: INFERENCE: Darren 'kept to himself' (shy/withdrawn) but became 'one of the most active gardeners' (social, engaged). The garden BROUGHT OUT NEW STRENGTHS in a quiet student.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 1, is it True or False that the students immediately knew how to grow vegetables when the project started? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The passage says the students were eager but curious — they had not grown vegetables before and needed to learn from scratch.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'True, they were eager.' Being eager is not the same as already knowing how.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: EAGER = wanting to try. 'Curious' = wanting to find out. Both words show the students did NOT already know — they were learning for the first time. Answer is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: What did the students learn about food from growing their own vegetables?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: They learned where food comes from and began to pay more attention to what they ate.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students describe only the effect without identifying the cause, or give only general statements.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 4: CAUSE = they GREW the vegetables themselves and understood where food comes from. EFFECT = they paid more attention to what they ate and WASTED FAR LESS FOOD. Link cause to effect clearly.

open_ended_questions.stem: How did the garden change Darren? Give TWO specific details from the passage.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) Darren had previously kept to himself, but the garden made him one of the most active gardeners. (ii) By the end of the year, he made three close friends through the garden.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'he became happier' without referencing specific details from the passage.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 5: (1) he went from 'keeping to himself' to being one of the MOST ACTIVE gardeners; (2) he made THREE CLOSE FRIENDS through gardening. Both details are explicit.

open_ended_questions.stem: How did the students use the vegetables from the garden in December?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: They cooked a simple vegetable soup using everything from the garden and invited parents and teachers to join them.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'they had a celebration' without describing what they did with the vegetables.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 6: they cooked VEGETABLE SOUP using everything from the garden and invited PARENTS and teachers to join them at the harvest festival.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on the passage, describe TWO character traits of the students who joined the gardening club. Give evidence for each.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) PERSISTENT: the students kept tending their plants through all seasons — from planting in January to harvesting in December — showing they did not give up even when progress was slow. (ii) CARING: they used their harvest to cook soup for parents and teachers, showing they wanted to share the results of their work with others.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'hardworking and kind' without precise traits or evidence. Name the trait and then give specific textual evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: TRAIT INFERENCE: Name the trait + give evidence from the passage. PERSISTENT = kept going for a full year. CARING = cooked for others. Trait + Evidence = full marks.

questions.stem: The princess ________ peacefully for one hundred years until the prince arrived at the castle.
questions.trap_type: 'Entered', 'avoided' and 'refused' all need an object after them, but the blank is followed by PEACEFULLY. Only 'slumbered' can stand alone with an adverb.
questions.learning_tip: SLUMBERED = slept deeply and peacefully, often for a long time. In fairy tales, enchanted characters SLUMBER for many years.
questions.retry_hint: The princess sleeps PEACEFULLY FOR ONE HUNDRED YEARS, and the blank is followed by that adverb, not by an object. Ask: which verb means to sleep deeply for a long time? 'Avoided' and 'refused' are the opposite of sleeping.

questions.stem: The dragon's roar echoed through the valley, as ________ as rolling thunder across a stormy sky.
questions.trap_type: 'Quiet' and 'soft' are opposites of thunder's sound. 'Swift' = fast, not relating to sound. LOUD = making a great amount of sound.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! The dragon's roar was AS LOUD AS rolling thunder = comparing its sound to a thunderstorm. Similes always use 'as ... as' to compare two different things directly.
questions.retry_hint: The roar ECHOED THROUGH THE VALLEY and is compared to ROLLING THUNDER. Ask: is thunder soft and gentle, or does it fill the whole sky with sound? 'Swift' is about speed, not about sound at all.

questions.stem: The brave knight ________ the fierce dragon with a sharp sword to rescue the village.
questions.trap_type: 'Fled from' means ran away from; 'admired' is a positive feeling; 'invited' is friendly. Only 'defeated' = overcame in battle.
questions.learning_tip: DEFEATED = overcame an opponent in a fight or contest. The knight DEFEATED the dragon = won the battle against it.
questions.retry_hint: The knight is BRAVE, he carries A SHARP SWORD, and he manages to RESCUE THE VILLAGE. Ask: which verb means to beat an enemy in battle? 'Fled from' means ran away, and 'invited' is friendly.

questions.stem: The young knight lived ________ after defeating the dragon and rescuing the village.

options.4: at the drop of a hat

questions.trap_type: 'Out of the blue' = unexpectedly; 'under the weather' = feeling ill; 'at the drop of a hat' = immediately. HAPPILY EVER AFTER = a fairy tale ending of permanent happiness.
questions.learning_tip: IDIOM: HAPPILY EVER AFTER = a life of permanent happiness, especially at the end of a fairy tale. 'He lived HAPPILY EVER AFTER' = he was happy for the rest of his life. This idiom comes from classic fairy tales!
questions.retry_hint: The knight has finished DEFEATING THE DRAGON and RESCUING THE VILLAGE - this is how fairy tales close. Ask: which idiom names an ending of lasting joy? 'Under the weather' means ill; 'out of the blue' means unexpectedly.

questions.stem: The young hero had to ________ the dragon's lair and rescue the princess before sunrise.
questions.trap_type: 'Run away from' = flee; 'give up on' = stop trying; 'look up to' = admire. BREAK INTO = enter a place by force.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: BREAK INTO = enter a place by force or without permission. The hero had to BREAK INTO the lair = he forced his way in. BREAK + INTO work together — never separate them!
questions.retry_hint: The hero must get inside THE DRAGON'S LAIR to RESCUE THE PRINCESS, and no dragon opens its door politely. Ask: which phrasal verb means to enter a place by force? 'Look up to' means admire; 'give up on' means stop trying.

questions.stem: Nobody in the fairy tale ________ that the old woman at the door is actually a powerful enchantress.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'know' thinking 'nobody in the fairy tale' = many people. NOBODY = singular → verb+S in present tense.
questions.learning_tip: NOBODY / EVERYONE / SOMEONE = Singular! Always use verb+S in present tense. Nobody KNOWS = add -S. 'Nobody know' is WRONG. Singular indefinite pronouns take singular verbs.
questions.retry_hint: The subject is NOBODY, not the people in the tale. Words like nobody act like ONE person, even when they feel like many. Ask: in the present tense, does a singular subject take the plain verb, or the verb ending in -s?

questions.stem: The miller's daughter ________ the strange little man's riddle and broke the curse.
questions.trap_type: The story is set in the past. 'Solve' is regular: solve → solved.
questions.learning_tip: The fairy tale is told in the past. 'Solve' is regular: solve → SOLVED. She SOLVED the riddle = completed the action in the past.
questions.retry_hint: The second half is finished and past: she BROKE THE CURSE. Ask: which tense must the first verb share with it? 'Solve' is a regular verb, so which ending does it take? A present form cannot sit beside 'broke'.

questions.stem: The three bears ________ their porridge when Goldilocks crept into their cottage.
questions.trap_type: 'Goldilocks crept into the cottage' is the sudden interrupting event. The bears were already eating = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: Goldilocks CREPT IN = sudden past event. The bears were already eating at that moment = WERE EATING (ongoing background).
questions.retry_hint: GOLDILOCKS CREPT INTO THEIR COTTAGE - a sudden event that interrupted the bears. Ask: which choice shows an action already in progress in the past? A plain past verb would report only a finished meal.

questions.stem: The fairy tale ________ enjoyed by generations of children all over the world for many centuries.
questions.trap_type: 'For many centuries' + implied continuation to the present = present perfect. 'The fairy tale' = singular → has been.
questions.learning_tip: 'For many centuries' (up to now) = present perfect. 'The fairy tale' = singular → HAS BEEN enjoyed. The enjoyment began long ago and continues.
questions.retry_hint: FOR MANY CENTURIES reaches from long ago right up to today, and THE FAIRY TALE is one single thing. Ask: which choice shows something that began in the past and still goes on? A plain past form would close the story off.

questions.stem: The dragon lives in that cave over there, ________ it?
questions.trap_type: Main clause is positive present simple ('lives') → negative tag. 'The dragon lives' = singular present simple → auxiliary 'does'. Negative tag = doesn't.
questions.learning_tip: Question tag for positive simple present singular: [positive] + DOESN'T + subject? The dragon LIVES there, DOESN'T it? Positive → negative tag; present simple → does.
questions.retry_hint: The statement is positive and in the simple present: THE DRAGON LIVES IN THAT CAVE. Ask: after a positive statement, must the tag turn negative? And which helping verb stands in for a plain present verb with one subject?

questions.stem: The children were not frightened by the giant's roar, ________ they?
questions.trap_type: Main clause is NEGATIVE past ('were not') → question tag must be POSITIVE. 'They were not' → positive tag = were they.
questions.learning_tip: Question tag for negative past: [negative statement] + WERE + subject? The children WERE NOT frightened, WERE they? Negative statement → positive tag; past 'were' → 'were'.
questions.retry_hint: Look at the statement: it contains the word NOT, so it is negative, and its verb is in the past. Ask: after a negative statement, does the tag turn positive or stay negative? The tag must reuse the statement's own verb.

questions.stem: The enchanted castle ________ deep in the forest by the wandering prince.
questions.trap_type: The castle did not discover itself. Past passive = was discovered.
questions.learning_tip: The castle was the receiver of the action. Past passive = WAS DISCOVERED. Passive = was/were + past participle.
questions.retry_hint: The CASTLE could not find itself: BY THE WANDERING PRINCE tells you who did it, and the castle simply received the action. Ask: which choice is passive and set in the past?

questions.stem: The fairy godmother told Cinderella ________ home before the clock struck midnight.
questions.trap_type: 'Told someone to do something' = reported speech: told + object + to + base verb.
questions.learning_tip: 'Told Cinderella TO + base verb': told Cinderella TO RETURN home before midnight.
questions.retry_hint: TOLD CINDERELLA = a reported command. Ask: after 'told + person', which form follows - the plain verb, the -ing form, the past form, or 'to' + verb? The rule never changes, whoever is being told.

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Reflexive pronouns)

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The queen looked at (1)________ in the magic mirror and asked who was the fairest in the land.' Signal: subject = 'the queen' (female singular) + reflexive object of 'looked at' = HERSELF. The queen looked at her own reflection.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'herself'. The hero is male, and 'he was brave' confirms it. TELL ONESELF = say something in your own head.
questions.learning_tip: HIMSELF = the reflexive pronoun for he. The hero told HIMSELF = the speaker and the listener are the same man.
questions.retry_hint: THE HERO is speaking, and the words 'HE WAS BRAVE' show that the speaker and the listener are the same person. Ask: which reflexive pronoun matches a single male? Match it to the hero, not to the princess.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The prince proved (2)________ worthy of the kingdom by completing the three tasks.' Signal: subject = 'the prince' (male singular) + reflexive object of 'proved' = HIMSELF. The prince proved his own worth.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'himself'. THE PRINCESS is one female, and she locked her own person in.
questions.learning_tip: HERSELF = the reflexive pronoun for she. She locked HERSELF in = she did it to her own person.
questions.retry_hint: THE PRINCESS is one female, and she LOCKED the door on her own person. Ask: which reflexive pronoun matches 'she'? 'Itself' belongs to things, and 'himself' belongs to one male.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The enchanted broom moved (3)________, sweeping the floor without anyone holding it.' Signal: subject = 'the broom' (thing/neuter singular) + reflexive = ITSELF. The broom moved by its own power.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'himself'. The dragon is an animal, not a man or a woman.
questions.learning_tip: ITSELF = the reflexive pronoun for it (a thing or an animal). The dragon stretched ITSELF out.
questions.retry_hint: THE DRAGON is an animal, neither a man nor a woman, and it STRETCHED its own body OUT on the treasure. Ask: which reflexive pronoun matches a single thing or creature?

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The three little pigs built their houses (4)________ without any help from their mother.' Signal: subject = 'the three little pigs' (plural, third person) + reflexive of 'built' = THEMSELVES. They did the building on their own.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'ourselves'. THE VILLAGERS are several people, and the storyteller is not talking about his own group here.
questions.learning_tip: THEMSELVES = the reflexive pronoun for they. The villagers hid THEMSELVES = they hid their own bodies.
questions.retry_hint: THE FRIGHTENED VILLAGERS are several people, and the storyteller is not talking about his own group here. Ask: which reflexive pronoun matches 'they'? 'Ourselves' would put the speaker inside the group.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'I thought to (5)________, this wolf does not seem as frightening as the stories say.' Signal: subject = 'I' (first person singular) + reflexive of 'thought to' = MYSELF. 'I thought to myself' = an internal private thought.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'yourself'. The king is speaking to HIS KNIGHTS - more than one listener.
questions.learning_tip: YOURSELVES = the reflexive pronoun for 'you' when 'you' means two or more people. 'Prepare YOURSELVES!' is said to a group.
questions.retry_hint: The king is speaking TO HIS KNIGHTS - count them: more than one listener. Ask: which reflexive pronoun matches 'you' when 'you' means a whole group? The singular form would fit only one knight.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The old wizard said to the young apprentice, "You must believe in (6)________ if you wish to master magic."' Signal: subject of the embedded clause = 'you' (second person singular) + reflexive = YOURSELF.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'yourselves'. Here the king turns to THE YOUNGEST KNIGHT alone - only one listener.
questions.learning_tip: YOURSELF = the reflexive pronoun for 'you' when 'you' is one person. Count the listeners before you choose.
questions.retry_hint: Now the king turns TO THE YOUNGEST KNIGHT alone: 'DO NOT BLAME ___ IF YOU FEEL AFRAID.' Ask: which reflexive pronoun matches 'you' when only one person is being spoken to?

questions.context_check: Passage: 'We found (7)________ lost deep inside the enchanted forest with no path home.' Signal: subject = 'we' (first person plural) + reflexive of 'found' = OURSELVES. We discovered our own situation.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'himself', matching the king from outside the speech marks. But the king says 'I', so the pronoun must match 'I'.
questions.learning_tip: MYSELF = the reflexive pronoun for I. 'I will ride out with you MYSELF' = the speaker in person, nobody else.
questions.retry_hint: Inside the speech marks the king says 'I WILL RIDE OUT WITH YOU ___' - so the subject is I, not 'the king'. Ask: which reflexive pronoun matches 'I'? 'Himself' would be the storyteller's word, never the king's own.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The fairy said, "Now go and enjoy (8)________ at the ball before midnight strikes."' Signal: subject of the command = 'you' (second person plural — addressed to Cinderella and her helpers together) + reflexive = YOURSELVES.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'themselves'. The narrator says WE VILLAGERS, so the speaker belongs to the group.
questions.learning_tip: OURSELVES = the reflexive pronoun for we. We promised OURSELVES = the promise is made by us, to us.
questions.retry_hint: WE VILLAGERS PROMISED - the speaker is standing inside that group. Ask: which reflexive pronoun matches 'we'? 'Themselves' would point at other people, away from the speaker.

C.passage: In the fairy tale, the hero told (1)________ that he was brave enough to face the dragon alone. The princess locked (2)________ in the tower and refused to cry. The dragon stretched (3)________ out on the pile of treasure and fell asleep. The frightened villagers hid (4)________ in the forest until the beast had flown away. The king said to his knights, 'Prepare (5)________ for battle!' Then he turned to the youngest knight and added, 'Do not blame (6)________ if you feel afraid.' 'I will ride out with you (7)________,' the king promised, 'for a king must share the danger.' At last the beast was gone, and we villagers promised (8)________ that we would never forget that day.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: Fairy tales often begin with a world that is (1)________ - filled with magic, talking creatures and impossible things. Many feature a humble hero who is (2)________, meaning ordinary and not gifted with special powers. When the hero makes a brave choice, a wish may be (3)________ by a fairy or a spirit. Evil characters who have (4)________ into thin air are often defeated by love or honesty. Each of these old stories has become a (5)________ - a tale so widely known and retold that everyone recognises it by name.

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'wicked'. The clue is 'FILLED WITH MAGIC, talking creatures and impossible things'.
questions.learning_tip: ENCHANTED = under a magic spell, full of magic. An ENCHANTED forest is a place where ordinary rules do not apply.
questions.retry_hint: The dash explains it: FILLED WITH MAGIC, TALKING CREATURES AND IMPOSSIBLE THINGS. Ask: which box word means 'under a magic spell'? 'Wicked' describes evil, and 'curse' is a noun, not a describing word.

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'disguised'. The clue is 'ORDINARY and NOT GIFTED WITH SPECIAL POWERS' - an everyday human being.
questions.learning_tip: MORTAL = an ordinary human, one who can be hurt and who will one day die, unlike gods and magical beings.
questions.retry_hint: The comma explains it: ORDINARY AND NOT GIFTED WITH SPECIAL POWERS. Ask: which box word names an everyday human being, one who can be hurt and who will one day die? 'Disguised' only means wearing a false appearance.

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'enchanted'. The blank follows 'a wish may be', so it must be a past participle, and a wish is something you GIVE.
questions.learning_tip: GRANTED = given or allowed. A fairy GRANTS a wish = she makes it come true.
questions.retry_hint: The blank follows A WISH MAY BE, so it must be a past participle, and a wish is something a FAIRY OR A SPIRIT gives you. Ask: which box word means 'given', or 'made to come true'?

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'disguised'. The clue is INTO THIN AIR - the characters are gone completely, not merely hidden behind a mask.
questions.learning_tip: VANISHED = disappeared suddenly and completely, leaving no trace at all.
questions.retry_hint: INTO THIN AIR - the villains are gone completely, not merely hiding behind a mask. Ask: which box word means to disappear all at once, leaving no trace? 'Disguised' only changes how someone looks.

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'curse'. The blank follows 'has become a', and the clue is 'a TALE so widely KNOWN AND RETOLD'.
questions.learning_tip: A LEGEND = an old story told again and again for generations until everybody knows it.
questions.retry_hint: The dash defines it: A TALE SO WIDELY KNOWN AND RETOLD that everyone recognises it by name. Ask: which box word names such an old and famous story? 'Curse' is a spell, not a story.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.trap_type: Students write 'fierce' (adjective) after the action verb 'roared'. A verb needs an adverb to describe how the action was done.
questions.learning_tip: After an action verb (roared), use an ADVERB: roared FIERCELY. 'Fierce' is an adjective — it describes nouns, not actions.
questions.retry_hint: The underlined word is meant to tell you HOW the dragon ROARED - and 'roared' is an action verb. Ask: does an action take an adjective, or an adverb? Which ending turns one into the other?

questions.trap_type: Students add -es to 'ox', producing 'oxes'. 'Ox' has a completely irregular plural form.
questions.learning_tip: 'Ox' has an irregular plural: ox → OXEN. Never write 'oxes'. Other irregular plurals: child → children, goose → geese.
questions.retry_hint: The farmer has TWO of them, so the noun must be plural - but OXES is not how English does it. Ask: how do you write more than one child, or more than one goose? Some plurals change their shape instead of adding -s.

questions.error_type: Spelling — -ing rule: silent -e is dropped before -ing
questions.trap_type: Students keep the final -e when adding -ing to 'make', producing 'makeing'. Drop the silent -e before adding -ing.
questions.learning_tip: 'Make' ends in silent -e: drop the -e before adding -ing → MAKING. Same rule: write → writing, ride → riding, give → giving.
questions.retry_hint: MAKEING keeps a letter it ought to drop. Ask: 'make' ends in a silent -e, so when you add -ing, does that -e stay or go? Compare: ride becomes riding, give becomes giving.

questions.trap_type: 'The villagers' is plural. Students write 'was' (singular).
questions.learning_tip: 'The villagers' = plural → WERE frightened. WAS is only for singular subjects.
questions.retry_hint: Find the subject: THE VILLAGERS - many people, and NOBODY DARED LEAVE their homes. Ask: does a plural subject take the singular past verb, or the plural one? Do not match the verb to the nearest word alone.

questions.trap_type: Students write a plain plural and leave out the apostrophe that shows ownership.
questions.learning_tip: The prayers BELONG TO the neighbours -> NEIGHBOURS' prayers (apostrophe after the -s for a plural). Singular: neighbour's.
questions.retry_hint: The PRAYERS belong to the neighbours, and there is more than one neighbour. Ask: does a plain -s show ownership, or only make a plural? Where does the apostrophe go when the owners are many?

E.passage: Once upon a time, a dragon lived on a hill above a small village. Every night, it roared fierce (1) and blew flames into the sky. The farmer who lived nearest to the hill used his two oxes (2) to plough the fields far away from the dragon. A travelling blacksmith began makeing (3) a special suit of armour to protect the village hero. The villagers was (4) so frightened that nobody dared leave their homes after dark. At last, the neighbours (5) prayers were answered when the hero returned from the lair in triumph, and peace returned to the valley.

questions.sentence_a: The princess touched the spindle.
questions.sentence_b: She immediately fell into a deep sleep.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'As soon as'.
questions.model_answer: As soon as the princess touched the spindle, she immediately fell into a deep sleep.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'The princess touched the spindle as soon as she immediately fell' — reversing the order.
questions.learning_tip: AS SOON AS + [the trigger], [the immediate result]. AS SOON AS the princess TOUCHED the spindle, she FELL into a deep sleep. The trigger comes after 'as soon as'.
questions.retry_hint: 'As soon as' must stand in front of the trigger - the event that happened FIRST. Ask: which came first, THE PRINCESS TOUCHED THE SPINDLE, or the deep sleep? The other half follows after a comma.

questions.sentence_a: Jack climbed the beanstalk.
questions.sentence_b: The beanstalk reached all the way up to the giant's castle.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using the relative pronoun 'which'.
questions.model_answer: Jack climbed the beanstalk, which reached all the way up to the giant's castle.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'Jack climbed the beanstalk which it reached all the way up to the giant's castle' — adding 'it' after 'which'.
questions.learning_tip: Use 'which' to add information about a THING. Jack climbed the beanstalk, WHICH reached up to the giant's castle. Do NOT add 'it' after 'which'.
questions.retry_hint: Both sentences name THE BEANSTALK, so mention it once and let 'which' stand in for the second mention. Ask: after 'which', do you still need the word 'it'? And where does the comma belong?

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
Long ago, a poor fisherman caught a golden fish in his net. The fish spoke in a clear, calm voice. 'Release me,' it said, 'and I will grant you one wish.'

The fisherman thought carefully. His family needed many things — a better boat, a larger house, enough food for winter. But instead, he made a simple request. 'I wish for my daughter to be healed,' he said, 'for she has been unwell for three years.'

The golden fish was quiet for a moment. Then it said, 'Your wish is granted.' The fish slipped back into the sea and disappeared.

When the fisherman returned home, his daughter was sitting up in bed, her cheeks pink and her eyes bright. She smiled when she saw him and said she felt better since noon.

The fisherman's neighbours were astonished. They asked him how he had managed it. He told them about the golden fish.

'You wasted the wish!' one neighbour said. 'You could have asked for gold, or a palace!'

The fisherman simply shook his head. He had no regrets.

Years later, when his daughter grew up to be a kind and generous woman, everyone in the village agreed that the fisherman made the wisest choice of all.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 2 has the same meaning as 'shining with a golden light'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Enormous' = very large; 'trembling' = shaking; 'ancient' = very old. GLEAMING = shining with a steady golden or silver light.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: GLEAMING = shining brightly with a soft, golden light. The fish was GLEAMING = it gave off a beautiful golden glow. GLEAM = shine; GLEAMING = currently shining.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 3, what does 'it' refer to in 'he knew it was the right choice'?

options.2: His decision to wish for his daughter's health rather than wealth
options.3: The fishing rod he used to catch the fish

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking 'it' = the fish. But 'it' refers to the fisherman's decision — the choice he made.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: PRONOUN REFERENCE: 'IT' refers to the fisherman's DECISION — the choice he made to wish for his daughter's health. The paragraph says 'he thought for a long time, then he knew IT was the right choice.' IT = his decision.

mcq_questions.stem: Why did the neighbours say the fisherman had wasted his wish?

options.1: Because they thought he should have wished for more fish.
options.2: Because they believed gold and palaces were more valuable than a person's health.
options.3: Because they did not know his daughter was ill.
options.4: Because they thought the golden fish would grant more wishes later.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking they wanted more fish. The passage says they suggested gold or a palace — material things.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph text: neighbours said 'he could have asked for GOLD or a PALACE.' They valued material wealth over health — showing they measured the wish's worth by money, not love.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 1, is it True or False that the fisherman caught the golden fish on purpose? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The passage says the fisherman cast his net as usual and was surprised when something golden appeared — he did not go looking for a magical fish.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'True, he caught it.' He caught it by accident, not on purpose.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: The fisherman cast his net 'as usual' = his normal routine. He was SURPRISED when the golden fish appeared. If he planned it, the passage would say so. Answer is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: What did the fisherman's neighbours say when they heard about the wish he made?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: They said he had wasted the wish and that he could have asked for gold or a palace.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'they were surprised' without quoting what they actually said.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 6: 'You WASTED the wish! You could have asked for GOLD, or a palace!' Quote the specific reaction, not just describe it.

open_ended_questions.stem: What was the CAUSE of the daughter's recovery, and what was the EFFECT it had on the fisherman when he returned home?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: CAUSE: The golden fish granted the fisherman's wish for his daughter to be healed. EFFECT: When the fisherman returned home, his daughter was sitting up in bed with pink cheeks and bright eyes, smiling — she had recovered fully.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students describe only the daughter's recovery without explaining what caused it.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: CAUSE = the golden fish GRANTED the wish. EFFECT = the daughter was SITTING UP in bed, cheeks pink, eyes bright, smiling. Link the cause (the wish) clearly to the effect (her recovery).

open_ended_questions.stem: Find ONE phrase from the last paragraph that shows the fisherman was satisfied with his decision.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: 'He had no regrets.'
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students quote from an earlier paragraph about the wish itself instead of the end of the passage.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 7: 'He had NO REGRETS.' This phrase directly tells us he was completely satisfied with the choice he made.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on his actions in the passage, describe TWO character traits of the fisherman with evidence from the passage.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) SELFLESS: when given a rare wish, the fisherman chose his daughter's health over wealth for himself — showing he put others' needs before his own. (ii) WISE: he ignored his neighbours' mocking and stayed firm in his decision, knowing that health and love matter more than gold.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'kind and brave' without precise traits or evidence from the passage.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: TRAIT INFERENCE: Name the trait + give evidence. SELFLESS = chose daughter's health over gold. WISE = ignored mockers and held firm. Trait + Evidence from passage = full marks.

questions.stem: The boy ________ the notice board for any message about his missing bicycle but found nothing.
questions.trap_type: 'Ignored' means paid no attention; 'decorated' means added ornaments; 'removed' means took away. Only 'scanned' = looked quickly across a surface to find something specific.
questions.learning_tip: SCANNED = looked quickly across something to find specific information. He SCANNED the notice board = looked rapidly for any relevant message.
questions.retry_hint: He is hunting for ANY MESSAGE ABOUT HIS MISSING BICYCLE, and his eyes sweep the whole NOTICE BOARD. Ask: which verb means to look rapidly across a surface for one piece of information? 'Removed' and 'decorated' change the board, not read it.

questions.stem: The lost kitten ________ under the staircase for two days before a neighbour found it.
questions.trap_type: 'Paraded' means walked proudly; 'galloped' = ran fast; 'scattered' = spread in different directions. Only 'huddled' = crouched close together for warmth or safety.
questions.learning_tip: HUDDLED = crouched or pressed close together in a small space, often for warmth or safety. The lost kitten HUDDLED under the stairs = curled up tightly in a small space.
questions.retry_hint: The kitten was LOST, alone UNDER THE STAIRCASE, and it stayed there FOR TWO DAYS. Ask: which verb shows a small animal curling up tightly in one spot for warmth and safety? 'Galloped' and 'paraded' would take it away from that spot.

questions.stem: Finding the owner of a lost wallet in a crowded city is like looking for a ________ — almost impossible without a clue.
questions.trap_type: 'A piece of cake' = something easy (opposite meaning); 'fish in water' = comfortable; 'drop in the ocean' = a tiny amount. NEEDLE IN A HAYSTACK = something almost impossible to find.
questions.learning_tip: IDIOM: A NEEDLE IN A HAYSTACK = something extremely difficult to find because it is hidden among many other things. Finding a lost owner is 'like A NEEDLE IN A HAYSTACK' = almost impossible. Idioms cannot be understood word by word!
questions.retry_hint: The dash explains the idiom: the search is ALMOST IMPOSSIBLE, because the CROWDED CITY hides the owner among millions. Ask: which idiom means something so tiny and so buried that you can hardly ever spot it? 'Piece of cake' means easy - the opposite.

questions.stem: The lost puppy's face was as ________ as a wilted flower — tired, drooping and in need of care.
questions.trap_type: 'Fierce' = aggressive; 'cheerful' = happy (opposite); 'alert' = watchful. FORLORN = appearing sad and abandoned.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! The puppy's face was AS FORLORN AS a wilted flower = comparing its sad, drooping look to a flower that has not been watered. FORLORN = pitifully sad and lonely.
questions.retry_hint: The dash tells you exactly how the face looked: TIRED, DROOPING AND IN NEED OF CARE, like a WILTED FLOWER. Ask: does that face look sad and abandoned, or fierce, or cheerful? Match the adjective to the wilted flower.

questions.stem: After finding the wallet on the bus, the honest girl decided to ________ it at the nearest police station.
questions.trap_type: 'Throw away' = discard; 'run off with' = steal; 'leave behind' = abandon. HAND IN = give something to someone in authority.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: HAND IN = give something to a person in authority (teacher, police, lost property office). She HANDED IN the wallet = she gave it to the police. HAND + IN work together — this means to submit or surrender something officially.
questions.retry_hint: The HONEST girl is giving the wallet up officially, at the NEAREST POLICE STATION. Ask: which phrasal verb means giving something you found over to someone with authority? 'Throw away' and 'run off with' are what a dishonest person would do.

questions.stem: Someone in this class ________ a water bottle in the canteen every single week.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'leave' thinking 'someone in class' = many people. SOMEONE = singular → verb+S in present tense.
questions.learning_tip: SOMEONE / EVERYONE / NOBODY / ANYONE = Singular! Always use verb+S. Someone LEAVES = add -S. 'Someone leave' is WRONG. Singular indefinite pronouns always take singular present-tense verbs.
questions.retry_hint: The subject is SOMEONE, not the whole CLASS. Words like someone, everyone and nobody act like ONE person. Ask: in the present tense, does a singular subject take the plain verb, or the verb ending in -s?

questions.stem: Ravi ________ his school pass somewhere between the canteen and the library last Thursday.
questions.trap_type: 'Last Thursday' = past. 'Lose' is irregular: lose → lost.
questions.learning_tip: 'Lose' is irregular: lose → LOST. 'Last Thursday' = past → LOST his school pass.
questions.retry_hint: LAST THURSDAY is finished time, so the verb must be past. Ask: what is the past form of this verb? Careful - it is irregular, so an -ed ending will not work; the vowel itself changes.

questions.stem: The teacher ________ the classroom for the missing scissors when a student found them in her own bag.
questions.trap_type: 'A student found them in her bag' is the sudden interrupting event. The teacher was already searching = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: The student FOUND them = sudden past event. The teacher was already searching at that moment = WAS SEARCHING (ongoing background).
questions.retry_hint: A STUDENT FOUND THEM suddenly, cutting across something already going on. Ask: which choice shows an action still in progress at that past moment? A plain past verb would report only a finished job.

questions.stem: The lost wallet ________ to the owner by a kind student who found it in the school field.
questions.trap_type: The wallet did not return itself — the student returned it. Past passive = was returned.
questions.learning_tip: The wallet was the receiver of the action. Past passive = WAS RETURNED. Passive = was/were + past participle.
questions.retry_hint: The WALLET did not do the action itself - A KIND STUDENT WHO FOUND IT did. Ask: which choice puts the subject on the receiving end, and sets it in the past? Passive = a form of 'be' + the past participle.

questions.stem: The library book was not where you left it, ________ it?
questions.trap_type: Main clause is NEGATIVE past ('was not') → question tag must be POSITIVE. 'Was not' → positive tag = was.
questions.learning_tip: Question tag for negative past: [negative statement] + WAS + subject? The book WAS NOT there, WAS it? Negative → positive tag; past 'was' → 'was'.
questions.retry_hint: Read the statement first: it is negative and it is set in the past ('not where you left it'). Ask: after a negative statement, does the tag turn positive or stay negative? And must the tag keep the tense of the statement?

questions.stem: You have handed in all the found items to the general office, ________ you?
questions.trap_type: Main clause is positive present perfect ('have handed') → negative tag. 'You have' → negative tag = haven't you.
questions.learning_tip: Question tag for positive present perfect: [positive] + HAVEN'T + subject? 'You HAVE handed in the items, HAVEN'T you?' Positive → negative tag; 'have' → 'haven't'.
questions.retry_hint: The statement is positive and it uses HAVE HANDED - a present perfect. Ask: after a positive statement, does the tag flip to negative or stay positive? The tag repeats the same helping verb; it never borrows 'did'.

questions.stem: There ________ no trace of the missing child's backpack anywhere near the playground when the search party arrived last night.
questions.trap_type: 'No trace' = a singular uncountable idea, and 'when the search party arrived last night' fixes the time in the past. Students write 'were' (plural) or 'is' (present).
questions.learning_tip: 'No trace' = singular uncountable concept. Past event → THERE WAS no trace of the backpack.
questions.retry_hint: 'NO TRACE' names one single thing, not many, and THE SEARCH PARTY ARRIVED LAST NIGHT fixes the time in the past. Ask: does a singular subject take a present form, or the past one? 'Were' would need a plural.

questions.stem: The general office assistant told students ________ their names and class when handing in lost items.
questions.trap_type: 'Told someone to do something' = reported speech: told + object + to + base verb.
questions.learning_tip: 'Told students TO + base verb': told students TO WRITE their names and class on a slip before handing in items.
questions.retry_hint: TOLD STUDENTS = a reported instruction. Ask: after 'told + person', which form comes next - the plain verb, the -ing form, or the infinitive with its little marker in front? 'Written' is a past participle and cannot follow.

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Verb forms of 'find')

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Siti enjoys (1)________ lost objects and returning them to their owners.' Signal: 'enjoys + ___' = gerund (verb-ing). Pattern: enjoy + verb-ing → finding.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'finds'. STUDENTS is plural, so the -s form cannot be used.
questions.learning_tip: Simple present for a weekly habit. Plural subject (students) -> plain verb: students FIND their items every week.
questions.retry_hint: Look at the subject of blank 1: STUDENTS - more than one - and EVERY WEEK signals a habit. Ask: in the simple present, does a plural subject take the plain verb, or the one ending in -s?

questions.context_check: Passage: 'She always (2)________ something interesting in the school's lost and found box every week.' Signal: 'always' = regular habit = simple present. Subject 'She' = singular → finds.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'find'. THE SECRETARY is one person, and 'always' signals a habit.
questions.learning_tip: Simple present, singular subject -> verb + S: the secretary always FINDS a way.
questions.retry_hint: The subject here is OUR SCHOOL SECRETARY - one person - and ALWAYS tells you this happens again and again. Ask: does a singular subject in the present tense take the plain verb, or the one with -s on the end?

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Last Monday, she (3)________ a wallet with over fifty dollars and a student ID card inside.' Signal: 'Last Monday' = past. 'Find' is irregular: find → found.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'finded' or 'finds'. YESTERDAY = finished past, and 'find' is irregular.
questions.learning_tip: 'Find' is irregular: find -> FOUND. Never 'finded'. Yesterday = simple past.
questions.retry_hint: YESTERDAY puts this action in finished time, and the verb is irregular. Ask: what does this verb become in the simple past? Adding -ed would give you a word that does not exist in English.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'While she (4)________ the owner's contact number, the student arrived at the office himself.' Signal: 'While she ___' = ongoing background action in the past. Subject 'she' = singular → was finding. Interrupted by 'the student arrived'.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'to find'. After SPEND + a period of time, English uses the -ing form.
questions.learning_tip: SPEND time + verb-ing: she spent the whole of Tuesday FINDING its owner. Never 'spent Tuesday to find'.
questions.retry_hint: 'SPENT THE WHOLE OF TUESDAY' - after 'spend' plus a stretch of time, English demands one particular form. Ask: which form follows 'spent an hour ___' - the plain verb, the infinitive, or the -ing form?

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Other students (5)________ clues about the wallet's owner at the same time.' Signal: same past time frame, plural subject 'other students' + ongoing parallel action → were finding.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'found'. WHILE signals an action already in progress when the boy walked in, and 'the secretary' is singular.
questions.learning_tip: WHILE + past continuous: WAS FINDING (singular subject) = the action was still going on when something else happened.
questions.retry_hint: WHILE means the action had already begun when A BOY WALKED IN, and the subject, THE SECRETARY, is one person. Ask: which past continuous form matches a singular subject?

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Siti always tries (6)________ the owner within the same day.' Signal: 'tries + ___' = infinitive. Pattern: try + to + base verb → to find.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'was finding'. TWO PRIMARY 3 BOYS is plural, so the plural past continuous is needed.
questions.learning_tip: Past continuous with a plural subject -> WERE + verb-ing. Two boys WERE FINDING it hard at that same moment.
questions.retry_hint: AT THE SAME MOMENT points back into the same past stretch of time, but now the subject is TWO PRIMARY 3 BOYS. Ask: does the past continuous of a plural subject begin with 'was', or with its plural partner?

questions.context_check: Passage: 'She says everyone should (7)________ a way to return lost things rather than keep them.' Signal: 'should + ___' = modal verb + base form. Never add -s or -ing after a modal.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'finding'. 'The most common item ___ at school' needs an infinitive of purpose.
questions.learning_tip: Infinitive after a noun: the most common item TO FIND = the item that people find most often.
questions.retry_hint: THE MOST COMMON ITEM ___ AT SCHOOL: the blank works like 'the best book ___ read'. Ask: which form goes straight after a noun like this - the plain verb, the -ing form, or the infinitive with its marker?

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Right now, Siti (8)________ the address of the student whose ID card was in the wallet.' Signal: 'Right now' = present continuous. Subject 'Siti' = singular → is finding.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'finds'. RIGHT NOW = happening at this moment, so the present continuous is needed.
questions.learning_tip: RIGHT NOW = present continuous: Siti IS FINDING out who owns the football at this very moment.
questions.retry_hint: RIGHT NOW tells you the action has not stopped - it goes on as you read. Ask: which form shows something happening at this very moment, and which helping verb matches SITI, one person?

C.passage: Every week, students at our school (1)________ their lost items at the general office. Our school secretary always (2)________ a way to return almost every one of them. Yesterday, a girl (3)________ a blue pencil case near the library door. She spent the whole of Tuesday (4)________ its owner, class by class. While the secretary (5)________ it hard to fit all the umbrellas onto one shelf, a boy walked in with a lost violin. At the same moment, two Primary 3 boys (6)________ it hard to describe the glasses they had lost. The most common item (7)________ at school is an umbrella - dozens are left behind on rainy days. Right now, Siti (8)________ out who owns a football that appeared last Friday.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: Losing something precious can be an upsetting experience. When something goes missing, the first reaction is often (1)________ - a mix of panic and helplessness as you search the same drawer again and again. A clear (2)________ of the lost item - its colour, its size and any special marks - helps other people to identify it. In a busy lost-property room it is hard to (3)________ one black school bag from another, so those details matter. Items that are (4)________, such as jewellery or important documents, must be reported at once. When the owner and the item are finally (5)________, relief and gratitude follow.

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'cheerful'. The dash explains the blank: A MIX OF PANIC AND HELPLESSNESS, searching the same drawer again and again.
questions.learning_tip: FRANTIC = wildly anxious or desperate. A FRANTIC search is one made in a panic.
questions.retry_hint: The dash explains the blank: A MIX OF PANIC AND HELPLESSNESS, searching THE SAME DRAWER AGAIN AND AGAIN. Ask: which box word describes someone wildly anxious? 'Cheerful' is the opposite feeling.

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'invitation'. The blank follows 'a clear', so it must be a noun, and the dashes list COLOUR, SIZE and SPECIAL MARKS.
questions.learning_tip: A DESCRIPTION = an account of what someone or something looks like. Give a clear DESCRIPTION so others can identify the item.
questions.retry_hint: 'A CLEAR ___ OF THE LOST ITEM' is followed by a list: ITS COLOUR, ITS SIZE and ANY SPECIAL MARKS. Ask: which box word names an account of what something looks like? It must be a noun, because 'a clear' comes first.

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'description' (a noun). The blank follows 'hard to', so it must be a base verb, and the clue is ONE BLACK SCHOOL BAG FROM ANOTHER.
questions.learning_tip: DISTINGUISH X FROM Y = tell two similar things apart. Small details help you DISTINGUISH one bag from another.
questions.retry_hint: The blank comes after HARD TO, so it must be a plain verb, and the job is telling ONE BLACK SCHOOL BAG FROM ANOTHER apart. Ask: which box word means to see the difference between two similar things?

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'frantic'. The examples give it away: JEWELLERY and IMPORTANT DOCUMENTS - things worth a great deal.
questions.learning_tip: VALUABLE = worth a lot of money, or very important. VALUABLE items must be reported at once.
questions.retry_hint: The examples do the work: JEWELLERY and IMPORTANT DOCUMENTS, and they MUST BE REPORTED AT ONCE. Ask: which box word describes things worth a great deal of money? 'Frantic' describes a person, not a possession.

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'celebrate' (a base verb). The blank follows 'are finally', so it must be a past participle, and the clue is THE OWNER AND THE ITEM coming back together.
questions.learning_tip: REUNITED = brought back together after being separated. Owner and item are REUNITED = they are together again.
questions.retry_hint: THE OWNER AND THE ITEM come back together, and RELIEF AND GRATITUDE FOLLOW. The blank sits after 'are finally', so it must be a past participle. Ask: which box word means joined again after being apart?

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.trap_type: Students write 'quick' (adjective) after the action verb 'searched'. A verb needs an adverb to describe how.
questions.learning_tip: After an action verb (searched), use an ADVERB: searched QUICKLY. 'Quick' is an adjective — it describes nouns, not actions.
questions.retry_hint: The underlined word tells us HOW the teacher SEARCHED - and searching is an action. Ask: do we describe an action with an adjective, or with an adverb? Most adverbs of manner take the same two-letter tail.

questions.trap_type: Students add -s to 'mouse', producing 'mouses'. 'Mouse' has a completely irregular plural form.
questions.learning_tip: 'Mouse' has an irregular plural: mouse → MICE. Never write 'mouses'. Other irregular plurals: goose → geese, tooth → teeth.
questions.retry_hint: TWO MOUSES cannot be right: this animal does not take a plain -s. Ask: how do you write more than one goose, or more than one tooth? The word changes shape instead of gaining an ending.

questions.error_type: Spelling — -ing rule: silent -e is dropped before -ing
questions.trap_type: Students keep the final -e when adding -ing to 'hide', producing 'hideing'. Drop the silent -e before adding -ing.
questions.learning_tip: 'Hide' ends in silent -e: drop the -e before adding -ing → HIDING. Same rule: make → making, slide → sliding, give → giving.
questions.retry_hint: 'HIDE' ends with a silent -e. Ask: when you add -ing, does that -e stay or drop away? Compare: make becomes making, ride becomes riding, slide becomes sliding.

questions.trap_type: 'The keys' is plural. Students write 'was' (singular).
questions.learning_tip: 'The keys' = plural → WERE eventually found. WAS is only for singular subjects.
questions.retry_hint: Find the real subject: A PAIR OF HOUSE KEYS AND A MOBILE PHONE - two things joined by 'and'. Ask: does a plural subject take 'was', or its plural partner? Do not match the verb to the nearest noun.

questions.trap_type: Students write a plain plural and leave out the apostrophe that shows ownership.
questions.learning_tip: The parents BELONG TO the students -> STUDENTS' parents (apostrophe after the -s for a plural). Singular: student's.
questions.retry_hint: The PARENTS belong to more than one student - the whole class of them. Ask: does a plain -s show ownership, or only make a plural? Where must the apostrophe sit when the owners are many?

E.passage: On the last day of school camp, the teacher searched quick (1) through all the tents for any items left behind. In one tent, she discovered a trail of footprints made by two mouses (2) that were hideing (3) under a sleeping bag all along. A pair of house keys and a mobile phone was (4) eventually found in the last tent, under a pile of damp towels. The teacher placed all the items in a bag labelled 'Lost Property' and returned them to the students (5) parents at the camp gate.

questions.sentence_a: You return the lost wallet to its owner.
questions.sentence_b: You will feel proud of yourself.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'If'.
questions.model_answer: If you return the lost wallet to its owner, you will feel proud of yourself.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'If you will return the lost wallet, you will feel proud' — adding 'will' in the 'if' clause.
questions.learning_tip: Conditional: IF + simple present, simple future. If you RETURN the wallet, you WILL FEEL proud. Never use 'will' in the 'if' clause.
questions.retry_hint: Sentence A is the condition; sentence B is the reward that follows it. Ask: after 'If', does the verb stay in the simple present, or take a future helper? Only ONE half of a conditional sentence looks forward - and it is not the 'If' half.

questions.sentence_a: A girl handed in a purse.
questions.sentence_b: The purse contained two hundred dollars.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using the relative pronoun 'which'.
questions.model_answer: A girl handed in a purse, which contained two hundred dollars.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'A girl handed in a purse which it contained two hundred dollars' — adding 'it' after 'which'.
questions.learning_tip: Use 'which' to add information about a THING. A girl handed in a purse, WHICH contained two hundred dollars. Never add 'it' after 'which'.
questions.retry_hint: Both sentences name the PURSE, so mention it once and let the relative pronoun carry the second mention. Ask: after 'which', do you still need the word 'it'? And what punctuation holds the extra fact apart?

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
Twelve-year-old Farah found a black notebook on the seat of Bus 67 on a Wednesday afternoon. She nearly left it where it was — it was not hers, and she was already running late. But she picked it up.

The notebook had no name on the cover. Inside, she found page after page of pencil drawings — birds, trees, faces, and at the back, a half-finished sketch of a street that looked familiar. She turned to the first page. Underneath the first drawing was a small inscription: 'For whoever finds this — please keep it safe.'

Farah brought the notebook home and placed it on her desk. She looked at the drawings every evening that week. She thought about the person who made them — someone careful, someone patient, someone who looked at the world closely.

She decided she had to return it. She went back to the bus stop and spoke to the driver of Bus 67. He did not recognise the notebook but told her to check with the transport company's lost property office.

At the lost property office, a young man was already waiting. He looked up when Farah walked in, saw the notebook in her hands and stood up quickly.

'That's mine,' he said.

Farah handed it over. The young man held the notebook for a moment and exhaled slowly. 'I looked for this for two weeks,' he said. 'Thank you.'

On the bus home, Farah felt lighter than she had in a long time.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 1 has the same meaning as 'looked quickly and carefully at something'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Raced' = moved fast; 'clutched' = held tightly; 'hesitated' = paused with uncertainty. SCANNED = looked quickly over something to find information.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: SCANNED = looked quickly and carefully across something to find specific details. Farah SCANNED the bus = she quickly looked around to see if anyone left the notebook. SCAN = quick, purposeful looking.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 3, what does 'someone' refer to in 'Farah thought about someone careful, someone patient'?

options.3: The unknown person who owned the notebook and drew in it with care

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking 'someone' = Farah. But Farah is imagining what the notebook's owner must be like — a stranger.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: PRONOUN REFERENCE: 'SOMEONE' here = the imagined, unknown OWNER of the notebook. Farah studies the drawings and thinks: what kind of person draws like this? She imagines SOMEONE careful, someone patient — a stranger she has never met.

mcq_questions.stem: What does 'Farah felt lighter than she had in a long time' at the end of the passage most likely mean?

options.1: Farah lost weight during the search for the owner.
options.2: Farah felt relieved and happy because she did the right thing.
options.3: Farah was tired from a long day and ready to sleep.
options.4: Farah felt confused about whether she made the right decision.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking 'lighter' = less weight. This is a metaphor for emotional relief.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: 'Felt LIGHTER' = a metaphor for feeling relieved and free from worry. Doing the right thing — returning the notebook — lifted the emotional weight from Farah's heart. She felt LIGHTER = happier and more at peace.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 1, is it True or False that Farah was in a hurry when she found the notebook? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: True. The passage says 'she was already running late' — she was rushing and did not have much time.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'False, she stopped to pick it up.' She did stop, but the passage makes clear she was in a hurry.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1: 'She was already RUNNING LATE.' = she was behind schedule and hurrying. Despite being in a hurry, she still stopped — showing her character. Answer is TRUE.

open_ended_questions.stem: What steps did Farah take to try to return the notebook? Name TWO steps.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) She went back to the bus stop and spoke to the driver of Bus 67. (ii) She went to the transport company's lost property office.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students name only one step or describe what she did at home (looking at drawings) instead of the steps she took to find the owner.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 4: (1) she spoke to the BUS DRIVER. (2) the driver told her to check the LOST PROPERTY OFFICE. These are the two steps she took to find the owner.

open_ended_questions.stem: What was the CAUSE of Farah's decision to return the notebook? What was the EFFECT on the young man when he got it back?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: CAUSE: Farah studied the drawings carefully and felt she understood what kind of person the artist was — careful, patient and observant. This made her feel she had to return it to its rightful owner. EFFECT: The young man stood up quickly when he saw the notebook, held it for a moment, exhaled slowly and told Farah he looked for this for two weeks.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students describe only the effect without identifying the cause in the passage.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: CAUSE: she studied the DRAWINGS and felt the owner deserved to have it back. EFFECT: the young man held it, exhaled slowly and said he looked for it for TWO WEEKS — showing great relief.

open_ended_questions.stem: Find a phrase in paragraph 1 that shows Farah had a reason NOT to pick up the notebook but chose to anyway.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: 'She was already running late.'
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students quote 'it was not hers' which is a reason not to take it, but the question asks for the specific personal inconvenience that made her hesitate.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1: 'She was already RUNNING LATE.' This is the personal inconvenience that gave her a reason to leave it — but she picked it up anyway.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on her actions throughout the passage, describe TWO character traits of Farah with evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) RESPONSIBLE: even though she was running late, Farah picked up the notebook and spent days trying to return it — she did not ignore it or keep it for herself. (ii) EMPATHETIC: she studied the drawings carefully and tried to understand what the owner must feel like, imagining them as 'someone careful, someone patient'.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'honest and kind' without naming precise traits or giving specific evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: TRAIT INFERENCE: Name the trait + give textual evidence. RESPONSIBLE = picked up notebook despite being late, spent days returning it. EMPATHETIC = imagined owner's feelings from the drawings. Trait + Evidence = full marks.

questions.stem: The student used an online dictionary to ________ the meaning of the unfamiliar word in his essay.
questions.trap_type: 'Delete' means to remove; 'ignore' means to pay no attention; 'print out' is a physical action. Only 'look up' = search for information in a reference source.
questions.learning_tip: LOOK UP = search for the meaning or definition of something in a dictionary or reference. He LOOKED UP the word = searched for its meaning.
questions.retry_hint: The student wants THE MEANING OF THE UNFAMILIAR WORD and he goes to AN ONLINE DICTIONARY. Ask: which phrasal verb means searching a reference source for a piece of information? 'Delete' and 'print out' never tell you what a word means.

questions.stem: The news ________ across the country within minutes after it was posted on social media.
questions.trap_type: 'Froze' means stopped; 'collected' means gathered; 'erased' means removed. Only 'spread' = moved quickly to many people or places.
questions.learning_tip: SPREAD = moved or extended rapidly to reach more people or places. News SPREADS quickly on social media because it reaches millions of people instantly.
questions.retry_hint: WITHIN MINUTES the news reached the whole COUNTRY after one post on SOCIAL MEDIA. Ask: which verb shows something moving out quickly to many people and places at once? 'Froze' would stop it; 'erased' would remove it.

questions.stem: The engineer worked to ________ the faulty software by fixing the errors in the code.
questions.trap_type: 'Delete' removes entirely; 'download' = transfer from internet; 'duplicate' = copy. Only 'debug' = find and fix errors in software code.
questions.learning_tip: DEBUG = find and fix errors (bugs) in a computer program or code. Engineers DEBUG software to make it work correctly.
questions.retry_hint: The clue follows the blank: the engineer is FIXING THE ERRORS IN THE CODE of the FAULTY SOFTWARE. Ask: which verb means hunting down and repairing mistakes inside a program? 'Duplicate' would only copy the same errors.

questions.stem: The teacher asked students to ________ their presentations to the class-sharing drive before Friday.
questions.trap_type: 'Delete', 'erase' = remove; 'disconnect' = break a connection. Only 'upload' = transfer a file from a device to a server or shared space.
questions.learning_tip: UPLOAD = send a file from your device to the internet or a shared server. Students UPLOAD their work to a shared drive so everyone can access it.
questions.retry_hint: The work must travel from the students' own devices TO THE CLASS-SHARING DRIVE. Ask: which verb means sending a file from your device onto a shared space online? 'Delete' and 'erase' would destroy the PRESENTATIONS instead.
