questions.stem: The ability to communicate ________ across cultures and languages is a key skill in today's connected world.
questions.trap_type: 'Vaguely' and 'carelessly' suggest poor communication; 'reluctantly' means unwillingly. Only 'effectively' = in a way that achieves the intended result.
questions.learning_tip: EFFECTIVELY = in a way that produces the desired result. Communicating EFFECTIVELY means getting your message across clearly and successfully.
questions.retry_hint: The sentence praises A KEY SKILL that works ACROSS CULTURES AND LANGUAGES - communication that succeeds. Ask: does the adverb describe a message that achieves its purpose, or one that fails? 'Vaguely' and 'carelessly' describe failure.

questions.stem: Every morning, the class monitor ________ the day's announcements on the whiteboard before lessons start.
questions.trap_type: 'Every morning' = regular habit = simple present. 'The class monitor' is singular → verb needs -s.
questions.learning_tip: 'Every morning' = regular habit = simple present. The class monitor (singular) → WRITES the announcements each morning.
questions.retry_hint: EVERY MORNING signals a habit that repeats, and the subject is THE CLASS MONITOR - one person. Ask: in the simple present, does a singular subject take the plain verb, or the verb with -s? 'Wrote' would push the habit into the past.

questions.stem: The engineers ________ the new app after two years of testing and improving the design.
questions.trap_type: 'After two years of testing' = completed past event. 'Launch' is regular: launch → launched.
questions.learning_tip: 'After two years of testing' = completed past action. 'Launch' is regular: launch → LAUNCHED.
questions.retry_hint: AFTER TWO YEARS OF TESTING - the work is over, so the moment is finished and past. Ask: which form shows a completed past action? This verb is regular, so the past takes the ordinary ending.

questions.stem: The students ________ their digital posters when the internet connection suddenly dropped.
questions.trap_type: 'The internet connection suddenly dropped' is the sudden interrupting event. The students were already creating = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: The connection DROPPED = sudden past event. The students were already creating at that moment = WERE CREATING.
questions.retry_hint: THE INTERNET CONNECTION SUDDENLY DROPPED - one sharp event cutting into something already under way. Ask: which choice shows an action still in progress at that past moment? A plain past verb reports only a finished job.

questions.stem: The new messaging app was easy to use, ________ it?
questions.trap_type: Main clause is positive past ('was easy') → negative tag. 'Was' → wasn't.
questions.learning_tip: Question tag for positive simple past: [positive] + WASN'T + subject? The app WAS easy to use, WASN'T it? Positive → negative tag.
questions.retry_hint: The statement is positive and set in the past: the app WAS EASY TO USE. Ask: after a positive statement, does the tag turn negative, or stay positive? And must the tag keep the tense the statement gives it?

questions.stem: The children have not checked their emails today, ________ they?
questions.trap_type: Main clause is NEGATIVE present perfect ('have not') → POSITIVE tag. 'Have not' → positive tag = have they.
questions.learning_tip: Question tag for negative present perfect: [negative] + HAVE + subject? 'They HAVE NOT checked, HAVE they?' Negative → positive tag.
questions.retry_hint: Look at the statement about THE CHILDREN and their EMAILS: it is a negative one. Ask: after a negative statement, does the tag stay negative or flip to positive? The tag must repeat the statement's own helping verb - 'did' belongs to another tense.

questions.stem: There ________ a great deal of confusion when the school's website crashed during the registration period.
questions.trap_type: 'A great deal of confusion' = singular uncountable. Past event → was.
questions.learning_tip: 'A great deal of confusion' = singular uncountable amount. Past event → THERE WAS a great deal of confusion.
questions.retry_hint: 'A GREAT DEAL OF CONFUSION' counts as one single amount, not many things, and THE WEBSITE CRASHED puts it firmly in the past. Ask: does a singular subject take a present form, or a past one? 'Were' would need a plural.

questions.stem: The school's podcast ________ by a group of Primary 5 and 6 students who take turns every week.
questions.trap_type: The podcast is produced by students (passive). Present regular action → is produced.
questions.learning_tip: The podcast is the receiver of the action. Present passive = IS PRODUCED. Plural agent 'students' → ARE; but the subject is 'the podcast' (singular) → IS PRODUCED.
questions.retry_hint: THE PODCAST cannot make itself - A GROUP OF PRIMARY 5 AND 6 STUDENTS makes it, and they TAKE TURNS EVERY WEEK. Ask: which choice puts the subject on the receiving end, in the present? Passive = a form of 'be' + past participle.

questions.stem: The tech teacher told his students ________ their passwords with anyone, even close friends.
questions.trap_type: Negative reported speech: told + object + not to + base verb.
questions.learning_tip: 'Told students NOT TO + base verb': told them NOT TO SHARE their passwords. After 'told + object', use 'not to' + base verb.
questions.retry_hint: TOLD HIS STUDENTS = a reported command, and this one is negative: PASSWORDS must stay secret, EVEN CLOSE FRIENDS included. Ask: which negative word comes first, and which verb form follows it - plain, -ing, or the infinitive?

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Modal verbs)

questions.context_check: Passage: 'With the internet, we (1)________ communicate with people on the other side of the world instantly.' Signal: present ability / general truth = CAN. CAN = present ability or general capability.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'could' (past ability) instead of 'can' (present ability). 'With the internet' = a current capability.
questions.learning_tip: CAN = present ability or general capability. We CAN communicate with anyone in the world = we have this ability right now.
questions.retry_hint: WITH THE INTERNET, the ability belongs to us right now, INSTANTLY, all over the world. Ask: which modal shows a present ability? A past-ability modal would suit the sentence about the days before smartphones, not this one.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'However, we (2)________ always check whether information online is accurate before sharing it.' Signal: advice or recommendation = SHOULD. SHOULD = what is advisable or right to do.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'must' (not in the box) or 'will'. SHOULD = strong advice; WILL = future certainty.
questions.learning_tip: SHOULD = advice or strong recommendation. We SHOULD always check facts before sharing = it is the right and responsible thing to do.
questions.retry_hint: The passage is giving advice: we ALWAYS CHECK whether information is ACCURATE BEFORE WE SHARE IT. Ask: which modal tells you the right and responsible thing to do? A modal of pure possibility would make the advice sound optional.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Sharing false information (3)________ cause serious harm to individuals and communities.' Signal: possibility with some likelihood = MAY. MAY = something is possible and may happen.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'might' (possibility) or 'should' (advice). This sentence is a school RULE about what pupils are allowed to do, not a possibility.
questions.learning_tip: MAY = permission. Pupils MAY use the laboratory only when a teacher is present = they are allowed to, but only under that condition.
questions.retry_hint: This sentence states A RULE: pupils use the laboratory ONLY WHEN A TEACHER IS PRESENT, and NOBODY IS ALLOWED to break it. Ask: which modal gives permission? 'Might' would only guess at a possibility, which no rule does.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Even a message that seems harmless (4)________ upset someone if it is misunderstood.' Signal: less certain or weaker possibility = MIGHT. MIGHT = something is possible but less certain than MAY.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'will' (certain) or 'would' (hypothetical). The message only possibly causes upset - it is not certain.
questions.learning_tip: MIGHT = a weaker or less certain possibility. Even a harmless message MIGHT upset someone = it is possible but not certain.
questions.retry_hint: A message THAT SEEMS HARMLESS could still upset someone IF IT IS MISUNDERSTOOD - the harm is possible, never certain. Ask: which modal shows the weaker possibility? 'Will' would promise that the upset happens every single time.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'In the future, technology (5)________ make communication even faster and more reliable.' Signal: future prediction or certainty = WILL. WILL = what is expected or predicted to happen in the future.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'would' (hypothetical) or 'shall' (formal/first person). WILL = expected future.
questions.learning_tip: WILL = expected future outcome. Technology WILL make communication faster = this is the expected direction of progress.
questions.retry_hint: IN THE FUTURE, technology makes communication EVEN FASTER AND MORE RELIABLE - this is what we expect to happen. Ask: which modal marks a plain future expectation? 'Would' belongs to an imagined situation, not a real one.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Many people said that without their phones, they (6)________ feel completely lost.' Signal: hypothetical or conditional outcome = WOULD. 'Without their phones' = a hypothetical situation; WOULD = the result in that hypothetical.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'will' (actual future) instead of 'would' (hypothetical conditional result).
questions.learning_tip: WOULD = hypothetical or conditional result. Without their phones, they WOULD feel lost = this is what they imagine would happen in that situation.
questions.retry_hint: WITHOUT THEIR PHONES is an imagined situation - these people are not actually without them. Ask: which modal shows the result of a situation that is only supposed, not real? A plain future modal belongs to things that really happen.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Before smartphones, people (7)________ only communicate by letter or telephone.' Signal: past ability or past possibility = COULD. 'Before smartphones' = a past time context; COULD = what was possible then.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'can' (present) instead of 'could' (past). 'Before smartphones' clearly sets the past context.
questions.learning_tip: COULD = past ability or possibility. Before smartphones, people COULD only communicate by letter or phone = that was their capability at the time.
questions.retry_hint: BEFORE SMARTPHONES EXISTED - the ability described is over and done with, and it was limited: BY LETTER OR TELEPHONE only. Ask: which modal shows a past ability? The present-ability modal is needed by blank 1.

questions.context_check: Passage: '(8)________ we use technology to bring people together rather than drive them apart? That is the choice we make every day.' Signal: suggestion or proposal = SHALL. 'Shall we' = a formal suggestion or invitation to consider something.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'should' (already used in blank 2) or 'will'. 'Shall we?' = a formal first-person suggestion.
questions.learning_tip: SHALL WE = used to make a suggestion or proposal. SHALL we use technology wisely? = a proposal to consider how we should behave.
questions.retry_hint: The blank opens a QUESTION, and the sentence proposes something: BRING PEOPLE TOGETHER rather than DRIVE THEM APART. Ask: which modal begins a suggestion made with 'we'? It is not the advice modal from blank 2.

C.passage: With the internet, we (1)________ communicate with people on the other side of the world instantly. However, we (2)________ always check whether the information we find online is accurate before we share it with others. In our school, pupils (3)________ use the computer laboratory only when a teacher is present - that is the rule, and nobody is allowed to break it. Even a message that seems harmless (4)________ upset someone if it is misunderstood, so think before you post. In the future, technology (5)________ make communication even faster and more reliable than it is today. Many people said that without their phones, they (6)________ feel completely lost. Before smartphones existed, people (7)________ only communicate by letter or telephone - a much slower process. (8)________ we use technology to bring people together rather than drive them apart? That is the choice we make every day.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: The internet has changed how information is shared around the world. In the past, only large organisations could (1)________ news to millions of people at once. Today, anyone with a phone can reach a global audience. However, not all information online is reliable. It is important to (2)________ what we read — separating facts from opinions and checking sources before believing or sharing content. One challenge is that some people post comments under (3)________ accounts, meaning their real names are hidden. This makes it harder to hold people responsible for harmful things they say. On the positive side, the internet has made knowledge (4)________ to people everywhere — even in remote areas. Scientists can (5)________ research findings to colleagues across the globe in seconds.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'news to millions of people at once' = send out widely = broadcast.
questions.learning_tip: BROADCAST = send out information, news or entertainment to a large audience at once. Television and radio stations BROADCAST programmes.
questions.retry_hint: IN THE PAST only LARGE ORGANISATIONS could reach MILLIONS OF PEOPLE AT ONCE - think of a radio or television station. Ask: which box word means sending news out widely to a huge audience? The blank follows 'could', so it must be a plain verb.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'separating facts from opinions and checking sources' = selecting carefully what to accept = filter.
questions.learning_tip: FILTER = carefully select or sort through information to keep only what is accurate or useful. We must FILTER what we read online.
questions.retry_hint: The dash tells you the job: SEPARATING FACTS FROM OPINIONS and CHECKING SOURCES before you believe anything. Ask: which box word means sifting information and keeping only what is trustworthy? It follows 'to', so it must be a plain verb.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'their real names are hidden' = without a name being known = anonymous.
questions.learning_tip: ANONYMOUS = having an unknown or hidden identity. An ANONYMOUS account = one where the real name of the user is not revealed.
questions.retry_hint: The clue sits right after the blank: THEIR REAL NAMES ARE HIDDEN, so nobody can be held RESPONSIBLE. Ask: which box word describes an account with no name attached to it? It must be a describing word, since 'accounts' follows.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'to people everywhere, even in remote areas' = available and easy to reach = accessible.
questions.learning_tip: ACCESSIBLE = available and easy to obtain or reach. The internet makes knowledge ACCESSIBLE to people all over the world.
questions.retry_hint: Knowledge now reaches PEOPLE EVERYWHERE - EVEN IN REMOTE AREAS. Ask: which box word means easy for anyone to reach or obtain? The blank follows 'has made knowledge', so it must describe knowledge, not a machine.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'research findings to colleagues across the globe in seconds' = send data or information electronically = transmit.
questions.learning_tip: TRANSMIT = send information, signals or data from one place to another. Scientists TRANSMIT their findings digitally to colleagues worldwide.
questions.retry_hint: Scientists send RESEARCH FINDINGS TO COLLEAGUES ACROSS THE GLOBE IN SECONDS. Ask: which box word means passing information electronically from one place to another? The blank follows 'can', so a noun cannot go here.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.trap_type: Students write 'clear' (adjective) after the action verb 'explained'. A verb needs an adverb.
questions.learning_tip: After an action verb (explained), use an ADVERB: explained CLEARLY. 'Clear' is an adjective — it describes nouns, not actions.
questions.retry_hint: The underlined word tells us HOW the teacher EXPLAINED - and explaining is an action. Ask: does an action take an adjective, or an adverb? Adverbs of manner nearly always gain the same two-letter tail.

questions.trap_type: Students add -s to 'woman'. 'Woman' has an irregular plural: the vowel changes instead.
questions.learning_tip: WOMAN -> WOMEN (irregular). Same pattern: man -> men, child -> children, foot -> feet.
questions.retry_hint: GROWN MEN AND WOMANS: this noun does not take a plain -s. Ask: what happens to 'man' when there is more than one? Apply exactly the same vowel change here.

questions.error_type: Spelling — doubling rule does not apply to 'connect' (two consonants before -ing)
questions.trap_type: Students double the 't' in 'connecting', writing 'connectting'. The doubling rule only applies when there is a SHORT VOWEL + SINGLE consonant. 'Connect' ends in -ct (two consonants) → no doubling.
questions.learning_tip: 'Connect' ends in two consonants (-c-t): do NOT double. Just add -ing → CONNECTING. Doubling only applies when a short vowel is followed by ONE consonant.
questions.retry_hint: Count the consonants at the end of 'CONNECT': there are two of them. Ask: do we double a final consonant when another consonant already stands in front of it? Doubling follows only a short vowel plus ONE consonant.

questions.trap_type: 'The messages' is plural. Students write 'was' (singular).
questions.learning_tip: 'The messages' = plural → WERE sent to the wrong address. WAS is only for singular subjects.
questions.retry_hint: THE MESSAGES is plural - more than one message went astray. Ask: does a plural subject take 'was', or its plural partner? Never let 'the wrong email address' sitting nearby decide the verb for you.

questions.trap_type: Students add a plain -s to 'children'. 'Children' is already plural, so the possessive needs 's.
questions.learning_tip: CHILDREN is already the plural of child, so the possessive is CHILDREN'S posters (apostrophe + s after an irregular plural). Never 'childrens'.
questions.retry_hint: The POSTERS belong to the CHILDRENS - and that spelling is wrong twice over. Ask: is 'children' already a plural on its own? So where must the apostrophe go, and does the extra -s stay or vanish?

E.passage: Last week, our digital literacy lesson taught us how to stay safe online. The teacher explained clear (1) how to spot fake news. She also reminded us that even grown men and womans (2) can be fooled by a clever headline. We spent part of the lesson connectting (3) our devices to the school network to practise checking verified sources. Unfortunately, the messages was (4) sent to the wrong email address by accident. At the end, the teacher displayed the childrens (5) digital safety posters on the classroom board for everyone to see.

questions.sentence_a: The teacher said to the class, 'You must verify information before sharing it online.'
questions.instruction: Rewrite using reported speech: The teacher told the class that ________.
questions.model_answer: The teacher told the class that they must verify information before sharing it online.
questions.trap_type: Students keep 'you' instead of changing to 'they', or keep 'must' unchanged without recognising the pronoun shift.
questions.learning_tip: In reported speech: change 'you' → 'they'. The teacher told the class that THEY must verify information before sharing it online.
questions.retry_hint: The teacher's exact words were spoken to THE CLASS, and inside the speech marks they are called 'YOU'. Ask: when you report those words to somebody else, which pronoun takes over from 'you'? The speech marks disappear with it.

questions.sentence_a: The school's new website was designed by a team of student volunteers.
questions.instruction: Rewrite beginning with: A team of student volunteers ________.
questions.model_answer: A team of student volunteers designed the school's new website.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'A team of student volunteers was designed the school's new website' — incorrectly keeping passive structure when making it active.
questions.learning_tip: Active voice: AGENT + VERB + OBJECT. A team of student volunteers DESIGNED the school's new website. Remove 'was' and 'by' when converting passive to active.
questions.retry_hint: The given sentence is passive: THE SCHOOL'S NEW WEBSITE receives the action, and A TEAM OF STUDENT VOLUNTEERS does it. Ask: when the doer moves to the front, what happens to 'was' and to the word 'by'? The verb becomes a plain past form.

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
On a Tuesday afternoon, eleven-year-old Dani received a message on the class group chat. It said that the science test on Friday was cancelled. She felt a wave of relief — she had not started studying yet.

But something felt off. The message was sent by an account she did not recognise. She checked with her friend Lena, who had not seen any official notice from the teacher.

Dani decided to check with Mr Woo directly. She sent him a polite message asking whether the test was still on. His reply came within minutes: the test was very much on.

The next day at school, Dani told her classmates. Several of them had already stopped studying, believing the false message. They were upset — but also relieved that Dani found out in time.

Mr Woo addressed the class about the incident. 'This is exactly why we must check the source of every message before we believe it,' he said. 'A single unverified message caused five students to waste a study night.'

Dani felt grateful she trusted her instincts. She learned something that no classroom lesson could fully teach: the importance of questioning what you read.

mcq_questions.stem: What made Dani suspicious about the message?

options.1: The message contained several spelling mistakes.
options.2: It was sent from an account she did not recognise.
options.3: Lena told her the message was fake.
options.4: Mr Woo had already warned them about fake messages.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 3 thinking Lena told her — but Lena only confirmed she had not seen an official notice, she did not say it was fake.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 2: 'The message was sent by an ACCOUNT SHE DID NOT RECOGNISE.' This unfamiliar sender made Dani suspicious.

mcq_questions.stem: What happened IMMEDIATELY AFTER Dani checked with Lena?

options.1: She stopped studying for the test.
options.2: She told her classmates the test was still on.
options.3: She sent Mr Woo a message to confirm whether the test was cancelled.
options.4: Mr Woo addressed the class about the incident.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 2 thinking she told classmates next. But telling classmates happened the NEXT DAY. Immediately after Lena, she messaged Mr Woo.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Sequence: checked with Lena → IMMEDIATELY decided to check with Mr Woo (paragraph 3). Telling classmates was the NEXT DAY (paragraph 4).

mcq_questions.stem: Mr Woo said 'A single unverified message caused five students to waste a study night.' What lesson was he trying to teach?

options.1: Students should not use group chats for school communication.
options.2: He was angry at the five students who stopped studying.
options.3: Even one piece of false information can have real consequences — so always verify before acting.
options.4: Students should only trust messages sent directly by the teacher.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking he was banning group chats. His point is about verifying information, not banning communication tools.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Mr Woo's lesson: ONE unverified message = FIVE students wasted a study night. The consequence was real. His lesson = always VERIFY before you believe and act.

open_ended_questions.stem: Why did Dani feel relief when she first read the message?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: She felt relief because the message said the science test was cancelled and she had not started studying yet.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'she was happy' without giving the specific reason.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1: the test was 'CANCELLED' and she 'had not started STUDYING yet'. Both reasons explain her relief.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 4, is it True or False that all of Dani's classmates had stopped studying because of the false message? Give a reason from the passage.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. Only SEVERAL of them had stopped studying, not all. The passage says 'Several of them had already stopped studying, believing the false message' — not the whole class.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'True, all students stopped studying.' The passage says 'several', not 'all'.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 4: 'SEVERAL of them had already stopped studying.' SEVERAL = some, not all. So it is FALSE that ALL classmates stopped studying.

open_ended_questions.stem: What TWO steps did Dani take to verify whether the message was true?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) She checked with her friend Lena to see if Lena had received any official notice. (ii) She sent Mr Woo a message directly asking whether the test was still on.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students give the same step twice in different words.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraphs 2–3: (1) she asked LENA if she had seen an official notice; (2) she messaged MR WOO directly to confirm. Two distinct verification steps.

open_ended_questions.stem: Find a phrase in the last paragraph that shows Dani gained something important that school lessons alone cannot fully provide.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: 'Something that no classroom lesson could fully teach: the importance of questioning what you read.'
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students quote 'she had learned something' without including the specific content of what she learned.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Last paragraph: 'something that NO CLASSROOM LESSON could fully teach: the importance of QUESTIONING what you read.' This phrase shows real-world learning beyond textbooks.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on her actions in the passage, describe TWO character traits of Dani with evidence from the passage.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: Dani is a cautious and responsible person. Firstly, her caution is shown when she did not immediately believe the message even though it brought her relief — instead, she noticed the sender was unfamiliar and decided to verify it first. Secondly, her sense of responsibility is shown when she took the time to tell her classmates the truth the following day, ensuring they had accurate information before the test, even though this was not her duty.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say she is 'smart and kind' without naming precise character traits or giving specific evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Name precise TRAITS then give EVIDENCE: (1) CAUTIOUS — felt something 'off' and chose to VERIFY despite initial relief; (2) RESPONSIBLE — told classmates the truth so they could prepare.

questions.stem: The boy ________ his fear of heights by climbing the wall at the adventure park step by step.
questions.trap_type: 'Avoided' and 'ignored' mean he did not face the fear. 'Increased' makes it worse. Only 'conquered' = overcame completely.
questions.learning_tip: CONQUERED = completely overcame a fear, difficulty or enemy. He CONQUERED his fear of heights = he faced it and won.
questions.retry_hint: He did not run from his FEAR OF HEIGHTS - he climbed the wall STEP BY STEP until the fear was beaten. Ask: which verb means to overcome something completely? 'Avoided' and 'ignored' would mean he never faced it at all.

questions.stem: The girl's hands ________ as she stood at the edge of the diving board for the first time.
questions.trap_type: 'Relaxed' = calm, which is the opposite; 'clapped' shows joy; 'stretched' = extended. Only 'trembled' = shook from nervousness or fear.
questions.learning_tip: TREMBLED = shook slightly from nervousness, cold or fear. Her hands TREMBLED = they shook because she was afraid.
questions.retry_hint: She is standing AT THE EDGE OF THE DIVING BOARD FOR THE FIRST TIME, and her body is showing her nerves. Ask: which verb shows hands shaking with fear? 'Relaxed' would mean she felt perfectly calm.

questions.stem: The coach ________ the nervous swimmer, telling her she had trained hard and was ready.
questions.trap_type: 'Criticised' and 'scolded' are negative; 'frightened' makes fear worse. Only 'reassured' = calmed someone by giving them confidence.
questions.learning_tip: REASSURED = calmed someone's worries by giving them confidence and encouragement. The coach REASSURED the swimmer = gave her confidence before the race.
questions.retry_hint: The coach's words are kind: SHE HAD TRAINED HARD AND WAS READY, and the swimmer is NERVOUS. Ask: which verb means calming someone by giving them confidence? 'Scolded' and 'criticised' would only make her feel worse.

questions.stem: After failing the audition twice, Maya showed great ________ by trying again a third time.
questions.trap_type: 'Cowardice', 'rudeness' and 'laziness' are all negative traits. Only 'perseverance' = continuing to try despite difficulties.
questions.learning_tip: PERSEVERANCE = the quality of continuing to try despite failure or difficulty. Trying again after two failures shows great PERSEVERANCE.
questions.retry_hint: She FAILED THE AUDITION TWICE and still went back A THIRD TIME. Ask: which noun names the quality of carrying on in spite of failure? 'Laziness' and 'cowardice' would have kept her at home.

questions.stem: The audience watched in ________ silence as the young gymnast performed her most difficult routine.
questions.trap_type: 'Bored' and 'restless' suggest disengagement; 'frightened' is for the gymnast not the audience. 'Tense silence' = the audience held their breath with suspense.
questions.learning_tip: TENSE silence = a silence filled with suspense, anticipation and anxiety. When everyone watches breathlessly, the atmosphere is TENSE.
questions.retry_hint: Nobody dares make a sound: the gymnast is performing HER MOST DIFFICULT ROUTINE and the AUDIENCE is holding its breath. Ask: which adjective describes a silence full of suspense? 'Bored' and 'restless' would mean nobody cared.

questions.stem: Every year, the school organises a camp to help students ________ new challenges and build resilience.
questions.trap_type: 'Every year' = regular event = simple present. 'Students' = plural → no -s.
questions.learning_tip: 'Every year' = a regular event = simple present. Help students FACE new challenges = infinitive after 'help'.
questions.retry_hint: The pattern is 'HELP + person + verb', and the person is STUDENTS, a plural. Ask: after 'help students', do we use the plain verb or the one with -s? EVERY YEAR keeps the whole sentence in the present.

questions.stem: The young athlete ________ her nerves and delivered a perfect performance at the finals.
questions.trap_type: 'At the finals' = past completed event. 'Control' is regular: control → controlled.
questions.learning_tip: 'At the finals' = completed past event. 'Control' is regular: control → CONTROLLED.
questions.retry_hint: AT THE FINALS she DELIVERED A PERFECT PERFORMANCE - both actions are over and done. Ask: which form shows a finished past action? This verb is regular, so no vowel change is needed, just the ordinary ending.

questions.stem: The students ________ the high ropes course when it started to rain heavily.
questions.trap_type: 'When it started to rain' = sudden interrupting event. Students were already attempting = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: The rain STARTED = sudden past event. The students were already in the middle of attempting the course = WERE ATTEMPTING.
questions.retry_hint: IT STARTED TO RAIN HEAVILY - a sudden event cutting into something already under way. Ask: which choice keeps the students in the middle of the HIGH ROPES COURSE at that past moment? A plain past verb would say the job was over.

questions.stem: You have never tried rock climbing before, ________ you?
questions.trap_type: Main clause is NEGATIVE present perfect ('have never') → POSITIVE tag. 'Have never' → positive tag = have you.
questions.learning_tip: Question tag for negative present perfect: [negative] + HAVE + subject? 'You have NEVER tried, HAVE you?' Negative → positive tag.
questions.retry_hint: NEVER TRIED ROCK CLIMBING BEFORE - the statement is a negative one. Ask: after a negative statement, does the tag stay negative or flip to positive? The tag must repeat the statement's own helping verb, so 'did' is out of place.

questions.stem: The speech was delivered bravely by the nervous student, ________ it?
questions.trap_type: Main clause is positive past passive ('was delivered') → negative tag. 'Was' → wasn't.
questions.learning_tip: Question tag for positive past: [positive] + WASN'T + subject? The speech WAS delivered bravely, WASN'T it? Positive → negative tag.
questions.retry_hint: The statement is positive and past: the speech WAS DELIVERED BRAVELY. Ask: after a positive statement, does the tag flip to negative, or stay positive? A tag always keeps the tense the statement gives it.

questions.stem: There ________ a long silence in the room when the results were announced.
questions.trap_type: 'A long silence' = singular. Past event → was.
questions.learning_tip: 'A long silence' = ONE silence = singular. Past event → THERE WAS a long silence in the room.
questions.retry_hint: 'A LONG SILENCE' is one thing, not several, and THE RESULTS WERE ANNOUNCED sets the time in the past. Ask: does a singular subject take a present form, or a past one? 'Were' would need a plural subject.

questions.stem: The gold medal ________ by the youngest competitor in the history of the championship.
questions.trap_type: The medal did not win itself. Past passive = was won.
questions.learning_tip: The medal was the receiver of the action. Past passive = WAS WON. Passive = was/were + past participle.
questions.retry_hint: THE GOLD MEDAL did nothing at all - THE YOUNGEST COMPETITOR did it. Ask: which choice puts the subject on the receiving end of a past action? Passive = a form of 'be' + the past participle.

questions.stem: The counsellor told the anxious student ________ herself too harshly when she made mistakes.
questions.trap_type: Negative reported speech: told + object + not to + base verb.
questions.learning_tip: 'Told the student NOT TO + base verb': told the student NOT TO JUDGE herself too harshly when she made mistakes.
questions.retry_hint: TOLD THE ANXIOUS STUDENT = a reported command, and a negative one: she must stop being HARSH with HERSELF. Ask: which negative word comes first, and which verb form follows it - plain, -ing, or the infinitive?

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Question words)

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Before her first public speech, Nora asked herself (1)________ the worst thing that could happen was.' Signal: blank = the content of the question (thing/event) = WHAT. 'What the worst thing was' = asking about a thing.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'who' (person) or 'when' (time). The question is about a thing (the worst outcome) = WHAT.
questions.learning_tip: WHAT = asking about a thing, event or action. 'What the worst thing could be' = asking about the nature of the event. WHAT asks about things.
questions.retry_hint: Nora is asking about a thing - THE WORST THING THAT COULD HAPPEN - not about a person or a time. Ask: which question word asks about things and events? A person word would need somebody to point at.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'She also asked herself (2)________ she was so afraid, and realised the fear was simply about being judged.' Signal: blank = the reason = WHY. 'Why she was afraid' = asking for the reason.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'how' (method) or 'what' (thing). WHY = the reason for something.
questions.learning_tip: WHY = asking for the reason or cause. 'Why she was afraid' = asking for the reason behind her fear. WHY asks for reasons.
questions.retry_hint: She wants a reason, and the passage supplies it at once: the fear was ABOUT BEING JUDGED BY OTHERS. Ask: which question word asks for a reason? 'How' would ask about the method instead.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'She thought about (3)________ in the audience she trusted and focused on their faces.' Signal: blank = a person = WHO. 'Who she trusted' = asking about a person in the audience.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'which' (choice between things) instead of 'who' (person). The blank refers to a PERSON she trusted.
questions.learning_tip: WHO = asking about a person. 'Who she trusted' = which PERSON she trusted. WHO is used for people.
questions.retry_hint: The blank points at people IN THE AUDIENCE she TRUSTED, and she focuses on THEIR FRIENDLY FACES. Ask: which question word asks about a person? 'Which' would force her to choose from a fixed list.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'She remembered (4)________ she had first practised — her bedroom, in front of the mirror.' Signal: blank = a place = WHERE. 'Where she practised' = asking about the location.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'when' (time) instead of 'where' (place). The clue 'her bedroom, in front of the mirror' = a place = WHERE.
questions.learning_tip: WHERE = asking about a place or location. 'Where she practised' = the location where practice took place. WHERE asks about places.
questions.retry_hint: The dash gives the answer away as a place: HER BEDROOM, STANDING IN FRONT OF THE MIRROR. Ask: which question word asks about a location? A time word would need a clock or a date, not a room.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'She also remembered (5)________ her teacher first told her she had a gift for public speaking.' Signal: blank = a time = WHEN. 'When her teacher told her' = asking about the time/moment this happened.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'where' (place, already used) or 'how' (method). WHEN = the time or moment something occurred.
questions.learning_tip: WHEN = asking about time or the moment something happened. 'When her teacher told her' = at what point in time. WHEN asks about time.
questions.retry_hint: This blank is about a moment in time - the day HER TEACHER FIRST TOLD HER she had a gift. Ask: which question word asks about time? The place word has already been used for her bedroom.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'As she walked to the podium, she focused on (6)________ she would deliver her opening line.' Signal: blank = the method or manner = HOW. 'How she would deliver it' = in what way she would speak.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'what' (thing) instead of 'how' (manner). HOW = the way or method in which something is done.
questions.learning_tip: HOW = asking about the method, manner or way something is done. 'How she would deliver the line' = in what way she would speak. HOW asks about manner.
questions.retry_hint: She is thinking about the manner of her OPENING LINE - she wants to deliver it WITH CONFIDENCE. Ask: which question word asks in what way something is done? A thing word would ask which line, not the way she says it.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'She paused to decide (7)________ of her two prepared endings she would use.' Signal: blank = a choice between specific, known options = WHICH. 'Which of her two endings' = selecting from a specific set.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'what' instead of 'which'. WHICH = choosing from a specific, defined set of options; WHAT = asking about something open-ended.
questions.learning_tip: WHICH = used when choosing from a specific, limited set. 'Which of her two endings' = choosing from exactly two options. WHICH asks about specific choices.
questions.retry_hint: Count them: OF HER TWO PREPARED ENDINGS - the choice comes from a fixed, limited set. Ask: does the open question word belong here, or the choosing one? Use the choosing word whenever the options are already listed.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'At the end, the teacher announced (8)________ speech had won the class competition.' Signal: blank = possessive question word before noun 'speech' = WHOSE. 'Whose speech had won' = belonging to which person.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'who' (subject pronoun, not possessive before a noun) instead of 'whose' (possessive before 'speech').
questions.learning_tip: WHOSE = possessive question word used before a noun. 'WHOSE speech had won' = the speech belonging to whom. WHOSE = asking who something belongs to.
questions.retry_hint: The blank stands directly in front of the noun SPEECH, and the sentence ends by naming the owner: IT WAS NORA'S. Ask: which question word asks who something belongs to? A plain person word cannot stand before a noun like this.

C.passage: Before her first public speech, Nora asked herself (1)________ the worst thing that could happen was. She also asked herself (2)________ she was so afraid, and realised the fear was simply about being judged by others. She thought about (3)________ in the audience she trusted and decided to focus on their friendly faces. She remembered (4)________ she had first practised — her bedroom, standing in front of the mirror. She also remembered (5)________ her teacher first told her she had a gift for public speaking. As she walked to the podium, she focused only on (6)________ she would deliver her opening line with confidence. Midway through, she paused to decide (7)________ of her two prepared endings she would use. At the end, the teacher announced (8)________ speech had won the class competition — and it was Nora's.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: Every person faces challenges in life, and learning to deal with them is part of growing up. For some, the biggest challenge is dealing with (1)________ — the feeling of worry and nervousness before doing something difficult. When twelve-year-old Marcus first joined the swimming team, he (2)________ at the edge of the pool for several minutes before his first dive, unsure whether he could do it. His coach told him that being (3)________ does not mean having no fear — it means acting despite the fear. Over time, each (4)________ Marcus overcame in training made him stronger and more confident. On the day of the inter-school finals, Marcus swam his best race ever. Standing on the podium, he felt the full joy of (5)________ — the reward for all his months of hard work.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'feeling of worry and nervousness before doing something difficult' = anxiety.
questions.learning_tip: ANXIETY = a feeling of worry, nervousness or fear about something uncertain. Many people experience ANXIETY before important events.
questions.retry_hint: The dash defines it: THE FEELING OF WORRY AND NERVOUSNESS before doing something difficult. Ask: which box word names that feeling? The blank follows 'dealing with', so it must be a noun, not a describing word.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'paused at the edge of the pool for several minutes before his first dive, unsure' = paused in uncertainty = hesitated.
questions.learning_tip: HESITATED = paused or waited before doing something because of uncertainty or fear. Marcus HESITATED at the pool edge = he stopped, unsure whether to jump.
questions.retry_hint: He stood AT THE EDGE OF THE POOL FOR SEVERAL MINUTES, UNSURE WHETHER HE COULD DO IT. Ask: which box word means paused because of doubt? 'Stumbled' would mean he tripped, and that is not what held him back.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'acting despite the fear' = having courage even when afraid = courageous.
questions.learning_tip: COURAGEOUS = showing bravery by acting even when afraid. Being COURAGEOUS does not mean having no fear — it means choosing to act despite it.
questions.retry_hint: The clue is in the very same sentence: it DOES NOT MEAN HAVING NO FEAR - it means ACTING DESPITE THE FEAR. Ask: which box word describes a person who acts although afraid? The blank follows 'being', so a noun cannot fit.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'each ___ Marcus overcame in training made him stronger' = a difficulty or challenge to get past = obstacle.
questions.learning_tip: An OBSTACLE = a difficulty or challenge that stands in the way of progress. Overcoming each OBSTACLE in training builds strength and confidence.
questions.retry_hint: Each one is something Marcus OVERCAME IN TRAINING, and each MADE HIM STRONGER AND MORE CONFIDENT. Ask: which box word names a difficulty standing in your way? After 'each', the noun must be singular.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'the reward for all his months of hard work' and 'standing on the podium' = a great victory or success = triumph.
questions.learning_tip: TRIUMPH = a great success or victory, especially after difficulty. Standing on the podium = the moment of TRIUMPH after months of effort.
questions.retry_hint: He is STANDING ON THE PODIUM after swimming HIS BEST RACE EVER, and it is THE REWARD for months of hard work. Ask: which box word names a great victory? 'Anxiety' is what he felt at the start, not here.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.trap_type: Students write 'brave' (adjective) after the action verb 'stepped'. A verb needs an adverb.
questions.learning_tip: After an action verb (stepped), use an ADVERB: stepped BRAVELY. 'Brave' is an adjective — it describes nouns, not actions.
questions.retry_hint: The underlined word describes HOW the students STEPPED onto the stage - and stepping is an action. Ask: can an adjective describe an action, or does an action need an adverb? Listen for the missing tail on the word.

questions.trap_type: Students add -s to 'child'. 'Child' has a completely irregular plural form.
questions.learning_tip: CHILD -> CHILDREN (irregular). Same group: man -> men, woman -> women, tooth -> teeth.
questions.retry_hint: MANY CHILDS is wrong twice over: this noun never takes a plain -s. Ask: what is the plural of 'child'? It is one of the few English nouns that grows a completely new ending instead.

questions.error_type: Spelling — y → i rule before -ed (try → tried)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'tryed' instead of applying the y→i rule before -ed.
questions.learning_tip: 'Try' ends in consonant + y: change y → i before -ed. try → TRIED. Same rule: cry → cried, carry → carried, study → studied.
questions.retry_hint: 'TRY' ends in a consonant plus -y. Ask: what happens to that -y before you add -ed? Compare: cry becomes cried, carry becomes carried, study becomes studied.

questions.trap_type: 'The students' is plural. Students write 'was' (singular).
questions.learning_tip: 'The students' = plural → WERE all trembling. WAS is only for singular subjects.
questions.retry_hint: THE STUDENTS is plural - the whole group is standing in the wings. Ask: does a plural subject take 'was', or its plural partner? Match the verb to the subject, never to the word standing beside it.

questions.trap_type: Students write a plain plural and leave out the apostrophe that shows ownership.
questions.learning_tip: The feedback BELONGS TO the coaches -> COACHES' feedback (apostrophe after the -s for a plural). Singular: coach's.
questions.retry_hint: The WARM FEEDBACK came from more than one coach - the whole coaching team. Ask: does a plain -s show ownership, or only number? Where does the apostrophe belong when the owners are many?

E.passage: On the day of the school's talent show, many students felt nervous but stepped brave (1) onto the stage. Many childs (2) from the lower primary classes performed as well, singing together in the opening item. Every student tryed (3) their best, even those who made small mistakes. Before the final act, the students was (4) all trembling in the wings. After the show, the coaches (5) warm feedback helped everyone feel proud of what they had achieved.

questions.sentence_a: You practise every day.
questions.sentence_b: Your confidence will grow over time.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'If'.
questions.model_answer: If you practise every day, your confidence will grow over time.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'If you will practise every day, your confidence will grow' — adding 'will' in the 'if' clause.
questions.learning_tip: Conditional: IF + simple present, simple future. If you PRACTISE every day, your confidence WILL GROW. Never 'will' in the 'if' clause.
questions.retry_hint: Sentence A sets the condition; sentence B is what follows from it. Ask: after 'If', does the verb stay in the simple present, or take a future helper? Only the second half of the sentence may look forward.

questions.sentence_a: The coach said to Marcus, 'You performed better than anyone expected today.'
questions.instruction: Rewrite using reported speech: The coach told Marcus that ________.
questions.model_answer: The coach told Marcus that he had performed better than anyone had expected that day.
questions.trap_type: Students keep 'you' instead of 'he', or keep 'today' instead of 'that day'.
questions.learning_tip: Reported speech: 'you' → 'he'; 'today' → 'that day'. The coach told Marcus that HE had performed better than anyone expected THAT DAY.
questions.retry_hint: The coach spoke straight to MARCUS and said 'YOU'. Ask: which pronoun takes over when the words are reported to somebody else? And when 'said' becomes 'told', what happens to the word TODAY, and to the tense of the verb?

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
Class 3F arrived at the adventure camp on a Monday morning. Their first challenge was a six-metre climbing wall. From the ground, it looked enormous.

Most students cheered and lined up eagerly. But a boy named Wei stood at the back. His palms were sweating. He had never liked heights.

When it was his turn, Wei put on his harness and approached the wall. He placed his hands on the first holds. Then he stopped. His feet felt glued to the ground.

'Take one step,' said the instructor quietly.

Wei looked up. The wall seemed impossibly high. He looked down at the instructor. Then he looked up again and took one step.

And then another. And another.

He did not reach the top. He stopped about halfway up. But when he came down, his classmates — even those who had reached the top — clapped for him.

'Why are they clapping?' Wei asked the instructor. 'I didn't make it to the top.'

The instructor smiled. 'They're clapping because they saw what it took for you to get even halfway.'

mcq_questions.stem: What happened IMMEDIATELY AFTER Wei placed his hands on the first holds?

options.1: He reached the top of the wall.
options.2: He stopped — his feet felt glued to the ground.
options.3: The instructor told him to take one step.
options.4: His classmates started clapping for him.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 3 thinking the instructor spoke first. But IMMEDIATELY after placing his hands, Wei stopped. The instructor spoke after that.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 3: Wei placed his hands on the holds → THEN he stopped, feet feeling glued. IMMEDIATELY after placing his hands = he stopped (option 2). The instructor spoke next.

mcq_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 2, is it True or False that Wei was the only student who did not want to climb the wall? Give a reason from the passage.
mcq_questions.model_answer: False. The passage says 'MOST students cheered and lined up eagerly' — implying not all students were equally eager. However, Wei is the only student specifically described as afraid. The passage does not say Wei was the only one who was nervous, only the only one whose fear is described in detail.
mcq_questions.trap_type: Students say 'True, Wei was the only afraid student.' The passage says 'most' students were eager, implying some may not have been — and Wei is simply the one highlighted.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 2: 'MOST students cheered' = not ALL. So there may have been others who were nervous. It is FALSE that Wei was confirmed as the ONLY nervous student.

mcq_questions.stem: The instructor said the classmates were clapping because 'they saw what it took for you to get even halfway.' What did the instructor mean?

options.1: The classmates felt sorry for Wei because he did not reach the top.
options.2: The classmates were clapping out of politeness, not genuine admiration.
options.3: Reaching halfway required more real courage from Wei than reaching the top did for others, because he faced and overcame his fear.
options.4: The instructor thought Wei should have tried harder to reach the top.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking the clapping = pity. But the instructor's words make clear it was ADMIRATION, not pity.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: The instructor means: for Wei, going halfway required GREATER COURAGE because he was genuinely afraid. Others climbed without that internal struggle. His courage was more visible — and more admirable.

open_ended_questions.stem: How tall was the climbing wall, and where did Wei stand when the students first lined up?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: The climbing wall was six metres tall. Wei stood at the back of the line.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students give only one of the two details.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1: wall was SIX METRES tall. Paragraph 2: Wei stood at the BACK. Give both specific details.

open_ended_questions.stem: What was the CAUSE of Wei's difficulty on the wall? What was the EFFECT on his classmates when they saw him climb?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: CAUSE: Wei had a fear of heights — his palms sweated and his feet felt glued to the ground when he stood in front of the wall. EFFECT: Even classmates who reached the top clapped for him when he came down, showing genuine admiration for the courage he displayed.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students describe only Wei's difficulty without explaining what effect his effort had on classmates.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: CAUSE: Wei had a FEAR OF HEIGHTS — sweating palms, feet feeling glued. EFFECT: his classmates CLAPPED for him in admiration, even those who reached the top.

open_ended_questions.stem: Find the phrase in paragraph 3 that shows Wei was paralysed by fear at the base of the wall.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: 'His feet felt glued to the ground.'
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students quote 'He placed his hands on the first holds' which describes action, not paralysis.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 3: 'His FEET FELT GLUED TO THE GROUND.' This phrase shows he could not move — paralysed by fear at the base of the wall.

open_ended_questions.stem: What advice did the instructor give Wei, and why was it effective?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: The instructor told Wei to 'take one step.' It was effective because it broke the overwhelming challenge into a single small action, which Wei could manage, and that first step led to more steps.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'the instructor encouraged him' without describing the specific advice or why it worked.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 4: 'Take ONE STEP.' The advice was effective because it reduced the overwhelming challenge to a SINGLE SMALL action. One step led to another.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on his actions in the passage, describe TWO character traits of Wei with evidence from the passage.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: Wei is a self-aware and persistent person. Firstly, his self-awareness is shown when he recognised and admitted his fear of heights — he stood at the back of the line, knowing he was afraid, rather than pretending to be fine. Secondly, his persistence is shown when, despite his feet feeling glued to the ground, he listened to the instructor and forced himself to take one step, then another, until he reached halfway — showing that he kept going even though every step required effort.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say he is 'brave and shy' without naming precise character traits or providing evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Name precise TRAITS then give EVIDENCE: (1) SELF-AWARE — stood at the back knowing he was afraid; (2) PERSISTENT — took ONE STEP at a time and kept going despite fear.

questions.stem: The hawker centre was ________ with the smell of freshly cooked char kway teow and laksa.
questions.trap_type: 'Silent' and 'empty' suggest absence; 'frozen' is for temperature. Only 'filled' = full of a smell, sound or quality.
questions.learning_tip: FILLED WITH = full of a smell, quality or thing. The hawker centre was FILLED WITH the smell of food = the smell was everywhere.
questions.retry_hint: The SMELL OF FRESHLY COOKED CHAR KWAY TEOW AND LAKSA is everywhere inside the HAWKER CENTRE. Ask: which word completes 'was ___ with' to mean full of something? 'Empty' and 'silent' say the exact opposite.

questions.stem: The Singapore Botanic Gardens is a ________ site, recognised by the United Nations for its natural and cultural importance.
questions.trap_type: 'Ordinary' and 'forgotten' suggest unimportance; 'damaged' is negative. Only 'heritage' = related to cultural or historical legacy worth preserving.
questions.learning_tip: A HERITAGE site = a place of cultural, historical or natural importance that is officially protected and preserved. Singapore's Botanic Gardens is a UNESCO HERITAGE site.
questions.retry_hint: The gardens are RECOGNISED BY THE UNITED NATIONS for their NATURAL AND CULTURAL IMPORTANCE - a place worth protecting for ever. Ask: which adjective names that kind of protected site? 'Ordinary' and 'forgotten' would mean nobody cared.

questions.stem: The Peranakan neighbourhood of Katong is known for its ________ shophouses painted in pastel shades.
questions.trap_type: 'Dull' and 'colourless' suggest plainness; 'crumbling' = falling apart. Only 'ornate' = richly decorated and detailed.
questions.learning_tip: ORNATE = richly and elaborately decorated with detailed patterns or carvings. Peranakan shophouses are ORNATE with floral tiles and colourful paintwork.
questions.retry_hint: The SHOPHOUSES are PAINTED IN PASTEL SHADES and covered with fine decoration. Ask: which adjective means richly and elaborately decorated? 'Dull' and 'colourless' describe plain walls, and 'crumbling' means falling apart.

questions.stem: Singaporeans from different races and religions ________ at public festivals, sharing food and celebrating together.
questions.trap_type: 'Separate' and 'compete' suggest division or rivalry. Only 'mingle' = mix socially with people from different backgrounds.
questions.learning_tip: MINGLE = mix or interact socially with others, especially people from different groups. At festivals, Singaporeans from all communities MINGLE freely.
questions.retry_hint: Singaporeans FROM DIFFERENT RACES AND RELIGIONS are SHARING FOOD AND CELEBRATING TOGETHER. Ask: which verb means mixing socially with people of other backgrounds? 'Separate' and 'argue' would pull the crowd apart.

questions.stem: The government's effort to ________ Singapore's old districts ensures that future generations can still experience the city's history.
questions.trap_type: 'Demolish' = destroy; 'relocate' = move elsewhere; 'replicate' = copy. Only 'conserve' = protect and preserve from damage or destruction.
questions.learning_tip: CONSERVE = protect something valuable from damage, destruction or change. The government CONSERVES old districts = works to keep them intact for future generations.
questions.retry_hint: The aim is that FUTURE GENERATIONS CAN STILL EXPERIENCE THE CITY'S HISTORY, so the OLD DISTRICTS must survive untouched. Ask: which verb means protecting something from damage or destruction? 'Demolish' would flatten them.

questions.stem: Every National Day, thousands of Singaporeans ________ at the Padang to watch the parade.
questions.trap_type: 'Every National Day' = regular annual event = simple present. 'Singaporeans' = plural → no -s.
questions.learning_tip: 'Every National Day' = a regular annual event = simple present. Singaporeans (plural) → GATHER at the Padang.
questions.retry_hint: EVERY NATIONAL DAY marks a habit repeated each year, and THOUSANDS OF SINGAPOREANS is plural. Ask: in the simple present, does a plural subject take the plain verb, or the one with -s on the end?

questions.stem: The architect ________ the design for the Esplanade building after studying the durian fruit.
questions.trap_type: Completed past action. 'Base' is regular: base → based.
questions.learning_tip: Completed past action. 'Base' is regular: base → BASED the design on the durian fruit.
questions.retry_hint: AFTER STUDYING THE DURIAN FRUIT - the studying is over, and the ESPLANADE design is done. Ask: which form shows a finished past action? This verb is regular, so the past takes the ordinary ending.

questions.stem: The tour guide ________ about the history of Chinatown when a visitor interrupted with a question.
questions.trap_type: 'A visitor interrupted' = sudden interrupting event. The guide was already speaking = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: The visitor INTERRUPTED = sudden past event. The guide was already speaking at that moment = WAS SPEAKING.
questions.retry_hint: A VISITOR INTERRUPTED WITH A QUESTION - a sudden event breaking into something already going on. Ask: which choice keeps the guide in the middle of his talk about CHINATOWN at that past moment?

questions.stem: The Marina Bay area looks especially beautiful at night, ________ it?
questions.trap_type: Main clause is positive present simple ('looks') → negative tag. 'Looks' = singular present → auxiliary 'does'. Negative tag = doesn't.
questions.learning_tip: Question tag for positive simple present: [positive] + DOESN'T + subject? The area LOOKS beautiful, DOESN'T it? Positive → negative tag; 'looks' → 'does'.
questions.retry_hint: The statement is positive and present: THE MARINA BAY AREA LOOKS beautiful. Ask: after a positive statement, does the tag flip to negative? And with no 'is' or 'are' in the statement, which helping verb must stand in for the plain present verb?

questions.stem: These shophouses have not been renovated for decades, ________ they?
questions.trap_type: Main clause is NEGATIVE present perfect ('have not been') → POSITIVE tag. 'Have not' → positive tag = have they.
questions.learning_tip: Question tag for negative present perfect: [negative] + HAVE + subject? 'These shophouses HAVE NOT been renovated, HAVE they?' Negative → positive tag.
questions.retry_hint: The statement about THESE SHOPHOUSES is negative - no renovation FOR DECADES. Ask: after a negative statement, does the tag turn positive? The tag must reuse the statement's own helping verb; it cannot borrow 'were'.

questions.stem: There ________ only a few traditional kampung houses remaining in Singapore today.
questions.trap_type: 'A few traditional kampung houses' = plural. Present fact → are.
questions.learning_tip: 'A few traditional kampung houses' = plural. Present fact → THERE ARE only a few remaining.
questions.retry_hint: ONLY A FEW TRADITIONAL KAMPUNG HOUSES means more than one, and TODAY sets the time in the present. Ask: does a plural subject take a singular verb, or a plural one? A past form would clash with 'today'.

questions.stem: The iconic Merlion statue ________ by many tourists every year and featured in countless photographs.
questions.trap_type: The Merlion is visited by tourists (passive). 'The Merlion statue' = singular → is visited.
questions.learning_tip: The Merlion statue is the receiver of the action. Present passive = IS VISITED. Singular subject = IS.
questions.retry_hint: THE ICONIC MERLION STATUE does not do the action - MANY TOURISTS do it EVERY YEAR. Ask: which choice puts the subject on the receiving end, in the present tense? Remember the statue counts as ONE thing, so its helping verb must be singular.

questions.stem: The heritage board told residents ________ the original tiles and wooden shutters when restoring old shophouses.
questions.trap_type: Reported speech: told + object + to + base verb.
questions.learning_tip: 'Told residents TO + base verb': told residents TO PRESERVE the original tiles and shutters.
questions.retry_hint: TOLD RESIDENTS = a reported instruction about THE ORIGINAL TILES AND WOODEN SHUTTERS. Ask: after 'told + person', which form comes next - the plain verb, the -ing form, or the infinitive with its marker? A past participle cannot follow.

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Prepositions of place and direction)

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Singapore is a small island nation located (1)________ South-East Asia.' Signal: inside a region/continent = IN. 'Located IN South-East Asia' = within the geographical region.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'at' or 'on' instead of 'in'. IN = inside a region, country or city.
questions.learning_tip: IN = inside a country, city or region. Singapore is located IN South-East Asia = it is within that geographical area.
questions.retry_hint: SOUTH-EAST ASIA is a whole region, and Singapore sits inside it. Ask: which preposition goes with countries, cities and large areas? The exact-point preposition is needed by a single named spot such as THE PADANG.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Families gather (2)________ the Padang on National Day to watch the celebrations.' Signal: specific location/event point = AT. 'Gather AT the Padang' = at that specific named place.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'in' (inside a large area) or 'on' (surface). AT = at a specific named location.
questions.learning_tip: AT = at a specific location or place. Families gather AT the Padang = at that exact named public area.
questions.retry_hint: THE PADANG is one exact, named place, and that is where families gather ON NATIONAL DAY. Ask: which preposition marks a specific point or spot, rather than a whole region or a surface?

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Hawker centres are found (3)________ almost every street in Singapore.' Signal: positioned along or throughout a surface/route = ON. 'ON every street' = along the street.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'in' (inside) or 'at' (a point). ON every street = located along each street.
questions.learning_tip: ON = used for surfaces and routes. Hawker centres are found ON almost every street = located along each street.
questions.retry_hint: HAWKER CENTRES are found along ALMOST EVERY STREET - and streets are routes you travel down, like roads and pavements. Ask: which preposition belongs with surfaces and routes? The region word is already needed by SOUTH-EAST ASIA.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The Gardens by the Bay Supertrees stand (4)________ the surrounding parkland, some reaching fifty metres high.' Signal: at a higher level, towering = ABOVE. The supertrees are elevated ABOVE the surrounding parkland.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'over' (crossing from one side to another) instead of 'above' (at a higher level, static position).
questions.learning_tip: ABOVE = at a higher level than something, used for static position. The supertrees stand ABOVE the parkland = they are taller and higher up.
questions.retry_hint: The SUPERTREES simply STAND there, SOME REACHING FIFTY METRES HIGH - they do not cross the parkland, they tower higher than it. Ask: which preposition shows a higher, motionless position? The crossing word is needed by the bridge.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The Henderson Waves Bridge arches (5)________ a forested valley connecting two hilltops.' Signal: spanning across from one side to another = OVER. 'Arches OVER a valley' = extends across it from above.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'above' (higher level, static) instead of 'over' (spanning or crossing). 'Over a valley' = the bridge spans it.
questions.learning_tip: OVER = spanning or extending across something. The bridge arches OVER the valley = it goes from one side to the other across the valley.
questions.retry_hint: The bridge ARCHES from one hilltop right across to the other, CONNECTING TWO HILLTOPS with A FORESTED VALLEY beneath. Ask: which preposition shows something spanning a gap from side to side?

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The old shophouses (6)________ Chinatown's main street hide courtyards full of history.' Signal: at the back of / further than = BEHIND. The courtyards are BEHIND (at the back of) the shophouses.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'under' or 'below'. The shophouses are not beneath the street - they stand at the BACK of it, away from the main road.
questions.learning_tip: BEHIND = at the back of something. The shophouses BEHIND the main street are the ones on the far side of it, hidden from the front.
questions.retry_hint: The SHOPHOUSES stand away from CHINATOWN'S MAIN STREET, and their INNER COURTYARDS are hidden from the front. Ask: which preposition puts one thing at the back of another? Nothing here is underneath the road.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Street vendors used to sell food (7)________ large umbrellas along the Singapore River.' Signal: sheltered directly beneath something = UNDER. Selling UNDER large umbrellas = beneath them for shade.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'below' (lower level, not necessarily sheltered beneath) or 'above' (higher). UNDER = directly beneath for shelter.
questions.learning_tip: UNDER = directly below and often sheltered by something. Vendors sold food UNDER large umbrellas = they were sheltered directly beneath the umbrellas.
questions.retry_hint: The STREET VENDORS needed shelter: they SELL FOOD directly beneath LARGE UMBRELLAS. Ask: which preposition means covered and sheltered right beneath something? The general lower-level word is needed by the MRT.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The MRT runs (8)________ the city streets, connecting different districts through an underground network.' Signal: at a lower level than the streets, not directly sheltered = BELOW. The MRT is BELOW the streets (underground), not sheltered under them.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'under' (directly beneath, sheltered) instead of 'below' (at a lower level in general). BELOW = at a lower level; UNDER = directly beneath and sheltered.
questions.learning_tip: BELOW = at a lower level than something. The MRT runs BELOW the city streets = it is at a lower level underground. 'Below' is used for general lower level position.
questions.retry_hint: The MRT RUNS through tunnels at a lower level than THE CITY STREETS, and nothing is sheltering it. Ask: which preposition means simply at a lower level? The sheltered-beneath word has already gone to the umbrellas.

C.passage: Singapore is a small island nation located (1)________ South-East Asia. Families gather (2)________ the Padang on National Day to watch the celebrations together. Hawker centres are found (3)________ almost every street in Singapore, serving food from all of the country's main communities. The Gardens by the Bay Supertrees stand (4)________ the surrounding parkland, some reaching fifty metres high. The Henderson Waves Bridge arches (5)________ a forested valley connecting two hilltops in the southern ridge. The old shophouses (6)________ Chinatown's main street hide inner courtyards full of history. Street vendors used to sell food (7)________ large umbrellas along the Singapore River over a century ago. Today, the MRT runs (8)________ the city streets, connecting different districts through one of the world's most efficient underground networks.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: Singapore is one of the most (1)________ countries in Asia. Its population includes Chinese, Malay, Indian and Eurasian communities, as well as people from many other parts of the world. Walking through the city, you will hear all four official languages, and older residents may still greet one another in a Chinese (2)________ such as Hokkien or Teochew. Temples, mosques, churches and synagogues stand side by side along the same street. This (3)________ mix of cultures, religions and traditions is a source of national pride. One of the most (4)________ images of the country is its city (5)________ at night - a glittering line of skyscrapers reflected in the waters of Marina Bay.

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'multicultural' (blank 3 needs it). The clue here is the LIST of communities: Chinese, Malay, Indian, Eurasian and many more.
questions.learning_tip: DIVERSE = made up of many different kinds. A DIVERSE population contains many different races and backgrounds.
questions.retry_hint: The clue is the list that follows: CHINESE, MALAY, INDIAN AND EURASIAN communities, plus people from MANY OTHER PARTS OF THE WORLD. Ask: which box word means made up of many different kinds? Blank 3 needs the longer word built from 'culture'.

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'ancestors'. The blank follows 'a Chinese', so it must be a singular noun, and the examples are HOKKIEN and TEOCHEW - ways of speaking.
questions.learning_tip: A DIALECT = a regional form of a language, with its own words and pronunciation. Hokkien and Teochew are Chinese DIALECTS.
questions.retry_hint: The blank follows 'A CHINESE', so it must be a singular noun, and the examples are HOKKIEN and TEOCHEW - ways of speaking, not people. Ask: which box word names a regional form of a language?

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'diverse' (blank 1 needs it). The clue is the noun that follows: a MIX OF CULTURES, RELIGIONS AND TRADITIONS.
questions.learning_tip: MULTICULTURAL = made up of many cultures living together. A MULTICULTURAL society celebrates the festivals of every community.
questions.retry_hint: The noun after the blank does the work: A MIX OF CULTURES, RELIGIONS AND TRADITIONS living side by side. Ask: which box word is built from 'many' plus 'culture'? The plain word for variety has already gone to blank 1.

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'diverse'. The clue is 'one of the most ___ IMAGES of the country' - the picture everyone recognises at once.
questions.learning_tip: ICONIC = famous and instantly recognised as a symbol of something. The Merlion is an ICONIC image of Singapore.
questions.retry_hint: The blank describes IMAGES OF THE COUNTRY - the picture the whole world recognises at a glance. Ask: which box word means famous as a symbol of a place? 'Diverse' describes people, not a photograph.

questions.trap_type: Students pick 'harmony'. The dash explains it: A GLITTERING LINE OF SKYSCRAPERS reflected in the water.
questions.learning_tip: A SKYLINE = the shape that a city's tall buildings make against the sky.
questions.retry_hint: The dash paints it for you: A GLITTERING LINE OF SKYSCRAPERS REFLECTED IN THE WATERS OF MARINA BAY. Ask: which box word names the shape a city's tall buildings cut against the sky? It follows 'its city', so it must be a noun.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.trap_type: Students write 'vivid' (adjective) after the action verb 'described'. A verb needs an adverb.
questions.learning_tip: After an action verb (described), use an ADVERB: described VIVIDLY. 'Vivid' is an adjective — it describes nouns, not actions.
questions.retry_hint: The underlined word tells us HOW the guide DESCRIBED the trade routes - and describing is an action. Ask: does an action take an adjective, or an adverb? Nearly every adverb of manner ends the same way.

questions.trap_type: Students simply add -s to 'shelf'. Nouns ending in -f or -fe usually change to -ves.
questions.learning_tip: SHELF -> SHELVES. Same rule: leaf -> leaves, knife -> knives, half -> halves, wolf -> wolves.
questions.retry_hint: WOODEN SHELFS breaks a rule: a noun ending in -f rarely takes a plain -s. Ask: how do you write more than one leaf, or more than one wolf? The -f must turn into something else first.

questions.error_type: Spelling — doubling rule: short vowel + single consonant before -ing
questions.trap_type: Students write 'stoping' with one 'p'. 'Stop' has a short vowel (o) + single consonant (p) → double the p before -ing.
questions.learning_tip: 'Stop' has a short vowel + single consonant: stop → STOPPING (double the p). Same rule: run → running, sit → sitting, jog → jogging.
questions.retry_hint: 'STOP' has a short vowel and ONE final consonant. Ask: what must happen to that consonant before -ing is added? Compare: run, sit and jog all do the very same thing.

questions.trap_type: 'The visitors' is plural. Students match the verb to the nearest word instead.
questions.learning_tip: 'The visitors' = plural -> WERE all amazed by the batik display. WAS is only for singular subjects.
questions.retry_hint: THE VISITORS is plural - a whole museum group standing in front of the BATIK CLOTH. Ask: does a plural subject take 'was', or its plural partner? The nearest noun must never decide the verb.

questions.error_type: Plural — consonant + y → drop y, add -ies (city → cities)
questions.trap_type: Students add -s to 'city', producing 'citys'. When a word ends in consonant + y, change y to i and add -es.
questions.learning_tip: 'City' ends in consonant + y → change y to i and add -es: city → CITIES. Same rule: country → countries, story → stories.
questions.retry_hint: TRADING CITYS is wrong: this noun ends in a consonant plus -y. Ask: what happens to that -y before the plural ending is added? Compare: country becomes countries, story becomes stories.

E.passage: Our class visited the Asian Civilisations Museum last Friday. Our guide described vivid (1) the ancient trade routes that connected Singapore to other parts of Asia. The oldest pottery bowls were arranged on wooden shelfs (2) inside a tall glass case. We spent time stoping (3) at each exhibit and reading the detailed captions. The visitors was (4) all amazed by a display of beautiful batik cloth from the region. At the end, we learned that Singapore's location made it one of the greatest trading citys (5) in South-East Asia.

questions.sentence_a: Singapore preserves its heritage buildings.
questions.sentence_b: Future generations will be able to experience the city's history.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'so that'.
questions.model_answer: Singapore preserves its heritage buildings so that future generations will be able to experience the city's history.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'Singapore preserves its heritage buildings so future generations will be able to' — omitting 'that' after 'so'.
questions.learning_tip: SO THAT = in order that (purpose). Singapore preserves heritage buildings SO THAT future generations CAN experience history. 'So that' introduces the purpose.
questions.retry_hint: Singapore protects its HERITAGE BUILDINGS for a reason, and sentence B is that reason. Ask: which two little words join a purpose to an action - and is it enough to write only the first of the two? Both are needed.

questions.sentence_a: The hawker centre near Tanjong Pagar serves traditional dishes.
questions.sentence_b: The hawker centre has been operating for over forty years.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using the relative pronoun 'which'.
questions.model_answer: The hawker centre near Tanjong Pagar, which has been operating for over forty years, serves traditional dishes.
