questions.context_check: Passage: 'The dentist said the decay would spread (7)________ the filling was done that day.' Signal: the decay will spread IF the filling is NOT done = UNLESS. UNLESS = if not / except if.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'if' instead of 'unless'. UNLESS = if not. 'Unless the filling was done' = 'if the filling was NOT done'.
questions.learning_tip: UNLESS = if not / except if. The decay would spread UNLESS the filling was done = it would spread IF the filling was NOT done.
questions.retry_hint: The DECAY WOULD SPREAD in one case only: the FILLING was NOT done that day. Ask: which single conjunction already carries a hidden negative inside it, so you never have to add one?

questions.context_check: Passage: '(8)________ Liam left the clinic, he felt a wave of relief wash over him.' Signal: at the same time as / in the moment that he was leaving = AS. AS = at the same time as, used for gradual or simultaneous actions.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'when' or 'while'. The easing of his shoulders and the passing of the minutes happen gradually, side by side.
questions.learning_tip: AS = at the same time as, used for gradual, side-by-side change: AS the minutes passed, the tightness slowly eased.
questions.retry_hint: THE MINUTES PASSED and, little by little, the TIGHTNESS in his shoulders EASED - both changes creep along together. Ask: which conjunction fits gradual, side-by-side change? A sudden-moment word would jar here.

C.passage: (1)________ Liam was nervous about his dentist appointment, he walked in calmly and sat down in the waiting room. His heart beat faster (2)________ the dentist switched on the drill. Liam counted the ceiling tiles (3)________ the dentist was working carefully on his tooth. He could not feel any pain (4)________ the anaesthetic had numbed the area around his gum. The dentist has treated Liam (5)________ he was six years old, so she knows exactly how nervous he gets and always speaks to him in a calm, steady voice. She told him to raise his hand (6)________ he felt any discomfort during the procedure. She warned him that the decay would spread further (7)________ the filling was done that day. (8)________ the minutes passed, the tightness in his shoulders slowly eased, and by the time he left the clinic he felt a wave of relief.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: Our dentist taught us a lot about keeping our teeth healthy during our last visit. She explained that (1)________ is a hard outer layer that protects the tooth from damage — and that eating too much sugar slowly wears it away. When bacteria combine with food particles, they form a sticky coating called (2)________ on the surface of the teeth. If not cleaned away regularly, this leads to tooth decay and a (3)________, which is a small hole that develops in the tooth. To prevent this, we should brush twice a day and (4)________ between our teeth every night to remove food particles that the toothbrush cannot reach. Before doing a filling, dentists inject medicine to (5)________ the area so the patient does not feel any pain during the procedure.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'hard outer layer that protects the tooth' = enamel.
questions.learning_tip: ENAMEL = the hard outer layer of a tooth that protects it from decay. Sugar slowly wears away ENAMEL.
questions.retry_hint: The clue is right in the sentence: HARD OUTER LAYER THAT PROTECTS THE TOOTH, worn away by SUGAR. Ask: which box word names that protective coat? The sticky film forms on top of it - it is not the tooth's own layer.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'sticky coating formed by bacteria and food particles on teeth' = plaque.
questions.learning_tip: PLAQUE = a sticky film of bacteria that forms on teeth. If not removed by brushing, PLAQUE causes tooth decay.
questions.retry_hint: BACTERIA combine with FOOD PARTICLES to form a STICKY COATING on the surface of the teeth. Ask: which box word names that film? A hole in the tooth comes later, and it is not the coating itself.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'a small hole that develops in the tooth' = cavity.
questions.learning_tip: A CAVITY = a small hole in a tooth caused by tooth decay. Dentists fill a CAVITY to prevent it from getting larger.
questions.retry_hint: The sentence defines it for you: A SMALL HOLE THAT DEVELOPS IN THE TOOTH after TOOTH DECAY. Ask: which box word names that hole? The sticky film and the hard outer layer are not holes.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'between our teeth every night to remove food particles the toothbrush cannot reach' = floss.
questions.learning_tip: FLOSS = use dental floss (a thin thread) to clean between teeth. You should FLOSS every day to remove plaque between teeth.
questions.retry_hint: You already BRUSH TWICE A DAY; this second action cleans BETWEEN OUR TEETH, where the TOOTHBRUSH CANNOT REACH. Ask: which box word is the verb for using thin thread between the teeth?

questions.trap_type: The clue 'inject medicine so the patient does not feel any pain' = make the area unable to feel = numb.
questions.learning_tip: NUMB = without feeling, unable to sense pain. Dentists inject anaesthetic to NUMB the area before doing a filling.
questions.retry_hint: Dentists INJECT MEDICINE so the patient DOES NOT FEEL ANY PAIN during the procedure. Ask: which box word is the verb meaning to take all feeling away from an area? A noun cannot follow 'medicine to ___'.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.error_type: Homophone confusion — its (possessive) vs it's (it is)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'its' (possessive pronoun) when the sentence needs 'it's' = it is. These look almost identical but have different meanings.
questions.learning_tip: ITS = belonging to it (possessive). IT'S = it is (contraction). 'IT'S important to brush your teeth' = 'It is important'. Use IT'S when you can replace it with 'it is'.
questions.retry_hint: Stretch the underlined word into its long form and read it before IMPORTANT: does 'belonging to it' make any sense? Ask: which spelling can be opened out into two words? A possessive never can. Test by expanding, not by sound.

questions.trap_type: Students write 'gentle' (adjective) after the action verb 'brushed'. A verb needs an adverb to describe how.
questions.learning_tip: After an action verb (brushed), use an ADVERB: brushed GENTLY. 'Gentle' is an adjective — it describes nouns, not actions.
questions.retry_hint: BRUSHED is an action, and the underlined word tells you HOW the brushing was done. Ask: does an action need an adjective, or a word carrying the -ly ending? Adjectives describe nouns, never verbs.

questions.trap_type: Students add -s to 'tooth', producing 'tooths'. 'Tooth' has a completely irregular plural form.
questions.learning_tip: 'Tooth' has an irregular plural: tooth → TEETH. Never write 'tooths'. Other irregular plurals: foot → feet, goose → geese.
questions.retry_hint: TOOTHS is the trap: this noun does not build its plural with -s at all. Ask: how do you write more than one FOOT, or more than one goose? The same kind of change happens here - the vowels shift.

questions.trap_type: 'The children' is plural. Students write 'was' (singular) by matching the verb to the nearest word.
questions.learning_tip: 'The children' = plural -> WERE very cooperative during their check-up. WAS is only for singular subjects.
questions.retry_hint: Count the subject: THE CHILDREN, not one child. Ask: does a plural subject take 'was', or its plural partner? Match the verb to the subject, never to the word standing nearest to it.

questions.error_type: Comparative form — more + adjective for two-syllable+ words (not -er)
questions.trap_type: Students add -er to 'painful', producing 'painfuller'. Two-syllable+ adjectives use 'more', never -er.
questions.learning_tip: PAINFUL is a long adjective (2+ syllables): use MORE PAINFUL, not 'painfuller'. Long adjectives always use MORE for the comparative form.
questions.retry_hint: PAINFULLER crams an ending onto a two-syllable adjective. Ask: do long adjectives take -er, or do they need a helper word placed in front? Compare: careful, helpful, useful - none of them take -er.

E.passage: Our dentist always reminds us that its (1) important to brush our teeth before bed. At our last appointment, the hygienist showed us how to hold the toothbrush and brushed gentle (2) on the gum line to prevent damage. She also pointed out that two of our tooths (3) had early signs of plaque build-up. The children was (4) very cooperative during their check-up and followed every instruction carefully. The dentist mentioned that a toothache left untreated will become painfuller (5) over time, so early visits are always the wisest choice.

questions.sentence_a: She brushes her teeth every morning.
questions.sentence_b: She has never had a cavity.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'Since'.
questions.model_answer: Since she brushes her teeth every morning, she has never had a cavity.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'She brushes her teeth every morning since she has never had a cavity' — reversing the cause and result.
questions.learning_tip: SINCE = because of an ongoing or established fact. SINCE she brushes every morning, she has never had a cavity. The reason comes after 'since'.
questions.retry_hint: One sentence is a cause, one is a result. She has NEVER HAD A CAVITY - is that the reason, or the outcome? Ask: after 'Since', which half must come first? Then a comma separates the two halves.

questions.sentence_a: You floss every day.
questions.sentence_b: Your teeth will not be as healthy as they could be.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'Unless'.
questions.model_answer: Unless you floss every day, your teeth will not be as healthy as they could be.
questions.trap_type: Students add 'will' in the 'unless' clause: 'Unless you will floss every day' — incorrect.
questions.learning_tip: UNLESS + simple present, simple future. UNLESS you FLOSS every day, your teeth WILL NOT BE as healthy. Never 'will' after 'unless'.
questions.retry_hint: 'Unless' packs a hidden negative inside itself, so nothing else in that half may be negative. Ask: which half is the condition - FLOSS EVERY DAY, or the state of your TEETH? And can 'will' ever sit after 'unless'?

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
Nine-year-old Priya had not been to the dentist in two years. Every time her mother suggested a visit, Priya found a reason to postpone it — a school project, a family outing, a stomach ache that appeared just in time.

But one Tuesday morning, Priya woke up with a sharp pain in her lower left molar. It throbbed steadily, like a tiny hammer tapping from the inside. She tried to ignore it, but by lunchtime, she could not chew her food properly.

Her mother made an appointment for that same afternoon. The clinic was small and brightly lit. Dr Nair, a tall woman with a gentle voice, welcomed Priya without any fuss. She examined the tooth quickly and explained that there was a cavity that needed to be filled.

'Will it hurt?' Priya asked.

'There will be a small pinch,' said Dr Nair. 'After that, you will feel nothing.'

She was right. The injection stung for two seconds. Then the whole left side of Priya's mouth felt like a thick cushion. The filling itself took twelve minutes.

Walking out, Priya felt something she had not expected: relief. Not just because it was over, but because it was so much smaller than the fear she carried for two years.

'You should have come sooner,' her mother said.

Priya nodded. She already knew.

mcq_questions.stem: Why had Priya not visited the dentist for two years?

options.1: Her mother forgot to make appointments.
options.2: There was no dentist near their home.
options.3: She always found excuses to avoid going.
options.4: She had no problems with her teeth.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 4 thinking she had no reason to go. But paragraph 1 says she found reasons to POSTPONE — implying she was avoiding it.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1: 'Every time her mother suggested a visit, Priya FOUND A REASON TO POSTPONE IT.' She was making excuses to avoid going.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 2 has the same meaning as 'pulsed with a steady pain'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick 'sharp' (the type of pain, not the rhythm) or 'tapping' (a simile, not the main word). 'Throbbed' = pulsed with a steady rhythm of pain.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: THROBBED = pulsed with a steady, rhythmic pain. 'It THROBBED steadily, like a tiny hammer tapping from the inside.' THROBBED = pulsed with steady pain.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 6, what does 'it' refer to in 'because it was so much smaller than the fear she carried for two years'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 2 thinking 'it' refers to the injection. But 'it' refers to the whole experience — the procedure — which was smaller than the FEAR she imagined.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: In context, 'IT had been so much smaller than the fear' = the entire dental PROCEDURE was far less frightening than the fear she built up over two years.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 5, is it True or False that the injection was completely painless? Give a reason from the passage.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The passage says 'The injection STUNG FOR TWO SECONDS.' It was not completely painless — it hurt briefly, but only for a short moment.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'True, Dr Nair said it would not hurt.' Dr Nair said 'you will feel nothing' AFTER the pinch — she acknowledged there would be a pinch.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 5: 'The injection STUNG FOR TWO SECONDS.' It was not completely painless — there was a brief sting. The answer is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: How long did the filling procedure take?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: The filling took twelve minutes.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'a short time' which is too vague.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 5: 'The filling itself took TWELVE MINUTES.' Give the exact duration stated in the passage.

open_ended_questions.stem: How did Priya feel when she walked out of the clinic, and why was the feeling unexpected?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: She felt relief. It was unexpected because she had dreaded the visit for two years — but the procedure was so much easier and smaller than the fear she built up in her mind.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'she was happy' without explaining why the feeling was unexpected.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 6: She felt RELIEF — unexpected because the procedure was 'SMALLER THAN THE FEAR she had carried for two years.' The reality was much less frightening than the imagined fear.

open_ended_questions.stem: How do we know that Dr Nair was a kind and reassuring dentist? Give ONE piece of evidence from paragraph 3.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: Dr Nair 'welcomed Priya without any fuss' and had a 'gentle voice', showing she was calm and reassuring rather than intimidating.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'she was kind' without quoting specific evidence from the passage.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 3: she 'welcomed Priya WITHOUT ANY FUSS' and had a 'GENTLE VOICE.' Both phrases show she was calm and reassuring — not intimidating or clinical.

open_ended_questions.stem: What is the most important lesson of this passage? Support your answer with TWO pieces of evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: The most important lesson is that fear of something is often worse than the thing itself — and that avoiding a problem only allows it to grow. Firstly, Priya avoided the dentist for two years and built up a large imagined fear, but the actual procedure took only twelve minutes and was far less painful than expected. Secondly, her delay caused the cavity to develop to the point where a filling was needed — had she gone earlier, the problem might have been caught sooner and treated more easily.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'we should brush our teeth' — too general. The lesson must be connected to specific events in the passage.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: LESSON: fear is often worse than reality; delaying makes problems worse. EVIDENCE: (1) the procedure was only TWELVE MINUTES — far smaller than two years of FEAR; (2) AVOIDING the dentist caused the cavity to worsen.

questions.stem: Grandma ________ her old photo albums to show her grandchildren what life was like when she was young.
questions.trap_type: 'Destroyed', 'hid' and 'discarded' all suggest the albums were not valued. Only 'treasured' = kept and valued something dearly.
questions.learning_tip: TREASURED = kept and valued something very dearly. Grandma TREASURED her photo albums = she valued them and kept them carefully.
questions.retry_hint: Grandma still has her OLD PHOTO ALBUMS and wants to SHOW them to her grandchildren. Ask: which verb means she valued and kept them dearly? 'Destroyed', 'hid' and 'discarded' would leave her nothing to show.

questions.stem: Grandfather's stories of life in the kampung ________ the children, who had never seen a village like that.
questions.trap_type: 'Bored', 'frightened' and 'angered' are all negative reactions. Kampung stories that captivate children = fascinated.
questions.learning_tip: FASCINATED = held someone's complete interest and attention. Grandfather's stories FASCINATED the children = they were completely captivated.
questions.retry_hint: The children HAD NEVER SEEN A VILLAGE like that KAMPUNG, so the stories gripped them completely. Ask: which verb means to hold somebody's whole attention? 'Bored', 'frightened' and 'angered' are all sour reactions.

questions.stem: My grandmother moves slowly and with great care, but her mind remains ________ and alert.
questions.trap_type: 'Dim', 'confused' and 'slow' all suggest mental weakness. 'Sharp' = mentally quick and clear even in old age.
questions.learning_tip: SHARP = mentally quick, alert and clear. Even in old age, Grandma's mind was SHARP = she was quick-thinking and mentally alert.
questions.retry_hint: BUT signals a contrast: her movements are slow, yet her MIND stays ALERT. Ask: which adjective matches 'alert'? 'Dim', 'confused' and 'slow' would repeat the weakness instead of contrasting with it.

questions.stem: Grandfather spent hours ________ old furniture in the garage, sanding it down and painting it a new colour.
questions.trap_type: 'Destroying' and 'ignoring' are negative; 'selling' means giving away for money. 'Restoring' = repairing and returning to original condition.
questions.learning_tip: RESTORING = repairing and returning something old to its original good condition. Grandfather RESTORED old furniture = fixed and repainted it.
questions.retry_hint: He spends hours SANDING it down and PAINTING it a new colour in the GARAGE. Ask: which verb means bringing something old back to its former good condition? 'Destroying' and 'ignoring' would undo all that work.

questions.stem: The afternoon visits to my grandparents were the most ________ part of my childhood — I remember every detail.
questions.trap_type: 'Forgettable', 'ordinary' and 'unpleasant' suggest unimportance or negativity. 'Cherished' = held dear in memory with great affection.
questions.learning_tip: CHERISHED = loved and kept in memory with deep affection. Those visits were CHERISHED memories = the most loved and treasured parts of childhood.
questions.retry_hint: The dash proves it: I REMEMBER EVERY DETAIL of those AFTERNOON VISITS. Ask: which adjective means loved and held dear in memory? 'Ordinary' and 'forgettable' contradict remembering every single detail.

questions.stem: Every Sunday, my grandmother ________ a pot of chicken rice for the whole family.
questions.trap_type: 'Every Sunday' = regular habit = simple present. 'My grandmother' is singular → verb needs -s.
questions.learning_tip: 'Every Sunday' = regular habit = simple present. My grandmother (singular) → COOKS a pot of chicken rice.
questions.retry_hint: EVERY SUNDAY marks a habit, so the verb stays present. The subject is MY GRANDMOTHER - one person, not the whole family she feeds. Ask: in the present tense, does a singular subject take the plain verb or the -s form?

questions.stem: Grandfather ________ us a long story about his school days whenever we visited him at his flat.
questions.trap_type: 'Whenever we visited' = past habit. 'Tell' is regular: tell → told (irregular). Students write 'telled'.
questions.learning_tip: 'Tell' is irregular: tell → TOLD. 'Whenever we visited' = past recurring action → TOLD us stories.
questions.retry_hint: WHENEVER WE VISITED is finished past time, repeated again and again. Ask: what is the past form of this irregular verb? Adding -ed would produce a word that does not exist in English.

questions.stem: My grandfather is the ________ storyteller in our family — nobody can hold our attention the way he does.
questions.trap_type: Superlative needed (best among all family members). 'Good' → irregular superlative = 'the best'. 'Most good' is wrong.
questions.learning_tip: SUPERLATIVE of 'good' = THE BEST (irregular). He is THE BEST storyteller in the family = better than anyone else. Never 'the most good'.
questions.retry_hint: NOBODY CAN HOLD OUR ATTENTION THE WAY HE DOES - he beats everyone in his family, not just one rival. Ask: for a whole group, comparative or superlative? 'Good' changes shape completely, and 'most good' is never English.

questions.stem: Grandma's chicken rice is ________ tastier ________ any version I have tried at a restaurant.
questions.trap_type: 'Far ... than' = 'far' is an intensifier used with comparative. 'Far tastier than' = much tastier than. Students may choose 'more ... than' but 'tastier' is already in comparative form.
questions.learning_tip: FAR + comparative + THAN = intensified comparison. 'Far TASTIER THAN' = much tastier than. 'Far' intensifies the comparative. Do not add 'more' before an adjective already in -er form.
questions.retry_hint: TASTIER already carries its own -er ending, so nothing may add a second comparison on top. Ask: which choice simply STRENGTHENS a comparative that is already formed? 'More tastier' doubles it, and 'as … as' would make them equal.

questions.stem: There is ________ advice I have received in life that was wiser than what my grandfather has given me.
questions.trap_type: 'Advice' is uncountable → use 'little' or 'much'. 'Few', 'a few', 'many' are for countable nouns.
questions.learning_tip: LITTLE = not much (uncountable). 'Advice' is uncountable → there is LITTLE advice wiser than what Grandfather gives. FEW is only for countable nouns.
questions.retry_hint: ADVICE cannot be counted - you never say 'two advices'. Ask: which word partners an uncountable noun? 'Few', 'a few' and 'many' all need separate things you can number one by one.

questions.stem: Grandmother's handmade kueh is just ________ delicious ________ the kueh sold at Bengawan Solo.
questions.trap_type: Equal comparison: 'just as delicious as' = the two are equally good.
questions.learning_tip: AS … AS = equal comparison. Grandmother's kueh is just AS DELICIOUS AS the shop-bought kueh = their quality is equal.
questions.retry_hint: JUST sits in front of the gap, and Grandmother's kueh is measured against BENGAWAN SOLO's - equally good, neither better. Ask: which pair keeps two things level? 'More … than' would push one in front.

questions.stem: The old rocking chair in the corner ________ by my grandfather himself when he was a young carpenter.
questions.trap_type: The chair was the receiver of the action. Past passive = was built.
questions.learning_tip: The rocking chair was the receiver of the action. Past passive = WAS BUILT. Passive = was/were + past participle.
questions.retry_hint: The ROCKING CHAIR did not make itself - BY MY GRANDFATHER HIMSELF names the maker, and he did it long ago. Ask: which choice is passive and past? Passive = a form of 'be' + a past participle.

questions.stem: Grandmother told the children ________ her silver bracelet without asking her first.
questions.trap_type: Negative reported speech: told + object + not to + base verb.
questions.learning_tip: 'Told the children NOT TO + base verb': told the children NOT TO TOUCH her silver bracelet without asking.
questions.retry_hint: TOLD THE CHILDREN = a reported order, and this one forbids something: hands off her SILVER BRACELET. Ask: after 'told' + person, which verb form follows? And where does a negative word sit - before that infinitive, or inside it?

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Personal pronouns — subject, object and possessive)

questions.context_check: Passage: 'My grandmother is eighty years old, but (1)________ still wakes up at five every morning.' Signal: blank = SUBJECT of 'wakes up'. My grandmother = female singular = SHE.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'her' (object form) instead of 'she' (subject). SHE is the subject pronoun for a female.
questions.learning_tip: SHE = subject pronoun for a female. My grandmother STILL WAKES UP — the subject is SHE. 'Her wakes up' is wrong.
questions.retry_hint: MY GRANDMOTHER is the one doing the WAKING, so the gap is the person who acts. Ask: does a subject slot take the acting pronoun, or the one that receives an action? A possessive would need a noun right after it.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'I visit (2)________ every Saturday morning without fail.' Signal: blank = OBJECT of 'visit'. Refers to grandmother (female) = HER (object pronoun).
questions.trap_type: Students write 'she' (subject) instead of 'her' (object after a verb).
questions.learning_tip: After the verb 'visit', use the OBJECT pronoun: visit HER. 'Visit she' is wrong.
questions.retry_hint: VISIT is a verb, and Grandmother receives that action - I am the one doing it. Ask: after a verb, do you use the acting pronoun or the receiving one? 'Visit she' is not English.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Mother sometimes calls (3)________ to help carry the grocery bags.' Signal: blank = OBJECT of 'calls'. Refers to grandfather = male = HIM (third person singular male object pronoun).
questions.trap_type: Students write 'his' (possessive) instead of 'he' (subject). HE is the subject of 'tends'.
questions.learning_tip: HE = subject pronoun for a male. Grandfather STILL TENDS the garden - the subject is HE. 'His tends the garden' is wrong.
questions.retry_hint: GRANDFATHER IS EIGHTY-FOUR, and the gap is whoever TENDS that garden. Ask: does an action-doer slot take a subject pronoun, an object pronoun, or a possessive? A possessive would need a noun after it.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Grandfather is eighty-four and (4)________ still tends the small garden behind the flat every day.' Signal: blank = SUBJECT of 'tends'. Grandfather = male singular = HE.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'he' (subject form) instead of 'him' (object form after the verb 'calls').
questions.learning_tip: After the verb 'calls', use the OBJECT pronoun: calls HIM to help. 'Calls he' is wrong. HIM is the object pronoun for a male.
questions.retry_hint: MOTHER CALLS somebody, and that somebody is on the receiving end of the calling. Ask: after a verb, do you use a subject pronoun or an object pronoun? 'Calls he' is not English.

questions.context_check: Passage: '(5)________ hands are rough from years of work, but they are always warm when he holds mine.' Signal: blank = BEFORE noun 'hands' = possessive adjective. Grandfather = male = HIS hands.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'he' (subject pronoun) instead of 'his' (possessive adjective before a noun).
questions.learning_tip: Before 'hands' (a noun), use a POSSESSIVE ADJECTIVE: HIS hands. 'He hands' is wrong.
questions.retry_hint: A noun follows the gap: HANDS. Ask: can a subject or object pronoun sit directly in front of a noun, or must that slot hold a possessive? 'He hands' and 'him hands' are both nonsense.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Together, (6)________ have taught me more about life than any book could.' Signal: blank = SUBJECT of 'have taught'. Refers to both grandparents (plural) = THEY.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'them' (object form) instead of 'they' (subject form).
questions.learning_tip: Both grandparents = plural = THEY have taught me. THEY is the subject pronoun for a group. 'Them have taught' is wrong.
questions.retry_hint: TOGETHER means both grandparents, and the gap is the pair who HAVE TAUGHT me about life. Ask: does an acting slot take a subject pronoun, or the object form? 'Them have taught' is not English.

questions.context_check: Passage: '(7)________ stories about growing up during a harder time in Singapore always leave me thinking.' Signal: blank = BEFORE noun 'stories' = possessive adjective. Both grandparents = THEIR stories.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'they' (subject) or 'them' (object) instead of 'their' (possessive adjective before 'stories').
questions.learning_tip: Before 'stories' (a noun), use a POSSESSIVE ADJECTIVE: THEIR stories. 'They stories' and 'them stories' are both wrong.
questions.retry_hint: STORIES is a noun, and it comes straight after the gap. Ask: which pronoun form is allowed to own a noun - subject, object, or possessive? 'They stories' and 'them stories' are both wrong.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'I hope I can spend as much time with (8)________ as possible before they grow too old to remember.' Signal: blank = OBJECT of 'spend time with'. Refers to grandparents (plural) = THEM (object pronoun).
questions.trap_type: Students write 'they' (subject form) instead of 'them' (object form after a preposition).
questions.learning_tip: After the preposition 'with', use the OBJECT pronoun: spend time with THEM. 'With they' is wrong.
questions.retry_hint: WITH is a preposition, and a preposition always takes the receiving form of a pronoun. Ask: which pronoun follows a preposition - the acting one, or the one that receives? 'With they' is not English.

C.passage: My grandmother is eighty years old, but (1)________ still wakes up at five every morning to prepare breakfast. I visit (2)________ every Saturday morning without fail. Grandfather is eighty-four, and (3)________ still tends the small garden behind the flat every day. When the bags of soil are heavy, Mother calls (4)________ to help carry them from the lift. (5)________ hands are rough from years of work, but they are always warm when he holds mine. Together, (6)________ have taught me more about life than any book could ever do. (7)________ stories about growing up in a harder Singapore always leave me thinking for days. I hope to spend as many afternoons with (8)________ as I can before those stories are forgotten.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: Spending time with grandparents is one of the most valuable things a child can do. As they grow older, grandparents may appear (1)________ in body, moving slowly and tiring easily, but their minds and hearts remain full of experience. The (2)________ they share — lessons about patience, hard work and kindness — is the kind that cannot be learned from a textbook. When grandparents (3)________ about the old days, they are sharing a living piece of family history that would otherwise be lost. These stories form part of a child's cultural (4)________ — a connection to the past that shapes their identity and values. Every family should (5)________ these moments together, for they grow rarer with every passing year.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'moving slowly and tiring easily' = physically weak = frail.
questions.learning_tip: FRAIL = physically weak, especially because of old age. An elderly person may look FRAIL but still be mentally sharp.
questions.retry_hint: MOVING SLOWLY AND TIRING EASILY, yet their MINDS AND HEARTS stay full. Ask: which box word describes a weak BODY in old age? A word about the mind would destroy the contrast the sentence is building.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'lessons about patience, hard work and kindness that cannot be learned from a textbook' = deep understanding gained through experience = wisdom.
questions.learning_tip: WISDOM = deep understanding and good judgement gained through long experience. Grandparents share WISDOM = valuable life lessons.
questions.retry_hint: The dash lists it: LESSONS ABOUT PATIENCE, HARD WORK AND KINDNESS, and it CANNOT BE LEARNED FROM A TEXTBOOK. Ask: which box word names deep understanding earned by living? It is a noun - 'the ___ they share'.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'talk about the old days' and 'sharing a living piece of family history' = recall and talk about past memories = reminisce.
questions.learning_tip: REMINISCE = recall and talk about past memories with pleasure and nostalgia. When grandparents REMINISCE, they share stories from their younger days.
questions.retry_hint: They talk ABOUT THE OLD DAYS and pass on A LIVING PIECE OF FAMILY HISTORY. Ask: which box word is the verb for fondly recalling the past aloud? A noun cannot follow 'when grandparents'.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'a connection to the past that shapes their identity and values' = cultural background passed down = heritage.
questions.learning_tip: HERITAGE = the cultural background, traditions and values passed down from previous generations. Family stories form part of a child's HERITAGE.
questions.retry_hint: A CONNECTION TO THE PAST THAT SHAPES THEIR IDENTITY AND VALUES - and the word CULTURAL sits right in front of the gap. Ask: which box word names what earlier generations hand down to a child?

questions.trap_type: The clue 'these moments grow rarer with every passing year' = hold dear and value deeply = cherish.
questions.learning_tip: CHERISH = hold something dear and value it deeply. Every family should CHERISH time with grandparents = treasure these increasingly rare moments.
questions.retry_hint: These moments GROW RARER WITH EVERY PASSING YEAR, so families are urged to hold them dear. Ask: which box word is the verb meaning to treasure something deeply? It follows 'should', so it must be a plain verb.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.error_type: Homophone confusion — they're (they are) vs their (possessive)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'they're' (they are) when the sentence needs 'their' (belonging to them).
questions.learning_tip: THEIR = belonging to them (possessive adjective before a noun). THEY'RE = they are. 'THEIR stories were amazing' = stories belonging to them. Test: can you replace it with 'they are'? If no, use THEIR.
questions.retry_hint: THEY'RE opens out into two words - try it: 'they are wonderful stories' about life BEFORE INDEPENDENCE. Does that read properly? Ask: which spelling shows the stories BELONG to the grandparents?

questions.trap_type: Students write 'patient' (adjective) after the action verb 'listened'. A verb needs an adverb.
questions.learning_tip: After an action verb (listened), use an ADVERB: listened PATIENTLY. 'Patient' is an adjective — it describes nouns, not actions.
questions.retry_hint: LISTENED is an action verb, and the underlined word says HOW Grandpa listened. Ask: which ending must an adjective take before it is allowed to describe an action? Adjectives belong to nouns only.

questions.trap_type: Students add -s to 'woman', producing 'womans'. 'Woman' has a completely irregular plural form.
questions.learning_tip: 'Woman' has an irregular plural: woman → WOMEN. Never write 'womans'. Other irregular plurals: man → men, child → children.
questions.retry_hint: WOMANS is the trap: this noun never builds its plural with a plain -s. Ask: what do you call more than one man, or more than one child? The vowel inside the word changes instead of an ending being tacked on.

questions.trap_type: 'The grandchildren' is plural. Students write 'was' (singular).
questions.learning_tip: 'The grandchildren' = plural → WERE gathered around the table. WAS is only for singular subjects.
questions.retry_hint: THE GRANDCHILDREN is the subject - many of them, folding dumplings. Ask: does a plural subject take 'was', or its plural partner? Match the verb to the subject, not to 'Grandma' standing next to it.

questions.error_type: Superlative required when selecting one from a group
questions.trap_type: Students use 'older' (comparative, for two things) when the sentence compares among all the siblings = superlative = oldest.
questions.learning_tip: OLDEST = superlative (comparing among three or more). 'He is the OLDEST of the four brothers' = more than two people being compared → need superlative, not comparative.
questions.retry_hint: Count them: FOUR BROTHERS, not two. Ask: does a comparative or a superlative pick the top one out of a group of four? Uncle Rajan is being ranked against all of them at once.

E.passage: Last weekend, our whole extended family gathered at Grandma's flat. We listened to they're (1) wonderful stories about life before independence. Grandpa listened patient (2) as each grandchild shared what they were doing in school. He mentioned that in the old days, the womans (3) in his village would wake before sunrise to cook breakfast for the whole family. The grandchildren was (4) gathered around the kitchen table, helping Grandma fold dumplings. Uncle Rajan, who is the older (5) of the four brothers, led everyone in singing a song that Grandma had taught them as children.

questions.sentence_a: My grandfather has been gardening for fifty years.
questions.sentence_b: He knows every plant in the garden by name.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'Since'.
questions.model_answer: Since my grandfather has been gardening for fifty years, he knows every plant in the garden by name.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'My grandfather has been gardening for fifty years since he knows every plant' — reversing the cause and result.
questions.learning_tip: SINCE = because of an ongoing or established fact. SINCE he has been gardening for fifty years, he knows every plant. The reason comes after 'since'.
questions.retry_hint: Which half is cause, and which is effect? FIFTY YEARS of gardening came first; knowing EVERY PLANT came afterwards. Ask: after 'Since', do you write the reason or the result? A comma then joins the halves.

questions.sentence_a: Grandmother's kueh is the best I have ever tasted.
questions.sentence_b: She has refined her recipe over forty years.
questions.instruction: Combine into one sentence using the relative pronoun 'which'.
questions.model_answer: Grandmother's kueh, which she has refined over forty years, is the best I have ever tasted.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'Grandmother's kueh is the best I have ever tasted which she has refined over forty years' — placing 'which' in the wrong position.
questions.learning_tip: Place 'which' immediately after the noun it refers to. Grandmother's kueh, WHICH she has refined over forty years, is the best I have ever tasted.
questions.retry_hint: Find the noun both sentences share: GRANDMOTHER'S KUEH. Ask: must 'which' hug that noun, or trail at the very end? And what punctuation fences off the extra fact about FORTY YEARS of refining?

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
Every Saturday morning, without fail, nine-year-old Nora took the bus to her grandfather's flat in Toa Payoh. It was a fifteen-minute ride she made so many times that she could close her eyes and know exactly when to pull the bell.

Grandpa Lin was always at the door before she knocked. He had a habit of watching for the bus from his kitchen window, and the moment he spotted her yellow school bag through the glass, he would shuffle towards the door.

Their Saturday mornings followed a comfortable routine. Grandpa made kaya toast and soft-boiled eggs while Nora set the table. They ate slowly, and Grandpa told stories — about growing up in a kampung, about his first job at the docks, about the time he cycled from Toa Payoh to Changi just to impress a girl.

'Was that girl Grandma?' Nora always asked.

'Every time,' Grandpa always replied, with a smile that had not changed in forty years.

One Saturday, Nora arrived to find Grandpa asleep in his armchair. She let herself in quietly with the spare key and made the kaya toast herself. When Grandpa woke, he looked at the table and then at her, and something moved across his face that sat between a smile and sadness — something in between.

'You are more like your grandmother every day,' he said.

mcq_questions.stem: How did Grandpa Lin know when Nora was arriving?

options.1: Nora always called him before taking the bus.
options.2: He watched for the bus from his kitchen window.
options.3: He heard her knock on the door.
options.4: Nora's mother sent him a message each time.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 3 thinking he heard her knock. But the passage says he came to the door BEFORE she knocked — because he watched from the window.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 2: 'He had a habit of WATCHING FOR THE BUS FROM HIS KITCHEN WINDOW.' He spotted her BEFORE she knocked — always at the door first.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 2 has the same meaning as 'walk slowly with short steps'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick 'spotted' (noticed) or 'moment' (a point in time). 'Shuffle' = walk slowly with short, dragging steps.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: SHUFFLE = walk slowly with short, dragging steps, as elderly people often do. Grandpa would SHUFFLE towards the door = walk slowly and carefully.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 6, what does 'it' refer to in 'it was something in between'?

options.3: Something in between a smile and sadness, like quiet emotion

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking 'it' refers to his eyes. But 'it' refers to the expression on his face — the emotion that was between a smile and sadness.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: In paragraph 6: 'something moved across his face... IT was something in between.' 'It' refers to that expression on his face — neither a smile nor sadness.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 1, is it True or False that Nora had to concentrate on her bus journey to know when to stop? Give a reason from the passage.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The passage says she 'could close her eyes and know exactly when to pull the bell' — she knew the route so well that she did not need to pay attention.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'True, she had to watch the stops carefully.' The passage says the opposite — she knew the route without needing to watch.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1: she 'could CLOSE HER EYES and know exactly when to pull the bell' = she knew the route by heart and did not need to concentrate. Answer is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: What did Nora do when she found Grandpa asleep on the last Saturday described?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: She let herself in quietly with the spare key and made the kaya toast herself.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'she woke him up' — she did not. She came in quietly and made breakfast herself.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 6: 'She LET HERSELF IN quietly with the SPARE KEY and made the KAYA TOAST HERSELF.' Two specific actions — she did not wake Grandpa.

open_ended_questions.stem: What TWO specific stories did Grandpa tell during their Saturday mornings? Give examples from paragraph 3.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) He told stories about growing up in a kampung and his first job at the docks. (ii) He told the story about cycling from Toa Payoh to Changi to impress a girl (who turned out to be Grandma).
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students give only one story or say 'he told many stories' without naming specific ones.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 3: (1) growing up in a KAMPUNG / first job at the DOCKS; (2) cycling from Toa Payoh to CHANGI to impress a girl. Give any two specific story topics.

open_ended_questions.stem: What did Grandpa mean when he said 'You are more like your grandmother every day'?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: He meant that Nora's actions — letting herself in quietly and preparing breakfast without being asked — reminded him of how his wife used to care for him, showing the same thoughtfulness and love.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'she looks like her grandmother' — the passage is about behaviour and character, not physical appearance.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Grandpa saw Nora MAKING BREAKFAST without being asked = caring for him without fuss. This reminded him of GRANDMA's character = quiet, thoughtful love.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on her actions in the passage, describe TWO character traits of Nora with evidence from the passage.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: Nora is a devoted and thoughtful person. Firstly, her devotion is shown by how she visits Grandpa Lin every single Saturday without fail — the passage says she has made the trip so many times that she knows when to pull the bell without looking. Secondly, her thoughtfulness is shown when she finds Grandpa asleep: instead of waking him, she quietly lets herself in and makes the kaya toast herself, showing she puts his comfort first and acts with care rather than convenience.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say she is 'kind and caring' without naming precise character traits or giving specific evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Name precise TRAITS then give EVIDENCE: (1) DEVOTED — visits every Saturday without fail, knows the route by heart; (2) THOUGHTFUL — did not wake Grandpa, QUIETLY made breakfast herself.

questions.stem: The magician ________ a white dove from beneath a silk handkerchief to the audience's delight.
questions.trap_type: 'Destroyed', 'borrowed' and 'swallowed' do not describe producing something in a magic act. 'Produced' = caused something to appear from seemingly nowhere.
questions.learning_tip: PRODUCED = caused to appear or brought out, often in a surprising way. The magician PRODUCED a dove = made it appear from a hidden place.
questions.retry_hint: A DOVE comes out FROM BENEATH A SILK HANDKERCHIEF, to the audience's DELIGHT. Ask: which verb means to make something appear from a hidden place? 'Swallowed' and 'destroyed' would leave no bird at all.

questions.stem: The magician told the audience he would make the ball ________ and reappear on the other side of the stage.
questions.trap_type: 'Grow' and 'expand' suggest getting bigger; 'bounce' = spring back. Only 'vanish' = disappear suddenly and completely.
questions.learning_tip: VANISH = disappear suddenly and completely. The ball seemed to VANISH from one hand and reappear in another — a classic magic effect.
questions.retry_hint: AND REAPPEAR tells you the ball must first go the other way. Ask: which verb means to disappear suddenly and completely? 'Grow', 'expand' and 'bounce' all keep the ball firmly in sight.

questions.stem: The audience gasped in ________ as the magician walked through a solid glass panel.
questions.trap_type: 'Boredom', 'sadness' and 'anger' are all inappropriate reactions to a stunning magic trick. 'Disbelief' = shock that something impossible seemed real.
questions.learning_tip: DISBELIEF = the feeling that something cannot be real or true. When the magician walked through glass, the audience gasped in DISBELIEF = they could not believe what they saw.
questions.retry_hint: The magician WALKED THROUGH A SOLID GLASS PANEL, and the audience GASPED. Ask: which noun names the shock of seeing something that cannot possibly be real? Boredom and anger never make a crowd gasp.

questions.stem: The magician asked for a ________ from the audience to use in his next trick.
questions.trap_type: 'Stranger', 'enemy' and 'suspect' all have negative connotations. A 'volunteer' = someone who willingly comes forward.
questions.learning_tip: A VOLUNTEER = someone who willingly offers to help or participate. Magicians ask for a VOLUNTEER from the audience to assist with a trick.
questions.retry_hint: The magician ASKED FOR somebody FROM THE AUDIENCE to help with his NEXT TRICK. Ask: which noun names a person who steps forward willingly? 'Enemy' and 'suspect' would turn a helper into a threat.

questions.stem: A skilled magician ________ the audience's attention with patter and movement so they miss the real trick.
questions.trap_type: 'Removes' and 'rewards' do not describe misdirection. 'Educates' is positive. 'Distracts' = diverts attention away from the real action.
questions.learning_tip: DISTRACTS = draws attention away from something. A magician DISTRACTS the audience = uses talk and movement to make them look the wrong way.
questions.retry_hint: The purpose is stated: SO THEY MISS THE REAL TRICK, using PATTER AND MOVEMENT. Ask: which verb means to pull attention away from what matters? 'Educates' and 'rewards' would help the audience, not fool them.

questions.stem: Every year, the school ________ a magic show for students during the end-of-year celebration.
questions.trap_type: 'Every year' = regular habit = simple present. 'The school' is singular → verb needs -s.
questions.learning_tip: 'Every year' = regular habit = simple present. The school (singular) → ORGANISES a magic show each year.
questions.retry_hint: EVERY YEAR marks a habit, so the tense stays present. The subject is THE SCHOOL - one thing, however many students it holds. Ask: does a singular subject take the plain verb, or the verb ending in -s?

questions.stem: The magician ________ his assistant into a large box and locked it shut with a golden key.
questions.trap_type: Past story. 'Lead' is irregular: lead → led. Students write 'leaded'.
questions.learning_tip: 'Lead' is irregular: lead → LED. The magician LED his assistant into the box = completed past action.
questions.retry_hint: The whole sentence is a finished story: he LOCKED IT SHUT WITH A GOLDEN KEY. Ask: what is the past form of this irregular verb? Adding -ed would produce a word that does not exist.

questions.stem: This magic show was ________ than the one we saw at the school carnival last year.
questions.trap_type: Comparing two shows = comparative. 'Exciting' is multi-syllable → use 'more exciting', not 'excitinger'.
questions.learning_tip: COMPARATIVE of multi-syllable adjectives: MORE + adjective. This show was MORE EXCITING than last year's = of the two, this one was better. Never 'excitinger'.
questions.retry_hint: THAN sets this show against THE ONE WE SAW AT THE SCHOOL CARNIVAL - exactly two shows. Ask: for two, comparative or superlative? And can a four-syllable adjective ever take -er? 'Excitinger' is not English.

questions.stem: Of all the tricks in the show, the disappearing act was ________ impressive.
questions.trap_type: Superlative needed (comparing among all tricks in the show). 'The most' + adjective = superlative.
questions.learning_tip: SUPERLATIVE: comparing among three or more. Of all the tricks, it was THE MOST IMPRESSIVE = best of all of them. 'The most' + multi-syllable adjective.
questions.retry_hint: Every trick in that show is in this race, not merely two of them. Ask: for three or several, do you need a comparative or a superlative? And IMPRESSIVE is long, so no -er ending can rescue you here.

questions.stem: There ________ only a little space left at the front of the hall, so some students sat further back.
questions.trap_type: 'A little space' = uncountable singular amount. Past context → was.
questions.learning_tip: 'A little space' = uncountable singular amount. Past event → THERE WAS only a little space left at the front.
questions.retry_hint: Two clues. A LITTLE SPACE is one uncountable amount, not a set of countable things, and SOME STUDENTS SAT FURTHER BACK - it is over and done. Ask: which form of 'be' is both singular and past?

questions.stem: The second performance was just ________ spectacular ________ the first one.
questions.trap_type: Equal comparison: 'just as spectacular as' = both performances were equally good.
questions.learning_tip: AS … AS = equal comparison. The second show was just AS SPECTACULAR AS the first = equally impressive.
questions.retry_hint: JUST tips you off: neither performance beat the other. Ask: which pair holds two things at exactly equal level? 'Less … than' would demote one, and 'the most … of' needs three or several.

questions.stem: Three volunteers from the audience ________ to come up to the stage by the magician.
questions.trap_type: The volunteers were the receivers of the action. Past passive = were invited.
questions.learning_tip: The volunteers were the receivers of the action. Past passive = WERE INVITED. Passive = was/were + past participle.
questions.retry_hint: THREE VOLUNTEERS did nothing themselves - BY THE MAGICIAN names who acted on them, and it is finished. Ask: which choice is passive and past, and does a plural subject take 'was' or its plural partner?

questions.stem: The magician told the audience ________ too loudly so as not to give away the ending of the trick.
questions.trap_type: Negative reported speech: told + object + not to + base verb.
questions.learning_tip: 'Told the audience NOT TO + base verb': told the audience NOT TO REACT too loudly.
questions.retry_hint: TOLD THE AUDIENCE = reported speech, and this is a warning against being TOO LOUD. Ask: after 'told' + person, which verb form follows? And where does a negative word stand - in front of that infinitive, or inside it?

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Verb forms of 'watch')

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Leo loves (1)________ magic shows on video every evening before bed.' Signal: 'loves + ___' = gerund (verb-ing). Pattern: love + verb-ing → watching.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'to watch'. ENJOY is one of the verbs that must be followed by the -ing form - 'enjoys to watch' is never correct.
questions.learning_tip: ENJOY + verb-ing: enjoys WATCHING magic shows. Same pattern: enjoy reading, enjoy swimming. The infinitive belongs after 'want', not after 'enjoy'.
questions.retry_hint: ENJOYS is the deciding word: some verbs demand the -ing form and refuse an infinitive. Ask: do you say 'enjoy to read' or 'enjoy reading'? Copy that same pattern here.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'He (2)________ every magician's hand carefully to try to spot the moment the trick happens.' Signal: 'every magician's hand' + habitual action = simple present. Subject 'He' = singular → watches.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'watch' (plural form) forgetting 'He' is singular.
questions.learning_tip: Regular habit = simple present. He (singular) → WATCHES every hand carefully.
questions.retry_hint: EVERY EVENING sets a habit, and HE is one person. Ask: in the present tense, does a singular subject take the plain verb, or the verb ending in -s? A past form would clash with his nightly routine.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Last Friday, Leo (3)________ a live magic show at the community centre for the first time.' Signal: 'Last Friday' = past. 'Watch' is regular: watch → watched.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'watch' (base form) ignoring the past signal 'Last Friday'.
questions.learning_tip: 'Last Friday' = past. 'Watch' is regular: watch → WATCHED.
questions.retry_hint: LAST FRIDAY is finished time, and it happened once - FOR THE VERY FIRST TIME. Ask: which form is simple past? A continuous form would claim the show was still running around some other event.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'While he (4)________ the magician closely, a dove appeared from nowhere and landed on the man's hat.' Signal: 'While he ___' = ongoing background action in the past. Subject 'he' = singular → was watching. Interrupted by 'a dove appeared'.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'watched' (simple past) missing the ongoing signal 'while he'.
questions.learning_tip: 'While he ___' = ongoing background past action = past continuous. He WAS WATCHING closely when the dove appeared.
questions.retry_hint: WHILE means one action had already begun when A DOVE APPEARED and cut across it. Ask: which form shows a past action still in progress? Leo is one person, so pick the singular helper, not the plural one.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'His friends (5)________ the same trick from different angles to see if they could spot the secret.' Signal: same past time frame, plural subject 'his friends' + ongoing parallel action → were watching.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'watched' (simple past). 'At that very moment' marks an action already in progress, and 'his friends' is plural.
questions.learning_tip: Plural subject + action in progress in the past = WERE + verb-ing. His friends WERE WATCHING at that very moment.
questions.retry_hint: HIS FRIENDS is plural, and they had their eyes on it AT THAT VERY MOMENT, FROM DIFFERENT ANGLES. Ask: which form shows a past action still in progress, and which helper belongs with a plural subject?

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Leo wants (6)________ as many different magicians as possible before he turns twelve.' Signal: 'wants + ___' = infinitive. Pattern: want + to + base verb → to watch.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'watching' instead of the infinitive after 'wants'.
questions.learning_tip: 'Want TO + base verb': wants TO WATCH as many magicians as possible. Always use the infinitive after 'wants'.
questions.retry_hint: WANTS refuses an -ing form after it. Ask: do you say 'she wants going', or 'she wants ___ go' with a small word slipped in front? Fill that same little word in before he TURNS TWELVE.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'His teacher says everyone should (7)________ a live magic show at least once in their life.' Signal: 'should + ___' = modal verb + base form. Never add -s or -ing after a modal.
questions.trap_type: Students add -es or -ing after the modal verb 'should'.
questions.learning_tip: After modal verbs (should, must, can, will), always use the BASE form: should WATCH. Never 'should watches' or 'should watching'.
questions.retry_hint: SHOULD is a modal, and a modal is always followed by a bare verb - no -s, no -ing, no infinitive marker. Ask: which single box form is the plain, unchanged verb? EVERYONE does not alter it either.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Right now, Leo (8)________ a slow-motion recording of the coin trick to see if he can finally figure it out.' Signal: 'Right now' = present continuous. Subject 'Leo' = singular → is watching.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'watches' (simple present habit) missing the 'right now' signal for present continuous.
questions.learning_tip: 'Right now' = present continuous. Leo (singular) → IS WATCHING a slow-motion recording right now.
questions.retry_hint: RIGHT NOW means at this very moment, so the action must be in progress. Ask: which form shows something happening as we speak? Leo counts as one person, so choose the singular helper, not 'are'.

C.passage: Leo enjoys (1)________ magic shows on video every evening before bed. He (2)________ every magician's hand carefully to try to spot the moment the trick happens. Last Friday, Leo (3)________ a live magic show at the community centre for the very first time. While he (4)________ the magician closely, a dove appeared from nowhere and landed on the man's hat. At that very moment, his friends (5)________ the same trick from different angles, hoping to catch any movement that would give away the secret. Leo wants (6)________ as many different magicians as possible before he turns twelve. His teacher says everyone should (7)________ a live magic show at least once in their life because no video can capture the feeling of being right there in the room. Right now, Leo (8)________ a slow-motion recording of the coin trick to see if he can finally figure out the secret.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: Magic tricks work by fooling the mind rather than actually doing the impossible. The most important tool in a magician's craft is (1)________ of hand — the ability to move objects with the fingers so quickly and smoothly that the eye cannot follow. A magician also uses (2)________ to guide the audience's attention away from what is really happening. For example, a dramatic gesture with one hand draws the eyes while the other hand secretly performs the real action. The result is an (3)________ — a false image that the brain accepts as real because it sees what it expects to see. A skilled magician makes every (4)________ in the audience feel as though the impossible has just happened right in front of them. At the end of some shows, the magician may choose to (5)________ how a trick works, which often surprises audiences — because the method is usually much simpler than they imagined.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'move objects with the fingers so quickly and smoothly that the eye cannot follow' = sleight of hand.
questions.learning_tip: SLEIGHT of hand = the skill of moving your hands and fingers so quickly and cleverly that the eye cannot follow. Magicians practice SLEIGHT of hand for years.
questions.retry_hint: The dash defines it: MOVE OBJECTS WITH THE FINGERS SO QUICKLY that THE EYE CANNOT FOLLOW. Ask: which box word completes the fixed phrase '___ OF HAND'? It names the skill itself, not the trick's effect.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'guide the audience's attention AWAY from what is really happening' = misdirection.
questions.learning_tip: MISDIRECTION = deliberately guiding someone's attention away from what is really happening. Magicians use MISDIRECTION to hide the real secret of the trick.
questions.retry_hint: The example spells it out: A DRAMATIC GESTURE WITH ONE HAND DRAWS THE EYES while the other hand works in secret. Ask: which box word names the art of steering attention AWAY from the real action?

questions.trap_type: The clue 'a false image that the brain accepts as real' = an illusion.
questions.learning_tip: An ILLUSION = a false image or impression that the mind accepts as real. Magic tricks create ILLUSIONS by exploiting how the brain processes visual information.
questions.retry_hint: The dash explains it: A FALSE IMAGE THAT THE BRAIN ACCEPTS AS REAL. Note 'an' in front of the gap - the word must begin with a vowel sound. Ask: which box word names that false picture in the mind?

questions.trap_type: The clue 'every ___ in the audience feel as though the impossible has just happened' = a person watching = spectator.
questions.learning_tip: A SPECTATOR = a person who watches an event, show or game. Every SPECTATOR in the audience felt the wonder of the trick.
questions.retry_hint: Every one of them sits IN THE AUDIENCE and FEELS AS THOUGH THE IMPOSSIBLE has just happened. Ask: which box word names one single person who watches a show? A skill or a false image cannot feel anything.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'choose to ___ how a trick works' = to show or disclose the secret = reveal.
questions.learning_tip: REVEAL = to show or disclose something that was previously hidden or secret. Some magicians REVEAL their secrets at the end of a show.
questions.retry_hint: AT THE END OF SOME SHOWS the magician gives the secret away, and audiences are SURPRISED at how simple the method is. Ask: which box word is the verb meaning to make a hidden thing known? It follows 'choose to'.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.trap_type: Students write 'to' when the meaning is 'excessively' or 'also'. 'Too' = also or excessively.
questions.learning_tip: TOO = also / excessively. 'The trick was TOO fast for us to follow' = excessively fast. TO = towards a destination / infinitive marker. Test: can you replace with 'also' or 'excessively'? If yes, use TOO.
questions.retry_hint: The underlined word is meant to say 'excessively': the trick moved FAST for anyone to FOLLOW WITH THEIR EYES. Ask: which spelling means 'more than enough'? It carries one extra letter.

questions.trap_type: Students write 'careful' (adjective) after the action verb 'watched'. A verb needs an adverb.
questions.learning_tip: After an action verb (watched), use an ADVERB: watched CAREFULLY. 'Careful' is an adjective — it describes nouns, not actions.
questions.retry_hint: WATCHED is the action, and the underlined word tells you HOW the class watched. Ask: which two letters must be added before an adjective may describe a verb? On its own, an adjective can describe only a noun.

questions.error_type: Irregular plural — half → halves (f → ves rule)
questions.trap_type: Students add -s to 'half', producing 'halfs'. Words ending in -f often change to -ves in the plural.
questions.learning_tip: 'Half' follows the -f → -ves rule: half → HALVES. Same pattern: leaf → leaves, loaf → loaves, knife → knives.
questions.retry_hint: HALFS is the trap: nouns ending in -f seldom take a plain -s. Ask: how do you write more than one leaf, or more than one loaf? Apply that same swap to this word.

questions.error_type: Subject-verb agreement — plural subject (the audience members)
questions.trap_type: 'The audience members' is plural. Students write 'was' (singular).
questions.learning_tip: 'The audience members' = plural → WERE stunned. WAS is only for singular subjects.
questions.retry_hint: The subject is THE AUDIENCE MEMBERS - many people, not one crowd-word. Ask: does a plural subject take 'was', or its plural partner? Count the people, not the group noun standing beside them.

questions.error_type: Comparative form - long adjectives take 'more', never an -er ending as well
questions.trap_type: Students add -er to the adjective even though MORE is already in front of it, comparing twice over.
questions.learning_tip: AMAZING is a multi-syllable adjective: MORE AMAZING. You may use 'more' OR an -er ending, never both.
questions.retry_hint: AMAZINGER piles an -er ending onto an adjective that already has MORE in front of it. Ask: which of those two must go? A long adjective takes a helper word, never an ending - and never both together.

E.passage: Last Saturday, our school hall hosted a wonderful magic show. The final trick moved to (1) fast for anyone to follow with their eyes. We watched careful (2) as the magician cut the rope into halfs (3) and then magically rejoined it. The audience members was (4) absolutely stunned when the rabbit appeared from the empty hat. Everyone agreed that the second half of the show was more amazinger (5) than the first, and we hoped the school would invite the same magician again next year.

questions.sentence_a: You look closely at the magician's right hand.
questions.sentence_b: You will miss what the left hand is doing.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'As'.
questions.model_answer: As you look closely at the magician's right hand, you will miss what the left hand is doing.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'You look closely as you will miss what the left hand is doing' — reversing the simultaneous/causal relationship.
questions.learning_tip: AS = at the same time that / because. AS you look at the right hand, you WILL MISS the left hand = the two things happen together. 'As' introduces the simultaneous trigger.
questions.retry_hint: Two things happen at once: your eyes lock onto the RIGHT HAND while the LEFT HAND works unseen. Ask: after 'As', which half comes first - the looking, or the missing? A comma then joins them.

questions.sentence_a: You pay attention to the magician's words and movements.
questions.sentence_b: You will be tricked every single time.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'Unless'.
questions.model_answer: Unless you pay attention to the magician's words and movements, you will be tricked every single time.
questions.trap_type: Students add 'will' in the 'unless' clause: 'Unless you will pay attention' — incorrect.
questions.learning_tip: UNLESS + simple present, simple future. UNLESS you PAY attention, you WILL BE tricked. Never 'will' after 'unless'.
questions.retry_hint: 'Unless' is a two-in-one word: it already contains a hidden negative. Ask: which half sets the condition - PAY ATTENTION, or being TRICKED EVERY SINGLE TIME? And what tense follows 'unless' - present, or future with 'will'?

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
The school hall was full. Three hundred students sat in rows, facing a small stage lit by a single spotlight. On the stage stood a man in a black suit. He introduced himself as Marco.

Marco performed seven tricks that evening. He made a coin pass through a solid table. He caused a handkerchief to change colour three times in a row. He invited a girl named Priya to choose any card from a deck, memorise it and return it to the pack — then he produced it from inside a sealed envelope that sat on a chair since the show began.

But the final trick was the one everyone remembered.

Marco asked the audience to think of any number between one and ten. He did not ask anyone to say it out loud. Then he turned his back to the audience and said, 'The number most of you are thinking of is seven.'

A roar went up from the hall.

Later, a boy named Ethan asked his teacher how the trick worked. 'When people are asked for a number between one and ten,' his teacher said, 'most people choose seven. It's simply how the human brain tends to work.'

Ethan was quiet for a moment. 'So it wasn't really magic at all,' he said.

'Perhaps not,' said the teacher. 'But it felt like it, didn't it?'

mcq_questions.stem: How many tricks did Marco perform in total that evening?
mcq_questions.trap_type: Students may guess a different number. The answer is stated directly in paragraph 2.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 2: 'Marco performed SEVEN tricks that evening.' The exact number is clearly stated.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 2 has the same meaning as 'a set of playing cards'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: Students may pick 'pack' — which is also a correct synonym for a set of cards. However, the question asks for the word IN paragraph 2 that has the same meaning, and 'deck' appears BEFORE 'pack' in the sentence. Both words appear; 'deck' is the first usage.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 2: 'choose any card from a DECK' — DECK = a complete set of 52 playing cards. The word 'pack' also appears later in the same sentence and means the same thing.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 4, what does 'it' refer to in 'He did not ask anyone to say it out loud'?

options.2: The number the audience was thinking of

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 3 thinking 'it' refers to the trick. But the instruction was to 'think of any number' — so 'it' = the number they were thinking of.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 4: Marco asked the audience to 'think of any number between one and ten.' He did not ask them to say IT = THE NUMBER out loud. 'It' = the number they were thinking of.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 2, is it True or False that the sealed envelope was prepared during the show? Give a reason from the passage.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The passage says the envelope 'sat on a chair SINCE THE SHOW BEGAN' — meaning it was placed there before any tricks started, not prepared during the show.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'True, Marco prepared it during the performance.' The envelope was on the chair from the start — before any tricks were performed.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 2: the envelope 'had been sitting on a chair SINCE THE SHOW BEGAN.' It was there from the very beginning, not prepared during the act. Answer is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: According to Ethan's teacher, why do most people choose the number seven?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: It is simply how the human brain tends to work — when asked for a number between one and ten, most people naturally think of seven.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'because it is a lucky number' — the passage gives a specific reason about how the BRAIN tends to work.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 6: 'It's simply how the HUMAN BRAIN tends to work.' When asked for a number between one and ten, most brains default to SEVEN.

open_ended_questions.stem: Describe TWO of the tricks Marco performed, using evidence from paragraph 2.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) He made a coin pass through a solid table. (ii) He caused a handkerchief to change colour three times in a row. (Accept also: he produced Priya's chosen card from a sealed envelope.)
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students describe the final trick (the number) which is in paragraph 4, not paragraph 2.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 2 gives THREE tricks: (1) coin through a TABLE; (2) handkerchief changing COLOUR; (3) card found in a sealed ENVELOPE. Give any two.

open_ended_questions.stem: What did the teacher mean when she said 'But it felt like it, didn't it?' at the end of the passage?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: She meant that even though the trick was based on psychology rather than real magic, the feeling of wonder and amazement it created was still real and valuable — the experience of magic does not require a supernatural secret.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'the teacher thought it was real magic' — she did not. She meant the FEELING it created was still genuine.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: The teacher means: even if the trick was not 'magic' in the supernatural sense, it still FELT like magic — and that feeling is what matters. The experience of WONDER is real.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on his conversation with his teacher, describe TWO character traits of Ethan with evidence from the passage.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: Ethan is a curious and intellectually honest person. Firstly, his curiosity is shown when he sought out his teacher after the show to ask how the final trick worked — he was not satisfied simply with the experience and wanted to understand the mechanics behind it. Secondly, his intellectual honesty is shown when, upon hearing the explanation, he said plainly 'So it wasn't really magic at all' — he accepted the truth directly rather than choosing to keep believing in something he now knew was not supernatural.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say he is 'smart and questioning' without naming precise character traits or providing specific evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Name precise TRAITS then give EVIDENCE: (1) CURIOUS — ASKED his teacher how the trick worked after the show; (2) INTELLECTUALLY HONEST — accepted the truth plainly ('it wasn't really magic at all').

questions.stem: The students lined up at the starting line, eager to ________ in the relay race.
questions.trap_type: 'Withdraw' means to pull out; 'ignore' and 'cancel' are negative. Only 'participate' = take part actively.
questions.learning_tip: PARTICIPATE = take part actively in an activity. All students were encouraged to PARTICIPATE in Sports Day events.
questions.retry_hint: They LINED UP AT THE STARTING LINE, EAGER for the RELAY RACE to begin. Ask: which verb means to take an active part in something? 'Withdraw' and 'cancel' would empty the track before the whistle.

questions.stem: The coach asked the team to ________ their efforts in the final quarter of the game.
questions.trap_type: 'Reduce' and 'abandon' mean giving up or doing less. 'Double' = increase effort to twice as much when it matters most.
questions.learning_tip: DOUBLE your efforts = increase what you are doing to twice as much. Coaches tell players to DOUBLE their efforts when the game is close.
questions.retry_hint: It is the FINAL QUARTER, so the coach wants their EFFORTS to grow, not shrink. Ask: which verb means to increase something to twice as much? 'Reduce' and 'abandon' would hand the game away.

questions.stem: The runners were ________ at the starting blocks, waiting for the starter's pistol.
questions.trap_type: 'Relaxed' and 'sleeping' suggest they were not ready; 'distracted' means not focused. 'Coiled' = tensed like a spring, ready to burst forward.
questions.learning_tip: COILED = tensed like a spring and ready to release energy. Athletes COIL at the starting blocks = they hold their muscles tight, ready to sprint.
questions.retry_hint: They are at the STARTING BLOCKS, WAITING FOR THE STARTER'S PISTOL - muscles tight, ready to burst forward. Ask: which adjective describes a body wound up like a spring? 'Relaxed' and 'sleeping' say the opposite.

questions.stem: Class 3B showed great ________ by encouraging their teammates even after falling behind.
questions.trap_type: All other options are negative qualities. SPORTSMANSHIP = fair and generous behaviour in sport.
questions.learning_tip: SPORTSMANSHIP = fair, generous and respectful behaviour towards teammates and opponents. Encouraging others even when losing shows great SPORTSMANSHIP.
questions.retry_hint: They kept ENCOURAGING THEIR TEAMMATES EVEN AFTER FALLING BEHIND - losing did not make them mean. Ask: which noun names fair, generous behaviour in sport? Every other choice names a fault.

questions.stem: The anchor runner on the red team ________ the baton and sprinted the final leg to clinch victory.
questions.trap_type: 'Dropped' would lose the race; 'ignored' and 'studied' don't fit the action. SEIZED = grasped quickly and firmly.
questions.learning_tip: SEIZED = grabbed firmly and quickly. The anchor runner SEIZED the baton = took it decisively and ran with it.
questions.retry_hint: The ANCHOR RUNNER took the BATON and SPRINTED THE FINAL LEG to win. Ask: which verb means to grab something firmly and quickly? 'Dropped' would lose the race, and 'studied' would stop it dead.

questions.stem: Our school has ________ the inter-class relay trophy three years in a row.
questions.trap_type: 'Has won' = present perfect. Students write 'win' or 'wins' ignoring the auxiliary 'has'.
questions.learning_tip: HAS + past participle = present perfect. Our school HAS WON the trophy = it won it at some point and the result stands today.
questions.retry_hint: HAS is already sitting in the sentence, waiting for its partner, and THREE YEARS IN A ROW reaches right up to today. Ask: after 'has', which form follows - plain, -s, -ing, or a past participle?

questions.stem: The students ________ their warm-up exercises when the sky suddenly turned dark.
questions.trap_type: 'The sky turned dark' is the sudden interrupting event. The students were already doing warm-ups = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: The sky TURNED DARK = sudden past event. Students were already in the middle of warm-ups = WERE DOING (ongoing background).
questions.retry_hint: THE SKY SUDDENLY TURNED DARK - a sharp event that cut into something already under way. Ask: which choice shows an action in progress in the past? A plain past verb would only report a finished job.

questions.stem: Running the 4x100m relay is ________ demanding than running a solo 100m sprint.
questions.trap_type: Comparing two events = comparative. 'Demanding' is multi-syllable → MORE, not -er.
questions.learning_tip: COMPARATIVE of multi-syllable adjectives: MORE + adjective. The relay is MORE DEMANDING than the solo sprint = comparing two things.
questions.retry_hint: THAN pits the RELAY against a SOLO 100M SPRINT - two events, not many. Ask: comparative or superlative? DEMANDING is long, so it needs a helper word, never an -er ending. 'Very' cannot pair with 'than'.

questions.stem: The PE teacher saw that the students ________ their stretches by the time the first event started.
questions.trap_type: 'By the time' forces the earlier of two past actions into the past perfect. Students write the simple past 'completed', which cannot show which action came first.
