questions.learning_tip: BY THE TIME + past = the other action must be PAST PERFECT (had + past participle). The stretches were finished BEFORE the first event started.
questions.retry_hint: Two past moments: the STRETCHES finished first, and only afterwards did THE FIRST EVENT start. Ask: which form shows the earlier of two past actions? BY THE TIME is the phrase that demands it.

questions.stem: There was ________ energy left in the team after the gruelling morning session.
questions.trap_type: 'Energy' is uncountable → use 'little' or 'much'. 'Few' and 'many' are for countable nouns.
questions.learning_tip: LITTLE = a small amount (uncountable). 'Energy' is uncountable → there was LITTLE energy left. 'Few' is only for countable things you can number.
questions.retry_hint: ENERGY cannot be counted - you never say 'three energies'. Ask: which word partners an uncountable noun after that GRUELLING MORNING SESSION? 'Few', 'many' and 'a few' all need countable things.

questions.stem: The winning team has not been announced yet, ________ it?
questions.trap_type: Main clause is NEGATIVE present perfect ('has not been') → POSITIVE question tag. 'Has not' → positive tag = has it.
questions.learning_tip: Negative statement → positive question tag. 'The team HAS NOT been announced, HAS it?' Negative → positive tag.
questions.retry_hint: A tag copies whichever helping verb runs the statement, and this statement ends with ANNOUNCED YET - a present perfect in negative form. Ask: after a negative statement, does its tag turn positive or stay negative?

questions.stem: The gold medal for the long jump event ________ by a student from Class 3C this morning.
questions.trap_type: The medal was the receiver of the action. Past passive = was won.
questions.learning_tip: The gold medal was the receiver of the action. Past passive = WAS WON. Passive = was/were + past participle.
questions.retry_hint: The GOLD MEDAL cannot win anything - BY A STUDENT FROM CLASS 3C tells you who acted, and THIS MORNING places it in past time. Ask: which choice is passive and past? Passive = a form of 'be' + past participle.

questions.stem: The PE teacher told the students ________ in the sun for too long without drinking water.
questions.trap_type: Negative reported speech: told + object + not to + base verb.
questions.learning_tip: 'Told students NOT TO + base verb': told students NOT TO STAND in the sun without drinking water.
questions.retry_hint: A reported order sits here: TOLD THE STUDENTS what they must never do IN THE SUN WITHOUT DRINKING WATER. Ask: which verb form follows 'told' + person? And does a negative word come before that infinitive, or inside it?

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Verb forms of 'run')

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Kai loves (1)________ more than any other sport.' Signal: 'loves + ___' = gerund (verb-ing). Pattern: love + verb-ing → running.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'to run'. ENJOY must be followed by the -ing form - 'enjoys to run' is never correct.
questions.learning_tip: ENJOY + verb-ing: enjoys RUNNING. Same pattern: enjoy cycling, enjoy swimming. The infinitive belongs after 'plans', not after 'enjoys'.
questions.retry_hint: ENJOYS decides it: this verb is always followed by an -ing form, never by an infinitive. Ask: do you say 'enjoy to swim' or 'enjoy swimming'? Copy that shape here - a SPORT is being named.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'He (2)________ fifty laps every morning before school as part of his training.' Signal: 'every morning' = regular habit = simple present. Subject 'He' = singular → runs.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'run' forgetting 'He' is singular in simple present.
questions.learning_tip: Regular habit = simple present. He (singular) → RUNS fifty laps every morning.
questions.retry_hint: FIFTY LAPS EVERY MORNING is a routine, so the tense stays present, and HE is one person. Ask: does a singular subject take the plain verb, or the verb ending in -s? A past form would break the routine.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Last Sports Day, Kai (3)________ the anchor leg and helped his team win the relay.' Signal: 'Last Sports Day' = past. 'Run' is irregular: run → ran.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'runned', not knowing 'run' is irregular.
questions.learning_tip: 'Last Sports Day' = past. 'Run' is irregular: run → RAN. Never write 'runned'.
questions.retry_hint: LAST SPORTS DAY is finished time, and he took the ANCHOR LEG in a race that is over. Ask: which form is simple past? This verb is irregular - the vowel changes, and no -ed ending is ever allowed.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'While Kai (4)________ the final stretch, the crowd began to cheer loudly.' Signal: 'while Kai ___' = ongoing background past action. Subject 'Kai' = singular → was running. Interrupted by 'the crowd began to cheer'.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'ran' (simple past) missing the ongoing signal 'while'.
questions.learning_tip: 'While Kai ___' = ongoing background past action = past continuous. Kai WAS RUNNING the final stretch when the crowd cheered.
questions.retry_hint: WHILE tells you this action had already begun when THE CROWD BEGAN TO CHEER. Ask: which form shows a past action still in progress? Kai is one person, so choose the singular helper, not the plural one.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'His teammates (5)________ alongside him on the track, shouting encouragement.' Signal: same past time frame, plural subject 'his teammates' + ongoing parallel action → were running.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'ran' (simple past) instead of past continuous for an ongoing parallel action.
questions.learning_tip: His teammates = plural. They were doing it at the same past moment = WERE RUNNING (past continuous).
questions.retry_hint: HIS TEAMMATES is plural, and they moved ALONGSIDE HIM at the same moment, SHOUTING ENCOURAGEMENT. Ask: which form shows an action in progress in the past, and which helper matches a plural subject?

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Kai plans (6)________ in the national school athletics championship next year.' Signal: 'plans + ___' = infinitive. Pattern: plan + to + base verb → to run.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'running' instead of the infinitive after 'plans'.
questions.learning_tip: 'Plan TO + base verb': plans TO RUN in the championship. Always use the infinitive after 'plans'.
questions.retry_hint: PLANS is the deciding word: it must be followed by an infinitive, never by an -ing form. Ask: do you say 'he plans going', or 'he plans ___ go' with a small word slipped in? Supply that word here.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'His coach says every athlete should (7)________ at least three races before a major competition.' Signal: 'should + ___' = modal verb + base form. Never add -s or -ing after a modal.
questions.trap_type: Students add -s or -ing after the modal verb 'should'.
questions.learning_tip: After modal verbs (should, must, can, will), always use the BASE form: should RUN. Never 'should runs' or 'should running'.
questions.retry_hint: SHOULD is a modal verb, and a modal always takes a bare, unchanged verb - no -s, no -ing, no infinitive marker. Ask: which box form is the plain one? EVERY ATHLETE adds nothing to it either.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Right now, Kai (8)________ his final practice lap before the championship next week.' Signal: 'Right now' = present continuous. Subject 'Kai' = singular → is running.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'runs' (simple present habit) missing the 'right now' signal for present continuous.
questions.learning_tip: 'Right now' = present continuous. Kai (singular) → IS RUNNING his final practice lap right now.
questions.retry_hint: RIGHT NOW pins the action to this very moment, so it must be in progress. Ask: which form shows something happening as you read? Kai counts as one person, so take the singular helper, not 'are'.

C.passage: Kai enjoys (1)________ more than any other sport on the school calendar. He (2)________ fifty laps every morning before school as part of his dedicated training routine. Last Sports Day, Kai (3)________ the anchor leg and helped his team win the relay by a single second. While Kai (4)________ the final stretch, the crowd began to cheer loudly from the sidelines. His teammates (5)________ alongside him on the track, shouting encouragement at every step. Kai already plans (6)________ in the national school athletics championship next year if he qualifies. His coach says every athlete should (7)________ at least three competitive races before a major championship. Right now, Kai (8)________ his final practice lap before the event next week.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: Sports Day at Greenfield Primary is one of the most exciting events of the year. Hundreds of (1)________ line the track and field, cheering for their classes and clapping for every athlete who crosses the finish line. In the relay race, each runner must pass a metal (2)________ to the next teammate without dropping it or stepping outside the exchange zone. Athletes who (3)________ in long-distance events need great (4)________ — the ability to keep going when their muscles are tired and their breathing is heavy. Gymnastic events test a different skill: how (5)________ a student can be, moving quickly and gracefully through a series of jumps and rolls.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'line the track and field, cheering for their classes' = people watching = spectators.
questions.learning_tip: SPECTATORS = people who watch an event. Hundreds of SPECTATORS lined the track to cheer for the athletes.
questions.retry_hint: HUNDREDS of them LINE THE TRACK AND FIELD, CHEERING for their classes. Ask: which box word names the people who watch? It must be plural - 'hundreds of ___'. The athletes are the ones being watched.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'pass a metal ___ to the next teammate' in a relay race = the object passed between runners = baton.
questions.learning_tip: A BATON = the short stick passed between runners in a relay race. Dropping the BATON in a relay usually means losing the race.
questions.retry_hint: In the RELAY RACE, each runner must pass a METAL object TO THE NEXT TEAMMATE without dropping it. Ask: which box word names that short stick? A person or a quality cannot be passed from hand to hand.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'athletes who ___ in long-distance events' = take part against others = compete.
questions.learning_tip: COMPETE = take part in a contest against others. Athletes COMPETE in long-distance events to test their stamina.
questions.retry_hint: The gap follows ATHLETES WHO, so it must be a verb, and the events are LONG-DISTANCE contests against others. Ask: which box word means to take part in a contest? A noun cannot follow 'who' here.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'ability to keep going when muscles are tired and breathing is heavy' = endurance.
questions.learning_tip: ENDURANCE = the ability to keep going for a long time despite fatigue and difficulty. Long-distance runners need great ENDURANCE.
questions.retry_hint: The dash defines it: KEEP GOING WHEN THEIR MUSCLES ARE TIRED and their BREATHING IS HEAVY. Ask: which box word names that staying power? It follows 'need great', so it must be a noun.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'moving quickly and gracefully through jumps and rolls' = agile.
questions.learning_tip: AGILE = able to move quickly and easily with great coordination. Gymnasts are AGILE — they move their bodies with speed and grace.
questions.retry_hint: GYMNASTIC events test MOVING QUICKLY AND GRACEFULLY through JUMPS AND ROLLS. Ask: which box word describes a body that changes direction with ease? It follows 'how', so it must be a describing word.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.trap_type: 'The runners' is plural. Students write 'was' (singular).
questions.learning_tip: 'The runners' = plural → WERE all ready at the starting line. WAS is only for singular subjects.
questions.retry_hint: THE RUNNERS is the subject - a whole line of them at the STARTING BLOCKS. Ask: does a plural subject take 'was', or its plural partner? Match the verb to the subject, not to the noun nearest the gap.

questions.trap_type: Students write 'their' (belonging to them) when the sentence needs 'there' (at that place).
questions.learning_tip: THERE = at that place. The judges stood THERE near the finish line. THEIR = belonging to them. Test: can you replace with 'at that place'? If yes, use THERE.
questions.retry_hint: The JUDGES did not own anything - they simply STOOD at a place NEAR THE FINISH LINE. Ask: which spelling means 'at that place'? The two words sound identical, so decide by meaning alone.

questions.trap_type: Students write 'quick' (adjective) after the action verb 'passed'. A verb needs an adverb.
questions.learning_tip: After an action verb (passed), use an ADVERB: passed QUICKLY. 'Quick' is an adjective — it describes nouns, not actions.
questions.retry_hint: PASSED is the action, and the underlined word describes HOW the BATON was handed over. Ask: which ending must be added before an adjective may describe an action? An adjective can only describe the baton itself.

questions.trap_type: Students write a plain plural and leave out the apostrophe that shows ownership.
questions.learning_tip: The names BELONG TO the winners -> WINNERS' names (apostrophe after the -s for a plural). Singular: winner's.
questions.retry_hint: The NAMES belong to more than one winner, and the coach read them out over the LOUDSPEAKER. Ask: does a plain -s show ownership, or only number? When many people own something, where does the apostrophe land?

questions.error_type: Irregular past tense - run -> ran (not runned)
questions.trap_type: Students add -ed to 'run', producing 'runned'. 'Run' is irregular: run -> ran.
questions.learning_tip: 'Run' is irregular: run -> RAN. Never write 'runned'. Other irregular verbs: swim -> swam, sing -> sang, throw -> threw.
questions.retry_hint: RUNNED is not a word at all: this verb never takes an -ed ending. Ask: how do you say it in the past - 'yesterday she ___ home'? The vowel inside changes, exactly as swim becomes swam.

E.passage: On Sports Day, the runners was (1) all lined up at the starting blocks, with hearts pounding in excitement. The judges stood their (2) near the finish line, holding clipboards and stopwatches. During the relay, each runner passed the baton quick (3) to the next teammate without slowing down. After the race, the coach read out the winners (4) names over the loudspeaker. Together, the team runned (5) their best race of the year and broke the school record.

questions.sentence_a: You train consistently every week.
questions.sentence_b: You will see a real improvement in your speed.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'As long as'.
questions.model_answer: As long as you train consistently every week, you will see a real improvement in your speed.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'As long as you will train' — adding 'will' after 'as long as', which follows the same rule as 'if'.
questions.learning_tip: AS LONG AS + simple present, simple future. AS LONG AS you TRAIN consistently, you WILL SEE improvement. Never 'will' after 'as long as'.
questions.retry_hint: Which half is the condition, and which is the reward? TRAIN CONSISTENTLY EVERY WEEK comes first. Ask: after 'As long as', does the verb stay simple present, or may 'will' sneak in? A comma joins the halves.

questions.sentence_a: The relay team trained for six months.
questions.sentence_b: The relay team finally won the district championship.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'After'.
questions.model_answer: After training for six months, the relay team finally won the district championship.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'After the relay team trained for six months, they won' — acceptable, but the model answer shows the more elegant reduction using -ing.
questions.learning_tip: AFTER + verb-ing (same subject): AFTER TRAINING for six months, the team finally WON. When the same subject does both actions, use 'after' + -ing for the first.
questions.retry_hint: Both halves share one subject: THE RELAY TEAM. Ask: which action came earlier - SIX MONTHS of work, or winning the DISTRICT CHAMPIONSHIP? The earlier one follows 'After', and a shared subject lets its verb change form.

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
The score between Red House and Blue House was tied at forty-eight points each going into the final event: the 4x100 metre relay. Whoever won this race would win the Sports Day championship.

Red House had the fastest individual sprinter in the school — a girl named Aisha. But the relay is not just about individual speed. The baton must be passed cleanly, and the team must run as one.

Blue House got off to a strong start. Their first two runners built a three-metre lead. By the third leg, the gap had widened to five metres.

Then Aisha stepped onto the track for the final leg. She ran not just with her legs but with everything she had. The crowd went quiet first — then erupted as she closed the gap metre by metre.

With twenty metres to go, she pulled level. With ten, she was ahead.

Red House crossed the finish line first by a fraction of a second.

In the changing room afterwards, Aisha sat quietly. Her teammates expected her to be celebrating. Instead, she said, 'I almost didn't catch up. We need to work on the third handover.'

That is what made her a leader.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 4 has the same meaning as 'burst out suddenly and loudly'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Quiet' is the opposite; 'closed' means reduced the gap; 'stepped' means moved onto. ERUPTED = burst out suddenly and with great force or noise.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: ERUPTED = burst out suddenly and with great energy or noise. The crowd ERUPTED = broke out in loud cheering all at once.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 3, what does 'it' refer to in 'the gap had widened to five metres'?

options.3: The distance between Blue House and Red House

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking 'it' refers to the race. But 'it' refers to the GAP — the lead Blue House built up.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 3: 'Their first two runners built a three-metre LEAD. By the third leg, IT had widened to five metres.' IT = the gap/lead between the two teams.

mcq_questions.stem: Why did the writer say 'That is what made her a leader' in the last line?

options.1: Because Aisha was the fastest runner in the school.
options.2: Because she had crossed the finish line first.
options.3: Because instead of celebrating, she focused on improving what went wrong.
options.4: Because her teammates listened to everything she said.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 or 2 thinking being fast or winning makes someone a leader. But the writer points to her THINKING after the victory.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: True leadership is shown in thinking about IMPROVEMENT, not just celebrating victory. Aisha spotted a weakness (the third handover) even after winning — that is what makes a leader.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 6, is it True or False that Red House won the relay by a wide margin? Give a reason from the passage.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The passage says Red House won 'BY A FRACTION OF A SECOND' — a fraction means an extremely small amount of time, not a wide margin.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'True, Red House won clearly.' The passage explicitly says 'by a fraction of a second' = an extremely narrow margin.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 6: 'Red House crossed the line first BY A FRACTION OF A SECOND.' A FRACTION of a second = extremely small. The win was very narrow, not wide. Answer is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: What advantage did Blue House have by the start of the third leg?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: Blue House had a five-metre lead over Red House by the start of the third leg.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'Blue House was winning' without stating the specific gap.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 3: 'by the third leg, the gap had widened to FIVE METRES.' Give the specific measurement from the passage.

open_ended_questions.stem: Paragraph 2 says 'the relay is not just about individual speed.' Explain what this means using TWO ideas from the passage.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) The baton must be passed cleanly between runners — if it is dropped, the team loses. (ii) The team must run as one — everyone's performance matters, not just the fastest runner.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'you need to be fast' — that is exactly what the passage says is NOT the only factor.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 2: (1) the BATON must be passed cleanly; (2) the TEAM must run as one. Two specific reasons why relay is about more than individual speed.

open_ended_questions.stem: What did Aisha say in the changing room, and how did this surprise her teammates?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: She said 'I almost didn't catch up. We need to work on the third handover.' Her teammates expected her to be celebrating their victory, but instead she focused on a weakness to improve.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'she was not happy' — she was not sad either. She was focused on improvement.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 7: teammates expected CELEBRATING, but Aisha talked about the THIRD HANDOVER — a weakness. This surprised them because she focused on improvement, not the win.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on her actions in the passage, describe TWO character traits of Aisha with evidence from the passage.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: Aisha is determined and analytical. (i) DETERMINED: she ran the final leg with a five-metre deficit and closed it to win by a fraction of a second, showing she never gave up. (ii) ANALYTICAL: after the win, she focused on the weak third handover rather than celebrating, showing she always thinks about improvement.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say she is 'fast and kind' without precise traits or evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: DETERMINED — ran with 'everything she had' to close a five-metre gap. ANALYTICAL — spotted the THIRD HANDOVER flaw even after winning.

questions.stem: The removal company arrived early and began to ________ the heavy furniture onto the lorry.
questions.trap_type: 'Paint', 'hide' and 'damage' do not describe moving furniture onto a vehicle. LOAD = place items onto a vehicle for transport.
questions.learning_tip: LOAD = place goods or items onto a vehicle or into a container. The workers LOADED the furniture onto the lorry.
questions.retry_hint: The lorry is waiting and the HEAVY FURNITURE has to go ONTO it. Ask: which verb means to place goods onto a vehicle? 'Paint' and 'damage' do something to the furniture; 'hide' keeps it out of sight.

questions.stem: Moving to a new neighbourhood can be ________ at first, but most people settle in within a few weeks.
questions.trap_type: 'Exciting', 'simple' and 'pleasant' are all positive. UNSETTLING = causing feelings of unease or discomfort — the contrast with 'settle in' makes 3 correct.
questions.learning_tip: UNSETTLING = making you feel uneasy or anxious because it disrupts your familiar routine. Moving is often UNSETTLING because everything is unfamiliar.
questions.retry_hint: The second half is the rescue: most people SETTLE IN WITHIN A FEW WEEKS. Ask: so at first the feeling must be the opposite of comfortable - which choice is the only uneasy one? 'Exciting', 'simple' and 'pleasant' are all happy words.

questions.stem: Mother spent the whole afternoon ________ boxes in the new living room, trying to decide where each item should go.
questions.trap_type: 'Destroying', 'hiding' and 'painting' do not describe organising boxes. STACKING = placing things one on top of another in a neat pile.
questions.learning_tip: STACKING = placing items neatly on top of each other. Mother STACKED the boxes = piled them up in an orderly way.
questions.retry_hint: Mother is TRYING TO DECIDE WHERE EACH ITEM SHOULD GO, so the boxes are being piled up neatly, not wrecked. Ask: which verb means placing things one on top of another? 'Destroying' and 'painting' organise nothing.

questions.stem: Father asked the children to ________ the old toys they no longer needed before the move.
questions.trap_type: 'Treasure' = value; 'multiply' = increase; 'break' = damage. SORT OUT = organise and decide what to keep or discard.
questions.learning_tip: SORT OUT = organise things by deciding what to keep, give away or throw away. Before moving, families SORT OUT their belongings.
questions.retry_hint: The toys are OLD and NO LONGER NEEDED, and this happens BEFORE THE MOVE. Ask: which choice means going through your things and deciding what to keep or give away? 'Treasure' means value them; 'break' destroys them.

questions.stem: Despite the chaos of moving, Mother was determined to ________ before evening so that the family could sleep comfortably that night.
questions.trap_type: 'Abandon' and 'demolish' need an object and mean giving up or destroying. 'Renovate' is weeks of building work, not something done before evening.
questions.learning_tip: SETTLE IN = make a new place feel like home. Mother wanted to SETTLE IN before night = unpack and organise so the home felt comfortable.
questions.retry_hint: Mother must finish the job BEFORE EVENING so that the family can SLEEP COMFORTABLY that night. Ask: which choice makes a new home liveable? 'Abandon' and 'demolish' give up or destroy, and building work takes weeks.

questions.stem: Our family has ________ to three different flats since I was born.
questions.trap_type: HAS + past participle = present perfect. 'Has moved' = it happened in the past and relates to the present.
questions.learning_tip: HAS + past participle = present perfect. Our family HAS MOVED to three flats = this is the total up to now. 'Move' is regular: move → moved.
questions.retry_hint: HAS is already sitting in the sentence, and SINCE I WAS BORN counts everything up to today. Ask: after 'has', which form completes a present perfect - the plain verb, the -s form, the -ing form, or the past participle?

questions.stem: The movers ________ the last box when the lift suddenly broke down.
questions.trap_type: 'The lift broke down' = sudden interrupting event. The movers were already carrying = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: The lift BROKE DOWN = sudden past event. The movers were already in the middle of carrying the box = WERE CARRYING.
questions.retry_hint: The lift SUDDENLY BROKE DOWN - one sharp event cutting across something longer. Ask: which choice shows an action already going on at that past moment? A plain past verb reports only a finished action.

questions.stem: Our new flat is ________ than our old one — it has an extra bedroom and a larger kitchen.
questions.trap_type: Comparing two flats = comparative. 'Spacious' is multi-syllable → MORE SPACIOUS. 'Spaciouser' is wrong.
questions.learning_tip: COMPARATIVE of multi-syllable adjectives: MORE + adjective. The new flat is MORE SPACIOUS than the old one. Never 'spaciouser'.
questions.retry_hint: THAN sets the new flat against the old one - just two things - and the adjective has three syllables. Ask: do long adjectives take -er, or do they need a comparing word in front? 'Spaciouser' is not English.

questions.stem: The new neighbourhood doesn't have ________ parks as our old one, but it's closer to the MRT.
questions.trap_type: 'Parks' is countable → use 'as many'. 'Much' is for uncountable. 'AS MANY as' = equal comparison for countable nouns.
questions.learning_tip: AS MANY ... AS = equal comparison for countable plural nouns. The neighbourhood doesn't have AS MANY parks AS the old one. MUCH is for uncountable nouns.
questions.retry_hint: PARKS can be counted one by one, and the two neighbourhoods are measured for an EQUAL number. Ask: which quantity phrase pairs countable plurals in an equal comparison? 'Much' belongs to uncountable things.

questions.stem: You have been to the new flat before, ________ you?
questions.trap_type: Main clause is positive present perfect ('have been') → negative question tag. 'Have been' → haven't you.
questions.learning_tip: Question tag for positive present perfect: [positive] + HAVEN'T + subject? 'You HAVE been to the flat, HAVEN'T you?' Positive → negative tag.
questions.retry_hint: The statement is POSITIVE and uses HAVE BEEN. Ask: after a positive statement, does the tag stay positive or flip to negative? A tag must repeat the helping verb it sees, so a form of 'be' cannot appear.

questions.stem: There ________ much noise from the road, so the family kept the windows closed.
questions.trap_type: 'Much noise' = uncountable singular amount. Past event → was.
questions.learning_tip: 'Much noise' = singular uncountable amount. Past event → THERE WAS much noise from the road.
questions.retry_hint: NOISE cannot be counted - there is no plural - and the family KEPT the windows closed, which is finished past time. Ask: does an uncountable amount take a singular verb or a plural one, and must the tense match 'kept'?

questions.stem: All the furniture ________ to the new flat within four hours by the removal team.
questions.trap_type: The furniture was the receiver of the action. Past passive = was delivered.
questions.learning_tip: All the furniture was the receiver of the action. Past passive = WAS DELIVERED. Passive = was/were + past participle.
questions.retry_hint: The FURNITURE did not carry itself: the REMOVAL TEAM did, and the job finished WITHIN FOUR HOURS. Ask: which choice is passive - the subject receives the action - and set firmly in the past?

questions.stem: Mother told us ________ in the rooms while the movers were still working.
questions.trap_type: Negative reported speech: told + object + not to + base verb.
questions.learning_tip: 'Told us NOT TO + base verb': told us NOT TO RUN in the rooms while the movers were working.
questions.retry_hint: Mother TOLD US something she forbade while the MOVERS were still working. Ask: after 'told + person', does the verb stay plain, take -ing, or follow the little word that introduces an infinitive? And where does the negative word sit?

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Time prepositions and adverbs)

questions.context_check: Passage: 'We said goodbye to our neighbours (1)________ the removal lorry arrived.' Signal: the goodbye happened earlier than the lorry's arrival = BEFORE. BEFORE = earlier in time than something else.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'after'. The lorry pulled up at eight and the farewells were over by then, so the goodbyes came first.
questions.learning_tip: BEFORE = earlier in time than something else. They said goodbye BEFORE the lorry arrived = the goodbye happened first.
questions.retry_hint: Read the clue that follows: WHEN IT FINALLY PULLED UP AT EIGHT, THE FAREWELLS WERE OVER. Ask: did the goodbyes happen earlier than the lorry's arrival, or later? Choose the word that puts the goodbye first.

questions.context_check: Passage: '(2)________ the last box was loaded, we took one final photo of our old home.' Signal: the photo was taken following the loading = AFTER. AFTER = later in time than something else.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'before'. The flat is EMPTY in the photograph, so the loading must already be finished.
questions.learning_tip: AFTER = later in time. AFTER the last box had been loaded, the flat was empty and the photograph could be taken.
questions.retry_hint: The photograph shows an EMPTY FLAT, so every box must be gone by then. Ask: does the photo come earlier or later than the loading? Pick the word that places one event later than another.

questions.context_check: Passage: '(3)________ the journey to our new home, I stared out of the window and thought about my old room.' Signal: happening throughout a period/event = DURING. DURING = throughout a particular time or event.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'after'. The lorries are being counted while the vehicle is still moving, so the whole stretch of travelling time is meant.
questions.learning_tip: DURING = all through a period or event. DURING the journey = at every moment of the journey, not once it has ended.
questions.retry_hint: I COUNTED THE LORRIES WE PASSED - that only happens while the vehicle is still moving. Ask: which preposition covers a whole stretch of travelling time, rather than the moment it ends?

questions.context_check: Passage: 'We have lived in the same block (4)________ I was five years old.' Signal: from a past point up to now = SINCE (used with present perfect). SINCE = from a specific point in the past up to now.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'until'. The blank names the starting point of a stretch of time that ran right up to moving day.
questions.learning_tip: SINCE = from a past starting point onwards. We had lived there SINCE I was five = from that age up to now.
questions.retry_hint: The blank names a starting point: I WAS FIVE YEARS OLD, and the living carried on from then. Ask: which word marks the moment a stretch of time began? 'Until' would mark its end instead.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The workers carried boxes (5)________ midnight before they finally finished.' Signal: continuing up to a point in time = UNTIL. UNTIL = up to a point in time.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'before'. FROM early evening names the start, so the blank must name the end of an unbroken stretch of work.
questions.learning_tip: FROM ... UNTIL = the start and the end of a continuous period. They worked FROM evening UNTIL midnight without a break.
questions.retry_hint: FROM EARLY EVENING names the start, and WITHOUT STOPPING ONCE tells you the work never paused. Ask: which word marks the end of an unbroken stretch, partnering 'from'?

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Mother wanted every box unpacked (6)________ the following morning.' Signal: a deadline — completed no later than a specific time = BY. BY = no later than a specific time.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'until'. Mother is naming a deadline, not a stretch of work: not a minute later than nine o'clock.
questions.learning_tip: BY = not later than a given time (a deadline). Unpacked BY nine o'clock = finished at nine o'clock at the latest.
questions.retry_hint: Mother sets a deadline: NINE O'CLOCK THE NEXT MORNING, AND NOT A MINUTE LATER. Ask: which word means 'no later than' a fixed time? The word for continuous work would say the unpacking never stops.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'By seven in the morning, Mother had (7)________ arranged the kitchen cupboards.' Signal: completed earlier than expected = ALREADY. ALREADY = sooner than expected, used with present or past perfect.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'yet'. The cupboards were done sooner than anyone expected, and the sentence is positive.
questions.learning_tip: ALREADY = sooner than expected, in positive sentences. She had ALREADY arranged the cupboards by seven.
questions.retry_hint: The cupboards were done WHEN I CAME DOWNSTAIRS AT SEVEN - sooner than anyone expected, and the sentence is positive. Ask: which adverb reports that something happened earlier than expected?

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Father had not found his reading glasses (8)________ — they were somewhere in the last unpacked box.' Signal: expected but not done up to now = YET. YET = expected to happen but hasn't happened up to now (used in negatives/questions).
questions.trap_type: Students write 'already'. The sentence is NEGATIVE - the glasses are still missing at the moment of speaking.
questions.learning_tip: YET = up to now, in negatives and questions. He had NOT found them YET = he expected to, but so far had not.
questions.retry_hint: Father HAD NOT FOUND his READING GLASSES - the sentence is negative and the search is still unfinished. Ask: which little word means 'up to now' and lives in negatives and questions?

C.passage: Moving day was full of surprises. We said goodbye to our neighbours (1)________ the removal lorry arrived; when it finally pulled up at eight, the farewells were over. (2)________ the last box had been loaded, we took a final photograph of the empty flat. (3)________ the long journey to the new estate, I stared out of the window and counted the lorries we passed. We had lived in the same block (4)________ I was five years old, so leaving it felt strange. The workers carried boxes from early evening (5)________ midnight, without stopping once for a meal. Mother wanted every box unpacked (6)________ nine o'clock the next morning, and not a minute later. When I came downstairs at seven, she had (7)________ arranged all the kitchen cupboards. Father, however, had not found his reading glasses (8)________ - they were in the very last box.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: Moving house is one of life's most (1)________ tasks — there are so many things to plan, pack and organise that it can feel overwhelming. Families who (2)________ to a different part of Singapore must get used to a new neighbourhood, new transport routes and new neighbours all at once. Before the move, many families choose to have their new flat (3)________, replacing old paint, flooring and fixtures to make the space feel fresh and welcoming. The hardest part for many people is leaving behind places and routines that feel (4)________ — the coffee shop downstairs, the park around the corner, the school nearby. After the move, the new home may feel (5)________ with boxes and furniture in unexpected places, but this usually sorts itself out within a few weeks.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'so many things to plan, pack and organise that it can feel overwhelming' = daunting.
questions.learning_tip: DAUNTING = seeming difficult and discouraging. Moving house is DAUNTING because of the sheer amount of things to do.
questions.retry_hint: The dash explains it: SO MANY THINGS TO PLAN, PACK AND ORGANISE that it can feel OVERWHELMING. Ask: which box word describes a task that looks too big to start? 'Familiar' says nothing about difficulty.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'move to a different part of Singapore' = move to a new location = relocate.
questions.learning_tip: RELOCATE = move to a different place, especially a new home or city. Families who RELOCATE must adjust to a new environment.
questions.retry_hint: The families are moving TO A DIFFERENT PART OF SINGAPORE, and the blank follows 'who', so it must be a verb. Ask: which box word means to move home to a new place? 'Renovated' is repair work, not a change of address.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'replacing old paint, flooring and fixtures to make the space feel fresh' = renovated.
questions.learning_tip: RENOVATED = repaired and improved by replacing old features. A newly RENOVATED flat has fresh paint, new flooring and updated fittings.
questions.retry_hint: The clue follows the comma: REPLACING OLD PAINT, FLOORING AND FIXTURES. Ask: which box word describes a flat repaired and made fresh again? After 'have their new flat' it must be a past participle.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'the coffee shop downstairs, the park around the corner' = well known and comfortable = familiar.
questions.learning_tip: FAMILIAR = well known through long experience. We miss places that feel FAMILIAR — places we know well and associate with comfort and routine.
questions.retry_hint: The examples are THE COFFEE SHOP DOWNSTAIRS and THE PARK AROUND THE CORNER - places the family knows by heart. Ask: which box word describes what you know well from long habit?

questions.trap_type: The clue 'boxes and furniture in unexpected places' = messy and disorganised = cluttered.
questions.learning_tip: CLUTTERED = filled with too many things in a disorganised way. A home full of unpacked boxes feels CLUTTERED.
questions.retry_hint: The clue is BOXES AND FURNITURE IN UNEXPECTED PLACES, and it SORTS ITSELF OUT within weeks. Ask: which box word describes a home too full of things lying in the wrong places?

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.error_type: Homophone confusion — it's (it is) vs its (possessive)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'it's' (it is) when the sentence needs 'its' (belonging to it). A room and its window = possessive.
questions.learning_tip: ITS = belonging to it (possessive adjective before a noun). 'The room and ITS window' = the window belonging to the room. IT'S = it is. Test: can you replace with 'it is'? If no, use ITS.
questions.retry_hint: The underlined word is short for 'it is', but the sentence is about the ROOM owning a BRIGHT WINDOW. Ask: can you replace it with 'it is' and still make sense? If you cannot, the apostrophe must go.

questions.trap_type: 'The boxes' is plural. Students write 'was' (singular).
questions.learning_tip: 'The boxes' = plural → WERE stacked neatly. WAS is only for singular subjects.
questions.retry_hint: Count the subject: THE BOXES - more than one. Ask: does a plural subject take the singular past verb or the plural one? Do not let 'one wall' pull the verb into the singular.

questions.trap_type: Students write 'careful' (adjective) after the action verb 'wrapped'. A verb needs an adverb.
questions.learning_tip: After an action verb (wrapped), use an ADVERB: wrapped CAREFULLY. 'Careful' is an adjective — it describes nouns, not actions.
questions.retry_hint: WRAPPED is an action verb, and the underlined word tells you HOW Mother wrapped the FRAGILE ITEMS. Ask: do we describe an action with an adjective, or with an adverb? Adjectives belong to nouns.

questions.error_type: Possessive apostrophe — singular possessive (family's, not familys)
questions.trap_type: Students add -s without an apostrophe for 'family's'. To show possession: family → family's (add 's).
questions.learning_tip: Singular possessive = noun + 's: the FAMILY'S belongings = the belongings belonging to the family. Never write 'familys' (that would be a wrong plural).
questions.retry_hint: The OLD BOOKS AND MAGAZINES belong to one family. Ask: does a plain -s show ownership, or only make a plural? Where must the apostrophe go when there is a single owner?

questions.error_type: Comparative — consonant+y adjectives: change y→i before -er (tidy → tidier)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'tidyer' without applying the y→i rule. Words ending in consonant+y change y to i before -er.
questions.learning_tip: 'Tidy' ends in consonant + y: change y → i before adding -er. tidy → TIDIER. Same rule: happy → happier, easy → easier, pretty → prettier.
questions.retry_hint: TIDY ends in a consonant plus -y, and the sentence compares today with THE NIGHT BEFORE. Ask: when you add -er to such a word, what happens to that y? Compare: happy, easy, pretty.

E.passage: On the first morning in our new flat, I woke up and looked at the room and it's (1) bright window facing east. The boxes was (2) stacked along one wall, waiting to be unpacked. Mother wrapped all the fragile items careful (3) in bubble wrap before placing them in the cupboards. Father sorted through the familys (4) old books and magazines, deciding which ones to donate to the community library. By lunchtime, our new home already looked tidyer (5) than it had when we arrived the night before.

questions.sentence_a: You do not visit the new neighbourhood before moving in.
questions.sentence_b: You will feel nervous on the first day.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'Unless'.
questions.model_answer: Unless you visit the new neighbourhood before moving in, you will feel nervous on the first day.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'Unless you will visit' — adding 'will' in the 'unless' clause.
questions.learning_tip: UNLESS + simple present, simple future. UNLESS you VISIT the new neighbourhood before moving in, you WILL FEEL nervous. Never 'will' after 'unless'.
questions.retry_hint: Sentence A is the condition, and notice that it is negative: you DO NOT visit. The joining word already carries that negative inside it. Ask: what tense follows it - present or future? Never add 'will' there.

questions.sentence_a: The removal team carried our belongings with great care.
questions.sentence_b: Not a single item was broken.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'Since'.
questions.model_answer: Since the removal team carried our belongings with great care, not a single item was broken.
questions.trap_type: Students reverse the order: 'Not a single item was broken since the removal team carried our belongings' — acceptable but less natural as an emphasis structure.
questions.learning_tip: SINCE = because of a background reason. SINCE the removal team carried everything carefully, not a single item was broken. The cause comes after 'since'.
questions.retry_hint: Sentence A gives the cause - the team carried everything WITH GREAT CARE - and sentence B gives the result. Ask: which half must follow the joining word, and where does the comma fall?

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
The removal lorry pulled away at seven in the evening, leaving the family of four standing in a flat full of boxes. Ten-year-old Zara had not said a word since they arrived.

Her mother noticed. 'It will feel like home soon,' she said.

Zara said nothing. She went to what was now her bedroom and sat on the bare mattress. The walls were white. There were no drawings pinned to them, no shelves of books, no familiar shadows.

Her father appeared in the doorway with a box in his arms. It was labelled 'ZARA — IMPORTANT'. He placed it gently on the floor and left without speaking.

Zara opened it slowly. Inside were her drawing pads, her coloured pencils, her stack of library books and — at the very bottom — a small framed photograph of her and her best friend Chloe, taken at the school garden on the last day of term.

She picked up a pencil and began drawing. First the outline of the window. Then the tree she could see outside. Then, slowly, the room itself.

By nine o'clock, there were three drawings pinned to the white wall.

When her mother came to say goodnight, Zara looked up and said, 'I think I can make this work.'

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 3 has the same meaning as 'well-known and comfortable through long experience'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Bare' = uncovered; 'white' is a colour; 'shadows' = dark shapes. FAMILIAR = known through long experience.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: FAMILIAR = well known and comfortable through long experience. 'No FAMILIAR shadows' = none of the shapes she knew from her old room.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 4, what does 'It' refer to in 'It was labelled ZARA — IMPORTANT'?

options.3: The box her father was carrying

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking 'It' refers to her father. But her father had 'a box in his arms' — 'It' = the box.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 4: 'Her father appeared with A BOX in his arms. IT was labelled ZARA — IMPORTANT.' IT = the box he was carrying.

mcq_questions.stem: Why did Father leave 'without speaking' after placing the box on the floor?

options.1: He was too tired to talk after the long day of moving.
options.2: He was angry that Zara was not helping to unpack.
options.3: He understood that Zara needed space and that the box would help more than any words could.
options.4: He did not know what was inside the box.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking he was just tired. But the deliberate, gentle action of leaving the specific 'IMPORTANT' box and then leaving quietly shows emotional intelligence.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Father chose the box labelled 'IMPORTANT' and left GENTLY without speaking — showing he understood Zara needed space, and that her special things would help her more than words.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 2, is it True or False that Zara's mother understood her daughter was upset? Give a reason from the passage.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: True. The passage says 'Her mother NOTICED' — and she spoke to Zara with reassurance, saying 'It will feel like home soon', showing she was aware of Zara's unhappiness.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'False, the mother was too busy unpacking.' The passage explicitly says the mother NOTICED Zara's silence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 2: 'Her mother NOTICED.' She said 'It will feel like home soon' — a reassurance. This shows the mother understood and cared. Answer is TRUE.

open_ended_questions.stem: Name THREE items that were inside the box labelled 'ZARA — IMPORTANT'.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: The box contained her drawing pads, her coloured pencils, and her stack of library books. (Accept also: a small framed photograph of her and her friend Chloe.)
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students name only one or two items.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 5: drawing pads, COLOURED PENCILS, LIBRARY BOOKS, and a FRAMED PHOTOGRAPH. Name any three.

open_ended_questions.stem: How did drawing help Zara feel more at home? Give TWO specific details from the passage.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) By nine o'clock, she had three drawings pinned to the white wall — filling the blank space that had reminded her of what was missing. (ii) She drew the view from her new window and the room itself, which shows she began to connect with and accept her new space.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'she felt better' without specific details.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 7: THREE DRAWINGS pinned to the WHITE WALL = the blank, unfamiliar room now had something personal in it. Drawing the NEW WINDOW and room = she started to see it as her own.

open_ended_questions.stem: What does Zara's final line — 'I think I can make this work' — tell us about how she is feeling by the end of the passage?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: She is feeling more hopeful and accepting. She no longer feels helpless about the move — she has taken action by drawing and making the space feel her own, and this has given her confidence.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'she is happy now' — she is not fully happy yet, but she is hopeful and determined.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: 'I think I CAN MAKE THIS WORK' = she is choosing to adapt rather than give up. This shows she is HOPEFUL and beginning to take ownership of her new home.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on his actions in the passage, describe TWO character traits of Zara's father with evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: Zara's father is perceptive and emotionally intelligent. (i) PERCEPTIVE: he chose the box labelled IMPORTANT — knowing which items would matter most to Zara. (ii) EMOTIONALLY INTELLIGENT: he placed the box gently and left without speaking, giving Zara space to recover in her own way.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'he is kind and caring' without naming precise traits or giving evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: PERCEPTIVE — chose the IMPORTANT box with her valued items. EMOTIONALLY INTELLIGENT — placed it GENTLY, left WITHOUT SPEAKING, giving her space and comfort without pressure.

questions.stem: At first, the skill seemed impossible, but Ben ________ by watching tutorials and practising daily.
questions.trap_type: 'Gave up' is the opposite; 'slept' and 'ignored' are irrelevant. PERSISTED = continued despite difficulty.
questions.learning_tip: PERSISTED = continued trying despite difficulty. Ben PERSISTED = he did not give up, even when progress was slow.
questions.retry_hint: The sentence turns on BUT: the skill SEEMED IMPOSSIBLE, and yet he kept WATCHING TUTORIALS AND PRACTISING DAILY. Ask: which verb means to keep trying despite difficulty? 'Gave up' is its exact opposite.

questions.stem: The music teacher ________ the student for holding the violin bow correctly for the first time.
questions.trap_type: 'Scolded' = told off; 'ignored' = paid no attention; 'confused' = made unsure. PRAISED = expressed admiration.
questions.learning_tip: PRAISED = expressed approval and admiration. The teacher PRAISED the student = told her she had done well.
questions.retry_hint: The student held the VIOLIN BOW CORRECTLY FOR THE FIRST TIME - that is good news. Ask: which verb means to tell someone they have done well? 'Scolded' tells them off, and 'ignored' says nothing at all.

questions.stem: After months of practice, her skills had ________ to a level where she could perform in front of a small audience.
questions.trap_type: 'Faded', 'collapsed' and 'disappeared' all suggest decline. IMPROVED = got better over time.
questions.learning_tip: IMPROVED = got better. After months of practice, her skills IMPROVED = they reached a higher level.
questions.retry_hint: AFTER MONTHS OF PRACTICE she can now PERFORM IN FRONT OF A SMALL AUDIENCE. Ask: did her skills climb or fall? 'Faded', 'collapsed' and 'disappeared' all point downwards.

questions.stem: The instructor demonstrated the technique, then asked the students to ________ it step by step.
questions.trap_type: 'Invent' = create something new; 'ignore' and 'destroy' are negative. REPLICATE = reproduce exactly what was demonstrated.
questions.learning_tip: REPLICATE = copy or reproduce something exactly. Students were asked to REPLICATE the instructor's technique = do it the same way she demonstrated.
questions.retry_hint: The instructor DEMONSTRATED the technique first, and the students must follow it STEP BY STEP. Ask: which verb means to copy exactly what you were shown? 'Invent' would create something new instead.

questions.stem: What sets great learners apart is the ability to learn from failure without becoming ________ by it.
questions.trap_type: 'Motivated', 'inspired' and 'rewarded' are all positive outcomes. DISCOURAGED = made to feel less confident or willing to continue.
questions.learning_tip: DISCOURAGED = made to feel less confident or willing to keep trying. Great learners fail but are not DISCOURAGED — they learn and keep going.
questions.retry_hint: Great learners LEARN FROM FAILURE and keep going. Ask: what feeling must they avoid? Choose the one word that would stop a person trying again - 'motivated', 'inspired' and 'rewarded' all push you forward.

questions.stem: Maya has ________ the piano for three years and can now play a full piece from memory.
questions.trap_type: HAS + past participle = present perfect. Students write 'study' or 'studies' ignoring 'has'.
questions.learning_tip: HAS + past participle = present perfect. Maya HAS STUDIED piano for three years = she started then and continues now.
questions.retry_hint: HAS is waiting for a partner, and FOR THREE YEARS runs right up to today. Ask: after 'has', which form builds a present perfect - the plain verb, the -s form, the -ing form, or the past participle?

questions.stem: The students ________ their coding project when the power cut suddenly knocked out all the computers.
questions.trap_type: 'The power cut knocked out the computers' = sudden interrupting event. The students were already finishing = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: The power cut KNOCKED OUT computers = sudden past event. Students were in the middle of finishing = WERE FINISHING.
questions.retry_hint: The POWER CUT SUDDENLY KNOCKED OUT the computers - one sharp event landing in the middle of something longer. Ask: which choice shows work already going on at that past moment?

questions.stem: Learning to code is far ________ than it looks if you follow a structured programme.
questions.trap_type: Comparative needed. 'Far' intensifies the comparative. 'Easy' → EASIER (one-syllable adjective adds -er).
questions.learning_tip: FAR EASIER THAN = much easier than. 'Easy' is one syllable → EASIER. FAR + comparative = intensified comparison.
questions.retry_hint: FAR needs a comparative to lean on, and THAN compares coding with how it LOOKS. Ask: is 'easy' a short adjective that takes -er, or a long one needing a comparing word? 'Easily' is an adverb and cannot follow 'far'.

questions.stem: There is ________ patience required when learning a new language than when learning a physical skill.
questions.trap_type: 'Patience' is uncountable → use 'more' or 'much'. 'Many', 'a few' and 'several' are for countable nouns.
questions.learning_tip: PATIENCE is uncountable. Comparative quantity for uncountable = MORE. There is MORE patience required = a larger amount is needed.
questions.retry_hint: PATIENCE cannot be counted - there is no plural - and THAN sets one amount against another. Ask: which quantity word compares two amounts of an uncountable thing? 'Many', 'a few' and 'several' need countable nouns.

questions.stem: You haven't tried the new pottery class yet, ________ you?
questions.trap_type: Main clause is NEGATIVE present perfect ('haven't tried') → POSITIVE question tag. 'Haven't' → positive tag = have you.
questions.learning_tip: Negative statement → positive question tag. 'You HAVEN'T tried, HAVE you?' Negative → positive tag.
questions.retry_hint: The statement is already NEGATIVE, and it is built in the present perfect (YET is the clue). Ask: after a negative statement, does the tag flip to positive or stay negative? The tag must reuse the same helping verb, so 'did' is out.

questions.stem: The new skill was ________ difficult to learn online ________ it was in a classroom setting.
questions.trap_type: Equal comparison: 'as difficult as' = both methods were equally hard.
questions.learning_tip: AS … AS = equal comparison. The skill was just AS DIFFICULT online AS in a classroom = the difficulty was the same in both settings.
questions.retry_hint: Read both halves: learning it online and learning it in a CLASSROOM were equal in DIFFICULT work - neither harder nor easier. Ask: which pair of words builds an EQUAL comparison? 'More ... than' says one side wins.

questions.stem: The best pottery pieces from the workshop ________ at the school's annual arts exhibition.
questions.trap_type: The pottery pieces were displayed by someone else. Past passive = were displayed.
questions.learning_tip: The pottery pieces were the receivers of the action. Past passive = WERE DISPLAYED. Plural subject → WERE.
questions.retry_hint: The POTTERY PIECES did not walk to the EXHIBITION - somebody put them there, and the subject is plural. Ask: which choice is passive, with the subject receiving the action, and set in the past?

questions.stem: The instructor told the students ________ when they made a mistake but to try again instead.
questions.trap_type: Negative reported speech: told + object + not to + base verb.
questions.learning_tip: 'Told students NOT TO + base verb': told students NOT TO GIVE UP when they made a mistake.
questions.retry_hint: The instructor is FORBIDDING one reaction and offering another instead - TRY AGAIN. Ask: after 'told + person', does the verb stay plain, take -ing, or follow the little word before an infinitive? And where does the negative word sit?

C.label: Section C - Grammar Cloze (Conjunctions: condition, contrast, reason, purpose)

questions.context_check: Passage: '(1)________ you practise every day, you will make steady progress.' Signal: conditional — progress depends on daily practice = IF. IF = standard conditional trigger.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'unless' or 'in case'. The mistake may or may not happen, and the advice follows from it - a plain open condition.
questions.learning_tip: IF = a plain condition: this may happen, and if it does, do that. IF you make a mistake, try again.
questions.retry_hint: The mistake may or may not happen, and the advice - DO NOT GIVE UP - follows only when it does. Ask: which joining word introduces a plain, open condition? A precaution word would mean you act beforehand.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'You cannot improve (2)________ you are willing to make mistakes.' Signal: if not = UNLESS. You CAN improve IF you ARE willing = you CANNOT improve IF you are NOT willing = UNLESS.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'if', forgetting that the sentence is already negative ('cannot improve').
questions.learning_tip: UNLESS = if not. You cannot improve UNLESS you are willing = you cannot improve IF you are NOT willing.
questions.retry_hint: Read the first half: YOU CANNOT IMPROVE - it is already negative. Ask: which joining word carries a hidden negative inside itself, meaning 'except when'? Adding a plain condition word would reverse the sense.

questions.context_check: Passage: '(3)________ learning something new can be frustrating, the feeling of achievement makes it worthwhile.' Signal: contrast between frustration and achievement = ALTHOUGH. ALTHOUGH = despite the fact that.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'because'. The two halves clash: the learning is unpleasant, yet the result is worthwhile - that is a contrast, not a reason.
questions.learning_tip: ALTHOUGH = despite the fact that. It introduces a fact that works AGAINST what follows.
questions.retry_hint: The two halves clash: learning something new can be FRUSTRATING, and yet the FEELING OF SUCCESS makes it worthwhile. Ask: does the joining word show a reason, or a contrast between two facts that pull opposite ways?

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Rina continued practising (4)________ her fingers hurt after every session.' Signal: stronger contrast — she practised DESPITE the pain (emphasis on difficulty overcome) = EVEN THOUGH. EVEN THOUGH = stronger form of 'although', emphasising surprise or difficulty.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'although'. There is no clash here: wanting to join the orchestra is exactly WHY she kept practising.
questions.learning_tip: BECAUSE = for this reason. It answers the question 'why?'. She practised BECAUSE she wanted a place in the orchestra.
questions.retry_hint: Nothing clashes here: wanting a place in the SCHOOL ORCHESTRA is exactly WHY Rina kept practising. Ask: does the second half fight the first, or explain it? A contrast word would spoil the sense.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'A teacher will always support you (5)________ you are genuinely trying your best.' Signal: continuous condition for ongoing support = AS LONG AS. AS LONG AS = on the condition that something remains true.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'more ... than'. The word TWICE measures the length of practice time, so the blank must be a phrase that compares durations.
questions.learning_tip: TWICE AS LONG AS = double the time. Use AS LONG AS to compare how long two people spent on something.
questions.retry_hint: The word TWICE measures how much time Ben spent, set beside Rina. Ask: which box phrase compares the DURATION of two people's practice? Nothing here is called better or worse - only longer or shorter.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'You can join the advanced class (6)________ you complete the beginner course first.' Signal: specific formal requirement/condition = PROVIDED THAT. PROVIDED THAT = on condition that (formal, specific requirement).
questions.trap_type: Students write 'because'. Slow explaining does not happen because nobody is left behind - it happens in order to reach that result.
questions.learning_tip: SO THAT = in order that. It gives the PURPOSE of an action: he explains slowly SO THAT everyone can follow.
questions.retry_hint: The teacher slows down deliberately, aiming at one result: NOBODY IS LEFT BEHIND. Ask: does the second half give a reason, or a PURPOSE - what he wants to achieve? Pick the phrase which introduces purpose.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Always bring a notebook to class (7)________ the instructor demonstrates a technique you want to remember.' Signal: preparing for a possible future event = IN CASE. IN CASE = as a precaution for something that might happen.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'if'. You cannot fetch the notebook after the demonstration starts - you bring it beforehand, as a precaution.
questions.learning_tip: IN CASE = as a precaution, because something might happen. Bring it IN CASE it is needed; IF means only when it does happen.
questions.retry_hint: You cannot fetch a NOTEBOOK once the demonstration has begun - you carry it beforehand, just as a precaution. Ask: which phrase means 'as a precaution, because it might happen'? A plain condition would mean you act only when it does.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'What matters in the end is not (8)________ you succeed on the first try, but whether you keep going.' Signal: expressing a choice between two possibilities = WHETHER. WHETHER = used when two alternatives are being considered (whether X or Y).
questions.trap_type: Students write 'if'. The structure 'not ___ ... but ...' sets two possibilities side by side.
questions.learning_tip: WHETHER = which of two possibilities. Use WHETHER (not 'if') after 'not ... but' and before 'or not'.
questions.retry_hint: The pattern is 'NOT ___ ... BUT ...' - two possibilities set side by side, and the second one wins. Ask: which joining word introduces a choice between two possibilities and can be followed by 'or not'?

C.passage: (1)________ you make a mistake, do not give up - simply try again the next day. You cannot improve (2)________ you are willing to make mistakes. (3)________ learning something new can be frustrating, the feeling of success makes every hour of practice worthwhile. Rina kept practising the violin (4)________ she wanted to join the school orchestra. Ben practised for twice (5)________ Rina did, and everyone noticed the difference at the concert. A good teacher explains each step slowly (6)________ nobody is left behind. Always bring a notebook (7)________ the instructor demonstrates something new - you will want to write it down at once. What matters is not (8)________ you succeed on the first try, but how many times you are willing to begin again.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: Learning any new skill requires time and commitment. For a complete (1)________, even the most basic steps can seem confusing at first. It takes (2)________ — the ability to show up and practise even when you do not feel like it — to make real progress. Over time, a student learns the correct (3)________ for each task: for example, how to hold a paintbrush, how to position the hands on a piano, or how to throw a ball accurately. The more you practise, the more naturally you (4)________ these methods, until they begin to feel automatic. True (5)________ of a skill takes years, but every small improvement along the way is worth celebrating.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'even the most basic steps can seem confusing' = someone just starting = beginner.
questions.learning_tip: A BEGINNER = someone at the very start of learning a skill. Even for a BEGINNER, the early stages are the most challenging.
questions.retry_hint: The clue is THE MOST BASIC STEPS CAN SEEM CONFUSING, and the blank follows 'a complete'. Ask: which box word names a person right at the start of learning? 'Discipline' and 'mastery' are things, not people.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'show up and practise even when you do not feel like it' = self-discipline.
questions.learning_tip: DISCIPLINE = the ability to make yourself do something regularly and consistently, even when it is hard. DISCIPLINE is what keeps you practising when motivation fades.
questions.retry_hint: The dash defines it: THE ABILITY TO SHOW UP AND PRACTISE EVEN WHEN YOU DO NOT FEEL LIKE IT. Ask: which box word names that inner strength? 'Technique' is about how you do a thing, not whether you turn up.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'how to hold a paintbrush, position hands on a piano, throw a ball' = the correct method = technique.
questions.learning_tip: TECHNIQUE = the correct or established method for doing something. Each skill has a specific TECHNIQUE that must be learned and practised.
questions.retry_hint: The examples follow the colon: HOW TO HOLD A PAINTBRUSH, HOW TO POSITION THE HANDS on a piano. Ask: which box word names the correct method for a task? After 'the correct' it must be a noun.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'feel automatic' and 'more naturally you ___' = take in and internalise = absorb.
questions.learning_tip: ABSORB = take in and internalise information or methods. As you practise, you ABSORB the technique until it feels natural.
questions.retry_hint: The clue is UNTIL THEY BEGIN TO FEEL AUTOMATIC - the methods sink in and become part of you. Ask: which box word is a verb here, after 'the more naturally you'? A noun cannot fill this blank.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'takes years' and 'true ___' = the highest level of skill = mastery.
questions.learning_tip: MASTERY = the highest level of skill or knowledge in a subject. True MASTERY takes years of dedicated practice.
questions.retry_hint: TRUE ___ TAKES YEARS, and it stands above every small improvement. Ask: which box word names the highest level of skill? 'Beginner' names the lowest, and 'discipline' is only the habit that gets you there.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.error_type: Homophone confusion — they're (they are) vs their (possessive)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'they're' (they are) when the sentence needs 'their' (belonging to them). 'Their skills' = belonging to them.
questions.learning_tip: THEIR = belonging to them. Students improve THEIR skills through practice. THEY'RE = they are. Test: can you replace with 'they are'? If no, use THEIR.
questions.retry_hint: The underlined word is short for 'they are', but the SKILLS belong to the students. Ask: can you replace it with 'they are' and still make sense? If not, drop the apostrophe and use the possessive spelling.

questions.trap_type: 'The students' is plural. Students write 'was' (singular).
questions.learning_tip: 'The students' = plural → WERE given time to practise independently. WAS is only for singular subjects.
questions.retry_hint: The subject is THE STUDENTS - many of them, not one. Ask: does a plural subject take the singular past verb or the plural one? Match the verb to the subject, never to the nearest noun.

questions.trap_type: Students write 'slow' (adjective) after the action verb 'improved'. A verb needs an adverb.
questions.learning_tip: After an action verb (improved), use an ADVERB: improved SLOWLY. 'Slow' is an adjective — it describes nouns, not actions.
questions.retry_hint: IMPROVED is an action verb, and the underlined word tells you HOW the handwriting improved. Ask: does an action take an adjective, or an adverb ending in -ly? 'Noticeably' beside it is your model.

questions.trap_type: Students write a plain plural and leave out the apostrophe that shows ownership.
questions.learning_tip: The best pieces BELONG TO the pupils -> PUPILS' best pieces (apostrophe after the -s for a plural). Singular: pupil's.
questions.retry_hint: The BEST PIECES belong to the pupils - more than one owner. Ask: does a plain -s show ownership, or only number? For plural owners, where does the apostrophe sit: before the -s, or after it?

questions.trap_type: Students add -er to 'good', producing 'gooder'. 'Good' has an irregular comparative form.
questions.learning_tip: 'Good' is irregular: good → BETTER (comparative), best (superlative). Never write 'gooder' or 'more good'.
questions.retry_hint: 'Good' refuses the -er ending, exactly as 'bad' does. Ask: what is the comparative of 'good'? It is an irregular word that changes shape completely, and GOODER is never English.

E.passage: Last term, all students in our class started learning calligraphy as part of our art module. At the start, they're (1) skills were very basic - they could barely control the thick ink brush. The students was (2) given time to practise independently while the teacher walked around and gave feedback. Their handwriting improved slow (3) but noticeably over the weeks. The teacher displayed the pupils (4) best pieces on the corridor wall for everyone to admire. By the end of term, most of us agreed that our calligraphy was gooder (5) than our regular handwriting had ever looked.

questions.sentence_a: You start with the simplest techniques.
questions.sentence_b: You will build a strong foundation for more advanced skills.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'As long as'.
questions.model_answer: As long as you start with the simplest techniques, you will build a strong foundation for more advanced skills.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'As long as you will start' — adding 'will' in the 'as long as' clause.
questions.learning_tip: AS LONG AS + simple present, simple future. AS LONG AS you START with simple techniques, you WILL BUILD a strong foundation.
questions.retry_hint: Sentence A is the condition: you START WITH THE SIMPLEST TECHNIQUES. Ask: after a condition phrase, does the verb take 'will', or stay in the simple present? Only the second half - the promise - looks to the future.

questions.sentence_a: Learning to cook seemed impossible at first.
questions.sentence_b: Mia now prepares three-course meals for her family.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'Although'.
questions.model_answer: Although learning to cook seemed impossible at first, Mia now prepares three-course meals for her family.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'Learning to cook seemed impossible although Mia now prepares' — less natural and buries the contrast.
questions.learning_tip: ALTHOUGH + [the difficult starting point], [the impressive result]. ALTHOUGH learning to cook SEEMED impossible, Mia NOW PREPARES three-course meals.
questions.retry_hint: The two facts pull against each other: cooking SEEMED IMPOSSIBLE AT FIRST, yet Mia now cooks for the whole family. Ask: which fact follows the contrast word, and where does the comma fall? The impressive result stays in the main clause.

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
Learning a new skill is one of the most rewarding experiences a person can have, but it rarely follows a straight line. Research shows that skill development typically happens in three stages.

In the first stage, everything feels clumsy and slow. A beginner has to think about every step — where to place their fingers, how to hold a tool, when to apply pressure. This conscious effort is tiring and mistakes are frequent.

In the second stage, some actions start to feel more natural. The learner no longer has to think about every small movement. This is when practice becomes most valuable, because the brain is beginning to form reliable pathways for the new skill.

In the third stage, the skill feels automatic. An expert pianist does not think about individual notes — they feel the music. A skilled chef does not measure every ingredient — they sense when something is right. At this stage, the learner has moved from thinking to feeling.

What makes the difference between those who reach stage three and those who stop at stage one? Research points to one factor above all others: the willingness to tolerate the discomfort of being a beginner.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 2 has the same meaning as 'happening regularly and with confidence'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Clumsy' = awkward; 'conscious' = deliberate; 'tiring' = exhausting. FREQUENT = happening often and regularly.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: FREQUENT = happening regularly and often. 'Mistakes are FREQUENT' = they happen often. Note: the question asks for 'happening regularly' — FREQUENT fits best.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 3, what does 'they' refer to in 'they feel the music'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 2 thinking 'they' = the fingers. But 'they' refers to the PIANISTS themselves — the experts described at the start of the paragraph.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 4: 'An EXPERT PIANIST does not think about individual notes — THEY feel the music.' THEY = the expert pianists = the people described.

mcq_questions.stem: The writer says learners move 'from thinking to feeling' in stage three. What does this mean?

options.1: Learners become more emotional about their skill.
options.2: The skill becomes so automatic that it no longer requires conscious thought.
options.3: Learners stop practising and start enjoying themselves.
options.4: The brain stops working and the body takes over completely.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 4 thinking it is literally about the body. The phrase is figurative — 'feeling' means acting intuitively without conscious thought.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: 'From THINKING to FEELING' = the skill no longer requires deliberate conscious thought. It becomes automatic and intuitive — done naturally, like breathing.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 3, is it True or False that stage two is the least important stage for practising? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The passage says stage two is when 'practice becomes MOST VALUABLE, because the brain is beginning to form reliable pathways.' It is actually the most important stage for practice.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'True, stage two is when things get easier so you don't need to practise as much.' The passage says the opposite.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 3: 'This is when practice becomes MOST VALUABLE' — stage two is described as the most valuable time to practise. Answer is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: According to the passage, what happens to a skilled chef in stage three?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: A skilled chef does not measure every ingredient — they sense when something is right, meaning the cooking process has become automatic and intuitive.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'the chef cooks well' without giving the specific detail about not measuring.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 4: 'A skilled chef does not MEASURE every ingredient — they SENSE when something is right.' The cooking has become automatic and feels natural.

open_ended_questions.stem: Describe what happens to a learner in Stage 1 and Stage 2, using TWO specific details from the passage.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: In Stage 1, everything feels clumsy and slow — the learner has to think about every step, such as where to place fingers or how to hold a tool. In Stage 2, some actions start to feel more natural and the learner no longer has to think about every small movement.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students describe only one stage, or describe stage 3 instead.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Stage 1: everything feels CLUMSY and slow; must think about every step. Stage 2: actions feel more NATURAL; no longer thinking about every movement.

open_ended_questions.stem: According to the last paragraph, what is the single most important factor in reaching stage three?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: The willingness to tolerate the discomfort of being a beginner — the ability to keep going even when you feel clumsy and slow.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'practising every day' — that is important, but the passage specifically identifies TOLERATING DISCOMFORT as the key factor.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Last paragraph: 'the willingness to TOLERATE THE DISCOMFORT of being a beginner.' This is identified as the factor above all others.

open_ended_questions.stem: This passage is an informational text. Describe TWO techniques the writer uses to make the explanation clear, with examples.
