open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) The writer divides skill learning into THREE CLEAR STAGES, making it easy to follow the progression from clumsy to automatic. (ii) The writer uses CONCRETE EXAMPLES — a pianist and a chef — so readers can picture what stage three feels like in real life.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students summarise the content rather than analysing the structure and techniques.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: STRUCTURE: THREE STAGES (clear progression). TECHNIQUES: (1) concrete EXAMPLES (pianist, chef); (2) rhetorical QUESTION before the conclusion. Analyse how, not just what.

questions.stem: The manatee ________ slowly through the warm river, using its broad, flat tail to steer.
questions.trap_type: 'Raced' implies speed; 'leaped' = jumped; 'dived' = went under. GLIDED = moved smoothly and slowly with minimal effort.
questions.learning_tip: GLIDED = moved smoothly and effortlessly, like a flat stone across ice or a large animal through calm water.
questions.retry_hint: It moves SLOWLY, and the BROAD, FLAT TAIL only steers - no effort, no splashing. Ask: which verb means to move smoothly and effortlessly? 'Raced' is fast, 'leaped' jumps, and 'dived' goes under.

questions.stem: The freshwater fish used its fins to ________ itself against the river current.
questions.trap_type: 'Hide' = conceal; 'push' = press; 'dissolve' = break down in liquid. STABILISE = keep balanced and steady.
questions.learning_tip: STABILISE = keep something steady and balanced. Fish use their fins to STABILISE themselves against currents.
questions.retry_hint: The fish is working AGAINST THE RIVER CURRENT and it uses its FINS. Ask: which verb means to keep something steady and balanced? 'Hide' conceals, 'push' presses, and 'dissolve' belongs to sugar in water.

questions.stem: The river ________ over rocks and boulders before widening into a calm, flat stretch near the town.
questions.trap_type: 'Froze' and 'evaporated' relate to water changing state. 'Disappeared' suggests it vanished. TUMBLED = moved over obstacles in a churning, rolling way.
questions.learning_tip: TUMBLED = moved in a rolling, churning manner over rocks. A fast-moving river TUMBLES over boulders before slowing down.
questions.retry_hint: The water crosses ROCKS AND BOULDERS before it becomes CALM and FLAT. Ask: which verb describes rolling, churning movement over obstacles? 'Froze' and 'evaporated' would turn the water into something else.

questions.stem: The giant river otter is one of the most ________ freshwater mammals — it can grow up to one and a half metres long.
questions.trap_type: 'Tiny', 'invisible' and 'shy' suggest something small or hidden. FORMIDABLE = impressively large, powerful or capable.
questions.learning_tip: FORMIDABLE = impressively large, powerful or capable. The giant otter is a FORMIDABLE predator in freshwater ecosystems.
questions.retry_hint: The dash gives the measurement: IT CAN GROW UP TO ONE AND A HALF METRES LONG. Ask: which adjective means impressively large and powerful? 'Tiny', 'invisible' and 'shy' all shrink the animal.

questions.stem: The wetlands serve as a ________ zone between the river and the dry land, supporting unique wildlife.
questions.trap_type: 'Separate' means apart; 'broken' = damaged; 'dangerous' = risky. TRANSITION = a zone of change between two different environments.
questions.learning_tip: A TRANSITION zone = an area of gradual change between two different environments. Wetlands are TRANSITION zones between rivers and dry land.
questions.retry_hint: The zone sits BETWEEN THE RIVER AND THE DRY LAND - neither one nor the other, but a gradual change from one into another. Ask: which word names a zone of change? 'Separate' would keep them apart.

questions.stem: Scientists have ________ more than three thousand species of freshwater fish worldwide.
questions.trap_type: HAVE + past participle = present perfect. Students write 'identify' or 'identifies' ignoring 'have'.
questions.learning_tip: HAVE + past participle = present perfect. Scientists HAVE IDENTIFIED more than 3,000 species = up to now.
questions.retry_hint: HAVE is already there, and MORE THAN THREE THOUSAND SPECIES have been counted up to now. Ask: after 'have', which form completes a present perfect - plain verb, -s form, -ing form, or past participle?

questions.stem: The family ________ the giant panda exhibit when the guides announced a surprise river cruise.
questions.trap_type: 'The guides announced' = sudden interrupting event. The family were already exploring = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: The guides ANNOUNCED = sudden past event. The family were already in the middle of exploring = WERE EXPLORING.
questions.retry_hint: The guides ANNOUNCED A SURPRISE RIVER CRUISE - a sudden event landing in the middle of something longer. Ask: which choice shows the family already busy at that past moment?

questions.stem: The Amazon River is ________ river in the world by volume of water discharged.
questions.trap_type: Superlative needed (the largest among all rivers worldwide). 'Large' → THE LARGEST (short adjective, add -est with 'the').
questions.learning_tip: SUPERLATIVE of short adjectives: THE + adjective + -est. The Amazon is THE LARGEST river = larger than all others.
questions.retry_hint: 'World' tells you every river on Earth is compared - ONE winner among all of them, not two rivals. Ask: does a short adjective take -er or -est in that situation? And which little word stands in front of a superlative?

questions.stem: River Safari has ________ animal species on display than any other freshwater wildlife park in Asia.
questions.trap_type: Comparing two parks = comparative. 'Species' is countable + comparative = MORE. 'Much' is for uncountable.
questions.learning_tip: COMPARATIVE quantity for countable plural (species): MORE. River Safari has MORE animal species = comparing two parks.
questions.retry_hint: SPECIES can be counted, and THAN ANY OTHER park sets two parks side by side. Ask: which quantity word raises one countable number above another? 'The most' would compare all parks at once; 'much' needs an uncountable noun.

questions.stem: The boat tour guide wasn't sure about the feeding schedule, ________ she?
questions.trap_type: Main clause is NEGATIVE past ('wasn't sure') → POSITIVE question tag. 'Wasn't' → positive tag = was she.
questions.learning_tip: Negative statement → positive question tag. 'She WASN'T sure, WAS she?' Negative → positive tag.
questions.retry_hint: The statement is already NEGATIVE, and it happened in the past: she wondered about the FEEDING SCHEDULE then. Ask: after a negative statement, does the tag flip to positive or stay negative? The tag must keep the same tense.

questions.stem: Freshwater is not ________ plentiful as saltwater — it makes up only about three percent of all the water on Earth.
questions.trap_type: The sentence uses 'not as ___ as' structure. The blank is the first 'as' in 'not as plentiful as'.
questions.learning_tip: NOT AS + adjective + AS = unequal comparison. Freshwater is not AS plentiful AS saltwater = there is less of it.
questions.retry_hint: The frame is half-built already: NOT ___ PLENTIFUL ... SALTWATER. Ask: which single little word opens an equal-comparison frame, so that the negative in front turns it into 'less'? The two-part option would repeat a word already printed.

questions.stem: The manatees at River Safari ________ by trained marine biologists who monitor their health daily.
questions.trap_type: The manatees are the receivers of the action. Present passive = are looked after.
questions.learning_tip: The manatees are the receivers of the action. Present passive = ARE LOOKED AFTER. Passive = am/is/are + past participle.
questions.retry_hint: The MANATEES do not care for themselves: TRAINED MARINE BIOLOGISTS do, and they MONITOR THEIR HEALTH DAILY, so it is still happening. Ask: which choice is passive, with the subject receiving the action, and set in the present?

questions.stem: The conservationist told visitors ________ the river otters without permission from the staff.
questions.trap_type: Negative reported speech: told + object + not to + base verb.
questions.learning_tip: 'Told visitors NOT TO + base verb': told visitors NOT TO FEED the river otters without staff permission.
questions.retry_hint: The conservationist is FORBIDDING an action near the RIVER OTTERS. Ask: after 'told + person', does a plain verb follow, an -ing form, or an infinitive with its little marker? And where does a negative word sit - ahead of that marker?

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Comparative structures)

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The manatee is (1)________ gentle ________ any animal in the river.' Signal: equal comparison (manatee's gentleness equals any animal's) = AS … AS.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'more ... than'. Nothing in the river is gentler - the manatee's gentleness is being matched, not raised above.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adjective + AS = an equal comparison. The manatee is AS gentle AS any other river animal.
questions.retry_hint: The manatee is measured against ANY ANIMAL FOUND IN THE RIVER and comes out level - nothing is gentler, nothing rougher. Ask: which box structure marks an EQUAL comparison, with neither side higher?

questions.context_check: Passage: 'River otters are (2)________ energetic ________ manatees, spending most of the day hunting and playing.' Signal: comparing two animals, river otters have a higher level of energy = MORE … THAN.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'as ... as'. Otters hunt and play all day, so their level of energy is HIGHER, not equal.
questions.learning_tip: MORE + long adjective + THAN = a higher level. Otters are MORE ENERGETIC THAN manatees.
questions.retry_hint: Otters spend MOST OF THE DAY HUNTING AND PLAYING, so their energy stands higher, not level. Ask: which box structure raises one side above another when the adjective is long, like ENERGETIC?

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Of all freshwater animals, the piranha is perhaps (3)________ feared.' Signal: superlative — comparing among all freshwater animals = THE MOST.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'more'. 'Of all freshwater animals' compares one against every other, not against a single rival.
questions.learning_tip: THE MOST + adjective = the top of the whole group. Of all the animals, the piranha is THE MOST feared.
questions.retry_hint: OF ALL FRESHWATER ANIMALS compares one creature against every other, not against a single rival. Ask: which box phrase crowns a winner over a whole group? A two-way comparative would beat only one rival.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Despite its fearsome reputation, the piranha is actually (4)________ aggressive ________ many sharks in salt water.' Signal: piranha has a lower level of aggression compared to sharks = LESS … THAN.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'more ... than'. DESPITE its fearsome reputation means the real number of attacks is LOWER than people expect, and swimmers can be counted.
questions.learning_tip: FEWER + countable plural + THAN = a smaller number. FEWER swimmers THAN people imagine. (Use LESS only for uncountable nouns.)
questions.retry_hint: DESPITE ITS FEARSOME REPUTATION tells you the true number of attacks is lower, not higher - and SWIMMERS can be counted one by one. Ask: which box structure lowers a COUNTABLE number? 'Less' needs something uncountable.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The Amazon River is (5)________ longer ________ the Nile in terms of the area it drains.' Signal: 'far' = intensifier for the comparative 'longer' = FAR … THAN.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'more ... than'. 'Larger' is already a comparative, so it needs an intensifier, not another comparing word.
questions.learning_tip: FAR + comparative + THAN = much bigger by a wide margin. The Amazon is FAR LARGER THAN the Nile in the water it carries.
questions.retry_hint: LARGER is already a comparative, so it cannot take another comparing word in front of it. Ask: which box structure adds an intensifier meaning 'by a wide margin' to a word that already ends in -er?

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Freshwater crocodiles are (6)________ dangerous ________ saltwater crocodiles.' Signal: freshwater crocodiles have lower danger level than saltwater = NOT AS … AS.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'more ... than'. The freshwater crocodile is the LESS dangerous of the two, and the sentence has no negative word yet.
questions.learning_tip: NOT AS + adjective + AS = a lower level than the other thing. They are NOT AS dangerous AS saltwater crocodiles.
questions.retry_hint: FRESHWATER CROCODILES are still to be respected, but SALTWATER CROCODILES are worse - and this clause carries no negative word yet. Ask: which box structure denies an equal comparison and so places one side lower?

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The deeper you go into a large river, (7)________ darker and colder the water becomes.' Signal: THE + comparative, THE + comparative = proportional change. Blank 7 = the second 'the' in the proportional structure. Answer = 'the … the' but blank fills only the second position word: 'the'.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'as ... as'. Two changes move together here: greater depth brings greater darkness and cold.
questions.learning_tip: THE + comparative, THE + comparative = two things changing together. THE deeper you go, THE colder it gets.
questions.retry_hint: Two changes move together: go DEEPER, and it grows DARKER AND COLDER. Ask: which box structure pairs two comparatives so that one rises with another? Nothing here is measured against a second river.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Scientists prefer to study freshwater animals in their natural habitat (8)________ in artificial tanks.' Signal: expressing a preference for one option over another = RATHER THAN.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'more ... than'. Nothing is being measured - one option is being CHOSEN over another.
questions.learning_tip: RATHER THAN = instead of, in preference to. They study animals in the wild RATHER THAN in a tank.
questions.retry_hint: Nothing is being measured here - one option is chosen over another: NATURAL HABITAT wins over A LABORATORY TANK. Ask: which box phrase means 'instead of'? Comparative structures all need an adjective, and there is none.

C.passage: The manatee is (1)________ gentle ________ any animal found in the river. River otters are (2)________ energetic ________ manatees, spending most of the day hunting and playing. Of all freshwater animals, the piranha is perhaps (3)________ feared. Despite its fearsome reputation, the piranha attacks (4)________ swimmers ________ most people imagine. The Amazon River is (5)________ larger ________ the Nile in the amount of water it carries to the sea each year. Freshwater crocodiles are (6)________ dangerous ________ saltwater crocodiles, but they are still to be respected in the wild. (7)________ deeper you go into a large river, ________ darker and colder the water becomes. Scientists prefer to study freshwater animals in their natural habitat (8)________ in the artificial conditions of a laboratory tank.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: A river is a complex (1)________ — a community of living things that depend on each other and on the water around them for survival. The fish, insects, plants and mammals that live in a river all rely on the same clean water and food sources. The speed of the water, or (2)________, determines what kinds of animals can survive in different parts of the river. Slow-moving water supports different life forms from fast-flowing rapids. Many (3)________ animals — those that live in water — have developed special features such as gills, webbed feet or streamlined bodies to help them move and breathe underwater. Plants and certain organisms also (4)________ the river water naturally, removing dirt and impurities as the water passes through their roots and stems. When humans pollute a river, they destroy the natural (5)________ that many species depend on, threatening the survival of entire communities of wildlife.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'a community of living things that depend on each other and the water' = ecosystem.
questions.learning_tip: An ECOSYSTEM = a community of living things and the environment they share, all interacting with each other.
questions.retry_hint: The dash defines it: A COMMUNITY OF LIVING THINGS THAT DEPEND ON EACH OTHER and on the water. Ask: which box word names a whole community plus its surroundings? 'Habitat' names only a home; 'current' is moving water.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'the speed of the water' in a river = current.
questions.learning_tip: A CURRENT = the flow or movement of water in a particular direction and at a particular speed. The river CURRENT determines which animals can live there.
questions.retry_hint: The clue sits just before the blank: THE SPEED OF THE WATER. Ask: which box word names that flow, slow in one place and fast in the RAPIDS? It follows 'or', so it must be a noun.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'those that live in water' = aquatic.
questions.learning_tip: AQUATIC = relating to or living in water. AQUATIC animals = those that live and breathe in water.
questions.retry_hint: The dash explains it: THOSE THAT LIVE IN WATER, with GILLS and WEBBED FEET. Ask: which box word is an adjective describing water-dwelling creatures? A noun cannot sit in front of 'animals' here.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'removing dirt and impurities as water passes through roots and stems' = filter.
questions.learning_tip: FILTER = remove impurities by passing through a material. Plants FILTER the river water = they clean it naturally.
questions.retry_hint: The blank follows 'Plants and certain organisms also', so it must be a verb, and the clue is REMOVING DIRT AND IMPURITIES. Ask: which box word means to clean water by passing it through something?

questions.trap_type: The clue 'many species depend on' for their survival = their natural home = habitat.
questions.learning_tip: A HABITAT = the natural environment where an animal or plant normally lives. Pollution destroys the HABITAT of river creatures.
questions.retry_hint: Humans POLLUTE the river and destroy this, and MANY SPECIES DEPEND ON it to survive. Ask: which box word names the natural home of a plant or animal? 'Ecosystem' is the whole community, not the place one creature lives.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.trap_type: 'The otters' is plural. Students write 'was' (singular).
questions.learning_tip: 'The otters' = plural → WERE swimming in tight circles. WAS is only for singular subjects.
questions.retry_hint: Count them: THE OTTERS, SWIMMING IN TIGHT CIRCLES - more than one animal. Ask: does a plural subject take a singular past verb, or a plural one? Never match the verb to 'the class'.

questions.trap_type: Students write 'quiet' (adjective) after the action verb 'moved'. A verb needs an adverb.
questions.learning_tip: After an action verb (moved), use an ADVERB: moved QUIETLY. 'Quiet' is an adjective — it describes nouns, not actions.
questions.retry_hint: MOVED is an action verb, and the guide takes care SO THAT THE ANIMALS WOULD NOT BE STARTLED. Ask: do we describe an action with an adjective, or with an adverb ending in -ly?

questions.trap_type: Students write 'to' when the meaning is 'excessively'. TOO = excessively, also.
questions.learning_tip: TOO = excessively. 'The water was TOO cold to swim in' = excessively cold. TO = direction or infinitive marker. Test: can you replace with 'excessively'? If yes, use TOO.
questions.retry_hint: The weather was excessively HUMID - past the point of COMFORT. Ask: which spelling means 'excessively', and which one only shows direction? The meaning-word carries one extra letter.

questions.error_type: Possessive apostrophe — singular possessive (otter's = one otter)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'otters'' (plural possessive) when the sentence refers to one specific otter. One otter → otter's.
questions.learning_tip: Singular possessive = noun + 's. ONE OTTER'S tail = the tail belonging to one otter. OTTERS' tail would be used if one tail belonged to many otters.
questions.retry_hint: Read it again: ONE OTTER kept using its webbed feet, and this LONG, FLAT TAIL belongs to that single animal. Ask: how many owners are there, and where does the apostrophe go when there is only one?

questions.trap_type: Students add -s to 'deer', producing 'deers'. Like 'fish', 'deer' has an invariant plural form.
questions.learning_tip: 'Deer' has an invariant plural: deer → DEER. 'Deers' is never correct. Similar invariants: fish → fish (in a group), sheep → sheep.
questions.retry_hint: A SMALL GROUP grazing at the RIVERBANK - and this animal behaves like 'sheep' and 'fish'. Ask: does its plural take an -s at all, or does the word stay exactly the same?

E.passage: Last weekend, our class visited River Safari for a field study. The otters was (1) swimming in tight circles when we arrived, chasing each other playfully. Our guide moved quiet (2) near the river otter enclosure so that the animals would not be startled. The weather was to (3) humid for comfort, but we pushed on and enjoyed every exhibit. One otter kept using its webbed feet to splash water - the otters' (4) long, flat tail helped it steer and turn with remarkable speed. Later, near the wetlands area, we spotted a small group of deers (5) grazing at the edge of the muddy riverbank.

questions.sentence_a: Freshwater makes up only three percent of the Earth's water.
questions.sentence_b: Freshwater is one of our most precious resources.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'Although'.
questions.model_answer: Although freshwater makes up only three percent of the Earth's water, it is one of our most precious resources.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'Freshwater makes up only three percent although it is precious' — less emphatic placement of the contrast.
questions.learning_tip: ALTHOUGH + [the surprising fact], [the important conclusion]. ALTHOUGH freshwater makes up only 3%, IT IS one of our most precious resources.
questions.retry_hint: The two facts clash: freshwater is ONLY THREE PERCENT of all the water, yet nothing is more precious. Ask: which fact follows the contrast word, and which becomes the main clause? Replace the repeated subject with a pronoun.

questions.sentence_a: The giant river otter hunts in groups.
questions.sentence_b: The giant river otter can catch fish more effectively.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'Since'.
questions.model_answer: Since the giant river otter hunts in groups, it can catch fish more effectively.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'The giant river otter hunts in groups since it can catch fish' — reversing the cause and effect.
questions.learning_tip: SINCE = because of a background reason. SINCE the giant river otter hunts in groups, IT CAN catch fish more effectively. The reason comes after 'since'.
questions.retry_hint: Which fact explains the other? HUNTS IN GROUPS is the cause; catching fish more easily is the result. Ask: does the reason follow the joining word, and where does the comma land? Use a pronoun for the second mention.

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
The sign at the entrance to the freshwater zone read: 'Seven percent of all known animal species live in freshwater. Yet freshwater makes up less than one percent of the Earth's habitable surface.'

Twelve-year-old Theo read the sign twice. He had always thought of rivers as ordinary. He grew up next to the Kallang River and never thought much about what lived beneath its surface.

Inside the exhibit, he pressed his face against the glass of the largest tank. A fat, slow-moving arapaima drifted past — one of the largest freshwater fish in the world, over two metres long. Beside it, a school of silver dollar fish caught the light and flashed like coins.

A keeper in a green vest appeared. 'Do you know how they breathe?' she asked Theo, nodding at the arapaima.

Theo shook his head.

'They can breathe air,' she said. 'Their swim bladder works like a lung. During dry season when rivers shrink and oxygen levels drop, they swim to the surface and gulp air.'

Theo stared. 'So they survive conditions that would kill most fish?'

'Exactly,' said the keeper. 'They've been doing it for two hundred million years.'

Theo looked at the arapaima again. It was not beautiful in the way that coral reef fish were beautiful. But there was something about it — something ancient and unstoppable — that he found more impressive.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 3 has the same meaning as 'a group of fish swimming together'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Tank' is the container; 'light' is illumination; 'coins' is a simile. SCHOOL = a group of the same species of fish swimming together.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: A SCHOOL (of fish) = a group of the same species of fish swimming together. 'A SCHOOL of silver dollar fish' = a group of them moving together.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 6, what does 'it' refer to in 'their swim bladder works like a lung'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking 'it' relates to breathing. But 'it' = the swim bladder, which is what works like a lung.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 6: 'Their SWIM BLADDER works like a lung. DURING dry season... IT helps them breathe air.' IT = the swim bladder.

mcq_questions.stem: In the last paragraph, why does Theo find the arapaima 'more impressive' than coral reef fish?

options.1: It was larger and more colourful than coral reef fish.
options.2: It had survived unchanged for two hundred million years by adapting to extreme conditions.
options.3: It was the only fish in the exhibit that could jump out of the water.
options.4: The keeper told Theo that arapaimas were the rarest fish in the world.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking beauty = impressiveness. But Theo explicitly says the arapaima is NOT beautiful in the way coral fish are — its impressiveness comes from its ancient, extreme survival.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Last paragraph: Theo says the arapaima is not beautiful like coral fish — but it is 'ancient and UNSTOPPABLE'. Its impressiveness comes from TWO HUNDRED MILLION YEARS of survival in extreme conditions.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 1, is it True or False that freshwater is common on Earth's surface? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The sign says freshwater makes up LESS THAN ONE PERCENT of the Earth's habitable surface — meaning it is very rare and limited.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'True, freshwater is found in many rivers and lakes.' The passage gives a specific percentage showing how rare it actually is.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1: freshwater makes up 'LESS THAN ONE PERCENT of the Earth's habitable surface.' That is extremely rare. Answer is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: How does the arapaima breathe during the dry season when oxygen levels drop?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: It swims to the surface and gulps air using its swim bladder, which works like a lung.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'it breathes through gills' — the arapaima has a special adaptation beyond gills.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 6: 'their SWIM BLADDER works like a lung... they swim to the SURFACE and gulp air.' This is the specific adaptation that allows them to survive low-oxygen conditions.

open_ended_questions.stem: What changed about Theo's view of rivers after his visit to the exhibit? Give TWO specific details from the passage.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) Before the visit, Theo 'had always thought of rivers as ordinary' — he grew up next to the Kallang River without thinking much about what lived beneath. (ii) After seeing the arapaima and learning about its survival abilities, he found it 'more impressive' than coral reef fish — his view of freshwater life had changed to one of genuine admiration.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'he learned a lot' without citing specific details from before and after.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: BEFORE: rivers seemed ORDINARY to Theo. AFTER: the arapaima seemed MORE IMPRESSIVE than coral fish. Track the change using specific evidence from paragraphs 2 and 9.

open_ended_questions.stem: How does the writer use the silver dollar fish in paragraph 3? What effect does it create?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: The writer describes the silver dollar fish as flashing 'like coins', using a simile. This creates a vivid, sparkling image in the reader's mind and gives the tank a sense of beauty and life.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students describe the fish physically without identifying the literary technique.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: 'Flashed LIKE COINS' = a SIMILE. The comparison creates a vivid sparkling IMAGE in the reader's mind, suggesting beauty and movement.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on his actions and words in the passage, describe TWO character traits of Theo with evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: Theo is curious and open-minded. (i) CURIOUS: he pressed his face against the glass to get close to the arapaima and asked the keeper questions to understand how it breathes. (ii) OPEN-MINDED: he found the arapaima MORE IMPRESSIVE than colourful coral fish — showing he values depth over surface beauty.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say he is 'smart and kind' without precise traits or evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: CURIOUS — PRESSED HIS FACE against the glass and asked questions. OPEN-MINDED — appreciated the arapaima's depth over the reef fish's beauty.

questions.stem: Maya ________ the butter and sugar together until the mixture was light and fluffy.
questions.trap_type: 'Divided' = split apart; 'scattered' = spread; 'dissolved' = melted into liquid. CREAMED = beat fat and sugar together until light and fluffy.
questions.learning_tip: CREAMED = beat butter and sugar together until the mixture becomes pale, light and fluffy. CREAM the butter and sugar is one of the first steps in many cake recipes.
questions.retry_hint: The result tells you everything: THE MIXTURE WAS LIGHT AND FLUFFY after the BUTTER AND SUGAR were beaten together. Ask: which verb names that beating step? 'Dissolved' belongs to sugar in liquid, not to butter.

questions.stem: The baker ________ flour over the work surface to prevent the dough from sticking.
questions.trap_type: 'Poured' = liquid; 'scattered' = threw in random directions; 'dissolved' = melted. DUSTED = sprinkled a fine powder lightly and evenly.
questions.learning_tip: DUSTED = sprinkled a fine powder lightly over a surface. The baker DUSTED flour over the surface = scattered a light, even layer.
questions.retry_hint: FLOUR is a fine powder, spread in a light layer TO PREVENT THE DOUGH FROM STICKING. Ask: which verb means to sprinkle a fine powder evenly over a surface? 'Poured' belongs to liquids.

questions.stem: The croissant dough needs to ________ undisturbed in the fridge overnight so the layers become flaky when baked.
questions.trap_type: 'Melt' and 'dissolve' destroy the dough. 'Harden' describes what the butter does, but nothing is left UNDISTURBED in order to harden - dough is left alone to develop.
questions.learning_tip: REST = allow food to sit undisturbed so it develops in texture or flavour. Croissant dough RESTS in the fridge so the butter layers stay distinct and become flaky.
questions.retry_hint: The dough is left UNDISTURBED IN THE FRIDGE OVERNIGHT so that the LAYERS BECOME FLAKY. Ask: which verb means to leave food alone so that it improves? 'Melt' and 'dissolve' would ruin it completely.

questions.stem: The freshly baked bread had a golden, ________ crust that made the whole kitchen smell wonderful.
questions.trap_type: 'Soggy' and 'raw' suggest undercooked; 'grey' is an unappealing colour. CRISPY = pleasantly firm and crunchy on the outside.
questions.learning_tip: CRISPY = pleasantly firm and crunchy, especially on the outside. A well-baked loaf has a CRISPY golden crust.
questions.retry_hint: The crust is GOLDEN and the whole KITCHEN SMELLS WONDERFUL - this loaf came out well. Ask: which adjective means pleasantly firm and crunchy? 'Soggy' and 'raw' would mean the baking failed.

questions.stem: The pastry chef was known for her ________ recipes — each one precise to the nearest gram.
questions.trap_type: 'Vague', 'approximate' and 'imprecise' all suggest a lack of accuracy. METICULOUS = showing great care and attention to detail.
questions.learning_tip: METICULOUS = very careful and precise, paying great attention to detail. A METICULOUS baker measures every ingredient to the nearest gram.
questions.retry_hint: The dash proves it: EACH ONE PRECISE TO THE NEAREST GRAM. Ask: which adjective means extremely careful about every detail? 'Vague', 'approximate' and 'imprecise' all mean the opposite.

questions.stem: Grandma has ________ the same pandan chiffon cake recipe for over thirty years.
questions.trap_type: HAS + past participle = present perfect. 'Use' is regular: use → used.
questions.learning_tip: HAS + past participle = present perfect. Grandma HAS USED the same recipe for thirty years = she started then and still uses it now.
questions.retry_hint: HAS is already in place, and FOR OVER THIRTY YEARS runs right up to today. Ask: after 'has', which form completes a present perfect? 'Use' is a regular verb, so its past participle is easy to build.

questions.stem: The baker ________ the croissants in the oven when she noticed the temperature was too low.
questions.trap_type: 'She noticed the temperature' = sudden observation interrupting the ongoing action. The baker was already baking = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: She NOTICED the temperature = sudden observation in the past. The baker was already in the middle of baking = WAS BAKING.
questions.retry_hint: SHE NOTICED the temperature - a sudden discovery cutting into a longer action. Ask: which choice shows the work already under way at that past moment? A one-word past form would end it too early.

questions.stem: This bakery's sourdough bread is ________ than the one at the supermarket — it has a deeper flavour.
questions.trap_type: Comparing two breads = comparative. 'Good' → irregular comparative = BETTER. 'Gooder' is wrong.
questions.learning_tip: 'Good' is irregular: good → BETTER (comparative). The bakery's bread is BETTER than the supermarket's = comparing two things. Never 'gooder'.
questions.retry_hint: THAN compares just two loaves, and 'good' refuses to take -er. Ask: what is the comparative of 'good'? GOODER is never English, and 'the best' would need three or more loaves.

questions.stem: There is ________ sugar in this recipe than I expected — only two tablespoons for the whole cake.
questions.trap_type: 'Sugar' is uncountable → use 'less'. 'Fewer' is for countable nouns. 'A few' is only for countable.
questions.learning_tip: LESS + uncountable noun: LESS sugar. 'Sugar' cannot be counted individually → LESS. FEWER is only for countable nouns (fewer cups, fewer eggs).
questions.retry_hint: SUGAR cannot be counted - there is no plural - and THAN sets this recipe against what I expected: ONLY TWO TABLESPOONS. Ask: which quantity word lowers an uncountable amount? 'Fewer' needs things you can count.

questions.stem: The oven was preheated to the right temperature, ________ it?
questions.trap_type: Main clause is positive past ('was preheated') → negative question tag. 'Was' → wasn't.
questions.learning_tip: Positive past statement → negative question tag. 'The oven WAS preheated, WASN'T it?' Positive → negative tag.
questions.retry_hint: The statement is POSITIVE and sits in the past: the oven WAS PREHEATED. Ask: after a positive statement, does the tag flip to negative or stay positive? The tag keeps the same tense, so a present form is out.

questions.stem: Homemade cookies are just ________ delicious ________ the ones sold in boutique bakeries.
questions.trap_type: Equal comparison: 'just as delicious as' = they are equally good.
questions.learning_tip: AS … AS = equal comparison. Homemade cookies are just AS DELICIOUS AS boutique bakery ones = their quality is equal.
questions.retry_hint: JUST is the giveaway: homemade cookies and the BOUTIQUE BAKERIES' ones are equally DELICIOUS, neither better nor worse. Ask: which pair of words builds an EQUAL comparison?

questions.stem: The winning cake at the bakery competition ________ by a fourteen-year-old who had been baking for only two years.
questions.trap_type: The cake was the receiver of the action. Past passive = was baked.
questions.learning_tip: The winning cake was the receiver of the action. Past passive = WAS BAKED. Passive = was/were + past participle.
questions.retry_hint: The CAKE did not bake itself: A FOURTEEN-YEAR-OLD did, and the COMPETITION is over. Ask: which choice is passive, with the subject receiving the action, and set firmly in the past?

questions.stem: The pastry instructor told the students ________ the dough too hard or it would become tough.
questions.trap_type: Negative reported speech: told + object + not to + base verb.
questions.learning_tip: 'Told students NOT TO + base verb': told students NOT TO KNEAD the dough too hard.
questions.retry_hint: The instructor is FORBIDDING something, warning that THE DOUGH would BECOME TOUGH. Ask: after 'told + person', does a plain verb follow, an -ing form, or an infinitive with its marker? And where does the negative word sit?

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Verb forms of 'bake')

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Grandma enjoys (1)________ every weekend, filling the flat with the smell of warm butter and sugar.' Signal: 'enjoys + ___' = gerund (verb-ing). Pattern: enjoy + verb-ing → baking.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'to bake' instead of the gerund after 'enjoys'.
questions.learning_tip: ENJOY + verb-ing: enjoys BAKING every weekend. After 'enjoys', always add -ING.
questions.retry_hint: ENJOYS is the deciding word. Ask: after 'enjoy', 'love' or 'keep', which form of the verb must follow - a plain one, an infinitive, or one ending in -ing? Grandma is not planning; she is doing what she likes.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'She (2)________ at least two different items every Saturday morning without fail.' Signal: 'every Saturday morning' = regular habit = simple present. Subject 'She' = singular → bakes.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'bake' (plural form) forgetting 'She' is singular.
questions.learning_tip: Regular habit = simple present. She (singular) → BAKES at least two items every Saturday.
questions.retry_hint: SHE is one person, the habit is regular (EVERY SATURDAY MORNING), and nothing here is finished past time. Ask: in the simple present, does a singular subject take the plain verb, or the one carrying -s?

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Last Sunday, she (3)________ a coconut layer cake for the whole family.' Signal: 'Last Sunday' = past. 'Bake' is regular: bake → baked.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'bake' (base form) ignoring the past signal 'Last Sunday'.
questions.learning_tip: 'Last Sunday' = past. 'Bake' is regular: bake → BAKED.
questions.retry_hint: LAST SUNDAY is finished time, and this is one completed action, not one in progress. Ask: which single-word past form fits? A continuous form would need a helper standing in front of it.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'While Grandma (4)________ the cake, the kitchen filled with the scent of toasted coconut.' Signal: 'while Grandma ___' = ongoing background past action. Subject 'Grandma' = singular → was baking.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'baked' (simple past) missing the ongoing signal 'while'.
questions.learning_tip: 'While Grandma ___' = ongoing background past action = past continuous. Grandma WAS BAKING when the scent filled the kitchen.
questions.retry_hint: WHILE tells you this action stretched on until THE KITCHEN FILLED with the scent - it had not finished. Ask: which past continuous form suits a SINGULAR subject like Grandma? A one-word past form would end it too soon.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Her grandchildren (5)________ smaller cakes in the toaster oven at the same time.' Signal: same past time frame, plural subject 'her grandchildren' + ongoing parallel action → were baking.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'baked' (simple past) instead of past continuous for a parallel ongoing action.
questions.learning_tip: Her grandchildren = plural. They were doing it at the same past moment = WERE BAKING (past continuous).
questions.retry_hint: HER GRANDCHILDREN is plural, and AT THE SAME TIME points back to Grandma's ongoing action. Ask: which past continuous form partners a plural subject? Check the helper before you choose.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'She wants (6)________ a French tart for the school charity fair next month.' Signal: 'wants + ___' = infinitive. Pattern: want + to + base verb → to bake.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'baking' instead of the infinitive after 'wants'.
questions.learning_tip: 'Want TO + base verb': wants TO BAKE a French tart. Always use the infinitive after 'wants'.
questions.retry_hint: WANTS is the deciding word. Ask: after 'want', 'hope' or 'decide', does the verb take -ing, or an infinitive with its little marker in front? Compare blank 1, where ENJOYS behaves differently.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Grandma says everyone should (7)________ from scratch at least once in their lives.' Signal: 'should + ___' = modal verb + base form. Never add -s or -ing after a modal.
questions.trap_type: Students add -s or -ing after the modal verb 'should'.
questions.learning_tip: After modal verbs (should, must, can, will), always use the BASE form: should BAKE. Never 'should bakes' or 'should baking'.
questions.retry_hint: SHOULD is a modal, and modals never let their verb take an ending. Ask: after 'should', 'must' or 'can', does the verb add -s, add -ing, or add nothing at all?

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Right now, Grandma (8)________ a pandan layered cake for a neighbour who just came home from hospital.' Signal: 'Right now' = present continuous. Subject 'Grandma' = singular → is baking.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'bakes' (simple present habit) missing the 'right now' signal for present continuous.
questions.learning_tip: 'Right now' = present continuous. Grandma (singular) → IS BAKING a pandan layered cake right now.
questions.retry_hint: RIGHT NOW means at this very moment, so the action has not finished. Ask: which present continuous form partners a singular subject like Grandma? A simple present would turn it into a weekly habit instead.

C.passage: Grandma enjoys (1)________ every weekend and fills the flat with the smell of butter and sugar. She (2)________ at least two items every Saturday morning. Last Sunday, she (3)________ a coconut layer cake for the whole family. While Grandma (4)________ the cake, the kitchen filled with the scent of toasted coconut. Her grandchildren (5)________ banana muffins in the toaster oven at the same time. She wants (6)________ a French almond tart for the school charity fair. Grandma says everyone should (7)________ something from scratch at least once to appreciate home-cooked food. Right now, Grandma (8)________ a pandan layered cake for a neighbour who just returned from hospital.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: Baking is both a science and an art. Every (1)________ — from flour and butter to eggs and vanilla — plays a specific role in the final product. The baker must measure each one precisely, because even a small change in quantity can affect the taste and texture of the result. (2)________ agents such as baking powder and yeast cause dough and batter to rise by producing bubbles of gas inside the mixture. Many bread recipes require the baker to (3)________ the dough by pressing and folding it repeatedly with the hands, which develops the gluten and gives the bread its chewy, elastic texture. When a large order must be filled, a baker may prepare many items in one (4)________ to save time. One of the most enjoyable parts of baking is the (5)________ that fills the kitchen — the smell of warm butter and sugar that reminds many people of home.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'from flour and butter to eggs and vanilla, plays a specific role' = a component used in cooking = ingredient.
questions.learning_tip: An INGREDIENT = a component or item used in a recipe. Each INGREDIENT in baking plays a specific chemical or flavour role.
questions.retry_hint: The dash lists them: FLOUR AND BUTTER, EGGS AND VANILLA, each with A SPECIFIC ROLE. Ask: which box word names any single item that goes into a recipe? 'Batch' counts finished goods, not what goes in.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'cause dough to rise by producing bubbles of gas' = leavening.
questions.learning_tip: A LEAVENING agent = something that causes baked goods to rise by producing gas. Yeast and baking powder are LEAVENING agents.
questions.retry_hint: The clue follows the blank: agents that CAUSE DOUGH AND BATTER TO RISE BY PRODUCING BUBBLES OF GAS, such as BAKING POWDER AND YEAST. Ask: which box word names that kind of agent?

questions.trap_type: The clue 'pressing and folding the dough repeatedly with the hands' = knead.
questions.learning_tip: KNEAD = press and fold dough repeatedly with the hands to develop gluten. You KNEAD bread dough to make it smooth and elastic.
questions.retry_hint: The blank follows 'require the baker to', so it must be a plain verb, and the clue is PRESSING AND FOLDING IT REPEATEDLY WITH THE HANDS. Ask: which box word names that action?

questions.trap_type: The clue 'prepare many items at one time to save time' = a batch.
questions.learning_tip: A BATCH = a quantity of something produced in one round of preparation. Bake a BATCH of cookies = make many at the same time.
questions.retry_hint: The clue is A LARGE ORDER and MANY ITEMS prepared in one go TO SAVE TIME. Ask: which box word names one round of baking that produces many items together?

questions.trap_type: The clue 'the smell of warm butter and sugar that fills the kitchen' = aroma.
questions.learning_tip: An AROMA = a pleasant and distinctive smell. The AROMA of baking fills the kitchen with warmth and comfort.
questions.retry_hint: The clue follows the dash: THE SMELL OF WARM BUTTER AND SUGAR that FILLS THE KITCHEN. Ask: which box word names a lovely smell? 'Crust' is something you can touch, not something you breathe in.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.trap_type: 'The croissants' is plural. Students match the verb to the nearest idea instead of the subject.
questions.learning_tip: 'The croissants' = plural -> WERE already in the oven. WAS is only for singular subjects.
questions.retry_hint: Count the subject: THE CROISSANTS - more than one, sitting in the oven. Ask: does a plural subject take the singular past verb, or the plural one? Never match the verb to 'the oven'.

questions.trap_type: Students write 'gentle' (adjective) after the action verb 'folded'. A verb needs an adverb.
questions.learning_tip: After an action verb (folded), use an ADVERB: folded GENTLY. 'Gentle' is an adjective — it describes nouns, not actions.
questions.retry_hint: FOLDED is an action verb, and the underlined word tells you HOW the baker folded the DOUGH. Ask: does an action take an adjective, or an adverb? Adjectives belong to nouns.

questions.trap_type: Students write 'their' (belonging to them) when the sentence needs 'there' (at that place).
questions.learning_tip: THERE = at that place. 'We stood THERE by the oven' = at that place. THEIR = belonging to them. Test: can you replace with 'at that place'? If yes, use THERE.
questions.retry_hint: Test it: WE STOOD ___ NEAR THE LARGE MIXING COUNTER - can you say 'at that place'? Nobody owns anything in this sentence. Ask: which spelling names a place, and which means 'belonging to them'?

questions.trap_type: Students leave out the apostrophe, turning the owner into a plain plural. One baker owns the apron.
questions.learning_tip: The apron BELONGS TO one baker -> BAKER'S apron (apostrophe + s). Plural owners: bakers'.
questions.retry_hint: ONE baker owns that CLEAN WHITE APRON, and the underlined word carries no apostrophe at all. Ask: can a plain -s ever show ownership? Where must the apostrophe go when there is a single owner?

questions.error_type: Irregular plural — shelf → shelves (f → ves rule)
questions.trap_type: Students add -s to 'shelf', producing 'shelfs'. Words ending in -f often change to -ves in the plural.
questions.learning_tip: 'Shelf' follows the -f → -ves rule: shelf → SHELVES. Same pattern: half → halves, leaf → leaves, loaf → loaves.
questions.retry_hint: SHELF ends in -f, and the WOODEN ones by the window are more than one. Ask: how do you write more than one leaf, or more than one loaf? Apply that same change here - a plain -s will not do.

E.passage: Last Saturday, our class visited a local artisan bakery for a baking workshop. The croissants was (1) already in the oven when we arrived, filling the air with a warm buttery smell. At the long wooden table, the baker showed us a fresh lump of dough and folded it gentle (2) three times before placing it back into the bowl to rest. We stood their (3) near the large mixing counter and watched her shape a baguette. The bakers (4) clean white apron had a small embroidered logo on the pocket - the bakery's symbol. After the croissants cooled, we placed them carefully on the wooden shelfs (5) by the window for the customers to see.

questions.sentence_a: You follow the recipe precisely.
questions.sentence_b: Your baked goods will turn out well every time.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'As long as'.
questions.model_answer: As long as you follow the recipe precisely, your baked goods will turn out well every time.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'As long as you will follow' — adding 'will' in the 'as long as' clause.
questions.learning_tip: AS LONG AS + simple present, simple future. AS LONG AS you FOLLOW the recipe precisely, your goods WILL TURN OUT well.
questions.retry_hint: Sentence A sets the condition: you FOLLOW THE RECIPE PRECISELY. Ask: after a condition phrase, may the verb take 'will', or must it stay in the simple present? Keep the future for the promise in the second half.

questions.sentence_a: The croissants looked perfect.
questions.sentence_b: They were made by an eleven-year-old student.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using the relative pronoun 'which'.
questions.model_answer: The croissants, which were made by an eleven-year-old student, looked perfect.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'The croissants looked perfect which they were made by an eleven-year-old' — adding 'they' after 'which'.
questions.learning_tip: Use 'which' to add information about a THING. The croissants, WHICH were made by an eleven-year-old, looked perfect. Never add 'they' after 'which'.
questions.retry_hint: Both sentences describe THE CROISSANTS, so name them once and let 'which' carry the second mention. Ask: after 'which', is the word 'they' still needed? And which punctuation marks fence off the extra information?

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
Thirteen-year-old Dev watched his grandmother bake bread for as long as he could remember. Her hands moved without measuring — a pinch of this, a handful of that. Dev had always wondered if he could do the same.

One Saturday morning, he decided to try. He found the recipe card in the back of the recipe book — her handwriting, faded but legible. He followed every step. He measured. He kneaded for eight minutes by the clock. He let the dough rise for an hour.

The result was dense and flat. Nothing like his grandmother's bread.

He said nothing at dinner. But his grandmother noticed. After the dishes were cleared, she came and sat across from him.

'You tried the bread,' she said. It was not a question.

Dev nodded. 'It was wrong,' he said. 'The recipe is the same but mine didn't come out like yours.'

His grandmother smiled. 'The recipe is the same. But you cannot bake it the way I do yet. I've made that bread four hundred times. Every time teaches you something the recipe doesn't say.'

Dev looked at his hands. 'So I just have to keep making it?' he asked.

'Yes,' she said. 'And one day your bread will taste different from mine. Not worse. Just yours.'

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 2 has the same meaning as 'able to be read clearly'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Faded' = grown lighter/harder to see; 'followed' = did what it said; 'measured' = checked quantities. LEGIBLE = clear enough to read.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: LEGIBLE = clear enough to be read. The handwriting was faded but still LEGIBLE = you could still make out the letters.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 7, what does 'it' refer to in 'Every time teaches you something the recipe doesn't say'?

options.3: Each time the bread is made

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking 'it' refers to the recipe. But 'every TIME' = each occasion of making the bread — 'it' = each of those occasions.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 7: 'I've made that bread four hundred times. EVERY TIME teaches you something the recipe doesn't say.' IT = every time / each occasion you bake the bread.

mcq_questions.stem: What did Grandmother mean by 'one day your bread will taste different from mine — not worse, just yours'?

options.1: Dev's bread would never be as good as hers.
options.2: Through repeated practice, Dev would develop his own style — different but equally valid.
options.3: Dev should try a different recipe instead of hers.
options.4: His bread was already good but needed more salt.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking 'different' = worse. But Grandmother specifically says 'not worse — just yours', emphasising personal development.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: 'Not worse, JUST YOURS' = through practice, Dev will develop his OWN unique result — different from hers but equally good. This is the nature of developing a craft.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 4, is it True or False that Dev told his family about the failed bread at dinner? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The passage says 'He said NOTHING AT DINNER' — he did not tell his family about the failed attempt.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'True, he told his grandmother.' His grandmother NOTICED, but Dev said nothing — she figured it out herself.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 4: 'He SAID NOTHING AT DINNER.' Dev stayed silent. His grandmother noticed on her own — he did not tell anyone. Answer is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: How did Dev's grandmother know that he tried to bake the bread?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: She noticed on her own — the passage says 'his grandmother noticed' after the dishes were cleared, suggesting she observed or sensed something without being told.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'Dev told her' — the passage says he said nothing. She NOTICED by herself.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 4: 'his grandmother NOTICED' — she figured it out herself, perhaps from his mood or the smell. Dev had said nothing.

open_ended_questions.stem: Why did Dev's bread not turn out like his grandmother's, even though he followed the same recipe? Give TWO reasons from the passage.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) Dev had never made the bread before — his grandmother has made it 'four hundred times', meaning she has accumulated experience that cannot be written in a recipe. (ii) Each time you bake the bread, you learn something the recipe cannot explain — Dev had none of that built-up knowledge yet.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'he made a mistake' — the passage does not say he made a mistake. He followed the recipe perfectly but lacked experience.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 7: (1) Grandmother made it FOUR HUNDRED TIMES = she has practised far more; (2) 'Every time teaches you something the RECIPE DOESN'T SAY' = experience beyond the instructions.

open_ended_questions.stem: Describe how Dev's grandmother bakes compared to the way Dev baked, using details from the passage.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: Grandmother bakes without measuring — using 'a pinch of this, a handful of that' from instinct and long experience. Dev baked by following every step of the recipe carefully, measuring precisely and timing everything by the clock.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'she is more experienced' without describing the specific contrast in method.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1: Grandmother's hands 'moved WITHOUT MEASURING'. Paragraph 2: Dev 'followed EVERY STEP', measured and timed. The contrast is precision vs instinct.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on her words and actions in the passage, describe TWO character traits of Dev's grandmother with evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: Dev's grandmother is perceptive and wise. (i) PERCEPTIVE: she noticed Dev tried the bread without being told — she came to sit with him after dinner and said "You tried the bread" without any prompting. (ii) WISE: she explained that 400 rounds of baking teach things a recipe cannot, and encouraged Dev with "not worse, just yours."
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say she is 'kind and patient' without naming precise traits or giving evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: PERCEPTIVE — noticed Dev's attempt WITHOUT BEING TOLD. WISE — explained the lesson of FOUR HUNDRED TIMES and encouraged him with 'not worse, just yours'.

questions.stem: During Deepavali, the streets were lit up and the whole neighbourhood was as ________ as a thousand stars.
questions.trap_type: Students pick 'noisy' for a festival atmosphere. But 'lit up' → the comparison is about light, not sound. 'As bright as a thousand stars' is the simile.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! It compares two things using 'as'. The street was AS BRIGHT AS a thousand stars = it shone like stars. Spot the simile by looking for 'as ... as'.
questions.retry_hint: 'As ___ as' is a simile, and the streets are LIT UP and compared with A THOUSAND STARS. Ask: are stars loud, or empty, or shining? Match the adjective to the stars, never to the crowd.

questions.stem: Mother asked the children to ________ their shoes before entering the temple during the festival.
questions.trap_type: 'Wash' is about cleaning, not removing. 'Buy' and 'repair' make no sense here. 'Take off' = remove shoes before entering a place of worship.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: TAKE OFF = remove (shoes, clothes). 'Take your shoes OFF before entering.' TAKE + OFF work together — never split this phrasal verb!
questions.retry_hint: Shoes must come away from your feet BEFORE ENTERING THE TEMPLE - that is what visitors do at a place of worship. Ask: which phrasal verb means to remove shoes or clothing? 'Wash' cleans them; 'repair' mends them.

questions.stem: The family ________ a large table of food offerings and placed it outside their door on the first day of the new year.
questions.trap_type: 'Removed' and 'destroyed' are negative actions. 'Ignored' = paid no attention. ARRANGED = set up carefully in an organised way.
questions.learning_tip: ARRANGED = set out items carefully and neatly. The family ARRANGED food offerings = they placed each item in a specific position for the ceremony.
questions.retry_hint: The LARGE TABLE OF FOOD OFFERINGS was set out neatly and PLACED OUTSIDE THEIR DOOR for the new year. Ask: which verb means to put things into careful order? 'Removed' and 'destroyed' would leave nothing there.

questions.stem: The Hari Raya celebration was a ________ occasion — relatives from across the island gathered for the first time in years.
questions.trap_type: 'Dull', 'ordinary' and 'silent' all suggest a quiet or unremarkable event. JOYOUS = full of great happiness and celebration.
questions.learning_tip: JOYOUS = full of great happiness. A JOYOUS occasion = a celebration filled with warmth, laughter and togetherness.
questions.retry_hint: The dash explains it: RELATIVES FROM ACROSS THE ISLAND GATHERED FOR THE FIRST TIME IN YEARS. Ask: does that feel dull, ordinary or silent - or full of happiness? Match the adjective to the reunion.

questions.stem: The Christmas choir performed with such ________ that even people passing on the street stopped to listen.
questions.trap_type: 'Silence' and 'anger' are negative; 'confusion' = disorder. HARMONY = notes or voices blending together beautifully.
questions.learning_tip: HARMONY = different notes or voices blending perfectly together. A choir performs in HARMONY = every voice fits together to create a beautiful sound.
questions.retry_hint: The CHRISTMAS CHOIR sang so beautifully that PEOPLE PASSING ON THE STREET STOPPED TO LISTEN. Ask: which noun names voices blending perfectly together? 'Silence' and 'confusion' would empty the street instead.

questions.stem: Everyone in our neighbourhood ________ a different festival, so there is always something to celebrate.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'celebrate' thinking 'everyone in our neighbourhood' = many people = plural. EVERYONE = singular → verb must have -s.
questions.learning_tip: EVERYONE / NOBODY / SOMEONE = Singular! Always use IS / HAS / verb+S. Everyone CELEBRATES = add -S. 'Everyone are celebrating' is WRONG.
questions.retry_hint: The subject is EVERYONE, not the neighbourhood around it. Words like everyone and nobody behave like ONE person. Ask: in the simple present, does a singular subject take the plain verb, or the one carrying -s?

questions.stem: Our family has ________ new lanterns every year for the Mid-Autumn Festival since I was very young.
questions.trap_type: HAS + past participle = present perfect. 'Make' is irregular: make → made.
questions.learning_tip: HAS + past participle = present perfect. Our family HAS MADE new lanterns every year = a repeated action from past to now. MAKE → MADE (irregular).
questions.retry_hint: HAS is waiting for its partner, and SINCE I WAS VERY YOUNG runs right up to now. Ask: after 'has', which form builds a present perfect? 'Make' is irregular, so no -ed ending will do.

questions.stem: The Deepavali light display this year is far ________ than the one last year.
questions.trap_type: Comparing two displays (this year vs last year) = comparative. 'Colourful' is multi-syllable → MORE COLOURFUL, not -er.
questions.learning_tip: MORE + long adj + THAN = comparative! Two displays compared → MORE COLOURFUL THAN. Never 'colourfullier'.
questions.retry_hint: FAR needs a comparative to lean on, and THAN sets THIS YEAR against THE ONE LAST YEAR - just two displays. Ask: does a three-syllable adjective take -er, or a comparing word in front? 'The most' would need several displays.

questions.stem: The children ________ their traditional costumes when the parade suddenly started early.
questions.trap_type: 'The parade suddenly started early' = sudden interrupting event. The children were already putting on costumes = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: The parade STARTED EARLY = sudden past event. Children were already in the middle of putting on costumes = WERE PUTTING ON (past continuous).
questions.retry_hint: THE PARADE SUDDENLY STARTED EARLY - a sharp event landing in the middle of something longer. Ask: which choice shows the children already busy with their TRADITIONAL COSTUMES at that past moment?

questions.stem: There was ________ food at the open house that we could not try everything on the table.
questions.trap_type: 'Food' is uncountable → use 'much/a little'. 'A few', 'many', 'several' are for countable nouns.
questions.learning_tip: SO MUCH + uncountable noun. 'Food' is uncountable → SO MUCH food. 'Many food' or 'a few food' are WRONG. Use MUCH/SO MUCH for uncountable things.
questions.retry_hint: FOOD cannot be counted - there is no plural - and the result clause (THAT WE COULD NOT TRY EVERYTHING) tells you the amount was huge. Ask: which choice suits an uncountable noun inside that frame? 'A few' and 'several' need countable things.

questions.stem: The Christmas carollers were not nervous at all, ________ they?
questions.trap_type: Main clause is NEGATIVE past ('were not nervous') → POSITIVE question tag. 'Were not' → positive tag = were they.
questions.learning_tip: Negative statement → positive tag. 'They WERE NOT nervous, WERE they?' NEGATIVE → POSITIVE tag. Past 'were' → tag uses 'were'.
questions.retry_hint: The statement is already NEGATIVE (NOT NERVOUS AT ALL) and it sits in the past. Ask: after a negative statement, does the tag flip to positive or stay negative? The tag must keep the past tense, so 'are' cannot appear.

questions.stem: The giant lion dance costume ________ by ten skilled performers moving in perfect coordination.
questions.trap_type: The costume was the receiver of the action. Past passive = was operated.
questions.learning_tip: WAS/WERE + past participle = passive! The costume WAS OPERATED by performers = performers did the action, costume received it.
questions.retry_hint: The giant COSTUME cannot move itself: TEN SKILLED PERFORMERS do the work, and the parade is over. Ask: which choice is passive, with the subject receiving the action, and set in the past?

questions.stem: The festival organiser told visitors ________ flash photography near the religious offerings.
questions.trap_type: Negative reported speech: told + object + not to + base verb.
questions.learning_tip: TOLD someone NOT TO + base verb. The organiser told visitors NOT TO USE flash photography. After 'told + object', use 'not to + base verb'.
questions.retry_hint: The organiser is FORBIDDING FLASH PHOTOGRAPHY near the RELIGIOUS OFFERINGS. Ask: after 'told + person', does a plain verb follow, an -ing form, or an infinitive with its marker? And where does the negative word sit?

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Quantity adjectives)

questions.context_check: Passage: 'There are (1)________ different festivals celebrated in Singapore throughout the year.' Signal: 'festivals' is countable + large number = MANY. MANY = a large number of countable things.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'much'. FESTIVALS can be counted one by one, and 'how ___' is a fixed question form.
questions.learning_tip: HOW MANY + countable plural noun. Ask HOW MANY festivals, but HOW MUCH excitement.
questions.retry_hint: HOW stands just in front of the blank, and FESTIVALS can be counted one by one. Ask: which quantity word partners countable plurals in a question? Its twin word belongs to things you cannot count, like EXCITEMENT.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'During Chinese New Year, there is so (2)________ excitement in the air.' Signal: 'excitement' is uncountable + large amount = MUCH. 'So much excitement' = a very large amount.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'many'. EXCITEMENT cannot be counted, and the fixed pattern 'so ___ ... that' needs a single quantity word.
questions.learning_tip: SO MUCH + uncountable noun: so MUCH excitement THAT the streets seem to sparkle. 'So a lot of' is never English.
questions.retry_hint: EXCITEMENT cannot be counted - it has no plural - and the fixed frame is 'so ___ ... THAT even the streets seem to sparkle'. Ask: which single quantity word fits an uncountable noun inside that frame?

questions.context_check: Passage: 'My mother prepared (3)________ kueh for the neighbours as a gift.' Signal: positive statement + unspecified amount (not large, not small) = SOME. SOME = an unspecified amount in positive sentences.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'any'. The sentence is POSITIVE - she really did prepare an unstated amount and handed it out.
questions.learning_tip: SOME = an unstated amount, used in positive statements. ANY belongs to negatives and questions.
questions.retry_hint: The sentence is POSITIVE: Mother really did prepare kueh and OFFERED A PLATE TO EVERYONE who walked past. Ask: which box word states an unstated amount in a positive statement? Its twin belongs to negatives and questions.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'I did not eat (4)________ pineapple tarts because I was already full.' Signal: negative sentence ('did not eat') + = ANY. ANY after a negative = 'not even one'.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'some' or 'many'. The sentence is NEGATIVE and ends with AT ALL - not even one tart was eaten.
questions.learning_tip: NOT ... ANY = none at all. Use ANY in negative sentences and questions; SOME in positive ones.
questions.retry_hint: Read the whole clause: I DID NOT EAT ... AT ALL - it is negative, and not even one tart was touched. Ask: which box word partners negatives and questions? Its positive twin cannot follow 'did not'.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'We lit (5)________ candles and placed them on the doorstep to welcome guests.' Signal: 'candles' is countable + small number = A FEW. A FEW = a small number of countable things.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'several' (four or five) or 'a little' (uncountable). The dash tells you the exact number: JUST THREE.
questions.learning_tip: A FEW = two or three countable things. A LITTLE is for uncountable nouns such as wax or oil.
questions.retry_hint: Count them: JUST THREE candles, and candles can be counted one by one. Ask: which box phrase means only two or three countable things? 'Several' would mean more, and 'little' belongs to things you cannot count.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Grandpa poured (6)________ rosewater into the lamp to make it smell pleasant.' Signal: 'rosewater' is uncountable + small amount = A LITTLE. A LITTLE = a small amount of an uncountable thing.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'a few'. ROSEWATER is a liquid - you cannot count it - and the amount is NO MORE THAN A TEASPOON.
questions.learning_tip: A LITTLE = a small amount of an uncountable thing. A FEW is only for countable plurals.
questions.retry_hint: ROSEWATER is liquid, so you cannot count it, and the clue NO MORE THAN says the quantity is tiny. Ask: which box phrase names small amounts that cannot be counted? Countable phrases belong with candles, not with liquid.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Our family visited (7)________ open houses on the first day of Hari Raya.' Signal: 'open houses' is countable + more than two but not a very large number = SEVERAL. SEVERAL = more than two, not very many.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'a few', which means only two or three. The dash gives the number: FIVE in a single afternoon.
questions.learning_tip: SEVERAL = more than two or three, but not a huge number. SEVERAL open houses = about four or five.
questions.retry_hint: The dash counts them: FIVE IN A SINGLE AFTERNOON - more than two or three, but hardly a crowd. Ask: which box word names that middle number of countable things? 'A few' would stop at three.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'There was (8)________ laughter and singing at the Christmas party that went on until late.' Signal: positive statement + large amount — works for both countable and uncountable = A LOT OF. 'Laughter' and 'singing' are both uncountable.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'much'. In a positive statement 'much laughter' sounds unnatural, and LAUGHTER AND SINGING is a large amount, not a small one.
questions.learning_tip: A LOT OF = a large amount, natural in positive statements with countable and uncountable nouns alike.
questions.retry_hint: LAUGHTER AND SINGING went on until very late - that is plenty, not scarcity, and the sentence is positive. Ask: which box phrase means large quantities in positive statements, countable or not? 'Much' sounds unnatural here.

C.passage: Do you know how (1)________ different festivals are celebrated in Singapore each year? During Chinese New Year, there is so (2)________ excitement in the air that even the streets seem to sparkle. My mother prepared (3)________ kueh for the neighbours, and she offered a plate to everyone who walked past our gate. I did not eat (4)________ pineapple tarts at all, because I was already full from dinner. We lit (5)________ candles - just three - and placed them on the doorstep to welcome our guests. Grandpa poured (6)________ rosewater, no more than a teaspoon, into the lamp to make the entrance smell pleasant. Our family visited (7)________ open houses on the first day of Hari Raya - five in a single afternoon - and each one offered a warm welcome. There was (8)________ laughter and singing at the Christmas party, which went on until very late.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: Singapore's four main communities each have rich (1)________ and traditions they share during festivals. During Deepavali, families (2)________ their homes with oil lamps and colourful kolam patterns. A (3)________ of worshippers carrying offerings may be seen moving through the streets near Hindu temples. Christmas brings a spirit of (4)________ — thankfulness for family and the blessings of the year. All these celebrations remind us that Singapore's strength comes from its (5)________ — different peoples coming together as one nation.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'rich ___ and traditions' = long-established practices = customs.
questions.learning_tip: CUSTOMS = traditional practices and ways of behaving that have been followed for a long time. Every culture has its own CUSTOMS during festivals.
questions.retry_hint: The blank is paired with AND TRADITIONS, so it names something similar: practices handed down for generations. Ask: which box word names those long-standing ways of doing things? After 'rich' it must be plural.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'homes with oil lamps and kolam patterns' = adorn for a special occasion = decorate.
questions.learning_tip: DECORATE = add colour, lights or ornaments to make a place look festive and beautiful. Families DECORATE their homes during Deepavali.
questions.retry_hint: The blank follows 'families', so it must be a verb, and the clue is OIL LAMPS AND COLOURFUL KOLAM PATTERNS on the home. Ask: which box word means to make a place look festive?

questions.trap_type: The clue is WORSHIPPERS CARRYING OFFERINGS MOVING THROUGH THE STREETS = an organised march, not a custom or a decoration.
questions.learning_tip: A PROCESSION = an organised group of people moving slowly together, often for a religious or ceremonial purpose.
questions.retry_hint: The clue is WORSHIPPERS CARRYING OFFERINGS, MOVING THROUGH THE STREETS in one organised line. Ask: which box word names that slow ceremonial march? 'Customs' are practices, not a moving group of people.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'a feeling of thankfulness for family, friends and blessings' = gratitude.
questions.learning_tip: GRATITUDE = the feeling of being thankful and appreciating what you have. Christmas is a time for expressing GRATITUDE to those we love.
questions.retry_hint: The dash defines it: THANKFULNESS FOR FAMILY AND THE BLESSINGS OF THE YEAR. Ask: which box word names that feeling? 'Unity' is about people joining together, not about giving thanks.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'coming together of different peoples to form one nation' = unity.
questions.learning_tip: UNITY = the state of being joined together as one, despite differences. Singapore's UNITY comes from its many communities celebrating together.
questions.retry_hint: The dash explains it: DIFFERENT PEOPLES COMING TOGETHER AS ONE NATION. Ask: which box word names that state of being joined into one? 'Customs' differ from group to group; this is what they all share.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.trap_type: 'The lanterns' is plural. Students write 'was' (singular).
questions.learning_tip: Plural subject → plural verb! The lanterns WERE glowing softly. WAS is only for singular subjects like 'the lantern' (one).
questions.retry_hint: Count the subject: THE LANTERNS GLOWING SOFTLY along the corridor - more than one. Ask: does a plural subject take a singular past verb, or a plural one? The corridor is not the subject.

questions.trap_type: Students write 'their' (belonging to them) when the sentence needs 'there' (at that place).
questions.learning_tip: THERE = at that place OR 'there is/are'. THEIR = belonging to them. 'We sat THERE on the mat' = at that place. Test: replace with 'at that place'. If it works → THERE.
questions.retry_hint: Test it: WE SAT ___ ON A MAT - can you say 'at that place'? Nobody owns the mat. Ask: which spelling names a place, and which one means 'belonging to them'?

questions.error_type: Spelling — ie/ei confusion (believe: I before E)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'beleive' putting E before I. The correct spelling is beLIEve — I comes before E.
questions.learning_tip: Rule: I before E, except after C! beLIEve = I before E ✅. reCEIve = after C, use EI ✅. Remember: 'beLIE' is in the word 'believe' — I before E!
questions.retry_hint: Grandmother holds this opinion about the FESTIVAL OF LIGHTS, but the underlined word has two letters swapped. Ask: does the rule say I before E, or E before I, when no C stands in front? Compare: relief, field, piece.

questions.trap_type: Students write 'gentle' (adjective) after the action verb 'placed'. A verb needs an adverb.
questions.learning_tip: After an action verb (placed), use an ADVERB: placed GENTLY. Rule: verb + adverb (-ly). 'Gentle' describes nouns; 'gently' describes actions.
questions.retry_hint: PLACED is an action verb, and the underlined word tells you HOW she placed each OIL LAMP. Ask: do we describe an action with an adjective, or with an adverb ending in -ly?

questions.error_type: Possessive apostrophe — singular possessive (family's, not familys)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'familys' without the apostrophe. To show possession: family → family's.
questions.learning_tip: Singular possessive: noun + 's! The FAMILY'S tradition = the tradition belonging to the family. 'Familys' is wrong — it is not a word. Add apostrophe + s: family's.
questions.retry_hint: It HAS ALWAYS BEEN OUR ___ TRADITION - one family owns this custom. Ask: can a plain -s ever show ownership? Decide where the apostrophe belongs when a single owner is named.

E.passage: Last week, we celebrated Deepavali with our neighbours. The lanterns was (1) glowing softly along the corridor of our block. We sat their (2) on a mat and watched the sparklers light up the night sky. My grandmother beleive (3) that the festival of lights reminds us to choose good over evil. She placed each oil lamp gentle (4) on the windowsill so the flame would not blow out. It has always been our familys (5) tradition to share a meal with our neighbours on Deepavali evening.

questions.sentence_a: You visit your neighbours during Hari Raya.
questions.sentence_b: The bond between communities will grow stronger.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'As long as'.
questions.model_answer: As long as you visit your neighbours during Hari Raya, the bond between communities will grow stronger.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'As long as you will visit' — adding 'will' in the 'as long as' clause.
questions.learning_tip: AS LONG AS + simple present, simple future. AS LONG AS you VISIT your neighbours, the bond WILL GROW stronger. Never use 'will' after 'as long as'.
