C.passage: Thunder rumbled (1)________ lightning lit up the whole sky in a single bright flash. We brought umbrellas (2)________ the strong wind turned them inside out immediately. The drain overflowed, (3)________ the road became flooded within just a few minutes. The children rushed inside (4)________ they were afraid of the lightning flashing across the dark sky. (5)________ the rain was heavy, Father still insisted on going out to buy dinner for the whole family. You can wait for the rain to stop (6)________ take a taxi home instead - the choice is yours. (7)________ the first rumble at noon, the sky has not brightened at all. The match will be cancelled (8)________ the rain stops within the next thirty minutes.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: Singapore experiences thunderstorms frequently, especially in the afternoons. Before a major storm, the weather (1)________ often warns of strong winds and heavy rain. A sudden (2)________ of wind can bend small trees and rattle windows. Heavy rain can (3)________ anyone caught outside within seconds. During a storm, it is important to find (4)________ — a covered area away from trees. Heavy rain also reduces (5)________, making it difficult for drivers to see clearly ahead.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'warns of strong winds and heavy rain before a storm' = a weather prediction = forecast.
questions.learning_tip: A FORECAST = a prediction of what the weather will be. The weather FORECAST warns us of coming storms so we can prepare.
questions.retry_hint: It comes BEFORE A MAJOR STORM and it WARNS OF STRONG WINDS AND HEAVY RAIN - a prediction made in advance. Ask: which box word names what the weathermen publish each morning? A 'drought' is dry weather, not a prediction.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'sudden ___ of wind can bend trees' = a sudden strong burst of wind = gust.
questions.learning_tip: A GUST (of wind) = a sudden, strong burst of wind. A GUST can bend small trees and knock over lightweight objects.
questions.retry_hint: It is SUDDEN, it can BEND SMALL TREES and RATTLE WINDOWS - a short, violent burst rather than a steady breeze. Ask: which box word names one sharp blast of wind? The blank is a noun, since 'a' sits in front of it.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'caught outside within seconds... even under an umbrella' = soaked completely = drench.
questions.learning_tip: DRENCH = soak something or someone completely with water. Heavy tropical rain can DRENCH you in seconds even if you have an umbrella.
questions.retry_hint: The blank follows CAN, so it must be a plain verb, and the victim is ANYONE CAUGHT OUTSIDE WITHIN SECONDS. Ask: which box word means to soak someone completely? 'Evaporate' does the opposite - it dries water away.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'find ___ — a covered area away from trees and open fields' = a place of protection = shelter.
questions.learning_tip: SHELTER = a covered place that provides protection from the rain, wind or sun. During a storm, find SHELTER in a covered area away from trees.
questions.retry_hint: The dash explains it: A COVERED AREA AWAY FROM TREES. Ask: which box word names a place that protects you from the rain? The blank follows 'find', so it must be a noun - a thing you can look for.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'reduces ___, making it difficult for drivers to see clearly' = the ability to see = visibility.
questions.learning_tip: VISIBILITY = how far or clearly you can see. Heavy rain reduces VISIBILITY = you cannot see very far ahead. Low VISIBILITY makes driving dangerous.
questions.retry_hint: The clue sits right after the comma: DRIVERS cannot SEE CLEARLY AHEAD. Ask: which box word names how far you are able to see? A 'rainbow' is a thing in the sky, not a measure of sight.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.trap_type: 'The puddles' is plural. Students write 'was' (singular).
questions.learning_tip: Plural subject → plural verb! The puddles WERE everywhere after the rain. WAS is only for singular. PUDDLES = more than one → WERE.
questions.retry_hint: THE PUDDLES is plural - many little pools, not one. Ask: which past form of 'to be' belongs with a plural subject? Decide by the subject, never by the word standing closest to the verb.

questions.error_type: Homophone confusion — they're (they are) vs their (possessive)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'they're' (they are) when the sentence needs 'their' (belonging to them).
questions.learning_tip: THEIR = belonging to them. THEY'RE = they are. 'They grabbed THEIR umbrellas' = umbrellas belonging to them. Test: 'They grabbed they are umbrellas' = WRONG. Use THEIR.
questions.retry_hint: Unfold the underlined word: it is short for THEY ARE. Ask: does 'they are raincoats' make any sense? The RAINCOATS belong to the children, so the possessive spelling is the one you need.

questions.error_type: Spelling — ie/ei confusion (weird: ei, exception to I-before-E rule)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'wierd' putting I before E. 'Weird' is an exception — it uses EI even though there is no C before it.
questions.learning_tip: WEIRD is an exception! I before E, except after C — but 'weird' breaks the rule. Remember: 'WEIRD is WEIRd' = spell it with EI. Just memorise this one: w-e-i-r-d.
questions.retry_hint: This one is the famous exception to the rhyme. Ask: does 'I before E, except after C' really work here, when there is no C anywhere in the word? The two vowels in 'WIERD' must swap places - simply memorise it.

questions.trap_type: Students write 'heavy' (adjective) after the action verb 'rained'. A verb needs an adverb.
questions.learning_tip: After an action verb (rained), use an ADVERB: rained HEAVILY. Rule: verb + adverb (-ly). 'Heavy' describes nouns (heavy rain). 'Heavily' describes the action (rained heavily).
questions.retry_hint: RAINED is the action, and the underlined word says HOW hard it came down. Ask: does an action verb take an adjective or an adverb? Careful - the same word is correct in 'heavy rain', where it describes a noun.

questions.trap_type: Students write a plain plural and leave out the apostrophe that shows ownership.
questions.learning_tip: The umbrellas BELONG TO the teachers -> TEACHERS' umbrellas (apostrophe after the -s for a plural). One teacher: teacher's.
questions.retry_hint: The umbrellas belong to the TEACHERS, and there is more than one of them - the sentence says THEY stepped out. Ask: for a plural owner already ending in -s, does the apostrophe come before that s, or after it?

E.passage: Yesterday afternoon, a thunderstorm hit our estate without warning. The puddles was (1) everywhere and the drains overflowed into the corridor. The children quickly grabbed they're (2) raincoats and boots before rushing outside to splash in the puddles. The sky had turned a wierd (3) yellow-green colour before the rain began. By four o'clock, it rained so heavy (4) that the bus was delayed by forty minutes. The teachers (5) umbrellas turned inside out as soon as they stepped out of the school building.

questions.sentence_a: You hear thunder.
questions.sentence_b: You should go indoors immediately.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'As soon as'.
questions.model_answer: As soon as you hear thunder, you should go indoors immediately.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'As soon as you will hear thunder' — adding 'will' in the 'as soon as' clause.
questions.learning_tip: AS SOON AS + simple present, imperative or simple future. AS SOON AS you HEAR thunder, you SHOULD go indoors. No 'will' after 'as soon as'.
questions.retry_hint: AS SOON AS means 'the moment that', so it goes in front of the event that happens FIRST. Ask: which of the two facts comes first in time? And does a time clause ever take 'will' inside it?

questions.sentence_a: The storm knocked down an old tree.
questions.sentence_b: The old tree had stood at the corner of the road for fifty years.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using the relative pronoun 'which'.
questions.model_answer: The storm knocked down an old tree, which had stood at the corner of the road for fifty years.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'an old tree which it had stood' — adding 'it' after 'which'. Also, 'had stood' is acceptable here as it is in a relative clause describing a prior state.
questions.learning_tip: WHICH = relative pronoun for things. The storm knocked down a tree, WHICH had stood for fifty years. Non-restrictive clause (extra info, commas) → use WHICH. Never add 'it' after 'which'.
questions.retry_hint: The OLD TREE appears in both facts. Ask: which fact is the main news, and which is extra background that can be tucked into a clause after a comma? The relative pronoun already stands for the tree, so do not repeat 'it'.

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage_title: How to Stay Safe During a Thunderstorm
G.passage:
Singapore experiences thunderstorms more than 170 days a year, making it one of the world's most storm-prone countries. Understanding what happens during a thunderstorm and how to stay safe can make a real difference.

A thunderstorm forms when warm, moist air rises rapidly and meets cooler air high in the atmosphere. This creates large storm clouds that produce lightning and thunder. Lightning is a powerful electrical discharge, and the thunder we hear is the sound it makes as it heats the air around it. Because light travels faster than sound, we always see lightning before we hear thunder. Counting the seconds between the flash and the bang tells you how far away the storm is — roughly one kilometre for every three seconds.

During a thunderstorm, there are several safety rules to follow. You should stay indoors and away from windows. Avoid using electrical appliances and unplug devices where possible. If you are outdoors, do not shelter under a tree, as trees attract lightning. Move to a low-lying area instead and crouch down with your feet together and your hands over your ears.

Thunderstorms in Singapore usually pass within thirty to sixty minutes. After the rain stops, it is important to check for flooded paths and fallen branches before going outside.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 2 has the same meaning as 'a release of electrical energy'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Atmosphere' is the sky; 'rapid' = fast; 'moist' = damp. DISCHARGE = a sudden release of electrical energy.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: DISCHARGE = a sudden release of energy, especially electrical energy. Lightning is an electrical DISCHARGE = a burst of electricity between clouds and the ground.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 2, what does 'it' refer to in 'the thunder we hear is the sound it makes'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking 'it' refers to the storm cloud. But 'it' refers to LIGHTNING, which heats the air and causes the sound of thunder.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 2: 'Lightning is a powerful electrical discharge, and the thunder we hear is the sound IT makes as it heats the air.' IT = LIGHTNING.

mcq_questions.stem: Why should you NOT shelter under a tree during a thunderstorm?

options.1: Trees are too wet to stand under.
options.2: You might be seen by lightning.
options.3: Trees attract lightning and could put you in danger.
options.4: Trees block the view of the storm.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking it is about getting wet. The passage specifically says trees 'attract lightning'.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 3: 'do not shelter under a tree, as TREES ATTRACT LIGHTNING.' If lightning hits the tree, you could be harmed. Move to a low-lying open area instead.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 1, is it True or False that Singapore has thunderstorms on fewer than 100 days a year? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The passage says Singapore experiences thunderstorms MORE THAN 170 DAYS A YEAR — far more than 100 days.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students may say 'True' guessing a lower number. The passage states '170 days a year' explicitly.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1: Singapore has thunderstorms MORE THAN 170 DAYS A YEAR. 170 > 100, so the statement is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: How can you estimate how far away a thunderstorm is?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: You count the seconds between the lightning flash and the thunder, then divide by three. Each three seconds is roughly one kilometre.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'count the seconds' without explaining the calculation.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 2: 'roughly ONE KILOMETRE for every THREE SECONDS.' Count the seconds → divide by three → distance in kilometres.

open_ended_questions.stem: Give TWO things you should do if you are caught OUTDOORS during a thunderstorm.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) Do not shelter under a tree — move away from it. (ii) Move to a low-lying area and crouch down with feet together and hands over ears.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students give indoor safety tips. The question specifies OUTDOORS.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 3 (OUTDOORS): (1) NOT UNDER A TREE (trees attract lightning); (2) CROUCH DOWN in a low-lying area, feet together, hands over ears. These are the two outdoor rules.

open_ended_questions.stem: Why do we see lightning before we hear thunder?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: Because light travels faster than sound. We see the lightning flash first, then hear the thunder after.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'lightning comes before thunder' without explaining why.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 2: 'Because LIGHT TRAVELS FASTER THAN SOUND, we always see lightning before we hear thunder.' This is the scientific reason for the sequence.

open_ended_questions.stem: This passage is an informational text. Describe TWO features the writer uses to make it useful to readers.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) PRACTICAL SAFETY RULES: the writer gives specific things to do and not do (e.g., avoid trees, crouch down), making the information actionable. (ii) SCIENTIFIC EXPLANATION: the writer explains WHY lightning and thunder happen, helping readers understand and remember the advice.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students summarise the content rather than analysing the features of the text.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: FEATURES of an informational text: (1) practical SAFETY RULES that readers can follow; (2) SCIENTIFIC EXPLANATION of why things happen. Analyse HOW it is written, not WHAT it says.

questions.stem: The firefighter was as ________ as a lion when he ran into the burning building to save the child.
questions.trap_type: 'Timid' and 'fearful' = afraid; 'slow' = not fast. BRAVE = showing courage in the face of danger.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! The firefighter was AS BRAVE AS a lion = comparing his courage to a lion's. 'As brave as a lion' is a common simile for great courage.
questions.retry_hint: He RAN INTO THE BURNING BUILDING TO SAVE THE CHILD, and he is compared to a LION. Ask: does a lion stand for courage or for fear? 'Timid' and 'fearful' say he was afraid, which the sentence flatly contradicts.

questions.stem: When the alarm went off, the firefighters ________ their gear and reached the fire truck in under a minute.
questions.trap_type: 'Threw away' and 'took off' mean removing; 'ignored' = paid no attention. PUT ON = dressed themselves in something.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: PUT ON = wear or dress in something. The firefighters PUT ON their gear = they dressed themselves in their protective suits and helmets quickly.
questions.retry_hint: The ALARM WENT OFF, so the crew must dress fast - the GEAR has to go onto their bodies before they reach the FIRE TRUCK. Ask: which phrasal verb means to get dressed in something? 'Took off' removes it again.

questions.stem: The fire engine ________ through the streets with its siren wailing loudly.
questions.trap_type: 'Crept' and 'tiptoed' suggest slow, quiet movement; 'floated' is for water or air. SPED = moved very fast.
questions.learning_tip: SPED = moved very quickly (past tense of 'speed'). The fire engine SPED through the streets = moved at high speed to reach the fire as fast as possible.
questions.retry_hint: The SIREN is WAILING LOUDLY and the engine is racing to an emergency. Ask: which past verb means moved very fast? 'Crept' and 'tiptoed' are slow and quiet, and nothing FLOATS along a street.

questions.stem: The firefighter worked quickly and carefully to ________ the people trapped inside the damaged building.
questions.trap_type: 'Forget', 'ignore' and 'delay' all mean not helping. RESCUE = save someone from danger.
questions.learning_tip: RESCUE = save someone from danger or a difficult situation. Firefighters RESCUE people trapped in fires or accidents — they bring them to safety.
questions.retry_hint: The people are TRAPPED INSIDE THE DAMAGED BUILDING, and he works QUICKLY AND CAREFULLY. Ask: which verb means to bring someone out of danger to safety? 'Forget', 'ignore' and 'delay' would leave them exactly where they are.

questions.stem: The fire safety officer emphasised that prevention is always more ________ than responding to a fire after it starts.
questions.trap_type: 'Exciting' and 'dangerous' are irrelevant comparisons. 'Tiring' is negative. EFFECTIVE = producing the desired result successfully.
questions.learning_tip: EFFECTIVE = producing the best results. Prevention is MORE EFFECTIVE than responding after a fire starts = stopping a fire before it happens works better than fighting it after.
questions.retry_hint: PREVENTION is weighed against RESPONDING TO A FIRE AFTER IT STARTS - the question is which one works better. Ask: which word means producing the result you want? 'Exciting' and 'tiring' measure feelings, not success.

questions.stem: Everyone in the group ________ amazed when they saw how quickly the firefighters could suit up.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'were' thinking 'everyone in the group' = many people. EVERYONE = singular → WAS. Past context = WAS.
questions.learning_tip: EVERYONE = Singular! Past context → EVERYONE WAS amazed. 'Everyone were' is WRONG. EVERYONE / NOBODY / SOMEONE = always singular → IS / WAS / HAS.
questions.retry_hint: The subject is EVERYONE, not 'the group' standing beside it. Words like everyone and nobody act like ONE person. Ask: which past form of 'to be' matches a singular subject? SAW tells you the time is past.

questions.stem: Our class has ________ to the fire station twice before, but this year's visit was the most memorable.
questions.trap_type: HAS + past participle = present perfect. 'Go' is irregular: go → gone.
questions.learning_tip: HAS + past participle = present perfect. Our class HAS GONE to the fire station twice = both visits happened before now. GO → GONE (irregular). Never 'has went'.
questions.retry_hint: HAS needs a past participle after it, and TWICE BEFORE ties those visits to now. Ask: what is the past participle of 'go' - the plain form, the -s form, the -ing form, or something irregular? 'Has went' is never English.

questions.stem: The fire station's ladder truck is the ________ vehicle in the whole fleet, able to extend to thirty metres.
questions.trap_type: Superlative needed (comparing to all vehicles in the fleet). 'Tall' → THE TALLEST (short adjective, add -est).
questions.learning_tip: THE + adjective + -EST = superlative for short adjectives! The TALLEST vehicle = taller than all others. TALL → TALLEST. Use -EST for one-syllable adjectives.
questions.retry_hint: The truck is ranked against THE WHOLE FLEET, not against one other vehicle, and it can EXTEND TO THIRTY METRES. Ask: for a short adjective, which ending marks the very top? And does a comparative ever follow 'the' like this?

questions.stem: The firefighters ________ the hose when the fire captain gave the order to stand down.
questions.trap_type: 'The captain gave the order' = sudden past event. Firefighters were already rolling the hose = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: The captain GAVE THE ORDER = sudden past event. Firefighters were already rolling the hose = WERE ROLLING (past continuous). Was/were + verb-ing.
questions.retry_hint: The FIRE CAPTAIN GAVE THE ORDER at one sudden moment, and the crew had already begun the job. Ask: which choice keeps an action running in the past until something cuts across it? Two options sit in the present, so they are out at once.

questions.stem: There was ________ smoke coming from the roof when the crew arrived — they had caught it early.
questions.trap_type: 'Smoke' is uncountable → use 'little' or 'much'. 'A few', 'many', 'several' are for countable nouns.
questions.learning_tip: LITTLE + uncountable noun. Smoke = uncountable → LITTLE smoke. 'A few smoke' is WRONG. LITTLE = not much of something uncountable. They were lucky — only LITTLE smoke.
questions.retry_hint: SMOKE cannot be counted, and THEY HAD CAUGHT IT EARLY tells you the amount was small. Ask: which word partners an uncountable noun? 'A few', 'many' and 'several' all need things you can count one by one.

questions.stem: The fire safety equipment hasn't been checked this month, ________ it?
questions.trap_type: Main clause is NEGATIVE present perfect ('hasn't been checked') → POSITIVE question tag. 'Hasn't' → positive tag = has it.
questions.learning_tip: Negative present perfect → positive tag. 'The equipment HASN'T been checked, HAS it?' NEGATIVE → POSITIVE tag. HAS → HASN'T; HASN'T → HAS.
questions.retry_hint: The statement is negative - the EQUIPMENT was not CHECKED THIS MONTH. Ask: after a negative statement, does the tag flip to positive? The tag must echo the same helping verb, so 'is' and 'isn't' cannot appear here.

questions.stem: The new fire safety leaflet ________ to every household in the estate last month.
questions.trap_type: The leaflet was the receiver of the action. Past passive = was delivered.
questions.learning_tip: WAS/WERE + past participle = passive! The leaflet WAS DELIVERED to households = the SCDF delivered it; the leaflet received the action.
questions.retry_hint: A LEAFLET cannot post itself TO EVERY HOUSEHOLD - the fire service did that LAST MONTH. Ask: which choice puts the receiver in the subject position and sets the action in the past? Two options make the leaflet the doer.

questions.stem: The fire safety officer told residents ________ candles unattended near curtains or paper.
questions.trap_type: Negative reported speech: told + object + not to + base verb.
questions.learning_tip: TOLD someone NOT TO + base verb. The officer told residents NOT TO LEAVE candles unattended. Formula: told + person + not to + base verb.
questions.retry_hint: The officer is passing on a rule about CANDLES left UNATTENDED. Ask: after 'told + person', does English use a plain verb, an -ing form, or 'to' + verb? And does the negative word come before that little word, or after it?

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Passive voice — 8 forms)

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Every fire engine (1)________ thoroughly after each call-out.' Signal: present simple passive — regular/routine action = IS + past participle. Subject 'every fire engine' = singular.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'is cleaning' (active) instead of 'is cleaned' (passive). The engine does not clean itself — people clean it.
questions.learning_tip: IS + past participle = present simple passive. The engine IS CLEANED = someone cleans it. Passive: IS/ARE + past participle. Rule: receiver + IS/ARE + pp.
questions.retry_hint: A FIRE ENGINE cannot wash itself - the crew does that AFTER EACH CALL-OUT, every single time. Ask: which box phrase makes one singular engine the receiver, in the present? Two box phrases talk about people being trained.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'All firefighters (2)________ for at least two years before they are allowed to attend a real fire.' Signal: present simple passive — plural subject 'all firefighters' = ARE + past participle.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'is trained' (singular) instead of 'are trained' (plural). 'All firefighters' = plural → ARE.
questions.learning_tip: ARE + past participle = present simple passive for PLURAL. All firefighters ARE TRAINED = they receive training (plural subject). ARE for plural; IS for singular. Rule: plural + ARE + pp.
questions.retry_hint: ALL FIREFIGHTERS is a plural subject, and the training lasts AT LEAST TWO YEARS before they may attend a real fire. Ask: which box phrase uses a plural present helping verb, with the firefighters receiving the action, not doing it?

questions.context_check: Passage: 'This fire station (3)________ in 1987 and has served the community ever since.' Signal: past simple passive — one completed past action = WAS + past participle. Subject 'this fire station' = singular.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'were built' (plural past) instead of 'was built' (singular past).
questions.learning_tip: WAS + past participle = past simple passive for SINGULAR. This station WAS BUILT in 1987 = someone built it then. Singular + WAS + pp. Rule: singular + WAS; plural + WERE.
questions.retry_hint: The date 1987 fixes the time in the past, and THIS FIRE STATION is one single building that could not build itself. Ask: which box phrase is singular, past and passive? A plural helping verb would clash with one station.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Three people (4)________ from the burning flat by the crew last Tuesday.' Signal: past simple passive — plural subject ('three people') + completed past action = WERE + past participle.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'was rescued' (singular past) instead of 'were rescued' (plural past).
questions.learning_tip: WERE + past participle = past simple passive for PLURAL. Three people WERE RESCUED = the crew rescued them. Plural + WERE + pp. Rule: plural past passive = WERE + pp.
questions.retry_hint: THREE PEOPLE is plural, BY THE CREW names the doer, and LAST TUESDAY EVENING fixes the time. Ask: which box phrase is plural, past and passive? The people trapped in the flat did not save themselves.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The fire safety manual (5)________ three times since it was first published.' Signal: present perfect passive — singular subject 'the manual' + action from past to now = HAS BEEN + past participle.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'have been updated' (plural) instead of 'has been updated' (singular).
questions.learning_tip: HAS BEEN + past participle = present perfect passive for SINGULAR. The manual HAS BEEN UPDATED = it was updated at some point(s) and is relevant now. Singular = HAS BEEN.
questions.retry_hint: THE FIRE SAFETY MANUAL is one single book, and SINCE IT WAS FIRST PUBLISHED runs from the past right up to now. Ask: which box phrase is a singular present perfect passive? A plural helping verb would not agree with one manual.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'New smoke detectors (6)________ in every flat in the estate since last year.' Signal: present perfect passive — plural subject 'new smoke detectors' = HAVE BEEN + past participle.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'has been installed' (singular) instead of 'have been installed' (plural).
questions.learning_tip: HAVE BEEN + past participle = present perfect passive for PLURAL. New detectors HAVE BEEN INSTALLED = they were installed (from past to now). Plural = HAVE BEEN.
questions.retry_hint: NEW SMOKE DETECTORS is plural, and SINCE LAST YEAR again stretches from the past up to now. Ask: which box phrase is a plural present perfect passive? The detectors certainly did not put themselves up.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'One of the hoses (7)________ right now after it was damaged during last week's call-out.' Signal: present continuous passive — singular subject 'one of the hoses' + happening right now = IS BEING + past participle.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'is repaired' (simple present passive) instead of 'is being repaired' (continuous passive, right now).
questions.learning_tip: IS BEING + past participle = present continuous passive. The hose IS BEING REPAIRED = it is being repaired right now. Rule: IS/ARE + BEING + pp = happening now (passive).
questions.retry_hint: RIGHT NOW tells you the work has not finished - it goes on as we speak. Ask: which box phrase shows a passive action in progress at this very moment? A simple present passive would mean it happens as a routine.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The new ladder truck (8)________ when the alarm suddenly sounded for a real fire.' Signal: past continuous passive — singular subject + ongoing past action interrupted = WAS BEING + past participle.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'was tested' (simple past passive, completed) instead of 'was being tested' (past continuous passive, ongoing when interrupted).
questions.learning_tip: WAS BEING + past participle = past continuous passive. The truck WAS BEING TESTED (ongoing) when the alarm sounded (interruption). Rule: WAS/WERE + BEING + pp = ongoing past passive.
questions.retry_hint: THE ALARM SOUNDED at one sudden moment, and work on the LADDER TRUCK had already begun. Ask: which box phrase shows a passive action still in progress in the PAST when something interrupted it? A finished past passive hides the interruption.

C.passage: Every fire engine (1)________ thoroughly after each call-out to ensure it is always ready for the next emergency. All firefighters (2)________ for at least two years before they are allowed to attend a real fire. This fire station (3)________ in 1987 and has served the community ever since. Three people (4)________ from the burning flat by the crew last Tuesday evening. The fire safety manual (5)________ three times since it was first published, to include new guidelines for high-rise buildings. New smoke detectors (6)________ in every flat in the estate since last year as part of a government safety programme. One of the hoses (7)________ right now after it was damaged during last week's call-out. The new ladder truck (8)________ when the alarm sounded for a real fire.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: Singapore Civil Defence Force firefighters are among the most highly trained (1)________ in the world. During school visits, they use a training room to (2)________ a fire emergency safely. Students learn to identify a fire (3)________ — anything that could start or spread a fire. They are also taught how to (4)________ a building quickly using stairways instead of lifts. Firefighters use specialist (5)________ such as breathing equipment and hydraulic cutting tools to carry out rescues.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'most highly trained ___ in the world' = the people who work there = personnel.
questions.learning_tip: PERSONNEL = the people who work in an organisation. SCDF PERSONNEL = the firefighters and staff who work for SCDF.
questions.retry_hint: The blank names the FIREFIGHTERS themselves - the people who do the job. Ask: which box word is a noun meaning the staff of an organisation? 'Apparatus' names their equipment, not the men and women who carry it.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'to ___ a fire emergency... without any real danger' = create a realistic copy of = simulate.
questions.learning_tip: SIMULATE = create a realistic copy or model of a situation for training purposes. Firefighters SIMULATE emergencies to train safely.
questions.retry_hint: The blank follows TO, so it must be a plain verb, and the fire is only pretend - it happens SAFELY inside a TRAINING ROOM. Ask: which box word means to copy a real situation for practice?

questions.trap_type: The clue 'anything that could start or spread a fire' = a source of danger = hazard.
questions.learning_tip: A HAZARD = a source of potential danger. An overloaded electrical socket is a fire HAZARD = it could cause a fire.
questions.retry_hint: The dash defines it: ANYTHING THAT COULD START OR SPREAD A FIRE. Ask: which box word names a source of danger? A 'casualty' is a person who gets hurt - that is the result, not the cause.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'leave a building quickly and safely using stairways' = evacuate.
questions.learning_tip: EVACUATE = leave a building or area quickly because of danger. During a fire, you must EVACUATE = exit the building immediately using the staircase.
questions.retry_hint: The clue is USING STAIRWAYS INSTEAD OF LIFTS - everyone is getting out fast. Ask: which box word means to leave a building because of danger? 'Extinguish' is what you do to the flames, not to the building.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'specialist ___ such as breathing equipment, hydraulic cutting tools and hoses' = specialised equipment = apparatus.
questions.learning_tip: APPARATUS = specialised equipment or tools for a particular purpose. Firefighters use specialist APPARATUS including breathing gear and hydraulic tools.
questions.retry_hint: The examples come after SUCH AS: BREATHING EQUIPMENT and HYDRAULIC CUTTING TOOLS. Ask: which box word is the general noun for specialist gear? 'Personnel' would name people, but the blank names things.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.trap_type: 'The firefighters' is plural. Students write 'was' (singular).
questions.learning_tip: Plural subject → plural verb! The firefighters WERE already dressed when the alarm rang. WAS is only for singular. FIREFIGHTERS = more than one → WERE.
questions.retry_hint: THE FIREFIGHTERS is plural - a whole crew standing there in FULL GEAR. Ask: which past form of 'to be' agrees with a plural subject? Find the subject first, then make the verb match it.

questions.error_type: Homophone confusion — its (possessive) vs it's (it is)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'its' (possessive) when the sentence needs 'it's' = it is.
questions.learning_tip: IT'S = it is. ITS = belonging to it. 'ITS important to test your smoke alarm' → can you replace with 'it is'? YES → use IT'S. Remember: IT'S = IT IS.
questions.retry_hint: Stretch the underlined word into two words: 'IT IS ESSENTIAL to check your smoke alarm'. Does that work? Then an apostrophe is missing. Without one, the word means 'belonging to it', and nothing here owns the checking.

questions.error_type: Spelling — ie/ei confusion (piece: I before E)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'peice' putting E before I. 'Piece' follows the I-before-E rule: pIEce.
questions.learning_tip: Rule: I before E, except after C! pIEce = I before E ✅. Remember: 'A pIEce of PIE' — the word PIE is hidden inside PIECE, with I before E.
questions.retry_hint: No C stands in front of the underlined word, so the plain rule holds: I before E. Ask: which two letters has the writer swapped in 'PEICE'? The same order shows up in shield, thief and relief.

questions.trap_type: Students write 'rapid' (adjective) after the action verb 'spread'. A verb needs an adverb.
questions.learning_tip: After an action verb (spread), use an ADVERB: spread RAPIDLY. Rule: verb + adverb (-ly). 'Rapid' describes nouns (a rapid spread). 'Rapidly' describes actions (spread rapidly).
questions.retry_hint: SPREAD is the verb, and the underlined word tells you HOW the fire travels - fast. Ask: which word class describes an action, the adjective or the adverb? An adjective would need a noun to describe, and there is none here.

questions.trap_type: Students write a plain plural and leave out the apostrophe that shows ownership.
questions.learning_tip: The masks BELONG TO the rescuers -> RESCUERS' masks (apostrophe after the -s for a plural). One rescuer: rescuer's.
questions.retry_hint: The breathing masks belong to the RESCUERS - a whole team of them. Ask: when the owners are plural and the word already ends in -s, where does the apostrophe sit? One owner would place it differently.

E.passage: Last Friday, our class visited Bukit Timah Fire Station for a learning journey. The firefighters was (1) already dressed in their full gear when we arrived, ready to demonstrate a mock rescue. The officer in charge said its (2) essential to check your smoke alarm every month. He showed us a peice (3) of melted plastic - the result of leaving a phone charger plugged in overnight. A small electrical fire can spread rapid (4) throughout a room in just two minutes if nothing is done. Before we left, we lifted one of the rescuers (5) heavy breathing masks, which weighed almost five kilograms.

questions.sentence_a: You test your smoke alarm regularly.
questions.sentence_b: You may not know it has stopped working.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'Unless'.
questions.model_answer: Unless you test your smoke alarm regularly, you may not know it has stopped working.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'Unless you will test' — adding 'will' in the 'unless' clause.
questions.learning_tip: UNLESS + simple present, simple future/modal. UNLESS you TEST your smoke alarm regularly, you MAY NOT KNOW it has stopped. No 'will' after 'unless'.
questions.retry_hint: Put the SMOKE ALARM fact first: it is the thing that has to be done. Ask: after UNLESS, does the verb stay in the present? And does that clause still need a 'not' inside it, when UNLESS already means 'if not'?

questions.sentence_a: The firefighter entered the burning building.
questions.sentence_b: She rescued two children from the third floor.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'After'.
questions.model_answer: After entering the burning building, the firefighter rescued two children from the third floor.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'After the firefighter entered the burning building, she rescued two children' — acceptable, but the model answer uses the -ing reduction.
questions.learning_tip: AFTER + verb-ing (same subject): AFTER ENTERING the building, the firefighter rescued two children. When the subject is the same for both actions, 'after + -ing' is elegant and concise.
questions.retry_hint: Both facts have the same doer, so the FIREFIGHTER is named only once. Ask: which action came earlier, and can that earlier verb be turned into an -ing form straight after AFTER? A comma then joins the two halves.

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
The alarm sounded at 2.47 in the afternoon. By 2.48, Senior Station Inspector Ravi had already led his team out of the station.

The call was for a kitchen fire in a third-floor flat on Clementi Avenue. When the engine arrived, smoke was pouring from an open window. Ravi's team pulled on their breathing masks and went in.

The fire was small — a forgotten pan on the stove. They put it out in under two minutes. But in the corridor outside, they found an elderly man who could not walk. He was trying to reach the staircase when the smoke overcame him.

Ravi lifted the man onto his back and carried him down three flights of stairs without stopping.

The paramedics were waiting outside. The man, who was seventy-eight years old, was taken to hospital and later confirmed to be in stable condition.

At the debrief that evening, Ravi reminded his team: 'The fire was the easy part. It is always the person who needs the most time.'

Ravi did not speak on the way back to the station. At the debrief, he set his helmet on the table and looked at his team. Each of them knew what the other was thinking: the man in the corridor could have been anyone's grandfather. That thought did not make the work harder. It made it more important.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 2 has the same meaning as 'flowing out in large amounts'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Arrived' = reached a place; 'pulled' = drew; 'open' = not closed. POURING = flowing out continuously and in large amounts.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: POURING = flowing out steadily and in large amounts. Smoke was POURING from the window = coming out in a continuous stream. 'Pour' = flow freely and in volume.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 3, what does 'them' refer to in 'They put it out in under two minutes'?

options.1: The smoke and flames from the fire

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 2 thinking 'it' = the pan. But 'put it out' = extinguished the FIRE. 'It' = the fire.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 3: 'The fire was small... They PUT IT OUT in under two minutes.' IT = the FIRE. 'Put out' = extinguish. They extinguished the fire in under two minutes.

mcq_questions.stem: Ravi said 'The fire was the easy part. It is always the person who needs the most time.' What did he mean?

options.1: Fires are usually small and easy to put out.
options.2: Rescuing people requires more care, effort and time than extinguishing the fire itself.
options.3: The team should have arrived faster.
options.4: Elderly people should not live in high-rise flats.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking he was dismissing the fire. His message is about what is truly difficult — the human rescue.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Ravi means: putting out the fire is technically straightforward, but RESCUING a PERSON — carrying them safely to safety — requires more time, care and effort. People are the priority.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 1, is it True or False that the team took more than two minutes to leave the station after the alarm? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The alarm sounded at 2.47 and 'BY 2.48, Senior Station Inspector Ravi had already LED HIS TEAM OUT of the station' — showing they left within one minute.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'True, it takes time to prepare.' The passage gives exact times — they left within one minute.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1: alarm at 2.47, team out by 2.48 = ONE MINUTE. 'By 2.48, Ravi had ALREADY led his team out.' They left in under one minute. Answer is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: What caused the fire, and where was it?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: The fire was caused by a forgotten pan left on the stove. It was in the kitchen of a third-floor flat on Clementi Avenue.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'a kitchen fire' without identifying the specific cause.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 3: 'a FORGOTTEN PAN on the stove' was the cause. Location: kitchen of a THIRD-FLOOR flat on Clementi Avenue. Give both the cause and the location.

open_ended_questions.stem: What TWO challenges did Ravi's team face that were more difficult than putting out the fire?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) They found an elderly man who could not walk and was overcome by smoke while trying to reach the staircase. (ii) Ravi had to carry the man on his back down three flights of stairs without stopping — a physically demanding and time-consuming rescue.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students describe the fire as a challenge. The question asks what was MORE DIFFICULT than the fire.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraphs 3–4: (1) finding a man who COULD NOT WALK and was overcome by smoke; (2) Ravi carrying him down THREE FLIGHTS of stairs on his back. The HUMAN rescue was the real challenge.

open_ended_questions.stem: How did the firefighters know where to go when they arrived at the flat?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: They could see smoke pouring from an open window, which showed them where the fire was.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'they got a call' — the call told them the address, but the visual clue (smoke from window) directed them to the exact location.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 2: 'SMOKE was POURING from an OPEN WINDOW.' This visual clue told them exactly where the fire was in the building. They could see it from outside.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on his actions and words in the passage, describe TWO character traits of Ravi with evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) DECISIVE: Ravi had his team out of the station within one minute of the alarm — no hesitation, immediate action. (ii) COMPASSIONATE: when he found the elderly man who could not walk, he lifted him onto his back and carried him down three flights of stairs without stopping, putting the man's safety entirely first.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'brave and fast' without precise traits or evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: DECISIVE = team out within ONE MINUTE, no hesitation. COMPASSIONATE = carried the elderly man on his BACK down THREE FLIGHTS without stopping — putting the person first.

questions.stem: The chapteh champion was as ________ as a cat, catching the feathered shuttlecock before it touched the ground.
questions.trap_type: 'Slow', 'clumsy' and 'heavy' all suggest the opposite of fast, skilled movement. QUICK = moving fast and reacting immediately.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! The champion was AS QUICK AS a cat = the simile compares his speed to a cat's. QUICK = fast and light in movement.
questions.retry_hint: He CATCHES THE FEATHERED SHUTTLECOCK BEFORE IT TOUCHED THE GROUND, and he is compared to a CAT. Ask: which word matches a cat's speed of reaction? 'Slow', 'clumsy' and 'heavy' all describe someone who would drop it.

questions.stem: Despite losing five rounds in a row, the young player refused to ________ and kept trying until the very end.
questions.trap_type: 'Continue', 'practise' and 'improve' all mean the opposite of stopping. GIVE UP = stop trying because something is too difficult.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: GIVE UP = stop trying because something feels too hard. The player refused to GIVE UP = he kept going despite losing. GIVE + UP work together — never split them!
questions.retry_hint: He KEPT TRYING UNTIL THE VERY END even after LOSING FIVE ROUNDS IN A ROW, and REFUSED flips the meaning of the blank. Ask: which phrasal verb means to stop trying because something feels too hard?

questions.stem: The kite flew higher and higher until it was barely ________, just a tiny speck against the blue sky.
questions.trap_type: 'Colourful' describes colour, not whether it can be seen from far away. 'Heavy' and 'broken' make no sense. VISIBLE = able to be seen.
questions.learning_tip: VISIBLE = able to be seen. The kite was barely VISIBLE = it was so far away it could hardly be seen. Opposite: invisible.
questions.retry_hint: It is only A TINY SPECK AGAINST THE BLUE SKY now that it has flown HIGHER AND HIGHER. Ask: which word means able to be seen at all? 'Colourful' talks about colour, and rising does not make a kite heavy or broken.

questions.stem: The old man showed the children how to ________ the gasing top so that it spun perfectly on the ground.
questions.trap_type: 'Break' = damage; 'ignore' = pay no attention; 'sell' = give for money. LAUNCH = send something into motion with force.
questions.learning_tip: LAUNCH = send something into motion with a controlled release of force. To LAUNCH a gasing top = to throw and release it so it spins perfectly.
questions.retry_hint: The top must end up SPINNING PERFECTLY ON THE GROUND, so it has to be thrown and released with force. Ask: which verb means to set something moving with a strong, controlled release? 'Break' and 'sell' have nothing to do with spinning.

questions.stem: The five stones game requires great ________ — both hands and eyes must work together at exactly the right moment.
questions.trap_type: 'Strength' = physical power; 'speed' = fast movement; 'silence' = no noise. COORDINATION = the ability to use hands and eyes together smoothly and accurately.
questions.learning_tip: COORDINATION = the ability to control different parts of your body together smoothly. Five stones needs great COORDINATION = your hands and eyes must work together at exactly the right time.
questions.retry_hint: The dash spells it out: BOTH HANDS AND EYES MUST WORK TOGETHER AT EXACTLY THE RIGHT MOMENT. Ask: which noun names that teamwork between body parts? 'Strength' is raw power, and 'speed' alone will not catch the stones.

questions.stem: Everyone in the playground ________ a different traditional game during recess.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'play' thinking 'everyone in the playground' = many people. EVERYONE = singular → verb must have -S in present tense.
questions.learning_tip: EVERYONE / NOBODY / SOMEONE = Singular! ALWAYS use verb+S. Everyone PLAYS = add -S. 'Everyone play' or 'Everyone are playing' are WRONG.
questions.retry_hint: Do not be fooled by THE PLAYGROUND full of children: the subject is EVERYONE, which counts as ONE. Ask: in the present tense, which ending does a singular subject put on its verb? 'Are playing' and 'have played' both treat it as plural.

questions.stem: Our school has ________ a traditional games festival every year since it was founded.
questions.trap_type: HAS + past participle = present perfect. 'Hold' is irregular: hold → held.
questions.learning_tip: HAS + past participle = present perfect. Our school HAS HELD a festival every year = from the past until now. HOLD → HELD (irregular).
questions.retry_hint: HAS is waiting for a past participle, and SINCE IT WAS FOUNDED stretches from the past to today. Ask: is 'hold' a regular verb that takes -ed, or an irregular one that changes its vowel? 'Has hold' and 'has holding' are impossible.

questions.stem: The gasing top spun ________ longer than the chapteh shuttlecock stayed in the air.
questions.trap_type: 'Too longer', 'most longer' and 'very longer' are all impossible. Only one of these words can strengthen a comparative that already ends in -er.
questions.learning_tip: FAR + comparative = much more. The gasing spun FAR LONGER THAN the chapteh stayed in the air. FAR makes the comparison stronger. 'Very longer' is WRONG.
questions.retry_hint: LONGER is already a comparative - it ends in -er - so the blank must strengthen it, not repeat it. Ask: can 'very', 'too' or 'most' ever stand in front of a comparative? Only one small word can do that job.

questions.stem: The children ________ their kites on the open field when a strong gust of wind suddenly snapped the string.
questions.trap_type: 'A gust snapped the string' = sudden interrupting event. The children were already flying kites = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: A gust SNAPPED the string = sudden past event. Children were already in the middle of flying kites = WERE FLYING (past continuous). Past continuous = was/were + verb-ing.
questions.retry_hint: A STRONG GUST OF WIND SUDDENLY SNAPPED THE STRING - there is the interruption. Ask: at that instant, had the children finished, or was the action still going on? Pick the past form that shows an action in mid-flow.

questions.stem: There was ________ space left on the mat for the five stones players to sit comfortably.
questions.trap_type: 'Space' is uncountable → use LITTLE. 'Few', 'many' and 'a few' are for countable nouns.
questions.learning_tip: LITTLE + uncountable noun. Space = uncountable → LITTLE space. 'Few space' or 'a few space' are WRONG. LITTLE = not much (uncountable).
questions.retry_hint: SPACE cannot be counted - you cannot say one space, two spaces, on a MAT. Ask: which option belongs with an uncountable noun? 'Few', 'many' and 'a few' all need things you can count, such as players.

questions.stem: Traditional games are more educational than most people think, ________ they?
questions.trap_type: Positive statement ('are more educational') → negative question tag. 'Are' → aren't they.
questions.learning_tip: Positive statement → negative tag. Traditional games ARE more educational, AREN'T they? POSITIVE → NEGATIVE tag. ARE → AREN'T.
questions.retry_hint: The statement is positive and its verb is ARE. Ask: after a positive statement, which way does the tag turn? The tag must repeat the same verb, so the singular forms 'is' and 'isn't' cannot match GAMES.

questions.stem: The zero-point rubber band rope ________ by the students before each game to make sure it was the right length.
questions.trap_type: The rope was the receiver of the action. Past passive: was/were + past participle.
questions.learning_tip: WAS/WERE + past participle = passive! The rope WAS MEASURED = someone measured it. The rope received the action. NEVER: 'was being measured' (P5 level).
questions.retry_hint: The word BY names the doer: THE STUDENTS. A ROPE cannot check its own length. Ask: which choice puts the receiver in the subject position and sets the action in past time? Two options are active, and one is present.

questions.stem: The games teacher told the students ________ their tops on the tiled corridor in case the surface was too slippery.
questions.trap_type: Negative reported speech: told + object + not to + base verb.
questions.learning_tip: TOLD someone NOT TO + base verb. The teacher told students NOT TO SPIN their tops on the tiles. Formula: told + person + not to + verb.
questions.retry_hint: The TILED CORRIDOR is TOO SLIPPERY, so this is a reported prohibition. Ask: after 'told + person', which pattern does the verb take - plain, -ing, -ed, or 'to' + verb? Then place the negative word correctly inside it.

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Prepositions of place and direction)

questions.context_check: Passage: 'We played five stones (1)________ the void deck of our block after school.' Signal: enclosed space (void deck) = IN. IN = inside an enclosed or defined space.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'at' or 'under'. THE SHADE is a space you stand inside, and 'at the shade' is never English.
questions.learning_tip: IN + an enclosed space or an area you are surrounded by: IN the shade, IN the hall, IN the classroom.
questions.retry_hint: THE SHADE is a patch you stand inside, wrapped around by it, not a point you touch. Ask: which box word suits a space that surrounds you? 'At the shade' is never English, so a point word cannot work.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Kai placed the gasing top (2)________ the smooth concrete surface and gave it a strong spin.' Signal: surface contact = ON. ON = touching the top of a surface.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'in' (enclosed space) instead of 'on' (surface contact).
questions.learning_tip: ON = on top of / touching a surface. The top is placed ON the concrete surface = it sits on top of it. ON is for surfaces.
questions.retry_hint: The key word is SURFACE: the top rests against the SMOOTH CONCRETE and touches it from above. Ask: which box word shows contact with a flat surface? A word for enclosed spaces would put the top underneath the concrete.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The children met (3)________ the corner of the field every Saturday morning to play chapteh.' Signal: a specific point or meeting place = AT. AT = at a specific point or location.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'in' (enclosed) instead of 'at' (specific point). AT is used for specific points, not enclosed spaces.
questions.learning_tip: AT = a specific point or location. We met AT the corner of the field = at that exact spot. AT is for specific places or points.
questions.retry_hint: A CORNER is a single exact point, not a room to stand inside. Ask: which box word marks a precise meeting point? The word for enclosed spaces is needed elsewhere, and you cannot meet 'under' a corner.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The kite flew (4)________ the tallest tree in the park before the wind changed direction.' Signal: movement above and across = OVER. OVER = above something, crossing from one side to the other.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'above' (not in word box) or 'through'. OVER = passing above and across.
questions.learning_tip: OVER = above something, moving from one side to the other. The kite flew OVER the tree = it passed above the tree. OVER shows crossing movement above.
questions.retry_hint: A KITE flies high above things, and it crossed THE TALLEST TREE without touching it. Ask: which box word means above and across the top of something? 'Through' would send the kite straight into the branches.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Priya hid the five stones bag (5)________ the bench so that nobody would take it during the break.' Signal: below and covered by = UNDER. UNDER = below and covered by something.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'behind' (at the back) instead of 'under' (below). The bag is below the bench, not at the back of it.
questions.learning_tip: UNDER = below something that is above you. The bag is UNDER the bench = below the seat of the bench. UNDER means something is directly above you.
questions.retry_hint: Priya HID the bag so that NOBODY WOULD TAKE IT - the safest spot is beneath the seat of the BENCH. Ask: which box word means below something? 'Behind' would put the bag at the back, still in plain sight.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The rubber band rope stretched (6)________ the narrow gap between the two pillars.' Signal: from one side to the other, passing inside = THROUGH. THROUGH = entering one side and exiting the other.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'over' (above) instead of 'through' (passing inside). The rope passes inside the gap, not over it.
questions.learning_tip: THROUGH = entering at one side and coming out the other. The rope stretched THROUGH the gap = it passed inside and came out the other side.
questions.retry_hint: The rope enters THE NARROW GAP at one side and comes out at the other, BETWEEN THE TWO PILLARS. Ask: which box word shows passage from one end of an opening to the other? 'Over' would carry the rope above the gap.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'He ran (7)________ the courtyard and grabbed the chapteh before it landed.' Signal: movement from outside to inside (entering) = INTO. INTO = movement entering an enclosed space.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'in' (static location) instead of 'into' (movement entering). INTO shows the direction of movement, not a static position.
questions.learning_tip: INTO = movement from outside to inside. He ran INTO the courtyard = he was outside, then moved inside. IN = where you are; INTO = the direction you move.
questions.retry_hint: HE RAN - he was outside, and then he arrived inside THE COURTYARD. Ask: which box word shows the DIRECTION of a movement rather than a still position? The plain word for enclosed spaces would mean he was already there.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The slowest player had to stand (8)________ the line and wait for the next round.' Signal: at the back of something = BEHIND. BEHIND = at the back of or further back than.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'under' (below) instead of 'behind' (at the back). The player is at the back of the line, not below it.
questions.learning_tip: BEHIND = at the back of something. Stand BEHIND the line = stand at the back, further away. BEHIND is about being at the rear or back of something.
questions.retry_hint: The SLOWEST PLAYER is sent to the back to WAIT FOR THE NEXT ROUND. Ask: which box word means at the rear of something? A line drawn on the ground has nothing beneath it, so 'under' is impossible.

C.passage: We played five stones (1)________ the shade of the void deck every day after school. Kai placed the gasing top (2)________ the smooth concrete surface and gave it a strong spin. The children met (3)________ the corner of the field every Saturday morning to play chapteh. The kite flew (4)________ the tallest tree in the park before the wind changed direction. Priya hid the five stones bag (5)________ the bench so nobody would take it during the break. The rubber band rope stretched (6)________ the narrow gap between the two pillars perfectly. He ran (7)________ the courtyard and grabbed the chapteh before it landed. The slowest player had to stand (8)________ the line and wait for the next round.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: Games like chapteh, gasing and five stones are part of Singapore's cultural (1)________ — people played them for generations and they connect us to our roots. These (2)________ games do not need expensive equipment or a large space, which makes them easy for anyone to enjoy. In a game of zero-point, a player must jump over a rope held by the (3)________ without touching it. Chapteh tests a player's (4)________ — the ability to move quickly and change direction without losing balance. After a round of five stones, players (5)________ the small cloth bags and prepare for the next throw.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'played for generations and connect us to our roots' = cultural legacy = heritage.
questions.learning_tip: HERITAGE = traditions and practices passed down through generations. These games are part of Singapore's cultural HERITAGE = they belong to our shared history.
questions.retry_hint: The clue comes after the dash: PLAYED THEM FOR GENERATIONS, and they CONNECT US TO OUR ROOTS. Ask: which box word names the customs handed down from our grandparents? A 'medal' is won, not inherited.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'have been played for generations' = old and long-established = traditional.
questions.learning_tip: TRADITIONAL = following practices that have been done for a long time. TRADITIONAL games are ones passed down from older generations.
questions.retry_hint: The blank describes GAMES that have come down through the GENERATIONS. Ask: which box word is an adjective meaning long-established and passed down? 'Clumsy' would describe a player, not a whole custom.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'jump over a rope held by the ___' = the other player in the game = opponent.
questions.learning_tip: An OPPONENT = the other player or team you are playing against. In zero-point, the OPPONENT holds the rope for you to jump over.
questions.retry_hint: The rope is HELD BY somebody, and it is not the jumper - a game needs two sides. Ask: which box word names the person playing against you? The blank follows 'the', so it must be a noun.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'move quickly and change direction without losing balance' = agility.
questions.learning_tip: AGILITY = the ability to move quickly and change direction smoothly. Chapteh tests your AGILITY — you must react fast and shift your body with control.
questions.retry_hint: The dash defines it exactly: THE ABILITY TO MOVE QUICKLY AND CHANGE DIRECTION WITHOUT LOSING BALANCE. Ask: which box word names that nimbleness? It follows 'a player's', so it must be a noun.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'pick up the cloth bags to prepare for the next throw' = retrieve.
questions.learning_tip: RETRIEVE = go and get something after it has been used or lost. Players RETRIEVE the five stones bags = they pick them up to use again.
questions.retry_hint: The round has ended, so the SMALL CLOTH BAGS are lying about and must be picked up before THE NEXT THROW. Ask: which box word is a verb meaning to fetch something back? 'Forfeit' would mean giving them away.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.trap_type: 'The players' is plural. Students write 'was' (singular).
questions.learning_tip: Plural subject → plural verb! The players WERE excited to compete. WAS is only for ONE thing. 'The players' = more than one → WERE.
questions.retry_hint: Count them: THE PLAYERS LINED UP AT THE STARTING ZONE are many, and each holds a top. Ask: does a plural subject take a singular past verb? The verb must agree with its subject, however far away that subject sits.

questions.trap_type: Students write 'there' (at that place) when the sentence needs 'their' (belonging to them).
questions.learning_tip: THEIR = belonging to them. The players held THEIR tops ready. THERE = at that place. Test: replace with 'belonging to them'. If YES → use THEIR.
questions.retry_hint: The TOPS belong to the players who GRIPPED them. Ask: is the underlined word pointing at a place over there, or showing ownership? Both spellings sound the same, so let the meaning of the sentence decide.

questions.error_type: Spelling — ie/ei confusion (achieve: I before E)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'acheive' putting E before I. The correct spelling is achIEve — I before E.
questions.learning_tip: Rule: I before E, except after C! achIEve = I before E ✅. Remember: 'achIEve' has IE in the middle — like 'PIE' — I before E always in this word!
questions.retry_hint: The letter in front of the two vowels is H, not C, so the ordinary rhyme applies. Ask: does 'ACHEIVE' put I before E, or E before I? Swap the pair, then compare with believe, relieve and grieve.

questions.trap_type: Students write 'careful' (adjective) after the action verb 'wrapped'. A verb needs an adverb.
questions.learning_tip: After an action verb (wrapped), use an ADVERB: wrapped CAREFULLY. Rule: verb + adverb (-ly). 'Careful' describes nouns; 'carefully' describes actions.
questions.retry_hint: WRAPPED tells you what the teacher did; the underlined word tells you HOW it was done. Ask: which word class modifies a verb - the adjective, or the adverb with its -ly ending? Adjectives belong to nouns, and no noun follows.

questions.trap_type: Students write a plain plural and leave out the apostrophe that shows ownership.
questions.learning_tip: The scores BELONG TO the winners -> WINNERS' scores (apostrophe after the -s for a plural). One winner: winner's.
questions.retry_hint: The FINAL SCORES belong to the WINNERS - more than one of them. Ask: for a plural owner that already ends in -s, does anything come after the apostrophe? Compare the singular form, where an s does follow it.

E.passage: Last Saturday, our class took part in the Traditional Games Carnival. The players was (1) lined up at the starting zone, each holding a top or a shuttlecock. They gripped there (2) tops tightly, waiting for the signal to begin. Every child wanted to acheive (3) the highest score and win the golden trophy. The teacher wrapped the gasing rope careful (4) around each top before handing it to the class. At the end of the day, the judges announced the winners (5) final scores and everyone cheered.

questions.sentence_a: You practise chapteh every day.
questions.sentence_b: You will improve your coordination and balance.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'If'.
questions.model_answer: If you practise chapteh every day, you will improve your coordination and balance.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'If you will practise' — adding 'will' in the 'if' clause.
questions.learning_tip: IF + simple present, simple future. IF you PRACTISE every day, you WILL IMPROVE. NEVER use 'will' after 'if' in the condition clause.
questions.retry_hint: IF opens the condition - the thing you must do first. Ask: which of the two facts is the condition, and which is the promised outcome? A condition clause keeps a present verb; 'will' belongs only in the other half.

questions.sentence_a: The gasing competition was held at the community centre.
questions.sentence_b: The gasing competition attracted players from five different schools.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using the relative pronoun 'which'.
questions.model_answer: The gasing competition, which attracted players from five different schools, was held at the community centre.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'The gasing competition which it attracted' — adding 'it' after 'which'.
questions.learning_tip: WHICH = relative pronoun for things. The competition, WHICH attracted players from five schools, was held at the centre. NEVER add 'it' after 'which'.
questions.retry_hint: THE GASING COMPETITION is named in both facts, so it should appear only once. Ask: which fact is the main statement, and which becomes the extra clause fenced off by two commas? The relative pronoun already stands for it.

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
It was the final round of the gasing competition, and nine-year-old Arif had one chance left.

All morning, he watched the older boys launch their tops with a single, practiced flick of the wrist. Their tops spun for minutes at a time, gliding slowly across the smooth concrete pad. Arif's best spin so far had lasted forty-three seconds.

His grandfather, who had taught him everything he knew about gasing, sat in the third row of the plastic chairs. He did not wave or call out. He simply watched.

Arif stepped to the line. He wound the rope around the top slowly, the way his grandfather had shown him — tight, even, patient.

He threw.

The top landed perfectly and spun without wobbling. Arif did not watch it. He watched his grandfather's face instead.

At sixty seconds, the crowd began to count. At seventy, some stood up. At eighty-three seconds, the judge raised the green flag.

Arif looked at his grandfather. The old man pressed his lips together and nodded once — the same nod he gave when something was done correctly.

That was enough.

Outside, the other competitors had already left. Arif stayed a little longer, watching the empty concrete pad where the tops had spun. He wanted to remember exactly how the rope felt in his hands.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 2 has the same meaning as 'moving smoothly without effort'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Spun' = rotated; 'practiced' = well-rehearsed; 'launched' = sent into motion. GLIDING = moving smoothly and effortlessly.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: GLIDING = moving smoothly, without effort or sound. The tops were GLIDING across the concrete = moving in a slow, effortless way.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 3, what does 'He' refer to in 'He simply watched'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 2 thinking 'He' = Arif. But the paragraph is describing Arif's grandfather — 'He' = the grandfather.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 3: 'His GRANDFATHER... sat in the third row. HE did not wave or call out. HE simply watched.' HE = the grandfather, not Arif.

mcq_questions.stem: Why did Arif watch his grandfather's face instead of his spinning top?

options.1: He was nervous and could not look at the top.
options.2: He could not see the top from where he was standing.
options.3: His grandfather's reaction meant more to him than the result on the judge's card.
options.4: He wanted to make sure his grandfather was safe.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking he was simply too nervous. But the whole passage builds to this moment — Arif cares deeply about his grandfather's approval.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Arif did not check the judge — he watched his GRANDFATHER'S FACE. This shows that his grandfather's reaction (approval, pride) meant MORE to him than the official result.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 2, is it True or False that Arif's best spin before the final lasted more than one minute? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The passage says 'Arif's best spin so far had lasted FORTY-THREE SECONDS' — which is less than one minute (sixty seconds).
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'True, the older boys' tops spun for minutes.' That is the older boys, not Arif.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 2: 'Arif's best spin had lasted FORTY-THREE SECONDS.' 43 seconds < 60 seconds (one minute). The answer is FALSE. Read carefully — the older boys spun longer, not Arif.

open_ended_questions.stem: How did Arif prepare the gasing top before throwing it?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: He wound the rope around the top slowly, tightly and evenly — exactly the way his grandfather had taught him.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'he got ready' — too vague. The passage gives specific details about how he wound the rope.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 4: 'He WOUND THE ROPE around the top SLOWLY — tight, even, patient.' Give these specific details, not a general answer.

open_ended_questions.stem: How did the crowd's reaction change as Arif's top kept spinning? Give TWO details from the passage.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) At sixty seconds, the crowd began to count — showing they were engaged and tracking the time. (ii) At seventy seconds, some stood up — showing their excitement was growing.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students describe only one stage of the reaction.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 7: At SIXTY seconds = crowd BEGAN TO COUNT. At SEVENTY seconds = some STOOD UP. These are two distinct reactions that show growing excitement.

open_ended_questions.stem: What did Arif's grandfather's nod mean to Arif?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: It meant that Arif did something correctly — it was his grandfather's sign of quiet approval and pride.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'the grandfather was happy' — too vague. The nod has a specific meaning explained in the passage.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Last paragraph: 'the same nod he gave when something was done CORRECTLY.' The nod = quiet signal of approval. That was enough for Arif.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on his actions in the passage, describe TWO character traits of Arif with evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) PATIENT: he wound the rope slowly and carefully — 'tight, even, patient' — not rushing despite the pressure of the final round. (ii) RESPECTFUL: instead of celebrating or checking the judge, he watched his grandfather's face — showing his grandfather's approval mattered most to him.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'brave and good at gasing' without precise traits or evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: TRAIT INFERENCE formula: TRAIT = evidence from text. PATIENT = wound rope 'SLOWLY, TIGHT, EVEN' despite final-round pressure. RESPECTFUL = watched GRANDFATHER'S FACE (not the judge). For G8, always name the TRAIT first, then give EVIDENCE from the passage.

questions.stem: The dragonfly hovered above the pond, its wings as ________ as paper, so delicate that sunlight shone right through them.
questions.trap_type: 'Heavy' and 'thick' are the opposite of delicate. 'Dark' doesn't fit because sunlight shines through them. THIN = having very little thickness, delicate and fine.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! The wings were AS THIN AS paper = comparing their delicate thinness to paper. THIN = very little thickness. A dragonfly's wings are among the thinnest structures in nature.
questions.retry_hint: The wings are compared to PAPER, and SUNLIGHT SHONE RIGHT THROUGH them. Ask: can light pass through something heavy, thick or dark? Match the adjective to the paper, not to the pond.

questions.stem: The scientist decided to ________ the rare beetle specimen carefully so it would not be damaged.
questions.trap_type: 'Destroy', 'ignore' and 'hide' are all harmful or unhelpful actions. LOOK AFTER = take care of something to keep it safe.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: LOOK AFTER = take care of something or someone. She decided to LOOK AFTER the beetle = keep it safe and in good condition. LOOK + AFTER work together — never split!
questions.retry_hint: The specimen is RARE and must NOT BE DAMAGED, so the scientist wants to keep it safe. Ask: which phrasal verb means to take care of something? 'Destroy', 'ignore' and 'hide' would all put the beetle at risk.

questions.stem: The butterfly ________ from a dull brown caterpillar into a creature with dazzling orange and black wings.
questions.trap_type: 'Disappeared' = vanished; 'shrank' = became smaller; 'escaped' = got away. TRANSFORMED = changed completely in form or appearance.
questions.learning_tip: TRANSFORMED = changed completely into something very different. The caterpillar TRANSFORMED into a butterfly = it became something entirely new and beautiful.
questions.retry_hint: It began as a DULL BROWN CATERPILLAR and ended with DAZZLING ORANGE AND BLACK WINGS - a complete change of body. Ask: which verb means to change completely into something new? 'Escaped' only tells you where it went.

questions.stem: The firefly's gentle light ________ in the darkness of the garden like a tiny dancing star.
questions.trap_type: 'Faded', 'disappeared' and 'shrank' all mean the light was going away or getting smaller. FLICKERED = shone with a rapidly changing, unsteady light.
questions.learning_tip: FLICKERED = shone with a rapidly changing, unsteady light. The firefly's light FLICKERED = it blinked on and off quickly, like a tiny flame.
questions.retry_hint: The light is GENTLE and compared to a TINY DANCING STAR - it keeps blinking, rather than dying away. Ask: which verb shows an unsteady, wavering light? 'Faded', 'disappeared' and 'shrank' all mean it is going away.

questions.stem: Ants are ________ insects — a single colony can contain millions of individuals all working together.
questions.trap_type: 'Solitary' = living alone; 'fragile' = easily broken; 'silent' = making no sound. SOCIAL insects live and work in large organised groups.
questions.learning_tip: SOCIAL insects = insects that live and work together in large organised groups. Ants are SOCIAL insects — they communicate, cooperate and build together as a community.
questions.retry_hint: A single COLONY holds MILLIONS OF INDIVIDUALS ALL WORKING TOGETHER. Ask: does that describe an insect that lives alone, or one that lives in an organised group? 'Solitary' says the exact opposite.

questions.stem: Nobody in the science class ________ that the stick insect on the leaf is actually a living creature.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'notice' thinking 'nobody in the science class' = many people. NOBODY = singular → verb must have -S in present tense.
questions.learning_tip: NOBODY = Singular! ALWAYS use verb+S in present tense. Nobody NOTICES = add -S. 'Nobody notice' or 'Nobody are noticing' are WRONG.
questions.retry_hint: Cover the words IN THE SCIENCE CLASS and look at what is left: NOBODY. That one word is the subject, and it counts as a single person. Ask: which present-tense ending does a singular subject demand?

questions.stem: Our school has ________ an insect garden in the science corner since last year.
questions.trap_type: HAS + past participle = present perfect. 'Create' is regular: create → created.
questions.learning_tip: HAS + past participle = present perfect. Our school HAS CREATED an insect garden = it was created at some point and is still there now. CREATE → CREATED (regular).
questions.retry_hint: SINCE LAST YEAR tells you the garden was made in the past and is still there, and HAS is already in place. Ask: which of the four forms can follow 'has' to build a present perfect?

questions.stem: The grasshopper can jump ________ than fifty times its own body length in a single leap.
questions.trap_type: Comparative needed (comparing to a standard distance). 'Far' → comparative = FARTHER (or further). 'Very' cannot be used with comparatives.
questions.learning_tip: FARTHER = comparative of 'far'. The grasshopper jumps FARTHER THAN fifty times its length = it goes more distance than that. FARTHER = more distance. 'Very farther' is WRONG.
questions.retry_hint: THAN is sitting in the sentence, so two distances are being measured against each other. Ask: does a comparison take the plain adjective, the -est form, or the -er form? 'Very' can never sit in front of a comparative.

questions.stem: The students ________ the monarch butterfly when it suddenly flew out of the net.
questions.trap_type: 'It suddenly flew out of the net' = sudden interrupting event. Students were already observing = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: The butterfly FLEW OUT = sudden past event. Students were already observing = WERE OBSERVING (past continuous). Past continuous = was/were + verb-ing.
questions.retry_hint: The butterfly SUDDENLY FLEW OUT OF THE NET - a short, sharp event cutting across a longer one. Ask: which choice shows the students already in the middle of watching it? A plain past verb reports only a finished action.

questions.stem: There is ________ information about beetles in this book — it covers almost every species in South-East Asia.
