questions.trap_type: 'Information' is uncountable → use 'a lot of' or 'much'. 'A few', 'many' and 'several' are for countable nouns.
questions.learning_tip: A LOT OF = large amount for BOTH countable and uncountable nouns. 'Information' is uncountable → A LOT OF information. 'Many information' or 'a few information' are WRONG.
questions.retry_hint: INFORMATION is a word you cannot count - never 'one information, two informations'. Ask: which quantity word goes with an uncountable noun? 'A few', 'many' and 'several' all need things you can count one by one.

questions.stem: The firefly display in the mangrove forest was the most beautiful thing you have ever seen, ________ it?
questions.trap_type: The tag copies the verb of the MAIN clause ('the display WAS the most beautiful thing'), not the verb inside 'you have ever seen'. 'Haven't it?' is not English.
questions.learning_tip: A question tag mirrors the main clause. Main verb WAS + positive statement -> negative tag WASN'T IT? Ignore the verbs inside the relative clause.
questions.retry_hint: Find the verb of the main clause: the display WAS the most beautiful thing. The tag copies THAT verb, not the 'have' hidden inside 'you have ever seen'. Ask: after a positive statement, is the tag positive or negative?

questions.stem: The rare Atlas moth specimen ________ to the national museum after it was discovered in the jungle last week.
questions.trap_type: The moth specimen was the receiver of the action. Past passive = was donated.
questions.learning_tip: WAS/WERE + past participle = passive! The specimen WAS DONATED = someone donated it; the specimen received the action. NEVER use 'was being donated' (P5 level).
questions.retry_hint: The specimen did not act - somebody FOUND it IN THE JUNGLE and moved it TO THE NATIONAL MUSEUM. Ask: which choice makes the subject the receiver of the action, and sets it in the past?

questions.stem: The nature guide told the children ________ the praying mantis or it might strike at their fingers.
questions.trap_type: Negative reported speech: told + object + not to + base verb.
questions.learning_tip: TOLD someone NOT TO + base verb. The guide told children NOT TO TOUCH the mantis. Formula: told + person + not to + verb.
questions.retry_hint: This is a reported command with a warning: OR IT MIGHT STRIKE AT THEIR FINGERS. Ask: after 'told + person', which form follows - the plain verb, the -ing form, or 'to' + verb? And where does the negative word sit?

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Personal pronouns — subject and object)

questions.context_check: Passage: '(1)________ spotted a bright green praying mantis on the wall of the science room.' Signal: blank = SUBJECT of 'spotted'. First person singular subject = I.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'Me' (object form). I is the SUBJECT pronoun — it does the action.
questions.learning_tip: I = subject pronoun — it DOES the action. I spotted the mantis. ME = object — it receives the action ('The mantis surprised ME'). SUBJECT = I; OBJECT = ME.
questions.retry_hint: The blank opens the sentence and DOES the spotting of the MANTIS on the wall. Ask: does a subject pronoun or an object pronoun belong here? The writer is the one telling the story, so pick the first-person subject form.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'My teacher asked (2)________ to draw the mantis in my science journal.' Signal: blank = OBJECT of 'asked'. The teacher asked → me (first person singular object). 'My teacher asked me' = ME is the receiver of asking.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'I' (subject) instead of 'me' (object after a verb).
questions.learning_tip: After a verb (asked), use OBJECT pronoun. My teacher asked ME = ME is what the verb 'asked' points to. 'My teacher asked I' is WRONG. After verbs: use ME, HIM, HER, THEM.
questions.retry_hint: The verb ASKED comes first, and the blank RECEIVES the asking - the teacher does the action, not the writer. Ask: after a verb, do we use the subject form or the object form of the first-person pronoun?

questions.context_check: Passage: 'My classmate Dion is the insect expert in our class — (3)________ knows the name of almost every bug.' Signal: blank = SUBJECT of 'knows'. Dion = male singular subject = HE.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'him' (object form) instead of 'he' (subject).
questions.learning_tip: HE = subject pronoun for a male. HE knows the names = HE does the action. 'Him knows' is WRONG. HE = subject; HIM = object (e.g., 'I told HIM').
questions.retry_hint: DION is a boy, and the blank DOES the knowing - 'knows the name of every bug'. Ask: which pronoun can stand as the subject of a sentence, and which one can only follow a verb? Subject form, single male.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'I always ask (4)________ for help when I cannot identify an insect.' Signal: blank = OBJECT of 'ask'. I ask → him (male singular object after a verb).
questions.trap_type: Students write 'he' (subject) instead of 'him' (object after a verb).
questions.learning_tip: After a verb (ask), use OBJECT pronoun. I always ask HIM for help = HIM is the receiver of asking. 'I ask he' is WRONG. After verbs: HIM, not HE.
questions.retry_hint: 'ASK' is the verb and the blank comes straight after it, so the blank receives the asking. Ask: which male pronoun follows a verb - the one that opens a sentence, or the object form? A subject pronoun never sits after a verb.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Our science teacher loves insects — (5)________ once kept a pet stick insect for a whole year.' Signal: blank = SUBJECT of 'kept'. Science teacher = female singular subject = SHE.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'her' (object form) instead of 'she' (subject).
questions.learning_tip: SHE = subject pronoun for a female. SHE kept a pet stick insect = SHE does the action. 'Her kept' is WRONG. SHE = subject; HER = object (e.g., 'I saw HER').
questions.retry_hint: The science teacher is female, and the blank DOES the keeping - 'ONCE KEPT a pet stick insect'. Ask: does the subject slot take the acting form or the receiving form? Pick the female form that can open a sentence.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The stick insect surprised (6)________ by shedding its skin overnight without any warning.' Signal: blank = OBJECT of 'surprised'. The insect surprised → her (female singular object after a verb).
questions.trap_type: Students write 'she' (subject) instead of 'her' (object after a verb).
questions.learning_tip: After a verb (surprised), use OBJECT pronoun. The insect surprised HER = HER is the receiver of 'surprised'. 'Surprised she' is WRONG. After verbs: HER, not SHE.
questions.retry_hint: The verb SURPRISED sits right in front of the blank, and the one who got the surprise is the female teacher. Ask: after a verb, do we use the form that acts, or the form that receives? Female plus object slot.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Ants are fascinating creatures — (7)________ can carry fifty times their own body weight.' Signal: blank = SUBJECT of 'can carry'. Ants = plural subject = THEY.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'them' (object form) instead of 'they' (subject).
questions.learning_tip: THEY = subject pronoun for a group. THEY can carry fifty times their weight = THEY do the action. 'Them can carry' is WRONG. THEY = subject; THEM = object.
questions.retry_hint: ANTS is plural, and the blank DOES the carrying - 'can carry fifty times their weight'. Ask: which plural pronoun is able to be the subject of a sentence? The other plural form can only follow a verb.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Scientists have studied (8)________ for thousands of years and still have new discoveries to make.' Signal: blank = OBJECT of 'studied'. Scientists studied → them (ants, plural object after a verb).
questions.trap_type: Students write 'they' (subject) instead of 'them' (object after a verb).
questions.learning_tip: After a verb (studied), use OBJECT pronoun. Scientists studied THEM = THEM is the receiver of 'studied'. 'Studied they' is WRONG. After verbs: THEM, not THEY.
questions.retry_hint: SCIENTISTS do the studying, and the ants RECEIVE it. Ask: after the verb STUDIED, does the plural subject form or the plural object form belong here? A subject pronoun can never sit after a verb.

C.passage: (1)________ spotted a bright green praying mantis on the wall. My teacher asked (2)________ to draw it. My classmate Dion is the insect expert — (3)________ knows the name of every bug. I always ask (4)________ for help when I cannot identify an insect. Our science teacher loves insects — (5)________ once kept a pet stick insect on her desk. The stick insect surprised (6)________ by shedding its skin overnight. Ants are fascinating creatures — (7)________ can carry fifty times their weight. Scientists have studied (8)________ for thousands of years.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: Insects have developed amazing ways to survive. Many use (1)________ to blend in with surroundings and hide from enemies. The stick insect looks exactly like a twig. A (2)________ is an animal that hunts and eats other animals. Insects use their (3)________ — the long feelers on their heads — to sense vibrations and communicate. Some insects begin life as (4)________, worm-like young that hatch from eggs. A healthy garden provides the ideal (5)________ for many insect species.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'blending in with surroundings to hide' = camouflage.
questions.learning_tip: CAMOUFLAGE = the ability to blend in with surroundings so as not to be seen. The stick insect uses CAMOUFLAGE = it looks like a twig so predators cannot spot it.
questions.retry_hint: The next sentence proves it: the STICK INSECT LOOKS EXACTLY LIKE A TWIG. Ask: which box word names the trick of blending into the background? 'Antennae' are feelers and 'larvae' are young - neither is a way of hiding.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'an animal that hunts and eats other animals' = predator.
questions.learning_tip: A PREDATOR = an animal that hunts and eats other animals. Birds and lizards are PREDATORS of insects = they catch and eat them.
questions.retry_hint: The sentence defines itself: AN ANIMAL THAT HUNTS AND EATS OTHER ANIMALS. Ask: which box word names the hunter rather than the hunted? A 'habitat' is a place, not a creature.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'long feelers on their heads — to sense vibrations, smell food and communicate' = antennae.
questions.learning_tip: ANTENNAE = the long, thin feelers on an insect's head used to sense the world. Insects use their ANTENNAE to detect smells, sounds and vibrations.
questions.retry_hint: The dashes explain it: THE LONG FEELERS ON THEIR HEADS, used to SENSE VIBRATIONS. Ask: which box word names those feelers? An insect has two of them, so the word must be plural.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'worm-like young that hatch from eggs before growing into their adult form' = larvae.
questions.learning_tip: LARVAE = the worm-like young of insects that hatch from eggs. Caterpillars are the LARVAE of butterflies. LARVA (singular) → LARVAE (plural).
questions.retry_hint: The clue is WORM-LIKE YOUNG THAT HATCH FROM EGGS - the stage that comes before the adult insect. Ask: which box word names the young of insects? A caterpillar is exactly this stage of a butterfly.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'ideal ___ for many insect species to feed, breed and shelter' = natural home = habitat.
questions.learning_tip: A HABITAT = the natural environment where a living thing normally lives. A healthy garden is the ideal HABITAT for insects to feed, breed and shelter.
questions.retry_hint: A HEALTHY GARDEN is a place, and the blank comes after 'the ideal'. Ask: which box word names the natural home where a creature feeds, breeds and shelters? 'Camouflage' is a trick, not a place.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.trap_type: 'The butterflies' is plural. Students write 'was' (singular).
questions.learning_tip: Plural subject → plural verb! The butterflies WERE resting on the flower. WAS is only for ONE thing (singular). BUTTERFLIES = more than one → WERE.
questions.retry_hint: Find the subject of the underlined verb: THE BUTTERFLIES - more than one. Ask: does a plural subject take the singular past form of 'to be', or the plural one? Never choose the verb by the word nearest to it.

questions.error_type: Homophone confusion — its (possessive) vs it's (it is)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'its' (possessive) when the meaning is 'it is'.
questions.learning_tip: IT'S = it is (contraction). ITS = belonging to it. 'ITS amazing how far ants can carry things' → can you say 'it is amazing'? YES → use IT'S. IT'S = IT IS.
questions.retry_hint: The underlined word as written means 'belonging to it', but the sentence is saying HARD TO BELIEVE. Ask: can you stretch it into the two words 'it is' and still make sense? If yes, an apostrophe is missing.

questions.error_type: Spelling — ie/ei confusion (chief: I before E)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'cheif' putting E before I. 'Chief' follows I-before-E: chIEf.
questions.learning_tip: Rule: I before E, except after C! chIEf = I before E ✅. Remember: the 'chIEf' has a PIE hidden inside him — chIEf. I before E!
questions.retry_hint: The underlined word sits in front of WORKER, and its two vowels are the wrong way round. Ask: with no C in front, does the I lead or does the E lead? Compare: field, brief, believe.

questions.trap_type: Students write 'slow' (adjective) after the action verb 'moved'. A verb needs an adverb.
questions.learning_tip: After an action verb (moved), use an ADVERB: moved SLOWLY. Rule: verb + adverb (-ly). 'Slow' describes nouns; 'slowly' describes HOW something moves.
questions.retry_hint: MOVED is an action verb, and the underlined word tells you HOW the caterpillar moved ALONG THE BRANCH. Ask: after a verb, do we use an adjective or an adverb? Manner words nearly always take the -ly ending.

questions.trap_type: Students write a plain plural and leave out the apostrophe that shows ownership.
questions.learning_tip: The notes BELONG TO the students -> STUDENTS' notes (apostrophe after the -s for a plural that already ends in -s). Singular: student's.
questions.retry_hint: The NOTES AND PHOTOGRAPHS belong to the whole class - the owners are many, not one. Ask: which mark shows ownership, and does it come before or after the -s when the plural already ends in -s?

E.passage: Our class went on a nature walk to study insects in the school garden. The butterflies was (1) resting on the flowers when we arrived, their wings open in the warm sunlight. Our teacher said that its (2) hard to believe that such delicate creatures can migrate across entire continents. The teacher pointed to a trail of ants and told us that the cheif (3) worker always leads the group back to the nest. The green caterpillar moved slow (4) along the branch, searching for fresh leaves to eat. At the end of the walk, the students (5) notes and photographs were collected and used to create a class insect guide.

questions.sentence_a: You remove fallen leaves and dead branches from your garden.
questions.sentence_b: You reduce the number of hiding places for harmful insects.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'As long as'.
questions.model_answer: As long as you remove fallen leaves and dead branches from your garden, you reduce the number of hiding places for harmful insects.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'As long as you will remove' — adding 'will' in the 'as long as' clause.
questions.learning_tip: AS LONG AS + simple present, simple present/future. AS LONG AS you REMOVE fallen leaves, you REDUCE hiding places. No 'will' after 'as long as'.
questions.retry_hint: 'AS LONG AS' sets the condition, so it goes in front of the sentence about REMOVING FALLEN LEAVES. Ask: after a condition word, do we use a present verb or 'will'? And where must the comma go?

questions.sentence_a: The firefly produces light using a chemical reaction in its body.
questions.sentence_b: The firefly uses light to attract a mate.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'Since'.
questions.model_answer: Since the firefly produces light using a chemical reaction in its body, it uses this light to attract a mate.
questions.trap_type: Students reverse the logic: 'The firefly uses light to attract a mate since it produces light using a chemical reaction' — acceptable but less natural as a causal structure.
questions.learning_tip: SINCE = because of a background reason. SINCE the firefly PRODUCES light using chemistry, IT USES this light to attract a mate. The background cause comes after 'since'.
questions.retry_hint: 'SINCE' introduces the background reason, so start with the sentence about the CHEMICAL REACTION. Ask: which fact explains the other? In the second half, a pronoun replaces the repeated FIREFLY.

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
Most people know that bees make honey. But the engineering inside a beehive is just as remarkable as the honey itself.

Bees build their hives from wax, which they produce inside their own bodies. A single worker bee produces only about one gram of wax in its entire lifetime. Yet a large hive may contain over one hundred thousand individual wax cells, all built to exactly the same six-sided shape.

The six-sided shape, called a hexagon, is not chosen by accident. It is the most efficient shape that exists: it uses the least amount of wax to create the most amount of storage space. Engineers and architects have studied the hexagon for centuries because of this property.

Inside each cell, bees store honey, pollen or eggs. The temperature inside the hive is kept at exactly thirty-five degrees Celsius at all times — warm enough for eggs to develop, cool enough to preserve the honey.

When a hive becomes too crowded, the queen bee leaves with half the colony to build a new home. The remaining bees raise a new queen. In this way, the colony survives and grows, generation after generation.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 3 has the same meaning as 'using the smallest amount of resources to get the best result'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Hexagon' is a shape; 'property' = a characteristic; 'chosen' = selected. EFFICIENT = using the least resources to produce the best result.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: EFFICIENT = using the least amount of resources to produce the best result. The hexagon is the most EFFICIENT shape = it uses the least wax but stores the most.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 4, what does 'this' refer to in 'The temperature inside the hive is kept at exactly thirty-five degrees Celsius at all times'?

options.3: A specific constant temperature maintained inside the hive
options.4: The number of bees in the colony

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 2 thinking 'this' refers to the cells. But the paragraph shifts to temperature — 'this' = the specific temperature of 35°C.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 4: 'The temperature inside the hive is kept at exactly THIRTY-FIVE DEGREES CELSIUS at all times.' THIS = this specific maintained temperature.

mcq_questions.stem: Why does the writer mention that 'engineers and architects have studied the hexagon for centuries'?

options.1: To show that humans are smarter than bees.
options.2: To suggest that bees learned to build from human engineers.
options.3: To show that bees discovered a mathematically perfect shape long before humans studied it.
options.4: To explain why beehives are always round.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking it is about human superiority. The writer's purpose is the opposite — to show that bees naturally discovered what humans took centuries to study.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 3: engineers studied the hexagon BECAUSE of its efficiency — the bees were already using it. This shows bees discovered a perfect shape BEFORE humans understood it scientifically.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 2, is it True or False that a single bee produces enough wax to build a complete hive on its own? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The passage says a single worker bee produces only about ONE GRAM OF WAX in its entire lifetime — far too little to build a whole hive.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'True, bees make their own wax.' They do make their own wax, but each bee only makes one gram — far too little to build an entire hive alone.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 2: 'a single worker bee produces only about ONE GRAM of wax in its ENTIRE LIFETIME.' One gram is a tiny amount — one bee alone could never build a hive. FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: Name THREE things that bees store inside the cells of the hive.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: Bees store honey, pollen and eggs inside the cells of the hive.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students name only one or two items.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 4: 'Inside each cell, bees store HONEY, POLLEN or EGGS.' All three are listed clearly in the passage. Name all three for full marks.

open_ended_questions.stem: Why is the hexagon shape so useful for building a beehive? Give TWO reasons from the passage.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) It uses the least amount of wax — meaning bees do not waste resources. (ii) It creates the most amount of storage space — so the bees can store the maximum amount of honey, pollen and eggs.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'it is strong and neat' — these may be true but are not stated in the passage.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 3: (1) uses the LEAST AMOUNT OF WAX; (2) creates the MOST AMOUNT OF STORAGE SPACE. Both are stated directly. Use the passage's own words.

open_ended_questions.stem: What happens when a beehive becomes too crowded?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: The queen bee leaves with half the colony to build a new home, while the remaining bees raise a new queen.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'the bees move away' — too vague. The passage gives specific details about what happens.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 5: 'The QUEEN BEE leaves with HALF the colony to build a new home. The remaining bees RAISE A NEW QUEEN.' Both actions are part of the answer.

open_ended_questions.stem: This passage is an informational text. Describe TWO techniques the writer uses to make the information interesting and clear.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) SURPRISING FACTS: the writer begins with what people already know ('bees make honey'), then immediately reveals something unexpected — that the engineering of the hive is equally remarkable. (ii) SPECIFIC NUMBERS: the writer uses exact figures (one gram of wax, one hundred thousand cells, thirty-five degrees) to make the facts feel real and precise.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students summarise the content instead of analysing the writer's techniques.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: TECHNIQUES of an informational text: (1) SURPRISING CONTRAST = writer says 'you know bees make honey — but the ENGINEERING is just as remarkable' = hooks the reader with an unexpected comparison. (2) SPECIFIC NUMBERS = 'one gram of wax', '100,000 cells', '35 degrees' = exact figures make information feel credible and precise. Analyse HOW the text is written, not WHAT it says.

questions.stem: Early in the morning, the farm was as ________ as a library — not a single animal had woken up yet.
questions.trap_type: 'Loud', 'busy' and 'dark' all suggest activity or noise. QUIET = making no or very little sound.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! The farm was AS QUIET AS a library = comparing the farm's silence to a library's. QUIET = making no sound. Similes always use 'as ... as'.
questions.retry_hint: The farm is compared to a LIBRARY, and NOT A SINGLE ANIMAL HAD WOKEN UP. Ask: does a library feel loud, busy or dark, or does it feel like silence itself? Match the adjective to the library.

questions.stem: Before the storm arrived, the farmer told his children to ________ for the market immediately.
questions.trap_type: 'Return' = come back; 'wait' = stay; 'sleep' = rest. SET OFF = begin a journey.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: SET OFF = start a journey or begin moving toward a destination. The farmer told them to SET OFF immediately = to start going right away. SET + OFF work together.
questions.retry_hint: The STORM is coming, and the children must leave for the MARKET IMMEDIATELY. Ask: which phrasal verb means to begin a journey? 'Return' means to come back, and 'wait' would keep them exactly where they are.

questions.stem: The farmer ________ the soil carefully before planting the seeds to make sure it was loose and rich.
questions.trap_type: 'Watered' = poured water; 'ignored' = paid no attention; 'painted' = applied colour. TILLED = turned over and prepared the soil for planting.
questions.learning_tip: TILLED = turned over and prepared the soil for planting. Farmers TILL the soil = they loosen it and enrich it before seeds are planted.
questions.retry_hint: The soil must end up LOOSE AND RICH, and the work is done BEFORE PLANTING THE SEEDS. Ask: which verb means to turn the earth over and prepare it? 'Watered' only adds water; 'painted' belongs to walls.

questions.stem: The goats were ________ in the meadow, eating grass and wandering wherever they pleased.
questions.trap_type: 'Sleeping' = resting; 'hiding' = concealing themselves; 'racing' = running fast competitively. GRAZING = eating grass or plants slowly while moving around.
questions.learning_tip: GRAZING = eating grass slowly while moving around a field. Goats and cows GRAZE in meadows = they wander and eat the grass as they go.
questions.retry_hint: The goats are EATING GRASS and WANDERING WHEREVER THEY PLEASED in the MEADOW. Ask: which verb describes an animal feeding slowly on grass as it moves about? 'Sleeping' and 'hiding' involve no eating at all.

questions.stem: The old farmer's vegetable garden was ________ — every patch of soil was used to grow something useful.
questions.trap_type: 'Empty' = nothing there; 'damp' = slightly wet; 'ordinary' = unremarkable. PRODUCTIVE = producing a large amount of useful output.
questions.learning_tip: PRODUCTIVE = producing a large useful output. A PRODUCTIVE garden = one where every patch grows food. Farmers want their land to be PRODUCTIVE = to yield as much as possible.
questions.retry_hint: The clue follows the dash: EVERY PATCH OF SOIL WAS USED TO GROW SOMETHING USEFUL. Ask: which adjective describes land that yields a great deal? 'Empty' says the opposite; 'damp' only talks about water.

questions.stem: Everyone on the farm ________ a different job to do before the sun rises each morning.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'have' thinking 'everyone on the farm' = many people. EVERYONE = singular → verb must be HAS in present tense.
questions.learning_tip: EVERYONE = Singular! Use HAS, not HAVE. Everyone HAS a job = singular. 'Everyone have a job' is WRONG. EVERYONE / NOBODY / SOMEONE = always singular → IS / HAS / verb+S.
questions.retry_hint: Cover ON THE FARM and read what is left: EVERYONE. Ask: is that one person, or many? Words like everyone, nobody and someone take a singular verb - choose the form you would use after 'he' or 'she'.

questions.stem: The farmer has ________ vegetables at the weekend market for over thirty years.
questions.trap_type: HAS + past participle = present perfect. 'Sell' is irregular: sell → sold.
questions.learning_tip: HAS + past participle = present perfect. The farmer HAS SOLD vegetables for thirty years = started then, still selling now. SELL → SOLD (irregular).
questions.retry_hint: FOR OVER THIRTY YEARS means the selling began long ago and still goes on, and HAS is already there. Ask: which form must follow 'has'? This verb is irregular, so an -ed ending will not do.

questions.stem: The harvest this year is much ________ than last year because of the long dry spell.
questions.trap_type: Comparing two harvests (this year vs last year) = comparative. 'Small' → SMALLER (short adjective adds -er).
questions.learning_tip: Short adjective + -ER = comparative. Small → SMALLER. The harvest is SMALLER THAN last year = comparing two harvests. 'Smallish' is informal and not standard.
questions.retry_hint: THAN LAST YEAR shows exactly two harvests being measured against each other. Ask: does a short adjective take -er, or 'the most'? A superlative is only for three or more, and 'smallish' is not exam English.

questions.stem: The children ________ the pigs when their father called them in for breakfast.
questions.trap_type: 'Their father called them in' = sudden interrupting event. The children were already feeding the pigs = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: Their father CALLED THEM = sudden past event. Children were already feeding the pigs = WERE FEEDING (past continuous). Past continuous = was/were + verb-ing.
questions.retry_hint: THEIR FATHER CALLED THEM IN - a sudden event breaking into something already happening. Ask: which choice shows the children in the middle of their chore at that past moment? A plain past verb shows a finished job.

questions.stem: There were ________ eggs in the basket — not enough to sell at the market.
questions.trap_type: 'Eggs' is countable → use FEW or A FEW. 'Little' and 'much' are for uncountable nouns. FEW = not many (negative implication).
questions.learning_tip: FEW = not many (countable noun, negative implication). EGGS = countable → FEW eggs. LITTLE is for uncountable nouns like 'milk'. FEW = not enough of something countable.
questions.retry_hint: Read the dash: NOT ENOUGH TO SELL AT THE MARKET, so the number is small. EGGS can be counted one by one. Ask: which quantity word goes with a countable plural and carries that 'not enough' feeling?

questions.stem: The cockerel crows every morning without fail, ________ it?
questions.trap_type: Positive simple present ('crows') → negative question tag. 'Crows' (singular present) → doesn't it.
questions.learning_tip: Positive simple present (third person singular) → negative tag. The cockerel CROWS every morning, DOESN'T it? DOES → DOESN'T. Positive → negative tag.
questions.retry_hint: The statement is positive, and its verb is CROWS - a plain present verb with no 'is' or 'are' in it. Ask: which helping verb stands in for it in the tag, and does a positive statement take a positive or a negative tag?

questions.stem: The freshly picked vegetables ________ to the market in a covered truck every Saturday at dawn.
questions.trap_type: The vegetables were the receivers of the action. Past passive: was/were + past participle.
questions.learning_tip: WAS/WERE + past participle = passive! The vegetables WERE DELIVERED = someone delivered them; vegetables received the action. WERE for plural subject.
questions.retry_hint: The VEGETABLES did nothing - somebody carried them TO THE MARKET IN A COVERED TRUCK. Ask: which choice makes the subject the receiver of the action? And is that subject singular or plural?

questions.stem: The farmer told his children ________ the greenhouse door open or the seedlings would dry out.
questions.trap_type: Negative reported speech: told + object + not to + base verb.
questions.learning_tip: TOLD someone NOT TO + base verb. The farmer told his children NOT TO LEAVE the door open. Formula: told + person + not to + verb.
questions.retry_hint: A reported command with a warning attached: OR THE SEEDLINGS WOULD DRY OUT. Ask: after 'told + person', is it the plain verb, the -ing form, or 'to' + verb? And does the negative word come before that little word, or after it?

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Time and condition conjunctions)

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The rooster crows (1)________ the sun begins to rise over the mountains.' Signal: at the same time as / at the moment that = WHEN. WHEN = at the moment something happens.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'while'. 'While he was seven years old' is not English: a stated age is a point in the past, not a stretch of activity.
questions.learning_tip: WHEN + a past age or a past occasion: WHEN he was seven years old. Use WHEN to say at what time in the past something happened.
questions.retry_hint: The clause names an age: HE WAS SEVEN YEARS OLD. Ask: which box word introduces a point or a period in the past? 'While' cannot take an age - 'while he was seven years old' is not English.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Father mends the fence (2)________ Mother tends to the vegetable patch nearby.' Signal: two actions happening at the same time, both ongoing = WHILE. WHILE = during the same period as.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'when'. Two people are busy with two different tasks over the same stretch of time, not at one single moment.
questions.learning_tip: WHILE = during the same period as another ongoing action. Father mends the fence WHILE Mother tends the patch = both jobs run side by side.
questions.retry_hint: Two people, two jobs, one stretch of time: FATHER MENDS the fence and MOTHER TENDS the vegetable patch side by side. Ask: which box word links two actions that run on together? A single-moment word will not do.

questions.context_check: Passage: '(3)________ the weather stays dry this week, we will harvest the sweet potatoes on Friday.' Signal: conditional — the harvest depends on dry weather = IF. IF = standard conditional.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'when'. WHEN treats dry weather as certain, but nobody can be sure of the weather - and the main clause uses 'will'.
questions.learning_tip: IF = an uncertain condition. IF + simple present, then simple future: IF the weather stays dry, we WILL harvest.
questions.retry_hint: Nobody can be sure of the weather, and the main clause says WE WILL HARVEST. Ask: which box word introduces something uncertain - a condition that may or may not come true? A time word would treat dry weather as certain.

questions.context_check: Passage: '(4)________ the milk is ready, Grandma pours it into glass bottles for the morning delivery.' Signal: immediately when something happens = AS SOON AS. AS SOON AS = immediately when.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'when'. The clue 'without wasting a single minute' shows there is no gap at all between the milk being ready and the pouring.
questions.learning_tip: AS SOON AS = the very moment something happens, with no delay. Use it when one action follows another instantly.
questions.retry_hint: The clue is WITHOUT WASTING A SINGLE MINUTE - there is no gap at all between the milk being ready and the pouring. Ask: which box phrase means 'at the very moment that'? A plain time word would still allow a wait.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The crops must be watered daily (5)________ the rainy season begins.' Signal: continuing up to a point = UNTIL. UNTIL = continuing up to that moment in time.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'before'. 'Stay under the net before they are strong enough' does not work: the seedlings STAY there right up to the moment they are ready.
questions.learning_tip: UNTIL = continuing all the way up to a point in time. STAY / WAIT / KEEP + UNTIL = go on doing it, then stop at that point.
questions.retry_hint: The seedlings STAY UNDER THE SHADE NET and only leave it once they are STRONG ENOUGH. Ask: which box word means 'right up to that point in time'? 'Before' would end their shelter far too early.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The children feed the chickens (6)________ they leave for school each morning.' Signal: the feeding happens earlier in time than leaving for school = BEFORE.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'after'. The hens are already pecking by the time the bus arrives, so the feeding must come first.
questions.learning_tip: BEFORE = earlier than the other event. Put BEFORE in front of the action that happens LATER, and the earlier action stands in the main clause.
questions.retry_hint: THE HENS ARE ALREADY PECKING HAPPILY BY THE TIME THE SCHOOL BUS ARRIVES, so the feeding must come first. Ask: which box word puts the chicken-feeding EARLIER than the leaving? Its opposite is needed in blank 7.

questions.context_check: Passage: '(7)________ the harvest is complete, the whole family gathers to share a meal together.' Signal: following the completion of the harvest = AFTER. AFTER = later in time, following an event.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'before'. The family can only celebrate once the crops are in, so the meal comes second.
questions.learning_tip: AFTER = later than the other event. AFTER the harvest is complete, the meal follows. AFTER marks the earlier event in its own clause.
questions.retry_hint: The family can only celebrate once the crops are in: THE WHOLE FAMILY GATHERS TO SHARE A BIG MEAL. Ask: which box word puts the meal LATER than the harvest? It is the opposite of the word blank 6 needs.

questions.context_check: Passage: '(8)________ the sun sets over the farm, the animals find their way back to the shelter on their own.' Signal: happening at the same time as / at the same rate as = AS. AS = happening simultaneously, or in proportion.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'if'. IF reverses the meaning: it is the absence of a storm that lets the animals come home by themselves.
questions.learning_tip: UNLESS = if not / except when. UNLESS a storm frightens them = they come back on their own every evening as long as no storm comes.
questions.retry_hint: Read the ending: the animals come home EACH EVENING WITHOUT ANY HELP. A sudden STORM is the one thing that would stop them. Ask: which box word means 'except when'? The plain condition word would flip the meaning.

C.passage: Life on a farm follows the rhythm of the sun. Grandpa still remembers milking the cows by hand (1)________ he was seven years old. Father mends the broken fence (2)________ Mother tends the vegetable patch nearby, each of them busy with their own task. (3)________ the weather stays dry this week, we will harvest the sweet potatoes on Friday afternoon. (4)________ the milk is ready, Grandma pours it into glass bottles without wasting a single minute. The tomato seedlings stay under the shade net (5)________ they are strong enough to face the afternoon sun. The children feed the chickens (6)________ they leave for school, so the hens are already pecking happily by the time the school bus arrives. (7)________ the harvest is complete, the whole family gathers to share a big meal together. (8)________ a sudden storm frightens them, the animals find their own way back to the shelter each evening without any help.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: A successful farm depends on the natural (1)________ — knowing when to plant, water and gather crops. Farmers (2)________ their plants from tiny seedlings into healthy produce using the right soil and water. The soil must be (3)________ — rich in nutrients to support healthy root growth. Many farms also keep (4)________ such as chickens, cows and pigs for eggs, milk and meat. At the end of each growing cycle, the farmer gathers the (5)________ — all the ripe fruits and vegetables ready to sell.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'knowing when to plant, water and gather' = the natural cycle of time on a farm = season.
questions.learning_tip: A SEASON = a period of time in the natural yearly cycle with specific weather and conditions. Farmers follow the SEASON = they know which activities belong to which part of the year.
questions.retry_hint: The dash explains it: KNOWING WHEN TO PLANT, WATER AND GATHER CROPS - a repeating part of the year. Ask: which box word names that stretch of time? 'Harvest' is only the gathering at the end, not the whole cycle.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'from tiny seedlings into strong, healthy produce by giving them the right care' = nurture.
questions.learning_tip: NURTURE = help something grow by giving it care, attention and the right conditions. Farmers NURTURE their plants = tend to them carefully from seedling to harvest.
questions.retry_hint: The farmers take plants FROM TINY SEEDLINGS INTO HEALTHY PRODUCE with the right soil and water. The blank follows 'Farmers', so a verb is needed. Ask: which box word means to care for something so that it grows?

questions.trap_type: The clue 'rich in nutrients and able to support healthy root growth' = fertile.
questions.learning_tip: FERTILE = (of soil) rich in nutrients and able to support healthy plant growth. FERTILE soil = the best kind for farming — plants grow well and produce a lot.
questions.retry_hint: The dash defines it: RICH IN NUTRIENTS TO SUPPORT HEALTHY ROOT GROWTH. The blank follows 'must be', so an adjective is needed. Ask: which box word describes soil that feeds plants well? 'Barren' means the exact opposite.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'chickens, cows and pigs — provide eggs, milk and meat' = livestock.
questions.learning_tip: LIVESTOCK = farm animals kept for their products or for food. Chickens, cows and pigs are all examples of LIVESTOCK kept on a working farm.
questions.retry_hint: The examples are listed for you: CHICKENS, COWS AND PIGS, kept FOR EGGS, MILK AND MEAT. Ask: which box word is the group name for farm animals? A 'scarecrow' is not an animal at all.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'fruits, vegetables and grains that are ready to be sold or stored' after the growing cycle = harvest.
questions.learning_tip: A HARVEST = the gathering of crops at the end of the growing season. The farmer gathers the HARVEST = all the crops that are ripe and ready.
questions.retry_hint: AT THE END OF EACH GROWING CYCLE the farmer gathers ALL THE RIPE FRUITS AND VEGETABLES READY TO SELL. Ask: which box word names that gathering-in of ripe crops? A 'season' is a period of time, not the crops.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.trap_type: 'The goats' is plural. Students write 'was' (singular).
questions.learning_tip: Plural subject → plural verb! The goats WERE grazing in the meadow. WAS is only for ONE thing. GOATS = more than one → WERE.
questions.retry_hint: The subject of the underlined verb is THE GOATS - more than one animal in the MEADOW. Ask: which past form of 'to be' belongs with a plural subject? Singular and plural never share the same form here.

questions.trap_type: Students write 'too' (also/excessively) when the sentence needs 'to' (infinitive marker).
questions.learning_tip: TO = infinitive marker before a verb (to water) or direction preposition. TOO = also or excessively. 'Forgot too water' is WRONG — 'to water' = the infinitive. Use TO before verbs.
questions.retry_hint: The underlined word sits in front of the verb WATER, and the sentence is not about 'also' or 'excessively'. Ask: which spelling marks an infinitive? The double-o spelling means 'as well' or 'more than enough'.

questions.error_type: Spelling — ie/ei confusion (field: I before E)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'feild' putting E before I. 'Field' follows I-before-E: fIEld.
questions.learning_tip: Rule: I before E, except after C! fIEld = I before E ✅. Remember: 'the fIEld has a PIE in the middle' — fIEld. I before E always!
questions.retry_hint: The underlined word names the LARGE open ground BEHIND THE MAIN BARN, and its vowels are the wrong way round. Ask: with no C in front, which vowel leads - the I or the E? Compare: brief, believe, piece.

questions.trap_type: Students write 'loud' (adjective) after the action verb 'crowed'. A verb needs an adverb.
questions.learning_tip: After an action verb (crowed), use an ADVERB: crowed LOUDLY. Rule: verb + adverb (-ly). 'Loud' describes nouns; 'loudly' describes HOW the rooster crowed.
questions.retry_hint: Look at what the underlined word is describing: not the rooster, but the way it CROWED. Ask: which class of word may describe a verb - an adjective or an adverb? Build the manner word by adding -ly.

questions.trap_type: Students write a plain plural and leave out the apostrophe that shows ownership.
questions.learning_tip: The vegetables BELONG TO all three farmers -> FARMERS' vegetables (apostrophe after the -s for a plural). One farmer: farmer's.
questions.retry_hint: The vegetables belong to ALL THREE FARMERS - the owners are more than one. Ask: a plain -s only makes a plural, so what must be added to show ownership, and on which side of the -s does that mark go?

E.passage: Last weekend, our class visited a working farm in Lim Chu Kang. The goats was (1) grazing peacefully in the meadow when we arrived, barely looking up from the grass. Our guide told us that one student forgot too (2) water the seedlings the previous week and several of them dried out. We walked across the large feild (3) behind the main barn, passing rows of cabbages and sweet potatoes stretching all the way to the trees. At five o'clock in the morning, the old rooster crowed so loud (4) that everyone on the farm woke up without needing an alarm clock. At the end of our visit, all three farmers (5) freshly harvested vegetables were packed neatly into crates for delivery.

questions.sentence_a: The soil is rich and well-watered.
questions.sentence_b: The crops will grow quickly and produce a large harvest.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'If'.
questions.model_answer: If the soil is rich and well-watered, the crops will grow quickly and produce a large harvest.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'If the soil will be rich' — adding 'will' in the 'if' clause.
questions.learning_tip: IF + simple present, simple future. IF the soil IS rich, the crops WILL GROW quickly. NEVER use 'will' after 'if' in the condition clause.
questions.retry_hint: 'IF' opens the condition, so the sentence about the SOIL goes first. Ask: does a condition clause ever take 'will'? Keep the future verb for the second half, and separate the two halves with a comma.

questions.sentence_a: The old barn stood at the edge of the paddy field.
questions.sentence_b: The old barn was built by the farmer's grandfather fifty years ago.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using the relative pronoun 'which'.
questions.model_answer: The old barn, which was built by the farmer's grandfather fifty years ago, stood at the edge of the paddy field.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'The old barn which it was built by' — adding 'it' after 'which'.
questions.learning_tip: WHICH = relative pronoun for things. The old barn, WHICH was built by the farmer's grandfather, stood at the edge of the field. NEVER add 'it' after 'which'.
questions.retry_hint: Both sentences name THE OLD BARN. Keep the one that says where it stood as the backbone, and slide the extra fact in straight after the barn. Ask: does 'which' still need 'it' after it, and where do the two commas go?

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
Eleven-year-old Priya grew up in a flat in Ang Mo Kio. She never visited a farm before.

On the first morning, she woke at five to help her aunt milk the cows. It was still dark. Everything smelled of earth and animals. She held the bucket so tightly her knuckles went white.

Her aunt did not explain. She simply showed her — slow, even strokes, the same rhythm again and again. Priya tried. The cow shifted, and she spilled half the bucket.

'Again,' said her aunt. There was no irritation in her voice. Just the word.

On the second morning, Priya woke at four-thirty — half an hour early. She was already in the barn when her aunt arrived.

'You came back,' said her aunt.

'I spilled,' said Priya.

Her aunt handed her the bucket. 'That is why you came back.'

By seven o'clock, the milk was done and the cows were calm. Priya's arms ached, but she did not mention it.

On the bus home, Priya sat without speaking. Her arms still ached. She looked at her hands and thought about the rhythm her aunt had shown her — slow, even, patient. She realised she could still feel the motion, like a small muscle memory she had not owned before that morning.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 4 has the same meaning as 'annoyance or frustration'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Rhythm' = pattern; 'shifted' = moved; 'simply' = in a plain way. IRRITATION = a feeling of mild anger or annoyance.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: IRRITATION = mild annoyance or frustration. 'There was no IRRITATION in her voice' = she was not annoyed at all, even though Priya spilled the milk.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 7, what does 'That' refer to in 'That is why you came back'?

options.3: The fact that Priya had spilled the milk and wanted to correct it

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking 'That' refers only to the spilled milk. But the aunt means the desire to come back and correct the mistake — the spilling and its consequence.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 7: Priya said 'I SPILLED.' Her aunt replied 'THAT is why you came back.' THAT = the fact that she spilled = the mistake that motivated her to return early to correct it.

mcq_questions.stem: Why does the writer end with 'Priya's arms ached, but she did not mention it'?

options.1: To show that Priya was too shy to talk to her aunt.
options.2: To show that Priya grew — she chose to complete the work quietly without complaining.
options.3: To show that the work was too hard for an eleven-year-old.
options.4: To show that her aunt would not have listened anyway.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 3 thinking the work was simply too hard. But the writer's point is about Priya's growth — she did not complain despite the pain.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: The ending shows Priya's growth: her arms ACHED (real physical pain), but she did not MENTION it = she chose to endure silently, without needing praise or comfort. This shows maturity.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 1, is it True or False that Priya visited a farm many times before this visit? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The passage says Priya 'had never been on a farm before' — this was her first time on a farm.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'True, she visited her aunt's farm' — the visit being described is her first time.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1: 'She HAD NEVER BEEN ON A FARM BEFORE.' This clearly states it was her first experience on a farm. Answer is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: What time did Priya arrive at the barn on the second morning?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: She arrived before four-thirty — she was already in the barn when her aunt arrived at four-thirty.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'five o'clock' (the first morning's time) instead of the second morning's time.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 5: 'On the second morning, Priya woke at FOUR-THIRTY — half an hour early. She was ALREADY IN THE BARN when her aunt arrived.' Second morning = four-thirty.

open_ended_questions.stem: How did Priya's aunt teach her? Give TWO specific details from the passage.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) She did not explain with words — she simply showed Priya by demonstrating the correct technique: 'slow, even strokes, the same rhythm again and again.' (ii) When Priya spilled, her aunt said only one word — 'Again' — without irritation, giving Priya the space to try again without embarrassment.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'she taught her patiently' without giving specific details from the text.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraphs 3–4: (1) Aunt SHOWED HER (demonstrated), not explained; (2) said only 'AGAIN' with NO IRRITATION — silent, patient encouragement. Two specific details.

open_ended_questions.stem: What reason does Priya's aunt give for why Priya came back early on the second morning?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: Her aunt says Priya came back because she had spilled — the mistake itself was what motivated her to return and try again.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'she wanted to learn more' — too vague. The aunt's specific point is that SPILLING itself = the reason.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 8: 'That is why you CAME BACK' — the aunt means: SPILLING = the reason for returning. Making a mistake and caring about it enough to return is the point.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on her actions across BOTH mornings, describe TWO character traits of Priya with evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) DETERMINED: on the second morning, she woke half an hour earlier than required and was already in the barn before her aunt arrived — she returned to face the same task that had defeated her. (ii) RESILIENT: despite her arms aching by seven o'clock, she did not mention it — she finished the work without complaining.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'hard-working and kind' without precise traits or evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: TRAIT INFERENCE formula: TRAIT = evidence from text. DETERMINED = woke at FOUR-THIRTY, ALREADY IN THE BARN before her aunt arrived. RESILIENT = arms ACHED but she DID NOT MENTION IT — endured without complaint. For G8, always: (i) Trait name: evidence. (ii) Trait name: evidence.

questions.stem: The librarian's memory was as ________ as a blade — she could recall the exact shelf location of any book within seconds.
questions.trap_type: 'Heavy', 'dull' and 'cold' do not describe a keen, precise memory. SHARP = quick and accurate in thinking and memory.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! Her memory was AS SHARP AS a blade = comparing her precise memory to the sharpness of a blade. SHARP = quick, accurate and precise.
questions.retry_hint: Her memory is compared to a BLADE: she can RECALL THE EXACT SHELF LOCATION of any book WITHIN SECONDS. Ask: is a blade dull and heavy, or keen and precise? Match the adjective to the blade, not to the library.

questions.stem: The children quickly ________ of stickers for decorating their reading journals and had to ask for more.
questions.trap_type: 'Gave up' = stopped trying; 'found out' = discovered; 'looked after' = cared for. RAN OUT OF = used up the entire supply of something.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: RUN OUT OF = use up the entire supply of something. They RAN OUT OF stickers = they used every single one and had none left. RUN + OUT + OF work together.
questions.retry_hint: The stickers are all gone, and the children HAD TO ASK FOR MORE. Ask: which phrasal verb means to use up the entire supply of something? 'Gave up' means to stop trying; 'looked after' means to take care of.

questions.stem: The library's reading room was completely ________ - not one person was speaking, not even in a whisper.
questions.trap_type: 'Crowded' = many people; 'colourful' = many colours; 'broken' = not working. SILENT = making no sound at all.
questions.learning_tip: SILENT = making no sound at all. The room was completely SILENT = nobody was talking, every sound was absent. Even a whisper would have been too loud.
questions.retry_hint: The clue follows the dash: NOT ONE PERSON WAS SPEAKING, NOT EVEN IN A WHISPER. Ask: which adjective means completely without sound? 'Crowded' counts people, and 'colourful' talks about what you see.

questions.stem: The librarian gently ________ the damaged page with clear tape so the book could still be used.
questions.trap_type: 'Tore' = damaged further; 'removed' = took away; 'replaced' = put something new. REPAIRED = fixed something that was damaged.
questions.learning_tip: REPAIRED = fixed something that was broken or damaged. The librarian REPAIRED the page = she mended it so the book could be used again.
questions.retry_hint: The librarian used CLEAR TAPE so that the book COULD STILL BE USED. Ask: which verb means to mend something damaged? 'Tore' would harm it further, and 'replaced' would throw the old page away.

questions.stem: The library's archive held rare ________ — old handwritten letters and maps that could not be found anywhere else.
questions.trap_type: 'Paintings', 'medals' and 'photographs' are specific formats. DOCUMENTS = written or printed records, especially rare or official ones.
questions.learning_tip: DOCUMENTS = written or printed records, especially formal or important ones. Rare DOCUMENTS = old handwritten letters or maps with historical value.
questions.retry_hint: The clue is the list after the dash: OLD HANDWRITTEN LETTERS AND MAPS. Ask: which word covers written records of every kind? 'Paintings', 'medals' and 'photographs' each name one narrow format only.

questions.stem: Somebody in the reading room ________ to switch off their mobile phone, and it keeps vibrating loudly on the table.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'forget' thinking 'somebody in the reading room' = plural. SOMEBODY = singular → present tense → FORGETS.
questions.learning_tip: SOMEBODY / SOMEONE / EVERYBODY / NOBODY = Singular! ALWAYS use verb+S. Somebody FORGETS = add -S. 'Somebody forget' is WRONG.
questions.retry_hint: The subject is SOMEBODY, not the readers sitting around them. Ask: does a word like somebody, anybody or nobody count as one person, or as many? In the present tense, a singular subject needs the -s ending.

questions.stem: Our school has ________ a reading corner in the library with bean bags and floor cushions.
questions.trap_type: HAS + past participle = present perfect. SET UP is a phrasal verb; past participle = 'set up' (no change in past participle form).
questions.learning_tip: HAS + past participle = present perfect. Our school HAS SET UP a reading corner = it was created at some point and is still there. SET UP (phrasal verb) → SET UP (past participle).
questions.retry_hint: HAS is waiting for a partner, and the corner is still there with its BEAN BAGS AND FLOOR CUSHIONS. Ask: after 'has', which form completes a present perfect? This phrasal verb does not change shape in the past participle.

questions.stem: The new library building is far ________ than the old one, with three floors and a rooftop garden.
questions.trap_type: Comparative needed (comparing new vs old building). 'Large' → LARGER (short adjective adds -er). 'More larger' is wrong (double comparative).
questions.learning_tip: Short adjective + -ER = comparative. Large → LARGER. The new library is LARGER THAN the old one. NEVER 'more larger' — that is a double comparative error.
questions.retry_hint: THAN THE OLD ONE shows two buildings being measured against each other. Ask: does a short adjective take -er, or the word 'more'? Putting 'more' in front of a word that already ends in -er is a double comparative.

questions.stem: The students ________ their book reports when the librarian announced the start of story time.
questions.trap_type: 'The librarian announced story time' = sudden interrupting event. Students were already writing = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: The librarian ANNOUNCED story time = sudden past event. Students were already writing = WERE WRITING (past continuous). Past continuous = was/were + verb-ing.
questions.retry_hint: THE LIBRARIAN ANNOUNCED THE START OF STORY TIME - a short event cutting across a longer one. Ask: which choice shows the students already in the middle of their book reports? A plain past verb reports a finished job.

questions.stem: There are ________ picture books in the children's section than in any other part of the library.
questions.trap_type: Comparing quantities of books = comparative 'more'. 'Much' and 'a little' are for uncountable; 'a few' is a small number, not comparative.
questions.learning_tip: MORE + countable plural noun = comparative quantity. There are MORE picture books = a larger number compared to other sections. 'Much books' is WRONG — MUCH is for uncountable.
questions.retry_hint: THAN is sitting in the sentence, so two sections are being compared for quantity. Ask: which word builds a comparison of number with a countable plural? 'Much' and 'a little' both need uncountable nouns.

questions.stem: You haven't returned last week's library book yet, ________ you?
questions.trap_type: Negative present perfect ('haven't returned') → positive question tag = have you.
questions.learning_tip: Negative present perfect → positive tag. 'You HAVEN'T returned the book, HAVE you?' NEGATIVE → POSITIVE tag. HAVEN'T → HAVE.
questions.retry_hint: The statement is already negative: YOU HAVEN'T RETURNED the book. Ask: after a negative statement, is the tag positive or negative? The tag also copies the helping verb that is standing there already.

questions.stem: The most popular book in the library ________ thirty times in a single month.
questions.trap_type: The book was the receiver of the action. Past passive = was borrowed.
questions.learning_tip: WAS/WERE + past participle = passive! The book WAS BORROWED thirty times = people borrowed it; the book received the action. Singular → WAS.
questions.retry_hint: The book did not act - THIRTY TIMES IN A SINGLE MONTH tells you what people did to it. Ask: which choice makes the subject the receiver of the action, set in the past? The subject is one book, so watch the number.

questions.stem: The librarian asked the children ________ their voices down while others were reading.
questions.trap_type: Requested action reported speech: asked + object + to + base verb.
questions.learning_tip: ASKED someone TO + base verb. The librarian asked children TO KEEP their voices down. Formula: asked + person + to + verb (positive reported speech).
questions.retry_hint: A reported request: the librarian ASKED THE CHILDREN, and gives a reason - WHILE OTHERS WERE READING. Ask: after 'asked + person', which form follows - the plain verb, the -ing form, or 'to' + verb?

C.label: Section C - Grammar Cloze (Verb 'read' - eight different forms)

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Aisha (1)________ at least two books every week.' Signal: 'every week' = regular habit = simple present. Subject 'Aisha' = singular → reads.
questions.trap_type: Students write the bare form. 'Every week without fail' = a present habit, and Aisha is one person.
questions.learning_tip: Simple present for a habit + a singular subject -> add -S: Aisha READS two books every week.
questions.retry_hint: AISHA is one person, and the habit repeats EVERY WEEK WITHOUT FAIL. Ask: in the simple present, does a singular subject take the plain verb, or the verb with -s? Two box forms describe one moment only - not this.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'She enjoys (2)________ adventure stories more than any other genre.' Signal: 'enjoys + ___' = gerund (verb-ing). Pattern: enjoy + verb-ing → reading.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'to read'. ENJOY never takes the infinitive.
questions.learning_tip: ENJOY + verb-ing: she enjoys READING. Same pattern: finish, avoid, keep and practise all take the -ing form.
questions.retry_hint: The verb ENJOYS comes first, and the box form must follow it directly. Ask: does 'enjoy' take 'to' + verb, or the -ing form? Same family: finish, avoid, keep and practise all behave in exactly the same way.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Last Saturday, she (3)________ a whole novel in a single afternoon.' Signal: 'Last Saturday' = past. 'Read' is irregular: read (present) → read (past) — same spelling, different pronunciation (present: /riːd/, past: /rɛd/).
questions.trap_type: Students write 'readed'. This verb is irregular: its past form is spelt exactly like its base form but said differently.
questions.learning_tip: Past simple with a finished time marker (LAST SATURDAY). The past of this verb keeps the same four letters - only the sound changes.
questions.retry_hint: LAST SATURDAY is finished time, and the novel was done in a single afternoon. Ask: which box form is the plain past? Careful - this verb is irregular, so its past looks exactly like its base form on paper.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'While she (4)________ the final chapter, the library lights flickered twice.' Signal: 'while she ___' = ongoing background past action. Subject 'she' = singular → was reading. Interrupted by 'lights flickered'.
questions.trap_type: Students write the simple past. WHILE + the lights suddenly flickering = a long action already in progress, cut across by a short one.
questions.learning_tip: Past continuous = was/were + verb-ing. Use it for the longer action that was already going on when something else happened.
questions.retry_hint: WHILE plus a sudden event - THE LIBRARY LIGHTS FLICKERED - means the longer action had already started. Ask: which box form shows an action still in progress in the past, with a singular subject?

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Her two younger brothers (5)________ picture books nearby at the same time.' Signal: same past time frame, plural subject 'her two brothers' + ongoing parallel action → were reading.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'was reading'. TWO younger brothers = a plural subject.
questions.learning_tip: Past continuous with a plural subject -> WERE + verb-ing. One brother WAS reading; two brothers WERE reading.
questions.retry_hint: Count the subject: HER TWO YOUNGER BROTHERS - that is more than one. Ask: for an action in progress in the past, which helping verb goes with a plural subject? One brother takes 'was'; two take the other one.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'After the lights came back on, she continued (6)________ without missing a single word.' Signal: 'continued + ___' = can take to-infinitive or -ing. Here we use 'continued to read' = infinitive. Pattern: continue + to + base verb.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'reading'. After 'her target IS', the noun-like slot is filled by an infinitive: her target is TO DO something.
questions.learning_tip: TO + base verb = the infinitive, used after 'my aim / my target / my plan is ...'. Never add -s or -ing after 'to'.
questions.retry_hint: HER LIBRARY TARGET FOR THIS YEAR IS ... - after 'is', an aim is expressed with an infinitive. Ask: which box form begins with the little word 'to'? After it, nothing may be added - no -s, no -ing.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Her library target is to (7)________ fifty books before the end of Primary Three.' Signal: 'to + ___' = infinitive = base verb. 'To' is already there → only base form follows.
questions.trap_type: Students write the simple past. SO FAR means 'up to now', which links the past to the present.
questions.learning_tip: Present perfect = has/have + past participle. Use it with SO FAR, ALREADY, YET and EVER, when the time period is still open.
questions.retry_hint: SO FAR means 'up to this moment', so the counting of THIRTY-EIGHT books is still open. Ask: which box form is a present perfect - a helping verb plus a past participle? A plain past would close the period.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Right now, Aisha (8)________ a book about ancient Egyptian civilisations.' Signal: 'Right now' = present continuous. Subject 'Aisha' = singular → is reading.
questions.trap_type: Students write the simple present. RIGHT NOW means at this very moment, not as a habit.
questions.learning_tip: Present continuous = is/are + verb-ing, for what is happening at this moment. RIGHT NOW / AT THE MOMENT are its signal words.
questions.retry_hint: RIGHT NOW points at this very moment, not at a habit. Ask: which box form shows an action happening as we speak, with a singular subject? The habit form would mean she does it regularly instead.

C.passage: Aisha (1)________ at least two books every week without fail. She enjoys (2)________ adventure stories more than any other genre in the library. Last Saturday, she (3)________ a whole novel in a single afternoon without stopping for lunch. While she (4)________ the final chapter, the library lights flickered twice and then came back on. Her two younger brothers (5)________ picture books nearby at that very same moment, keeping themselves quietly entertained. Her library target for this year is (6)________ fifty books before the end of Primary Three. So far, she (7)________ thirty-eight of them and she is well ahead of her plan. Right now, Aisha (8)________ a book about ancient Egyptian civilisations that she found on the top shelf.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: A public library contains many types of books. Readers often (1)________ the shelves freely, picking up books that catch their eye. Many libraries have an online (2)________ — a searchable list of every book available. Books in the (3)________ section, such as encyclopaedias, cannot be borrowed and must be used inside. Readers borrow (4)________ — made-up stories — for pleasure. If a book is not returned by the due date, it becomes (5)________ and a small fine may be charged.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'picking up books that catch their eye before deciding what to borrow' = browse.
questions.learning_tip: BROWSE = look casually at items without a specific goal. You BROWSE the shelves = you look along them, picking up books that interest you without a fixed plan.
questions.retry_hint: Readers move along the shelves FREELY, PICKING UP BOOKS THAT CATCH THEIR EYE, with no fixed plan. The blank follows 'often', so a verb is needed. Ask: which box word means to look casually along the shelves?

questions.trap_type: The clue 'a searchable list of every book and resource available' = catalogue.
questions.learning_tip: A CATALOGUE = a complete searchable list of all available items. A library CATALOGUE = the system that lists every book and tells you where to find it.
questions.retry_hint: The dash defines it: A SEARCHABLE LIST OF EVERY BOOK AVAILABLE, and it is ONLINE. Ask: which box word names that complete list? A 'bookmark' only keeps your place on one page.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'encyclopaedias and atlases... cannot be borrowed... used inside the library' = reference section.
questions.learning_tip: A REFERENCE section = the part of a library containing books like encyclopaedias that cannot be borrowed and must be used inside. You go there to look up specific information.
questions.retry_hint: The clue is that ENCYCLOPAEDIAS CANNOT BE BORROWED and MUST BE USED INSIDE. Ask: which box word names the section you may only look things up in? 'Fiction' books go home with you.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'stories that are made up and not based on real events' = fiction.
questions.learning_tip: FICTION = stories that are made up and imaginary (not real). Novels, fairy tales and adventure stories are FICTION. Opposite: non-fiction = true or factual.
questions.retry_hint: The dash spells it out: MADE-UP STORIES, borrowed FOR PLEASURE. Ask: which box word names invented writing - novels, fairy tales, adventures? The opposite kind of book is factual and true.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'not returned by the due date... a small fine may be charged' = overdue.
questions.learning_tip: OVERDUE = not returned or completed by the required date. A library book is OVERDUE = it should have been returned but has not been yet. A fine is charged as a reminder.
questions.retry_hint: The book was NOT RETURNED BY THE DUE DATE, and A SMALL FINE MAY BE CHARGED. Ask: which box word describes a book that is late? To 'renew' it would have kept it out of trouble.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.trap_type: 'The books' is plural. Students write 'was' (singular).
questions.learning_tip: Plural subject → plural verb! The books WERE arranged neatly on the shelf. WAS is only for ONE thing (singular). BOOKS = more than one → WERE.
questions.retry_hint: THE BOOKS is the subject of the underlined verb, and they fill the whole shelf. Ask: does a plural subject take the singular past form of 'to be', or the plural one? Look at the subject, not at the word beside it.

questions.error_type: Homophone confusion — they're (they are) vs their (possessive)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'they're' (they are) when the sentence needs 'their' (belonging to them).
questions.learning_tip: THEIR = belonging to them. Students must return THEIR books on time. THEY'RE = they are. Test: can you replace with 'they are'? 'they are books' — NO. Use THEIR.
questions.retry_hint: Stretch the underlined word out: 'they are BORROWED BOOKS' makes no sense at all. Ask: which spelling shows that the books belong to the students? The two spellings sound alike, so decide by meaning, not by ear.

questions.error_type: Spelling — ie/ei confusion (grief: I before E)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'greif' putting E before I. 'Grief' follows I-before-E: grIEf.
questions.learning_tip: Rule: I before E, except after C! grIEf = I before E ✅. The story was full of grIEf — remember: grief has an IE inside, like beLIEve and frIEnd.
questions.retry_hint: The underlined word names the deep sadness felt when HER FAVOURITE LIBRARY WAS CLOSED DOWN, and its vowels are swapped. Ask: with no C in front, which vowel leads? Compare: believe, brief, piece.

questions.trap_type: Students write 'soft' (adjective) after the action verb 'spoke'. A verb needs an adverb.
questions.learning_tip: After an action verb (spoke), use an ADVERB: spoke SOFTLY. Rule: verb + adverb (-ly). 'Soft' describes nouns; 'softly' describes HOW someone speaks.
questions.retry_hint: SPOKE is the action, and the underlined word answers 'in what manner did she speak?'. Ask: can an adjective ever describe a verb? Manner words are built by adding -ly to the describing word.

questions.error_type: Possessive apostrophe — singular possessive (librarian's = one librarian)
questions.trap_type: Students use plural possessive (librarians') when only one librarian is meant.
questions.learning_tip: ONE LIBRARIAN'S desk = the desk belonging to one librarian. LIBRARIANS' desk = belonging to many librarians. Check: is it ONE or MANY? ONE → librarian's.
questions.retry_hint: Count the owners: the passage speaks of THE LIBRARIAN, one single person, all the way through. Ask: for a single owner, does the apostrophe come before the -s, or after it? The underlined form claims there are many.

E.passage: Every Tuesday afternoon, our class visits the school library for reading time. The books was (1) arranged neatly on the shelves, sorted by subject and author. Students must remember to return they're (2) borrowed books by Friday or they will receive an overdue notice. In one of the storybooks, the main character experienced great greif (3) when her favourite library was closed down to make way for a new road. The librarian spoke soft (4) to each student, helping them find a book that matched their interests. After the session, we tidied the librarians' (5) desk and placed all the returned books in the sorting trolley.

questions.sentence_a: You read at least thirty minutes a day.
questions.sentence_b: Your vocabulary and comprehension will improve significantly.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'As long as'.
questions.model_answer: As long as you read at least thirty minutes a day, your vocabulary and comprehension will improve significantly.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'As long as you will read' — adding 'will' in the 'as long as' clause.
questions.learning_tip: AS LONG AS + simple present, simple future. AS LONG AS you READ thirty minutes a day, your vocabulary WILL IMPROVE. NEVER 'will' after 'as long as'.
questions.retry_hint: 'AS LONG AS' states the condition, so the THIRTY MINUTES A DAY sentence goes first. Ask: does a condition clause ever take 'will'? Keep the future verb for the result half, and put a comma between the two.

questions.sentence_a: The library holds a rare collection of old maps.
questions.sentence_b: The rare collection is not available to borrow.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using the relative pronoun 'which'.
questions.model_answer: The library holds a rare collection of old maps, which is not available to borrow.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'a rare collection which it is not available' — adding 'it' after 'which'.
questions.learning_tip: WHICH = relative pronoun for things. A rare collection of old maps, WHICH is not available to borrow. NEVER add 'it' after 'which'. The collection is the antecedent.
questions.retry_hint: The second sentence adds a fact about the same COLLECTION, so it can hang off the first with 'which'. Ask: after 'which', is a pronoun still needed? And which mark separates the extra fact from the main sentence?

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
The book was always in the same corner. Every Saturday, nine-year-old Jonas walked past the other shelves — the adventure books, the science books, the graphic novels — and went straight to that corner.

The book was too difficult for him. He knew that. The words were long and the sentences ran over two lines. But he liked the cover: a boy standing at the edge of a cliff, looking out at a sea of clouds.

He never borrowed it. He just sat down and tried to read it. Sometimes he got through one page. Once, on a day when the library was particularly quiet, he got through three.

One Saturday, the corner was empty. The book was gone.

Jonas stood and stared at the gap in the shelf for a long time. Then he went to the librarian.

'Someone borrowed the book in the corner,' he said. 'The one with the boy on the cliff.'

The librarian checked the screen. 'It will be back in three weeks,' she said.

Jonas nodded. 'I'll be here,' he said.

He sat down in the corner with a different book. But he did not read it. He thought about the boy on the cliff and the sea of clouds below.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 3 has the same meaning as 'especially or noticeably'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Difficult' = hard; 'borrowed' = taken from the library; 'sometimes' = occasionally. PARTICULARLY = especially or to a notable degree.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: PARTICULARLY = especially or to a notable degree. 'The library was PARTICULARLY quiet' = noticeably quieter than usual, more so than normally.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 6, what does 'It' refer to in 'It will be back in three weeks'?

options.3: The book with the boy on the cliff

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 2 thinking 'it' refers to the empty shelf. But Jonas asked about the book — the librarian's 'it' = the book.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 6: Jonas told the librarian about THE BOOK in the corner. The librarian replied 'IT will be back in three weeks.' IT = the book Jonas asked about.

mcq_questions.stem: Jonas sat with a different book but 'did not read it'. What does this tell us about his feelings?

options.1: He was too tired to read anything.
options.2: He could only think about the book on the cliff — he was so attached to it that no other book could hold his attention.
options.3: He had already read every other book in the library.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking he was tired. But the passage ends with him thinking about the boy and the cliff — showing deep attachment to that specific book.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Last paragraph: Jonas sat with another book but THOUGHT ABOUT THE BOY ON THE CLIFF. He could not read anything else because his mind was fully on that one book — deep attachment.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 2, is it True or False that Jonas found the book easy to read? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The passage says 'The book was too difficult for him' — the words were long and the sentences ran over two lines.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'True, he read it every week.' He tried to read it every week — but the passage says it was too difficult for him.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 2: 'The book was TOO DIFFICULT for him. The WORDS WERE LONG and the sentences RAN OVER TWO LINES.' He tried but it was hard. Answer is FALSE.
